Example: Neoprene isolation pads under a fast fan on a solid floor mainly stop noise and fretting at the feet.

docs.title: Nested Inlet Vanes
docs.text: Variable inlet vanes built into the inlet funnel rather than a separate housing, applied to clean airstreams up to 600°F.

docs.title: Noise Limits
docs.text: The maximum sound a fan installation may produce, stated as sound power, sound pressure at a location, an A-weighted number, or octave band values.

docs.title: Nominally Leak-Tight Fan
docs.text:
A fan built to reduce leakage to a level agreed with the customer, verified by shop testing and recorded on the inspection form.

Example: A nominally leak-tight fan uses continuous welds, close bolt spacing, and double gaskets.

docs.title: Non-Drive End Bearing
docs.text: The bearing nearer the impeller on a two-bearing fan shaft; also called the inboard bearing.

docs.title: Non-Ferrous Material
docs.text: A metal or alloy not based on iron, such as aluminum, bronze, brass, copper, or Monel, far less likely to throw sparks when rubbing steel.

docs.title: Non-Overloading Power Curve
docs.text:
A brake horsepower curve that rises to a maximum and then falls as airflow increases, so a motor sized for that maximum cannot be overloaded at that speed.

Example: Backward inclined, backward curved, and airfoil fans have non-overloading power curves.

docs.title: Nozzle and Windband
docs.text:
The discharge parts at the top of a lab exhaust fan: the nozzle accelerates exhaust into a jet, and the surrounding windband draws in outside air.

Example: The nozzle and windband produce the entrained flow that dilutes lab fumes.

docs.title: Octave Band
docs.text:
A range of frequencies whose upper limit is twice its lower limit, identified by its center frequency.

Example: Fan sound data are published in eight octave bands.

docs.title: Octave Band Sound Data
docs.text:
A fan's sound power level reported separately in each of eight octave bands centered from 63 to 8,000 Hz.

Example: A guide specification requires octave band sound data tested to AMCA Standard 300.

docs.title: ODP Motor
docs.text:
An open drip proof motor whose internal fan blows surrounding air directly across the windings, with openings shielded from dripping water.

Example: An ODP motor suits a clean, dry mechanical room but not a dusty plant.

docs.title: Oil Mist Lubrication
docs.text:
A bearing oil system in which compressed air breaks metered oil into fine droplets carried to the bearings by one pump unit.

Example: Oil mist lubrication keeps a slight overpressure in the bearing housing that keeps dust out.

docs.title: Open Radial Paddle Impeller
docs.text:
A radial impeller with single-thickness paddle blades on the hub, braced by gussets, with no back plate or rings.

Example: The catalog's RBO uses an open radial paddle impeller for coarse, sticky material.

docs.title: Open Spring Isolator
docs.text:
A bare coil spring between two load plates with no restriction of aerodynamically caused motion.

Example: Twin City Fan typically does not use floor-mounted open spring isolators.

docs.title: Operating Point
docs.text: The single airflow and pressure at which a fan actually runs in a system, where its fan curve intersects the system curve.

docs.title: Opposed Blade Damper
docs.text:
A damper whose adjacent blades rotate in opposite directions, giving airflow that follows control-arm movement closely over the whole range.

Example: An opposed blade damper costs about 10 percent more but suits systems modulated across their entire range.

docs.title: Outlet Damper
docs.text:
A damper mounted on a fan discharge that controls airflow by adding resistance, typically the least expensive flow-control option.

Example: An outlet damper suits a hot, humid, or dusty system that only occasionally runs at reduced capacity.

docs.title: Outlet Flange
docs.text:
A flat frame around a fan outlet, drilled with a bolt-hole pattern, for a bolted connection to downstream ductwork.

Example: The rectangular outlet flange of a housed centrifugal fan bolts to a matching duct flange.

docs.title: Outlet Silencer
docs.text:
A sound-absorbing duct section on a fan discharge that reduces noise carried through the outlet into the duct or atmosphere.

Example: An exhaust stack near a property line gets an outlet silencer to protect neighbors.

docs.title: Outlet System Effect
docs.text: Loss of fan performance caused by the outlet connection, such as a missing or short outlet duct, a close elbow or damper, or an abrupt expansion.

docs.title: Outlet Velocity
docs.text:
The average speed of air leaving a fan, in feet per minute, equal to airflow volume divided by outlet area.

Example: 6,000 CFM through a 2 ft² outlet gives an outlet velocity of 3,000 fpm.

docs.title: Outlet Velocity Pressure
docs.text: The velocity pressure corresponding to a fan's outlet velocity, expressing the kinetic energy of the leaving air in in. wg.

docs.title: Overhung Impeller
docs.text:
An impeller mounted on the end of the shaft beyond both bearings.

Example: An Arrangement 1 fan has an overhung impeller, with both bearings on a pedestal outside the housing.

docs.title: Overloading Power Curve
docs.text:
A brake horsepower curve that keeps rising as airflow increases, so a motor sized for the design point can be overloaded at higher airflow.

Example: A forward curved fan whose access door is left open can overload its motor.

docs.title: Paint Booth Exhaust Fan
docs.text:
A fan that removes fumes and overspray from a spray booth at controlled velocity and is easy to clean.

Example: Twin City Fan meets the cleaning need of a paint booth exhaust fan with swingout or clamshell construction.

docs.title: Panel Fan
docs.text:
An axial fan whose impeller is centered in a flat mounting panel, usually installed in a wall opening.

Example: A warehouse wall panel fan carries an inlet safety screen and a weatherhood with a bird screen.

docs.title: Paper Handling Impeller
docs.text:
A material handling impeller made extra rugged for high-impact loading, with a full back plate, trapezoidal gussets, and a paper deflector cone over the hub face.

Example: The catalog's RBP conveys corrugated paper trim, and its deflector cone keeps paper from wrapping around the hub.

docs.title: Parallel Blade Damper
docs.text:
A damper whose blades all rotate in the same direction and stay parallel, recommended for modulating airflow from full open to about 75 percent open.

Example: A parallel blade outlet damper gives low-cost control over the top quarter of a fan's airflow range.

docs.title: Particulate-Laden Airstream
docs.text:
An airstream carrying solid material such as dust, grit, chips, fibers, lint, or granular product that can erode or build up on fan parts.

Example: A woodworking dust collection system moves a particulate-laden airstream, favoring rugged radial or radial tip impellers.

docs.title: Peak Efficiency
docs.text:
The highest efficiency on a fan's efficiency curve, together with the airflow and pressure where it occurs.

Example: Selecting near peak efficiency keeps both power and noise down.

docs.title: Peak Pressure Point
docs.text:
The highest static pressure on a fan curve and the airflow at which it occurs, marking the boundary of the stall region.

Example: A fan whose peak pressure point is 4.9 in. wg at 4,000 CFM is stable only to the right of 4,000 CFM.

docs.title: Performance Table
docs.text: A grid in a product catalog giving, for one model and size at standard air, the RPM and BHP needed for each combination of airflow and static pressure.

docs.title: Performance Table Header
docs.text:
The block above and around a performance table grid—size block, model line, column heads, and footer—that states what the grid's numbers mean.

Example: On a Catalog 902 page, the header's footer gives the maximum RPM for each class and the legend for shading and italics.

docs.title: Pie Split Housing
docs.text:
A split housing with a wedge cut at 90 degrees or more so the impeller can be removed without disturbing inlet or outlet ductwork.

Example: A pie split housing lets a worn impeller be replaced while the ducts stay connected.

docs.title: Piezometer Ring
docs.text: Tubing around the throat of a fan's inlet funnel that, with a tap on the funnel face, measures the pressure drop used to calculate airflow.

docs.title: Pillow Block Bearing
docs.text:
A bearing in a housing that bolts to a mounting surface parallel to the shaft axis, such as the top of a fan pedestal, in solid or split styles.

Example: A belt-driven Arrangement 1 fan carries its shaft on two pillow block bearings.

docs.title: Pivot Motor Base
docs.text:
A motor base with the motor on a plate hinged at one edge, so belt tension is set by swinging the motor about the pivot.

Example: Arrangement 9SS swingout fans use an automotive pivot base, which restricts motor location by rotation.

docs.title: Plenum Arrangement 3SM
docs.text: A horizontal Arrangement 3 plenum fan with the motor on the side of the fan frame on a slide base.

docs.title: Plenum Arrangement 4V
docs.text: The vertical, direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fan, available for vertical up or vertical down airflow.

docs.title: Plenum Arrangements 3HS and 3HA
docs.text:
Horizontal Arrangement 3 plenum fans with the motor mounted on top: 3HS on a slide base and 3HA on a heavy-duty adjustable motor base.

Example: An air handler short on floor space uses Plenum Arrangement 3HA.

docs.title: Plenum Arrangements 3VA and 3VS
docs.text:
Vertical Arrangement 3 plenum fans with a side-mounted motor: 3VA on an adjustable motor base and 3VS on a slide base.

Example: An air handler that turns airflow vertically uses Plenum Arrangement 3VA.

docs.title: Plenum Fan
docs.text:
An unhoused centrifugal fan that runs inside an air-filled space within a structure and pressurizes that space, which then distributes air to its outlets.

Example: An air handling unit with a plenum fan can take its discharge ducts off any side of the cabinet.

docs.title: Plenum Fan Arrangements
docs.text:
The set of standard arrangements describing how a plenum fan's motor and drive mount on its frame inside the plenum.

Example: Arrangement 3 is the most common plenum fan arrangement, with variants 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VA, and 3VS.

docs.title: Plenum Motor Positions
docs.text:
The motor locations defined for belt-driven plenum fan arrangements, named differently from housed fan positions because there is no scroll.

Example: On plenum Arrangement 3HS the top-mounted motor sits in the Standard (S) or Optional (O) position.

docs.title: Plug Fan
docs.text:
An unhoused centrifugal fan mounted on a panel fastened to the outside of a plenum wall, with the impeller inside the plenum.

Example: A plug fan on an oven plenum keeps its motor and bearings outside the hot space.

docs.title: Plug Fan Arrangements
docs.text:
The set of standard arrangements describing how a plug fan, with impeller inside the enclosure and drive outside, is supported and driven; seven are listed: 1P, 4, 4P, 8, 8P, 9, and 9P. In Twin City Fan model names, the suffix PL (as in BCPL) means that style of wheel in a plug fan arrangement.

Example: Plug fans come wall-hung, as in Arrangement 9, or grade-mounted, as in Arrangement 9P.

docs.title: Plume Dilution
docs.text:
The mixing of fresh outside air into contaminated exhaust, followed by high-velocity discharge, so the exhaust leaves at lower concentration and rises away from the building.

Example: Bypass flow and entrained flow together provide plume dilution for lab exhaust.

docs.title: Post Mount Motor Base
docs.text:
An adjustable motor base whose motor plate rides on threaded posts so the motor can be moved to tension the belts, used on small motors.

Example: A tubular Arrangement 9 axial fan with a 184T motor uses a standard post mount motor base.

docs.title: Power Roof Ventilator
docs.text:
A motor-driven fan unit, centrifugal or axial, built to mount on a roof opening to exhaust or supply air; abbreviated PRV.

Example: Upblast, downblast, louvered, and hooded roof units are all power roof ventilators.

docs.title: Power Varies With Speed Cubed
docs.text:
The fan law stating that brake horsepower changes in proportion to the cube of the speed ratio.

Example: Cutting speed 20 percent reduces power to 0.8³ = 0.512, about half.

docs.title: Pre-Spin
docs.text:
Swirl given to air entering an impeller, in the same direction the impeller rotates, by inlet vanes or an inlet box damper.

Example: Because pre-spin does part of the impeller's work, variable inlet vanes save power at reduced flow.

docs.title: Premium Efficiency Motor
docs.text: A motor built with more and better active material, such as copper and electrical steel, so less of its input becomes heat; comparable to NEMA Premium and IEC IE3.

docs.title: Pressure Blower
docs.text:
A housed centrifugal fan with narrow housing and impeller widths, built to produce high pressure at relatively low airflow.

Example: A pressure blower supplying combustion air can be turned down to zero flow with a discharge damper.

docs.title: Pressure Rise
docs.text:
The increase in pressure a fan produces between its inlet and its outlet, stated as fan total pressure or fan static pressure.

Example: A fan moving air from a room into a duct at 2 in. wg static pressure provides that pressure rise.

docs.title: Pressure Transmitter
docs.text:
A device that converts a measured pressure difference into a signal a controls system can use, with or without a local display.

Example: A pressure transmitter on a piezometer ring sends airflow data to the building automation system.

docs.title: Pressure Varies as Speed Squared
docs.text:
The fan law stating that a fan's pressure changes in proportion to the square of the speed ratio.

Example: A 10 percent speed increase raises pressure by 1.1² = 1.21, or 21 percent.

docs.title: Product Catalog
docs.text:
A manufacturer's published document for one product line, giving its models, sizes, classes, arrangements, options, construction, limits, and often rated performance.

Example: Catalog 300 covers the BC-SW and BC-DW backward inclined fans.

docs.title: Product Options
docs.text:
The construction choices and accessories a catalog offers beyond the standard fan, with statements of what each does and when to use it.

Example: Spark-resistant construction, inlet boxes, and variable inlet vanes are product options.

docs.title: Radial Bladed Fan
docs.text:
A housed centrifugal fan with flat blades pointing straight out from the hub, built heavy for dirty, abrasive, sticky, or bulky airstreams.

Example: A radial bladed fan conveys wood chips because material slides off the flat blades instead of building up.

docs.title: Radial Bladed Impeller
docs.text:
A centrifugal impeller with flat blades pointing straight out from the hub along radii, with no backward or forward lean.

Example: A radial bladed impeller handles heavy dust because material flies off its tips rather than building up.

docs.title: Radial Tip Fan
docs.text:
A housed centrifugal fan whose blades curve forward at the entering edge and become radial at the tip, more efficient than a radial bladed fan at high airflow.

Example: A radial tip fan suits a dusty dryer exhaust where airflow is large and particulate is present.

docs.title: Radial Tip Impeller
docs.text:
A centrifugal impeller whose blades curve forward at the entering edge and become radial at the tip of the leaving edge.

Example: A radial tip impeller combines a self-cleaning tip with better efficiency than a radial blade.

docs.title: Rating Conditions
docs.text: The conditions under which catalog performance numbers apply: air density, installation type, and what BHP includes or excludes.

docs.title: Reading a Performance Table
docs.text:
Finding the row for the required airflow and the column for the required static pressure and taking the RPM and BHP printed where they meet.

Example: Reading a performance table for 10,000 CFM at 4 in. wg gives the cell's RPM and BHP, and its shading shows the fan class.

docs.title: Recess Cone
docs.text:
A cone-shaped pocket formed into the insulated plug or wall of a plug fan or air kit that gives the shaft cooler and shaft seal a recessed space with outside air; also called a drive cone.

Example: "Design #2" for Arrangement 9 plug fans uses a recess cone.

docs.title: Regenerative Thermal Oxidizer
docs.text:
An industrial air pollution control process, abbreviated RTO, that destroys pollutants in process exhaust by oxidizing them at high temperature using heat-storing ceramic beds.

Example: An automotive paint booth sends its exhaust through an RTO driven by a leak-tight fan.

docs.title: Relieved Inlet Transition
docs.text: A transition shaped to smooth the flow of paper trim and similar material into a fan so it does not snag or pile up.

docs.title: Restrained Bearing
docs.text:
A pillow block bearing whose housing is mechanically prevented from shifting on its pedestal by dowel pins, stop blocks, or spring pins.

Example: Type A and Type B spark-resistant construction includes restrained bearings.

docs.title: Restrained Spring Isolator
docs.text:
A spring isolator with a housing or frame that restrains the spring's vertical or horizontal motion.

Example: A fan that must not lift or rock at startup sits on restrained spring isolators.

docs.title: Reverse Bore Hub
docs.text: An axial impeller hub bored from the opposite face so the impeller can be mounted facing the other way on the shaft, paired with PM airflow.

docs.title: Reversible Impeller
docs.text:
An axial impeller designed to move air in either direction along the shaft, with standard flow (MP) and reverse flow (PM) modes.

Example: A tunnel ventilation fan uses a reversible impeller so it can supply or exhaust on demand.

docs.title: Ring Fan
docs.text:
An axial fan whose impeller is centered in a short mounting ring rather than a full tube or flat panel.

Example: A ring fan can be mounted in a wall or partition opening to move air between spaces.

docs.title: Roof Curb
docs.text:
A raised frame built into a roof around an opening and flashed into the roofing, on which a rooftop fan sits.

Example: A roof exhauster's curb cap rests on the roof curb, keeping the fan above standing water and snow.

docs.title: Roof Exhauster Shroud
docs.text: The sheet-metal shell around the impeller of a centrifugal roof exhauster that guides the air the impeller throws off.

docs.title: Roof Mounted Axial Fan
docs.text: An axial fan mounted on a roof curb to supply or exhaust air, offered with a stack cap for straight-up discharge or a hood that deflects air downward.

docs.title: Roof Mounted Panel Fan
docs.text: A panel fan used as the base model of a roof unit with roof accessories such as a stack cap or hood.

docs.title: Roof Ventilator
docs.text:
In the current Twin City Fan catalog, an axial, motor-driven rooftop fan unit built on a tubeaxial impeller, offered in upblast, low profile, hooded, filtered supply, and smoke and heat forms.

Example: TUD and TUB upblast units are listed as roof ventilators, not as centrifugal roof exhausters.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
The direction in which a fan's impeller turns, stated for centrifugal fans as clockwise or counterclockwise viewed from the drive side.

Example: A backward inclined wheel turning the wrong way moves only a fraction of its rated air while drawing power.

docs.title: Rotation and Discharge Code
docs.text:
A short designation stating both a centrifugal fan's rotation and its outlet direction, written as a name or as an angle.

Example: "CW THD" and "CW 90" are equivalent rotation and discharge codes.

docs.title: Rotation Arrow
docs.text:
A curved arrow marked on drawings and on the fan housing showing the required direction of impeller rotation.

Example: An electrician checks the motor's bump-start direction against the rotation arrow on the housing.

docs.title: RTO Service Conditions
docs.text:
The operating facts an RTO fan must survive that only the customer or RTO builder knows, which sales must specify.

Example: Temperature swings during the RTO's flow reversals are part of the RTO service conditions.

docs.title: Rub Plate
docs.text:
A non-ferrous plate, typically aluminum, at the housing opening where the shaft passes through, protecting against steel shaft-to-housing contact; also called a striker or spark plate.

Example: A Type B fan with an outside protruding hub does not need a rub plate.

docs.title: Rub Ring
docs.text:
A non-ferrous ring mounted where an impeller could shift into a stationary part, so the ring is touched first instead of steel.

Example: Radial bladed fans and pressure blowers use an inlet rub ring of Monel.

docs.title: Rubber-in-Shear Isolator
docs.text:
An isolator that carries its load through a rubber element loaded in shear, giving moderate isolation with about 0.2 to 0.5 in. deflection; abbreviated RIS.

Example: A floor-mounted RIS pad has two steel load plates embedded in rubber.

docs.title: Scroll Housing
docs.text:
The snail-shaped casing around a housed centrifugal impeller whose clearance from the impeller grows steadily toward the outlet.

Example: The scroll housing collects the air thrown off the impeller tips and converts part of its velocity into static pressure.

docs.title: Scroll Wrapper
docs.text:
The curved band of sheet metal that wraps around the impeller between the two side plates and runs out to the discharge.

Example: The scroll wrapper's growing spiral clearance slows the air and turns velocity into static pressure.

docs.title: Seismic Restraint
docs.text:
A device that holds an isolated fan in place during an earthquake by limiting how far it can move on its soft mounts.

Example: Seismic springs and snubbers are the two seismic restraint forms FanPedia shows.

docs.title: Seismic Spring Isolator
docs.text:
A restrained spring isolator whose housing nearly surrounds the spring so it withstands earthquake loads.

Example: A hospital rooftop fan in a seismic zone sits on seismic spring isolators.

docs.title: Selection Trade-Offs
docs.text:
The conflicts between good properties that no single fan can have at once and that a selection must settle deliberately.

Example: A larger, slower fan trades higher first cost for lower operating cost.

docs.title: Separated Pedestal
docs.text: A fan pedestal for high-temperature applications that leaves a gap between the fan housing and the pedestal, reducing heat conducted to the bearings and leaving room for insulation.

docs.title: Set Screw Mount
docs.text: A bearing locking method in which two set screws in the inner ring are tightened onto the shaft.

docs.title: Setback Outlet Flange
docs.text:
The bolted flange frame around a DWDI fan's discharge opening, set back from the end of the outlet.

Example: Duct connections to a setback outlet flange are taken from the certified dimensional drawing.

docs.title: Severe Duty Motor
docs.text:
A motor built to keep running in moisture, chemical fumes, dust, washdown, or outdoor exposure where a general duty motor would fail early.

Example: A paper mill fan uses an IEEE 841 severe duty motor.

docs.title: Shaft and Coupling Alignment
docs.text:
The positioning of motor and fan bearings so the two shaft centerlines form one straight line through the coupling, correcting offset and angular misalignment.

Example: Poor shaft and coupling alignment shows up as vibration and early coupling wear.

docs.title: Shaft and Coupling Guards
docs.text:
Guards that cover a fan's exposed shaft and bearings and enclose the flexible coupling on direct-drive arrangements.

Example: An Arrangement 8 fan needs a coupling guard over the joint between motor and fan shaft.

docs.title: Shaft Cooler
docs.text:
A cast aluminum part mounted on the shaft between the shaft seal and the bearings that dissipates heat conducted along the shaft from the airstream.

Example: Shaft coolers are recommended for applications over 300°F.

docs.title: Shaft Coupling
docs.text:
A device that connects two shafts end to end so one drives the other, such as fan shaft to motor shaft.

Example: Arrangements 7 and 8 use a flexible shaft coupling between the motor and fan shaft.

docs.title: Shaft Grounding Ring
docs.text:
A ring of conductive fibers around a motor shaft that gives VFD-induced shaft voltages a low-resistance path to ground, bypassing the bearings.

Example: A fan run on a VFD may get a shaft grounding ring to keep shaft current from pitting the bearing raceways.

docs.title: Shaft Keyway
docs.text: A groove cut lengthwise into a shaft to accept a key that transmits torque to a hub, bushing, coupling, or sheave.

docs.title: Shaft Locking Collar
docs.text:
A ring clamped to a shaft that holds it in place axially so it cannot slide and strike a bearing or the impeller.

Example: Vertical fans use a shaft locking collar because gravity pulls the shaft along its axis.

docs.title: Shaft Material Grades
docs.text:
The specific steel or alloy specifications from which fan shafts are made, such as Grade 1045 or 4140 mild steel and Types 304, 316, or 2205 stainless.

Example: A marine axial fan needing AMCA A spark resistance uses an AMPCO-45 shaft.

docs.title: Shaft Seal
docs.text:
A seal mounted on the fan housing around the shaft where it passes through the housing wall, reducing leakage of air or gas along the shaft.

Example: An overhung fan needs one shaft seal on the drive side; a center hung fan with the shaft through both sides needs two.

docs.title: Shaft Sleeve
docs.text:
A tube fitted over a shaft where it would otherwise be exposed to the airstream, shielding a shaft of dissimilar material.

Example: A stainless steel fan with a steel shaft uses a stainless shaft sleeve inside the housing.

docs.title: Shaft Turndown
docs.text:
A section of shaft machined to a smaller diameter than the rest, on one or both ends, to fit a standard bearing, seal, hub, or coupling.

Example: A center hung Arrangement 3DI shaft may carry several turndowns along its length.

docs.title: Sheave
docs.text:
A grooved pulley mounted on the motor shaft or the fan shaft that carries the drive belts, fastened with or without a bushing; the motor-shaft one is the drive pulley and the fan-shaft one the driven pulley.

Example: Swapping a 6-inch motor sheave for a 7-inch one raises fan speed about 17 percent.

docs.title: Shutoff Pressure
docs.text:
The static pressure a fan develops at zero airflow, with the inlet or outlet completely blocked.

Example: Shutoff pressure is the most pressure a fan can impose on its ductwork at a given speed.

docs.title: Single Width Single Inlet
docs.text: A centrifugal impeller and housing configuration, abbreviated SWSI, that takes air in through one side only, with one back plate, one shroud, and one inlet.

docs.title: Size Change Calculation
docs.text:
An application of the fan laws to a geometrically similar fan of another size, with airflow scaling by the diameter ratio cubed, pressure squared, and power to the fifth power.

Example: At the same RPM, a size 1.12 times larger moves 1.405 times the airflow and absorbs 1.762 times the power.

docs.title: Slide Base
docs.text:
A motor base in which the motor plate slides along a fixed base, moved by an adjusting screw to set belt tension.

Example: Arrangement 9 fans carry the motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal.

docs.title: Slide Gate Damper
docs.text: A flat gate that slides across the airway in a frame to throttle flow manually, offered for cast aluminum pressure blowers.

docs.title: Slip Connection
docs.text:
A joint made by sliding one collar or pipe over or into another and sealing it, typically with a rubber sleeve and clamps.

Example: A slip connection between a fan and a free-standing inlet box tolerates small movement.

docs.title: Smoke and Heat Exhaust Fan
docs.text:
A fan built to keep running while moving smoke and hot gas out of a burning building, rated for a minimum temperature and duration.

Example: The current catalog rates its smoke and heat fans for 500°F for four hours or 1,000°F for 15 minutes.

docs.title: Snubber
docs.text:
A pair of brackets with elastomeric material between them, one on the fan or base and one on the floor, that limits excessive movement in any direction.

Example: A snubber engages only when an earthquake or startup jolt pushes the fan beyond its normal float.

docs.title: Soap Bubble Test
docs.text:
A shop leak check in which a pressurized fan housing's seams, joints, and seals are coated with soap solution so bubbles reveal leaks.

Example: An RTO fan passes a soap bubble test before shipment, and the result goes on the inspection form.

docs.title: Solid Pillow Block Bearing
docs.text:
A pillow block bearing with a one-piece cast housing, the common choice on standard fans.

Example: Replacing a solid pillow block bearing usually means sliding it off the shaft end after pulling the sheave.

docs.title: Sone Rating
docs.text:
A measure of perceived loudness on a linear scale, where 1 sone is the loudness of a 1,000 Hz tone at 40 dB sound pressure level.

Example: A 10-sone exhauster sounds about twice as loud as a 5-sone one.

docs.title: Sound Power Level
docs.text:
The total acoustic power a fan radiates, in decibels relative to 10⁻¹² watt, independent of room or distance; abbreviated Lw.

Example: Fan manufacturers publish sound power levels in eight octave bands.

docs.title: Sound Pressure Level
docs.text:
The magnitude of sound pressure fluctuations at one location, in decibels relative to 20 micropascals; abbreviated Lp.

Example: A fan's sound pressure level falls as a listener moves farther away, while its sound power stays the same.

docs.title: Space Constraints
docs.text:
The physical limits on where a fan can go, including footprint, height, duct locations, service clearances, rigging paths, and supporting structure.

Example: A fixed footprint in a mechanical room often decides the arrangement before performance does.

docs.title: Spark Resistant Construction
docs.text: Fan construction that lowers the chance of the fan striking a spark by using non-ferrous airstream parts and arranging parts so rotating and stationary components are unlikely to touch.

docs.title: Spark Resistant Type A
docs.text:
The highest degree of spark resistance, requiring all fan components in the airstream to be non-ferrous and assembled to reduce stationary-to-rotating contact.

Example: A Type A centrifugal fan has a non-ferrous housing, impeller, inlet funnel, and shaft sleeve.

docs.title: Spark Resistant Type B
docs.text:
Spark-resistant construction requiring a non-ferrous impeller and an assembly that reduces stationary-to-rotating contact, usually with a non-ferrous rub plate.

Example: A Type B fan has an aluminum impeller and rub plate while the housing and shaft stay steel.

docs.title: Spark Resistant Type C
docs.text:
The minimal spark-resistant construction, keeping a steel impeller and housing but adding non-ferrous parts where a shifting rotor would touch first.

Example: A Type C centrifugal fan uses an aluminum inlet funnel and rub plate with a steel impeller.

docs.title: Specific Speed
docs.text:
A single number that characterizes a fan design by combining its speed, airflow, and pressure at the point of rating, usually peak efficiency.

Example: Axial fans have high specific speed, while radial blowers have low specific speed.

docs.title: Specification Performance Clause
docs.text:
The paragraph in Part 2 of a fan specification stating what the fan must deliver, at what air conditions, and how ratings must be proven.

Example: A specification performance clause names the airflow, pressure, temperature, elevation, and AMCA rating standards.

docs.title: Specification Review
docs.text:
The check of a specification, or a submittal against one, for completeness and internal consistency before it is issued or approved.

Example: Specification review catches a duty point stated with no air condition.

docs.title: Speed Change Calculation
docs.text:
An application of the fan laws that finds the new speed, pressure, and power when a fan on the same system must deliver a different airflow.

Example: To raise airflow from 8,000 to 9,000 CFM, speed rises by 9,000/8,000 = 1.125.

docs.title: Speed Control
docs.text:
A flow-control method that reduces airflow by slowing the impeller, using the least power of any method.

Example: Slowing a fan to 80 percent speed cuts its airflow to 80 percent and its power to about half.

docs.title: Spherical Roller Bearing
docs.text:
A rolling bearing with crowned, barrel-shaped rollers in a spherical outer raceway, suited to high and shock loads and tolerant of slight misalignment.

Example: A heavy industrial fan with a large shaft runs on spherical roller bearings.

docs.title: Split Housing
docs.text:
A fan housing built in sections that bolt together along planned joints so it can be opened or shipped in pieces.

Example: Horizontal, pie, and three-way splits are the three centrifugal split housing styles.

docs.title: Split Pillow Block Bearing
docs.text:
A pillow block bearing whose housing splits horizontally through the shaft centerline so the cap lifts off for inspection and replacement.

Example: Larger heavy-duty fans often use split pillow block bearings.

docs.title: Spring Isolator
docs.text:
A steel coil spring with load plates placed between a fan or its base and the structure, giving high deflection and high isolation.

Example: A 2-inch-deflection spring isolator lets a fan run far above its natural frequency.

docs.title: Square Inline Centrifugal Fan
docs.text:
An inline centrifugal fan with a square housing and removable side panels that can pass air straight through or turn it 90 degrees.

Example: A square inline fan fits a rectangular duct run above a ceiling, and its side panels come off for service.

docs.title: Stack Cap
docs.text: A short, open-topped discharge stack on the outlet of a roof-mounted or vertically mounted fan that sends air straight up in a vertical jet.

docs.title: Stainless Steel Construction
docs.text:
Construction in which airstream parts, and where specified the shaft, are made of stainless steel, an iron-based alloy made corrosion resistant by chromium.

Example: A food-plant washdown exhaust fan uses Type 304 stainless steel construction.

docs.title: Stall Region
docs.text: The part of a fan curve to the left of the pressure peak, where airflow separates from the blades and performance becomes unsteady.

docs.title: Standard Air
docs.text:
The reference air condition used to rate fans: air with a density of 0.075 lb/ft³, very nearly that of dry air at 70°F and 29.92 in. Hg barometric pressure.

Example: Unless a catalog table says otherwise, its static pressures and brake horsepowers are standard-air values.

docs.title: Standard Motor Position Rule
docs.text:
FanPedia's default pairing of motor side with rotation on pedestal-mounted motors: clockwise fans take position L and counterclockwise fans take position R.

Example: A CCW Arrangement 9 fan normally has its motor in position R.

docs.title: Static Efficiency
docs.text: Fan efficiency computed from air power based on fan static pressure, divided by brake horsepower.

docs.title: Static Oil Lubrication
docs.text: A bearing oil system that keeps a constant oil level in a sump in each bearing housing, topped up by a constant-level oiler.

docs.title: Static Pressure
docs.text:
The pressure that air exerts equally in all directions on the walls of a duct or housing, independent of air motion, measured perpendicular to the flow.

Example: A manometer tube connected flush to the side of a duct reads static pressure.

docs.title: Straight Bore Hub
docs.text: An impeller hub whose bore runs straight through, fastened to the shaft with a key and set screws.

docs.title: Straightening Vanes
docs.text:
Fixed vanes inside a tubular housing downstream of the impeller that remove swirl and return the air to straight-through flow.

Example: Straightening vanes in a tubular inline centrifugal fan turn the radially thrown air back along the duct.

docs.title: Stuffing Box Seal
docs.text: A shaft seal in which rings of packing are stacked in a housing around the shaft and compressed by an outer plate, like valve-stem packing; also called a packing gland or Graphoil seal.

docs.title: Submittal Data
docs.text:
The package of documents sent for the engineer's review before a fan is released for manufacture, confirming it meets the specification.

Example: Submittal data include performance curves, octave band sound data, motor ratings, and dimensioned drawings.

docs.title: Surge
docs.text:
An unstable, cycling condition left of the pressure peak in which airflow and pressure oscillate between the fan and the air volume in the ductwork.

Example: Surge shows up as rhythmic "breathing" of the ductwork and fluctuating motor amps.

docs.title: Swingout Door Assembly
docs.text:
The hinged door and reinforced framework that carry a swingout fan's rotating parts out of the housing.

Example: On Arrangement 9ST, the motor, shaft, bearings, and impeller ride on the swingout door assembly.

docs.title: Swingout Fan
docs.text:
A fan whose impeller, shaft, and bearing assembly is mounted on a large hinged door so it swings out of the housing for cleaning and inspection.

Example: A food plant uses a swingout fan where the impeller must be washed often.

docs.title: Swingout Motor Position Rule
docs.text:
The rule tying motor position to the swing side of an Arrangement 9ST and to both rotation and swing side of an Arrangement 9SS.

Example: A 9SS left-swing fan must be CCW with the motor in position R and an F2 conduit box.

docs.title: Synchronous Motor Speed
docs.text:
The speed of the rotating magnetic field in an induction motor, set by supply frequency and number of poles: 120 times frequency divided by poles.

Example: A four-pole motor on 60 Hz has a synchronous motor speed of 1,800 RPM.

docs.title: System Curve
docs.text:
A parabola-shaped graph of one duct system's resistance against airflow, starting at zero pressure at zero airflow.

Example: A system needing 2 in. wg at 5,000 CFM has a system curve passing 8 in. wg at 10,000 CFM.

docs.title: System Effect
docs.text:
The loss of fan performance caused by the way a fan is connected to its system, expressed as an added pressure loss the selection must account for.

Example: An elbow bolted directly to a fan inlet creates system effect that a catalog rating does not include.

docs.title: System Effect Curve
docs.text:
A lettered chart in AMCA 201 giving system effect in in. wg against velocity at the fan inlet or outlet for a given connection.

Example: A designer looks up the system effect curve assigned to an inlet elbow, then reads the loss at the inlet velocity.

docs.title: System Resistance
docs.text:
The pressure needed to push a given airflow through everything connected to a fan, rising with the square of airflow.

Example: Doubling airflow through a duct system raises its system resistance to four times the original.

docs.title: Taconite Seal
docs.text:
A bearing seal for dirty or abrasive environments that combines a labyrinth with a grease-purged cavity that pushes contaminants out.

Example: A mining-plant fan on split pillow blocks is ordered with taconite seals.

docs.title: Taper Lock Hub
docs.text: An impeller hub with a tapered bore that is clamped to the shaft by a tapered bushing drawn in by screws.

docs.title: TEAO Motor
docs.text:
A totally enclosed air over motor with no cooling fan of its own, relying on the fan's airstream for cooling.

Example: A direct-drive vaneaxial fan with the motor inside the tube uses a TEAO motor.

docs.title: Technical Description
docs.text:
A short written paragraph in FanPedia or a catalog that defines one component, arrangement, or option and states its restrictions.

Example: The technical description of Arrangement 1 SWSI states that the motor can go in any of the four AMCA motor positions.

docs.title: TEFC Motor
docs.text:
A totally enclosed fan cooled motor with sealed windings and an external fan that blows air over the ribbed outer frame.

Example: A TEFC motor is the usual choice for a fan in a dusty or damp industrial space.

docs.title: Temperature Correction
docs.text: The density correction factor for an air temperature other than 70°F, computed from absolute temperatures in degrees Rankine.

docs.title: TENV Motor
docs.text:
A totally enclosed non-ventilated motor with no cooling fan, dissipating heat through its frame alone.

Example: A TENV motor is chosen where lint would clog the fan cover of a TEFC motor.

docs.title: Thermal Expansion
docs.text:
The increase in a part's dimensions as its temperature rises, proportional for a straight part to its length and temperature rise.

Example: Thermal expansion lengthens a hot fan's shaft, which the floating bearing must accommodate.

docs.title: Three-Way Split Housing
docs.text: A split housing cut into three sections, up to 180 degrees, used for shipping or to pass the fan through a restricted opening.

docs.title: Thrust Restraint
docs.text:
A device that prevents excessive fan motion on isolators caused by the aerodynamic reaction force of the moving air.

Example: A fan on soft springs pushing 4 in. wg through a 4 ft² outlet needs a thrust restraint against an 83 lb reaction.

docs.title: Tip Speed
docs.text:
The linear speed of the outermost point of the impeller blades, in feet per minute, set by impeller diameter and rotating speed.

Example: A 3-foot-diameter impeller at 1,000 RPM has a tip speed of about 9,425 fpm.

docs.title: Top Angular Down Discharge
docs.text:
The centrifugal discharge position, coded TAD at 135 degrees, with the outlet near the top of the housing and air heading downward at 45 degrees.

Example: A TAD outlet can collide with a motor on that side, restricting motor position.

docs.title: Top Angular Up Discharge
docs.text:
The centrifugal discharge position, coded TAU at 45 degrees, with the outlet near the top of the housing and air heading upward at 45 degrees.

Example: A TAU outlet meets an exhaust duct climbing toward an offset roof penetration.

docs.title: Top Horizontal Discharge
docs.text:
The centrifugal discharge position, coded THD at 90 degrees, with the outlet at the top of the housing pointing sideways.

Example: A fan feeding a duct that runs near the ceiling uses top horizontal discharge.

docs.title: Total Pressure
docs.text: The sum of static pressure and velocity pressure at a point in an airstream, representing all of the energy the air carries there.

docs.title: Totally Split Roller Bearing
docs.text:
A specialty bearing whose housing and every internal part are split in halves so it can be replaced without removing the shaft.

Example: A large fan where pulling the shaft means a long outage may justify a totally split roller bearing.

docs.title: Transition Piece
docs.text: A section of ductwork that connects a fan opening to a duct of different shape or size; usually called a transition.

docs.title: Transmission Losses
docs.text:
The power lost between the motor shaft and the fan shaft in the drive, such as belt flexing and slip and drive bearing friction.

Example: A belt-driven fan's motor must supply the catalog BHP plus transmission losses.

docs.title: Trantorque Hub
docs.text:
An axial impeller hub that uses a keyless compression bushing which grips the shaft when tightened.

Example: A Trantorque hub needs no shaft key, unlike a taper lock hub.

docs.title: Tri-Directional Positioner
docs.text: A motor positioner combining horizontal positioners with vertical jack screws, giving adjustment horizontally and vertically.

docs.title: Tube Adapter and Sleeve
docs.text:
A flexible outlet connection for pressure blowers: a metal collar and flange bolted to the discharge plus a molded rubber slip sleeve with hose clamps.

Example: A tube adapter and sleeve connects a pressure blower to a pipe line rated up to 5 psi and 180°F.

docs.title: Tubeaxial Fan
docs.text:
An axial fan in a plain cylindrical housing with no guide vanes, so air leaves with some rotational swirl.

Example: A tubeaxial fan provides general ventilation through a wall or short duct run.

docs.title: Tubular Housing
docs.text:
A round, straight-through cylindrical housing in which air enters one end and leaves the other in line with the duct.

Example: Tubeaxial, vaneaxial, tubular inline centrifugal, and mixed flow fans all use tubular housings.

docs.title: Turndown
docs.text:
The range over which a flow-control method can reduce airflow and still control it well, stated as a ratio of maximum to minimum controllable airflow.

Example: A method with 4:1 turndown can control a 10,000 CFM fan down to 2,500 CFM.

docs.title: Two and Four Hole Mount
docs.text:
The two pillow block base styles: a two hole mount with one hold-down bolt on each side of the shaft, and a four hole mount with two on each side.

Example: A replacement bearing from another maker may not match the pedestal holes if it offers only a two hole mount.

docs.title: Two-Bearing Housing
docs.text: A specialty housing, also called a monoblock bearing, holding both shaft bearings in one casting to preserve their alignment.

docs.title: Unhoused Centrifugal Fan
docs.text: A centrifugal fan whose impeller runs without a scroll housing, discharging radially in all directions into a surrounding plenum or cabinet.

docs.title: Unitary Base
docs.text:
A fan base of structural channel, also called a channel base, designed to bolt directly to the floor without isolators.

Example: A fan on a solid industrial slab with no vibration-sensitive neighbors sits on a unitary base.

docs.title: Up Blast Discharge Position
docs.text:
The centrifugal discharge position, coded UBD at 360 degrees, with the outlet pointing straight up.

Example: A fan exhausting into a vertical stack uses the up blast discharge position so no outlet elbow is needed.

docs.title: Upblast Discharge
docs.text:
A fan discharge configuration that sends exhaust straight up, away from the roof surface and nearby air intakes.

Example: Kitchen exhaust fans use upblast discharge so the grease plume clears the roof.

docs.title: Utility Set
docs.text:
A compact single-inlet centrifugal fan package, belt or direct driven, for general exhaust and supply in commercial and light industrial buildings.

Example: A utility set with a weather cover exhausts a paint storage room from an outdoor pad.

docs.title: V-Belt
docs.text:
A drive belt with a trapezoidal cross section that wedges into the matching V-shaped groove of a sheave.

Example: A 25 hp fan drive uses three V-belts side by side on multi-groove sheaves.

docs.title: Vaneaxial Fan
docs.text:
An axial fan whose tubular housing includes a section of stationary guide vanes that straighten the airflow as it passes through.

Example: A vaneaxial fan reaches higher pressure and efficiency than a tubeaxial fan of the same diameter.

docs.title: Variable Frequency Drive
docs.text:
An electronic controller, abbreviated VFD, that converts fixed-frequency AC power to adjustable-frequency power, changing induction motor speed in proportion.

Example: Running a VFD at 45 Hz slows a 60 Hz fan to about 75 percent speed.

docs.title: Variable Inlet Vanes
docs.text:
A ring of adjustable radial vanes at a fan inlet that, when partly closed, pre-spin entering air to control flow; also called inlet guide vanes or a vortex damper.

Example: Variable inlet vanes with an actuator let a building automation system modulate a large centrifugal fan.

docs.title: Velocity Pressure
docs.text:
The pressure that a moving airstream would produce if brought to rest, representing the kinetic energy of the air.

Example: At standard air, air moving at 4,005 fpm has a velocity pressure of 1 in. wg.

docs.title: Velocity Pressure Equation
docs.text: The equation converting between air velocity and velocity pressure; for standard air, velocity in fpm equals 4,005 times the square root of velocity pressure in in. wg.

docs.title: Ventilating Set
docs.text: The trade name for a compact Arrangement 10 centrifugal fan in Class I or II, sizes 122 through 365.

docs.title: Vertical Arrangement
docs.text:
A fan arrangement in which the shaft is vertical, so air enters or leaves the impeller vertically.

Example: Plenum Arrangement 4V can be built for vertical up or vertical down airflow.

docs.title: Vertical Inline Motor Location
docs.text: The place a motor occupies on a belt-driven Arrangement 9 vertical inline fan, centered on the curb cap or between the support brackets, with no motor position letter.

docs.title: Vertical Jack Screws
docs.text: Screws threaded through drilled and tapped motor feet that lift the motor so shims can be set, removed after shimming.

docs.title: Vibration
docs.text:
The repeated back-and-forth motion of a machine or structure about its resting position, mainly caused in fans by rotating unbalance.

Example: A fan whose impeller collects dirt develops vibration once per revolution.

docs.title: Vibration Isolation
docs.text: The prevention or limitation of the force an operating fan transmits to its supporting structure, using resilient isolators.

docs.title: Viewed From Drive Side
docs.text:
The convention of describing a centrifugal fan's rotation, discharge, and motor position as seen from the side where the sheave, coupling, or motor is located.

Example: A fan that is clockwise viewed from the drive side appears counterclockwise from the inlet side.

docs.title: Wall Mounted Fan
docs.text:
A fan installed in or on a wall to supply or exhaust air directly through it, usually without ductwork.

Example: A belt-driven wall mounted fan provides cost-effective general ventilation for a warehouse.

docs.title: Wall Type Gravity Damper
docs.text:
A parallel blade, end-pivoted gravity damper mounted in a vertical plane for fans and openings in a wall.

Example: A wall exhaust fan uses a wall type gravity damper whose blades hang closed.

docs.title: Weather Cover
docs.text:
A cover that protects a fan's motor from rain, snow, and sun when installed outdoors.

Example: An Arrangement 10 fan with an optional weather cover is suitable for roof installation.

docs.title: Weatherhood
docs.text:
A hood mounted over the outdoor side of a wall fan that keeps rain and snow out while letting air pass.

Example: A panel fan's weatherhood carries a bird screen across its open side.

docs.title: Weep Hole
docs.text:
A small open hole at the lowest point of a fan housing that drains wash water before painting and moisture after installation.

Example: When water must be piped away rather than dripped, a housing drain replaces the weep hole.

docs.title: Welded Housing
docs.text:
A fan housing whose scroll, sides, and framing are joined by welds into one permanent piece.

Example: Nominally leak-tight construction calls for a welded housing with continuous welds.

docs.title: Wet Airstream
docs.text:
An airstream carrying enough water vapor, mist, or steam that liquid water can condense and collect inside the fan.

Example: Commercial dishwasher exhaust is a wet airstream, so the fan may need a housing drain and corrosion-resistant coating.

docs.title: Wiper Bar
docs.text: A strip mounted inside a centrifugal housing in the inlet funnel area that directs air to prevent turbulence and increase efficiency.

docs.title: Zero Speed Switch
docs.text:
A sensor that detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft; also called a speed sensor.

Example: A zero speed switch alarms when a belt breaks even though the motor starter is still on.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 27 chapters covering 581 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Air, Pressure and the Fan - Introduces airflow, CFM, air velocity, static pressure, air density and temperature, the core vocabulary every later chapter uses to describe what a fan does.
  2. Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air - Covers velocity and total pressure, standard air, and the hot, wet, corrosive, dusty and explosive airstreams that shape how a fan must be built.
  3. Basic Fan Anatomy - Names the core parts of every fan (housing, impeller, shaft, bearings, motor, inlet, outlet and drive train) and basic housing features such as access doors and screens.
  4. Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans - Presents the three fan families, scroll and tubular housings, inline fans, roof and wall ventilators, and the difference between commercial and industrial duty.
  5. Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans - Covers kitchen, smoke and heat, fiberglass, plenum, tubeaxial and gravity relief units, roof exhauster styles, and upblast versus downblast discharge.
  6. Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines - Covers plug fans, vaneaxials, pressure blowers, radial fans, utility sets, filtered supply and dust collection fans, and lab exhaust plume dilution.
  7. Housing Construction and Exploded Views - Details scroll side plates, cutoffs, split housings, framing, access panels and roof exhauster parts, and how to read an exploded view.
  8. Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types - Introduces impeller blades, back plates, shrouds and hubs; backward inclined, forward curved, mixed flow and axial impellers; orientation and balancing.
  9. Impeller Construction and Material Handling - Covers airfoil and backward curved designs, double width double inlet impellers, axial blade geometry, hub types, and radial, material-handling and paper-handling impellers.
  10. Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings - Explains brake horsepower, fan efficiency, fan and system curves, the operating point, stall, density corrections, sound ratings and fan class.
  11. Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements - Compares direct and belt drive, couplings, sheaves and belts, overhung and center-hung impellers, and the standard Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7.
  12. Discharge Positions and Rotation - Introduces viewing a fan from the drive side, discharge positions and angles, angular discharges, rotation, and the basic motor positions.
  13. Rotation and Discharge Codes - Covers clockwise and counterclockwise designation, the complete rotation and discharge code, motor position restrictions, and the conventions for inline and axial fans on orders.
  14. Fan Motors and Enclosures - Introduces induction and EC motors, NEMA frames, ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV and explosion-proof enclosures, service factor, insulation class and motor bases.
  15. Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners - Covers variable frequency drives, inverter-duty, premium-efficiency and hazardous-location motors, thermal protection, slide and pivot bases, and the positioners used to adjust belt tension.
  16. Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - Covers bearing types and life, mounting, lubrication, bearing seals, positioners and sensors, shaft features, and the family of shaft seals.
  17. Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals - Covers L-10 and L-50 life, split and solid pillow blocks, oil-mist and static-oil lubrication, labyrinth and taconite seals, fixed and floating rules, and pedestals.
  18. Inlets, Outlets and Flow Control - Covers inlet boxes and funnels, evasés, transitions, silencers, the damper families, inlet vanes, speed control and turndown, and how each one changes a fan's airflow.
  19. Damper Details and Duct Connections - Details gravity damper styles, blade types, actuators, blast and slide gates, lab exhaust dampers, flexible connectors and flange bolt patterns.
  20. Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance - Covers construction classes, materials and coatings, spark-resistant construction, high-temperature and high-moisture basics, and insulated fans, matching a fan's build to its airstream.
  21. High Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - Covers cooler boxes, heat shields, thermal expansion, spark-resistant Types A and B, leak-tight fans and leakage testing, and the service conditions of RTO duty.
  22. Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation - Introduces unitary, isolation and inertia bases, isolator deflection, neoprene pads, rubber-in-shear isolators, seismic restraint, and piezometer rings for measuring a fan's airflow.
  23. Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement - Covers spring isolator types and how they mount, snubbers, thrust restraints, shaft alignment, anti-backspin devices, and verifying a fan's airflow in the field.
  24. Advanced Arrangements and Configuration Variants - Covers Arrangements 8, 9 and 10, plug, plenum, swingout and clamshell variants, and the motor position rules specific to each arrangement.
  25. Fan Laws, System Effect and Sound - Applies the fan laws and speed-change calculations, and covers system effect, fans in parallel and series, the efficiency curve, Fan Energy Index and octave-band sound.
  26. Reading Catalogs and Performance Tables - Teaches catalog structure, model codes, performance tables and interpolation, rating conditions, operating limits, and how FanPedia relates to current catalogs.
  27. Fan Selection and Writing the Specification - Brings everything together: application requirements, selecting family, impeller, arrangement, construction, motor, drive and accessories, writing and reviewing the specification, and the capstone.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Read the chapters in order. Every concept is introduced only after the concepts it depends on, so each chapter builds on the ones before it. Each chapter lists the earlier chapters it relies on; if a term is unfamiliar, go back to the chapter that introduced it.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the physical quantities used to describe air in motion: airflow volume in cubic feet per minute, air velocity, static pressure in inches of water gauge, and air density as it changes with temperature and altitude. It defines a fan as a machine that moves air by turning at a given speed and power. Every later chapter builds on this vocabulary. After completing it, readers can state what a fan delivers and in which units.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Air Movement 13733 Fan Speed 11322 Horsepower 2706 Airflow Volume 1382 Air Pressure 1283 Air Density 374 Airstream 371 Fan 10322 Cubic Feet Per Minute 59 Air Velocity 103 Inches of Water Gauge 59 Static Pressure 1101 Air Temperature 200 Altitude 107 Contaminated Airstream 194

docs.text: This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

docs.title: Why This Chapter Comes First
docs.text:
Every fan order, catalog page and specification in this book reduces to a short sentence: move this much air, against this much resistance, at these conditions, without the air destroying the fan. Before you can read that sentence on a performance table or write it in a submittal, you need the handful of quantities it is built from: airflow volume in cubic feet per minute, air velocity, pressure in inches of water gauge, fan speed in revolutions per minute, horsepower, and the density of the air itself. This chapter defines each one, shows how they connect, and works a realistic number for every idea so you can check a catalog value instead of just copying it.

Meet Breeze

Hi, I'm Breeze, a hummingbird. My wings beat dozens of times a second, so I take airflow personally, and I care about exact designations the way an application engineer does. Here is what I do when I show up in this book:

  1. Welcome: I open each chapter and tell you what it will let you do on the job.
  2. Thinking: I stop you at an idea worth rethinking, so you can build the right mental model.
  3. Tip: I hand you a shortcut or a quick check that saves time on a real order.
  4. Warning: I warn you about a common mistake, why it happens and how to avoid it.
  5. Encouraging: I encourage you when a topic is genuinely hard, and point to a way through it.
  6. Celebration: I celebrate at the end of a chapter by naming the skill you just gained.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Air Movement: Why We Move Air at All
docs.text:
Air movement is the transfer of a mass of air from one place to another, driven by a difference in pressure. Buildings and plants move air for a small number of practical reasons: to supply fresh air to people, to carry heat into or out of a space, to deliver air a process needs (combustion air for a burner, drying air for a dryer), and to capture and remove something unwanted (fumes from a lab hood, dust from a grinder, steam from a kitchen). In each case the air is not the product; it is the vehicle. The fan's job is to keep that vehicle moving at the rate the job requires.

Two physical facts make air movement an engineering problem rather than an afterthought. First, air has mass. A cubic foot of air at room conditions weighs about 0.075 pound, which sounds negligible until you multiply it by the volume of a building. Second, air moves only when something pushes it: it always flows from a region of higher pressure toward a region of lower pressure, and it resists being speeded up, turned and squeezed through filters and ducts. A fan supplies the pressure difference that keeps the air moving against that resistance.

The following table organizes the common jobs of air movement that the paragraph above described, with a typical site for each and the property of the air that matters most for that job.

Job of air movement Typical site What matters most Ventilation (fresh air for people) Office, school, warehouse Enough volume, delivered quietly Heating or cooling Air handler, cooling tower, oven Volume and the air temperature Process air Burner combustion air, dryer, kiln Volume, pressure and temperature, often high Contaminant capture and removal Lab hood, paint booth, dust collector, kitchen hood What the air carries, and where it is discharged Pressurization or exhaust balance Clean room, stair tower, plenum Pressure difference between spaces

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Air Is in a Room?
docs.text:
A small machine shop measures 40 ft by 30 ft with a 12 ft ceiling. The owner wants the room air replaced ten times every hour.

  1. Room volume: \( 40 \times 30 \times 12 = 14{,}400 \) cubic feet.
  2. Weight of that air at room conditions: \( 14{,}400 \times 0.075 = 1{,}080 \) pounds, more than half a ton.
  3. Ten changes per hour means the fan must move \( 14{,}400 \times 10 = 144{,}000 \) cubic feet, or about 10,800 pounds of air, every hour.
  4. Per minute, that is \( 144{,}000 \div 60 = 2{,}400 \) cubic feet.

The last number, 2,400 cubic feet every minute, is the form in which a fan's airflow is ordered and cataloged. You will meet it again below as a duct calculation and as a MicroSim challenge.

Air Is Heavy Enough to Matter

Think of a fan as a machine that keeps lifting and throwing a steady stream of mass, not as something that "stirs" weightless air. Once you picture those 10,800 pounds an hour, it stops being surprising that a modest ventilation fan needs a real motor, and that the weight of each cubic foot changes the work the fan must do.

docs.title: The Airstream
docs.text:
The airstream is the moving body of air that passes through a fan and its connected ductwork, together with everything that air carries: heat, moisture, dust, fibers, fumes or vapors. FanPedia uses the term constantly because so many construction decisions depend on which parts of a fan sit in the airstream and which sit out of it. The impeller and the inside of the housing are always in the airstream. Bearings, motors and belts may or may not be, depending on how the fan is arranged.

The properties of the airstream decide what the fan must be built from and how it must be laid out. Temperature changes the air's weight and the strength of metals and seals. Moisture and corrosive gases attack materials. Solids wear blades and build up on them. Flammable vapors and dusts make a spark dangerous. Before looking at a worked example, the following table summarizes those airstream properties and what each one changes in a fan selection; later chapters treat each in depth.

Airstream property What it changes in the fan Where this book covers it Temperature Air density, material strength, bearing and seal choice This chapter; Chapter 21 Altitude (site elevation) Air density, and therefore pressure and power This chapter Moisture Drains, coatings, materials Chapter 2 Solids (dust, fibers, chips) Impeller type, wear protection Chapter 9 Corrosive gases Materials and coatings Chapter 20 Flammable vapors or dusts Spark-resistant construction Chapter 20

docs.title: Worked Example: Which Parts Sit in a 300°F Airstream?
docs.text:
A customer needs a belt-driven centrifugal fan to exhaust 300°F air from a curing oven. Compare two arrangements described in FanPedia's technical descriptions:

  • Arrangement 1, single width, single inlet: the impeller is overhung on the end of the shaft, and "the two fan bearings are mounted on the bearing pedestal, out of the airstream," which FanPedia says makes the arrangement suited to high-temperature or contaminated air (FanPedia, p. 162).
  • Arrangement 3, double width, double inlet: the impeller is mounted between the bearings, and "both bearings are located in the airstream," so standard double width, double inlet fans should be used for clean air with air temperatures limited to 130°F (FanPedia, p. 167).

Trace the airstream: in Arrangement 3 the 300°F air flows directly past both bearings, which is well above the 130°F limit for the standard design. In Arrangement 1 the hot air stays inside the housing while the bearings sit outside on the pedestal. Arrangement 1 is the natural starting point for this job. Arrangements themselves are the subject of Chapter 11; the point here is that you cannot pick one until you know what is in the airstream.

docs.title: The Fan
docs.text:
A fan is a machine that moves air by turning a bladed wheel, the impeller, inside or in front of a housing. The rotating blades push on the air, raise its pressure slightly and send it on its way. A motor turns the impeller either directly (the impeller is mounted on the motor shaft) or through belts and pulleys. FanPedia describes the main families by the path the air takes: housed centrifugal fans draw air in along the shaft and discharge it "at a right angle to the fan shaft," while axial and inline fans "move air straight through the fan with a rotating impeller" (FanPedia, pp. 4, 6-7). Chapter 3 names every part, and Chapter 4 compares the families.

What separates a fan from a compressor is how little it raises the pressure. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 14.7 pounds per square inch, and a fan adds only a small fraction to that. Because the air is squeezed so little, it barely changes volume passing through, and for most work you can treat the cubic feet per minute entering a fan as equal to the cubic feet per minute leaving it.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Big Is a Fan's Pressure Rise?
docs.text:
A heavy-duty industrial fan develops 10 inches of water gauge (a unit defined in the pressure section below; atmospheric pressure is about 407 of these units).

  1. Pressure rise as a fraction of atmospheric pressure: \( 10 \div 407 = 0.025 \), or about 2.5 percent.
  2. The air's volume therefore shrinks by only about 2.5 percent through the fan; at a typical HVAC pressure of 2 inches of water gauge, about 0.5 percent.
  3. Conclusion: in catalog work the fan's inlet and outlet airflow are taken as the same number, and the fan is rated by the airflow at its inlet.

Every fan rating states what the fan delivers in a fixed set of quantities: airflow, pressure, speed, power and the air density the rating assumes. The sections that follow define each one, and the chapter closes with an interactive duty statement that puts them back together.

docs.title: Airflow Volume and Cubic Feet Per Minute
docs.text:
Airflow volume is the volume of air a fan moves in a unit of time. It is a rate: not "how much air is in the duct" but "how much air passes a point each minute." In the United States the unit is cubic feet per minute, abbreviated CFM. One CFM is one cubic foot of air passing a point every minute. The machine-shop example above needed 2,400 CFM; a large industrial exhaust fan may move several hundred thousand CFM.

Airflow volume is not the same as the amount of air in pounds. A cubic foot of hot air weighs less than a cubic foot of cool air, so the same CFM carries different masses at different temperatures. The connection is the mass flow equation below; air density, its key ingredient, gets its own section later in this chapter.

docs.title: Mass Flow from Airflow Volume
docs.text:
\[ \dot{m} = Q \times \rho \]

where:

  • \( \dot{m} \) is the mass flow rate in pounds per minute
  • \( Q \) is the airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
  • \( \rho \) is the air density in pounds per cubic foot

docs.title: Worked Example: Same CFM, Different Air
docs.text:
A process fan moves 10,000 CFM.

  1. At 70°F and sea level, density is 0.075 lb/ft³: \( 10{,}000 \times 0.075 = 750 \) lb of air per minute.
  2. At 400°F and sea level, density falls to about 0.0462 lb/ft³: \( 10{,}000 \times 0.0462 = 462 \) lb per minute.
  3. The fan is moving the same 10,000 CFM in both cases but nearly 40 percent less air by weight when it is hot.

This is why fan catalogs and specifications always state CFM at a stated condition. Fan airflow is rated as the actual volume at the fan inlet, at the density of the air actually entering the fan. When a specification lists CFM without a temperature and elevation, ask for them before selecting anything.

docs.title: Air Velocity
docs.text: Air velocity is how fast the air is moving at a point, in feet per minute. Velocity and airflow volume are linked by the area the air passes through: the same CFM moves slowly through a large duct and quickly through a small one. Velocity matters because fast air is noisy, costs pressure to push through ducts, and can carry dust that slow air would drop. Chapter 2 turns this relationship into the continuity equation and shows how velocity creates its own pressure; here we need only the basic calculation.

docs.title: Airflow, Velocity and Area
docs.text:
\[ Q = V \times A \]

where:

  • \( Q \) is the airflow volume in CFM
  • \( V \) is the average air velocity in feet per minute
  • \( A \) is the flow area in square feet

docs.title: Worked Example: Velocity in a Rectangular Duct
docs.text:
The machine shop's 2,400 CFM flows through a 16 in by 12 in duct.

  1. Convert the duct size to square feet: \( (16 \times 12) \div 144 = 1.333 \) ft².
  2. Solve for velocity: \( V = Q \div A = 2{,}400 \div 1.333 = 1{,}800 \) feet per minute.
  3. If the same air were carried in a 24 in by 16 in duct (2.667 ft²), velocity would halve to 900 feet per minute.

Check the Units Before the Arithmetic

Duct sizes come in inches but the equation wants square feet, so divide width times height by 144 (or use \( \pi D^2 \div 576 \) for a round duct of diameter \( D \) inches) before you divide CFM by area. If your answer comes out 144 times too small, you skipped that step.

The calculator below lets you practice that conversion and the velocity equation on the kinds of ducts you will see on drawings, including the 16 in by 12 in example above.

docs.title: Diagram: Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator
docs.text:
Run Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator Fullscreen

Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch01-duct-airflow-velocity-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate air velocity, airflow volume or required flow area from the other two quantities for rectangular and round ducts, to within 2 percent of the model value.

Prerequisites: airflow volume, cubic feet per minute (CFM), air velocity in feet per minute, flow area in square feet, the equation Q = V × A, converting duct dimensions in inches to square feet (all defined in the sections "Airflow Volume and Cubic Feet Per Minute" and "Air Velocity" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For four fixed challenges, the learner types one number (velocity, CFM or area) before the sim reveals the model value. An answer is correct when it is within ±2% of the model value. Mastery is 4 of 4 correct, with at most two attempts each. Free exploration with the duct and airflow controls is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Velocity can be found by dividing CFM by the duct dimensions in inches without converting to square feet. (2) A bigger duct moves more air at the same fan airflow; in fact the CFM is the same and only the velocity drops. (3) A round duct of diameter D has the same area as a square duct of side D.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with an immediate check, so each challenge requires a committed number before the answer appears. The free mode afterward lets the learner see the inverse relationship between area and velocity at fixed CFM, which addresses misconception 2.

Content:

Adjustable quantities in free mode:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Duct shape rectangular or round rectangular Rectangular width 6 48 2 16 in Rectangular height 6 48 2 12 in Round diameter 6 60 2 18 in Airflow Q 200 20,000 100 2,400 CFM

Displayed values in free mode: flow area in ft² (3 decimals), velocity in feet per minute (nearest 10), and the equation with the current numbers substituted.

Challenges, in this order:

# Given Asked Model answer Feedback when wrong 1 2,400 CFM in a 16 in × 12 in rectangular duct Velocity (ft/min) 1,800 Area is (16 × 12) ÷ 144 = 1.333 ft²; V = 2,400 ÷ 1.333 = 1,800 ft/min. Did you forget to divide by 144? 2 5,000 CFM in a 24 in round duct Velocity (ft/min) 1,592 Round area is π × 24² ÷ 576 = 3.142 ft², not 24 × 24 ÷ 144; V = 5,000 ÷ 3.142 = 1,592 ft/min. 3 A 20 in × 10 in rectangular duct at 1,500 ft/min Airflow (CFM) 2,083 Area is 200 ÷ 144 = 1.389 ft²; Q = V × A = 1,500 × 1.389 = 2,083 CFM. 4 10,000 CFM with velocity no higher than 2,000 ft/min Minimum flow area (ft²) 5.00 A = Q ÷ V = 10,000 ÷ 2,000 = 5.00 ft². A larger area lowers the velocity further.

Provenance: Equations and conversions from the chapter section "Air Velocity". Challenge 1 values come from the chapter's machine-shop worked example. Challenges 2-4 are illustrative; the sim labels them "illustrative values".

Rules: Rectangular area A = (W × H) ÷ 144 ft². Round area A = π × D² ÷ 576 ft². V = Q ÷ A, displayed rounded to the nearest 10 ft/min in free mode and to the nearest 1 ft/min in challenges. Q = V × A rounded to the nearest 1 CFM. A = Q ÷ V rounded to 0.01 ft². A learner answer x is correct when |x − model| ≤ 0.02 × model. Non-numeric or empty input is rejected with "Enter a number" and does not use an attempt. Because every dimension is at least 6 in, area is never zero.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types a velocity, then presses Check. The sim shows the model value beside the learner's answer and highlights the step where the learner's number departs from the worked calculation, if it does.
  2. The learner completes challenges 2, 3 and 4 the same way.

Hint after a first wrong attempt: the slip the learner's number matches (for example "You divided by 12 instead of 144. One square foot is 144 square inches."), or else the challenge's rule (challenge 1: "Convert the duct size to square feet first (W × H ÷ 144), then solve V = Q ÷ A."); the step titles are listed with the step to check marked, with no model value and no worked numbers. After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge; the model value and worked calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 4" is shown. Challenges cannot be re-answered after they are revealed.
