Schedule label Hours per day Days per week Hours per year 24 h/day, 7 days/week 24 7 8,736 24 h/day, 5 days/week 24 5 6,240 16 h/day, 5 days/week 16 5 4,160 8 h/day, 5 days/week 8 5 2,080 2 h/day, 5 days/week 2 5 520

Each bar shows L-10 years; a second series shows L-50 years. Hovering a bar shows the rating, the schedule, the hours per year, the L-10 years and the L-50 years.

Challenge cases, in this order:

# L-10 rating (h) Schedule Model L-10 years Feedback when wrong 1 40,000 16 h/day, 5 days/week 9.6 16 × 5 × 52 = 4,160 h per year; 40,000 / 4,160 = 9.6 years. 2 40,000 24 h/day, 7 days/week 4.6 Around-the-clock service is 8,736 h per year; 40,000 / 8,736 = 4.6 years. 3 20,000 8 h/day, 5 days/week 9.6 8 × 5 × 52 = 2,080 h per year; 20,000 / 2,080 = 9.6 years. Half the rating at a quarter of the hours of around-the-clock service still gives about ten years.

Provenance: L-10 and L-50 definitions, the L-50 = 5 × L-10 rule, the available TCF ratings, and the example values for 40,000 h and 20,000 h from FanPedia, page 90. Values for 60,000, 80,000 and 100,000 h are computed with the Rules.

Rules: Hours per year = hours per day × days per week × 52. L-10 years = L-10 hours / hours per year. L-50 hours = 5 × L-10 hours; L-50 years = L-50 hours / hours per year. Display years rounded to 0.1 year. The rating is chosen from the five listed values only; schedules are the five listed only.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types the L-10 life in years.
  2. The learner presses Check. The chart switches to that rating, highlights the matching schedule bar, and shows its value next to the learner's answer.
  3. After all three challenges, the learner can choose any of the five ratings. All ten bars (five L-10, five L-50) update at once. The learner should notice that every bar scales in proportion to the rating, and that the 2 h/day bar is about 17 times the 24/7 bar.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: years." Hint after a first wrong attempt: the slip the answer matches (every day of the year counted, around-the-clock hours used, weeks instead of years, the wrong rating), or else the rule "Hours per year = hours per day × days per week × 52; then L-10 years = L-10 hours ÷ hours per year."; the bars stay hidden. After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge; the model value and calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box. The chart shows the five schedule labels with the bars hidden. The question reads "A 40,000-hour L-10 bearing runs 16 hours a day, 5 days a week. How many years is its L-10 life?"

Chapter Anchors: L-10 = 40,000 h at 16 h/day, 5 days/week gives 4,160 h/year and 9.6 years; L-50 is 200,000 h and 48 years; 24/7 service is 8,736 h/year and 4.6 years; L-50 = 5 × L-10; ratings 20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000 and 100,000 h.

docs.title: The Fan Motor
docs.text:
The fan motor is the machine that converts electrical energy into the mechanical rotation that turns the impeller. FanPedia (page 68) notes that the electric motor is by far the most common way to power a ventilating fan, and that two technologies are used.

An induction motor is an alternating-current (AC) motor in which the current in the rotor, needed to produce torque, is created by electromagnetic induction from the magnetic field of the stator winding, so no electrical connection to the rotor is needed. An electronically commutated (EC) motor uses on-board electronics to run and control the motor: a rectifier converts the AC supply to direct current (DC), and a controller sends the right amount of current, in the right direction, at the right time, through each winding. The EC motor's speed can be set by its own speed controller or by a 0-10 V signal from an outside source, and it runs efficiently even at reduced speed.

FanPedia (page 69) names the parts of an induction motor, the more common of the two. You will see them on drawings and nameplates:

  • The stator is the stationary part; its windings carry current and produce the magnetic field.
  • The rotor assembly (rotor and motor shaft) is the rotating part that delivers power to the fan.
  • The motor bearings support the rotor at each end, inside the endplates.
  • The conduit box is where the power wiring connects, usually in position F1 or F2 on the side of the motor (F3 is on top). F1 or F3 is the standard location; F2 is standard on IEC frames but a special modification on NEMA motors (FanPedia page 75).
  • The nameplate identifies the manufacturer, serial number, and ratings.

docs.title: Diagram: Induction Motor Parts
docs.text:
Run Induction Motor Parts Fullscreen

Induction Motor Parts

sim-id: ch03-induction-motor-overlay Library: html + FP.Overlay Status: built Bloom Level: Remember Learning Objective: The learner will identify the ten labeled parts of an electric induction motor on an exploded view, given each part's function.

Content: Ten numbered markers on the exploded view: fan cover, endplates, nameplate, stator, rotor assembly, external fan, conduit box, frame, motor bearings, and motor shaft.

Provenance: FanPedia page 69, "Motors: Typical Electric Induction Motor Components" (exploded view), with the printed labels removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 69.

The table below compares the two technologies on the points just described.

Feature Induction motor EC motor Supply AC AC, converted to DC on board How the rotor gets its magnetism Current induced from the stator field Permanent magnets in the rotor How speed is varied External speed control Built-in electronics, own controller or 0-10 V signal Where it is common Most fans in the industry Smaller fans where efficient speed control matters

docs.title: Service Factor
docs.text: Two nameplate ratings matter most when you match a motor to a fan. The horsepower (HP) rating is the power the motor can deliver continuously. The fan's brake horsepower (BHP), from Chapter 1, is the power the fan actually draws at its operating point. The service factor (S.F.) is the multiplier above the rated horsepower at which the motor may be used. FanPedia gives the example of a 100 HP motor with a 1.15 service factor, which may be operated at 115 HP, and lists 1.0 (when operated on a variable frequency drive, VFD) and 1.25 as other common values (page 69).

docs.title: Worked Example: Is the Motor Large Enough?
docs.text:
A fan selection shows 53 BHP at the design point. The proposed motor is 50 HP with a 1.15 service factor.

  1. Across the line, the motor may be loaded to \( 50 \times 1.15 = 57.5 \) HP. 53 BHP is within that limit, but it uses the service factor every hour the fan runs, leaving no margin for the motor to run cooler or handle denser air.
  2. The specification then adds a VFD. On a VFD the service factor is 1.0, so the limit becomes \( 50 \times 1.0 = 50 \) HP. 53 BHP is now above the limit.
  3. The next standard size, a 60 HP motor, carries 53 BHP with margin under either condition.

Result: change the motor to 60 HP before the order is entered. Chapter 14 covers motor enclosures and insulation classes, and Chapter 15 covers speed control.

Service Factor Is Not Spare Horsepower

A frequent mistake is selecting a motor whose nameplate horsepower is below the fan's brake horsepower and counting on the service factor to cover the gap. Size the motor so the fan's BHP at the design point is at or below the nameplate horsepower, and remember that a motor on a VFD usually has a service factor of 1.0.

docs.title: The Drive Train
docs.text:
The drive train is the set of parts that carries power from the motor shaft to the impeller. It decides whether the impeller turns at the motor's speed or at some other speed, and whether the motor sits in line with the fan or beside it. There are three basic ways to connect them:

  • Direct drive, impeller on the motor shaft. The impeller mounts straight onto the motor shaft, as in Arrangement 4. The drive train is just the motor and the impeller hub. FanPedia (page 174) notes that Arrangement 4 offers low maintenance since there are no fan bearings, fan shaft, or drive parts to maintain.
  • Direct drive through a coupling. The motor shaft and the fan shaft are joined end to end by a coupling, a device that connects two shafts so they turn together. FanPedia (page 174) describes Arrangement 8 as Arrangement 1 with the bearing pedestal extended to carry the motor, and a flexible coupling connecting the fan and motor shafts. Arrangement 7 is the coupled version of Arrangement 3.
  • Belt drive. A sheave (also called a pulley), a grooved wheel, is mounted on the motor shaft and another on the fan shaft, and V-belts run in the grooves between them. A bushing may connect a sheave to its shaft. The motor sits on a motor base or slide base that moves to tension the belts. A belt guard encloses the belts and sheaves.

docs.title: Diagram: Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan Parts
docs.text:
Run Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan Parts Fullscreen

Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan Parts

sim-id: ch03-direct-drive-centrifugal-overlay Library: html + FP.Overlay Status: built Bloom Level: Remember Learning Objective: The learner will identify the twelve labeled parts of an Arrangement 8 direct drive centrifugal fan on an exploded view, given each part's function.

Content: Twelve numbered markers on the exploded view: inlet collar, inlet funnel, impeller, housing, outlet flange, access hole for mounting bolts, pedestal, bearings, shaft, coupling, motor, and inlet flange (in the inset).

Provenance: FanPedia page 9, "Exploded Views: Centrifugal Fans", Direct Drive Centrifugal Fans (Arrangement 8), with the printed labels removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 9.

In a direct drive the impeller turns at motor speed. In a belt drive, the ratio of the two sheave diameters sets the fan speed, so changing a sheave changes the fan's speed and, with it, the fan's airflow. FanPedia notes that belt-driven fans can reach the exact point of rating through a simple sheave change (page 173).

docs.title: Belt Drive Speed Ratio
docs.text:
\[ N_{fan} = N_{motor} \times \frac{D_{motor}}{D_{fan}} \]

where:

  • \( N_{fan} \) is the fan shaft speed in RPM
  • \( N_{motor} \) is the motor speed in RPM
  • \( D_{motor} \) is the pitch diameter of the motor sheave in inches
  • \( D_{fan} \) is the pitch diameter of the fan sheave in inches

The pitch diameter is the diameter at which the belt actually rides in the sheave groove, slightly smaller than the outside diameter. Real drives lose a small amount of speed to belt slip; the formula gives the ideal value.

docs.title: Worked Example: Fan Speed on a Belt Drive
docs.text:
An illustrative motor runs at 1,760 RPM. Its sheave has a 5.0-inch pitch diameter, and the fan sheave has an 8.0-inch pitch diameter.

  1. Find the ratio: \( 5.0 / 8.0 = 0.625 \).
  2. Find the fan speed: \( 1{,}760 \times 0.625 = 1{,}100 \) RPM.
  3. Now suppose the system needs a bit more air. Replacing the motor sheave with a 5.4-inch sheave gives \( 1{,}760 \times 5.4 / 8.0 = 1{,}188 \) RPM, about 8 percent faster.

A larger motor sheave, or a smaller fan sheave, speeds the fan up. Because the fan's power draw rises much faster than its speed, a sheave change must always be followed by a check that the motor can still carry the load.

One Fan, Many Speeds

Notice what the belt drive buys you: the same fan, impeller, and motor can be set to many different speeds just by choosing two sheaves. That is why belt drive is the flexible choice for matching a fan to a system exactly, and direct drive is the low-maintenance choice when the motor speed already fits.

The MicroSim below lets you practice the speed-ratio calculation and see how each sheave moves the fan speed.

docs.title: Diagram: Belt Drive Speed Calculator
docs.text:
Run Belt Drive Speed Calculator Fullscreen

Belt Drive Speed Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch03-belt-drive-speed-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the fan shaft speed of a belt drive from the motor speed and the two sheave pitch diameters, to within ±10 RPM.

Prerequisites: drive train, sheave, V-belt, pitch diameter, motor speed, direct drive, belt drive (defined in "The Drive Train" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge drives, the learner types the fan speed in RPM before the drive runs. An answer is correct when it is within ±10 RPM of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing sheaves in free exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A larger fan sheave makes the fan turn faster (it makes it turn slower). (2) A belt drive always slows the fan down (if the motor sheave is larger than the fan sheave, the fan turns faster than the motor). (3) Fan speed depends on the difference between the sheave sizes rather than their ratio.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a speed from a ratio is an Apply-level procedure, so the learner commits a number before the drive turns and the sim shows the result. Free exploration afterward confronts misconception 1 and 2 directly, because the learner can watch the fan speed fall as the fan sheave grows.

Content:

Quantities the learner can change in free exploration:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Motor sheave pitch diameter 3.0 12.0 0.2 5.0 in Fan sheave pitch diameter 4.0 24.0 0.2 8.0 in

Motor speeds the learner can choose: 1,160 RPM; 1,760 RPM; 3,500 RPM. Default: 1,760 RPM. The sim labels these "illustrative nominal motor speeds".

Challenge drives, in this order:

# Motor speed (RPM) Motor sheave (in) Fan sheave (in) Model fan speed (RPM) Feedback when wrong 1 1,760 5.0 8.0 1,100 Multiply motor speed by motor sheave over fan sheave: 1,760 × 5.0 / 8.0 = 1,100 RPM. 2 1,760 6.0 12.0 880 The fan sheave is twice the motor sheave, so the fan turns at half the motor speed: 1,760 / 2 = 880 RPM. 3 1,160 9.0 6.0 1,740 Here the motor sheave is larger, so the fan turns faster than the motor: 1,160 × 9.0 / 6.0 = 1,740 RPM.

The display always shows the ratio (motor sheave / fan sheave) to three decimals and the fan speed in RPM, and labels the drive "fan slower than motor", "fan same as motor" or "fan faster than motor".

Provenance: The speed-ratio formula is standard belt-drive kinematics, ignoring belt slip. Motor speeds and sheave sizes are illustrative and labeled as such. The idea that a sheave change sets the exact point of rating comes from FanPedia, page 173.

Rules: Fan speed = motor speed × motor sheave / fan sheave, rounded to the nearest 1 RPM. Ratio label: "fan slower than motor" when ratio < 1.000; "fan same as motor" when ratio = 1.000; "fan faster than motor" when ratio > 1.000. Belt slip is not modeled, and the sim says so in a note. The largest possible fan speed is 3,500 × 12.0 / 4.0 = 10,500 RPM and the smallest is 1,160 × 3.0 / 24.0 = 145 RPM; the display covers that whole range.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 (motor speed and both sheaves, shown as labeled numbers and drawn to scale) and types the fan speed.
  2. The learner presses Check. The drive turns, and the fan speed is shown next to the learner's answer.
  3. After all three challenges, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes either sheave or the motor speed; the drawing, ratio, label and fan speed update immediately.
  4. The first time the learner enlarges the fan sheave, the sim notes "Bigger fan sheave: fan speed went down."

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: RPM." Hint after a first wrong attempt: the slip the answer matches (the ratio inverted, the motor speed unchanged), or else the rule "Fan speed = motor speed × motor sheave ÷ fan sheave." (challenge 3 also asks whether the fan turns faster or slower than the motor); the drive stays at rest. After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge; the model value and calculation are revealed and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box and the drive at rest. The question reads "The motor turns at 1,760 RPM with a 5.0-inch sheave driving an 8.0-inch fan sheave. How fast does the fan turn?"

Chapter Anchors: 1,760 RPM with a 5.0-inch motor sheave and 8.0-inch fan sheave gives a ratio of 0.625 and 1,100 RPM; a 5.4-inch motor sheave gives 1,188 RPM, about 8 percent faster. The 5.4-inch value lies on the motor sheave step grid.

With the drive train in place, every major part of the fan has been named. The interactive exploded view below brings them back together in the drawing you will meet on submittals and in FanPedia.

docs.title: Diagram: Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan
docs.text:
Run Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan Fullscreen

Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan

Type: infographic sim-id: ch03-exploded-centrifugal-fan Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify each of the 14 labeled parts in an exploded view of a belt-driven Arrangement 9 centrifugal fan when given the part's name or function.

Prerequisites: exploded view, fan housing, impeller, inlet funnel, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange, shaft, bearing, sheave, V-belt, motor, slide base, pedestal (all defined in this chapter above).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner answers 10 prompts by selecting a part on the drawing. A selection is correct when it is the part named in the Content quiz table. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The inlet funnel and inlet collar are the same part (the funnel shapes the air into the impeller; the collar is a duct connection). (2) The pedestal is part of the housing (it is a separate support for the bearings and shaft). (3) The sheave on the fan shaft is the same size as the motor sheave (their ratio sets fan speed).

Instructional Rationale: Identifying parts on the same kind of drawing used in submittals and in FanPedia is the Remember-level skill this chapter promises. Explore mode lets the learner attach each name to a location and a function; quiz mode requires the learner to retrieve the part from a name or a function rather than read a label.

Content:

The drawing shows a belt-driven SWSI centrifugal fan, Arrangement 9, exploded along the shaft line, with these 14 parts. Each part, when selected in explore mode, opens an infobox with the text below.

# Part Infobox text 1 Inlet collar Short sleeve at the inlet for a slip-fit duct connection, clamped, with no bolt holes. 2 Flanged inlet (inlet flange) Flat ring with a bolt-hole pattern for a bolted duct connection; mates with a companion flange shipped loose. 3 Inlet funnel Aerodynamically shaped ring that funnels air smoothly into the impeller; also called inlet cone or inlet bell. 4 Impeller The rotating part that adds energy to the air; air enters at its center and leaves at the blade tips. 5 Housing The scroll-shaped shell that encloses the impeller and guides air to the outlet; also called side, scroll or casing. 6 Access hole for mounting bolts Opening in the housing used to reach the bolts that mount the housing. 7 Outlet flange Flat frame around the outlet with a bolt-hole pattern for the downstream duct or accessory. 8 Shaft Steel bar that carries the impeller and transmits torque from the drive; with the impeller it forms the rotor assembly. 9 Bearings Two bearings on the pedestal that support and locate the shaft, outside the airstream in Arrangement 9. 10 Sheave (pulley) Grooved wheel on the fan shaft; with the motor sheave and belts it sets the fan speed. 11 Belt V-belts that carry power from the motor sheave to the fan sheave. 12 Motor Converts electrical energy into rotation; here it sits beside the fan and drives through belts. 13 Motor slide base Adjustable base that slides the motor to tension the belts. 14 Pedestal Support structure that carries the bearings and shaft, and in Arrangement 9 the motor slide base on its side.

Quiz prompts, in this order:

# Prompt Correct part Why (shown as feedback) 1 Select the part that adds energy to the air. Impeller It is the only rotating part in the air path. 2 Select the part that funnels air smoothly into the impeller. Inlet funnel The funnel shapes the inlet air; the collar and flange are duct connections. 3 Select the part a duct slips over and is clamped to. Inlet collar A collar has no bolt holes; a flanged inlet is bolted. 4 Select the part that the downstream duct is bolted to. Outlet flange The outlet flange carries the bolt pattern for the discharge duct. 5 Select the part that carries the impeller and transmits torque to it. Shaft The shaft and impeller form the rotor assembly. 6 Select the parts that support and locate the shaft. Bearings Two bearings on the pedestal hold the shaft radially and axially. 7 Select the part that you would change to change fan speed. Sheave (pulley) The ratio of the motor and fan sheaves sets fan speed. 8 Select the part that moves to tension the belts. Motor slide base Sliding the motor away from the fan tightens the belts. 9 Select the part also called the scroll or casing. Housing Side, scroll and casing are field names for the housing. 10 Select the structure that holds the bearings and the motor slide base. Pedestal The pedestal is a separate support, not part of the housing.

Provenance: Part list and arrangement from FanPedia, page 10 (exploded view, belt-driven centrifugal fans, Arrangement 9). Infobox definitions from this chapter's sections, which cite FanPedia pages 59, 79, 90 and 188.

Rules: Explore mode: selecting any part opens its infobox; one infobox is open at a time. Quiz mode: one selection per prompt per attempt; a prompt is correct only when the exact part in the Correct part column is selected.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner starts in explore mode and selects parts to read their infoboxes. A part that has been opened is marked as visited.
  2. The learner can collapse the drawing to the assembled view and expand it again to see how each part moves into place.
  3. The learner switches to quiz mode. Labels are hidden. Each prompt appears in turn and the learner selects a part.
  4. After the tenth prompt, a summary shows which prompts were missed, with their Why text.

Feedback: Ten prompts, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct:" followed by the Why text, and the part's label appears. Hint after a first wrong attempt: "That is the ." followed by a hint that points to the correct part without naming it (prompt 1: "Look for the part that turns in the air path; the parts around it only guide the air."). After the final attempt: "That is the ." followed by the Why text of the correct answer; the correct part is highlighted and the prompt counts as missed. Score "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The exploded drawing in explore mode with all 14 labels visible and no infobox open. The prompt reads "Select any part to see what it does. When you are ready, switch to quiz mode."

Chapter Anchors: 14 labeled parts; Arrangement 9, belt-driven SWSI centrifugal fan; 10 quiz prompts; the bearings sit outside the airstream in Arrangement 9.

Lots of Names, One Machine

If the part names are starting to blur together, that is normal; most people need a couple of passes through an exploded view before the names stick. Go back to the airflow MicroSim and say each part's name out loud as the air reaches it, then try the exploded view quiz again.

docs.title: Housing Features for Access and Service
docs.text: Fans need to be inspected, cleaned, and repaired, often without removing the ductwork. Three housing features make that possible. The split housing, covered earlier, opens the housing for impeller removal. The other two are the access door and the inspection port.

docs.title: Access Door
docs.text:
An access door is a removable or hinged cover over an opening in the fan housing, large enough to let a person reach or see into the housing to inspect, clean, or service the impeller and interior. Access doors appear on centrifugal housings, on the tubes of axial and inline fans (where FanPedia labels them impeller access doors, page 63), and on most inlet boxes, where FanPedia lists the access door as standard (page 145). FanPedia (page 125) shows three common styles:

  • A bolted access door is a plate bolted to the housing, either on the housing face or wrapped over the edges of the housing. It seals well but takes time to open.
  • A raised access door is built up above the housing surface. On insulated fans FanPedia notes it is usually raised 2 inches above the insulation (page 117), so the door can be opened without cutting through the insulation.
  • A quick-open access door is held with latches or handles, so it can be opened without tools for frequent inspection or cleaning.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing the Access Door
docs.text:
A customer is ordering three centrifugal fans: one for a clean-air supply system, one for a bakery exhaust that must be cleaned weekly, and one insulated fan for a hot dryer exhaust.

  1. Clean-air supply: inspection is rare, so a standard bolted access door on the scroll is enough and seals well.
  2. Bakery exhaust: buildup must be removed every week. A quick-open access door saves removing and replacing a ring of bolts each visit.
  3. Insulated dryer exhaust: a flush door would be buried in insulation. Specify a raised access door, usually raised 2 inches above the insulation.

Result: three fans, three access doors, each chosen by how often the inside of the fan will be reached. For a fan that must be cleaned more often than a door allows, FanPedia describes swingout and clamshell constructions, covered in Chapter 24.

Ask How Often the Fan Gets Cleaned

Here is a shortcut for any access question: ask the customer how often someone will need to see the impeller. Once a year points to a bolted door; every week points to a quick-open door or even swingout construction.

docs.title: Inspection Port
docs.text: An inspection port is a small, closable opening in the fan housing that lets a technician look into the fan, or insert a light, gauge, or probe, without opening an access door. FanPedia lists the inspection port as a standard housing accessory alongside the access door and the split housing (page 59), and a belt-driven tubeaxial fan in its exploded views carries a separate inspection door near the bearing housing (page 15). Because the port is smaller than an access door, it is quicker to open and adds less leakage risk, but it allows viewing only, not cleaning or impeller removal. Specify one when the owner wants to check impeller buildup or wear between full inspections.

docs.title: Accessories That Protect the Openings
docs.text: Fans that draw air from, or discharge it to, the open air need protection at their openings: to keep people and objects out of the impeller, to keep birds and weather out, and to keep air from flowing backward when the fan is off. Three accessories handle those jobs.

docs.title: Bird and Safety Screens
docs.text:
A screen is a wire mesh or grille fastened across a fan opening. The two common kinds do different jobs. A bird screen keeps birds and large debris out of an opening that faces the outdoors, such as the discharge of a roof exhauster or the hood of a wall fan. A safety screen guards an opening against a person's hand, tools, or loose objects reaching the impeller, and is used on any opening someone could reach.

FanPedia's exploded views show both. Upblast and downblast centrifugal roof exhausters carry a bird screen (page 19). A panel fan carries an inlet safety screen on the side people can reach and a bird screen on its outdoor weatherhood (page 18). High-temperature centrifugal fans include a safety screen as part of their general construction (page 110).

docs.title: Worked Example: Screens for a Wall-Mounted Exhaust Fan
docs.text:
A warehouse will have a panel fan in the outside wall, 8 feet above a walkway, exhausting through a weatherhood.

  1. Inside opening (the inlet): it faces the warehouse and is within reach of a ladder or a forklift mast. Specify an inlet safety screen.
  2. Outside opening (the weatherhood): it faces the outdoors, where birds nest in sheltered openings. Specify a bird screen on the weatherhood.
  3. When the fan is off: cold outside air will blow back through the opening. That calls for a backdraft damper, covered next.

Result: two screens with two different jobs, one on each side of the same fan. A screen also adds a small resistance to airflow, which the fan selection should account for.

A Bird Screen Is Not a Safety Screen

Watch out for specifications that list "screen" without saying which kind, because a mesh sized to stop birds is not designed to keep fingers out of an impeller. Write "bird screen" or "safety screen" and name the opening each one covers.

docs.title: Backdraft Damper
docs.text:
A backdraft damper is a damper that lets air flow out through the fan in the normal direction and closes to stop air from flowing back in when the fan stops. A damper is a set of movable blades that can open or close an opening. The most common backdraft damper is the gravity damper, which needs no actuator. FanPedia (page 181) describes three types:

  • A butterfly-type gravity damper is built into roof-mounted upblast fans. It prevents a backdraft of outside air and provides weather protection when the fan is not running.
  • Ceiling-type and wall-type gravity dampers have parallel, end-pivoted blades that open automatically when the fan is energized and close by gravity when power is turned off. They prevent air from flowing back through the system and also keep out rain and snow.

Panel fans use a similar part called a backdraft shutter, mounted between the fan and its weatherhood (page 18).

docs.title: Worked Example: Stopping Winter Backdraft
docs.text:
The warehouse in the previous example runs its wall exhaust fan only during the day shift. At night, wind pushes cold air in through the idle fan, and the heating bill climbs.

  1. Diagnose the flow: with the fan off, nothing holds the opening shut, so wind pressure drives air backward through the fan.
  2. Choose the damper: the fan is wall-mounted, so a wall-type gravity damper fits. When the fan starts, the airflow pushes its blades open; when the fan stops, the blades fall shut by gravity.
  3. Check for flutter: if the fan runs at low airflow, a gravity damper may only partly open. FanPedia (page 182) notes that low flow can leave automatic damper blades partly open, causing flutter and noise, and that a motorized damper, opened by an actuator, avoids this. For this fan, which runs at full speed, the gravity damper is fine.

Result: one accessory that closes the opening every night with no wiring or controls.

docs.title: Stack Cap
docs.text: A stack cap is a short, open-topped discharge stack fitted to the outlet of a roof-mounted or vertically mounted fan, so the air leaves straight up in a vertical jet. FanPedia (pages 7 and 8) contrasts it with a hood: a fan with a stack cap moves air in a straight line through the fan, while a hooded fan deflects the discharge down and outward. Roof-mounted axial fans and panel fans are offered with either. For vertical inline, mixed flow, and axial fans, FanPedia's discharge codes include "VUS", vertical up with stack cap (page 51). Choose a stack cap when the exhaust should be thrown up and away from the roof, as in many fume and heat exhaust applications, and a hood when the opening needs protection from rain more than a high discharge.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text: You now have names for every major part of a fan and the features around it. The last activity asks you to apply them to short job-site requests.

docs.title: Diagram: Which Housing Feature Does the Job?
docs.text:
Run Which Housing Feature Does the Job? Fullscreen

Which Housing Feature Does the Job?

Type: microsim sim-id: ch03-housing-feature-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify 12 job-site requests by the housing feature or opening accessory that meets each one, choosing from four options per request.

Prerequisites: welded housing, bolted housing, split housing, access door, inspection port, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange, companion flange, bird screen, safety screen, backdraft damper, gravity damper, stack cap, hood (all defined in this chapter above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers all 12 requests by choosing one of four options and committing the answer. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct option column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Bird screens and safety screens are interchangeable. (2) An inspection port allows cleaning and impeller removal (it allows viewing only). (3) A collar and a flange are the same connection. (4) A backdraft damper controls airflow while the fan runs (it only stops reverse flow when the fan is off). (5) A split housing is only for maintenance (it is also used for shipping and tight openings).

Instructional Rationale: Classifying realistic requests requires the learner to connect each feature's function to a need, which is the Understand-level step between naming a part and selecting one. The distractors are features that share a location or a word with the right answer, so a correct choice shows the learner knows what each feature does.

Content:

Requests, in this order, each with four options in the order shown:

# Request shown to the learner Options Correct option Why (shown as feedback) 1 "We need to look at the impeller for buildup between cleanings without opening a door." Access door; Inspection port; Pie split housing; Safety screen Inspection port A port is a small, closable opening for viewing; an access door is for reaching in. 2 "The impeller must be pulled out without disconnecting the inlet or outlet duct." Horizontal split housing; Pie split housing; Raised access door; Inlet collar Pie split housing A pie split cuts a wedge of 90 degrees or more so the impeller comes out without disturbing inlet or outlet. 3 "The fan has to fit through a doorway smaller than the assembled housing." 3-way split housing; Quick-open access door; Welded housing; Stack cap 3-way split housing A 3-way split divides the housing into three sections for shipping or for passing through a specific opening. 4 "The fan is insulated, and we need to open the door without cutting the insulation." Bolted access door; Raised access door; Inspection port; Inlet flange Raised access door A raised access door is built up above the insulation, usually by 2 inches. 5 "Our flexible sleeve slips over the inlet and is held with clamps." Inlet flange; Inlet collar; Companion flange; Outlet flange Inlet collar A collar is a plain sleeve for slip-fit connections; a flange is bolted. 6 "The contractor needs a part to attach to the duct in the field so the bolt holes match the fan inlet." Companion flange; Inlet collar; Evasé; Inspection port Companion flange Companion flanges are attached to the duct in the field and are shipped loose to match the fan flange. 7 "The downstream duct must bolt rigidly to the fan discharge." Outlet flange; Inlet collar; Stack cap; Bird screen Outlet flange The outlet flange carries the bolt pattern for the discharge duct. 8 "Birds keep nesting in the roof exhauster's discharge." Safety screen; Bird screen; Backdraft damper; Inspection port Bird screen A bird screen keeps birds and debris out of outdoor-facing openings. 9 "A panel fan inlet is within reach of people on a ladder." Bird screen; Safety screen; Stack cap; Gravity damper Safety screen A safety screen keeps hands and objects away from the impeller. 10 "Cold air blows in through the wall fan every night when it is off." Backdraft damper; Safety screen; Stack cap; Quick-open access door Backdraft damper A gravity backdraft damper opens when the fan runs and closes by gravity when it stops. 11 "The fume exhaust must discharge straight up, away from the roof." Hood; Stack cap; Backdraft damper; Bird screen Stack cap A stack cap moves air straight through and up; a hood deflects it down and outward. 12 "The housing seams must not leak, so we want no bolted seams in the scroll." Bolted housing; Welded housing; 3-way split housing; Inspection port Welded housing Continuous welds join the housing permanently with no bolted seams to leak.

Provenance: Feature definitions from this chapter's sections, which cite FanPedia pages 7, 8, 18, 19, 59, 117, 120, 125, 156, 157, 180, 181 and 194. Requests are illustrative job-site wording written for this chapter.

Rules: Twelve requests, fixed order, four options each in the order listed. One option is correct per request. Answers are committed one request at a time and cannot be changed after the second attempt.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads request 1 and its four options.
  2. The learner chooses one option and commits it. Feedback appears immediately.
  3. The learner moves to the next request. After request 12, a summary lists every request with the learner's choice, the correct option and the Why text.
  4. The learner can retry only the missed requests in a second round; the first-attempt score is kept.

Feedback: Two attempts per request. Correct: "Correct:" followed by the Why text. Incorrect on the first attempt: the Why text for the option the learner chose is not shown; instead, a hint names the job of the correct feature without naming it (for request 1: "Think of the smallest opening that still lets you see inside."). Hints for requests 2 to 12, in order: "Which split keeps the inlet and outlet in place?"; "Which split divides the housing for shipping?"; "Which door sits above the insulation?"; "Which connection has no bolt holes?"; "Which part goes on the duct, not the fan?"; "Which part has the bolt pattern at the discharge?"; "Which mesh is meant for animals?"; "Which mesh is meant for people?"; "Which part acts only when the fan stops?"; "Which part throws air straight up?"; "Which joining method leaves no seams to gasket?". Incorrect on the second attempt: the correct option is revealed with its Why text and the request counts as missed. Score "Correct on first attempt: n of 12" is shown at the end.

Starting State: Request 1 is shown with its four options and no selection. The heading reads "A customer calls with a request. Which feature does the job?"

Chapter Anchors: 12 requests; pie splits are 90 degrees or more; raised access doors are usually raised 2 inches above insulation; companion flanges are shipped loose; gravity dampers close by gravity when power is turned off.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The fan housing (side, scroll, or casing) encloses the impeller, guides the air from inlet to outlet, and supports the other components. Plenum, panel, and ring fans have no housing; a plug fan's housing is optional.
  • A welded housing is one permanent, stiff piece with no bolted seams to leak; a bolted housing comes apart for shipping and service but needs close bolt spacing and gaskets for leak-tight service. Split housings (horizontal, pie, 3-way) are planned bolted joints for shipping, tight openings, or impeller removal.
  • The impeller is the only part that adds energy to the air. Its blade shape names its type, and it is either overhung (Arrangements 1, 4, 8, 9, 10) or center-hung (Arrangements 3 and 7). Tip speed is \( \pi D N / 12 \) in ft/min.
  • The fan inlet brings air in through an inlet funnel, with an inlet collar (slip fit) or an inlet flange (bolted). The fan outlet connects through an outlet flange, a transition, or an evasé that lowers outlet velocity.
  • The fan shaft carries the impeller and transmits torque; it has keyways, keystock, a tach hole, and turndowns. Two bearings, one fixed and one floating, support and locate it. L-10 life in years is the hours rating divided by hours run per year; L-50 is five times L-10.
  • The fan motor is an induction or EC motor. Size it so the fan's BHP is at or below nameplate horsepower; service factor is 1.0 on a VFD.
  • The drive train is direct (impeller on the motor shaft, or a coupling) or belt drive, where fan speed equals motor speed times motor sheave over fan sheave.
  • Access doors (bolted, raised, quick-open) let people reach inside; inspection ports let them look inside. Bird screens keep animals out, safety screens keep people out, backdraft dampers stop reverse flow when the fan is off, and stack caps throw the discharge straight up.

You Can Name Every Part of a Fan

You can now trace the air from inlet flange to outlet flange, find the shaft and bearings from the arrangement number, and convert a bearing's L-10 hours into years for a real schedule. That vocabulary is the foundation for the centrifugal, axial, and mixed flow fan families in Chapter 4.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Basic Fan Anatomy
docs.text: Test your understanding of the housing, impeller, shaft, bearings, motor, drive train and housing features that every fan shares with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which part of a fan is the only one that adds energy to the airstream?
docs.text:
1. The housing scroll
  2. The inlet funnel
  3. The evasé
  4. The impeller
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The impeller is the rotating part that does the work on the air, and it is the only part of the fan that adds energy to the airstream. Every other part guides the air, supports the impeller or turns it. The scroll and the evasé convert some of the air's velocity into static pressure, and the inlet funnel smooths the air into the impeller, but none of them adds energy.

Concept Tested: Impeller

See: The Impeller

docs.title: 2. Besides "housing," which names are used in the field for the stationary shell that encloses the impeller?
docs.text:
1. Rotor, hub or shroud
  2. Side, scroll or casing
  3. Pedestal, framing or base
  4. Funnel, cone or bell
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. FanPedia describes the fan housing as the main structure of the fan, which directs the air through the system and supports the inlet, outlet, framing and structural supports; in the field it is also called the side, scroll or casing. Rotor, hub and shroud are rotating parts or impeller parts. Pedestal and framing are supports. Funnel, cone and bell are other names for the inlet funnel.

Concept Tested: Fan Housing

See: The Fan Housing

docs.title: 3. What distinguishes an inlet collar from an inlet flange?
docs.text:
1. A collar is bolted to the duct, while a flange is clamped to a flexible sleeve
  2. A collar is used only on axial fans, while a flange is used only on centrifugal fans
  3. A collar is a plain sleeve for a clamped slip-fit connection, while a flange is a drilled ring for a bolted connection
  4. A collar guides air smoothly into the impeller, while a flange holds the impeller on the shaft
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An inlet collar is a short, plain cylindrical sleeve with no bolt holes: a duct or flexible connector slips over it and is clamped. An inlet flange is a flat ring drilled with a bolt-hole pattern, giving a rigid, sealable joint that mates with a companion flange. When the connection must be bolted, rigid or sealed, specify a flange. Option D describes the inlet funnel and the hub, and option A reverses the two parts.

Concept Tested: Inlet Collar

See: Inlet Collar

docs.title: 4. What does a bearing's L-10 life rating mean?
docs.text:
1. The operating hours at which 10 percent of a population of identical bearings, at a given speed and load, are expected to have failed
  2. The operating hours that every bearing in the population is guaranteed to reach
  3. The operating hours at which half of a population of identical bearings are expected to have failed
  4. The operating hours a single bearing runs before it loses 10 percent of its load capacity
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Bearing life is a statistical estimate. FanPedia defines L-10 life as the hours at which 10 percent of a population of bearings, at a given speed and load, are expected to have failed. It is not a guarantee for every bearing. The hours at which 50 percent have failed is L-50 life, the average life, calculated as five times the L-10 life. Most Twin City Fan models offer an L-10 life of 40,000 hours.

Concept Tested: Bearing

See: Bearing Life

docs.title: 5. A fan's bearings are rated L-10 = 60,000 hours. The fan runs 12 hours a day, 6 days a week. What is the expected L-10 life in years?
docs.text:
1. 6.9 years
  2. 13.7 years
  3. 16.0 years
  4. 80.1 years
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Hours per year are 12 × 6 × 52 = 3,744. The L-10 life in years is 60,000 ÷ 3,744 = 16.0 years. Option A assumes the fan runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (8,736 hours per year). Option B counts 12 hours on every day of the year instead of 6 days a week, and option D is the L-50 life, five times the L-10 figure.

Concept Tested: Bearing

See: Bearing Life

docs.title: 6. A motor turning 1,760 RPM has a 6-inch motor sheave, and the fan sheave is 8 inches (pitch diameters). What is the ideal fan speed?
docs.text:
1. 2,347 RPM
  2. 1,760 RPM
  3. 1,100 RPM
  4. 1,320 RPM
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In a belt drive, fan speed equals motor speed times motor sheave pitch diameter divided by fan sheave pitch diameter: 1,760 × 6 ÷ 8 = 1,320 RPM. Option A inverts the ratio, option B is the direct-drive case where the impeller turns at motor speed, and option C uses the chapter's 5-inch motor sheave instead of 6 inches. Real drives lose a little speed to belt slip, so the formula gives the ideal value.

Concept Tested: Drive Train

See: The Drive Train

docs.title: 7. On an Arrangement 4 direct-drive fan, where are the bearings that carry the rotating impeller?
docs.text:
1. On a bearing pedestal outside the housing, both on one side of the impeller
  2. Inside the motor frame, because the impeller is mounted on the motor shaft
  3. One on each side of the impeller, mounted on the housing framing
  4. In the inlet funnel, where they are cooled by the incoming air
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In Arrangement 4, the impeller mounts on the end of the motor shaft, so there is no separate fan shaft and no fan bearings to service; the only bearings are the motor bearings inside the motor frame. Option A describes overhung arrangements such as 1 and 9, with two fan bearings on a pedestal. Option C describes center-hung Arrangements 3 and 7. FanPedia notes that Arrangement 4 offers low maintenance for this reason.

Concept Tested: Fan Shaft

See: The Fan Shaft

docs.title: 8. What does an evasé do at the fan outlet?
docs.text:
1. It enlarges the outlet to reduce the outlet velocity and increase static pressure capability
  2. It changes a round outlet to a square one without changing the outlet area
  3. It closes the outlet to stop air flowing backward when the fan is off
  4. It sets the outlet flange back from the end of the outlet on double-width fans
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An evasé is a transition that enlarges the outlet; its outlet is larger than its inlet. FanPedia gives its purpose as reducing the fan's outlet velocity and increasing its static pressure capability. In the chapter's example, enlarging a 3.0 ft² outlet to 5.0 ft² cuts the leaving velocity from 3,000 to 1,800 ft/min. Option B describes a transition, option C a backdraft damper, and option D a setback outlet flange.

Concept Tested: Fan Outlet

See: The Fan Outlet

docs.title: 9. What does the service factor on a motor nameplate mean, and how should it be used when sizing a motor for a fan?
docs.text:
1. It is spare horsepower meant to cover a fan brake horsepower above the nameplate rating
  2. It is the ratio of the fan's brake horsepower to its air horsepower at the design point
  3. It is always 1.15 for fan motors, whether or not they run on a variable frequency drive
  4. It is the multiplier above rated horsepower at which the motor may be used, but the fan's BHP should still be at or below nameplate horsepower
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The service factor is the multiplier above the rated horsepower at which a motor may be used; FanPedia's example is a 100 HP motor with a 1.15 service factor operated at 115 HP. It is not spare horsepower: size the motor so the fan's BHP at the design point is at or below nameplate horsepower. Common values include 1.0 for a motor on a variable frequency drive and 1.25, so 1.15 is not universal.

Concept Tested: Fan Motor

See: Service Factor

docs.title: 10. A customer orders three centrifugal fans: a clean-air supply fan inspected about once a year, a bakery exhaust fan cleaned every week, and an insulated fan on a hot dryer exhaust. Which access door choices fit, in that order?
docs.text:
1. Quick-open door, bolted door, raised door
  2. Raised door, quick-open door, bolted door
  3. Bolted door, quick-open door, raised door
  4. Bolted door, raised door, quick-open door
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The choice follows how often someone must reach inside and what surrounds the door. Rare inspection of clean air suits a bolted door, which seals well. Weekly cleaning favors a quick-open door held with latches, so nobody removes a ring of bolts each visit. On an insulated fan a flush door would be buried, so a raised door, usually 2 inches above the insulation, can be opened without cutting the insulation.

Concept Tested: Access Door

See: Access Door

docs.title: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
Summary
docs.text: This chapter sorts fans into their three families: centrifugal fans, which turn air through a right angle; axial fans, which move air parallel to the shaft; and mixed flow fans, which combine the two. It introduces scroll and tubular housings, guide vanes, housed and unhoused centrifugal fans, inline centrifugal fans, panel and ring fans, power roof ventilators, and laboratory fume exhaust fans, along with the commercial and industrial duty classes in Twin City Fan's catalogs. After completing it, readers can recognize a fan's family from its shape and airflow path.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy

docs.title: Three Families, One Question
docs.text:
Every fan in a Twin City Fan catalog, from a quiet restroom exhauster to a vaneaxial fan in a tunnel, answers one question the same way: which way does the air travel as it passes through the impeller? The answer sorts every fan into one of three groups, and that sorting comes before arrangement, impeller type, construction class or accessories. A sales engineer who gets the family wrong will get every later line of the order wrong too, because each family has its own housings, mounting options and catalog pages.

Sorting the Fan Zoo

Walk onto any rooftop or into any mechanical room and you will find a crowd of fans that look nothing alike. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at one, or at its drawing, and say which family it belongs to and which part of the catalog to open. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Fan Families
docs.text:
A fan family is a group of fans that share the same airflow path through the impeller. Recall from Chapter 3 that the impeller is the rotating part that does the work, and that the fan shaft is the axis it turns on. Every family is defined by the direction air is moving, relative to that shaft, when it leaves the impeller. FanPedia's technical descriptions put it this way: what sets axial and centrifugal impellers apart is how the air passes through the impeller.

There are three families:

  1. Centrifugal fans. Air enters the impeller along the shaft (axially), is accelerated by the blades, and leaves the impeller radially, at a right angle to the shaft.
  2. Axial fans. Air enters along the shaft and leaves along the shaft, with a swirling motion added by the rotating blades. The flow never turns the corner.
  3. Mixed flow fans. Air enters along the shaft and leaves the impeller on a diagonal, partly axial and partly radial. FanPedia describes the mixed flow impeller as a hybrid axial-centrifugal design.

The family is set by the impeller, not by the box around it. That distinction matters because Twin City Fan builds several families into the same outer shape. A round tube bolted into a duct run can hold an axial impeller, a centrifugal impeller or a mixed flow impeller. A rooftop unit with a hood can be axial or centrifugal. If you classify by silhouette alone, you will misfile fans on every job.

The Impeller Decides

Notice that the housing only guides air the impeller has already pointed somewhere. Think of the impeller as the decision and the housing as the paperwork that follows: to find the family, find out which way the impeller throws the air.

The families also lean toward different jobs. FanPedia describes axial impellers as built for moving large volumes of air against relatively low pressures as economically as possible, while centrifugal impellers come in several blade types, each with its own application range. Twin City Fan's current catalog describes its mixed flow and inline centrifugal lines as giving the performance of a centrifugal fan with the space-saving advantages of an axial-type fan. You will meet the pressure and efficiency differences properly in Chapter 10; for now, the airflow path is the sorting key.

docs.title: Worked Example: Classifying Three Fans on One Drawing Set
docs.text:
A mechanical drawing set for a small manufacturing plant shows three fans. You need to tell your inside sales colleague which catalog section to open for each.

  • Fan EF-1 is drawn as a round tube in a straight duct run. The schedule note reads "vaneaxial." Vaneaxial is a type of axial fan, so air goes straight through along the shaft. Family: axial.
  • Fan SF-2 is drawn with a snail-shaped housing. Duct enters the side of the housing and leaves out the top at a right angle. A right-angle turn through a snail-shaped housing is the signature of a housed centrifugal fan. Family: centrifugal.
  • Fan EF-3 is drawn as a round tube in a straight duct run, just like EF-1, but the schedule note reads "tubular inline centrifugal." The outside shape matches EF-1, yet the impeller throws air outward at a right angle; vanes inside the tube then turn the air back to the duct direction. Family: centrifugal.

The trap is EF-3. It looks like EF-1 from outside, but the impeller decides the family. When a drawing is ambiguous, the schedule's fan type, the model designation, or a call to the engineer settles it.

The table below gathers the three families side by side, using FanPedia's own descriptions of the airflow path.

Family Air enters the impeller Air leaves the impeller FanPedia's description Centrifugal Along the shaft At a right angle to the shaft (radially) Air "enters the impeller axially and is accelerated by the blades and discharged radially" Axial Along the shaft Along the shaft, with swirl Air is propelled "in an axial direction with a swirling tangential motion" Mixed flow Along the shaft On a diagonal, between the two A "hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller design"

docs.title: Centrifugal Fans
docs.text:
A centrifugal fan draws air into the center of the impeller along the shaft and throws it outward, at a right angle to the shaft, off the tips of the blades. FanPedia's description of housed centrifugal fans is short and exact: air is drawn through one side (single inlet) or both sides (double inlet) and is discharged at a right angle to the fan shaft. The impeller does two things to the air at once. Its spinning blades accelerate the air in the direction of rotation, and the outward throw raises its pressure as it moves from the small radius at the inlet to the larger radius at the blade tips.

Two widths cover most housed centrifugal fans:

  • Single width, single inlet (SWSI). Air enters one side of the housing through one inlet. The drive (bearings, shaft, belt or motor) sits on the other side, out of the inlet's way.
  • Double width, double inlet (DWDI). The impeller is roughly twice as wide and takes air in from both sides. A DWDI fan moves more air from the same impeller diameter, which is why Twin City Fan's catalog describes most centrifugal models as available single-wide or double-wide "for even higher volumes of air." Because both sides are inlets, the shaft passes through an inlet.

The blades can be shaped several ways, and FanPedia lists the options a housed centrifugal fan can carry: backward inclined, airfoil, backward curved, radial tip, forward curved and radial bladed. Those impeller types are the subject of Chapter 8. In this chapter, the point is that every one of them throws the air outward, so every one of them is a centrifugal fan.

Not every centrifugal fan has a housing. A housed centrifugal fan wraps the impeller in a scroll housing that collects the air and delivers it to one outlet. An unhoused centrifugal fan runs the impeller without that scroll, inside a plenum. Both are covered below, and Chapter 5 returns to housed centrifugal and plenum fans as product lines.

The table below gathers the centrifugal configurations this chapter discusses, so you can compare where air enters and leaves each one.

Configuration Housing Where air enters Where air leaves the fan Example current Twin City Fan lines Housed centrifugal, SWSI Scroll One side, along the shaft One outlet, at a right angle to the shaft BC-SW, BAF-SW, NFC-SW Housed centrifugal, DWDI Scroll Both sides, along the shaft One outlet, at a right angle to the shaft BC-DW, BAF-DW, NFC-DW Plenum fan (unhoused) None; sits in a plenum Inlet funnel, along the shaft All around the impeller, into the plenum Plenum fan lines Plug fan (unhoused) None; mounted through a plenum wall Inlet funnel, along the shaft All around the impeller, into the plenum Plug fan lines Tubular inline centrifugal Tubular One end of the tube Other end of the tube, along the shaft TSL Square inline centrifugal Square, removable side panels One end Straight through or at a 90-degree turn, depending on the ductwork BSI, DSI Centrifugal roof exhauster Roof unit with shroud or hood Roof opening below Upblast, downblast, louvered or hooded VC, DCRD, BCRD, BCRU

docs.title: Worked Example: Letting the Fan Make the Turn
docs.text:
A plant engineer has a horizontal exhaust duct that runs along the ceiling of a paint-mixing room and must turn straight up through the roof. The engineer asks whether the fan or a duct elbow should make the 90-degree turn.

  1. Read the geometry. Air arrives horizontally and must leave vertically: a right-angle turn.
  2. Match it to a family. A housed centrifugal fan takes air in along its shaft and discharges it at a right angle to the shaft. Mount the fan with its shaft horizontal, in line with the incoming duct, and choose a discharge that points straight up.
  3. Check the alternative. An axial fan would discharge in the same direction the air entered, so the design would need an elbow before or after it. Every elbow costs pressure and space.
  4. Choose the width. If the airflow is large and both sides of the fan are open to the room or a plenum, a DWDI fan can take air in from both sides. Here the air arrives through a single duct, so an SWSI fan with its inlet on the duct end is the natural fit.
  5. Pass it on. The order still needs a discharge position, a rotation and an arrangement. Those are designated from the drive side and are covered in Chapter 11 and Chapter 12.

The housed centrifugal fan does the turn and the pressure rise in one component. That combination is the most common reason it ends up on the drawing.

docs.title: Scroll Housings
docs.text:
The scroll housing is the snail-shaped casing around the impeller of a housed centrifugal fan. FanPedia notes that the housing is also called the side, scroll or casing, and that it is the main structure supporting the inlet, outlet, framing and structural supports. Its shape has a job: the gap between the impeller tips and the housing wall starts narrow and grows steadily as the scroll wraps around the impeller, ending at the outlet.

Why grow? Each blade throws a little more air into the gap as it passes. Further around the scroll, more air has joined the flow, so the passage must be larger to carry it. The expanding passage also slows the air down. Recall from Chapter 2 that total pressure is the sum of static pressure and velocity pressure. Air leaving the blade tips is moving fast and carries much of its energy as velocity pressure. As the scroll widens, the air slows and part of that velocity pressure is recovered as static pressure, the pressure that pushes air through ductwork, filters and coils.

The parts of a scroll housing have names you will see on drawings and in FanPedia's exploded views (pp. 9-10) and its SWSI housing construction drawing (p. 60):

  • The housing scroll is the curved wrapper sheet that forms the spiral.
  • The housing sides are the flat side sheets that close the spiral; the inlet is cut into a side.
  • The cutoff is the point near the outlet where the scroll passes closest to the impeller tips. It splits the air leaving through the outlet from the air that would otherwise keep circling.
  • The wiper bar, which FanPedia groups with the cutoff, helps direct air through the housing in the inlet funnel area to prevent turbulence and increase efficiency.
  • The inlet funnel (also called the inlet cone) guides air smoothly into the impeller eye.
  • The inlet collar and inlet flange are the duct connections on the inlet side: a collar is a short round sleeve, and a flange is a bolting rim.
  • The outlet (discharge) flange is the bolting rim around the outlet.
  • The framing is the structural steel that stiffens the housing and supports it.
  • The pedestal is the structure that carries the bearings and drive on some arrangements.

Fast Air In, Useful Pressure Out

The scroll is not just a cover; it is a pressure converter. Think of it like a funnel run backwards: the passage widens, the air slows, and the speed it gave up shows up as static pressure the duct system can use.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Pressure Can the Scroll Recover?
docs.text:
The numbers in this example are illustrative, chosen to show the idea; they are not ratings for any Twin City Fan model. Use the velocity pressure equation from Chapter 2 for standard air, where \( V \) is velocity in feet per minute and \( VP \) is velocity pressure in inches of water gauge:

\[ VP = \left( \frac{V}{4005} \right)^2 \]

Suppose air leaves the impeller tips at about 4,000 fpm, and the scroll and outlet slow it to about 2,000 fpm by the time it reaches the outlet flange.

\[ VP_{\text{tip}} = \left( \frac{4000}{4005} \right)^2 \approx 1.00 \text{ in. wg} \qquad VP_{\text{outlet}} = \left( \frac{2000}{4005} \right)^2 \approx 0.25 \text{ in. wg} \]

Halving the velocity cuts velocity pressure to one quarter, because velocity pressure goes with the square of velocity. Up to about \( 1.00 - 0.25 = 0.75 \) in. wg of velocity pressure is available to become static pressure. A real scroll recovers only part of it, because friction and turbulence take a share, which is one reason details such as the cutoff and the wiper bar matter.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading Rotation From the Scroll
docs.text:
A field technician sends you a photo of an unlabeled housed centrifugal fan, taken from the drive side, and asks which way the impeller turns. The scroll answers the question. The impeller carries air around the scroll in its direction of rotation, and the passage grows in that same direction. Start at the cutoff, follow the scroll the way the gap gets wider, and you arrive at the outlet. The direction you just traced is the direction of rotation. If that path runs clockwise in the photo, the impeller turns clockwise as viewed from the drive side. Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 turn this observation into the formal rotation and discharge designation.

Trace It From the Cutoff

Here's a shortcut for any scroll you can see: put a finger on the cutoff and slide it along the housing toward the wide end. The direction your finger moves is the impeller's rotation. Check it from the drive side.

Before trying the interactive diagram, make sure each of the ten housing terms in the list above is familiar. The diagram shows a single width, single inlet housing based on FanPedia's construction drawing and asks you to locate each part.

  2. The learner switches to quiz mode. All labels disappear.
  3. For each prompt, the learner clicks a region. The sim marks it right or wrong.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists ten housing terms and states that the diagram is based on FanPedia's SWSI construction drawing. The chapter states that the scroll passage grows from the cutoff to the outlet.

docs.title: Unhoused Centrifugal Fans
docs.text:
An unhoused centrifugal fan is a centrifugal impeller and inlet funnel run without a scroll housing. FanPedia states plainly that not every fan needs a housing, and lists plenum fans and plug fans among the fans that run without one. With no scroll to collect it, air leaves the impeller all the way around its circumference and fills the space the fan sits in. That space is a plenum, which FanPedia defines as an air-filled space within a structure that the fan pressurizes. The plenum, not a scroll, then delivers air to wherever it goes next.

FanPedia describes two types:

  • A plenum type unhoused fan is designed for air handling applications where the fan operates within an air plenum, such as inside an air handling unit cabinet.
  • A plug type unhoused fan is designed for circulating or recirculating air within a plenum. The fan is "plugged" into the plenum wall: the mounting panel attaches to the outside of the wall and the impeller sits inside. FanPedia lists high-temperature ovens and OEM paint booths among the common industrial uses.

docs.title: Worked Example: An Oven Builder's Fan
docs.text:
An OEM oven builder needs a fan to recirculate hot air inside an oven chamber and wants the motor and bearings outside the hot zone where they can be reached for service.

  1. Family. The air only needs to be stirred and pressurized inside the chamber; no ductwork leaves the fan. An unhoused centrifugal fan pressurizes the space it sits in, which is exactly the job.
  2. Type. The impeller must be inside the chamber while the drive stays outside. That is the plug type: FanPedia's exploded views of plug fans (pp. 13-14) show a mounting panel and an insulation plug between the impeller on one side and the shaft, bearings, pedestal and motor on the other.
  3. What to confirm. Oven temperature affects construction, bearings and materials. High-temperature construction is covered in Chapter 21; for now, record the operating temperature on the inquiry so the selection can account for it.

A plenum type fan would suit the same builder if the job were an air handler cabinet instead of an oven wall. The difference is where the drive lives relative to the wall.

docs.title: Axial Fans
docs.text:
An axial fan moves air parallel to the shaft. Its impeller looks like a propeller: blades are attached to a central hub, and as they turn they push air along the axis of rotation. FanPedia describes the result as air propelled in an axial direction with a swirling tangential motion created by the rotating blades. That swirl is important. It is energy the impeller put into the air that is moving around the duct rather than down it, so it does no useful work unless something recovers it.

Axial impellers come with many blade profiles and blade counts. FanPedia states that the emphasis in axial design is on moving large volumes of air against relatively low pressures as economically as possible. Some axial impellers have fixed blade pitch, and some have adjustable pitch, meaning the blade angle can be reset to change performance. The impeller types, including the hub position, appear in Chapter 8.

Axial fans take several forms in Twin City Fan's lines:

  • An inline axial fan sits in a tubular housing in a duct run. FanPedia notes that inline axial fans can be mounted horizontally or vertically, ducted or unducted.
  • A tubeaxial fan is an inline axial fan with a plain tubular housing.
  • A vaneaxial fan is an inline axial fan whose housing includes a vane section, guide vanes that straighten the airflow as it moves through the fan.
  • Panel fans and ring fans center an axial impeller in a flat panel or a ring, usually mounted in a wall.
  • Roof mounted axial fans start from a tubeaxial fan or a panel fan and add roof accessories such as a hood or stack cap.

Twin City Fan's current catalog describes the two inline types by the job they do. Tubeaxial fans cover a wide range of requirements "from general ventilation to process air supply." Vaneaxial fans are for applications where "large volumes of air are required at moderate to high pressures." The table summarizes the axial forms just described.

Axial form Housing Vanes Typical use described in FanPedia or the current catalog Example current lines Tubeaxial Plain tube None General ventilation to process air supply TD, TB, TCTA, TCTS Vaneaxial Tube with vane section Guide vanes Large volumes at moderate to high pressures TCVA, TCVX, TCVS Panel fan Flat panel None Wall mounted, straight-through flow TCWPF, WPD, WPB Ring fan Ring None Wall mounted, straight-through flow (FanPedia type) Roof mounted axial Tubeaxial or panel fan plus hood or stack cap None Rooftop exhaust or supply TUD, TUB, THD, THB

docs.title: Worked Example: Tubeaxial or Vaneaxial?
docs.text:
A specifying engineer is choosing an axial fan for a straight duct run and asks a representative to explain the difference between Twin City Fan's tubeaxial and vaneaxial lines.

  1. Same family, same path. Both are axial fans in tubular housings; air enters and leaves along the shaft. Both catalogs list direct-drive and belt-driven models and fixed or adjustable pitch impellers.
  2. The difference is the vane section. FanPedia's exploded views of direct drive tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans (pp. 15-16) show the same housing, impeller, shaft and motor; the vaneaxial adds guide vanes.
  3. What the vanes buy. The tubeaxial discharges air that is still swirling. The vaneaxial's guide vanes turn that swirl into straight flow, recovering part of the energy as static pressure. That is why the catalog positions the vaneaxial for moderate to high pressures and the tubeaxial for general ventilation and process air supply.
  4. The recommendation. If the duct system's pressure requirement is modest and cost matters most, start with the tubeaxial section. If the system needs more pressure or the downstream equipment is sensitive to swirling air, start with the vaneaxial section. Either way, the final selection is made from the published performance, as shown in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Tubular Housings
docs.text: A tubular housing is a round, straight-through cylinder that holds the impeller and lets air enter one end and leave the other, in line with the duct. FanPedia's housing drawings place the tubular fan next to the centrifugal scroll, and its fan type pages show tubular housings on three different families: inline axial fans (tubeaxial and vaneaxial), tubular inline centrifugal fans, and mixed flow fans. A tubular housing usually carries flanges at each end, an impeller access door, and a motor support or, for belt drive, a motor base and a belt tube (also called a belt fairing) that shelters the belt as it passes through the airstream to the shaft.
