  4. The learner presses Next. After 13 jobs, the sim shows both scores and lists the missed jobs with their "Why" text.

Feedback: 13 jobs, shuffled order, one scored attempt per job for the line and one for the feature. Correct line: "Correct: . ". Incorrect line: "The better fit is . ". Correct feature: "Right: decides this job." Incorrect feature: "The deciding feature is ." Answers are revealed after each check. Scores "Lines correct: n of 13" and "Features correct: n of 13" are shown; the summary states that 10 of 13 lines is the mastery level.

Starting State: The first shuffled job is shown with no line selected. The prompt reads "Which product line would you recommend for this job?"

Chapter Anchors: 13 product lines, as named in this chapter's sections. The chapter states that backward inclined fans serve the clean side of a filter and radial bladed fans serve cyclone applications, that radial tip fans are more efficient than radial blade fans at high airflow, and that air kit enclosures and insulation are provided by others.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A plug fan mounts through a plenum wall, keeping motor and drive out of the process air; Arrangement 9 is most common, and P versions mount to grade.
  • A vaneaxial fan uses guide vanes to straighten swirl for moderate to high pressure in a compact tube; a roof mounted panel fan is a panel fan with a stack cap or hood.
  • Radial bladed fans survive abrasive, sticky or bulky material; radial tip fans handle dirty air more efficiently at high airflow; pressure blowers give high pressure at relatively low volume.
  • Utility sets are packaged Arrangement 10 ventilating sets; duct fans are double-inlet scroll fans in an enclosure; filtered supply fans filter outside make-up air; air kits are forward curved DWDI impellers for enclosures built by others.
  • Paint booth exhaust fans need precise velocity and easy cleaning; dust collection fans depend on fan position: backward inclined on the clean side, radial bladed for cyclones.
  • Inline lab exhaust fans achieve plume dilution with bypass flow and entrained flow. Fan flow is contaminated plus bypass; lab exhaust total flow adds entrained flow.

The Product-Line Map Is Complete

You can now take an industrial job description, from a hot oven wall to a dusty cyclone to a lab roof, and name the product line built for it along with the feature that decides it. Every later chapter on impellers, arrangements and construction builds on that map.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines
docs.text: Test your understanding of plug, vaneaxial, radial, pressure blower and packaged fan lines, application fans, and lab exhaust flow with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What feature of a plug fan keeps the motor and drive components out of the process air?
docs.text:
1. A section of stationary guide vanes behind the impeller
  2. A gusseted mounting panel fastened to the outside of the plenum wall
  3. A belt tube that carries the belts across the airstream
  4. A scroll housing that surrounds the impeller inside the plenum
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A plug fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan "plugged" into a plenum wall. The mounting panel fastens to the outside of the wall while the impeller sits inside, so the panel separates the motor and drive from the process air and lets the fan be installed and removed as a unit. Guide vanes belong to vaneaxial fans, a belt tube to belt driven tubular fans, and a plug fan has no scroll housing of its own; the plenum does that job.

Concept Tested: Plug Fan

See: Plug Fans: The Impeller Goes In, the Drive Stays Out

docs.title: 2. Why can a vaneaxial fan reach pressures that a plain tubeaxial fan cannot deliver efficiently?
docs.text:
1. Its impeller turns faster because it is always direct driven
  2. It draws air through two inlets, one on each side of the impeller
  3. Its housing is narrower than a tubeaxial housing of the same size
  4. Its stationary guide vanes turn part of the swirl's rotational energy into static pressure
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Air leaving any axial impeller swirls around the axis, and that swirl carries energy that does not appear as useful duct pressure. A vaneaxial fan adds a section of stationary guide vanes that straighten the flow and recover part of that rotational energy as static pressure. That is why the catalog describes vaneaxial fans as moving large volumes at moderate to high pressures in a compact tube. Vaneaxial fans come in both direct and belt driven versions, and double inlets and narrow housings belong to other fan types.

Concept Tested: Vaneaxial Fan

See: Vaneaxial Fans and Roof Mounted Panel Fans

docs.title: 3. A customer wants a direct drive plug fan, but the airstream is hot, so the impeller should not sit on the motor shaft. The plenum wall can carry the fan and there is room for a long assembly. Which arrangement fits?
docs.text:
1. Arrangement 8
  2. Arrangement 4
  3. Arrangement 9P
  4. Arrangement 4P
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Work the three questions in order. Direct drive leaves Arrangements 4, 4P, 8 and 8P. A hot airstream may limit Arrangement 4 and 4P, where the impeller is mounted on the motor shaft, so the motor-coupled-to-fan-shaft design, Arrangement 8, is used. The wall is adequate, so the wall-mounted version applies rather than 8P. Arrangement 9P is belt driven and grade mounted, which the customer did not ask for.

Concept Tested: Plug Fan

See: Plug Fans: The Impeller Goes In, the Drive Stays Out

docs.title: 4. Which statement best describes the trade-off between a radial tip fan and a radial bladed fan?
docs.text:
1. The radial bladed fan is more efficient at high airflow, while the radial tip fan is more rugged
  2. Both have identical efficiency, so the choice depends only on the housing material
  3. The radial tip fan is much more efficient at high airflow, while the radial bladed fan still wins when the material is bulky, sticky or abrasive
  4. The radial tip fan is meant only for clean air on the clean side of a filter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A radial tip impeller is curved forward at the entering edge and radial at the tip, so it suits dirty, particulate-laden air while letting air onto the blade more smoothly. The current catalog states that at high airflows it is much more efficient than a comparable radial blade fan. The radial bladed fan, the industry's "workhorse," remains the choice when durability must outrank efficiency because the material is bulky, sticky or abrasive. Option A reverses the trade-off.

Concept Tested: Radial Tip Fan

See: Radial Tip Fans

docs.title: 5. A process fan must move 20,000 CFM at 10 in. wg total pressure with a total efficiency of 65%. Using BHP = (Q × TP) / (6356 × η), about how much brake horsepower does it draw?
docs.text:
1. About 31.5 BHP
  2. About 20.5 BHP
  3. About 48.4 BHP
  4. About 74.5 BHP
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Multiply airflow by total pressure: 20,000 × 10 = 200,000. Multiply the constant by the efficiency: 6356 × 0.65 = 4,131. Then 200,000 / 4,131 ≈ 48.4 BHP. Option A leaves out the efficiency (that is the air power), option B multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing, and option D divides by the efficiency twice. Lower efficiency always means more brake horsepower for the same duty.

Concept Tested: Radial Tip Fan

See: Radial Tip Fans

docs.title: 6. Which description fits a pressure blower?
docs.text:
1. A housed centrifugal with a narrower housing and impeller width, built for high pressure at relatively low airflow
  2. A double-inlet scroll fan mounted inside an enclosure for large volumes at low pressure
  3. An axial impeller in a flat panel housing with a stack cap or hood
  4. A forward curved double inlet impeller sold without a housing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. FanPedia notes that pressure blowers have narrower housings and impeller widths than standard centrifugal fans. The current catalog adds that their performance is stable through the operating range and that they can be turned down to zero flow with a discharge damper. Option B describes a duct fan, option C a roof mounted panel fan, and option D an air kit.

Concept Tested: Pressure Blower

See: Pressure Blowers

docs.title: 7. A customer asks for a fan for a dust collector and says only that the air is "dirty." Which fact should you pin down first to decide between a high-efficiency clean-air fan and a rugged dirty-air fan?
docs.text:
1. Whether the collector is indoors or outdoors
  2. Whether the motor will be direct drive or belt driven
  3. The color and finish the customer wants on the housing
  4. Whether the fan sits on the clean side of the filter or handles dust-laden air, as on a cyclone
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The current application page states the split: backward inclined fans are used on the clean side of a filter, where the dust has already been removed, and radial bladed fans are used for cyclone applications, where dust-laden air reaches the fan. The fan's position relative to the filter decides which family survives the airstream. Location, drive type and finish matter to the order, but none of them decides between an efficient clean-air fan and a rugged dirty-air fan.

Concept Tested: Dust Collection Fan

See: Application Fans: Paint Booths and Dust Collectors

docs.title: 8. A lab's fume hoods exhaust 6,000 CFM of contaminated air, the bypass damper admits 4,000 CFM, and the nozzle entrains another 10,000 CFM. What is the fan flow the fan is selected on, and what is the lab exhaust total flow?
docs.text:
1. Fan flow 20,000 CFM; total flow 20,000 CFM
  2. Fan flow 10,000 CFM; total flow 20,000 CFM
  3. Fan flow 6,000 CFM; total flow 16,000 CFM
  4. Fan flow 16,000 CFM; total flow 20,000 CFM
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Contaminated air and bypass air both pass through the impeller, so fan flow is 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000 CFM. Entrained air joins only after the air leaves the fan, so total flow is 10,000 + 10,000 = 20,000 CFM. Option A sizes the fan to the total flow, which the chapter warns against. Option C leaves out the bypass air, and option D counts the entrained air in the fan flow.

Concept Tested: Lab Exhaust Total Flow

See: Laboratory Exhaust: Dilute, Then Throw It High

docs.title: 9. Why should a quotation for an air kit state clearly who supplies the enclosure, insulation and supports?
docs.text:
1. An air kit is supplied without a housing; FanPedia states the enclosure and insulation are provided by others
  2. Air kits are always shipped with a pedestal that replaces the enclosure
  3. Air kits are complete roof units that only need a curb
  4. An air kit's enclosure is welded at the factory, so it cannot be modified on site
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An air kit is forward curved, double-width, double-inlet impellers on a shaft, sold as a component for someone else's enclosure, such as an oven or plenum. FanPedia shows the enclosure and insulation as provided by others in the field and notes that air kits need support supplied by Twin City Fan or others rather than a pedestal. Quoting an air kit as if it were a finished fan is a common trap, so the scope split belongs on the quote.

Concept Tested: Air Kit

See: Filtered Supply Fans and Air Kits

docs.title: 10. At night, fume hood sashes close and contaminated exhaust drops, and the bypass damper opens by the same amount. With entrained flow unchanged, what happens at the stack?
docs.text:
1. Fan flow drops, so the plume rises less and may return to the building
  2. Entrained flow falls to zero because the fan flow has changed
  3. Fan flow and stack velocity stay steady, and the contaminated share of the plume falls
  4. The bypass damper closes to save energy, so total flow doubles
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Fan flow is contaminated plus bypass flow, so when bypass rises by exactly as much as contaminated air falls, fan flow and stack velocity hold steady. That is the purpose of bypass flow in common practice. In the chapter's example, contaminated air falls from 8,000 to 5,000 CFM while bypass rises from 2,000 to 5,000 CFM; fan flow stays at 10,000 CFM and the contaminated share of a 20,000 CFM plume falls from 40% to 25%.

Concept Tested: Bypass Flow

See: Laboratory Exhaust: Dilute, Then Throw It High

docs.title: References: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines
docs.text:
1. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia - Overview of housed centrifugal fans, their blade types and drive arrangements. Background for the plug fan, radial bladed, radial tip, pressure blower, utility set and duct fan lines in this chapter.

  2. Axial fan design - Wikipedia - Explains axial impellers, blade swirl and the role of guide vanes. Useful context for why a vaneaxial fan's vane section recovers pressure that a plain tubeaxial loses.

  3. Fume hood - Wikipedia - Describes laboratory fume hoods, sashes and exhaust systems. Explains where the contaminated air in a lab exhaust fan's flow comes from and why sash position changes exhaust volume.

  4. Fan Handbook: Selection, Application, and Design - Frank P. Bleier - McGraw-Hill - Bleier organizes fans by type and by application, pairing each design with the jobs it suits; that job-first approach mirrors this chapter's product-line survey.

  5. Industrial Ventilation: A Manual of Recommended Practice for Design - ACGIH - American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists - The standard design manual for local exhaust and dust collection systems, known for its worked design plates; context for dust collector and exhaust fan duties.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Source for the plug fan arrangements (pp. 170-172), radial bladed impeller styles (p. 32), air kits, swingout and clamshell construction, and lab exhaust flow diagrams.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Online edition of FanPedia with the fan basics, components, construction and accessories sections this chapter draws on. Handy for quick lookups of product family definitions.

  8. Plug Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for industrial plug fans, describing the gusseted mounting panel, unit removal, high-temperature and spark resistant options, and the BEPL, BFPL, AFPL and BCPL models.

  9. Radial Bladed Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page calling the radial bladed fan the industry "workhorse" and listing the RBO, RBR, RBW, RBP, RBA and JRW models by impeller type.

  10. Laboratory Fume Exhaust Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for lab exhaust fans, including inline TVIFE, QIFE, QFE and TFE models, explaining plume dilution and why lab fumes must not re-enter the building.

  11. BEPL and BFPL High Efficiency Plug Fans, Catalogs 355 and 360 (PDF, April 2024) - Twin City Fan - Arrangements page: "Available in Arrangement 1P, 9 and 9P (Belt Driven) and Arrangement 4, 4P and 8P (Direct Drive) configurations." Basis for the availability note in the plug fan section. The BFPL catalog is at Catalog 360.

  12. BCPL and AFPL Plug Fans, Catalog 350 (PDF, April 2024) - Twin City Fan - Lists Arrangements 1P, 9 and 9P (belt driven) and 4 and 8P (direct drive), and describes Arrangement 1P as belt driven, mounted to grade, with the motor mounted separate from the fan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter takes a closer look at how fan housings are built: scroll side plates and wrappers, the cutoff, straightening vanes, horizontal, three-way, and pie split housings, housing framing, access panels, cast housings, discharge cones, belt guards and belt tubes, and roof exhauster shrouds and curb caps. It shows how to read the exploded views FanPedia uses to name every part. After completing it, readers can read an exploded view and explain what each housing feature is for.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Housing Side Plate 3 Scroll Wrapper 1 Cutoff 2 Straightening Vanes 2 Horizontal Split Housing 1 Three-Way Split Housing 1 Pie Split Housing 1 Motor Cover 1 Roof Exhauster Shroud 1 Curb Cap 1 Exploded View 3 Belt Guard 2 Belt Tube 1 Housing Framing 2 Discharge Cone 1 Housing Access Panel 1 Nozzle and Windband 1 Cast Housing 1 Mounting Panel 2 Insulation Plug 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
  • Chapter 6: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines

Taking the Fan Apart on Paper

A customer calls about a "bent piece of sheet metal near the outlet" and wants a replacement. By the end of this chapter you will open the right FanPedia drawing, put a name and a purpose to that part, and know whether the housing can come apart to reach it. Let's follow the airflow.

In Chapter 3 you learned that a fan housing directs air from the inlet to the outlet and supports the other key components. FanPedia puts it the same way: the housing is the "main structure to support other key components such as inlet, outlet, framing and structural supports," and it is also known as the side, scroll or casing (FanPedia p. 59). Not every fan has one. Plenum fans, plug fans, panel fans and ring fans run without a housing of their own.

This chapter works through the pieces a housing is built from, the ways a housing can be split, and the guards, covers and panels that attach to it. First, though, you need the tool FanPedia uses to name all of those pieces.

docs.title: Reading an Exploded View
docs.text:
An exploded view is a drawing of an assembly with its parts pulled apart along the lines they assemble on, so each part is visible and can carry its own label. Parts that bolt together sit on a shared line of travel, so the drawing shows both what each part is called and roughly where it goes. FanPedia's Fan Basics section opens with eleven pages of them (pp. 9–19), one or two fan families per page, each labeled in the shop's own vocabulary. The Housing Construction pages (pp. 59–66) add housing-only views that zoom in on the shell.

The table below lists where each family's exploded view sits, so you can open the right page while you read this chapter.

Fan family Exploded view pages Housing detail pages Housed centrifugal, direct drive and belt driven 9–10 60 (SWSI), 61 (DWDI) Plenum fans 11–12 none (unhoused) Plug fans 13–14 66 Tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans 15–16 63 Inline centrifugal and mixed flow fans 17 64 Panel fans 18 none Centrifugal roof exhausters 19 none Pressure blowers (cast) none 62 Square inline fans none 65

Three habits make an exploded view easier to read:

  1. Find the airflow first: inlet funnel or collar on one side, outlet flange or discharge on the other.
  2. Separate the housing parts (the shell and what is welded or bolted to it) from the rotating parts (impeller, shaft, bearings) and the drive parts (motor, belt, sheave).
  3. Note the caption under the drawing, such as "Arr. 9 Fan" or "Direct Drive Shown," because the same family can show different parts in different arrangements.

A Drawing Is a Parts List

Notice that every label in an exploded view is a word you can put on an order or a replacement-parts request. Read the drawing as a parts list with pictures, and the vocabulary of this whole book starts to hang together.

docs.title: The Scroll Housing: Side Plates, Wrapper and Cutoff
docs.text:
A housed centrifugal fan's shell is built from three kinds of pieces. FanPedia's SWSI housing view (p. 60) labels them HOUSING SIDE, HOUSING SCROLL and CUTOFF.

A housing side plate is one of the two flat sides of a scroll housing. On a single width, single inlet (SWSI) fan, the inlet side plate carries the round inlet opening, which in turn holds the inlet collar, inlet funnel or inlet flange; the opposite side plate faces the drive. On a double width, double inlet (DWDI) fan (p. 61), both side plates carry inlets, and each side also supports a bearing on a structural support. Because the side plates hold the inlet hardware and often the bearing supports, they are the stiffest, most load-bearing panels of the shell.

The scroll wrapper (FanPedia's "housing scroll") is the curved band of sheet metal that wraps around the impeller between the two side plates and runs out to the discharge. In standard fan engineering terms, the scroll's spiral shape gives the space between impeller and housing a gradually growing cross-section. That shape collects the air the impeller throws off, slows it down, and turns part of its velocity into static pressure before it leaves through the outlet. When FanPedia describes housed centrifugal fans as having "single or double width scroll housings" (p. 4), the width it refers to is the width of this wrapper.

The cutoff is the point near the outlet where the scroll wrapper comes closest to the impeller, like a tongue that separates air leaving through the discharge from air that would otherwise keep circling the housing. FanPedia groups it with the wiper bar as a feature that "helps to direct air through the housing ... to prevent turbulence and to increase efficiency" (p. 59). On the p. 60 drawing the cutoff sits at the discharge end of the scroll, while the wiper bar is a curved fin mounted on the inner end of the inlet funnel, so it sits in the inlet funnel area; Chapter 18 covers the wiper bar.

Before you look at the interactive drawing below, recall the inlet and outlet hardware from Chapter 3: the inlet collar is a short cylinder at the inlet opening, the inlet funnel is the shaped piece that guides air into the impeller, and the inlet and outlet flanges are the bolting rims that connect to ductwork. Framing is covered in the next section, and the pedestal is the stand that carries the bearings (and, on some arrangements, the motor).

docs.title: Diagram: SWSI Housing Callout Explorer
docs.text:
Run SWSI Housing Callout Explorer Fullscreen

SWSI Housing Callout Explorer

Type: infographic sim-id: ch07-swsi-housing-callout-explorer Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify ten labeled parts of a single width, single inlet centrifugal fan housing from a one-sentence description of each part's job.

Prerequisites: exploded view, housing side plate, scroll wrapper, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet collar, inlet funnel, inlet flange, outlet flange, housing framing, pedestal (all defined in the chapter sections above and in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner is shown one description at a time and clicks the part it describes. An answer is correct when the clicked part matches the "Part" column below. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Clicking callouts in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The cutoff and the wiper bar are the same piece in the same place. (2) The side plate and the scroll are one continuous part. (3) The inlet collar and the inlet funnel are interchangeable names.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level identification needs retrieval practice with immediate correction, so the learner first explores labeled callouts, then retrieves each name from its function with the labels hidden.

Content:

# Part (callout label) Description shown on click and in quiz mode 1 Housing Side One of the two flat sides of the scroll housing; on an SWSI fan the inlet side carries the round inlet opening. 2 Housing Scroll The curved wrapper between the side plates that collects air from the impeller and carries it to the outlet. 3 Cutoff The tongue near the outlet where the scroll comes closest to the impeller, separating discharged air from air that would keep circling. 4 Wiper Bar A bar near the inlet funnel area that helps direct air through the housing to reduce turbulence. 5 Inlet Collar A short cylinder at the inlet opening that the inlet hardware mounts to. 6 Inlet Funnel The shaped piece that guides air smoothly into the impeller eye. 7 Inlet Flange The bolting rim at the inlet that connects the fan to inlet ductwork. 8 Outlet (Discharge) Flange The bolting rim at the outlet that connects the fan to discharge ductwork. 9 Framing The angles or channels fastened to the housing that stiffen it and support it on its base. 10 Pedestal The stand that carries the bearings and, on some arrangements, the motor.

The drawing is a line drawing of an SWSI housed centrifugal fan with the ten callouts above; no other parts are labeled. A note on the drawing reads "Based on FanPedia p. 60. Rubbing bars, shown there on spark-resistant fans only, are covered in Chapter 20."

Provenance: Part names and positions: FanPedia p. 60 (Centrifugal Fans SWSI). Cutoff and wiper bar function: FanPedia p. 59. Housing, framing and structural support role: FanPedia pp. 59 and 185. Scroll description and cutoff tongue description: standard fan engineering, as stated in this chapter's section "The Scroll Housing."

Rules: Explore mode: clicking a callout shows its description; any number of clicks. Quiz mode: the 10 descriptions appear once each in shuffled order. A click on the matching part is correct. Clicking a non-callout area does nothing and uses no attempt.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner clicks each callout in explore mode and reads its description.
  2. The learner switches to quiz mode. Callout labels are hidden; a description appears.
  3. The learner clicks the part the description fits. The part is marked correct or incorrect and its label is revealed.
  4. After 10 descriptions the score and a list of missed parts are shown, and the learner can retry the quiz with a new shuffle.

Feedback: 10 items, shuffled, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect: "That is the . The is ." For item 3 or 4 answered with the other, add: "The cutoff sits at the outlet end of the scroll; the wiper bar sits near the inlet funnel." The correct part is revealed after each answer. A running count "Correct: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: Explore mode with all ten callouts visible and the prompt "Click any part to see what it does."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the drawing is based on FanPedia p. 60, that the cutoff sits at the discharge end of the scroll, and that the wiper bar sits near the inlet funnel.

docs.title: Housing Framing and Cast Housings
docs.text:
Housing framing is the structural steel (formed angles or channels) fastened to the outside of the housing to stiffen the sheet metal and give the fan feet to sit on. FanPedia labels FRAMING along the bottom of both the SWSI and DWDI housing views (pp. 60–61), and shows separate STRUCTURAL SUPPORTS on the DWDI fan, where each side plate carries a bearing. Unhoused fans need framing too: the plenum fan views (pp. 11–12) and the square inline view (p. 65) label a FRAME that holds the inlet panel, motor and pedestal together in place of a housing.

Most fan housings are fabricated: cut from sheet or plate and welded or bolted together, as Chapter 3 described. A cast housing is instead poured as a single metal casting. FanPedia's p. 62 shows pressure blowers built two ways, with a cast aluminum housing and with a cast iron housing, each with its inlet, outlet, pedestal and structural support. A casting gives a pressure blower's narrow housing its shape in one piece. Cast parts appear elsewhere on these blowers as well; FanPedia lists a slide gate damper with a cast aluminum frame for cast aluminum pressure blowers (p. 192).

docs.title: Split Housings
docs.text:
Chapter 3 introduced the split housing: a housing built in sections that bolt together, so it can be taken apart. FanPedia names three kinds for centrifugal fans (pp. 156–157 and 194), and each one is named by where the cut runs.

A horizontal split housing is cut along the housing's horizontal centerline, so the upper half lifts off the lower half. FanPedia calls this the "standard split" and notes that size 807 and above may be split by the shop for shipping purposes.

A three-way split housing is cut into three sections, up to 180 degrees. FanPedia says this split is "normally required either for shipping or to enable the fan to enter a specific sized opening," such as a doorway or roof hatch on a retrofit job. Three-way splits need additional drafting and engineering time, so they should be identified early in a quote.

A pie split housing is cut at angles of 90 degrees or greater, removing a wedge of the housing so the impeller can come out "without disturbing inlet or outlet" ductwork. FanPedia shows two styles:

  • Mohawk (newer style): splits between the scroll and the inlet housing side; the inlet side itself has no split. It is not used on double width fans or on fans with attached inlet boxes.
  • Standard (older style): splits all the way down to the funnel or inlet plate. Weld nuts on the inside of the split take bolts from outside the housing, and studs are welded to the outside.

FanPedia's arrangement descriptions show where pie splits are built in: Arrangements 3SI and 7SI (single inlet fans with an attached or integrated inlet box) and 7DI include a pie split housing "for easy impeller removal" (pp. 164–168).

The table below summarizes the three splits you have just read about.

Split Where the cut runs Main reason Note Horizontal Along the horizontal centerline Standard split; shipping large sizes Shop may split size 807 and above for shipping Three-way Three sections, up to 180 degrees Shipping, or passing through a specific opening Extra drafting and engineering time Pie A wedge at 90 degrees or greater Impeller removal without disturbing inlet or outlet Mohawk or standard style

Splits and Tight Housings Don't Mix Easily

Watch out for split housings on nominally leak-tight or RTO jobs: every split is another joint that can leak. FanPedia says split housings are "not recommended" for nominally leak-tight construction, and when a split is used there, it needs gasketing, close bolt spacing and centering plates to seal around the shaft seal and inlet (pp. 120–121), so flag it before the quote goes out. Chapter 21 covers those requirements.

The following MicroSim gives you a set of job situations and asks you to pick the split each one calls for, using the rules from this section.

docs.title: Diagram: Split Housing Selector
docs.text:
Run Split Housing Selector Fullscreen

Split Housing Selector

Type: microsim sim-id: ch07-split-housing-selector Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend a horizontal, three-way, Mohawk pie, standard pie or no split housing for eight described centrifugal fan situations, justifying each choice with a FanPedia rule.

Prerequisites: split housing, horizontal split housing, three-way split housing, pie split housing, Mohawk and standard pie styles, attached inlet box, double width fan, nominally leak-tight construction (defined in the section "Split Housings" above and in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: For each situation the learner commits one recommendation and then picks one justification from four offered. A situation is correct when both the recommendation and the justification match the table below. Mastery is 6 of 8 situations correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Any split will let the impeller out without touching the ductwork. (2) The Mohawk pie split works on any fan. (3) Adding a split is always harmless. (4) A horizontal split is only for maintenance, never shipping.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judgment needs the learner to weigh a situation against stated criteria and defend the choice, so each recommendation is paired with a chosen justification rather than a bare answer.

Content:

Choices for every situation: Horizontal split; Three-way split; Pie split, Mohawk style; Pie split, standard style; No split recommended.

# Situation Correct recommendation Correct justification (shown as feedback) 1 A size 807 SWSI housing is too large to ship assembled. The customer only needs it in two halves. Horizontal split The standard split runs along the horizontal centerline, and size 807 and above may be split by the shop for shipping. 2 A replacement fan must pass through an existing doorway that is smaller than the housing even when split in two. Three-way split A three-way split is normally required to ship a fan or to enter a specific sized opening. 3 Maintenance wants to pull the impeller of an SWSI fan with no inlet box without disturbing the ductwork, and wants the inlet side left unsplit. Pie split, Mohawk style The Mohawk splits between the scroll and the inlet housing side; the inlet side has no split. 4 The same impeller-removal need, but on a double width, double inlet fan. Pie split, standard style The Mohawk style is not used on double width fans. 5 An Arrangement 3SI fan with an attached inlet box needs easy impeller removal. Pie split, standard style Arrangement 3SI includes a pie split, and the Mohawk style is not used on fans with attached inlet boxes. 6 An Arrangement 1 fan in nominally leak-tight service. Nothing about shipping or access requires a split. No split recommended FanPedia states split housings are not recommended for nominally leak-tight construction. 7 A replacement SWSI housing must match the existing pie split on an older fan, which runs all the way down to the inlet plate. Pie split, standard style The standard (older style) pie split runs all the way down to the funnel or inlet plate. 8 A retrofit fan must be lowered through a roof hatch smaller than half the housing, and the quote has not yet allowed for drafting time. Three-way split Three sections fit the opening, and three-way splits need additional drafting and engineering time, so the quote must allow for it.

Justification options offered for situation n are its own justification plus the justifications of the next three rows after n (counting past row 8 back to row 1) whose correct recommendation differs from row n's, so no distractor is a valid reason for the same split.

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 156–157 and 194 (split housing types, Mohawk and standard styles, size 807, three-way drafting time); pp. 164 and 168 (Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 7DI include a pie split); p. 120 (split housings not recommended for nominally leak-tight construction). The situations are illustrative and must be labeled "illustrative situations."

Rules: One recommendation and one justification per situation. A situation counts correct only when both match the table. Situations 3, 4, 5 and 7 all involve a pie split; the style is decided only by the facts stated in each situation text (inlet side left whole, double width, attached inlet box, matching an older split), and the sim gives no other hint.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads situation 1 and selects one of the five recommendations. The choice is locked.
  2. Four justifications appear in shuffled order. The learner selects one.
  3. The sim marks the recommendation and justification correct or incorrect and shows the feedback.
  4. The learner moves to the next situation until all eight are done, then sees a summary table of their answers beside the correct ones.

Feedback: 8 situations in fixed order, one attempt each. Both correct: "Correct: . ." Recommendation wrong: "Not quite. The better choice is : ." Recommendation right but justification wrong: "Right split, wrong reason. ." The correct answer is revealed after each situation. A running count "Situations correct: n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Situation 1 shown with the five recommendation choices and the question "Which split, if any, should this fan have?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the shop may split size 807 and above for shipping, that a three-way split has up to 180 degrees and three sections, that a pie split is at 90 degrees or greater, that the Mohawk style is not used on double width fans or fans with attached inlet boxes, and that split housings are not recommended for nominally leak-tight construction.

docs.title: Getting Inside: Housing Access Panels
docs.text:
Chapter 3 introduced the access door, a small bolted or quick-opening door in the housing for inspecting and cleaning the impeller. FanPedia shows access doors on the housings of tubeaxial, vaneaxial, inline centrifugal and mixed flow fans (pp. 63–64) and lists bolted, raised and quick-open styles among its common accessories (p. 125).

A housing access panel is larger: a whole removable side of the housing rather than a door cut into it. The clearest example is the square inline fan. FanPedia describes square inline centrifugal fans as "built with square housings and removable side panels" (p. 6), and its p. 65 view labels the ACCESS PANEL as "REMOVABLE, 3 SIDES." Taking off a panel exposes the impeller, motor and drive at once, which is why square inline fans are easy to service in tight ceiling spaces.

docs.title: Tubular Housings: Straightening Vanes, Discharge Cone and Belt Tube
docs.text:
Inline centrifugal, mixed flow and axial fans use a tubular housing, and their exploded views (pp. 15–17) show three parts a scroll housing does not have.

Straightening vanes are fixed vanes inside a tubular housing, downstream of the impeller, that take the swirl out of the air leaving the impeller and turn it back into straight-through flow. FanPedia labels STRAIGHTENING VANES on both the inline centrifugal and the mixed flow views (pp. 17 and 64). On a vaneaxial fan the same job is done by the guide vanes of Chapter 4, which FanPedia says "help straighten the airflow as it moves through the fan" (p. 7). Recovering that swirl as useful pressure is why a vaned tubular fan can develop more pressure than a plain tube.

A discharge cone is a tapered section at the outlet end of the tubular housing. FanPedia's belt driven inline centrifugal and mixed flow view (p. 17) labels it at the discharge, where it guides the air leaving the impeller and vanes toward the outlet connection.

A belt tube (FanPedia: "BELT TUBE, aka Belt Fairing") is an enclosed passage through the side of a belt driven tubular housing. In an axial or inline fan the motor sits outside the tube while the impeller shaft is inside it, so the belts have to cross the airstream. The belt tube shields the belts and sheaves from the moving air and from whatever the air carries. It appears on the belt driven tubeaxial, vaneaxial, inline centrifugal and mixed flow views (pp. 15–17, 63–64).

Inline Centrifugal and Mixed Flow Fan Parts

sim-id: ch07-inline-centrifugal-mixed-flow-overlay Library: html + FP.Overlay Status: built Bloom Level: Remember Learning Objective: The learner will identify the twelve labeled parts of a direct drive inline centrifugal fan and a belt driven mixed flow fan on FanPedia's exploded views, given each part's function or appearance.

Content: 12 numbered markers: Tubular housing, Straightening vanes, Shaft, Impeller (inline centrifugal), Inlet funnel, Motor, Impeller (mixed flow), Bearing housing, Belt guard, Belt tube, Sheave, Discharge cone

Provenance: FanPedia page 17, "Exploded Views: Inline Centrifugal & Mixed Flow Fans, direct drive (left) and belt driven (right)", with the printed labels removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 17.

docs.title: Guards and Covers
docs.text:
A belt guard encloses the belts and sheaves on the outside of a belt driven fan so that no one can reach the moving drive. FanPedia shows one beside the belt tube on the belt driven inline view (p. 17) and lists it as a common accessory (p. 125). FanPedia also notes that spark-resistant axial fans keep a mild steel belt guard (p. 109); Chapter 20 explains why that matters. A related accessory, the shaft/bearing guard and coupling guard, protects the exposed shaft and coupling on direct drive fans (p. 126).

A motor cover, also called a weather cover, is a hood placed over the motor to protect it from rain, snow and sun. FanPedia lists "Motor Cover / Weather Cover" as a common accessory (p. 126), and the centrifugal roof exhauster view (p. 19) labels a MOTOR COVER on top of the unit, above the MOTOR HOUSING that encloses the motor.

Guard or Tube? Ask Where the Belt Runs

Here's a quick check when a drawing shows a belt drive: if the belts cross the airstream inside a tube, you need a belt tube; if they run outside the housing where people can reach them, you need a belt guard. A belt driven inline fan, as on p. 17, has both.

docs.title: Plug Fan Hardware: Mounting Panel and Insulation Plug
docs.text:
A plug fan has no housing; it is "plugged" into the wall of the customer's plenum, which acts as the fan housing (FanPedia pp. 5 and 172). Two parts take the place of the housing's structure.

The mounting panel is the flat plate that fastens the fan to the customer's wall. FanPedia explains that "the mounting panel is mounted to the outside wall and the impeller inside the plenum wall" (p. 5); the inlet funnel and impeller hang inside the plenum, while the shaft, bearings and motor stay outside the process airstream. On Arrangement 9 plug fans the wall carries the whole fan. On the grade-mounted versions (Arrangements 1P, 4P, 8P and 9P), the fan stands on the foundation instead, and FanPedia lists the mounting panel as optional (pp. 170–172). Not every plug fan model is built in every arrangement; Chapter 6 gives the arrangements the current catalogs list.

The insulation plug is an insulated section mounted with the panel that fills the opening in the plenum wall around the fan, so the wall keeps its insulating value where the fan passes through it. It appears on both plug fan exploded views (pp. 13–14) and on the Arr. 9P detail "Mounting Panel with Insulation Plug" (p. 66). Plug fans often serve hot equipment such as ovens, so the plug matters in high-temperature service. For Arrangement 9 high-temperature plug fans, FanPedia's two designs set the rule by the thickness of the plug or wall (p. 113, which refers to Fan Engineering Letter FE-3200). With a plug or wall less than 4" thick (Design #1, a gap for the shaft cooler), the insulated plug is optional up to 500°F. With a plug or wall 4" or more thick (Design #2, a recess cone for the shaft cooler), the insulated plug is required at 301°F and above. The two statements do not conflict because they apply to different wall thicknesses.

docs.title: Rooftop Hardware: Shroud, Curb Cap, Nozzle and Windband
docs.text:
Roof-mounted fans need parts that seal them to the building and send the exhaust where it should go.

A curb cap is the base plate or frame of a roof-mounted fan that sits on and covers the roof curb, the raised frame built around the roof opening. FanPedia's centrifugal roof exhauster view (p. 19) stacks CURB CAP directly on ROOF CURB, and its roof mounted axial fans are shown "with hood and curb cap" or "with stack cap and curb cap" (p. 7). On vertical inline and axial fans mounted on a roof, the motor is centered on the curb cap (p. 57).

A roof exhauster shroud is the sheet-metal shell around the impeller of a centrifugal roof exhauster that guides the air the impeller throws off. FanPedia labels the SHROUD between the impeller and the curb cap on its upblast and downblast views (p. 19), with a SKIRT and bird screen around the downblast unit, where air is turned down and outward. Chapter 5 described these upblast and downblast discharges.

A nozzle and windband sit at the top of a lab exhaust fan. The nozzle accelerates the contaminated exhaust into a high-velocity jet, and the windband around it draws in fresh outside air, which FanPedia calls entrained flow (pp. 4 and 6). The fresh air mixes with the contaminated air to dilute it and carry it up and away from the building. Chapter 5 introduced entrained flow; here you can see that the nozzle and windband are the housing parts that produce it.

The last MicroSim pulls the chapter together: you sort parts into the fan family whose FanPedia exploded view shows them.

docs.text:

Which Exploded View Shows This Part

Type: microsim sim-id: ch07-exploded-view-part-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute twelve housing parts to the fan family whose FanPedia exploded view or housing detail shows them, using what each part does to decide.

Prerequisites: exploded view, housing side plate, scroll wrapper, cutoff, straightening vanes, guide vanes, discharge cone, belt tube, mounting panel, insulation plug, roof exhauster shroud, curb cap, motor cover (all defined in this chapter above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner drops each of 12 part cards into one of four family bins and presses Check. A card is correct when its bin matches the "Correct family" column below. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first check.

Misconceptions: (1) Straightening vanes belong to scroll housings. (2) A plug fan has a scroll. (3) A belt tube is the same as a belt guard and appears on every belt driven fan. (4) Curb caps are only for centrifugal roof exhausters.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level attribution asks the learner to connect each part's function to the airflow path of a family, so the learner commits all placements before any feedback, then reads the reason for each.

Content:

Bins: Housed Centrifugal (scroll housing); Tubular (axial, inline centrifugal, mixed flow); Plug Fan; Centrifugal Roof Exhauster.

# Part card Correct family Why (shown as feedback) 1 Housing Side Housed Centrifugal A flat side plate of the scroll housing (FanPedia pp. 60–61). 2 Housing Scroll Housed Centrifugal The curved wrapper exists only on scroll housings (p. 60). 3 Cutoff Housed Centrifugal The tongue where the scroll meets the outlet (p. 60). 4 Straightening Vanes Tubular Fixed vanes that remove swirl in inline centrifugal and mixed flow housings (pp. 17, 64). 5 Guide Vanes Tubular The vaneaxial version of straightening vanes (pp. 16, 63). 6 Discharge Cone Tubular Tapered outlet section on the belt driven inline and mixed flow view (p. 17). 7 Belt Tube Tubular Carries belts across the airstream to a shaft inside the tube (pp. 15–17). 8 Mounting Panel Plug Fan Fastens the fan to the customer's plenum wall (pp. 13–14, 66). 9 Insulation Plug Plug Fan Insulates the plenum wall opening around the fan (pp. 13–14, 66). 10 Shroud Centrifugal Roof Exhauster Shell around the roof exhauster impeller (p. 19). 11 Curb Cap Centrifugal Roof Exhauster Sits on the roof curb in the exploded view (p. 19); roof mounted axial fans also use one (p. 7). 12 Motor Cover Centrifugal Roof Exhauster Weather cover on top of the roof exhauster (p. 19).

Provenance: FanPedia exploded views pp. 13–19 and housing detail pages pp. 60–61, 63–64 and 66, as cited in each row.

Rules: Each card goes in exactly one bin. The answer key is the family whose FanPedia exploded view (pp. 9–19) or housing detail (pp. 59–66) labels the part; for Curb Cap the exploded view on p. 19 decides, and the feedback notes the roof mounted axial use. Cards can be moved freely until Check is pressed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees 12 cards in shuffled order and four empty bins.
  2. The learner drags each card into a bin. Cards can be moved between bins before checking.
  3. The learner presses Check. Each card is marked correct or incorrect, and clicking a card shows its "Why" text.
  4. The learner can press Retry to send the incorrect cards back to the pool and place them again; retries are not counted toward mastery.

Feedback: 12 cards, shuffled, one first check counted for mastery, unlimited retries. Correct card: "Correct: belongs to . ." Incorrect card: "Not . " For card 4 placed in Housed Centrifugal, add: "A scroll housing turns the air with its spiral shape; vanes are needed only when the air leaves the impeller swirling inside a tube." A score "First check: n of 12" is shown.

Starting State: All 12 cards in the pool, the four bins empty, and the question "Which fan family's exploded view shows each part?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that FanPedia's exploded views run from p. 9 to p. 19, that straightening vanes appear on pp. 17 and 64, that the belt tube is also called a belt fairing, and that roof mounted axial fans are shown with a curb cap on p. 7.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An exploded view separates an assembly along its assembly lines so each part carries a label; FanPedia's run from p. 9 to p. 19, and its housing details from p. 59 to p. 66.
  • A scroll housing is built from two housing side plates and a curved scroll wrapper; the cutoff at the outlet keeps discharged air from recirculating.
  • Housing framing stiffens the shell and supports it; a cast housing, as on cast aluminum or cast iron pressure blowers, is poured in one piece.
  • A horizontal split housing is the standard split; a three-way split housing is for shipping or passing through a specific opening; a pie split housing lets the impeller out without disturbing the ducts, in Mohawk or standard style.
  • Housing access panels remove a whole side (three sides on square inline fans), while access doors are cut into the housing.
  • Tubular housings add straightening vanes, a discharge cone and, on belt drives, a belt tube; a belt guard and motor cover protect people and the motor outside the airstream.
  • Plug fans use a mounting panel and an insulation plug at the plenum wall; roof fans use a curb cap, a roof exhauster shroud, and on lab exhaust a nozzle and windband.

You Can Read the Drawing Now

You can now open any FanPedia exploded view, find the cutoff, the side plates, the straightening vanes or the curb cap, and say what each one is for. That "bent piece near the outlet" from the start of the chapter is most likely the cutoff, and you know to confirm it on p. 60 before anyone orders a part.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Housing Construction and Exploded Views
docs.text: Test your understanding of scroll housing parts, split housings, tubular housing parts, guards, plug fan hardware and rooftop hardware with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. On a housed centrifugal fan, what is the cutoff?
docs.text:
1. The flat side of the scroll housing that carries the inlet opening
  2. The structural steel that stiffens the housing and gives the fan its feet
  3. The point near the outlet where the scroll wrapper comes closest to the impeller
  4. The bolted joint along the housing's horizontal centerline
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The cutoff sits at the discharge end of the scroll, where the wrapper comes closest to the impeller. Like a tongue, it separates air leaving through the discharge from air that would otherwise keep circling the housing, and FanPedia groups it with the wiper bar as a feature that helps prevent turbulence and increase efficiency. Option A describes a housing side plate, option B housing framing, and option D a horizontal split.

Concept Tested: Cutoff

See: The Scroll Housing: Side Plates, Wrapper and Cutoff

docs.title: 2. According to FanPedia, why is a three-way split housing normally required?
docs.text:
1. For shipping, or to let the fan pass through a specific sized opening
  2. To let the impeller come out without disturbing inlet or outlet ductwork
  3. To make the housing nominally leak-tight
  4. To reduce the drafting and engineering time on a quote
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. FanPedia says the three-way split, which cuts the housing into three sections up to 180 degrees, is "normally required either for shipping or to enable the fan to enter a specific sized opening," such as a doorway or roof hatch on a retrofit. Option B is the purpose of a pie split. Splits are not recommended for leak-tight construction, and a three-way split adds drafting and engineering time rather than saving it, so it should be identified early in a quote.

Concept Tested: Three-Way Split Housing

See: Split Housings

docs.title: 3. Why does a scroll wrapper give the space between the impeller and the housing a gradually growing cross-section?
docs.text:
1. To make room for the bearings inside the housing
  2. To let the housing be split into sections for shipping
  3. To hold the inlet collar and inlet funnel in place
  4. To collect the air the impeller throws off, slow it down and turn part of its velocity into static pressure
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The scroll wrapper is the curved band of sheet metal between the two side plates that runs out to the discharge. Its spiral shape gives the air a gradually growing passage, so it collects the air leaving the impeller, slows it, and converts part of its velocity into static pressure before the air leaves through the outlet. The inlet collar and funnel are carried by the side plate, and splitting is a separate housing feature.

Concept Tested: Scroll Wrapper

See: The Scroll Housing: Side Plates, Wrapper and Cutoff

docs.title: 4. A plant wants to be able to pull the impeller out of a housed centrifugal fan without disconnecting the inlet or outlet ductwork. Which housing feature meets that need?
docs.text:
1. A horizontal split housing
  2. A pie split housing
  3. A three-way split housing
  4. A bolted access door
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A pie split housing removes a wedge of the housing, cut at 90 degrees or greater, so the impeller can come out "without disturbing inlet or outlet" ductwork. FanPedia builds pie splits into Arrangements 3SI, 7SI and 7DI for easy impeller removal. A horizontal split is the standard split, a three-way split serves shipping or tight openings, and an access door is only large enough to inspect and clean the impeller.

Concept Tested: Pie Split Housing

See: Split Housings

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between a belt tube and a belt guard on a belt driven fan?
docs.text:
1. They are two names for the same part, used by different manufacturers
  2. A belt tube shields belts that cross the airstream; a belt guard keeps people away from belts outside the housing
  3. A belt tube is used only on centrifugal roof exhausters; a belt guard is used only on plug fans
  4. A belt guard protects the belts from the airstream; a belt tube protects people from the moving drive
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In a belt driven axial or inline fan, the motor sits outside the tube while the impeller shaft is inside it, so the belts must cross the airstream; the belt tube (also called a belt fairing) shields them from the air and whatever it carries. A belt guard encloses belts and sheaves outside the housing so people cannot reach the moving drive. Option D reverses the two jobs. A belt driven inline fan has both.

Concept Tested: Belt Tube

See: Guards and Covers

docs.title: 6. A technician must reach the impeller, motor and drive of a square inline fan in a tight ceiling space. Which housing feature gives the most direct access?
docs.text:
1. A quick-open access door cut into the housing
  2. The cutoff at the discharge
  3. A three-way split housing
  4. The removable housing access panels, which take off a whole side of the housing
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A housing access panel is a whole removable side of the housing rather than a door cut into it. FanPedia describes square inline fans as built with square housings and removable side panels, and its view labels the access panel "removable, 3 sides." Removing a panel exposes the impeller, motor and drive at once, which is why these fans are easy to service in tight ceiling spaces. An access door is smaller, and splits and cutoffs do not provide service access.

Concept Tested: Housing Access Panel

See: Getting Inside: Housing Access Panels

docs.title: 7. What is the job of the insulation plug on a plug fan?
docs.text:
1. It fills the opening in the plenum wall around the fan so the wall keeps its insulating value
  2. It seals the shaft where it passes through the housing side plate
  3. It replaces the mounting panel on grade-mounted arrangements
  4. It insulates the motor from the weather on outdoor installations
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The insulation plug is an insulated section mounted with the panel that fills the opening in the plenum wall where the fan passes through, so the wall keeps its insulating value. It appears on both FanPedia plug fan exploded views and on the Arrangement 9P "Mounting Panel with Insulation Plug" detail. Because plug fans often serve hot equipment such as ovens, the plug matters in high-temperature service. A motor cover, not an insulation plug, protects the motor from weather.

Concept Tested: Insulation Plug

See: Plug Fan Hardware: Mounting Panel and Insulation Plug

docs.title: 8. A customer orders a nominally leak-tight fan and also asks for a split housing so it can be shipped in sections. What should you do before the quote goes out?
docs.text:
1. Quote the split as requested, since splitting a housing does not add any leakage paths
  2. Drop the leak-tight requirement, because leak-tight construction and split housings can never be combined
  3. Flag the conflict: splits are not recommended for leak-tight fans, and one used there needs gasketing and close bolt spacing
  4. Replace the split with a pie split, because a pie split joint is sealed and never leaks
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Every split is another joint that can leak. FanPedia says split housings are "not recommended" for nominally leak-tight construction, and when a split is used there it needs gasketing, close bolt spacing and centering plates to seal around the shaft seal and inlet. The right move is to flag the requirement before quoting, not to ignore it or abandon the leak-tight construction. A pie split is still a split joint.

Concept Tested: Horizontal Split Housing

See: Split Housings

docs.title: 9. What is the underlying reason that inline centrifugal and mixed flow fans carry straightening vanes downstream of the impeller?
docs.text:
1. The air leaving the impeller swirls, and the vanes turn it back into straight-through flow so the swirl is recovered as useful pressure
  2. The vanes carry the bearings in the middle of the airstream
  3. The vanes block reverse airflow when the fan is shut down
  4. The vanes protect the belts from the airstream
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Air leaving the impeller of a tubular fan carries a swirl. Straightening vanes are fixed vanes downstream of the impeller that take the swirl out and turn the air back into straight-through flow. Recovering that swirl as useful pressure is why a vaned tubular fan can develop more pressure than a plain tube, the same job guide vanes do on a vaneaxial fan. The vanes do not carry bearings, act as a backdraft damper, or shield belts; the belt tube does that last job.

Concept Tested: Straightening Vanes

See: Tubular Housings: Straightening Vanes, Discharge Cone and Belt Tube

docs.title: 10. An exploded view labels a MOTOR COVER at the top, a SHROUD below the impeller, a CURB CAP, and a ROOF CURB at the bottom. Which fan family's drawing is this?
docs.text:
1. A housed centrifugal fan with a scroll housing
  2. A belt driven plug fan
  3. A square inline fan
  4. A centrifugal roof exhauster
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FanPedia's centrifugal roof exhauster view stacks the curb cap directly on the roof curb, places a shroud around the impeller to guide the air it throws off, and labels a motor cover above the motor housing. A housed centrifugal would show side plates, a scroll and a cutoff; a plug fan would show a mounting panel and insulation plug; and a square inline fan would show removable access panels. Sorting labels this way is how an exploded view becomes a parts list.

Concept Tested: Roof Exhauster Shroud

See: Rooftop Hardware: Shroud, Curb Cap, Nozzle and Windband

docs.title: References: Housing Construction and Exploded Views
docs.text:
1. Exploded-view drawing - Wikipedia - Explains how exploded views separate an assembly along its assembly lines so each part can be labeled. The drawing convention FanPedia uses to name every housing part.

  2. Volute (pump) - Wikipedia - Describes the spiral casing whose growing cross-section collects flow from an impeller and converts velocity to pressure. The same principle as a fan's scroll wrapper and cutoff.

  3. Metal casting - Wikipedia - Overview of casting processes and materials such as aluminum and iron. Background for the cast housings used on pressure blowers, as opposed to fabricated sheet and plate housings.

  4. Fan Handbook: Selection, Application, and Design - Frank P. Bleier - McGraw-Hill - Bleier's handbook presents housing construction alongside fan types and accessories, with practical guidance on how construction choices follow from installation and service needs.

  5. Fans and Ventilation: A Practical Guide - William Cory - Elsevier - Cory writes from long fan-industry experience, explaining fan components, accessories and installation in plain practical terms suited to readers learning the parts of a fan.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Source for the exploded views (pp. 9-19), housing construction details (pp. 59-66), split housings (pp. 156-157, 194) and plug fan insulation plug notes cited in this chapter.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Online edition of FanPedia, including the housing construction and accessories sections. Use it to look up a housing part name quickly while reading an exploded view.

  8. Plug Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for plug fans, describing the gusseted mounting panel that separates motor and drive from the process air and lets the fan be removed as a unit.

  9. Inline Centrifugal Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for tubular and square inline centrifugal fans, the families whose housings carry straightening vanes, discharge cones, belt tubes and removable access panels.

  10. Centrifugal Roof & Wall Exhausters - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for upblast, downblast and wall exhausters, the product family whose FanPedia exploded view shows the shroud, curb cap and motor cover covered in this chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the impeller, the part that does the work of moving air. It covers blades, back plates, shrouds, and hubs; the main centrifugal types (single width single inlet, backward inclined, and forward curved); mixed flow impellers; and axial impellers with fixed or adjustable pitch, including hub position on the intake or discharge side and reversible impellers. It also covers straight bore and taper lock hubs and why impellers are balanced. After completing it, readers can identify an impeller type and explain how air flows through it.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 22 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Impeller Blade 26 Impeller Back Plate 4 Impeller Shroud 2 Impeller Balancing 47 Blade Leading Edge 1 Impeller Hub 9 Centrifugal Impeller 55 Axial Impeller 17 Impeller Orientation 5 Back Plate Fins 1 Single Width Single Inlet 10 Backward Inclined Impeller 13 Forward Curved Impeller 5 Mixed Flow Impeller 2 Fixed Pitch Impeller 1 Adjustable Pitch Impeller 3 Fiberglass Axial Impeller 2 Hub on Intake Side 2 Hub on Discharge Side 2 Reversible Impeller 1 Straight Bore Hub 2 Taper Lock Hub 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans

Welcome to the Impeller Chapter

Every fan you will ever quote, specify, or troubleshoot has exactly one part that actually moves the air, and that part is the impeller. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at a wheel on a shop floor or a picture in a catalog and say what type it is, which way the air goes through it, and what the order has to say about it. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: The Part That Does the Work
docs.text:
In Chapter 3 you met the impeller as one part among many: housing, shaft, bearings, motor, inlet, and outlet. Every other part of a fan exists to hold the impeller, spin it, or guide air into and out of it. The impeller is the only part that adds energy to the airstream. When it turns, its blades push on the air, raising the air's velocity and pressure, which is the total pressure rise you studied in Chapter 2.

In Chapter 4 you sorted fans into three families by the path the air takes. That sorting is really a statement about the impeller inside. This chapter opens the fan up and looks at the impeller itself: what its parts are called, how the main centrifugal and axial types differ, how an axial impeller's hub position follows from the airflow direction, how the hub fastens to the shaft, and why every impeller is balanced before it ships. Chapter 9 then goes further into airfoil, backward curved, radial, and material handling designs.

docs.title: Impeller Parts
docs.text: Before comparing impeller types, it helps to name the parts that most of them share. FanPedia's centrifugal impeller drawing (FanPedia PDF p. 31) labels four of them: the blade, the back plate, the impeller front plate, and the hub. A fifth idea, the blade's leading edge, appears on every axial airflow page (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–41).

docs.title: Impeller Blade
docs.text:
An impeller blade is the surface that pushes on the air. Every impeller, centrifugal or axial, has a set of blades arranged evenly around the axis of rotation, and the shape, angle, and number of those blades decide most of what the impeller can do: how much pressure it can build, how efficiently it runs, and how well it tolerates dust. Blade shape is also the quickest way to identify an impeller type in the field. A blade that leans or curves back, away from the direction of rotation, belongs to the backward family; a blade whose tip curves toward the direction of rotation belongs to a forward curved impeller; a blade that runs straight out from the center is radial.

On an axial impeller the blades are shaped like propeller blades. FanPedia describes their action in one sentence: the concave side of the blade "cups the air and pushes it away from the impeller" (FanPedia PDF p. 37). The concave side is the hollow, inside face of the curved blade.

docs.title: Worked Example: Checking Rotation from the Blades
docs.text:
A facilities technician calls about a new housed centrifugal fan that "runs but doesn't move much air." You ask them to lock out the motor, open the access door, and describe the blades. They report flat blades whose outer ends lean back, away from the direction the arrow on the housing shows.

  1. Flat, single-thickness blades that lean backward identify a backward inclined impeller (FanPedia PDF p. 31).
  2. On a backward inclined impeller, the blade tips should trail the direction of rotation. The technician's description says the tips lean away from the arrow, which is correct for the arrow.
  3. You then ask them to bump the motor and watch the shaft. If the shaft turns against the arrow, the wiring is reversed. A centrifugal impeller turning backward still moves some air, but far less than its rating, which matches the complaint.
  4. The fix is to swap two motor leads (a job for an electrician) and recheck the rotation.

The blade shape told you what "correct" looks like before anyone measured anything. Chapter 12 shows how rotation is formally designated on a drawing.

docs.title: Blade Leading Edge
docs.text: The blade leading edge is the edge of the blade that meets the incoming air first. On an axial impeller, FanPedia states that "air is drawn through the impeller from the leading edge of the blades" (FanPedia PDF p. 37), so the leading edge always faces the intake side of the fan. On a centrifugal impeller the leading edge is the inner edge of each blade, near the inlet, and the opposite edge at the outer diameter is the trailing edge, or blade tip, where air leaves. Knowing which edge leads is how you check that an axial impeller is mounted facing the right way: if the leading edges face the discharge, the impeller is backward on its shaft.

docs.title: Impeller Back Plate and Impeller Shroud
docs.text:
The impeller back plate is the solid disc on the closed side of a centrifugal impeller. The blades are welded to it, and on most centrifugal impellers the hub is attached to it, so the back plate carries the blade loads to the hub and shaft. It also forms one wall of the air passage, so air entering the open side has nowhere to go except outward between the blades.

The impeller shroud is the ring-shaped plate on the inlet side of a centrifugal impeller. FanPedia labels it the impeller front plate (FanPedia PDF p. 31), and both names are common in the trade. The shroud has a large hole in its center where air enters, and it closes the other side of the blade passages so air is guided outward instead of leaking around the blade edges. Together, the back plate and shroud sandwich the blades. Not every impeller has both: FanPedia's open paddle impeller has neither, and its material handling impeller has a back plate only (FanPedia PDF p. 32), designs that Chapter 9 covers.

docs.title: Back Plate Fins
docs.text:
Back plate fins are small radial vanes welded to the outside of the back plate, on the side away from the blades. FanPedia lists this accessory as "fins on impeller back plate" and notes that it is also known by these names, any of which may appear on drawings and orders (FanPedia PDF p. 126):

  • thrust fins
  • thrust vanes or anti-thrust vanes
  • back plate fins
  • back pressure fins
  • cooling fins

FanPedia also gives their purpose: the fins "reduce the thrust load on the bearings," and they "can create a negative pressure behind the impeller to draw air into the fan through the shaft hole in the housing," which "helps reduce the possibility of leakage of the airstream to atmosphere" (FanPedia PDF pp. 126, 184). Thrust load is the push along the shaft's axis that the bearings must resist. Back plate fins therefore show up when bearing life or airstream leakage around the shaft is a concern.

docs.title: Impeller Hub
docs.text: The impeller hub is the thick central piece that connects the impeller to the shaft. Its bore, the hole through its center, fits the shaft, and the hub transmits the motor's torque into the blades. On a centrifugal impeller the hub is fastened to the back plate; on an axial impeller the hub is the center body that the blades attach to. FanPedia's axial overview (FanPedia PDF p. 35) names five axial parts: the blade, the blade tip, the hub, the hub boss (the raised center of the hub that holds the bore), and, on adjustable pitch impellers, the shank, which is the root of a blade that fits into the hub.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a Hub Callout on a Replacement Order
docs.text:
A plant sends a purchase order for "one replacement impeller, same as existing," with a photo of the old wheel. Before it can be quoted, the hub has to be described. You work through it like this:

  1. What fastens the hub to the shaft? The photo shows set screws on the side of the hub and a keyway in the bore. That is a straight bore hub (defined later in this chapter).
  2. What size is the bore? A straight bore must match the shaft diameter, so you need the shaft size from the nameplate data or the original order. The photo cannot give it.
  3. Is it centrifugal or axial? A back plate and front plate are visible, so it is centrifugal, and the hub sits on the back plate.
  4. Anything attached to the back plate? The photo shows short vanes on the back of the back plate, so the replacement must also have back plate fins.

The order now names the hub type, the bore, and the fins instead of "same as existing." That is the habit to build: name each part, and an order can be checked.

Before moving on, the table below collects the parts you have just read about.

Part Where it is What it does Blade Around the axis, between plates (centrifugal) or on the hub (axial) Pushes on the air Blade leading edge Edge of the blade that meets the incoming air Faces the intake; shows mounting direction Back plate Closed side of a centrifugal impeller Carries blades to the hub; closes the air passage Shroud (front plate) Inlet side of a centrifugal impeller Guides air outward; closes the blade passages Back plate fins Outside of the back plate Reduce bearing thrust; help limit shaft-hole leakage Hub Center of the impeller Connects the impeller to the shaft

docs.title: Centrifugal Impellers
docs.text:
A centrifugal impeller draws air in along the shaft axis and throws it outward, at a right angle to the shaft, off the blade tips. Air enters through the shroud opening, turns, and is flung outward through the passages between the blades by the impeller's rotation. FanPedia's housed centrifugal fan description states the result: air is drawn in through one or both sides and "is discharged at a right angle to the fan shaft" (FanPedia PDF p. 4). In a housed fan the scroll housing collects the air leaving the blade tips and turns its velocity into useful pressure; in a plenum fan, the plenum does that job; in an inline centrifugal fan, the tubular housing turns the air back in line with the duct.

FanPedia lists the centrifugal impeller types built into housed centrifugal fans: backward inclined, airfoil, backward curved, radial tip, forward curved, and radial bladed (FanPedia PDF p. 4). This chapter covers backward inclined and forward curved; the others are in Chapter 9.

One number connects impeller size and speed to how hard the impeller works on the air: the tip speed, the velocity of the blade tips as they travel around the circle. Higher tip speed means the blades can build more pressure, and it also means more stress in the impeller. For an impeller diameter \( D \) in inches turning at \( N \) revolutions per minute, the circumference in feet is \( \pi D / 12 \), and the tip speed is:

\[ V_{tip} = \frac{\pi D N}{12} \]

where \( V_{tip} \) is the tip speed in feet per minute (ft/min), \( D \) is the impeller diameter in inches, and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

docs.title: Worked Example: Tip Speed of a Centrifugal Impeller
docs.text:
A 30-inch centrifugal impeller runs at 1,200 rpm (illustrative values, not a specific catalog size).

\[ V_{tip} = \frac{\pi \times 30 \times 1200}{12} = 9{,}425 \text{ ft/min} \]

If a belt change raises the speed to 1,800 rpm, the tip speed rises in proportion to 14,137 ft/min, 50% higher. The fan laws in Chapter 25 show that pressure rises with the square of speed, so this change raises the pressure the impeller can develop by a factor of \( 1.5^2 = 2.25 \). The impeller's structure has to be rated for that speed, which is why a speed increase is always checked against the maximum speed the current catalog allows for that fan and its construction.

Same Spin, Different Path

A centrifugal impeller works mostly by flinging air outward, so its pressure comes from the radius the air travels through. An axial impeller works by lifting air along the shaft, like a propeller. Once you see which way the air leaves the wheel, the housing, the arrangement, and even the drawing conventions start to make sense.

docs.title: Single Width Single Inlet
docs.text:
A single width single inlet (SWSI) impeller takes air in through one side only. It has one back plate, one shroud, and one inlet opening, and its housing has one inlet. The alternative is the double width double inlet (DWDI) impeller, which is essentially two single-width impellers placed back to back on a common center plate, drawing air in from both sides; it is covered in Chapter 9. FanPedia's housed centrifugal fan figure shows both (FanPedia PDF p. 4), and the arrangement pages list the SWSI arrangements separately (FanPedia PDF pp. 20–22).

Because a SWSI impeller has one open side and one closed side, its shaft can come in through the closed side. That allows the impeller to hang on the end of the shaft, with no bearing on the inlet side to block the airflow.

docs.title: Worked Example: Can This Be Arrangement 4?
docs.text:
A mechanical contractor asks for "a direct-drive fan, impeller on the motor shaft, double inlet, to save space." You check it against FanPedia:

  1. Arrangement 4 is direct drive with the "impeller mounted to motor shaft" and appears on the SWSI arrangement pages (FanPedia PDF p. 20).
  2. A double inlet impeller takes air from both sides, so a shaft cannot end inside it with a motor on one side without blocking one inlet. FanPedia's double width, double inlet arrangement page lists only Arrangement 3 and 7 variants (3, 3DI, 3F, 7, and 7DI) (FanPedia PDF p. 23), and its orientation page shows those arrangements with the impeller between two bearings (FanPedia PDF p. 30).
  3. The request is inconsistent. You go back to the contractor with two options: an Arrangement 4 SWSI fan, or a double width fan in Arrangement 3 or 7.

The words "single width single inlet" carry a real constraint on arrangement, so they belong on every centrifugal order.

docs.title: Impeller Orientation
docs.text:
Impeller orientation describes where the impeller sits on the shaft relative to the bearings. FanPedia names two orientations for centrifugal fans (FanPedia PDF p. 30):

  • Overhung impeller: the impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, outboard of the bearings. FanPedia lists Arrangements 1, 8, 9, and 10, and Arrangement 4, where the impeller hangs on the motor shaft.
  • Center hung impeller: the impeller is mounted between the bearings. FanPedia lists Arrangement 3 and Arrangement 7, single and double width.

Orientation matters for the order because it fixes which arrangements are possible and where the bearings sit relative to the airstream. Chapter 11 develops the arrangements in full.

docs.title: Backward Inclined Impeller
docs.text:
A backward inclined impeller has flat, single-thickness blades tilted backward, so each blade's outer end trails behind its inner end as the impeller turns. FanPedia's caption reads "impeller with flat, single thickness, backward inclined blades" (FanPedia PDF p. 31). Its close relatives are the backward curved impeller, whose single-thickness blades are curved backward, and the airfoil impeller, whose backward inclined blades have a hollow airfoil section; both are in Chapter 9.

Backward inclined impellers are widely used for general ventilation and clean or lightly dusty air because they combine good efficiency with a useful property called a non-overloading power curve. On a fan curve, which Chapter 10 covers in detail, the brake horsepower of a backward inclined fan at a fixed speed rises to a peak and then falls as airflow keeps increasing. A motor sized for that peak cannot be overloaded at that speed, wherever the fan ends up operating on its curve.

docs.title: Worked Example: Will the Motor Overload?
docs.text:
A rooftop filtered supply unit is being selected for a building whose duct system is still being designed. The engineer worries that the real duct resistance may be lower than calculated, which would push the fan to more airflow than planned. FanPedia notes that filtered units use either forward curved or backward inclined impellers (FanPedia PDF p. 4). Which is safer here?

  1. Lower system resistance moves the operating point to the right on the fan curve, toward more airflow.
