  2. With a backward inclined impeller, power peaks and then falls toward higher airflow, so a motor sized for the peak power at the selected speed covers this case.
  3. With a forward curved impeller, power keeps rising with airflow (next section), so the same shift can overload a motor that was sized only for the design point.
  4. When the system resistance is uncertain, the backward inclined unit, or a forward curved unit with a motor sized for the highest airflow it could reach, protects the motor.

docs.title: Forward Curved Impeller
docs.text: A forward curved impeller has many short, shallow blades that curve forward, so their tips point in the direction of rotation. FanPedia's caption is "impeller with single thickness, forward curved blades," and its drawing shows the end ring and tie rods that hold the narrow blades in place (FanPedia PDF p. 31). The forward curve throws air off the tips at high velocity, so a forward curved impeller moves a given airflow at a lower speed and in a smaller size than a backward inclined impeller, which suits compact, low-pressure equipment. The trade-offs are lower efficiency, a power curve that keeps rising with airflow (an overloading curve), and shallow blade pockets that collect dust, so forward curved impellers belong in clean air.

docs.title: Mixed Flow Impeller
docs.text:
A mixed flow impeller is a hybrid of axial and centrifugal designs: air leaves it partly along the shaft and partly outward. FanPedia calls it a "hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller design" used in mixed flow fans with tubular housings (FanPedia PDF p. 6), and describes its shape: "airfoil blades taper from impeller front plate to hub end resulting in a larger tip width" (FanPedia PDF p. 32). Because the air turns only partway, a mixed flow fan can sit in a straight duct like an axial fan while developing more pressure than a comparable axial impeller.

Now that the centrifugal family and the mixed flow hybrid have been described, the comparison below summarizes them.

Impeller Blade shape (FanPedia caption) Air leaves Power curve Best airstream Backward inclined Flat, single thickness, tilted backward Outward, at a right angle to the shaft Non-overloading Clean to lightly dusty Forward curved Single thickness, curved forward; many short blades Outward, at a right angle to the shaft Overloading Clean Mixed flow Airfoil blades tapering from front plate to hub, larger tip width Partly along the shaft, partly outward Depends on design; see the catalog Clean

Do Not Judge a Wheel by Its Width

A common trap is calling any wheel with many narrow blades "forward curved" without checking which way the blades curve against the rotation. Before you write the impeller type on an order, find the rotation arrow and confirm the blade tips point with it (forward curved) or trail it (backward inclined).

docs.title: Axial Impellers
docs.text:
An axial impeller moves air parallel to the shaft. Its blades are attached to a central hub and, as the impeller turns, the concave side of each blade "cups the air and pushes it away from the impeller" (FanPedia PDF p. 37). Air enters at the blades' leading edges and leaves straight through, so an axial fan can sit in a duct with no change of direction. Axial impellers are used in tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans, roof mounted axial fans, and panel fans; FanPedia notes that inline centrifugal fans can share the same arrangements but use different impellers (FanPedia PDF p. 28).

FanPedia lays out three steps for configuring an axial fan (FanPedia PDF p. 36):

  1. Select the model and impeller type, for example "Model TCTA with 'TCTA' impeller."
  2. Choose the airflow direction: air through the impeller then over the motor (airflow = PM), or air over the motor then through the impeller (airflow = MP).
  3. Determine the rotation the impeller needs to produce that airflow direction.

FanPedia adds two notes to every axial airflow page: airflow direction and rotation "must be correct for the fan to operate at 100% performance," and if the impeller rotates in the wrong direction, "you will not get any airflow in the proper direction" (FanPedia PDF pp. 37–40). For axial fans, rotation is determined by viewing the impeller from the discharge side of the fan.

docs.title: Fixed Pitch and Adjustable Pitch Impellers
docs.text:
The pitch of an axial blade is its angle relative to the plane of rotation. A steeper pitch takes a bigger bite of air per revolution.

A fixed pitch impeller has its blades set at one angle that cannot be changed. FanPedia shows fixed pitch impellers as cast or fabricated (FanPedia PDF p. 35); its axial type pages mark the "TCTS," "TCTA," "Z Series," and "L Series" impellers as fixed (FanPedia PDF p. 34).

An adjustable pitch impeller has separate blades whose shanks are clamped into the hub, so the blade angle can be reset to a different pitch. Resetting the pitch moves the fan to a different performance curve without changing the impeller diameter or speed. FanPedia marks the "B Series," "E Series," "TCVX," "A," and "AXIAD" impellers as adjustable and the "C Series" as adjustable only (FanPedia PDF p. 33). Blade count and pitch angle are covered in more depth in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Fiberglass Axial Impeller
docs.text: A fiberglass axial impeller has blades, and sometimes a hub, molded from fiberglass-reinforced plastic instead of metal, which suits corrosive airstreams that would attack steel or aluminum. FanPedia shows a fiberglass group (FanPedia PDF p. 34): the "TF" and "FG7" impellers, marked fixed, and the adjustable "F4/F6" impellers with an aluminum hub and "FG4/FG6" impellers with a fiberglass hub. Whether the hub is aluminum or fiberglass is part of the impeller designation, so it has to be stated on the order.

docs.title: Worked Example: Configuring an Axial Fan
docs.text:
A customer needs a direct-drive tubeaxial fan to exhaust warm air from a process area, and asks how the order should describe the impeller. Following FanPedia's three steps:

  1. Model and impeller. Suppose the selection, made from the current catalog, is a fan with a fixed pitch cast impeller. (The model is not the point of this example.)
  2. Airflow direction. With airflow = PM, air passes through the impeller and then over the motor. With airflow = MP, air passes over the motor first. In a direct-drive axial fan the motor is in the airstream either way; when that is a problem, a belt-driven arrangement is the answer, which Chapter 11 covers. Here the customer chooses MP to match an existing duct layout.
  3. Rotation. Rotation is read from the discharge side. The rotation must match the impeller hand (left hand or right hand), because FanPedia shows both left hand and right hand fixed and adjustable impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43). A right hand impeller is ordered with right hand rotation.

The finished line on the order states the impeller, the airflow direction (MP), and the rotation, and the next section shows how MP also fixes the hub position.

docs.title: Hub on Intake Side and Hub on Discharge Side
docs.text:
FanPedia gives each airflow direction an alternative name based on where the hub's boss faces (FanPedia PDF pp. 36–40):

  • Hub on intake side: airflow = PM, air through the impeller then over the motor. The hub faces the incoming air.
  • Hub on discharge side: airflow = MP, air over the motor then through the impeller. The hub faces the leaving air.

In FanPedia's side views (pp. 37–40) the motor is on one side of the impeller and the hub on the other, so in both builds the hub faces away from the motor: in PM the side away from the motor is the intake, and in MP it is the discharge.

The hub bore follows the same choice. On FanPedia's left hand and right hand pages, a standard bore hub goes with MP airflow and a reverse bore hub goes with PM airflow, for both adjustable and fixed cast impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43). In other words, "MP," "hub on discharge," and "standard bore hub" all describe the same build, and "PM," "hub on intake," and "reverse bore hub" describe the other.

Airflow code Air path Also called Hub bore (FanPedia pp. 42–43) PM Through impeller, then over motor Hub on intake Reverse bore hub MP Over motor, then through impeller Hub on discharge Standard bore hub

One Letter Order, Three Answers

Read the airflow code left to right as the air's path; FanPedia capitalizes the P in "imPeller" to make the point, so PM means impeller first, then motor. If the impeller comes first, the hub faces the intake and the bore is reversed; if the motor comes first, the hub faces the discharge and the bore is standard.

docs.title: Reversible Impeller
docs.text: A reversible impeller is an axial impeller designed to move air in either direction along the shaft. FanPedia shows one reversible impeller in two modes (FanPedia PDF p. 41): standard flow, with airflow = MP and the hub on the discharge side, and reverse flow, with airflow = PM and the hub on the intake side. In both modes, air is drawn in at the blades' leading edge for that flow direction. FanPedia labels the rotation the same in both modes; since rotation is always viewed from the discharge side and the discharge switches ends when the flow reverses, the motor's actual direction of turning reverses with the flow. Reversible impellers are used where a single fan must both supply and exhaust, such as a space that is ventilated in one direction during some operations and the other direction at other times.

docs.title: Diagram: Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator
docs.text:
Run Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator Fullscreen

Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-axial-airflow-hub-configurator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply FanPedia's axial airflow rules to state the hub position and hub bore for an axial fan order, given its airflow code or air path, with at least 7 of 8 orders correct.

Prerequisites: axial impeller, blade leading edge, airflow = PM, airflow = MP, hub on intake side, hub on discharge side, standard bore hub, reverse bore hub, reversible impeller, rotation viewed from the discharge side (all defined in the section "Axial Impellers" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 orders the learner commits two answers before the fan is animated: hub position (intake side or discharge side) and hub bore (standard bore or reverse bore). An order is correct when both answers match the answer table. Mastery is 7 of 8 orders correct on the first attempt. Running the free model is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "Hub on intake" means the motor is on the intake side. (2) PM and MP are rotation codes rather than airflow codes. (3) A reversible impeller has a fixed hub position. (4) Running an axial impeller backward simply gives less airflow in the same direction.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a rule set to new orders, with a committed answer checked against the rule, is the Apply-level evidence; animating the air path only after the answer lets the learner see why the rule holds.

Content:

A side view of a direct-drive axial fan: tubular housing, motor, impeller with hub and blades, and labels "Intake" and "Discharge" that move with the airflow direction. The free model has two settings: airflow code (PM or MP) and rotation (correct for the impeller, or reversed).

The 8 orders, in this fixed order:

# Order text shown Hub position Hub bore Why (feedback) 1 Airflow = PM, adjustable pitch Intake side Reverse bore PM is air through the impeller then over the motor, also called hub on intake, built with a reverse bore hub. 2 Airflow = MP, fixed pitch cast Discharge side Standard bore MP is air over the motor then through the impeller, also called hub on discharge, built with a standard bore hub. 3 Air passes over the motor first, then through the impeller Discharge side Standard bore Motor first is MP, which is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub. 4 Air passes through the impeller first, then over the motor Intake side Reverse bore Impeller first is PM, which is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub. 5 Reversible impeller, standard flow Discharge side Standard bore FanPedia shows standard flow as MP, hub on discharge. 6 Reversible impeller, reverse flow Intake side Reverse bore FanPedia shows reverse flow as PM, hub on intake. 7 Right hand adjustable pitch impeller, airflow = MP Discharge side Standard bore Impeller hand does not change the rule: MP is a standard bore hub on the discharge side. 8 Left hand fixed cast impeller, airflow = PM Intake side Reverse bore Impeller hand does not change the rule: PM is a reverse bore hub on the intake side.

Provenance: Airflow codes, "aka" names, leading-edge statement and rotation viewing side from FanPedia PDF pp. 36–40; reversible impeller modes from FanPedia PDF p. 41; standard bore with MP and reverse bore with PM for left hand and right hand, adjustable and fixed cast impellers from FanPedia PDF pp. 42–43; wrong-rotation note from FanPedia PDF pp. 37–40.

Rules: PM gives hub on intake side and reverse bore hub. MP gives hub on discharge side and standard bore hub. Impeller hand (left or right) and pitch type (fixed or adjustable) do not change hub position or bore. Reversible impeller: standard flow = MP, reverse flow = PM. In the free model, correct rotation shows air entering at the leading edges and leaving at the discharge; reversed rotation shows no airflow in the intended direction, with the message "Wrong rotation: no airflow in the proper direction (FanPedia note 2)." The rotation is always labeled as viewed from the discharge side.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads an order and chooses a hub position and a hub bore, then presses Check.
  2. The fan is drawn with the hub on the correct side and animated with air moving in the order's direction, intake to discharge.
  3. Feedback appears; the learner moves to the next order.
  4. After order 8, the free model unlocks. The learner switches between PM and MP and watches the hub and the intake and discharge labels move, then reverses the rotation and sees the airflow stop in the intended direction.

Feedback: 8 orders, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct (both answers right): "Correct." followed by the Why text. Incorrect (either answer wrong): "Not quite." followed by the correct hub position and bore and the Why text. A running count "Orders correct: n of 8" is shown. No retry of scored items; the learner can restart the whole set.

Starting State: Order 1 is shown with the fan drawn without its hub, and the question "Which side does the hub face, and which hub bore does this build use?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that PM is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub, MP is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub, reversible standard flow is MP and reverse flow is PM, rotation is viewed from the discharge side, and wrong rotation gives no airflow in the proper direction. Mastery is 7 of 8.

Two Codes, Many Names

If PM, MP, hub on intake, hub on discharge, standard bore, and reverse bore feel like six things to memorize, most people feel the same on first pass. There are really only two builds with three names each, so learn the air path for one of them and the other is just its opposite; the configurator above lets you test that before it goes on an order.

docs.title: Hub Types
docs.text: The hub's bore has to grip the shaft tightly enough to carry full motor torque and stay put under vibration, and it must also come off when the impeller or shaft needs service. FanPedia shows two common ways to do this, for both centrifugal and axial impellers (FanPedia PDF pp. 44–45). A third, the Trantorque hub, is in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Straight Bore Hub
docs.text: In a straight bore hub, "the bore of the hub is straight through. Shafts are keyed and mounted to the hub" (FanPedia PDF p. 45). A key, a small square bar, sits half in a keyway in the shaft and half in a matching keyway in the hub, so it carries the torque. On centrifugal impellers, set screws through the hub press on the key and shaft to stop the hub sliding along the shaft. On axial impellers FanPedia shows two versions: with key and set screws, and with key, retaining washer, and bolt at the shaft end (FanPedia PDF p. 44). A straight bore has to be machined to suit one shaft diameter.

docs.title: Taper Lock Hub
docs.text: In a taper lock hub, "the hub bore is tapered with respect to the fan shaft. The hub is locked to the shaft using a tapered bushing" (FanPedia PDF p. 45). The bushing has a straight bore that fits the shaft and a tapered outside that fits the hub. Tightening the bushing's screws draws it into the tapered hub, which squeezes the bushing onto the shaft for a tight clamping fit along its whole length. Loosening the screws, and using the bushing's removal holes, releases it. FanPedia's axial version is shown "with key and hardware" (FanPedia PDF p. 44).

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing Between Two Hubs
docs.text:
A plant engineer replaces impellers every few years because of wear and wants the change-outs to be quick. The current impeller has a straight bore hub that has seized to the shaft twice. Compare the two hub types for this customer:

Question Straight bore hub Taper lock hub How is torque carried? Key in matching keyways Clamping fit of the bushing, with a key How is it held in place along the shaft? Set screws (or washer and bolt on axial) The bushing's grip on the shaft What does removal require? Pulling the hub off a close-fitting bore Loosening the bushing screws to release the taper Does the hub bore have to match the shaft? Yes, machined to one shaft diameter The bushing's bore matches the shaft

For this customer, the taper lock hub answers the stated problem: the taper releases the grip when the screws are backed out, so change-outs do not depend on forcing a close-fitting bore off the shaft. The hub type then goes on the replacement order along with the shaft diameter. Confirm in the current catalog that the impeller is offered with that hub.

docs.title: Impeller Balancing
docs.text:
An impeller is never perfectly symmetric. Slight differences in plate thickness, weld beads, and blade position leave more mass on one side of the axis than the other. When the impeller spins, that off-center mass is pulled outward and the whole rotor is pushed around in a circle once per revolution, which the bearings, shaft, and structure feel as vibration. Impeller balancing is the process of measuring that unbalance, usually by spinning the impeller on a balancing machine, and correcting it by adding or removing small weights until what is left, the residual unbalance, is within an allowed limit. Detailed balancing procedures are outside the scope of this course; what an application or sales engineer needs is why it matters and how the limit is set.

The force from a given unbalance grows with the square of speed. For a residual unbalance \( U \) in ounce-inches turning at \( N \) rpm, the rotating force is approximately:

\[ F \approx 1.77 \, U \left( \frac{N}{1000} \right)^2 \]

where \( F \) is the force in pounds-force (lbf), \( U \) is the unbalance (the unbalance mass in ounces multiplied by its distance from the axis in inches), and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

The allowed residual unbalance is set by a balance quality grade, \( G \), from the international balancing standard ISO 21940-11 (formerly ISO 1940-1). The grade is a speed in millimeters per second; a smaller grade is tighter balance. The fan industry standard AMCA 204 assigns balance grades by fan application category, with grades such as G6.3 and G2.5 common for industrial fans. For an impeller weighing \( W \) pounds running at a maximum service speed of \( N \) rpm, the permissible residual unbalance is:

\[ U_{per} = \frac{6.015 \, G \, W}{N} \]

where \( U_{per} \) is the permissible residual unbalance in ounce-inches, \( G \) is the balance grade in mm/s, \( W \) is the impeller weight in pounds, and \( N \) is the speed in rpm.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Unbalance Is Allowed?
docs.text:
A 200 lb impeller runs at 1,200 rpm and is balanced to grade G6.3 (illustrative values; the grade for a real fan comes from the specification or catalog).

  1. Permissible residual unbalance: \( U_{per} = 6.015 \times 6.3 \times 200 / 1200 = 6.32 \) oz·in.
  2. If the balancer corrects at a radius of 15 in, the largest uncorrected mass allowed there is \( 6.32 / 15 = 0.42 \) oz, less than half an ounce on a 200 lb wheel.
  3. At G2.5 the limit drops to \( 2.51 \) oz·in, or \( 0.17 \) oz at 15 in.
  4. The force from the G6.3 limit at 1,200 rpm is \( 1.77 \times 6.32 \times 1.2^2 \approx 16 \) lbf. Run the same impeller at 1,800 rpm and the force is about 36 lbf; at 2,400 rpm, twice the speed, about 64 lbf, four times as much.

That last step is the practical lesson: an impeller balanced for one speed is not automatically acceptable at a higher one, which is one more reason a speed increase is checked against the catalog before it is made.

docs.title: Diagram: Impeller Balance Calculator
docs.text:
Run Impeller Balance Calculator Fullscreen

Impeller Balance Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-impeller-balance-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the permissible residual unbalance and the matching correction mass for an impeller from its weight, speed, balance grade and correction radius, to within 2% of the model value.

Prerequisites: impeller balancing, residual unbalance, balance quality grade G, ounce-inch, correction radius (all defined in the section "Impeller Balancing" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge impellers the learner types the permissible residual unbalance (oz·in) and the correction mass (oz) before the answer is shown. A value is correct when it is within ±2% of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges with both values correct. Moving the free-exploration controls is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A heavier impeller is allowed less unbalance (it is allowed more, in proportion to weight). (2) Force from unbalance grows in proportion to speed (it grows with the square of speed). (3) A larger grade number means tighter balance (it means looser balance).

Instructional Rationale: Calculation at the Apply level needs practice with a committed, checked number; the free model afterward lets the learner see the speed-squared force growth that the misconceptions get wrong.

Content:

Adjustable quantities in free exploration:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Impeller weight W 20 2000 10 200 lb Maximum service speed N 300 3600 50 1200 rpm Correction radius r 4 40 1 15 in

Balance grade G choices: G16, G6.3, G2.5, G1.0. Default G6.3.

Displayed results: permissible residual unbalance U (oz·in, two decimals), correction mass m (oz, two decimals), rotating force F at the selected speed (lbf, whole number), and a line showing F at half and at double the selected speed when those speeds lie within 300–3600 rpm.

Challenge impellers, in this order (all illustrative):

# W (lb) N (rpm) G r (in) U (oz·in) m (oz) Feedback when wrong 1 200 1200 G6.3 15 6.32 0.42 U = 6.015 × 6.3 × 200 / 1200 = 6.32 oz·in; m = 6.32 / 15 = 0.42 oz. 2 200 1200 G2.5 15 2.51 0.17 A tighter grade lowers the limit: U = 6.015 × 2.5 × 200 / 1200 = 2.51 oz·in; m = 2.51 / 15 = 0.17 oz. 3 600 1800 G6.3 20 12.63 0.63 U = 6.015 × 6.3 × 600 / 1800 = 12.63 oz·in; m = 12.63 / 20 = 0.63 oz.

Provenance: Formulas from the chapter section "Impeller Balancing": U = 6.015 G W / N (ISO 21940-11 permissible residual unbalance converted to US units) and F ≈ 1.77 U (N/1000)². Grade choices are ISO balance quality grades. All weights, speeds and radii are illustrative and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: U = 6.015 × G × W / N, with G in mm/s, W in lb, N in rpm, U in oz·in. m = U / r. F = 1.77 × U × (N/1000)². Speed N is the speed used for both U and F. Values are rounded only for display. Answers are judged within ±2% of the unrounded model value.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types U and m.
  2. The learner presses Check. The model values and the worked calculation appear next to the learner's answers.
  3. After the three challenges, free exploration unlocks: the learner changes W, N, G and r, and U, m and F update at once.
  4. The learner sets N to 1,200 rpm and then to 2,400 rpm. The force line and bars keep the same impeller's U fixed, as in the chapter's worked example, so F at double the speed is four times larger (about 16 lbf to about 64 lbf for the default impeller). A separate line notes that the grade limit at 2,400 rpm is half of U, so the same impeller would have to be balanced tighter to run that fast.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct (both values within ±2%): "Correct: U = oz·in, m = oz." Hint after a first wrong attempt: which value is off ("Your U is within 2%; your m is not.") and the rule for it, never the model values: "Use U = 6.015 × G × W / N, with G in mm/s, W in lb and N in rpm." / "The correction mass is m = U / r, with r in inches." Slip notes replace the rule when they apply: U without the 6.015 factor ("Multiply by the 6.015 unit-conversion factor as well."), W and N swapped ("A heavier impeller is allowed more unbalance: W goes on top and N underneath."), divided by G ("Multiply by the grade G; do not divide by it."), m = U × r ("m = U / r: divide by the correction radius, do not multiply."), m consistent with a wrong U ("Your m follows from your U, so fixing U fixes m."); challenge 2 adds "A tighter grade (a smaller G) lowers the limit." After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge with the model values and calculation, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 with empty answer boxes and the question "How much unbalance may this 200 lb impeller keep at 1,200 rpm and grade G6.3?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses W = 200 lb, N = 1,200 rpm, G6.3, r = 15 in and gets U = 6.32 oz·in and m = 0.42 oz; G2.5 gives 2.51 oz·in and 0.17 oz; F is about 16 lbf at 1,200 rpm, about 36 lbf at 1,800 rpm and about 64 lbf at 2,400 rpm.

docs.title: Identifying an Impeller Type
docs.text: You now have the vocabulary to name an impeller from what you can see. The decision runs in a fixed order: first the air path (outward, straight through, or partway), then for centrifugal impellers the blade shape against rotation and the number of inlets, and for axial impellers the pitch type, material, and hub position. The classifier below gives you practice on descriptions like the ones you will meet in field photos and catalog pages.

docs.title: Diagram: Impeller Type Classifier
docs.text:
Run Impeller Type Classifier Fullscreen

Impeller Type Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: ch08-impeller-type-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify written descriptions of impellers into the impeller types named in this chapter, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: centrifugal impeller, axial impeller, mixed flow impeller, backward inclined impeller, forward curved impeller, single width single inlet, fixed pitch impeller, adjustable pitch impeller, fiberglass axial impeller, reversible impeller (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner sorts each of 10 description cards into one of six bins before any feedback is shown for that card. A card is correct when its bin matches the answer column. Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Many narrow blades always means forward curved. (2) Any impeller in a tubular housing is axial. (3) Adjustable pitch means the blades can be changed while the fan runs. (4) Fiberglass impellers are always fixed pitch.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying new descriptions requires the learner to apply the defining features of each type rather than recall a picture, and asking for a prediction before feedback makes the learner commit to a reason.

Content:

Bins: Backward inclined (centrifugal); Forward curved (centrifugal); Mixed flow; Axial, fixed pitch; Axial, adjustable pitch; Axial, reversible.

# Card text Correct bin Why (feedback) 1 Flat, single-thickness blades whose tips trail the direction of rotation; air leaves at a right angle to the shaft Backward inclined (centrifugal) Flat blades tilted backward against rotation define backward inclined. 2 Many short, shallow blades curved so their tips point in the direction of rotation, held by an end ring and tie rods Forward curved (centrifugal) Tips pointing with rotation, plus end ring and tie rods, define forward curved. 3 Airfoil blades that taper from the front plate to the hub end, giving a larger tip width; air leaves partly along the shaft Mixed flow A tapered blade with partly axial discharge is the hybrid axial-centrifugal impeller. 4 Cast impeller with blades formed at one angle that cannot be changed Axial, fixed pitch Cast or fabricated blades at one angle are fixed pitch. 5 Separate blades whose shanks clamp into the hub so the blade angle can be reset Axial, adjustable pitch Clamped shanks allow the pitch to be reset. 6 One axial impeller shown in two modes: standard flow MP and reverse flow PM Axial, reversible An impeller built to move air either way along the shaft is reversible. 7 Fiberglass blades on an aluminum hub, sold as the "F4/F6" impeller Axial, adjustable pitch FanPedia marks F4/F6 and FG4/FG6 as adjustable; fiberglass does not mean fixed. 8 Fiberglass "TF" impeller with molded blades Axial, fixed pitch FanPedia marks the TF impeller as fixed. 9 A single width single inlet wheel with backward-tilted flat blades in an inline (tubular) centrifugal fan Backward inclined (centrifugal) Air still leaves the wheel outward; the tubular housing turns it back in line, so the impeller is centrifugal. 10 "TCTA" impeller, as listed in FanPedia's axial impeller types Axial, fixed pitch FanPedia marks the TCTA impeller as fixed.

Provenance: Centrifugal captions from FanPedia PDF p. 31; mixed flow caption from FanPedia PDF p. 32 and hybrid description from p. 6; fixed and adjustable markings from FanPedia PDF pp. 33–34; fixed pitch "cast or fabricated" from p. 35; reversible modes from p. 41.

Rules: Each card has exactly one correct bin, given in the table. Cards are judged on the first placement only for the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. A card appears; the learner drags or assigns it to one bin.
  2. The card is marked correct or incorrect and the Why text is shown.
  3. Incorrectly placed cards return to a review pile that the learner can redo after card 10.

Feedback: 10 cards in shuffled order, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "This one is ." plus the Why text. Score "n of 10" shown at the end; the review pile does not change the score.

Starting State: Six empty bins and the first card, with the prompt "Where does the air go, and what do the blades look like?"

Chapter Anchors: Mastery is 8 of 10. The chapter states that TCTA, TF and FG7 are fixed, F4/F6 and FG4/FG6 are adjustable, and reversible standard flow is MP and reverse flow is PM.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The impeller is the only part of a fan that adds energy to the air; its blades push the air, and the blade leading edge meets the incoming air first.
  • A centrifugal impeller's blades sit between a back plate and a shroud (FanPedia's impeller front plate); back plate fins on the back reduce bearing thrust and help limit leakage at the shaft hole.
  • The hub connects the impeller to the shaft. A straight bore hub is keyed and held by set screws (or a washer and bolt); a taper lock hub clamps to the shaft through a tapered bushing.
  • A centrifugal impeller throws air outward at a right angle to the shaft. A single width single inlet impeller takes air from one side and can be overhung; double width impellers are center hung in Arrangements 3 and 7.
  • Backward inclined impellers have flat blades tilted against rotation and a non-overloading power curve; forward curved impellers have many short blades curved with rotation, run slower and smaller, and have an overloading power curve.
  • A mixed flow impeller is a hybrid whose airfoil blades taper from front plate to hub, sending air partly along the shaft.
  • An axial impeller moves air parallel to the shaft, with fixed pitch (cast or fabricated) or adjustable pitch blades; fiberglass axial impellers come in both.
  • Airflow PM is hub on intake with a reverse bore hub; airflow MP is hub on discharge with a standard bore hub. A reversible impeller runs standard flow MP and reverse flow PM. Axial rotation is viewed from the discharge side, and wrong rotation gives no airflow in the proper direction.
  • Impeller balancing limits residual unbalance to \( U_{per} = 6.015\,G\,W/N \); the vibration force from unbalance grows with the square of speed.

You Can Name the Wheel

You can now name every major impeller part, tell backward inclined from forward curved by the blades alone, and turn an axial airflow code into a hub position and bore. That is exactly what an impeller line on an order needs.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types
docs.text: Test your understanding of impeller parts, centrifugal and axial impeller types, airflow codes and hub position, hub types, and impeller balancing with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does FanPedia's centrifugal impeller drawing call the ring-shaped plate on the inlet side of the impeller, also known as the impeller shroud?
docs.text:
1. The hub boss
  2. The back plate
  3. The wiper bar
  4. The impeller front plate
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The impeller shroud is the ring-shaped plate on the inlet side of a centrifugal impeller, with a large central hole where air enters. FanPedia labels it the impeller front plate, and both names are common in the trade. Together with the back plate on the closed side, it sandwiches the blades and guides air outward. The hub boss is the raised center of an axial hub, and the wiper bar is a housing part near the inlet funnel.

Concept Tested: Impeller Shroud

See: Impeller Back Plate and Impeller Shroud

docs.title: 2. According to FanPedia, what do back plate fins (also called thrust fins or anti-thrust vanes) do?
docs.text:
1. They add airflow by acting as a second set of blades
  2. They reduce the thrust load on the bearings and help limit airstream leakage through the shaft hole
  3. They hold the blades of a forward curved impeller in a drum shape
  4. They lock the hub to the shaft without a key
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Back plate fins are small radial vanes on the outside of the back plate. FanPedia says they "reduce the thrust load on the bearings" and can create a negative pressure behind the impeller that draws air in through the shaft hole, which helps reduce leakage of the airstream to atmosphere. They are not working blades. End rings hold forward curved blades, and a keyless hub lock is a different part entirely.

Concept Tested: Back Plate Fins

See: Back Plate Fins

docs.title: 3. What does it mean that a backward inclined fan has a non-overloading power curve?
docs.text:
1. Its brake horsepower is the same at every airflow
  2. Its brake horsepower keeps rising as airflow increases
  3. At a fixed speed, its brake horsepower rises to a peak and then falls, so a motor sized for the peak cannot be overloaded at that speed
  4. It can never draw more than its design-point horsepower, whatever the speed
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. On a backward inclined fan's curve, brake horsepower at a fixed speed rises to a peak and then falls as airflow keeps increasing. A motor sized for that peak cannot be overloaded at that speed, wherever the fan ends up operating on its curve. Option B describes the overloading curve of a forward curved impeller. Option D overstates the idea: the protection holds only at that speed, not at any speed.

Concept Tested: Backward Inclined Impeller

See: Backward Inclined Impeller

docs.title: 4. A 24-inch centrifugal impeller runs at 1,750 rpm. Using V = πDN / 12, what is its tip speed?
docs.text:
1. About 11,000 ft/min
  2. About 132,000 ft/min
  3. About 3,500 ft/min
  4. About 5,500 ft/min
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Tip speed is π × 24 × 1,750 / 12 = π × 3,500 ≈ 10,996 ft/min, about 11,000 ft/min. Option B forgets to divide by 12 to convert inches to feet, option C leaves out π, and option D uses the radius instead of the diameter. Tip speed matters because higher tip speed lets the blades build more pressure and also puts more stress on the impeller.

Concept Tested: Centrifugal Impeller

See: Centrifugal Impellers

docs.title: 5. A tubeaxial fan order specifies airflow = PM. Which hub position and hub bore go with that build?
docs.text:
1. Hub on intake side, with a reverse bore hub
  2. Hub on discharge side, with a reverse bore hub
  3. Hub on discharge side, with a standard bore hub
  4. Hub on intake side, with a standard bore hub
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Read the code as the air's path: PM means through the impeller first, then over the motor. FanPedia calls that build hub on intake side, and its left hand and right hand pages pair it with a reverse bore hub. The opposite build, MP (over the motor, then through the impeller), is hub on discharge side with a standard bore hub. Options B and D mix the two builds.

Concept Tested: Hub on Intake Side

See: Hub on Intake Side and Hub on Discharge Side

docs.title: 6. A contractor asks for a direct drive fan with a double inlet impeller mounted on the motor shaft (Arrangement 4). Why is that request inconsistent?
docs.text:
1. Arrangement 4 is a belt drive arrangement
  2. Double inlet impellers are used only on axial fans
  3. A double inlet impeller takes air from both sides, so a motor shaft ending inside it would block one inlet; double width fans are center hung in Arrangements 3 and 7
  4. Arrangement 4 requires a forward curved impeller
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A single width single inlet impeller has one closed side, so a shaft can enter from that side and the impeller can hang on the end of the motor shaft. A double inlet impeller takes air from both sides, so a shaft cannot end inside it without blocking one inlet. FanPedia's double width, double inlet page lists only Arrangement 3 and 7 variants, with the impeller between two bearings. Arrangement 4 is direct drive, not belt drive.

Concept Tested: Single Width Single Inlet

See: Single Width Single Inlet

docs.title: 7. Why does a taper lock hub make impeller change-outs easier than a straight bore hub?
docs.text:
1. It needs no bushing at all
  2. Loosening the bushing screws releases the taper's grip, so the hub does not have to be forced off a close-fitting bore
  3. It is welded to the shaft, so the shaft and impeller are replaced together
  4. Its bore is machined to match one shaft diameter exactly
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In a taper lock hub, a tapered bushing with a straight bore is drawn into the tapered hub by its screws, clamping it onto the shaft. Backing the screws out, using the bushing's removal holes, releases the grip, so change-outs do not depend on pulling a hub off a close-fitting bore. Option D describes the straight bore hub, which must be machined to one shaft diameter and is the type that can seize.

Concept Tested: Taper Lock Hub

See: Taper Lock Hub

docs.title: 8. A 100 lb impeller with a maximum service speed of 1,800 rpm is balanced to grade G6.3. Using U = 6.015 G W / N, what is the permissible residual unbalance?
docs.text:
1. About 0.21 oz·in
  2. About 21.1 oz·in
  3. About 6.32 oz·in
  4. About 2.11 oz·in
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Multiply 6.015 × 6.3 × 100 = 3,790, then divide by 1,800 rpm to get about 2.11 oz·in. Options A and B are off by a factor of ten, a decimal slip. Option C is the chapter's worked example for a 200 lb impeller at 1,200 rpm. A higher speed or a tighter grade (smaller G) lowers the permissible unbalance.

Concept Tested: Impeller Balancing

See: Impeller Balancing

docs.title: 9. An impeller balanced for 1,200 rpm is later run at 2,400 rpm with the same residual unbalance. How does the rotating force from that unbalance change?
docs.text:
1. It stays the same, because the unbalance has not changed
  2. It becomes about four times as large
  3. It doubles, in proportion to speed
  4. It falls by half, because the impeller is better centered at speed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The force from a given unbalance grows with the square of speed, F ≈ 1.77 U (N/1000)². Doubling the speed multiplies the force by 2² = 4; in the chapter's example, about 16 lbf at 1,200 rpm becomes about 64 lbf at 2,400 rpm. Option C assumes a straight proportion. This is why an impeller balanced for one speed is not automatically acceptable at a higher one, and why speed increases are checked against the catalog.

Concept Tested: Impeller Balancing

See: Impeller Balancing

docs.title: 10. A colleague calls a wheel "forward curved" because it has many narrow blades. What should be checked before that impeller type goes on the order?
docs.text:
1. The impeller diameter, since forward curved wheels are always larger
  2. Whether the hub is straight bore or taper lock
  3. Whether the blade tips point in the direction of rotation or trail it, using the rotation arrow
  4. Whether the fan has back plate fins
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Blade count and width do not identify the type; the direction of the blade curve against rotation does. Forward curved blade tips point in the direction of rotation, while backward inclined tips trail it. Find the rotation arrow and confirm the curve before writing the impeller type. Forward curved wheels actually move a given airflow in a smaller size, and hub type and back plate fins say nothing about blade shape.

Concept Tested: Forward Curved Impeller

See: Forward Curved Impeller

docs.title: References: Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types
docs.text:
1. Impeller - Wikipedia - General overview of impellers, their blades, shrouds and hubs in pumps and fans. A good companion to this chapter's naming of impeller parts.

  2. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia - Compares backward inclined, forward curved and radial blade centrifugal fans, including their power characteristics. Supports the chapter's discussion of overloading and non-overloading curves.

  3. Rotating unbalance - Wikipedia - Explains how an off-center mass on a rotor produces a force that grows with the square of speed. The physics behind the chapter's impeller balancing section.

  4. Fans: Design and Operation of Centrifugal, Axial-Flow and Cross-Flow Fans - Bruno Eck - Pergamon Press - Eck's classic text explains fan behavior from the blade outward, relating blade shape and angle to pressure and flow for centrifugal and axial impellers.

  5. Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Turbomachinery - S. L. Dixon and C. A. Hall - Butterworth-Heinemann - Widely used for its clear velocity-triangle treatment, which shows why forward, radial and backward blade angles change the pressure an impeller develops.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Source for the impeller drawings (pp. 31-35), axial airflow and hub position pages (pp. 36-43), hub types (pp. 44-45) and back plate fins cited in this chapter.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Online edition of FanPedia, including the fan components section on impellers and hubs. Useful for checking impeller and airflow-code terminology.

  8. AMCA Publications - Air Movement and Control Association - Lists AMCA Standard 204, Balance Quality and Vibration Levels for Fans, the standard the chapter cites for assigning balance grades by fan application category.

  9. Axial Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans, including adjustable pitch models such as TCVX. Shows how the axial impeller types in this chapter appear as products.

  10. Centrifugal Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page listing SWSI and DWDI housed centrifugal fans with backward inclined, backward curved, airfoil and forward curved impellers, the types compared in this chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter goes deeper into impeller design: airfoil and backward curved blades, double width double inlet impellers, impeller width and airflow path, end rings, gussets and tie rods, axial blade tips, blade count and pitch angle, and fiberglass and Trantorque hubs. It then covers impellers built for dirty airstreams: radial bladed, radial tip, open radial paddle, material handling, and paper handling designs. After completing it, readers can explain why a given impeller suits clean air, high efficiency, or a particulate-laden airstream.
