docs.text:
Run Operating Point Finder Fullscreen

Operating Point Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch10-operating-point-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve for the operating point of an illustrative fan in a stated duct system by predicting where the fan curve and system curve intersect, to within ±300 CFM and ±0.15 in. wg.

Prerequisites: fan curve, system resistance, system curve, operating point, stall region, brake horsepower (all defined in the sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge systems, the learner commits a predicted operating point (airflow in CFM and pressure in in. wg) before the intersection is revealed. A prediction is correct when the airflow is within ±300 CFM and the pressure within ±0.15 in. wg of the model intersection. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Free changes to the system curve after the challenges are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A fan always delivers its rated airflow, whatever the system. (2) A dirtier, more resistant system makes the fan move more air "because it works harder." (3) The system curve is a straight line, so 20% more air needs 20% more pressure.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level solving needs the learner to use the two curves to reach a number, so each challenge asks for a committed prediction before the intersection is drawn. Free exploration afterward lets the learner watch the operating point slide along the fan curve as the system curve steepens or flattens.

Content:

The fan curve is Curve A from the Fan Curve Explorer (illustrative backward inclined fan at one fixed speed, standard air), joined by straight lines between points:

Airflow (CFM) FSP (in. wg) BHP 0 4.6 4.0 2,000 4.8 5.0 4,000 4.9 6.0 6,000 4.8 7.0 8,000 4.5 8.1 10,000 4.0 9.0 12,000 3.2 9.5 14,000 2.0 9.4 16,000 0.4 8.8

Challenge systems, in this fixed order:

# System described to the learner Model operating point BHP at that point Feedback when wrong 1 "As designed: 4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM." 10,000 CFM, 4.00 in. wg 9.0 The fan curve passes through 4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM, exactly where the system needs 4.0 in. wg, so the curves cross at the design point. 2 "Filters loaded: 4.0 in. wg at 8,000 CFM." 8,390 CFM, 4.40 in. wg 8.3 A steeper system curve crosses the fan curve further left. At 8,000 CFM the fan offers 4.5 in. wg and the system needs 4.0, so the fan pushes on until about 8,390 CFM. 3 "Resistance overestimated: 2.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM." 11,600 CFM, 3.36 in. wg 9.4 A flatter system curve crosses further right. The fan moves more air than designed, and BHP rises toward its 9.5 maximum.

Readouts shown after each reveal: operating airflow (nearest 10 CFM, shown to the exact CFM when rounding would cross the 4,000 CFM stall boundary, so a stall-region point never reads 4,000), operating pressure (two decimals), BHP at that airflow (one decimal, interpolated linearly from the table), and whether the point is in the stall region.

Free-exploration input (unlocked after the challenges): the system's resistance at 10,000 CFM.

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit System resistance at 10,000 CFM 1.0 35.0 0.1 4.0 in. wg

Provenance: The fan curve is illustrative (the chapter's illustrative fan curve table) and must be labeled "Illustrative fan curve." The three challenge systems and their model intersections are from the chapter section "The Operating Point." The square law is standard fan engineering.

Rules: System curve: P = R × (Q ÷ 10,000)², where R is the resistance at 10,000 CFM (challenge 2's system has R = 6.25 in. wg, equivalent to 4.0 in. wg at 8,000 CFM; challenge 3's has R = 2.5 in. wg). Fan pressure and BHP between table points are linearly interpolated. The operating point is the airflow, searched in 1 CFM steps from 0 to 16,000 CFM, where |fan pressure − system pressure| is smallest. An operating point with airflow < 4,000 CFM is flagged "In the stall region: select a different fan." If R is so high that the curves cross at less than 4,000 CFM, the flag is shown; the default range always produces an intersection. Prediction correct when |predicted CFM − model CFM| <= 300 and |predicted pressure − model pressure| <= 0.15.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1. The fan curve and the system curve are drawn; the intersection is not marked.
  2. The learner places a predicted operating point (airflow and pressure) and presses Check. The sim marks the true intersection, shows the readouts, and compares the prediction.
  3. The learner repeats for challenges 2 and 3. Each new challenge redraws the system curve and hides the previous intersection.
  4. After the third challenge, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes the system resistance at 10,000 CFM, and the system curve, intersection and readouts update at once. The learner should notice that above about R = 30.6 in. wg the operating point falls below 4,000 CFM and enters the stall region.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: the curves cross at CFM and in. wg." Hint after a first wrong attempt, with no intersection values and nothing drawn: challenge 1 "The operating point is where the fan curve and the dashed system curve meet. Follow the dashed curve out from the origin until it reaches the fan curve, then read the airflow and pressure at that crossing."; challenge 2 "A steeper system curve crosses the fan curve further left. Where the fan offers more pressure than the system needs, the airflow keeps rising until the two pressures match."; challenge 3 "A flatter system curve crosses further right: the fan moves more air than designed. Follow both curves to the right until they meet." One note about the prediction is added when it applies: airflow within tolerance ("Your airflow is close; read the pressure where the two curves meet."), pressure within tolerance (the same for airflow), or a point on only one curve ("Your point is on the fan curve but not on the system curve; slide along the fan curve until it meets the dashed curve." and the reverse). After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge, the intersection is revealed and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with the fan curve and the as-designed system curve and no intersection marked. The prompt reads: "Where will this fan actually run in this system?"

Chapter Anchors: As designed: 10,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg and 9.0 BHP. Dirty filters (4.0 in. wg at 8,000 CFM): about 8,390 CFM at 4.40 in. wg and about 8.3 BHP. Resistance overestimated (2.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM): about 11,600 CFM at 3.36 in. wg and about 9.4 BHP. The system curve through 4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM needs 5.76 in. wg at 12,000 CFM and 2.56 in. wg at 8,000 CFM. Curve A's stall region begins below 4,000 CFM, which this system family reaches only above about R = 30.6 in. wg.

docs.title: System Effect
docs.text:
A catalog rating is measured with the fan connected to ideal test ductwork: long, straight, uniform runs that deliver a smooth, even airflow into the inlet and carry it away from the outlet without disturbance. Real installations seldom look like that. An elbow bolted directly to the fan inlet, a short or missing discharge duct, or an abrupt transition makes the fan perform worse than its rating. System effect is that loss of fan performance caused by the way the fan is connected to the system, expressed as an extra pressure the fan must overcome. It is not a loss in the ductwork itself; it exists only because the fan's inlet or outlet airflow is disturbed.

System effect matters because neither the fan curve nor the designer's system curve contains it. If it is ignored, the actual operating point falls short of the design point, even though both the fan and the duct calculations are correct. FanPedia gives a practical example: inlet boxes are used when the installation does not allow a straight run of duct into the fan, and the inlet box "is designed to minimize the system effect of a 90 degree turn into the fan" (FanPedia p. 187). Values for system effect come from AMCA Publication 201, Fans and Systems, which tabulates the loss for common inlet and outlet connections. The detailed inlet and outlet cases and the system effect curve are covered in Chapter 25.

docs.title: Worked Example: Allowing for System Effect
docs.text:
A designer calculates 4.0 in. wg of duct resistance at 10,000 CFM and selects the fan at exactly that point. The fan is installed with an elbow directly on its inlet, which carries a system effect of 0.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM (illustrative). The fan must now overcome 4.5 in. wg to move 10,000 CFM, but the illustrative fan curve offers only 4.0 in. wg there. Because the system effect also rises with airflow squared, the effective system curve passes through 4.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM, and it crosses the fan curve at about 9,560 CFM and 4.11 in. wg. The job is about 4% short of its air, and nothing in the duct calculation or the catalog explains why. A larger system effect, or a fan selected on a steeper part of its curve, makes the shortfall larger.

The correct practice is to add the system effect to the design pressure before selection, so the fan is chosen at 10,000 CFM and 4.5 in. wg (a higher speed or a larger fan), or to change the connection so the system effect disappears, for instance by adding straight duct or an inlet box. The ordered steps are:

  1. Calculate the duct system resistance at the design airflow.
  2. Identify each non-ideal fan connection and look up its system effect at the design airflow.
  3. Add the system effects to the duct resistance.
  4. Select the fan at the design airflow and the sum.

System Effect Is Not in the Fan Curve

Watch out for field complaints that blame the fan for a shortfall caused by its connection. The catalog rating assumes ideal ductwork, so an elbow on the inlet costs pressure no table shows. Before you quote, ask what is bolted to the inlet and outlet, and add the system effect to the design pressure.

docs.title: Density Corrections
docs.text:
Every catalog rating assumes standard air: 0.075 lb/ft³, which is dry air at 70°F at sea-level barometric pressure (29.92 in. Hg). Real jobs are hotter, colder, higher or wetter. A fan running at a fixed speed moves the same volume of air (the same CFM) whatever the density, because the impeller sweeps the same volume each revolution. But the pressure it develops and the power it absorbs are both proportional to density. Lighter air means less pressure and less horsepower; heavier air means more of both.

The density correction factor is the ratio of the actual air density to standard density. It converts between catalog (standard-air) values and actual job values:

docs.title: Density Correction Factor
docs.text:
\[ K_d = \frac{\rho_{actual}}{0.075} \] \[ P_{actual} = P_{std} \times K_d \qquad BHP_{actual} = BHP_{std} \times K_d \]

where:

  • \( K_d \) is the density correction factor (dimensionless)
  • \( \rho_{actual} \) is the actual air density in lb/ft³
  • \( P \) is fan pressure in in. wg and \( BHP \) is brake horsepower, at standard or actual conditions as subscripted

To select a fan from a standard-air catalog for a job at non-standard density, the procedure runs in the opposite direction: divide the actual required pressure by \( K_d \) to get the equivalent standard-air pressure, look up the fan at the actual CFM and that pressure, then multiply the catalog BHP by \( K_d \) to get the actual BHP. The two most common causes of non-standard density are temperature and altitude, and each has its own factor.

docs.title: Temperature Correction
docs.text: Air expands as it is heated, so hot air is less dense than standard air. A temperature correction is the density correction factor for a temperature other than 70°F. Since density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature, the factor uses absolute temperatures in degrees Rankine (°F + 460):

docs.title: Temperature Correction Factor
docs.text:
\[ K_t = \frac{70 + 460}{T + 460} = \frac{530}{T + 460} \]

where:

  • \( K_t \) is the temperature correction factor (dimensionless)
  • \( T \) is the actual air temperature at the fan inlet in °F

The table lists the factor at several temperatures. All values come from the equation and are standard engineering values.

Air temperature (°F) Temperature correction factor 0 1.152 70 1.000 120 0.914 200 0.803 300 0.697 400 0.616 600 0.500 800 0.421

docs.title: Worked Example: A Hot Exhaust Fan
docs.text: An oven exhaust fan must handle 8,000 CFM of 200°F air against 2.0 in. wg of actual static pressure at sea level. The temperature factor is \( 530/660 = 0.803 \). The equivalent standard-air pressure is \( 2.0 / 0.803 = 2.49 \) in. wg, so the fan is selected from the catalog at 8,000 CFM and 2.49 in. wg. If the catalog shows, illustratively, 4.6 BHP at that point, the fan absorbs \( 4.6 \times 0.803 = 3.7 \) BHP when running hot. When the same fan starts up cold, the air is denser and the BHP is higher, which is why hot fans need a cold-start motor check (cold start horsepower is covered in Chapter 25).

docs.title: Altitude Correction
docs.text: Barometric pressure falls with elevation, and air density falls with it. An altitude correction is the density correction factor for a site above sea level, equal to the ratio of the local standard barometric pressure to the sea-level value. It can be computed from the standard atmosphere:

docs.title: Altitude Correction Factor
docs.text:
\[ K_a = \left( 1 - 6.875 \times 10^{-6} \times h \right)^{5.2559} \]

where:

  • \( K_a \) is the altitude correction factor (dimensionless)
  • \( h \) is the site elevation in feet above sea level

The table gives the factor at 1,000-foot steps. Combined temperature and altitude effects multiply: \( K_d = K_t \times K_a \).

Elevation (ft) Altitude correction factor 0 1.000 1,000 0.964 2,000 0.930 3,000 0.896 4,000 0.864 5,000 0.832 6,000 0.801 7,000 0.772 8,000 0.743

docs.title: Worked Example: A Hot Fan at Altitude
docs.text:
A dryer exhaust fan in a plant at 5,000 ft must move 10,000 CFM of 200°F air against 3.0 in. wg actual static pressure.

  1. Temperature factor: \( K_t = 530/660 = 0.803 \).
  2. Altitude factor: \( K_a = 0.832 \) from the table.
  3. Combined factor: \( K_d = 0.803 \times 0.832 = 0.668 \).
  4. Equivalent standard-air pressure: \( 3.0 / 0.668 = 4.49 \) in. wg.
  5. Select the fan from the catalog at 10,000 CFM and 4.49 in. wg. Suppose the catalog shows 11.0 BHP at that point (illustrative).
  6. Actual BHP when running hot at altitude: \( 11.0 \times 0.668 = 7.35 \) BHP.

A salesperson who skips steps 1 through 4 and selects at 3.0 in. wg will deliver a fan that falls about a third short on pressure at the job.

Two Directions, One Factor

If density corrections feel slippery, that's normal; most people mix up the dividing and multiplying direction at first. You already handle the factor itself, so anchor on one sentence: pressure goes into the catalog divided by the factor, and horsepower comes out of the catalog multiplied by it. Work the dryer example once more with your own numbers and it will stick.

docs.title: Diagram: Density Correction Calculator
docs.text:
Run Density Correction Calculator Fullscreen

Density Correction Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch10-density-correction-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the combined density correction factor for a stated air temperature and site elevation, and use it to convert an actual static pressure to the standard-air pressure used for catalog selection, to within ±0.01 on the factor and ±0.05 in. wg on the pressure.

Prerequisites: standard air, density correction factor, temperature correction, altitude correction, degrees Rankine (all defined in the section "Density Corrections" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge jobs the learner types the combined factor and, for challenge 3, the standard-air pressure, before the model values are shown. A factor is correct when within ±0.01 of the model value; a pressure is correct when within ±0.05 in. wg. Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges fully correct. Moving the exploration inputs is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The fan moves less CFM in hot or thin air at the same speed. (2) The actual pressure is multiplied by the factor to get the catalog pressure, instead of divided. (3) Temperature in °F can be used directly in the ratio, without adding 460.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check on each step, so the learner commits each factor before it is revealed. Free exploration afterward shows that a hot fan at altitude can need a catalog pressure half again as large as the job pressure.

Content:

Challenge jobs, in this fixed order:

# Job shown to the learner Asked Model answer Feedback when wrong 1 200°F air at sea level (0 ft) Combined factor 0.803 Use absolute temperatures: 530 ÷ (200 + 460) = 0.803. Sea level has an altitude factor of 1.000. 2 70°F air at 5,000 ft Combined factor 0.832 At 70°F the temperature factor is 1.000; the altitude factor at 5,000 ft is 0.832. 3 200°F air at 5,000 ft, 3.0 in. wg actual static pressure, 10,000 CFM Combined factor, then standard-air pressure 0.668, then 4.49 in. wg Multiply the two factors: 0.803 × 0.832 = 0.668. Divide the actual pressure by the factor: 3.0 ÷ 0.668 = 4.49 in. wg. The CFM does not change.

Free-exploration inputs (unlocked after the challenges):

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Air temperature at fan inlet 0 800 10 70 °F Site elevation 0 10,000 500 0 ft Actual static pressure 0.5 15.0 0.1 3.0 in. wg Catalog BHP at the standard-air point 1.0 200.0 0.5 11.0 BHP

Readouts in exploration: temperature factor, altitude factor, combined factor (each to three decimals), standard-air pressure for catalog selection (two decimals), actual BHP (two decimals), and the unchanged CFM statement "Airflow volume is the same at any density for a fan at fixed speed."

Provenance: Equations are standard engineering: K_t = 530 ÷ (T + 460) and the standard-atmosphere altitude formula. The challenge jobs and the 11.0 BHP default are illustrative and must be labeled "Illustrative values." Challenge 3 and the 11.0 BHP default match the chapter's worked example "A Hot Fan at Altitude."

Rules: K_t = 530 ÷ (T + 460), T in °F. K_a = (1 − 6.875 × 10⁻⁶ × h)^5.2559, h in feet. K_d = K_t × K_a. Standard-air pressure = actual pressure ÷ K_d. Actual BHP = catalog BHP × K_d. Factors rounded to three decimals, pressures to two. A factor is correct when |answer − model| <= 0.01; a pressure when |answer − model| <= 0.05. All input ranges keep T + 460 > 0 and K_a > 0.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types the combined factor.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the model factor and the one-line calculation.
  3. The learner completes challenge 2, then challenge 3 in two parts: the factor first, then the standard-air pressure. The second part appears only after the first is checked.
  4. After challenge 3, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes temperature, elevation, actual pressure and catalog BHP, and every readout updates at once. The learner should notice that at 800°F the combined factor at sea level is 0.421, so the catalog pressure is more than twice the job pressure.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts per answer. Correct: "Correct: ." Hint after a first wrong attempt, never the model value or a finished calculation: challenge 1 "Use absolute temperatures: Kt = 530 ÷ (T + 460). Sea level has an altitude factor of 1.000."; challenge 2 "At 70°F the temperature factor is 1.000, so Kd is the altitude factor: Ka = (1 − 6.875 × 10⁻⁶ × h)^5.2559, with h in feet."; challenge 3 part 1 "Kd = Kt × Ka: multiply the temperature factor for 200°F by the altitude factor for 5,000 ft."; part 2 "Standard-air pressure = actual pressure ÷ Kd, using the Kd from part 1. The CFM does not change." Slip notes are added when they apply: a challenge-3 pressure close to 3.0 × 0.668 = 2.00: "That multiplies by the factor; to enter a standard-air catalog, divide by it."; a challenge-1 factor close to 70 ÷ 200 = 0.35: "Add 460 to each temperature first."; an inverted challenge-1 factor: "Hot air is lighter than standard air, so the factor is below 1: put 530 on top."; challenge 2 without the exponent: "Raise (1 − 6.875 × 10⁻⁶ × h) to the 5.2559 power." or inverted: "Thinner air at altitude is lighter, so the factor is below 1."; challenge 3 with only one factor: "That is only one of the two factors." or the sum: "Multiply the factors; do not add them." After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text (with the 2.00 and 0.35 notes when they apply), the model value is shown and the answer counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box. The prompt reads: "This fan handles 200°F air at sea level. By what factor do its pressure and horsepower change from the catalog?"

Chapter Anchors: Temperature factor at 200°F is 0.803. Altitude factor at 5,000 ft is 0.832. Combined factor at 200°F and 5,000 ft is 0.668; 3.0 in. wg actual becomes 4.49 in. wg for catalog selection; 11.0 catalog BHP becomes 7.35 actual BHP. The temperature factor at 800°F is 0.421.

docs.title: How Ratings Are Measured: the AMCA 210 Rating Standard
docs.text:
Catalog ratings are only comparable if every manufacturer measures fans the same way. The AMCA 210 rating standard is ANSI/AMCA Standard 210 (also published as ASHRAE Standard 51), Laboratory Methods of Testing Fans for Certified Aerodynamic Performance Rating. It defines how a fan is mounted on a test chamber or test duct, where pressures are measured, how airflow is measured (with calibrated nozzles or a Pitot traverse), how speed and power are measured, and how the results are converted to standard air density and a reference speed. A fan is tested at many points from no flow to full open flow, so the test traces the whole fan curve, not one point.

AMCA 210 also defines four installation types, the combinations of a free or ducted inlet with a free or ducted outlet, because the same fan performs differently in each. A certified rating states which installation type it applies to. Manufacturers who participate in the AMCA Certified Ratings Program may place the AMCA seal on the catalog; the program checks that published ratings match independent test results. Certified sound ratings are tested under companion standards (AMCA 300 for the test and AMCA 311 for certification). Installation types are covered in Chapter 25, and how to read the certified-ratings statement in a catalog in Chapter 26.

docs.title: Worked Example: Converting a Test Point to Standard Air
docs.text:
In an illustrative AMCA 210 test, a fan running at the reference speed is measured at 9,800 CFM, 3.85 in. wg fan static pressure and 8.6 BHP, on a day when the test air density is 0.073 lb/ft³. To publish the point at standard air, the lab applies the density correction from the previous section in the reverse direction:

\[ K_d = \frac{0.075}{0.073} = 1.027 \] Quantity Measured at 0.073 lb/ft³ Published at 0.075 lb/ft³ Rule Airflow 9,800 CFM 9,800 CFM Unchanged at fixed speed Fan static pressure 3.85 in. wg 3.96 in. wg Multiply by 1.027 BHP 8.6 8.84 Multiply by 1.027

The published table is therefore a set of standard-air values that no customer's job may exactly match. That is the reason the density correction, system effect and installation type all exist: they translate a laboratory rating back into a real installation.

Check the Seal and the Footnote

What does the current catalog say? Before quoting a rating, read the certified-ratings footnote under the table: it names the installation type and whether the BHP includes drive losses. Thirty seconds there prevents most "the fan doesn't match the catalog" calls.

docs.title: Fan Sound
docs.text: Every fan makes noise, and many specifications limit it. Fan sound is the airborne noise a fan generates, produced mainly by the impeller blades passing the housing cutoff, by turbulence in the airflow, and to a lesser degree by bearings, belts and motors. Fan sound is described with a small set of terms, and two of them, sound power and sound pressure, are easily confused.

docs.title: Decibel
docs.text: The ear responds to an enormous range of acoustic energy, from a whisper to a jet engine, so sound is measured on a logarithmic scale. The decibel (dB) is a unit equal to ten times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of a quantity to a fixed reference quantity. Because it is a ratio, a decibel value always implies a reference. A 3 dB increase means the acoustic energy has doubled, and a 10 dB increase means it has risen tenfold. Decibels do not add arithmetically: two identical fans, each 90 dB, together produce 93 dB, not 180 dB.

docs.title: Sound Power Level
docs.text: Sound power level (Lw) is the total acoustic power a fan radiates, expressed in decibels relative to a reference of 10⁻¹² watts. It is a property of the fan at its operating point, like BHP, and it does not depend on the room or the distance from the fan. That is why fan manufacturers publish sound power, usually in eight octave bands (octave bands are covered in Chapter 25).

docs.title: Sound Power Level
docs.text:
\[ L_w = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{W}{10^{-12}} \right) \]

where:

  • \( L_w \) is the sound power level in dB
  • \( W \) is the acoustic power in watts
  • \( 10^{-12} \) W is the reference power

Sound pressure level, by contrast, is what a microphone measures at one location; it depends on distance, room size and reflections, and it is developed in Chapter 25. A specification that asks for "85 dB" without saying whether it means sound power or sound pressure, and at what distance, cannot be checked.

docs.title: Worked Example: Adding Fans
docs.text:
A plant installs two identical exhaust fans, each rated at a sound power level of 90 dB in one octave band. The combined level is:

\[ L_{w,total} = 10 \log_{10} \left( 10^{90/10} + 10^{90/10} \right) = 90 + 10 \log_{10} 2 = 93 \text{ dB} \]

Ten identical fans would produce \( 90 + 10 \log_{10} 10 = 100 \) dB. When one fan is 10 dB louder than the other, the quieter fan adds only about 0.4 dB to the total, so treating the loudest source first is almost always the right noise-control priority. The rules of thumb are:

Change Effect on combined level Two equal sources +3 dB Ten equal sources +10 dB Add a source 10 dB quieter About +0.4 dB

docs.title: Sone Rating
docs.text: A sone rating is a measure of perceived loudness on a linear scale, where 1 sone is defined as the loudness of a 1,000 Hz tone at a sound pressure level of 40 dB, and a sound of 2 sones is judged twice as loud as one of 1 sone. Because the scale is linear, sones are easier for non-specialists to compare than decibels: a 10-sone fan sounds about twice as loud as a 5-sone fan. Sone ratings are common on commercial products such as roof and wall exhausters, ceiling and cabinet ventilators, and are calculated from measured sound data under AMCA procedures for a stated listening distance.

docs.title: Blade Pass Frequency
docs.text: The blade pass frequency (BPF) is the rate at which impeller blades pass a fixed point such as the housing cutoff, equal to the fan speed in revolutions per second times the number of blades. It often appears as a distinct tone in a fan's sound spectrum. For example, a 10-blade impeller at 1,770 RPM has a blade pass frequency of \( 1{,}770 \times 10 / 60 = 295 \) Hz. Knowing it helps an engineer recognize whether a tonal complaint comes from the fan or from something else in the system.

docs.title: Blade Pass Frequency
docs.text:
\[ BPF = \frac{N \times B}{60} \]

where:

  • \( BPF \) is the blade pass frequency in hertz (Hz)
  • \( N \) is the fan speed in RPM
  • \( B \) is the number of impeller blades

You Can Read a Fan Curve

You just learned to find a fan's operating point from its fan curve and a system curve, and to explain why it moves when filters load or a damper closes. Add density correction and system effect, and you can turn a catalog rating into what the fan will really do on the job.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A performance rating is five numbers, not one: airflow volume, pressure, speed, brake horsepower and the density they assume. A CFM without a pressure cannot be checked or ordered.
  • Fan static pressure equals fan total pressure minus outlet velocity pressure. Outlet velocity pressure comes from outlet velocity, which is airflow divided by fan outlet area; confirm which pressure a specification means.
  • BHP equals air power divided by efficiency: \( BHP = Q \times P / (6356 \times \eta) \), using static pressure with static efficiency or total pressure with total efficiency.
  • Tip speed (\( \pi D N / 12 \)) governs pressure and impeller stress. Every selection speed must be below the maximum safe speed for the fan's AMCA class, after any temperature derate.
  • A fan curve shows every possible operating point at one speed and density. Never select left of the pressure peak, in the stall region.
  • Non-overloading BHP curves (backward inclined, airfoil) have a ceiling; overloading curves (forward curved, radial) do not, so their motors must be sized for the highest airflow the fan may see.
  • System resistance rises with airflow squared, and the system curve is a parabola through the design point. The operating point is where the fan curve and system curve cross, and it moves when either one changes.
  • System effect is lost performance caused by poor fan connections. It is not in the fan curve; add it to the design pressure before selecting.
  • Correct for density: divide actual pressure by \( K_d = K_t \times K_a \) to enter a standard-air catalog, and multiply the catalog BHP by \( K_d \) to get actual BHP. CFM does not change.
  • AMCA 210 defines how fans are tested and rated, so certified catalog ratings from different manufacturers can be compared.
  • Fan sound is published as sound power level in decibels; sones express loudness on a linear scale, and the blade pass frequency (\( N \times B / 60 \)) identifies the fan's characteristic tone.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings
docs.text: Test your understanding of fan pressures, power and efficiency, fan class, fan and system curves, density corrections, AMCA 210 ratings and fan sound with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Under the AMCA definition used in North American fan catalogs, what is fan static pressure?
docs.text:
1. The static pressure reading on a gauge at the fan outlet
  2. Fan total pressure minus the fan outlet velocity pressure
  3. Fan total pressure plus the fan outlet velocity pressure
  4. The total pressure at the fan inlet
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fan total pressure is the rise in total pressure across the fan, outlet minus inlet. Fan static pressure is fan total pressure minus the outlet velocity pressure: all the energy the fan adds except the kinetic energy of the air leaving the outlet. The chapter warns that a gauge reading across the fan is not the same thing, because the definition is built from total pressures, not gauge readings.

Concept Tested: Fan Static Pressure

See: Fan Total Pressure and Fan Static Pressure

docs.title: 2. Why is "10,000 CFM" by itself not a usable fan performance rating?
docs.text:
1. CFM is not a recognized unit of airflow in fan catalogs or AMCA ratings
  2. Airflow is always stated in pounds per minute in a fan rating, never in CFM
  3. A fan has only one possible airflow, so stating the number is redundant
  4. Without the pressure, speed, power and density it assumes, the airflow cannot be checked or ordered
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Fan performance is the complete statement of what a fan does at one set of conditions: airflow, pressure, speed, brake horsepower and the air density those numbers assume. The same fan at the same speed can deliver a whole family of airflow and pressure pairs, and the system picks which one. Remove any qualifier and the number cannot be checked. Option C is the misconception the chapter corrects: a fan has a curve, not a single airflow.

Concept Tested: Fan Performance

See: What a Fan Performance Rating Says

docs.title: 3. A fan moves 12,000 CFM through an outlet with an inside area of 3.0 ft² against 3.0 in. wg fan static pressure, at standard air. What is the fan total pressure?
docs.text:
1. About 4.0 in. wg
  2. About 3.0 in. wg
  3. About 2.0 in. wg
  4. About 3.5 in. wg
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Outlet velocity is 12,000 / 3.0 = 4,000 FPM. Outlet velocity pressure at standard air is (4,000 / 4005)² ≈ 1.00 in. wg. Fan total pressure is fan static pressure plus outlet velocity pressure: 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0 in. wg. Option B ignores the velocity pressure, and option C subtracts it instead of adding it. On high-velocity fans, confusing the two pressures can shift a selection by a full inch of water gauge.

Concept Tested: Outlet Velocity Pressure

See: The Fan Outlet: Area, Velocity and Velocity Pressure

docs.title: 4. A specification requires a minimum static efficiency of 75%. At the selected point, the fan's static efficiency is 70% and its total efficiency is 77%. What is the correct conclusion?
docs.text:
1. The fan complies, because its total efficiency exceeds 75%
  2. The fan complies, because the average of the two efficiencies is above 73%
  3. The fan does not comply; total efficiency is always the larger of the two and cannot be substituted for static efficiency
  4. The two efficiencies cannot both apply to the same point, so the data is wrong
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Static efficiency uses fan static pressure and total efficiency uses fan total pressure, so total efficiency is always the larger at a given point. Both are valid at once; the chapter's worked example has 70% static and about 77% total at the same point. A specification that names static efficiency must be met on static efficiency, so 70% fails a 75% requirement even though the total efficiency would pass a total-efficiency requirement.

Concept Tested: Fan Efficiency

See: Brake Horsepower and Fan Efficiency

docs.title: 5. Where on a backward inclined fan's pressure curve is the stall region?
docs.text:
1. To the left of the peak of the pressure curve, toward zero flow
  2. At the far right end of the curve, near maximum airflow
  3. At the point of peak efficiency
  4. Wherever the brake horsepower curve reaches its maximum
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. For a backward inclined or airfoil fan, the stall region begins at the airflow of peak pressure and extends left toward zero flow. There the airflow is too low for the blade angles, air separates from the blades and recirculates, and the fan may pulse, surge, vibrate and rumble. Catalog tables usually stop short of this region, which is why some cells at low airflow and high pressure are blank. Never select a fan left of the peak.

Concept Tested: Stall Region

See: The Stall Region

docs.title: 6. Why must the motor on a forward curved fan be sized for the highest airflow the fan could realistically see, not just the design point?
docs.text:
1. Forward curved fans always run in the stall region
  2. Forward curved fans cannot use belt drives
  3. Its brake horsepower keeps rising with airflow, so lower-than-designed system resistance pushes power above the design value
  4. Its maximum safe speed is lower than any other fan's
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Forward curved and radial bladed fans have an overloading power curve: brake horsepower keeps rising as airflow increases, all the way to the right end of the curve. If the duct system has less resistance than calculated, an access door is left open, or a damper is removed, the fan moves more air and draws more power than at the design point. A motor sized only for the design point can then trip. Non-overloading curves have a ceiling instead.

Concept Tested: Overloading Power Curve

See: Overloading and Non-Overloading Power Curves

docs.title: 7. An exhaust fan must handle 300°F air (temperature correction factor 0.697) against 2.5 in. wg actual static pressure at sea level. At what static pressure should it be looked up in a standard-air catalog?
docs.text:
1. About 1.74 in. wg
  2. 2.5 in. wg
  3. About 3.08 in. wg
  4. About 3.59 in. wg
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. To enter a standard-air catalog, divide the actual required pressure by the density correction factor: 2.5 / 0.697 ≈ 3.59 in. wg. The fan is selected at the actual CFM and that equivalent pressure, and the catalog BHP is then multiplied by 0.697 to get the BHP when running hot. Option A multiplies instead of dividing, the most common direction error, and option B skips the correction, which would leave the fan short on pressure at the job.

Concept Tested: Temperature Correction

See: Temperature Correction

docs.title: 8. Which statement best describes system effect?
docs.text:
1. The pressure loss of the ductwork, elbows and filters, which is already in the system curve
  2. A loss of fan performance caused by the way the fan is connected to the system, which appears in neither the fan curve nor the duct calculation
  3. The reduction in fan pressure caused by hot, low-density air
  4. The extra airflow a fan delivers when the system resistance is overestimated
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Catalog ratings are measured with ideal test ductwork. An elbow on the inlet, a short or missing discharge duct, or an abrupt transition makes the fan perform worse than its rating. System effect is that loss, expressed as extra pressure the fan must overcome; it exists only because the fan's inlet or outlet airflow is disturbed. Because it is in neither the fan curve nor the system curve, it must be added to the design pressure before selection.

Concept Tested: System Effect

See: System Effect

docs.title: 9. A selection needs 1,500 RPM. The catalog lists maximum safe speeds of 1,300 RPM (Class I), 1,650 RPM (Class II) and 2,000 RPM (Class III) for this size, and the job temperature carries a derate factor of 0.95. Which class should be ordered?
docs.text:
1. Class I
  2. Class III
  3. Class II
  4. None of these classes; a larger fan size is required
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Apply the derate first: Class I becomes 1,300 × 0.95 = 1,235 RPM, Class II becomes 1,650 × 0.95 ≈ 1,568 RPM, and Class III becomes 1,900 RPM. The selection speed of 1,500 RPM exceeds the derated Class I limit but not the derated Class II limit. The rule is to choose the lightest class whose derated limit is at or above the selection speed, so Class II is ordered. Class III would work but is heavier than needed.

Concept Tested: Fan Class

See: Fan Class

docs.title: 10. A fan's airflow has dropped since start-up. Its speed has not changed and nothing in the fan is damaged. Which explanation fits the fan curve and system curve picture?
docs.text:
1. The fan curve has shifted to the right because the impeller has worn in
  2. The system curve has become steeper, for example from a loaded filter or a closed damper, moving the operating point left along the unchanged fan curve
  3. The system curve has become flatter, moving the operating point to the left
  4. The air has become denser, which lowers the airflow at a fixed speed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The operating point is where the fan curve and system curve cross. With speed unchanged, the fan curve stays the same, so the change must be in the system. A loaded filter, a closed damper or an iced coil makes the system curve steeper, and the crossing moves left to less airflow. A flatter system curve would move the point right. Density does not change CFM at a fixed speed; it changes pressure and horsepower.

Concept Tested: Operating Point

See: The Operating Point

docs.title: 11. What does a sone rating measure?
docs.text:
1. Perceived loudness on a linear scale, where 2 sones is judged twice as loud as 1 sone
  2. The total acoustic power a fan radiates, in decibels relative to 10⁻¹² watts
  3. The rate at which impeller blades pass the housing cutoff
  4. The sound pressure a microphone measures at one location
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A sone is a unit of perceived loudness on a linear scale; 1 sone is the loudness of a 1,000 Hz tone at 40 dB sound pressure level, and a 10-sone fan sounds about twice as loud as a 5-sone fan. That makes sones easier for non-specialists to compare than decibels. Option B describes sound power level, option C blade pass frequency, and option D sound pressure level.

Concept Tested: Sone Rating

See: Sone Rating

docs.title: 12. Why do fan manufacturers publish sound power level rather than sound pressure level?
docs.text:
1. Sound power is always the lower number, so it looks better in a catalog
  2. Sound power can be added arithmetically when several fans run together
  3. Sound pressure cannot be measured in decibels
  4. Sound power is a property of the fan at its operating point and does not depend on the room or the distance from the fan
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Sound power level is the total acoustic power a fan radiates, a property of the fan at its operating point, like brake horsepower. Sound pressure level is what a microphone measures at one spot and depends on distance, room size and reflections. Decibels never add arithmetically: two identical 90 dB fans together produce 93 dB, not 180 dB. A specification asking for "85 dB" without saying power or pressure, and at what distance, cannot be checked.

Concept Tested: Sound Power Level

See: Sound Power Level

docs.title: References: Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings
docs.text:
1. Density of air - Wikipedia - Explains how air density depends on temperature, pressure and humidity, with standard values. The basis for the chapter's temperature and altitude correction factors.

  2. Sound power - Wikipedia - Defines sound power and sound power level and contrasts them with sound pressure. Supports the chapter's explanation of why fan catalogs publish sound power.

  3. Sone - Wikipedia - Defines the sone as a unit of perceived loudness and relates it to phons and decibels. Background for the sone ratings published on commercial fans.

  4. Fan Engineering: An Engineer's Handbook on Fans and Their Applications - Robert Jorgensen (ed.) - Buffalo Forge Company - A long-standing industry handbook, valued for presenting fan performance, fan and system curves, and density corrections in the units and form catalogs use.

  5. Fans and Ventilation: A Practical Guide - William Cory - Elsevier - Cory explains fan pressures, efficiencies, system effect and fan-system interaction in practical, application-focused terms, with attention to how test ratings relate to installed performance.

  6. AMCA Publications - Air Movement and Control Association - Lists the standards this chapter names: AMCA 210 (ANSI/ASHRAE 51) for fan testing, Publication 201 on fans and systems, Standard 99, and Standard 300 for sound testing.

  7. AMCA Certified Ratings Program - Air Movement and Control Association - Explains AMCA certification and the standards it relies on, including AMCA 210, AMCA 300 and Publication 311. Context for the AMCA seal on catalog ratings.

  8. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Source for the evasé and outlet area (p. 146), ventilating sets (p. 167), damper effect on the operating point (p. 182) and inlet box system effect (p. 187) cited here.

  9. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Online edition of FanPedia, including the accessories and technical description sections that discuss flow control and system effect. Useful when reading a catalog rating.

  10. Centrifugal Fans - Twin City Fan - Current catalog page for SWSI and DWDI housed centrifugal fans, the entry point to the product catalogs and performance data this chapter teaches you to read and correct.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explains how the motor turns the impeller: direct drive, belt drive with sheaves and V-belts and its drive service factor, and shaft couplings. It introduces overhung and center-hung impellers and the standard numbered fan arrangements that combine them: Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 4, and 7, with the plug, plenum, vertical, axial, inline, and lab exhaust arrangement families. It also explains why some arrangements keep the bearings out of a hot airstream. After completing it, readers can name a fan's arrangement from a drawing.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 22 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Direct Drive 497 Shaft Coupling 28 Overhung Impeller 470 Center Hung Impeller 456 Motor Support Base 1 Belt Drive 713 Sheave 24 Drive Service Factor 23 Fan Arrangement 445 V-Belt 23 Arrangement 1 83 Arrangement 3 10 Arrangement 4 28 Plug Fan Arrangements 68 Plenum Fan Arrangements 5 Vertical Arrangement 3 Axial and Inline Arrangements 15 Lab Exhaust Arrangements 22 Bearings Out of Airstream 22 Arrangement 2 1 Arrangement 3 SI and DI 3 Arrangement 7 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
  • Chapter 6: Industrial Fans and Application Product Lines
  • Chapter 9: Impeller Construction and Material Handling

From Motor Shaft to Impeller

Every quote, drawing and field call eventually asks the same question: how is this fan driven, and where do its bearings sit? By the end of this chapter you will look at an outline drawing and say "that's an Arrangement 9 with the motor on the pedestal" before anyone points at the title block. Let's follow the airflow.

A motor turns, and an impeller turns. Everything between those two shafts decides how fast the fan runs, how easily its speed can change later, how much maintenance it needs, where the bearings live and what temperature of air the fan can handle. This chapter starts with the two basic ways to connect a motor to an impeller, direct drive and belt drive, then looks at the two ways an impeller can sit on its shaft, overhung and center hung. Those two choices, combined with where the motor and bearings are mounted, are what a numbered fan arrangement describes.

You already know the parts from Chapter 3: the impeller, the housing, the shaft, the bearings and the motor. You also met the fan families in Chapter 4 through Chapter 6. Here those parts get assembled into the standard layouts that appear on every Twin City Fan drawing and order.

docs.title: Two Ways to Turn an Impeller
docs.text: A drive is the mechanical connection that carries power from the motor shaft to the fan impeller. There are two families. In a direct drive fan, the impeller turns at the motor's speed. In a belt drive fan, belts and pulleys sit between the motor and the fan shaft, so the impeller can turn faster or slower than the motor. Many fan types are offered both ways. FanPedia's exploded views, for example, show a direct drive tubeaxial fan beside a belt driven one, and a direct drive inline centrifugal beside a belt driven version (FanPedia pp. 15–17).

docs.title: Direct Drive
docs.text:
A direct drive fan has no speed change between the motor and the impeller: the impeller turns at the motor's speed. There are two ways to build one.

  • Impeller on the motor shaft. The impeller hub is keyed or clamped straight onto the motor shaft. There is no separate fan shaft and no fan bearings; the motor's own bearings carry the impeller. FanPedia describes Arrangement 4 this way: "the impeller is mounted directly to the motor shaft," and the arrangement "offers low maintenance since there are no fan bearings, fan shaft or drive parts to maintain" (FanPedia p. 164).
  • Motor coupled to a fan shaft. The fan has its own shaft and bearings, and a shaft coupling (covered next) joins that shaft end to end with the motor shaft. FanPedia's Arrangements 7 and 8 are built this way (FanPedia p. 21).

The first form is compact and simple. The second keeps the impeller's weight and the shaft's loads on fan bearings sized for the job, which matters on larger and heavier rotors.

Because the impeller turns at motor speed, a direct drive fan can only run at the speeds motors actually come in, unless a variable frequency drive (VFD) changes the motor speed electrically. An AC induction motor's synchronous speed is set by the supply frequency and the number of magnetic poles in its winding:

\[ N_s = \frac{120\, f}{p} \]

where:

  • \( N_s \) is the synchronous speed in revolutions per minute (rpm)
  • \( f \) is the supply frequency in hertz (60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in much of the world)
  • \( p \) is the number of poles in the motor winding

A loaded induction motor runs a little below its synchronous speed; the difference is called slip, and the nameplate shows the actual full-load speed. Chapter 14 covers motors in detail. For now, the table below lists the synchronous speeds the formula gives for common pole counts.

Poles Synchronous speed at 60 Hz Synchronous speed at 50 Hz 2 3,600 rpm 3,000 rpm 4 1,800 rpm 1,500 rpm 6 1,200 rpm 1,000 rpm 8 900 rpm 750 rpm

Worked example: can this duty be direct driven? A selection program shows that a centrifugal fan meets its airflow and pressure at 1,140 rpm. On 60 Hz power, a 6-pole motor (1,200 rpm synchronous, a little less at full load) lands near that speed, so a direct drive selection is realistic. If the same fan instead needed 1,450 rpm, no fixed motor speed matches: a 4-pole motor would spin the fan far too fast, and a 6-pole motor too slow. The application engineer then has three choices. Pick a different fan size or impeller width that meets the duty at a standard motor speed; drive the fan with a VFD that slows a faster motor; or use a belt drive. FanPedia notes this exact trade on direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fans: "Fans can be selected with varying impeller widths to provide desired performance at direct drive motor speeds," and "performance changes in the field are usually achieved by means of variable inlet vanes or VFD" (FanPedia p. 170). On direct drive axial fans, adjusting the blade angle does the same fine-tuning job (FanPedia p. 172).

The trade-off, then, is simplicity against flexibility. A direct drive fan has fewer wearing parts (no belts to tension or replace), no belt dust in the airstream, and no belt losses. FanPedia calls out the cleanliness benefit for Arrangement 4 plenum fans: the compact fan and motor unit "eliminates belt residue and requires less maintenance than other arrangements," which is why they are "widely used in cleanroom, pharmaceutical and other critical applications" (FanPedia p. 170). The cost is that the fan speed is locked to the motor speed unless a VFD is added, and on impeller-on-motor-shaft designs the motor sits close to the airstream, which limits the air temperature (FanPedia p. 171).

docs.title: Shaft Coupling
docs.text:
A shaft coupling connects two shafts end to end so that one drives the other. FanPedia lists the coupling among the shaft accessories and defines its two jobs on a fan: it is "used to connect the fan shaft to the motor shaft or fan shaft to fan shaft (i.e. twin fan assembly)" (FanPedia p. 129). Fans use a flexible coupling, which transmits torque while tolerating a small amount of misalignment between the two shafts. Even so, the motor and fan shafts must be aligned carefully when the fan is installed, and they must stay aligned while it runs. FanPedia explains that concrete inertia bases are typically used on longer direct drive fans "to mitigate assembly deflection, maintaining proper alignment between the motor, coupling, shaft and bearings" (FanPedia p. 175). Chapter 22 covers those bases.

When you see the word "Coupling" on an arrangement drawing, it tells you three things at once:

  • the fan is direct driven, so fan speed equals motor speed;
  • the fan has its own shaft and bearings, so it is not an impeller-on-motor-shaft Arrangement 4;
  • the motor sits in line with the fan shaft, not beside it as on a belt drive.

Worked example: reading the coupling clue. A customer emails a photo of a single inlet centrifugal fan. The motor sits on an extension of the bearing pedestal, in line with the fan shaft, and a short guarded section between them joins the two shafts. There is no belt guard. Reasoning from the coupling: the fan is direct driven, but not Arrangement 4, because Arrangement 4 has no fan shaft to couple to. FanPedia describes exactly this layout as Arrangement 8, "a modified version of Arrangement 1 used for direct drive. The Arrangement 1 bearing pedestal is extended to accommodate the motor. A flexible coupling connects the fan and motor shaft" (FanPedia p. 165). If the impeller had instead sat between two bearings with the coupled motor on a pedestal, the answer would be Arrangement 7. If a motor is ever replaced on a coupled fan, the coupling alignment must be checked again before restart.

docs.title: Motor Support Base
docs.text: On a direct drive tubular fan, the motor often sits inside the tube, in line with the airflow, with the impeller on its shaft. The motor support base is the structure inside the tubular housing that carries that motor. FanPedia labels it "Motor Support Base" in the exploded view of a direct drive inline centrifugal and mixed flow fan (FanPedia p. 17); the direct drive axial exploded views show the matching support structure under the motor (FanPedia pp. 15–16). Compare the belt driven versions on the same pages, where the motor sits outside the tube on a motor base and saddle and the drive runs inside a belt tube. The motor support base is a structural part, not an adjustable base; there are no belts to tension on a direct drive fan.

docs.title: Belt Drive
docs.text:
A belt drive transmits power from the motor shaft to the fan shaft through belts running on grooved pulleys. Because the two pulleys can be different sizes, the fan can turn at almost any speed, not just at a motor speed. FanPedia summarizes the benefit plainly: "Belt driven configurations offer performance flexibility" (FanPedia p. 162). On axial and inline fans, "any future change in rating can be accomplished through a simple sheave change or blade angle adjustment" (FanPedia p. 173). A belt drive also lets the motor sit outside the airstream, beside or above the fan instead of in line with it.

The price of that flexibility is maintenance and a little efficiency. Belts stretch and wear, so they need periodic tensioning and eventual replacement, which is why belt driven motors sit on adjustable mounts such as slide bases (Chapter 15). Belts shed dust, and some power is lost in the drive. The table below summarizes the two drive families described so far.

Question Direct drive Belt drive Fan speed Fixed at motor speed (unless a VFD is used) Set by the sheave ratio; changeable with a sheave change Parts between motor and impeller None, or a flexible coupling Two sheaves, belts, often bushings Routine maintenance Lowest; no belts Belt tension checks and belt replacement Belt residue in the air None Possible; belt dust Where the motor goes On the fan shaft line Beside, above or on the pedestal; can be out of the airstream FanPedia examples Arrangements 4, 7, 8 Arrangements 1, 3, 9, 10

docs.title: Sheave
docs.text:
A sheave is the grooved pulley that a V-belt runs on; FanPedia writes "sheave/pulley" on its exploded views (FanPedia p. 15). A belt drive has two: the motor sheave (also called the drive sheave) on the motor shaft and the fan sheave (the driven sheave) on the fan shaft. FanPedia's shaft accessories page describes drive sheaves as "sheave mounted to fan shaft and motor shaft," which "can be with or without a bushing," a bushing being the tapered sleeve that clamps a sheave to its shaft (FanPedia p. 128). A sheave's working size is its pitch diameter, the diameter at which the belt effectively rides in the groove; drive calculations use pitch diameter, not the outside diameter.

Because the belt does not slip appreciably, the belt surface moves at the same speed over both sheaves. That makes the speed ratio the inverse of the diameter ratio:

\[ N_{fan} = N_{motor} \times \frac{D_{motor}}{D_{fan}} \]

where:

  • \( N_{fan} \) is the fan shaft speed in rpm
  • \( N_{motor} \) is the motor's full-load speed in rpm (from the nameplate)
  • \( D_{motor} \) is the pitch diameter of the motor sheave in inches
  • \( D_{fan} \) is the pitch diameter of the fan sheave in inches

A larger fan sheave slows the fan; a larger motor sheave speeds it up.

Worked example: sizing a fan sheave. A belt driven fan must run at 1,250 rpm. The motor runs at 1,760 rpm at full load (an illustrative 4-pole nameplate value), and the motor sheave has a 6.0 in pitch diameter. Rearranging the formula:

\[ D_{fan} = D_{motor} \times \frac{N_{motor}}{N_{fan}} = 6.0 \times \frac{1760}{1250} = 8.45 \text{ in} \]

Stock sheaves come in discrete sizes. If the nearest available pitch diameter is 8.4 in (illustrative), the fan runs at \( 1760 \times 6.0 / 8.4 = 1{,}257 \) rpm, about half a percent fast, which is normally acceptable; the selection should be rechecked at that speed. If the customer later needs more air, a smaller fan sheave or a larger motor sheave raises the fan speed, but horsepower rises steeply with speed, so the motor must be checked before any speed increase (Chapter 25 covers the fan laws that predict it).

Sanity-Check the Ratio in Your Head

Before trusting a drive calculation, ask which sheave is bigger. If the fan must turn slower than the motor, the fan sheave must be the larger one; if your answer says otherwise, the ratio is upside down.

docs.title: V-Belt
docs.text:
A V-belt is a drive belt with a trapezoidal cross-section that wedges into the matching V-shaped groove of a sheave. The wedging action multiplies the grip between belt and sheave, so a V-belt can carry useful power at modest tension. Fan drives commonly use several V-belts side by side on multi-groove sheaves; each belt carries a share of the load. FanPedia refers to "V-belt drive" throughout its arrangement descriptions; for example, double width fans "are generally supplied in Arrangement 3 for V-belt drive" (FanPedia p. 167), and belt driven axial fans use "either a fixed or adjustable V-belt drive system" (FanPedia p. 173). A fixed drive has sheaves of set pitch diameter; an adjustable drive uses a motor sheave whose groove width can be changed to vary its pitch diameter, which lets a technician trim the fan speed during balancing.

The speed at which the belt travels matters because a belt's power capacity depends on it. Belt speed in feet per minute follows from the motor sheave's circumference:

\[ V = \frac{\pi \, D_{motor} \, N_{motor}}{12} \]

where:

  • \( V \) is the belt speed in feet per minute (ft/min)
  • \( D_{motor} \) is the motor sheave pitch diameter in inches (divide by 12 to get feet)
  • \( N_{motor} \) is the motor speed in rpm

Worked example: belt speed and belt count. A drive uses a 5.0 in motor sheave on a 1,760 rpm motor. Belt speed is \( \pi \times 5.0 \times 1760 / 12 = 2{,}304 \) ft/min. The drive manufacturer's rating table gives the horsepower one belt of the chosen section can carry at that belt speed and sheave size; suppose it is 6.0 hp per belt (illustrative). If the drive must carry a design load of 19.5 hp (computed in the next section), the number of belts is \( 19.5 / 6.0 = 3.25 \), rounded up to 4 belts, because a fraction of a belt cannot share the load. Rounding down would overload every belt. The real per-belt rating must always come from the current drive manufacturer's data.

docs.title: Drive Service Factor
docs.text:
A belt drive is not sized for the motor's nameplate horsepower alone. The drive service factor is a multiplier, at least 1.0, that the drive designer applies to the motor's power to allow for the duty the drive will see: starting loads, hours of operation per day, and the character of the driven machine. The result is the design horsepower the belts and sheaves are selected to carry:

\[ HP_{design} = HP_{motor} \times SF_{drive} \]

where:

  • \( HP_{design} \) is the design horsepower used to select belts and sheaves
  • \( HP_{motor} \) is the motor nameplate horsepower
  • \( SF_{drive} \) is the drive service factor from the belt drive manufacturer's table for the driven machine and duty

Worked example: design horsepower. A belt driven fan has a 15 hp motor and runs around the clock. Suppose the belt maker's table gives a drive service factor of 1.3 for a fan in continuous service (illustrative; use the current table for the actual value). Design horsepower is \( 15 \times 1.3 = 19.5 \) hp, the figure used in the belt count example above. A drive selected for only 15 hp would run its belts near their limit every hour of every day and wear them out early.

Two Different Service Factors

A common trap is reading the motor nameplate's service factor and treating it as the drive service factor. The motor service factor says how far above rated horsepower the motor may run (FanPedia's example on page 69: 1.15 on a 100 HP motor allows 115 HP), while the drive service factor is a sizing multiplier for belts and sheaves from the drive manufacturer's table. Keep them in separate lines of your calculation.

The microsim below puts the three belt drive formulas side by side, so you can see how sheave sizes, fan speed, belt speed and belt count move together.

docs.text:

Belt Drive Speed Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch11-belt-drive-speed-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the fan speed, belt speed and required belt count of a V-belt fan drive from the motor speed, the two sheave pitch diameters, the motor horsepower and the drive service factor, with fan speed within ±5 rpm and belt count exact.

Prerequisites: belt drive, sheave, pitch diameter, motor sheave, fan sheave, V-belt, belt speed, drive service factor, design horsepower (all defined in the "Belt Drive" section of this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: For four challenge drives, the learner types the fan speed in rpm and the number of belts before the answer is revealed. A fan speed is correct when it is within ±5 rpm of the model value; a belt count is correct only when it equals the model value. Mastery is 4 of 4 challenges with both answers correct. Moving the free-exploration controls is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A larger fan sheave makes the fan run faster. (2) The speed ratio equals the diameter ratio the same way up (fan/motor) rather than inverted. (3) A belt count of 3.25 rounds down to 3. (4) The motor's nameplate service factor is the drive service factor.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a drive is an Apply-level procedure, so the learner commits numbers for fixed challenges and gets the worked calculation as feedback; free exploration afterward lets them see the inverse diameter relationship directly.

Displayed outputs: fan speed (rpm, rounded to the nearest whole rpm), speed ratio (motor rpm ÷ fan rpm, to two decimals), belt speed (ft/min, nearest whole number), design horsepower (to one decimal), belts required (whole number). The two sheaves are drawn to scale relative to each other, joined by a belt, and each rotates at a rate proportional to its computed speed; the relative size of the two sheaves is itself content being taught.

A label reads: "Motor speeds, per-belt ratings and service factors are illustrative. Use the current drive manufacturer's tables for real selections."

Provenance: Formulas: standard belt drive engineering, as stated in this chapter's "Sheave", "V-Belt" and "Drive Service Factor" sections. All numeric values are illustrative; challenge 1 matches the chapter's worked examples. The motor service factor contrast is from FanPedia p. 69.

Rules:

  • Fan rpm = motor rpm × motor sheave ÷ fan sheave.
  • Belt speed (ft/min) = π × motor sheave (in) × motor rpm ÷ 12.
  • Design hp = motor hp × drive service factor.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1's motor speed, sheave sizes, horsepower, service factor and per-belt rating, and types a fan rpm and a belt count.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sheaves turn at the model speeds, and the sim shows the model values beside the learner's entries.
  3. The learner completes challenges 2, 3 and 4. In challenge 3 the learner should notice the fan turning faster than the motor.
  4. After challenge 4, free-exploration mode unlocks. The learner changes any quantity and every output updates at once. The first time the fan sheave is increased, the sim notes "Bigger fan sheave, slower fan."

Feedback: Four challenges, fixed order, two attempts each; fan rpm and belt count are judged separately. Correct: "Correct: ." Hint after a first wrong attempt, never the model rpm, belt count or worked sums: which field is off ("Your fan speed is right; the belt count is not." and the reverse, or "Both the fan speed and the belt count are off."), then for a wrong fan speed "Fan rpm = motor rpm × motor sheave ÷ fan sheave." (replaced by "Your ratio is inverted: the larger sheave turns slower." when the fan rpm equals motor rpm × fan sheave ÷ motor sheave within ±5 rpm; challenge 3 adds "Here the motor sheave is the larger one."), and for a wrong belt count "Belts = design hp (motor hp × drive service factor) ÷ rating per belt, rounded up." (replaced by "Round belt counts up; a partial belt cannot carry its share." when the count equals the quotient rounded down, or by "A whole-number quotient is not rounded up." when it is one more than an exact whole-number quotient). After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge, with the inverted-ratio and rounded-down notes when they apply; the model value and worked calculation are shown, and the item counts as missed. A running count "Challenges fully correct: n of 4" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with empty answer boxes and the sheaves at rest. The question on screen is "How fast will the fan turn, and how many belts does this drive need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples use a 1,760 rpm motor, a 5.0 in motor sheave and an 8.0 in fan sheave (challenge 1: 1,100 rpm); a belt speed of 2,304 ft/min; a 15 hp motor with a drive service factor of 1.3 giving 19.5 design hp; 6.0 hp per belt giving 3.25, rounded up to 4 belts; and a 6.0 in motor sheave with an 8.4 in fan sheave giving 1,257 rpm. The chapter states that a larger fan sheave slows the fan and that the motor S.F. example on FanPedia p. 69 is 1.15 on a 100 HP motor.

docs.title: Where the Impeller Sits on the Shaft
docs.text: The drive answers how the impeller is turned. The next question is where the impeller sits relative to the bearings that carry it. FanPedia's shaft overview states it directly: the shaft "is supported by two bearings in one of two basic mounting arrangements: 1. Overhung impeller 2. Center hung impeller" (FanPedia p. 79). Every centrifugal arrangement number is built on one of these two.

docs.title: Overhung Impeller
docs.text:
An overhung impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, beyond both bearings. FanPedia's arrangement descriptions put it the same way: "The impeller is overhung on the shaft, i.e., mounted at the end of the shaft" (FanPedia p. 162). Picture a diving board: the board is clamped at two points near one end and the load sits out past the end. The two bearings sit together on a bearing pedestal, the stand outside the housing that carries the bearings, and the shaft reaches from the pedestal through the housing side into the impeller.

Three consequences follow from that geometry.

  • The bearings stay outside the housing. Air flows through the housing; the pedestal stands beside it. FanPedia says of Arrangement 1 that the two fan bearings "are mounted on the bearing pedestal, out of the airstream, which makes them ideal for high temperature or contaminated air applications" (FanPedia p. 162).
  • The bearing nearest the impeller carries the most load. Like the support nearest the end of a diving board, it reacts to the impeller's weight plus the leverage of the overhang, so the overhang distance and the bearing spacing matter in the design.
  • The impeller can come out from one side. With nothing on the far side of the impeller, the rotor can be serviced without disturbing a second bearing on the inlet side.

FanPedia's impeller orientation page lists the overhung arrangements as Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10, plus Arrangement 4 (FanPedia p. 30). Arrangement 4 is a special case: the impeller is overhung on the motor shaft, and the shaft's "two bearings [are] located within motor frame" (FanPedia p. 79).

Worked example: tracing the load path of an Arrangement 1 fan. Start at the impeller and follow the weight to the floor. The impeller hangs on the end of the shaft inside the housing. The shaft passes out through the housing side, usually through a shaft seal, to the two pillow block bearings bolted to the top of the pedestal. The pedestal carries the bearing loads to the fan base. The housing carries no shaft load at all; it only contains the air. The motor sits separately on the floor or fan base and drives the shaft through belts. If this fan moves 450°F oven exhaust, nothing in the load path from bearing to floor is in that air, which is why FanPedia lists Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 9F and 10 for its high temperature centrifugal construction, for airstream temperatures from 276°F to 1,000+°F (FanPedia p. 110).

docs.title: Center Hung Impeller
docs.text:
A center hung impeller is mounted between the two bearings, one on each side of the impeller. FanPedia: "the impeller center hung on the shaft, i.e., mounted between the bearings making it structurally sound and compact" (FanPedia p. 163). Picture a bridge span supported at both ends: the load sits between the supports, so each bearing carries roughly its share of the impeller weight and there is no overhang leverage. The shaft can be shorter and stiffer for a given impeller, which suits large and heavy rotors and double width impellers.

The catch is that one bearing has to sit on the inlet side of the impeller, and air enters the fan there. On a single width fan, that inlet-side bearing is usually carried by a bracket in the inlet, in the airstream. FanPedia states that "Arrangement 3 has one bearing located in the airstream" (FanPedia p. 163). On a double width, double inlet (DWDI) fan, both sides are inlets, so "both bearings are located in the airstream," and FanPedia limits standard DWDI fans to "clean air applications with air temperatures limited to 130°F" (FanPedia p. 167).

FanPedia's impeller orientation page lists the center hung arrangements as Arrangement 3 and Arrangement 7, each in single and double width (FanPedia p. 30).

The table below sets the two impeller positions side by side.

Feature Overhung impeller Center hung impeller Impeller location At the end of the shaft, beyond both bearings Between the two bearings Load on the bearings Nearest bearing carries weight plus overhang leverage Shared between the bearings, no overhang Bearings in the airstream No; both on a pedestal outside the housing (or inside the motor, Arrangement 4) Inlet-side bearing in the airstream (both on DWDI), unless inlet boxes move them out FanPedia arrangements (p. 30) 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4 3 and 7, single and double width

Worked example: why a center hung fan for a large clean-air supply? An air handling job needs a very large DWDI fan moving outdoor air at ambient temperature. The rotor is wide and heavy. Center hanging it between two bearings gives a short, stiff shaft span with no overhang leverage, and the 130°F limit for bearings in the airstream is not a concern at ambient temperature, so a standard DWDI Arrangement 3 fits. Change one fact: the same fan must handle 300°F process air. Now the in-airstream bearings rule out the standard Arrangement 3, and the engineer needs either an overhung arrangement or a center hung design that moves its bearings out of the air, which is what the SI and DI arrangements covered below do.

Diving Board or Bridge

Notice that the overhung-versus-center-hung choice is really a choice about where the bearings must stand. An overhung impeller keeps both bearings on one side, out of the air but carrying leverage; a center hung impeller shares the load evenly but has to put a bearing on the inlet side, where the air is.

The sorter below asks you to classify arrangements by impeller position and to say where the bearings are.

Type: microsim sim-id: ch11-overhung-center-hung-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify twelve fan arrangements as overhung or center hung and state whether each arrangement's bearings sit in or out of the airstream, from a one-line description of each arrangement.

Prerequisites: overhung impeller, center hung impeller, bearing pedestal, airstream, single width single inlet (SWSI), double width double inlet (DWDI), inlet box, direct drive, belt drive, shaft coupling (defined in this chapter and in Chapters 3 and 4).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 12 cards, the learner commits two choices: impeller position (Overhung or Center hung) and bearing location (All out of airstream, At least one in airstream, or No fan bearings). A card is correct only when both choices match the answer columns below. Mastery is 10 of 12 cards correct on the first attempt.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying described arrangements into a two-way scheme makes the learner apply the defining feature (where the impeller sits relative to the bearings) rather than memorize numbers, and the second choice links that geometry to bearing exposure, which is why it matters.

the Arrangement 1 pedestal extended to carry the motor; flexible coupling Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 8 is a modified Arrangement 1, so the impeller stays at the shaft end with both bearings on the pedestal (FanPedia pp. 79, 165). 11 Arrangement 9 SWSI: belt driven; motor on a slide base on the side of the bearing pedestal Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 9 is in the overhung group with Arrangements 1, 8 and 10 (FanPedia p. 30). 12 Arrangement 10 SWSI: belt driven; motor on an adjustable base inside the bearing pedestal Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 10 is in the overhung group, with its bearings on the pedestal (FanPedia pp. 30, 167).

Provenance: FanPedia p. 30 (impeller orientation: overhung for Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4; center hung for Arrangements 3 and 7, single and double width), p. 79 (shaft overview), and pp. 162–168 (technical descriptions cited per card).

Rules: Each card has two answer fields; both must be chosen before Check is enabled. A card is correct only when both fields match. There is no partial credit in the score, but feedback states which field was wrong.

Learner Activity:

  1. A card appears with its text. The learner predicts the impeller position, then the bearing location.
  2. The learner presses Check. A simple side-view schematic of that arrangement appears, showing the impeller, the shaft, the bearings and the edge of the airstream, with the correct answers.
  3. The learner moves to the next card. Cards already answered cannot be re-answered in the same round.
  4. After 12 cards, the learner sees the score and the list of missed cards and may start a new shuffled round.

Feedback: 12 cards, shuffled, one attempt each per round. Correct: "Correct: , ." Incorrect: names the wrong field and shows the "Why" text. If card 6 or card 10 is marked center hung, the feedback adds: "Direct drive does not decide impeller position; Arrangements 4 and 8 are direct drive and overhung." The schematic and answer appear after each check. A running count "Correct: n of 12" is shown.

Starting State: Card 1 of a shuffled deck is shown with both answer fields empty and the question "Where is the impeller, and where are the bearings?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that FanPedia p. 30 lists Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4 as overhung and Arrangements 3 and 7 as center hung; that Arrangement 3 SWSI has one bearing in the airstream; that standard DWDI fans have both bearings in the airstream and are limited to 130°F clean air; and that Arrangement 4's only bearings are in the motor frame.

docs.title: The Fan Arrangement
docs.text:
A fan arrangement is a standard numbered description of how a fan's drive, impeller, bearings and motor are put together. The number tells the reader, in one or two characters, whether the fan is direct or belt driven, whether the impeller is overhung or center hung, what carries the bearings, and where the motor is mounted. The numbering comes from the Air Movement and Control Association (AMCA) arrangement standard, and Twin City Fan, like other manufacturers, uses those base numbers on its drawings and catalogs. Suffix letters then mark variants: SI for a single inlet fan with an integral inlet box, DI for a double inlet fan with integral inlet boxes, F for an extended frame that carries the motor, P for a pedestal (grade mounted) plug fan, and so on (FanPedia pp. 20–29).

Arrangements are always defined for a fan type. FanPedia groups its arrangement drawings by family: centrifugal fans (SWSI on pp. 20–22 and DWDI on p. 23), plenum fans (pp. 24–25), plug fans (pp. 26–27), axial and inline centrifugal fans (p. 28), and fume exhaust fans (p. 29). The same base number can look different from one family to the next. An Arrangement 4 centrifugal fan has its motor on a pedestal beside the housing, while an Arrangement 4 axial fan has its motor inside the tube; both are "impeller mounted to motor shaft."

The table below collects the base arrangements this chapter covers and the defining features of each; the sections that follow explain each one. The table reinforces what you already know about drives and impeller positions.

Arrangement Drive Impeller position Bearings carried by Motor mounted 1 Belt (direct drive possible) Overhung Pedestal, out of airstream On floor or fan base, separate from fan 2 Belt or direct Overhung Bracket on the fan housing Separate from fan 3 Usually belt Center hung Housing; one bearing on each side of impeller On floor or fan base 4 Direct Overhung on motor shaft No fan bearings (motor bearings only) On a pedestal; impeller on motor shaft 7 Direct, coupled Center hung Housing and a pedestal that also carries the motor On the pedestal, coupled to fan shaft 8 Direct, coupled Overhung Extended Arrangement 1 pedestal On the extended pedestal, coupled 9 Belt only Overhung Pedestal On the side of the pedestal 10 Belt only Overhung Pedestal Inside the pedestal

Arrangements 8, 9 and 10, and the many lettered variants, are developed in Chapter 24. They appear here so you can see the whole numbering pattern.
