Worked example: naming an arrangement from a drawing. An outline drawing shows a single inlet centrifugal fan. Working through it systematically:

  1. Find the drive. There is a belt guard and two sheaves, so the fan is belt driven. That rules out 4, 7 and 8.
  2. Find the impeller relative to the bearings. Both bearings sit together on a pedestal on the drive side; nothing is on the inlet side. The impeller is overhung. That rules out 3 (and 7).
  3. Find the motor. The motor is bolted to a slide base on the side of the bearing pedestal, so the fan ships as one assembly with motor and drive mounted.

Overhung, belt driven, motor on the side of the pedestal: Arrangement 9. Had the motor stood on its own base on the floor beside the fan, it would be Arrangement 1; had it been tucked inside the pedestal, Arrangement 10 (FanPedia pp. 165–167).

Three Questions Make the Number

Think of an arrangement number as a compressed answer to three questions: how is it driven, where is the impeller relative to the bearings, and what carries the motor? Once you can answer those from a drawing, the number almost names itself.

docs.title: Arrangement 1
docs.text:
Arrangement 1 is an overhung impeller fan with both bearings on a pedestal and the motor mounted separately on the floor or fan base. FanPedia's drawing caption reads "Direct Drive or Belt Driven; Motor Mounted on Floor or Fan Base" (FanPedia p. 20), and the technical description adds that it "is usually belt driven" and that its pedestal bearings sit "out of the airstream, which makes them ideal for high temperature or contaminated air applications" (FanPedia p. 162). With belt drive, "the motor can be mounted in any of the four AMCA standard motor positions: W, X, Y or Z"; motor positions are defined in Chapter 12.

Arrangement 1 is also the parent of other arrangements. Arrangement 8 is "a modified version of Arrangement 1 used for direct drive," with the pedestal extended to carry a coupled motor (FanPedia p. 165), and Arrangement 9F extends the frame to carry a motor "similar to an Arrangement 1 fan" (FanPedia p. 166).

Worked example: checking a motor position. A customer orders an Arrangement 1 fan with clockwise (CW) rotation and a bottom horizontal discharge (BHD), and asks for the motor in position Z. FanPedia lists these motor position restrictions for Arrangement 1, all because the motor would interfere with the housing outlet or not fit (FanPedia p. 162):

  • BHD discharge: CW rotation, position Z not allowed; CCW rotation, position W not allowed.
  • TAD (top angular down) discharge: CW rotation, position W not allowed; CCW rotation, position Z not allowed.
  • THD (top horizontal) discharge: CW rotation, position W, and CCW rotation, position Z, face a height restriction because the motor may not fit below the discharge.

The requested combination, BHD with CW rotation and motor position Z, is on the list. The application engineer offers W, X or Y instead, or a different discharge. The same check applies to Arrangements 3 and 3F, which carry the identical restriction list (FanPedia p. 163). For the THD cases, FanPedia adds that "on Arrangement 1 fan the motor will fit if pedestal is lengthened to accommodate motor" (FanPedia p. 162).

docs.title: Arrangement 2
docs.text: Arrangement 2 is defined in the AMCA arrangement standard as an overhung impeller fan, belt or direct driven, whose bearings are mounted in a bracket supported by the fan housing rather than on a separate pedestal. It is essentially Arrangement 1 with the pedestal replaced by a bracket on the housing. FanPedia's arrangement drawings (pp. 20–29) do not include an Arrangement 2, so treat it as a code you may meet on older drawings or other manufacturers' equipment. If a customer asks for one, check what the current Twin City Fan catalog offers before quoting; an Arrangement 1 or 9 usually meets the same need.

docs.title: Arrangement 3
docs.text:
Arrangement 3 is a center hung impeller fan with one bearing on each side of the impeller, the bearings supported by the fan housing, and the motor mounted separately on the floor or fan base. FanPedia shows it for single width fans as "Belt Driven; Motor Mounted on Floor or Fan Base" (FanPedia p. 20) and for double width fans as "Direct Drive or Belt Driven" (FanPedia p. 23). The description calls it "structurally sound and compact" and notes that the single width version "has one bearing located in the airstream" (FanPedia p. 163). Double width fans "are generally supplied in Arrangement 3 for V-belt drive" (FanPedia p. 167), and Arrangement 3 is also "the most common plenum fan arrangement," frequently used in OEM and site-built air handlers (FanPedia p. 168).

Worked example: matching Arrangement 3 to the air. Two DWDI fan requests arrive on the same day. The first is a supply fan for an office air handler moving filtered outdoor air. The second exhausts 200°F air from a dryer. For the first, a standard Arrangement 3 DWDI is a natural choice: it is compact, belt driven for easy speed adjustment, and the air is clean and well under 130°F. For the second, the same arrangement fails on FanPedia's own limit: both bearings sit in the airstream, and standard DWDI fans are for clean air "limited to 130°F" (FanPedia p. 167). The engineer looks instead at Arrangement 3DI, which uses integrated inlet boxes to move the bearings out of the airstream (next section), or at an overhung arrangement.

Arrangement 3 Is Not Automatically Hot-Air Ready

A common trap is assuming that because Arrangement 3 is common and robust, it suits any temperature. Its inlet-side bearing (both bearings on a DWDI) sits in the air; check the air temperature and cleanliness first, and move to an SI/DI or overhung arrangement when the air is hot or dirty.

docs.title: Arrangement 3 SI and DI
docs.text: Arrangement 3SI and Arrangement 3DI are center hung arrangements that add integral inlet boxes so that the bearings can stand outside the airstream. In 3SI (single inlet), a single width fan "utilizes an attached inlet box to locate the bearing outside of the airstream on independent bearing pedestals that allows for elevated operating temperatures and relatively clean air" (FanPedia p. 164). In 3DI (double inlet), a double width fan uses "integrated inlet boxes to locate the bearings outside of the airstream on independent bearing pedestals" (FanPedia p. 167). Both are usually direct drive: "the motor is located by the customer off the fan assembly and direct-coupled to the shaft," and both include a pie split housing for easy impeller removal (FanPedia pp. 164, 167). The inlet box turns the incoming air through a right angle, which is what clears a path for the shaft to pass out of the box to a bearing that the air never touches.

docs.title: Arrangement 4
docs.text:
Arrangement 4 is a direct drive fan with the impeller mounted on the motor shaft and the motor mounted on a pedestal. FanPedia's caption: "Direct Drive; Impeller Mounted to Motor Shaft" (FanPedia p. 20). It has no fan shaft and no fan bearings, which gives it the lowest maintenance of any arrangement: "there are no fan bearings, fan shaft or drive parts to maintain" (FanPedia p. 164). It is also compact. The limits come from the same simplicity. The motor's bearings carry the whole impeller, which limits size: FanPedia notes that "Arrangement 4 fans are typically limited up to size 365" (FanPedia p. 164). And the motor sits close to the air, so "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171). FanPedia's high temperature page for Arrangement 4 centrifugal fans describes a shaft seal, a shaft cooler, a cooler guard and a hub for airstream temperatures from 181°F to 1,000+°F (FanPedia p. 111). Current practice is more conservative: Twin City Fan engineering says Arrangement 4 is not used for high-temperature applications, and its standard ranges are typically up to about 180°F (for example EPQN 0-180°F, QSL 0-160°F, TCTA 0-105°F, from Twin City Fan's model temperature tables). Other ranges are special order.

Several variants build on it (FanPedia pp. 20–21):

  • 4S: swingout construction for easy access to the impeller and housing interior.
  • 4VI and 4HI: mounted directly on the fan inlet, vertical or horizontal; "the entire fan is supported by the inlet flange only."
  • Plenum, plug, axial, inline and lab exhaust Arrangement 4: covered later in this chapter.

Worked example: when Arrangement 4 fits. A small exhaust fan serves a clean, room-temperature process with no one available for belt maintenance. Direct drive at a standard motor speed meets the duty, and the selected fan size is well under the size where Arrangement 4 is typically limited. Arrangement 4 is the natural choice: no belts, no fan bearings to grease, compact footprint. Now raise the air temperature to 600°F. Arrangement 4 is no longer the right choice: Twin City Fan engineering does not use it for high-temperature applications. An overhung Arrangement 1, 8, 9 or 10 with the bearings and motor well away from the heat is the answer (FanPedia pp. 110–111).

docs.title: Arrangement 7
docs.text: Arrangement 7 is a direct drive, center hung fan whose motor is coupled to the fan shaft and mounted on a pedestal. FanPedia captions it "similar to Arr. 3 but with motor pedestal" (FanPedia p. 21) and describes it as an arrangement in which "the impeller is mounted between the bearings, but the Arrangement 7 incorporates a pedestal designed to accommodate the motor, flexible coupling and one bearing" (FanPedia p. 168). The SI and DI versions, 7SI and 7DI, add integrated inlet boxes to move the bearings out of the airstream and are mounted on a unitary base as standard, with an inertia base available as an option (FanPedia pp. 165, 168). Choose Arrangement 7 over 3 when the duty suits a direct drive motor speed and you want the motor carried on the fan's own pedestal instead of driving through belts.

docs.title: Bearings Out of the Airstream
docs.text:
You have now seen one idea several times: some arrangements are chosen because they keep the bearings out of the airstream. Bearings are lubricated precision parts. Hot air thins and breaks down their grease; dusty, corrosive or wet air attacks their seals; and in spark-resistant construction, a bearing in the airstream is a potential ignition source. FanPedia's spark-resistant construction pages state flatly: "Bearings not allowed in airstream" (FanPedia p. 104). Keeping the bearings outside the housing also makes them easier to reach for lubrication and inspection.

An arrangement keeps its bearings out of the airstream in one of three ways:

  1. Overhang the impeller so both bearings sit on a pedestal outside the housing: Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10 (FanPedia pp. 30, 162).
  2. Add inlet boxes to a center hung fan so the inlet-side bearing stands outside the box: Arrangements 3SI, 3DI, 7SI and 7DI (FanPedia pp. 164–168).
  3. Put the whole rotating assembly outside the air path, as plug fans do: in Arrangement 9 plug fans, "motor, shaft and bearings are outside of the process airstream" (FanPedia p. 172), and belt driven axial and inline Arrangement 9 fans are "the perfect choice for applications that require the motor to be out of the airstream" (FanPedia p. 173).

Worked example: screening arrangements for a hot, dirty exhaust. A foundry needs a belt driven centrifugal exhaust fan for 350°F air carrying dust. The application engineer screens the arrangements:

Candidate Bearings in the airstream? Verdict Arrangement 3 SWSI Yes, one (FanPedia p. 163) Reject: hot, dusty air at a bearing Arrangement 3 DWDI Yes, both; limited to 130°F clean air (FanPedia p. 167) Reject Arrangement 4 No fan bearings, but the motor is close to the air (FanPedia p. 171) Reject: Twin City Fan engineering does not use Arrangement 4 for high-temperature applications, and it is not belt driven anyway Arrangement 1 No; both on the pedestal (FanPedia p. 162) Keep Arrangement 9 or 10 No; overhung, bearings on the pedestal (FanPedia p. 30) Keep; choose by where the motor should go

The shortlist is Arrangements 1, 9 and 10, which also appear in FanPedia's high temperature centrifugal construction list, for 276°F to 1,000+°F (FanPedia p. 110). The final choice comes down to motor location and footprint, the subject of Chapter 24.

The Code Alphabet Takes a Few Passes

If 3SI, 7DI, 4VI and 9SS are starting to blur together, that's normal; most people need a few drawings before the suffixes stick. Anchor each one to its base number first (overhung or center hung, belt or direct), then read the letters as modifications, and keep FanPedia pp. 20–29 open beside you while you practice.

The microsim below lets you practice naming the base arrangement from the features a drawing shows.

docs.title: Diagram: Arrangement Identifier
docs.text:
Run Arrangement Identifier Fullscreen

Arrangement Identifier

Type: microsim sim-id: ch11-arrangement-identifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish ten centrifugal fan arrangements (1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10) from schematic side-view drawings by identifying the drive type, the impeller position relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor.

Prerequisites: direct drive, belt drive, shaft coupling, sheave, overhung impeller, center hung impeller, bearing pedestal, inlet box, SWSI, DWDI, fan arrangement, Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10 (defined in this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 10 drawings, the learner first answers three feature questions (drive: Belt / Direct with coupling / Direct on motor shaft; impeller: Overhung / Center hung; bearings carried by: Pedestal / Fan housing (at least one bearing) / Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes / Motor only), then names the arrangement from a list of the ten. The arrangement answer is correct when it matches the "Arrangement" column. Mastery is 8 of 10 arrangements correct on the first attempt. Feature answers are scaffolding and are scored separately.

Misconceptions: (1) Every direct drive fan is Arrangement 4. (2) Any fan with a coupling is Arrangement 7, whatever the impeller position. (3) Arrangement 1 and Arrangement 9 differ in impeller position (they differ only in motor location). (4) Arrangement 2 and Arrangement 1 are the same (Arrangement 2's bearings are on a bracket carried by the housing).

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing arrangements is an Analyze task: the learner must break each drawing into its defining features before naming the whole. Asking for the features first, and committing them before the name, makes the learner perform that decomposition rather than pattern-match a picture.

Content:

Each drawing is a simple schematic side view (viewed from the side of the shaft) showing only the parts listed for it. The parts drawn are the content being taught.

# Parts shown in the drawing Drive Impeller Bearings carried by Arrangement Why (feedback) 1 SWSI housing; two bearings together on a pedestal beside the drive side of the housing; impeller at the shaft end; motor on its own base on the floor, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 1 Overhung on a pedestal with a separately mounted motor is Arrangement 1 (FanPedia pp. 20, 162). 2 SWSI housing; two bearings in a bracket bolted to the drive side of the housing; impeller at the shaft end; separate motor with belts Belt Overhung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 2 Overhung with bearings in a bracket on the housing is AMCA Arrangement 2. 3 SWSI housing; one bearing on the drive side and one on a bracket across the inlet; impeller between them; motor on the floor beside the fan, belts to the fan sheave Belt Center hung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 3 Center hung with bearings carried by the housing and a separate motor is Arrangement 3 (FanPedia pp. 20, 163). 4 SWSI housing with an attached inlet box; impeller between two bearings, each on its own pedestal outside the housing and inlet box; a coupled motor off the fan assembly Direct with coupling Center hung Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes 3SI The attached inlet box puts the bearing outside the air on independent pedestals (FanPedia p. 164). 5 DWDI housing with an inlet box on each side; impeller between two bearings on independent pedestals; a coupled motor off the fan assembly Direct with coupling Center hung Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes 3DI Double width with integrated inlet boxes and independent bearing pedestals is Arrangement 3DI (FanPedia p. 167). 6 SWSI housing; motor on a pedestal; impeller hub on the motor shaft; no separate shaft, no fan bearings Direct on motor shaft Overhung Motor only 4 Impeller mounted to the motor shaft is Arrangement 4 (FanPedia pp. 20, 164). 7 DWDI housing; impeller between two bearings; a pedestal on the drive side carrying one bearing, a flexible coupling and the motor Direct with coupling Center hung Fan housing (at least one bearing) 7 Center hung with a pedestal for motor, coupling and one bearing is Arrangement 7 (FanPedia pp. 21, 168). 8 SWSI housing; two bearings on a long pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; a flexible coupling and the motor on the far end of the same pedestal Direct with coupling Overhung Pedestal 8 An Arrangement 1 pedestal extended for a coupled motor is Arrangement 8 (FanPedia p. 165). 9 SWSI housing; two bearings on a pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 9 Overhung with the motor on the side of the bearing pedestal is Arrangement 9 (FanPedia p. 165). 10 SWSI housing; two bearings on a pedestal; impeller at the shaft end; motor on an adjustable base inside the pedestal, belts to the fan sheave Belt Overhung Pedestal 10 Overhung with the motor inside the bearing pedestal is Arrangement 10 (FanPedia p. 167).

Answer list for the arrangement question, in this order: 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10.

A note on screen reads: "Schematics are simplified. Twin City Fan arrangement drawings: FanPedia pp. 20–23. Arrangement 2 is from the AMCA standard and is not shown in FanPedia."

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 20–23 (arrangement drawings and captions), p. 30 (impeller orientation), pp. 162–168 (technical descriptions cited per row). Arrangement 2: AMCA arrangement standard definition, as stated in this chapter's "Arrangement 2" section.

Rules: Drawings are shown in shuffled order. The arrangement question unlocks only after all three feature questions are answered. Feature answers are scored but do not block the arrangement answer. If the three committed features match the drawing's columns, the arrangement list highlights the arrangements consistent with those features (for drawing 1, features Belt / Overhung / Pedestal highlight 1, 9 and 10). If any feature is wrong, no highlighting is shown.

Learner Activity:

  1. A drawing appears. The learner answers the drive question, the impeller question and the bearings question.
  2. The learner presses Check Features. Each feature is marked correct or incorrect, with the correct answer shown.
  3. The learner selects an arrangement from the list and presses Check Arrangement. The drawing's parts are labeled and the "Why" text appears.
  4. After 10 drawings the learner sees separate scores for features and arrangements and may start a new shuffled round.

Feedback: 10 drawings, shuffled, one attempt per question per round. Correct arrangement: "Correct: Arrangement ." Incorrect: "This is Arrangement . ." Added messages for likely confusions: choosing 4 for drawings 4, 5, 7 or 8: "There is a coupling and a separate fan shaft, so this is not Arrangement 4." Choosing 7 for drawing 8: "The impeller is overhung, not between the bearings; a coupled overhung fan is Arrangement 8." Choosing 1 for drawing 9 or 10, or 9 for 10: "Look at where the motor is mounted; Arrangements 1, 9 and 10 differ only in motor location." Choosing 1 for drawing 2: "The bearings are on a bracket carried by the housing, not on a pedestal." The answer is revealed after each check. Running counts "Features correct: n of 30" and "Arrangements correct: n of 10" are shown.

Starting State: The first drawing of a shuffled set is shown with all questions unanswered and the prompt "How is this fan driven, where is the impeller, and what carries the bearings?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example names an Arrangement 9 from a drawing with a belt guard, an overhung impeller with both bearings on a pedestal, and the motor on a slide base on the side of the pedestal, and states that Arrangements 1, 9 and 10 differ in motor location. The chapter states that Arrangement 2 is not shown in FanPedia's arrangement drawings (pp. 20–29).

Read a Drawing in Three Glances

Want to name an arrangement in ten seconds? Glance once for a belt guard or a coupling, once to see whether anything stands on the inlet side of the impeller, and once to find the motor; check it from the drive side, and the number follows.

docs.title: Arrangement Families Beyond the Housed Centrifugal
docs.text: The numbers above were defined for housed centrifugal fans. The other fan families from Chapters 4 through 6 reuse many of the same base numbers, with letters that describe how each family is mounted. This section introduces the families; Chapter 24 covers each lettered variant in detail.

docs.title: Plug Fan Arrangements
docs.text:
A plug fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan whose impeller and inlet funnel sit inside the customer's enclosure, while the shaft, bearings and motor stay outside it, mounted through a wall panel; "the system plenum acts as the fan housing" (Chapter 7; FanPedia p. 172). Plug fan arrangements describe how that fan is supported and driven. FanPedia shows six (FanPedia pp. 26–27):

  • Arrangement 9: belt driven, "fully supported by the customer's wall"; FanPedia calls it "the most common plug fan arrangement" (FanPedia p. 172).
  • Arrangement 4: direct drive, impeller on the motor shaft, wall mounted; compact and low maintenance, though "high airstream temperatures may limit the use of this arrangement" (FanPedia p. 171).
  • Arrangement 8: direct drive, motor coupled to the fan shaft, wall mounted; "the least common plug fan arrangement due to the length of the assembly" (FanPedia p. 171).
  • Arrangements 1P, 4P, 8P and 9P: the "P" (pedestal plug) versions are floor mounted. FanPedia explains why: they are "typically used on larger fans and/or larger HP motors where the customer's wall may not be sufficient by itself," and "mounting to the foundation also makes it better for meeting lower vibration requirements" (FanPedia pp. 170–172).

Worked example: wall or floor? An oven builder wants a large belt driven plug fan to recirculate hot air, and the oven wall is light-gauge insulated panel. The default plug fan choice is Arrangement 9, which hangs the whole fan on the wall. Here the wall may not carry a large fan and motor, and an oven line usually cares about vibration. Arrangement 9P mounts the same belt driven fan on its own pedestal at grade, so the wall only seals around the fan, with the mounting panel optional (FanPedia p. 172). Because the bearings and motor are outside the oven in both versions, the hot air never reaches them.

docs.title: Plenum Fan Arrangements
docs.text: A plenum fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan that sits inside an air plenum and pressurizes it, with its motor and drive inside the plenum too, unlike a plug fan (FanPedia pp. 5, 172). Plenum fan arrangements describe how the motor and drive are mounted on the fan frame. FanPedia shows belt driven Arrangements 1 and 3, the top-mounted motor versions 3HS and 3HA, the side-mounted 3SM, the vertical 3VA and 3VS, and direct drive Arrangements 4 and 4V (FanPedia pp. 24–25). Arrangement 3 is "the most common plenum fan arrangement" in OEM and site-built air handlers, and direct drive Arrangement 4 plenum fans serve cleanroom and pharmaceutical work (FanPedia pp. 168, 170).

docs.title: Vertical Arrangement
docs.text: A vertical arrangement is one in which the fan shaft is vertical, so air enters or leaves the impeller vertically. FanPedia's vertical arrangements include Arrangement 4VI, a centrifugal fan "designed to mount directly on the inlet of the fan" with "a vertical airflow into the fan (vertical motor shaft)" (FanPedia p. 164); the vertical plenum arrangements 3VA and 3VS (FanPedia pp. 169–170); and plenum Arrangement 4V, available "with either vertical up airflow (inlet under the motor) or vertical down airflow (inlet above the motor)" (FanPedia p. 170). Vertical fans need bearing and shaft details suited to a vertical shaft, covered in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Axial and Inline Arrangements
docs.text:
Axial and inline arrangements apply the same numbering to tubular fans: axial fans and inline centrifugal fans. FanPedia shows two base arrangements with access variants, and notes that "inline centrifugal fans are available with the same arrangements but use different impellers" (FanPedia p. 28):

  • Arrangement 4 (direct drive): "the impeller is mounted directly on the fan motor shaft," making it "the logical choice when space is at a premium or a simple, dependable fan with minimum maintenance is required." Exact performance is reached by adjusting the blade angle (FanPedia p. 172). The motor sits inside the tube on its support.
  • Arrangement 9 (belt driven): "the perfect choice for applications that require the motor to be out of the airstream," with "either a fixed or adjustable V-belt drive system," so a rating change is "a simple sheave change or blade angle adjustment" (FanPedia p. 173). The motor sits outside the tube and the belts run through a belt tube.
  • CS and SO variants (4CS, 4SO, 9CS, 9SO) add a clamshell door or a swingout rotor for maintenance access (FanPedia pp. 172–173).

Worked example: an inline fan for oily, moist exhaust. A designer specifies a tubeaxial exhaust fan for air that carries oil mist and moisture. A direct drive Arrangement 4 would put the motor inside the tube, in that air. Arrangement 9 keeps the motor outside the tube with the belts shielded by the belt tube, so the motor stays clean and cool, and if the system turns out to need a little more air after balancing, a sheave change handles it without replacing the motor. If cleaning access matters, the 9CS (clamshell) or 9SO (swingout) variant adds a door to reach the rotor (FanPedia p. 173).

docs.title: Lab Exhaust Arrangements
docs.text:
Lab exhaust arrangements are the arrangements offered on laboratory fume exhaust fans, the high-plume fans that dilute and discharge hazardous fumes above a building (Chapter 5 and Chapter 6). FanPedia's fume exhaust arrangement page (FanPedia p. 29) and descriptions (FanPedia pp. 174–175) show five, each tied to particular models. The table below gathers them; the models were introduced in Chapter 4.

Arrangement Drive Models shown (FanPedia p. 29) Notes from FanPedia pp. 174–175 1 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE Overhung; two bearings on the pedestal, out of the airstream 4 Direct BAIFE, BCIFE, TVIFE Impeller on motor shaft; motor on a pedestal (BAIFE, BCIFE) or motor drive plate (TVIFE) 8 Direct (coupled) BAIFE, BCIFE Arrangement 1 pedestal extended for the motor; flexible coupling 9 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE, TFE, QFE, QIFE Motor slide base on the pedestal (BAIFE, BCIFE) or adjustable motor base on the housing exterior (inline models, excluding TVIFE) 10 Belt BAIFE, BCIFE Scroll-type centrifugal only; motor base inside the pedestal; weather cover option for roof or outdoor use

Worked example: matching a lab exhaust model to an arrangement. A lab project calls for an induced-flow mixed flow fan and asks for "belt drive with the motor out of the exhaust." Of the two induced-flow mixed flow models, FanPedia shows TVIFE only in direct drive Arrangement 4 (on a motor drive plate) and QIFE in belt driven Arrangement 9 (FanPedia pp. 29, 174–175). So the request points to a QIFE in Arrangement 9, with its adjustable motor base on the outside of the housing. If the project had specified a scroll housed BCIFE with a compact rooftop footprint, Arrangement 10, with the motor inside the pedestal and the optional weather cover, would be worth offering.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Direct drive turns the impeller at motor speed, either with the impeller on the motor shaft (Arrangement 4) or through a shaft coupling to a fan shaft (Arrangements 7 and 8). It is simple and low maintenance, but fan speed is fixed unless a VFD is added. A direct drive tubular fan carries its motor on a motor support base inside the tube.
  • Belt drive sets fan speed through the sheave ratio, \( N_{fan} = N_{motor} \times D_{motor} / D_{fan} \). A larger fan sheave slows the fan. V-belts wedge into sheave grooves; belt count is design horsepower divided by per-belt rating, rounded up.
  • The drive service factor multiplies motor horsepower to give design horsepower for belts and sheaves. It is not the motor nameplate's service factor.
  • An overhung impeller sits at the end of the shaft with both bearings on one side (Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 10 and 4); a center hung impeller sits between the bearings (Arrangements 3 and 7).
  • A fan arrangement number answers three questions: how the fan is driven, where the impeller sits relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and motor. Arrangement 1 is overhung with a separate motor; Arrangement 2 (AMCA, not in FanPedia) carries its bearings on a housing bracket; Arrangement 3 is center hung with one bearing (SWSI) or both (DWDI) in the airstream; Arrangement 4 puts the impeller on the motor shaft; Arrangement 7 is a coupled, center hung fan with a motor pedestal.
  • Arrangements 3SI and 3DI (and 7SI, 7DI) use inlet boxes to move center hung bearings out of the air.
  • Keeping the bearings out of the airstream matters for hot, dirty, corrosive and spark-resistant duty; overhung arrangements, inlet-box arrangements and plug fans all achieve it.
  • The same numbers reappear in the plug, plenum, vertical, axial and inline, and lab exhaust families, with letters that describe the mounting.

You Can Name the Arrangement

You can now size a belt drive from its sheaves, tell an overhung rotor from a center hung one, and turn a drawing into an arrangement number by asking three questions. That's the vocabulary every order, outline drawing and field service call in the rest of this book will use.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
docs.text: Test your understanding of direct and belt drives, overhung and center hung impellers, and the standard numbered fan arrangements with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which statement best describes an overhung impeller?
docs.text:
1. The impeller is mounted between two bearings, one on each side of it
  2. The impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, beyond both bearings
  3. The impeller is mounted on a shaft that is carried by bearings inside the inlet
  4. The impeller is mounted on a vertical shaft above the motor
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An overhung impeller sits at the end of the shaft, past both bearings, like the load on a diving board. The two bearings sit together on a bearing pedestal outside the housing. An impeller mounted between the bearings (A) is a center hung impeller. A bearing in the inlet (C) belongs to a center hung single width fan, and a vertical shaft (D) describes a vertical arrangement, not the impeller's position on the shaft.

Concept Tested: Overhung Impeller

See: Overhung Impeller

docs.title: 2. Which arrangement has the impeller mounted directly on the motor shaft, with no fan shaft and no fan bearings?
docs.text:
1. Arrangement 1
  2. Arrangement 7
  3. Arrangement 3
  4. Arrangement 4
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In Arrangement 4 the impeller is mounted directly to the motor shaft, so the motor's own bearings carry it. FanPedia notes that it offers low maintenance because there are no fan bearings, fan shaft or drive parts to maintain. Arrangement 1 has two fan bearings on a pedestal, Arrangement 3 carries its bearings on the housing, and Arrangement 7 couples the motor to a separate fan shaft.

Concept Tested: Arrangement 4

See: Arrangement 4

docs.title: 3. Why does FanPedia describe Arrangement 1 as ideal for high temperature or contaminated air?
docs.text:
1. Its two bearings sit on a pedestal outside the housing, out of the airstream
  2. Its impeller is center hung, so the bearing loads are shared evenly
  3. Its motor is mounted inside the housing, where the airflow cools it
  4. It is always direct driven, so there are no belts to degrade in the heat
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Arrangement 1 overhangs the impeller, so both bearings sit together on a pedestal beside the housing, out of the airstream. Hot air would thin and break down bearing grease, and dirty air would attack the seals, so keeping the bearings out of the air is the advantage. Arrangement 1 is overhung, not center hung (B); its motor is mounted separately on the floor or fan base (C); and it is usually belt driven (D).

Concept Tested: Bearings Out of Airstream

See: Bearings Out of the Airstream

docs.title: 4. How does the drive service factor differ from the motor service factor on the nameplate?
docs.text:
1. They are the same number, written once on the nameplate and once on the drive order
  2. The drive service factor is always lower than 1.0, while the motor service factor is above 1.0
  3. The drive service factor multiplies motor horsepower to size belts and sheaves; the motor service factor says how far above rated horsepower the motor may run
  4. The drive service factor applies only to direct drive fans, and the motor service factor only to belt drives
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The drive service factor comes from the belt drive manufacturer's table and multiplies motor horsepower to give the design horsepower used to select belts and sheaves. The motor service factor is a nameplate rating: FanPedia's example is 1.15 on a 100 HP motor, allowing 115 HP. Confusing the two (A) is the trap the chapter warns about. The drive service factor is at least 1.0 (B) and applies to belt drives (D).

Concept Tested: Drive Service Factor

See: Drive Service Factor

docs.title: 5. An arrangement drawing shows a flexible coupling joining the motor shaft to the fan shaft. What can you conclude?
docs.text:
1. The fan is belt driven, and the coupling replaces the fan sheave
  2. The fan is direct driven, has its own shaft and bearings, and is therefore not Arrangement 4
  3. The fan must be Arrangement 4, because every direct drive fan is Arrangement 4
  4. The impeller must be center hung, because couplings are used only on center hung fans
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A coupling joins two shafts end to end, so fan speed equals motor speed and the fan has its own shaft and bearings. Arrangement 4 has no fan shaft to couple to, so a coupled fan is a different arrangement, such as 7 (center hung) or 8 (overhung). A coupling is not part of a belt drive (A). Arrangement 8 shows that a coupled fan can be overhung, so D is wrong.

Concept Tested: Shaft Coupling

See: Shaft Coupling

docs.title: 6. A belt drive has a motor running at 1,760 rpm, a motor sheave with a 5.0 in pitch diameter and a fan sheave with an 8.0 in pitch diameter. How fast does the fan turn?
docs.text:
1. 1,100 rpm
  2. 2,816 rpm
  3. 1,760 rpm
  4. 1,320 rpm
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Fan speed equals motor speed times the motor sheave diameter divided by the fan sheave diameter: 1,760 × 5.0 / 8.0 = 1,100 rpm. The larger fan sheave slows the fan, so the answer must be below motor speed. Option B, 2,816 rpm, comes from inverting the ratio. Option C ignores the sheaves, as if the fan were direct driven.

Concept Tested: Sheave

See: Sheave

docs.title: 7. A 20 hp belt-driven fan uses a drive service factor of 1.3, and the chosen V-belt section can carry 7.0 hp per belt at this belt speed. How many belts does the drive need?
docs.text:
1. 2 belts
  2. 3 belts
  3. 4 belts
  4. 5 belts
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Design horsepower is 20 × 1.3 = 26 hp. Dividing by the per-belt rating gives 26 / 7.0 = 3.71, which is rounded up to 4 belts because a fraction of a belt cannot share the load. Rounding down to 3 (B) would overload every belt. Three belts also results from forgetting the service factor (20 / 7.0 = 2.86, rounded up).

Concept Tested: V-Belt

See: V-Belt

docs.title: 8. An outline drawing shows a belt-driven single inlet centrifugal fan. Both bearings sit together on a pedestal, nothing is on the inlet side of the impeller, and the motor is on an adjustable base inside the bearing pedestal. Which arrangement is it?
docs.text:
1. Arrangement 1
  2. Arrangement 3
  3. Arrangement 9
  4. Arrangement 10
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Belt drive with both bearings on a pedestal means an overhung fan: Arrangement 1, 9 or 10. These three differ only in where the motor goes. A motor on its own base on the floor is Arrangement 1, a motor on the side of the pedestal is Arrangement 9, and a motor inside the pedestal is Arrangement 10. Arrangement 3 is center hung, with a bearing on each side of the impeller.

Concept Tested: Fan Arrangement

See: The Fan Arrangement

docs.title: 9. An oven builder needs a large belt-driven plug fan to recirculate hot air. The oven wall is a light-gauge insulated panel, and the line is sensitive to vibration. Which plug fan arrangement fits best, and why?
docs.text:
1. Arrangement 9, because it is the most common plug fan arrangement
  2. Arrangement 4, because a direct drive fan has no belts to wear in the heat
  3. Arrangement 9P, because the pedestal carries the fan at grade instead of the wall and helps with lower vibration
  4. Arrangement 8, because the coupled motor shortens the assembly
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Arrangement 9 is the most common plug fan arrangement (A), but it hangs the whole fan on the customer's wall. FanPedia says the pedestal versions suit larger fans where the wall may not be enough, and that mounting to the foundation helps meet lower vibration requirements. Arrangement 4 is direct drive and limited by hot air (B). Arrangement 8 is the least common plug fan arrangement because of its long assembly (D).

Concept Tested: Plug Fan Arrangements

See: Plug Fan Arrangements

docs.title: 10. A large DWDI fan works well in a standard Arrangement 3 when it moves ambient outdoor air, but the same fan must now handle 300°F process air. What explains the problem, and what change addresses it?
docs.text:
1. Both center hung bearings sit in the airstream, so moving to Arrangement 3DI, whose inlet boxes put the bearings outside the air, addresses it
  2. The overhung impeller puts too much leverage on the bearing nearest the housing, so switching to a center hung fan addresses it
  3. The V-belts lose grip in hot air, so switching to an Arrangement 3 with a larger fan sheave addresses it
  4. The housing cannot withstand 300°F, so changing the discharge position addresses it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A DWDI fan has inlets on both sides, so both center hung bearings are in the airstream, and FanPedia limits standard DWDI fans to clean air at 130°F. Arrangement 3DI uses integrated inlet boxes to locate both bearings outside the airstream on independent pedestals. Option B describes an overhung fan, not a DWDI Arrangement 3. Belt grip (C) and discharge position (D) have nothing to do with the bearing temperature limit.

Concept Tested: Arrangement 3 SI and DI

See: Arrangement 3 SI and DI

docs.title: References: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
docs.text:
1. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia - Overview of centrifugal fan construction with a section on drive mechanisms, comparing direct and belt drive and noting where bearings sit. Useful background for this chapter's drive and impeller-position sections.

  2. Belt (mechanical) - Wikipedia - Explains V-belts, how the wedge-shaped section grips the sheave groove, and how pulley diameters set the speed ratio. Supports the chapter's sheave, V-belt and fan-speed calculations.

  3. Coupling - Wikipedia - Surveys shaft coupling types, including flexible couplings that tolerate small misalignment, and the alignment and maintenance issues they raise. Background for the chapter's coupled direct-drive Arrangements 7 and 8.

  4. Fan Handbook: Selection, Application, and Design (1998) - Frank P. Bleier - McGraw-Hill - Bleier writes from the viewpoint of a working fan application engineer, organizing fan knowledge around selection and installation decisions rather than aerodynamic theory, the same practical lens this chapter takes on drives and arrangements.

  5. Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design - Richard G. Budynas and J. Keith Nisbett - McGraw-Hill - Its flexible-elements chapter sizes V-belt drives from tabulated belt ratings corrected by service factors, the systematic design-horsepower method behind this chapter's belt count worked example.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - The chapter's primary source: arrangement drawings (pp. 20-29), impeller orientation (p. 30), shafts and couplings (pp. 79, 128-129) and arrangement technical descriptions (pp. 162-175).

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - The online edition of FanPedia, whose Fan Arrangements, Exploded Views and Technical Descriptions galleries show the arrangement drawings and descriptions this chapter cites, page by page.

  8. ANSI/AMCA Standard 99-16, Standards Handbook (PDF) - AMCA International - The AMCA handbook containing the drive arrangement drawings for centrifugal, axial and tubular centrifugal fans (sections 9 and 13), the numbering system this chapter's arrangement numbers come from.

  9. Fan Arrangements, Rotation, Discharge and Motor Position (FE-3900) - Twin City Fan - Engineering letter reproducing the AMCA 99-2404 centrifugal drive arrangements, including Arrangement 2 with bearings in a casing bracket, which FanPedia does not show.

  10. V-Belt Drive Selection for Fans (FE-1400) - Twin City Fan - Engineering letter on belt sections, sheaves, bushings, fixed versus variable pitch drives and service factors. A practical companion to the chapter's sheave, V-belt and drive service factor sections.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the conventions used to describe a fan's orientation. It establishes the rule that a fan is viewed from the drive side, then covers discharge positions and angles (up blast, top horizontal, bottom horizontal, down blast, and the angular discharges), inlet box position, rotation, inline configurations, and the standard W, X, Y, Z and axial motor positions. After completing it, readers can describe which way a fan discharges and where its motor sits.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Discharge Position 164 Discharge Angle 115 Inlet Box Position 19 Up Blast Discharge Position 22 Top Horizontal Discharge 22 Bottom Horizontal Discharge 22 Down Blast Discharge Position 22 Angular Discharge 5 Viewed From Drive Side 111 Motor Position 48 Top Angular Up Discharge 1 Top Angular Down Discharge 1 Bottom Angular Up Discharge 1 Rotation 87 Inline Configuration 5 Motor Positions W X Y Z 20 Axial Motor Positions 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements

docs.title: Why Orientation Needs a Shared Language
docs.text:
A fan that arrives on a job site with its outlet pointing the wrong way is not a small problem. The housing of a centrifugal fan is cast or welded around a fixed scroll, so the outlet cannot simply be turned to meet the duct. The installing contractor either rebuilds the ductwork, returns the fan, or waits for a replacement, and all three cost time and money. Almost every one of these mistakes traces back to two people describing the same fan from opposite sides.

This chapter gives you the vocabulary that prevents that mistake. You will learn the single viewing rule the industry uses, then the names for which way the impeller turns, which way the outlet points, where an inlet box sits, and where the motor goes. Chapter 13 turns these names into the compact codes written on orders; this chapter makes sure you can see what each code means before you write one.

Point It the Right Way the First Time

Every order you write, quote you check, or drawing you approve carries a rotation, a discharge and a motor position. Get them right and the fan bolts straight onto the duct; get one wrong and a crane sits idle while the outlet points at the wrong wall. By the end of this chapter you will read any fan's orientation as easily as reading a clock. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: Viewed From the Drive Side
docs.text:
Before you can name a fan's rotation or discharge, you must agree where the observer is standing. A fan housing seen from one side is the mirror image of the same housing seen from the other side: the outlet that points right from one side points left from the other, and a wheel that turns clockwise from one side turns counterclockwise from the other. Without a fixed viewpoint, every orientation word is ambiguous.

The convention that resolves this is to describe a centrifugal fan viewed from the drive side. The drive side is the side of the fan where the drive is located: the sheave and belts on a belt-driven fan, the coupling on a coupled fan, or the motor on a direct-drive fan. FanPedia's discharge pages show a person standing beside the bearing pedestal and looking at the housing, under the heading "Rotation View From Drive Side" (FanPedia pp. 46-49). Rotation, discharge position, inlet box position and the centrifugal motor positions are all read from that spot.

Two practical consequences follow. First, on a single-inlet fan with the drive on the pedestal, the drive side is the side opposite the inlet, so an installer standing at the inlet sees everything mirrored. Second, on a double-width, double-inlet (DWDI) fan, both faces of the housing have inlets, so "the inlet side" means nothing; only the end of the shaft carrying the drive identifies the viewpoint.

Worked example. A field technician sends a photo taken from the inlet of an Arrangement 1 single-inlet fan. In the photo the outlet is at the top of the housing and points to the technician's left, and the rotation arrow on the housing appears counterclockwise. The order says CW, Top Horizontal. Is the fan wrong?

  1. The photo was taken from the inlet side, which on this fan is opposite the drive side.
  2. Mirror the photo left to right. The outlet now points right, and the rotation arrow now reads clockwise.
  3. From the drive side, the fan is clockwise with a top horizontal outlet pointing right, which is exactly what was ordered.

The fan is correct. The only error was the viewpoint, which is the most common cause of a false "wrong fan" report.

Ask Where the Photo Was Taken

A common trap is comparing a job-site photo or sketch with the order without asking which side it was taken from. Before you agree that a fan is wrong, find the sheave, coupling or motor in the picture; if it is on the far side of the housing, mirror the image before you compare. Check it from the drive side.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
Rotation is the direction in which the impeller turns. For centrifugal fans it is stated as clockwise (CW) or counterclockwise (CCW), judged from the drive side. Rotation is not a free choice once the housing is built: a centrifugal impeller must turn toward the outlet, so that the air spinning off the blades travels around the scroll and leaves through the outlet. A backward-inclined or airfoil wheel turned the wrong way still moves some air, but at a fraction of its rated performance, while drawing power and making noise.

Axial impellers use a different reference. FanPedia's airflow and rotation pages state that axial rotation "is determined by viewing the impeller from the discharge side of the fan," and name the result left-hand (LH) or right-hand (RH) rotation (FanPedia pp. 37-41). The same pages warn that airflow direction and rotation must both be correct for the fan to deliver full performance, and that an impeller turning the wrong way will not move air in the proper direction. Chapter 13 develops the axial convention fully; for now, remember that the viewing rule depends on the fan family.

The following list summarizes the two viewpoints just described:

  • Centrifugal fans: view from the drive side; rotation is CW or CCW.
  • Axial impellers: view from the discharge side; rotation is LH or RH.

Worked example. After a motor replacement on a belt-driven SWSI fan, a facilities technician bumps the motor to check rotation. Standing at the sheave guard (the drive side), they see the wheel turning counterclockwise. The nameplate and order say CW.

  1. The observer is on the drive side, so no mirroring is needed: the wheel really is turning CCW.
  2. The required rotation is CW, so the wheel is turning backward.
  3. On a three-phase motor, interchanging any two of the three supply leads reverses the motor. The electrician swaps two leads, and the next bump shows clockwise rotation.

Had the technician stood at the inlet, the wheel would have appeared clockwise and the backward wheel would have been missed. That fan would then have run at reduced airflow with no obvious fault, which is the expensive version of this mistake.

docs.title: Discharge Position
docs.text:
The discharge position of a centrifugal fan is the direction in which air leaves the housing outlet, described from the drive side. Because the housing scroll wraps around the impeller in the direction of rotation, the outlet always sits where the spinning air naturally leaves the wheel. That ties discharge position to rotation: a given outlet direction can be built on a clockwise housing or on a counterclockwise housing, and the two are mirror images that are not interchangeable.

FanPedia defines eight standard discharge positions for single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) centrifugal fans, each 45 degrees apart (FanPedia pp. 46-47). Each has a full name and a three-letter abbreviation:

  • UBD, Upblast: the outlet points straight up.
  • TAU, Top Angular Up: the outlet is near the top and points upward at 45 degrees.
  • THD, Top Horizontal: the outlet is at the top and points horizontally.
  • TAD, Top Angular Down: the outlet is near the top and points downward at 45 degrees.
  • DBD, Downblast: the outlet points straight down.
  • BAD, Bottom Angular Down: the outlet is near the bottom and points downward at 45 degrees.
  • BHD, Bottom Horizontal: the outlet is at the bottom and points horizontally.
  • BAU, Bottom Angular Up: the outlet is near the bottom and points upward at 45 degrees.

The name alone does not tell you whether a horizontal outlet points left or right. That comes from the rotation. On a clockwise fan, air at the top of the wheel is moving to the right, so a CW top horizontal outlet points right; on a counterclockwise fan, the same outlet points left. A complete discharge description therefore always pairs a rotation with a position.

docs.title: Discharge Angle
docs.text:
The discharge angle is the number of degrees from the upblast position to the actual outlet direction, measured in the direction of rotation. Upblast is both 0 and 360 degrees, and FanPedia writes it as 360. Each step of 45 degrees moves the outlet one position around the housing, so the angle and the name carry the same information: FanPedia lists "CW 90" as also known as "Clockwise 90°" for Top Horizontal, and so on around the circle (FanPedia pp. 46-47).

Measuring in the direction of rotation is what makes the system work for both hands. A CW 90 outlet and a CCW 90 outlet are both top horizontal, one pointing right and the other pointing left. If you want the outlet direction as a single compass-style angle, measured clockwise from straight up as seen from the drive side, it is:

\[ \theta = \begin{cases} N & \text{for clockwise rotation} \\ 360^\circ - N & \text{for counterclockwise rotation} \end{cases} \]

where \( N \) is the discharge angle in degrees (45 to 360) and \( \theta \) is the direction the air leaves, with 0 degrees straight up, 90 degrees to the right, 180 degrees straight down, and 270 degrees to the left (360 is treated as 0).

Worked example. A submittal lists a fan as CCW 135. Which way does the air leave?

  1. The angle is \( N = 135^\circ \) and the rotation is counterclockwise.
  2. \( \theta = 360^\circ - 135^\circ = 225^\circ \), which is down and to the left as seen from the drive side.
  3. An outlet that points downward at 45 degrees from near the top of the housing is Top Angular Down, so CCW 135 is TAD with the air heading down and to the left.

A CW 135 fan is also TAD, but with \( \theta = 135^\circ \) the air heads down and to the right. The two housings are mirror images.

The table below gathers the eight positions with their angles and the outlet direction for each rotation, using the rule you just applied.

Abbreviation Name Discharge angle Air leaves toward (CW) Air leaves toward (CCW) UBD Upblast 360 Straight up Straight up TAU Top Angular Up 45 Up and right Up and left THD Top Horizontal 90 Right Left TAD Top Angular Down 135 Down and right Down and left DBD Downblast 180 Straight down Straight down BAD Bottom Angular Down 225 Down and left Down and right BHD Bottom Horizontal 270 Left Right BAU Bottom Angular Up 315 Up and left Up and right

The Angle Follows the Wheel

Notice that the discharge angle is not a compass bearing; it counts degrees in whichever direction the wheel turns, starting from upblast. That is why one table of names serves both rotations, and why "CW 90" and "CCW 90" are the same name with mirror-image housings.

Even upblast and downblast, which point the same way for both rotations, are not interchangeable between hands. On a CW upblast fan the outlet sits on the left side of the housing top, because that is where air on a clockwise wheel is moving upward; on a CCW upblast fan it sits on the right. Duct centerlines on a drawing reveal the difference immediately.

Before working through the interactive explorer below, make sure the three ideas it uses are clear: rotation is read from the drive side, the discharge angle counts from upblast in the direction of rotation, and a view from the opposite side is a mirror image.

docs.title: Diagram: Discharge Position Explorer
docs.text:
Run Discharge Position Explorer Fullscreen

Discharge Position Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: ch12-discharge-position-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the drive-side viewing rule and the discharge-angle convention to name the rotation and discharge position of ten SWSI centrifugal housing drawings, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: drive side, viewed from the drive side, rotation (CW and CCW), discharge position, discharge angle, the eight position names and abbreviations, mirror image of an opposite-side view (all defined in the sections "Viewed From the Drive Side", "Rotation", "Discharge Position" and "Discharge Angle" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the ten challenge drawings, the learner commits one rotation (CW or CCW) and one of the eight discharge abbreviations before pressing Check. An answer is correct only when both the rotation and the abbreviation match the answer column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Exploration mode (changing rotation, angle and viewpoint and watching the housing redraw) is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The rotation seen from the inlet side is the fan's rotation. (2) The discharge angle is a fixed compass bearing that ignores rotation, so CW 90 and CCW 90 point the same way. (3) Upblast and downblast housings are the same for both rotations because the air points the same way. (4) "Top Horizontal" alone tells you which way the air goes.

Instructional Rationale: Naming an orientation from a drawing is an Apply-level skill that needs practice with a judged answer, so the learner commits rotation and position before feedback. Exploration mode first lets the learner see each angle step move the outlet around the housing and see the mirror flip when the viewpoint changes, which confronts misconceptions 2 and 3 with the drawing itself; the inlet-side challenge items confront misconception 1.

Content:

Exploration mode. The learner can set three things, and the sim draws an SWSI centrifugal housing with a rotation arrow, the outlet, and a label stating the viewpoint:

Quantity Values Default Rotation CW, CCW CW Discharge angle 45 to 360 in steps of 45 degrees (eight values) 360 Viewpoint Drive side, Inlet side (opposite drive) Drive side

For the current setting the sim shows: the abbreviation and full name; the designation in the form "CW 90"; the FanPedia "also known as" form ("Clockwise 90°"); and the direction the air leaves as seen from the drive side, from the "Air leaves toward" columns of the chapter's discharge table. When the viewpoint is Inlet side, the drawing is mirrored left to right and a note reads: "You are looking from the inlet side. The fan's rotation and discharge are still named as seen from the drive side."

The eight positions (abbreviation, name, discharge angle): UBD Upblast 360; TAU Top Angular Up 45; THD Top Horizontal 90; TAD Top Angular Down 135; DBD Downblast 180; BAD Bottom Angular Down 225; BHD Bottom Horizontal 270; BAU Bottom Angular Up 315.

Challenge mode. Ten drawings in this fixed order. "Viewpoint" is what the drawing shows; the arrow and outlet are described as they appear in that drawing.

# Viewpoint shown Rotation arrow as drawn Outlet as drawn Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Drive side Clockwise At the top, pointing right CW THD (CW 90) From upblast, 90 degrees clockwise is top horizontal, and a CW wheel throws air to the right at the top. 2 Drive side Counterclockwise On the right side of the top, pointing straight up CCW UBD (CCW 360) Straight up is upblast; it sits on the right because air on the right of a CCW wheel moves upward. 3 Drive side Clockwise At the bottom, pointing left CW BHD (CW 270) 270 degrees clockwise from upblast is bottom horizontal; a CW wheel moves air to the left at the bottom. 4 Drive side Counterclockwise On the left side, pointing straight down CCW DBD (CCW 180) Straight down is downblast; it sits on the left because air on the left of a CCW wheel moves downward. 5 Drive side Clockwise Near the top on the left, pointing up and to the right at 45 degrees CW TAU (CW 45) One 45-degree step clockwise from upblast is top angular up. 6 Drive side Counterclockwise Near the top on the left, pointing down and to the left at 45 degrees CCW TAD (CCW 135) Three 45-degree steps counterclockwise from upblast is top angular down; the air heads down and left. 7 Drive side Clockwise Near the bottom on the left, pointing up and to the left at 45 degrees CW BAU (CW 315) Seven 45-degree steps clockwise from upblast is bottom angular up. 8 Inlet side Counterclockwise At the top, pointing left CW THD (CW 90) From the inlet side everything is mirrored; from the drive side the wheel is CW and the top outlet points right. 9 Inlet side Clockwise On the left side of the top, pointing straight up CCW UBD (CCW 360) Mirror the inlet-side view: from the drive side the wheel is CCW and the upblast outlet is on the right. 10 Drive side Counterclockwise At the bottom, pointing right CCW BHD (CCW 270) 270 degrees counterclockwise from upblast is bottom horizontal; a CCW wheel moves air to the right at the bottom.

Provenance: Position names, abbreviations, angles and the "also known as" forms come from FanPedia pp. 46-47 (SWSI Centrifugal Fans, Clockwise and Counterclockwise, "Rotation View From Drive Side"), local copy fanpedia.pdf in the course source folder. The outlet-location rule follows the housing drawings on those pages. Challenge items are constructed for this chapter from those rules.

Rules: Let N be the discharge angle (45, 90, ..., 360) and let all directions be measured clockwise from straight up, as seen from the drive side, with 360 treated as 0. Air direction: theta = N for CW; theta = (360 - N) mod 360 for CCW. Outlet location on the housing: for CW, location = (theta - 90) mod 360; for CCW, location = (theta + 90) mod 360. Inlet-side view: draw the mirror image, so every direction d becomes (360 - d) mod 360 and the drawn rotation arrow reverses; the correct name does not change. Position names map from N exactly as in Content. A challenge answer is correct when rotation equals the answer's rotation AND abbreviation equals the answer's abbreviation; there is no partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. In exploration mode the learner steps the discharge angle from 360 through 45, 90 and on to 315 with CW selected, and watches the outlet move clockwise around the housing one position per step while the name and designation update.
  2. The learner switches rotation to CCW at the same angle. The housing redraws as a mirror image and the "Air leaves toward" text changes side; the learner should notice that the name and angle stayed the same.
  3. The learner sets the viewpoint to Inlet side. The drawing mirrors and the arrow appears reversed, while the name and designation do not change; the learner should notice that only the picture changed.
  4. The learner starts the challenge. For each drawing they choose a rotation and an abbreviation, then press Check.
  5. After the tenth item a summary shows the score and lists any missed items with their feedback.

Feedback: Ten items, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ( )." Incorrect on the first attempt: if the rotation is wrong on an inlet-side item, "Check the viewpoint: this drawing is from the inlet side, so mirror it before naming the rotation."; if the rotation is wrong on a drive-side item, "Read the arrow as drawn: this view is from the drive side."; if only the abbreviation is wrong, "Count 45-degree steps from upblast in the direction of rotation." After a second wrong attempt the correct answer and the Why text are shown and the item counts as missed. Only first-attempt answers count toward the score. A running count "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: Exploration mode, CW, discharge angle 360, viewpoint Drive side. The housing shows a CW upblast outlet on the left side of the top. The prompt reads: "Step the angle and predict where the outlet will go before it moves."

Chapter Anchors: Eight positions, 45 degrees apart; upblast written as 360; the discharge angle is measured from upblast in the direction of rotation; theta = N for CW and 360 - N for CCW; CCW 135 is TAD with the air heading down and to the left; a CW upblast outlet sits on the left of the housing top and a CCW upblast outlet on the right; the challenge has ten items with mastery at 8 of 10.

docs.title: Up Blast Discharge Position
docs.text:
The up blast discharge position (UBD, 360 degrees) points the outlet straight up. It is the natural choice when a fan exhausts vertically through a roof or into a stack, because the air leaves the housing already moving in the direction it must travel and no elbow is needed at the outlet. Avoiding an elbow close to the outlet matters because a fan's outlet velocity profile is uneven for several duct diameters downstream, and an elbow placed in that region costs pressure that the fan rating does not account for. Chapter 25 treats this loss, called system effect, in detail.

Worked example. A dust collector exhaust fan sits on a pad beside a building and must discharge into a vertical stack directly above it.

  1. The air must leave going up, so the discharge position is UBD.
  2. The stack foundation was poured before the fan was selected, and from the drive side its centerline sits to the left of the fan shaft.
  3. For UBD the outlet sits on the left side of the housing top for CW and on the right side for CCW, so only the CW housing puts the outlet over the existing foundation. The order reads CW 360.
  4. Had the order been written as "upblast" with no rotation, the factory could have built either hand, and half the time the outlet would miss the stack.

docs.title: Top Horizontal Discharge
docs.text:
Top horizontal discharge (THD, 90 degrees) puts the outlet at the top of the housing, pointing sideways. It suits a fan that feeds an overhead horizontal duct, a common layout in mechanical rooms and plants where ducts run near the ceiling. Because the air leaves at the top of the housing and travels horizontally, the duct can start at roughly the height of the housing top without an elbow.

THD also has a practical interaction with the motor. FanPedia's technical descriptions for Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F note a height restriction for THD: the motor "may not fit below the discharge" in one of the four standard motor positions, a limit described later in this chapter and in detail in Chapter 13 (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

Worked example. A supply fan in a penthouse must feed a duct running to the east at the ceiling. The fan will be set so that, standing on the drive side, the observer faces north.

  1. Facing north, east is on the observer's right.
  2. The air must leave horizontally at the top, toward the right: THD.
  3. From the discharge table, a CW top horizontal outlet throws air to the right. The order reads CW 90 (CW THD).
  4. Had the fan been set with the drive side facing south, east would be on the observer's left, and the same duct would need CCW 90.

The same duct can need either hand, depending on which way the fan is set on its base, which is why layout drawings must show the drive side.

docs.title: Bottom Horizontal Discharge
docs.text:
Bottom horizontal discharge (BHD, 270 degrees) puts the outlet at the bottom of the housing, pointing sideways. It suits fans that feed a duct running at floor level or below grade, a tunnel, or an under-floor plenum. A bottom horizontal outlet keeps the duct low, which helps when headroom is limited or when the discharge feeds equipment at grade.

BHD has its own interaction with the motor. FanPedia notes that on Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F a BHD outlet can collide with the motor in one standard position, because the motor "interferes with outlet opening of housing" (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

Worked example. A boiler forced-draft fan must deliver air into a windbox inlet located low on the boiler front, to the observer's left when they stand on the fan's drive side.

  1. The air must leave horizontally at the bottom of the housing: BHD.
  2. From the discharge table, a CW bottom horizontal outlet throws air to the left.
  3. The order reads CW 270 (CW BHD).
  4. Because a CW BHD outlet projects to the left at floor level, the motor cannot be placed on the left side of the fan in the position the outlet occupies. The motor position must be chosen with the outlet in mind, as the motor position section below shows.

docs.title: Down Blast Discharge Position
docs.text:
The down blast discharge position (DBD, 180 degrees) points the outlet straight down. It suits a fan mounted above the space it serves: a fan on a platform or mezzanine discharging down into a duct or chamber below it, or a fan supported on structural steel above a process. A downblast fan's outlet usually connects through a floor opening or into a plenum, so the support frame must leave room around the outlet flange.

Like upblast, downblast points the same direction for both rotations, but the housings differ: a CW downblast outlet sits on the right side of the housing bottom, and a CCW downblast outlet on the left, because those are the sides where the wheel moves air downward.

Worked example. A fan on a mezzanine must discharge through a floor sleeve into a supply chamber below. The sleeve is already cast in the slab, and the architect's drawing shows the sleeve centerline offset to the right of the fan shaft when viewed from the drive side.

  1. Air must leave straight down: DBD.
  2. The outlet must sit to the right of the shaft.
  3. A CW downblast outlet sits on the right of the housing bottom, so the order reads CW 180.
  4. Ordering CCW 180 would put the outlet on the left, off the sleeve, and the slab would need a new opening.

docs.title: Angular Discharge
docs.text: An angular discharge is any of the four positions that point the outlet at 45 degrees rather than straight up, straight down or horizontally: TAU (45), TAD (135), BAD (225) and BAU (315). Angular discharges let the outlet meet a duct that rises or falls at an angle, or clear an obstruction without a full elbow. They are named by where the outlet is (top or bottom of the housing) and which way the air heads (up or down). Not every fan type offers all four: FanPedia's DWDI discharge pages list seven positions and omit Bottom Angular Down, a limit covered in Chapter 13 (FanPedia pp. 48-49).

docs.title: Top Angular Up Discharge
docs.text: Top angular up discharge (TAU, 45 degrees) places the outlet near the top of the housing with the air heading upward at 45 degrees, one step past upblast in the direction of rotation. For a CW fan the air heads up and to the right; for a CCW fan, up and to the left. A TAU outlet is a good fit when an exhaust duct must climb toward a roof penetration that is offset from the fan, because it replaces an elbow with the housing's own geometry.

docs.title: Top Angular Down Discharge
docs.text: Top angular down discharge (TAD, 135 degrees) places the outlet near the top of the housing with the air heading downward at 45 degrees. For a CW fan the air heads down and to the right; for a CCW fan, down and to the left. Because the outlet projects down beside the housing, it can collide with a motor placed on that side; FanPedia lists TAD among the discharges that restrict motor position on Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F (FanPedia pp. 162-163).

docs.title: Bottom Angular Up Discharge
docs.text: Bottom angular up discharge (BAU, 315 degrees) places the outlet near the bottom of the housing with the air heading upward at 45 degrees. For a CW fan the air heads up and to the left; for a CCW fan, up and to the right. BAU is one step short of upblast in the direction of rotation, and it suits a duct that leaves low and climbs away from the fan at an angle, for instance to rise over a walkway beside the unit.

docs.title: Inlet Box Position
docs.text:
Some centrifugal fans are fitted with an inlet box, a sheet-metal box attached to the fan inlet that turns the incoming air 90 degrees so the inlet duct can approach from the side, top or bottom instead of along the shaft. An inlet box also lets the bearing on an Arrangement 3 fan sit outside the airstream; Chapter 18 covers inlet boxes as accessories. The inlet box position states where the box's opening faces.

FanPedia defines inlet box position by an angle measured around the fan as viewed from the drive side, in 45-degree steps from 45 to 360, with 360 at the top and the angle increasing clockwise (FanPedia p. 144). Unlike the discharge angle, this angle does not change direction with rotation: it is a fixed clock around the housing. Each position also has a description of how the air enters:

  • 45 — Angular Down Intake (box at the upper right)
  • 90 — Horizontal Right Intake (box on the right)
  • 135 — Angular Up Intake (box at the lower right)
  • 180 — Bottom Up Intake (box at the bottom)
  • 225 — Angular Up Intake (box at the lower left)
  • 270 — Horizontal Left Intake (box on the left)
  • 315 — Angular Down Intake (box at the upper left)
  • 360 — Top Down Intake (box at the top)

The descriptions repeat for the angular positions: 45 and 315 are both Angular Down Intake, and 135 and 225 are both Angular Up Intake. The number, not the description, is what pins down the side.

Worked example. A fan with an inlet box must take air from a horizontal duct that arrives from the observer's left when standing on the drive side, and the fan's outlet is CW top horizontal, pointing right.

  1. The box opening must face left to meet the duct: Horizontal Left Intake.
  2. Horizontal Left Intake is position 270.
  3. Check for conflicts: the outlet is at the top pointing right, and the box is on the left, so the two connections do not compete for the same space.
  4. The order specifies CW 90 discharge with the inlet box at 270.

If the duct instead arrived from above at an angle on the left, the position would be 315, Angular Down Intake.

Two Angles, Two Rules

Watch out for treating the inlet box angle like the discharge angle. The discharge angle counts from upblast in the direction of rotation, but the inlet box angle is always counted clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side, so a CCW fan's inlet box at 90 is still on the right. Write each angle with its own label on the order so no one converts one into the other.

Before working through the next interactive element, recall that the inlet box angle runs clockwise from the top in 45-degree steps and that two pairs of positions share a description.

docs.title: Diagram: Inlet Box Position Dial
docs.text:
Run Inlet Box Position Dial Fullscreen

Inlet Box Position Dial

Type: microsim sim-id: ch12-inlet-box-position-dial Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the drive-side inlet box angle convention to set the correct inlet box position for eight duct-approach descriptions, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: inlet box, inlet box position, viewed from the drive side, the eight inlet box position numbers and their descriptions, the difference between the inlet box angle and the discharge angle (all defined in the sections "Viewed From the Drive Side", "Discharge Angle" and "Inlet Box Position" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of eight challenge items, the learner sets the inlet box to one of the eight positions on a drive-side view of the fan and presses Check. An answer is correct when the position number equals the answer column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rotating the box freely in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The inlet box angle counts in the direction of rotation, like the discharge angle. (2) The description alone ("Angular Down Intake") identifies one position. (3) The inlet box angle is read from the inlet side.

Instructional Rationale: Setting a position from a described duct approach makes the learner perform the conversion an order writer performs, and judging each setting gives immediate correction. Items 5 to 8 share descriptions in pairs so that the learner must use the location, not the words, which confronts misconception 2; item 8 is shown on a CCW fan to confront misconception 1.

Content:

Exploration mode. A drive-side view of a centrifugal housing with an inlet box that the learner can move to any of eight positions. For the current position the sim shows the number and its FanPedia description:

Position Description Box location seen from the drive side 45 Angular Down Intake Upper right 90 Horizontal Right Intake Right 135 Angular Up Intake Lower right 180 Bottom Up Intake Bottom 225 Angular Up Intake Lower left 270 Horizontal Left Intake Left 315 Angular Down Intake Upper left 360 Top Down Intake Top

The learner can also switch the fan's drawn rotation between CW and CCW; the position numbers do not move.

Challenge mode. Eight items in this fixed order:

# Fan rotation shown Duct approach described to the learner Correct position Why (shown as feedback) 1 CW The inlet duct runs horizontally and arrives from the right of the drive-side observer. 90 A box opening facing right is Horizontal Right Intake, position 90. 2 CW The inlet duct drops vertically from the roof directly above the fan. 360 Air entering downward from the top is Top Down Intake, position 360. 3 CW The inlet duct rises from a trench directly below the fan. 180 Air entering upward from the bottom is Bottom Up Intake, position 180. 4 CW The inlet duct runs horizontally and arrives from the left of the drive-side observer. 270 A box opening facing left is Horizontal Left Intake, position 270. 5 CW The inlet duct comes down at 45 degrees from the upper right. 45 Angular Down Intake on the upper right is 45; the upper-left one is 315. 6 CW The inlet duct comes down at 45 degrees from the upper left. 315 Angular Down Intake on the upper left is 315, counted clockwise from the top. 7 CW The inlet duct rises at 45 degrees from the lower left. 225 Angular Up Intake on the lower left is 225; the lower-right one is 135. 8 CCW The inlet duct rises at 45 degrees from the lower right. 135 The inlet box angle always runs clockwise from the top, whatever the rotation, so lower right is 135.

Provenance: Position numbers, descriptions and the drive-side viewing rule come from FanPedia p. 144 (Inlet Boxes: Positions, "Inlet Box Positions Determined From Drive Side"), local copy fanpedia.pdf in the course source folder. Challenge items are constructed for this chapter.

Rules: Positions are 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315 and 360 degrees, measured clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side; 360 is the top. The position does not depend on the fan's rotation. An answer is correct only when the selected number equals the answer; there is no partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. In exploration mode the learner moves the box around the housing one position at a time and reads each number and description.
  2. The learner switches the drawn rotation from CW to CCW; the box and its number stay where they were. The learner should notice that rotation does not change the inlet box angle.
  3. The learner starts the challenge, reads each duct description, moves the box to a position and presses Check.
  4. After item 8 a summary shows the score and lists missed items with their feedback.

Feedback: Eight items, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: position , ." Incorrect on the first attempt: if the learner chose the mirror position (for example 315 instead of 45), "Same description, other side: the angle counts clockwise from the top as seen from the drive side."; if the learner's answer equals the correct position counted counterclockwise on item 8, "The inlet box angle does not follow rotation; count clockwise from the top."; otherwise "Find where the duct arrives, then read that position's number." After the second wrong attempt the correct answer and the Why text are shown and the item counts as missed. Only first-attempt answers count. A running count "Correct on first attempt: n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Exploration mode, CW fan, inlet box at 360 (Top Down Intake). The prompt reads: "Move the box. Which positions share a description?"
