Shaft Seal Identifier

Type: microsim sim-id: ch16-shaft-seal-identifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify a fan shaft seal into one of seven FanPedia seal types from a description of its parts, materials or order-line name, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: shaft seal, friction shaft seal, V-ring (axial) shaft seal, lip shaft seal, carbon ring seal (single and double), lantern ring, purge, stuffing box seal, stuffing box with gas purge, Graphoil, carbon yarn packing (all defined in the "Shaft Seals" section above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 12 cards, the learner commits a card to one of seven seal-type bins. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct bin" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Opening the reference cross-sections in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any seal with a purge is a carbon ring seal (stuffing boxes can be purged too). (2) A lip shaft seal and a bearing lip seal are the same part (the shaft seal is on the fan housing and sealing air; the bearing seal keeps dirt out of the bearing). (3) "Labyrinth" always means a bearing seal (FanPedia also lists "labyrinth shaft seal" as another name for carbon ring shaft seals). (4) Single and double carbon ring seals differ only in size (the double ring adds a lantern ring and purge).

Instructional Rationale: Classifying unfamiliar descriptions into categories requires the learner to recognize each seal's defining parts rather than recall a label. Each card asks for a prediction committed before feedback, and the feedback states the identifying part so the learner builds the part-to-type mapping.

Content:

Seven bins, each with a reference infobox (shown in explore mode and after each answer):

Bin Reference infobox Friction shaft seal Standard type; soft seal material (tacky cloth, Teflon, Viton, Nomex mineral wool, silicone sheet or Fiber Frax ceramic felt) held by a cover plate, typically aluminum. Also called tacky cloth seal. V-ring shaft seal Teflon plate design with Chekseal and PTFE joint sealant. Also called axial shaft seal or Teflon shaft seal. Lip shaft seal Elastomer lip (Buna-N standard, Viton special) in a seal housing with a grease fitting. Also called grease seal, grease purge, double lip seal. Single carbon ring seal One split carbon ring in a seal housing behind a cover plate; vendor supplied. Also called floating circumferential carbon ring seal, labyrinth shaft seal. Double carbon ring seal Two split carbon rings with a lantern ring at a purge hole; vendor supplied. Stuffing box seal Inside plate with seal housing, Graphoil split inner rings, carbon yarn packing outer rings, outside plate with retaining ring. Also called Graphoil seal, packing gland seal. Stuffing box seal with gas purge Stuffing box with a Teflon lantern ring at a purge hole; ships with a 1/8-inch NPT pipe plug replaced in the field by the customer's purge line.

Twelve cards:

# Card text shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 An aluminum cover plate clamps a strip of tacky cloth against the shaft. Friction shaft seal Soft material held by a cover plate is the friction (standard) seal. 2 Order line: "Shaft Seal: Buna Rubber (lip type), Standard". Lip shaft seal Buna rubber lip is the standard lip seal. 3 A seal housing on the fan housing wall carries a grease fitting. Lip shaft seal Only the lip seal is greased through its own housing. 4 One split carbon ring sits in a seal housing behind a cover plate; there is no purge hole. Single carbon ring seal One carbon ring without a purge is the single ring mechanical seal. 5 Two split carbon rings with a lantern ring between them at a purge hole. Double carbon ring seal Two carbon rings plus a lantern ring is the double ring mechanical seal. 6 Graphoil split rings inside, carbon yarn packing outside, and an outside plate with a retaining ring; no purge hole. Stuffing box seal Graphoil and carbon yarn packing compressed in a box is a stuffing box. 7 Carbon yarn packing and a Teflon lantern ring at a hole closed by a 1/8-inch NPT pipe plug. Stuffing box seal with gas purge Packing plus a lantern ring and purge plug is the purged stuffing box. 8 A Teflon plate with Chekseal, called an axial shaft seal. V-ring shaft seal "Axial shaft seal" is another name for the V-ring type. 9 Seal material is Fiber Frax ceramic felt under a cover plate. Friction shaft seal Fiber Frax is one of the friction seal's materials. 10 The order calls it a "packing gland seal" and lists no purge. Stuffing box seal Packing gland seal is another name for the stuffing box. 11 Order line: "Shaft Seal: Viton (lip type), Special". Lip shaft seal Viton is the special lip material; the part is still a lip seal. 12 Order line: "Shaft Seal: Graphoil Stuffing Box With Purge". Stuffing box seal with gas purge "With Purge" adds the lantern ring and purge connection.

Provenance: FanPedia (Twin City Fan, 2021), Shaft Seals pages 149 (friction), 150 (V-ring), 151 (lip), 152 (single ring mechanical), 153 (double ring mechanical), 154 (stuffing box) and 155 (stuffing box with gas purge). Card wording is written for this chapter from those pages.

Rules: Each card has exactly one correct bin. A card is answered by committing it to a bin; once committed it cannot be moved except on the second attempt after a wrong first attempt. Score counts first-attempt correct answers only.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner opens any bin's reference infobox to review the seven seal types.
  2. The learner starts the quiz. One card is shown at a time.
  3. The learner commits the card to a bin. The sim marks it right or wrong, shows the feedback, and opens the correct bin's infobox.
  4. After 12 cards the sim shows the first-attempt score and lists any missed cards with their correct bins.
  5. The learner can restart; cards reshuffle.

Feedback: 12 cards, shuffled order, two attempts per card. Correct: "Correct: . ." Incorrect on the first attempt: "Not this one." plus a hint naming the mix-up between look-alike seals, never the correct bin (for example, single versus double carbon ring: "Count the rings and look for a lantern ring at a purge hole."; plain versus purged stuffing box: "Look for a lantern ring, a purge hole or a purge plug on the card."; friction versus lip: soft material under a cover plate versus an elastomer lip with its own greased housing); when no specific pair applies, "Look again at the parts named on the card." Incorrect on the second attempt: "This is a . ." and the card counts as missed. A running count "First-try correct: n of 12" is shown. Mastery message at the end when the count is >= 10: "You can identify FanPedia's seven shaft seal types from their parts."

Starting State: Explore mode showing the seven bins and the prompt "Every shaft seal is identified by what touches the shaft. Open the bins, then start the quiz."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter describes seven seal types (friction, V-ring, lip, single carbon ring, double carbon ring, stuffing box, stuffing box with gas purge) in three families (contact, carbon ring, stuffing box). The purge plug is 1/8-inch NPT. Mastery is 10 of 12.

Supported and Sealed

You can now trace a rotating assembly from the keyway at the sheave to the seal at the housing wall, and say why each bearing, collar, sensor and seal is there. Next time an order line reads "Graphoil Stuffing Box With Purge," you will know exactly what ships and what the contractor must connect.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The shaft and impeller form the rotating assembly, carried on two bearings in an overhung or center hung layout.
  • Keyways carry torque through keystock; turndowns step the shaft diameter down at hubs, seals, bearings and couplings; locking collars keep the shaft from moving axially.
  • Shaft sleeves shield a shaft from an airstream of a different material (typical on Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10, but not used on nominally leak-tight fans); clad shafts do the same job on shafts of 9 inches and larger at lower cost.
  • Bearing life is a fatigue statistic; most Twin City Fan models offer L-10 life of 40,000 hours, which is about 9.6 years at 16 hours a day, 5 days a week.
  • Ball bearings suit lighter, smoother duty; spherical roller bearings carry high and shock loads at more limited speed.
  • Pillow blocks mount parallel to the shaft, flange bearings perpendicular to it, and two-bearing housings hold both bearings in precise alignment for special jobs.
  • Set screw mounts lock the inner ring with two screws; fixed bearings locate the shaft axially, and above 300°F every fan uses one fixed and one floating bearing.
  • Positioners adjust bearing location; dowel pins and stop blocks restrain it, as spark-resistant Types A and B require.
  • Grease is standard, high temperature grease is needed on hot fans, and static oil and oil mist systems are special-application options.
  • Bearing seals (lip, labyrinth, taconite) protect the bearing and set its speed limit; insulated bearings block VFD shaft currents.
  • RTDs, thermocouples and vibration sensors mount on tapped bearing housings and give early warning of bearing trouble.
  • Shaft seals limit leakage where the shaft enters the housing. Friction and lip seals are simple contact seals; carbon ring and stuffing box seals limit leakage further, and their purged versions use a lantern ring and a customer-supplied purge line.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals
docs.text: Test your understanding of fan shafts, bearings, bearing monitoring and shaft seals with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does an L-10 bearing life rating describe?
docs.text:
1. The number of hours after which every bearing in a population is expected to have failed
  2. The number of hours by which 10% of a large population of identical bearings, at a given speed and load, are expected to have failed
  3. The guaranteed minimum life of one individual bearing, stated in years of operation
  4. The number of hours a bearing can run without lubrication before 10% of its raceway wears away
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Bearing life is a statistical estimate of fatigue failure, and L-10 life is the hours by which 10% of a large population of identical bearings at a given speed and load are expected to have failed. It is not the point where every bearing fails (A), it is not a guarantee for one bearing (C), and FanPedia's life figures assume proper lubrication rather than describing running without it (D).

Concept Tested: Bearing Life

See: Bearing Life

docs.title: 2. Which shaft seal does FanPedia describe as its standard type?
docs.text:
1. The lip shaft seal with a Buna-N elastomer lip
  2. The stuffing box seal with Graphoil rings
  3. The double carbon ring seal with a lantern ring
  4. The friction shaft seal, also called a tacky cloth seal
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The friction shaft seal is FanPedia's standard type: a ring of soft seal material, most often tacky cloth, clamped by a cover plate so that it rubs lightly on the shaft. The lip seal (A) is the next step up when leakage must be reduced. Stuffing box (B) and double carbon ring (C) seals limit leakage further but are more expensive and are chosen for demanding constructions such as nominally leak-tight fans.

Concept Tested: Friction Shaft Seal

See: Lip and Friction Shaft Seals

docs.title: 3. Which statement correctly distinguishes a bearing seal from a shaft seal?
docs.text:
1. A bearing seal keeps dirt out of the bearing and lubricant in; a shaft seal on the housing wall limits air or gas leakage along the shaft
  2. A bearing seal limits air leakage out of the fan housing; a shaft seal keeps grease inside the bearing
  3. A bearing seal is used only on ball bearings; a shaft seal is used only on spherical roller bearings
  4. A bearing seal and a shaft seal are two names for the same part on the drive side of the fan
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A bearing seal is built into the bearing housing and protects the bearing from dust and moisture while keeping lubricant in; its type also sets the bearing's speed limit. A shaft seal is mounted on the fan housing where the shaft passes through the wall, and its job is the airstream, not lubrication. Option B reverses the two jobs, a common mix-up. Options C and D confuse two separate parts.

Concept Tested: Bearing Seal

See: Bearing Seals

docs.title: 4. Why does a hot fan normally use one fixed bearing and one floating bearing rather than two fixed bearings?
docs.text:
1. A floating bearing runs cooler because it carries no radial load
  2. Two fixed bearings would let the impeller slide axially into the inlet funnel
  3. The shaft grows longer as it heats, and two fixed bearings would turn that growth into thrust load on the bearings
  4. A floating bearing lets the shaft be removed without pulling the impeller
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Only one bearing should control the shaft's axial position. A shaft that warms by hundreds of degrees gets measurably longer, and if both bearings clamp it, the growth has nowhere to go except into the bearings as thrust load. The floating bearing still supports the shaft radially (A is wrong) and simply lets it slide. Two fixed bearings hold the shaft more firmly, not less (B), and the floating bearing has nothing to do with shaft removal (D).

Concept Tested: Fixed Bearing

See: Fixed Bearings

docs.title: 5. A fan has bearings rated at an L-10 life of 40,000 hours and runs 12 hours a day, 5 days a week. About how many calendar years is that L-10 life?
docs.text:
1. 6.4 years
  2. 9.6 years
  3. 12.8 years
  4. 25.6 years
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Use Y = L-10 ÷ (hours per day × days per week × 52). The fan runs 12 × 5 × 52 = 3,120 hours a year, and 40,000 ÷ 3,120 ≈ 12.8 years. 9.6 years (B) is the answer for 16 hours a day, 5 days a week, the chapter's own example. 6.4 years (A) is roughly the figure for 24 hours a day, 5 days a week. 25.6 years (D) comes from counting only half the hours.

Concept Tested: Bearing Life

See: Bearing Life in Calendar Years

docs.title: 6. An Arrangement 1, horizontally mounted fan handles 450°F air on split spherical roller pillow blocks. How should the two bearings be ordered?
docs.text:
1. Both bearings fixed, because the fan is horizontal
  2. Fixed bearing on the drive end and floating bearing on the inboard end near the impeller
  3. Floating bearing on the drive end and fixed bearing on the inboard end near the impeller
  4. Both bearings floating, because the airstream is above 300°F
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. At 301°F and above, every bearing type uses one fixed and one floating bearing, so two fixed bearings (A) are ruled out; split roller bearings use one of each even below 300°F. On horizontally mounted fans the fixed bearing goes on the drive side, so the floating bearing sits on the inboard end. Option C is the layout for vertically mounted fans. Two floating bearings (D) would leave nothing to locate the shaft axially.

Concept Tested: Fixed Bearing

See: Fixed Bearings

docs.title: 7. A fan for an aggregate drying plant will run in heavy dust on split spherical roller pillow blocks. Which bearing seal choice best follows the chapter's guidance?
docs.text:
1. A lip seal, because contact seals give the tightest fit at any speed
  2. A standard labyrinth seal, because it is the only non-contact option
  3. No bearing seal, because the shaft seal on the housing already keeps the dust out
  4. A taconite seal, after checking the fan speed against its speed limit and allowing for the wider bearing it needs
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Taconite seals are designed for dirty or abrasive environments on split pillow block spherical roller bearings. Two checks follow: the standard taconite seal has a lower speed limit than a labyrinth (a non-contact Canadian type exists for higher speeds), and it makes the bearing wider, which can mean a longer shaft or a larger bearing support. Lip seals (A) are for ball bearings at low to moderate speeds. The shaft seal (C) protects the airstream, not the bearing.

Concept Tested: Bearing Seal

See: Bearing Seals

docs.title: 8. A specification says: "Provide provisions for vibration monitoring in the horizontal and vertical directions at each fan bearing. Sensors by others." What does the fan order need on a two-bearing fan?
docs.text:
1. Four drilled and tapped holes in the bearing housings, with no sensors shipped
  2. Four accelerometers shipped loose, with sensor cords supplied by Twin City Fan
  3. Two tapped holes, one per bearing, because each sensor reads both directions
  4. Bearing RTDs installed through a T-fitting on each grease fitting
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. "Provisions" means drilled and tapped holes in the bearing housings, not the sensors themselves. Two bearings times two directions gives four holes, and "sensors by others" means nothing is shipped loose; the standard tap is 1/4"-28 UNF with a 1-inch spot face unless the plant asks for 1/4"-18 NPT. Option B ignores "by others," and sensor cords are supplied by others in any case. Option C undercounts the directions. Option D describes temperature sensors, not vibration sensors.

Concept Tested: Bearing Vibration Sensor

See: Monitoring the Bearings

docs.title: 9. A nominally leak-tight Arrangement 8 fan handles a gas that must not escape. Why is a double carbon ring seal chosen over a single carbon ring seal?
docs.text:
1. The double ring uses larger carbon rings, so it seals with zero clearance and no leakage at all
  2. The lantern ring between its two rings lets customer-supplied purge gas at a slightly higher pressure fill the seal, so any leakage is purge gas flowing into the fan
  3. The double ring needs no purge supply, while the single ring must be purged with nitrogen
  4. The single ring cannot be installed without first removing the impeller from the shaft
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The double ring seal places a lantern ring at a purge hole between two split carbon rings. When clean air or inert gas is supplied there slightly above the gas pressure in the fan, leakage across the inner ring is purge gas entering the fan rather than process gas escaping. FanPedia's leak-tight list includes the double ring but not the single ring. No seal reaches zero leakage (A), the purge belongs to the double ring (C), and both seals use split rings that install around the shaft (D).

Concept Tested: Carbon Ring Seal

See: Carbon Ring Seals

docs.title: 10. FanPedia's nominally leak-tight construction says not to use a shaft sleeve and cap. What is the underlying reason?
docs.text:
1. Shaft sleeves cannot be made from the same material as the airstream parts
  2. Shaft sleeves are allowed only on Arrangement 4 fans
  3. A sleeve makes the shaft too large to fit the shaft seal's bore
  4. The joint between the sleeve and the shaft is one more path for gas to leak along
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A shaft sleeve shields the shaft from an airstream of a different material, but the gap between sleeve and shaft creates an additional leak path, which defeats the purpose of leak-tight construction. Option A is not a reason the chapter gives; the sleeve exists to shield a shaft whose material differs from the airstream parts. Sleeves are typical on Arrangements 1, 8, 9 and 10, while Arrangement 4 fans can use a protruding hub instead (B is reversed). Seal fit (C) is a machining detail, not the reason FanPedia gives.

Concept Tested: Shaft Sleeve

See: Shaft Features

docs.title: References: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals
docs.text:
1. Spherical roller bearing - Wikipedia - Describes barrel-shaped rollers in a spherical outer raceway, their high load capacity and tolerance of misalignment. Background for why heavy industrial fans use spherical roller pillow blocks.

  2. Radial shaft seal - Wikipedia - Explains rotary lip seals: an elastomer lip pressed against a turning shaft, common materials and failure modes. Supports the chapter's lip shaft seal and bearing lip seal descriptions.

  3. Stuffing box - Wikipedia - Covers the gland assembly that houses packing compressed around a rotating or sliding shaft to limit leakage. The same principle behind the chapter's Graphoil stuffing box seal and its retightenable packing.

  4. Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (11th ed.) - Richard G. Budynas and J. Keith Nisbett - McGraw-Hill - Known for its step-by-step rolling-bearing selection method linking catalog load rating, L-10 rating life and reliability, plus clear treatment of keys, setscrews and collars on shafts.

  5. Seals and Sealing Handbook (6th ed.) - Robert K. Flitney - Butterworth-Heinemann - Flitney's handbook is valued for comparing rotary lip seals, compression packings, mechanical seals and clearance seals side by side, which mirrors the chapter's contact, carbon ring and stuffing box families.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - The chapter's primary source: shaft features, bearing types and mounts, fixed and floating bearings, bearing seals and sensors, and the shaft seal pages with exploded views.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Web edition of FanPedia with the Fan Components bearing and shaft image galleries and the Accessories pages, useful for quick visual lookup of the parts named in this chapter.

  8. Fan Bearing Selection (FE-1200) - Twin City Fan Engineering Letter - The letter FanPedia cites for bearing seals: bearing construction, lip, labyrinth and taconite seals, L-10 life, and fixed and expansion bearing practice.

  9. Sealing of Fan Housings (FE-700) - Twin City Fan Engineering Letter - Explains why housing leakage matters (energy, hazards, bearing damage, noise) and compares shaft seal types and degrees of sealing, expanding the chapter's shaft seal section.

  10. VFD Induced AC Motor Shaft Current and Bearing Damage (FE-4000) - Twin City Fan Engineering Letter - Shows how drive-induced shaft voltage pits bearing raceways and how insulated bearings and grounding mitigate it, the problem behind the chapter's insulated bearing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter adds the details needed to specify bearings and their supports. It covers L-10 and L-50 bearing life, split, solid, and totally split pillow blocks, adapter sleeve and concentric mounts, fixed and floating bearings and the rules for placing them, drive-end and non-drive-end bearings, grease fittings, static oil and oil mist lubrication, labyrinth, taconite, and gas purge seals, seal speed limits, and bearing stop blocks and dowel pins. It closes with fan pedestals, separated and bolt-on pedestals, and shaft and coupling guards. After completing it, readers can choose bearing and lubrication options for a given duty.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation
  • Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals

Two Small Blocks, One Long Fan Life

Most fan service calls start at the bearings, and most bearing questions on a quote come down to a short list of choices: which life rating, which housing, which seal, which lubricant, and what holds it all up. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read a bearing and pedestal line on an order and say why each choice is there. Let's follow the airflow, and then follow the shaft out to where it meets the steel.

Chapter 16 introduced bearings as parts: ball and spherical roller elements, pillow block and flange housings, the fixed bearing, lubrication in general, and the shaft seals that keep air inside the housing. This chapter adds the details that show up when a fan is actually specified and built. You will learn how bearing life is rated and converted to calendar time, how the bearing housing and its mount are chosen, which bearing on the shaft is fixed and which floats, how oil replaces grease on special jobs, how bearing seals and gas purge shaft seals differ, and how the pedestal, its options and the guards around the drive complete the assembly.

docs.title: Bearing Life: L-10 and L-50
docs.text:
Even a bearing that is perfectly installed, loaded and lubricated eventually fails from metal fatigue in its rolling elements and races. Because fatigue varies from one bearing to the next, bearing life is a statistical estimate: it predicts when a given percentage of a large population of identical bearings, running at a stated speed and load, will have failed. FanPedia (p. 90) puts it plainly: all bearings have a finite life.

L-10 bearing life is the number of operating hours at which 10% of a population of bearings at a given speed and loading condition is expected to fail. Equivalently, 90% of the bearings are expected to survive past that number of hours. This is the rating Twin City Fan catalogs quote. Most TCF fan models offer L-10 life of 40,000 hours, and some models are offered at 20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000 or 100,000 hours; the product catalog for each model states which.

L-50 bearing life, also called average life, is the number of hours at which 50% of the population is expected to fail. FanPedia gives a simple conversion: L-50 is five times L-10. A bearing selected for L-10 of 40,000 hours therefore has an L-50 of 200,000 hours. The two numbers describe the same bearing; L-50 only sounds longer because it describes a later point in the failure curve. When a competitor quotes "200,000-hour average life" and a TCF quote says "L-10 40,000 hours," the two may be identical selections.

Hours become meaningful to a customer only when they are converted to years of that customer's operating schedule. The conversion divides the rated hours by the hours the fan runs in a year:

\[ \text{Years} = \frac{\text{Rated life (h)}}{\text{hours per day} \times \text{days per week} \times \frac{365}{7}} \]

The factor \( 365/7 \approx 52.14 \) is the number of weeks in a year. The table below reproduces FanPedia's two examples (p. 90).

Rating Hours 24 h/day, 7 days/wk 24 h/day, 5 days/wk 16 h/day, 5 days/wk 8 h/day, 5 days/wk 2 h/day, 5 days/wk L-10 40,000 4.6 years 6.4 years 9.6 years 19 years 77 years L-50 200,000 22.8 years 32 years 48 years 96 years 385 years L-10 20,000 2.3 years 3.2 years 4.8 years 9.6 years 39 years L-50 100,000 11.5 years 16 years 24 years 48 years 193 years

The calculation lands within a few tenths of a year of every cell in the table; the small differences come from rounding and from whether a year is counted as exactly 52 weeks or as 365 days.

The 8,760 Shortcut

A year of continuous running is 8,760 hours, so for a 24/7 process fan just divide the L-10 hours by 8,760: 40,000 hours is about 4.6 years. For anything less than 24/7, multiply that answer by 168 and divide by the fan's actual hours per week.

The MicroSim below lets you practice the conversion for both ratings and several duty schedules before you have to do it on a customer call.

docs.title: Diagram: Bearing Life to Calendar Years
docs.text:
Run Bearing Life to Calendar Years Fullscreen

Bearing Life to Calendar Years

Type: microsim sim-id: ch17-bearing-life-calendar-years Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the expected calendar life in years of an L-10 or L-50 bearing rating for a stated daily and weekly duty schedule, to within 2% of the model value.

Prerequisites: bearing life as a statistical estimate, L-10 bearing life, L-50 bearing life, the L-50 = 5 × L-10 conversion, and the years formula (all defined in the section "Bearing Life: L-10 and L-50" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For five challenge problems, the learner types the expected life in years before the answer is revealed. An answer is correct when it is within ±2% of the model value computed by the Rules. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Changing the inputs in free-exploration mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) L-50 is a better or longer-lived bearing than L-10, rather than a different statistical point on the same bearing. (2) L-10 hours equal calendar hours regardless of how many hours a day the fan runs. (3) L-10 is the time at which every bearing fails.

Instructional Rationale: Converting a rating to years is a calculation applied to new duty schedules, so the learner commits a number before seeing the model value. Free exploration afterwards lets the learner see how strongly the duty schedule, not just the rating, sets the calendar life.

Content:

The learner can set four inputs:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit L-10 rating 20,000 100,000 20,000 40,000 hours Hours per day 1 24 1 24 h/day Days per week 1 7 1 7 days/week Rating shown L-10 or L-50 L-10

Challenge problems, in this order:

# Rating given to learner Hours per day Days per week Model answer (years) Feedback when wrong 1 L-10 40,000 h 24 7 4.6 24 × 7 × 52.14 = 8,760 h per year; 40,000 ÷ 8,760 = 4.6 years. 2 L-10 40,000 h 8 5 19.2 Only 2,086 operating hours a year: 40,000 ÷ 2,086 = 19.2 years. Calendar life depends on the schedule. 3 L-50 for a bearing rated L-10 20,000 h 24 7 11.4 First convert: L-50 = 5 × 20,000 = 100,000 h. Then 100,000 ÷ 8,760 = 11.4 years. 4 L-10 60,000 h 16 5 14.4 16 × 5 × 52.14 = 4,171 h per year; 60,000 ÷ 4,171 = 14.4 years. 5 L-10 100,000 h 12 6 26.6 12 × 6 × 52.14 = 3,754 h per year; 100,000 ÷ 3,754 = 26.6 years.

A comparison table of FanPedia's published values (the four rows of the chapter table above) is shown after challenge 5 so the learner can check the model against the source.

Provenance: L-10 and L-50 definitions, the L-50 = 5 × L-10 rule, the available L-10 ratings (20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000 and 100,000 hours) and the published year tables: FanPedia p. 90 (Bearings: Bearing Life Overview). Challenge values 4 and 5 and all free-exploration values are computed from the Rules; the 12 h/day, 6 days/week schedule is illustrative and is labeled "illustrative schedule".

Rules: Annual hours = hours per day × days per week × 365/7. Years = rated hours ÷ annual hours, rounded to 0.1 year. L-50 hours = 5 × L-10 hours. An answer is correct when |answer − model| ≤ 0.02 × model. Annual hours can never be zero because both minimums are 1. When the learner switches between L-10 and L-50, the hours and years shown both update and the rating label changes; the underlying L-10 rating is unchanged.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 (rating and schedule) and types an answer in years.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the annual operating hours, the model answer and the learner's answer side by side.
  3. The learner completes challenges 2 to 5 the same way. Challenge 3 asks for an L-50 answer from an L-10 rating, so the learner must apply the five-times rule first.
  4. After challenge 5, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes any input and the annual hours and years update immediately, with a bar comparing L-10 and L-50 years for the same bearing. The learner should notice that switching from L-10 to L-50 changes the years by exactly five times while the bearing itself is unchanged.

Feedback: Five challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: years." Hint after a first wrong attempt: a hint that names the slip or the step, with no model answer and no worked numbers: forgetting the L-50 = 5 × L-10 conversion, dividing by weekly hours instead of annual hours, dividing by operating days instead of hours, counting 7 days or 24 hours when the schedule is shorter, inverting the division; otherwise the two steps (annual hours = hours per day × days per week × 365/7; years = rated hours ÷ annual hours). After the final attempt: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge, with the model answer and the worked calculation, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box. The question on screen is "A process fan runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week on bearings rated L-10 40,000 hours. How many years until 10% of such bearings are expected to fail?"

Chapter Anchors: L-10 40,000 h at 24/7 is 4.6 years; L-50 is five times L-10; L-10 40,000 h has L-50 of 200,000 h; 8,760 hours in a continuous year; the chapter table's 20 year values (4 rows by 5 schedules); TCF offers L-10 20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000 and 100,000 hours on some models.

docs.title: Pillow Block Housings: Solid, Split and Totally Split
docs.text:
A pillow block bearing is a bearing insert carried in a housing that bolts to a surface parallel to the shaft, which on most fans is the top of the pedestal. FanPedia describes three housing styles (pp. 92, 178-179), and the difference among them is how much of the bearing must come off the shaft for inspection or replacement.

A solid pillow block bearing has a one-piece cast housing. It is offered with ball or spherical roller elements, its bolt holes are usually slotted for adjustment during mounting, and it is the common choice on standard fans. To replace one, the mechanic generally has to slide it off the end of the shaft, which may mean pulling the sheave or coupling first.

A split pillow block bearing has a housing split horizontally through the shaft centerline, so the top cap lifts off. FanPedia notes that the split exists "for easy bearing replacement and inspection." Split pillow blocks are offered with ball or spherical roller elements and are common on larger, heavy-duty fans.

A totally split roller bearing goes one step further: the housing is split and every internal part (inner ring, roller cage, outer ring) is split into two halves. The internal parts can be removed without removing the shaft at all. FanPedia lists it as a specialty bearing for special applications only, which typically means a large fan where pulling the shaft is a major outage.

Housing style What splits What a bearing change involves FanPedia note Solid pillow block Nothing Slide the bearing off the shaft end Standard on most fans Split pillow block Housing only Lift the cap; the insert still slides on the shaft Easy inspection and replacement Totally split roller Housing and all internal parts Remove halves with the shaft in place Special applications only

docs.title: Locking the Bearing to the Shaft
docs.text:
A bearing insert has to grip the shaft so the inner ring turns with it. Chapter 16 described the set screw mount, in which two set screws bear directly on the shaft. The alternative family is the concentric bearing mount, in which the inner ring is clamped evenly around the whole circumference of the shaft instead of being pushed to one side by screws. FanPedia shows two concentric styles (p. 92), and both tighten to the shaft using a partially segmented inner ring.

  • D-Lok / Skwezloc style: a split locking collar is tightened with a cap screw, squeezing the segmented inner ring onto the shaft. FanPedia shows it on solid pillow blocks.
  • Adapter mount: the locking collar is tightened with a spanner wrench. FanPedia notes this style is used for both solid and split pillow block bearings.

The adapter sleeve mount is the common industrial form of the adapter mount: a thin, slit, tapered sleeve sits between the shaft and a bearing with a tapered bore. Tightening the locknut with a spanner wrench draws the sleeve into the taper, which closes it onto the shaft and seats the bearing. Because the clamp is uniform around the shaft, a concentric mount runs truer than a set screw mount and is less likely to mark or fret the shaft, which is why it is the usual partner for spherical roller bearings on heavier fans.

docs.title: Diagram: Pillow Block Bearings and Shaft Mounts
docs.text:

Pillow Block Bearings and Shaft Mounts

sim-id: ch17-pillow-block-bearing-overlay Library: html + FP.Overlay Status: built Bloom Level: Remember Learning Objective: The learner will identify the solid (ball and spherical roller) and split pillow block housings and the set screw, D-Lok / Skwezloc and adapter shaft mounts on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each.

Content: Six numbered zones: solid pillow block bearing, ball type; solid pillow block bearing, spherical roller type; split pillow block bearing; set screw mount; D-Lok / Skwezloc style (concentric); adapter mount (concentric).

Provenance: FanPedia page 92, "Bearings: Pillow Block Bearings" (top row) and "How Bearings Connect to Shaft" (bottom row), with the captions removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 92.

Bearings are not the only parts that must turn with the shaft. Keystock is the method FanPedia (p. 80) gives for connecting the shaft to a rotating element such as an impeller hub, bushing, coupling or sheave. A piece of keystock sits half in the shaft keyway and half in the matching keyway of the hub, so torque passes through the key rather than through friction alone. A square key is typically supplied; a stepped key, which is wider on one side than the other, is used only when a square key is not possible. Keystock also reappears later in this chapter as a material for bearing stop blocks.

docs.title: Bolting the Bearing Down: Two and Four Hole Mounts
docs.text:
The pillow block housing is held to the pedestal by bolts through its base. A two hole mount has one bolt on each side of the shaft; a four hole mount has two on each side. More bolts spread the load and resist the housing rocking under larger shaft loads. FanPedia (p. 91) gives the TCF standard by shaft diameter:

Fan shaft diameter TCF standard mount 2-15/16 in. and below 2 hole mount 3-7/16 in. and above 4 hole mount

FanPedia adds that some bearing manufacturers offer only a two hole or only a four hole mount beyond these ranges, so a replacement bearing from a different manufacturer may not drop onto the existing pedestal holes. That is worth checking before a field replacement is ordered.

docs.title: Drive End and Non-Drive End Bearings
docs.text:
On a fan with two shaft bearings, the bearings are named by which end of the shaft they serve. The drive end bearing is the one nearest the sheave or coupling that brings power into the shaft. FanPedia (p. 91) also calls it the outboard bearing, and notes that on a pedestal it is set 3/4 in. in from the end of the pedestal top plate. The non-drive end bearing is the one nearer the impeller, also called the inboard bearing.

Which side of the fan the drive end falls on depends on the arrangement. For SWSI Arrangements 1, 8, 9, 9F and 10, the drive end is on the side away from the housing. For SWSI Arrangements 3, 3SI, 7 and 7SI, and for DWDI Arrangements 3, 3DI, 7 and 7DI, the bearings sit on both sides of the impeller; FanPedia notes that on Arrangement 3 inlet-driven fans the drive end bearing is on the inlet side. The same drawing shows which face of each bearing carries the locking collar, so the assembler knows how to orient it.

docs.title: Fixed and Floating Bearings
docs.text:
A steel shaft grows longer as it warms. On a fan handling hot air, the shaft between the two bearings may grow by a noticeable amount compared with the pedestal that holds the bearings. If both bearings clamp the shaft axially, that growth has nowhere to go, and it turns into an axial load that shortens bearing life.

FanPedia's answer (pp. 97-99) is to let only one bearing locate the shaft. The fixed bearing (also called the non-expansion, thrust or locating bearing, covered in Chapter 16) controls the shaft's axial position. The floating bearing (also called the expansion or non-locating bearing) supports the shaft radially but lets the outer ring slide axially inside its housing, so the shaft can grow or shrink without loading the bearings.

One Bearing Decides, One Bearing Follows

Think of the fixed bearing as the shaft's anchor and the floating bearing as its slide. The shaft always grows away from the anchor, so where you put the anchor decides where all the thermal movement goes.

docs.title: The Fixed-Floating Bearing Rules
docs.text:
FanPedia states the placement and quantity rules as guidelines. These fixed-floating bearing rules have two parts: where the fixed bearing goes, and whether a floating bearing is needed at all.

Placement depends on how the fan is mounted:

  • Horizontal mounted fans: the fixed bearing is on the drive side, and the floating bearing is on the non-drive side.
  • Vertical mounted fans (for example, Arrangement 9 axial or plug fans mounted vertically, or plenum Arrangements 3VA and 3VS): the floating bearing is on the drive side.

Whether a floating bearing is needed depends on bearing type and operating temperature:

Operating temperature Ball type Roller type Split roller type 300°F and below 2 fixed 1 fixed, 1 floating 1 fixed, 1 floating 301°F and above 1 fixed, 1 floating 1 fixed, 1 floating 1 fixed, 1 floating

There is one footnote to watch. On Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI, where the bearings straddle the impeller and the shaft between them is long, FanPedia notes that ball type bearings at 300°F and below may still require one fixed and one floating bearing. Treat that case as an engineering review item rather than a lookup. FanPedia's high-temperature construction pages (Chapter 21) repeat the rule: hot fans use fixed and floating bearings and high-temperature grease.

Four Questions, in Order

The rules look like a lot at first because they mix orientation, bearing type, temperature and arrangement. Ask them in a fixed order (horizontal or vertical, ball or roller, above or below 300°F, straddle arrangement or not) and every case comes out in under a minute; the sim below lets you practice exactly that.

docs.title: Diagram: Fixed or Floating Bearing Assignment
docs.text:
Run Fixed or Floating Bearing Assignment Fullscreen

Fixed or Floating Bearing Assignment

Type: microsim sim-id: ch17-fixed-floating-bearing-assignment Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the fixed-floating bearing rules to assign the correct bearing configuration to ten fan scenarios defined by mounting orientation, bearing type, operating temperature and arrangement, with at least 8 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: drive end bearing, non-drive end bearing, fixed bearing, floating bearing, ball, roller and split roller bearing types, horizontal and vertical mounting, and the fixed-floating bearing rules (all defined in the sections "Drive End and Non-Drive End Bearings" and "Fixed and Floating Bearings" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 10 scenario cards, the learner selects one of four configurations and commits it. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct configuration column. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the shaft diagram before committing is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every fan needs a floating bearing. (2) The fixed bearing is always on the drive end, regardless of orientation. (3) Temperature does not matter for ball bearings. (4) The 300°F cutoff applies the same way to straddle arrangements with ball bearings.

Instructional Rationale: The rules are a decision procedure, so the learner applies them to new combinations and commits an answer per card. Showing the shaft with the bearings labeled after each answer connects the rule to the physical layout.

Content:

The four configurations offered for every card:

  • A. Two fixed bearings
  • B. Fixed bearing at the drive end, floating bearing at the non-drive end
  • C. Floating bearing at the drive end, fixed bearing at the non-drive end
  • D. Flag for engineering review: may need one fixed and one floating

Scenario cards, in this order:

# Scenario shown to the learner Correct configuration Why (shown as feedback) 1 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 1, horizontal mount, ball bearings, 150°F A Ball bearings at 300°F and below use two fixed bearings. 2 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 1, horizontal mount, spherical roller solid pillow blocks, 200°F B Roller bearings always use one fixed and one floating; on a horizontal fan the fixed bearing is on the drive side. 3 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 8, horizontal mount, split roller bearings, 650°F B Above 301°F every type uses one fixed and one floating; horizontal puts the fixed bearing at the drive end. 4 Axial fan, Arrangement 9, vertical floor mount, roller bearings, 120°F C On vertical mounted fans the floating bearing is on the drive side. 5 Plug fan, Arrangement 9, vertical up mount, ball bearings, 100°F A Ball bearings at 300°F and below use two fixed bearings, whatever the orientation. 6 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 9, horizontal mount, ball bearings, exactly 300°F A The two-fixed rule covers 300°F and below, and 300°F is included. 7 DWDI centrifugal, Arrangement 3, horizontal mount, roller bearings, 180°F B Roller bearings use one fixed and one floating; horizontal puts the fixed bearing at the drive end. 8 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 3SI, horizontal mount, ball bearings, 250°F D FanPedia's footnote: on 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI, ball bearings at 300°F and below may require one fixed and one floating. 9 Plenum fan, Arrangement 3VA, vertical down mount, split roller bearings, 200°F C Split roller bearings use one fixed and one floating, and a vertical fan puts the floating bearing on the drive side. 10 SWSI centrifugal, Arrangement 1, horizontal mount, ball bearings, 301°F B At 301°F and above every bearing type uses one fixed and one floating; horizontal puts the fixed bearing at the drive end.

Provenance: All rules and arrangement lists: FanPedia pp. 97-99 (Bearings: Fixed & Floating Bearings), including the footnote on Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI. Drive end and non-drive end definitions: FanPedia p. 91. The scenario temperatures are illustrative and are labeled "illustrative scenario".

Rules: Step 1: if the operating temperature is >= 301°F, the configuration has one fixed and one floating bearing; go to step 3. Step 2: if the temperature is <= 300°F and the bearings are ball type, the answer is A, except for Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI, where it is D. Roller and split roller types at <= 300°F have one fixed and one floating. Step 3: for a configuration with a floating bearing, a horizontal mount gives B and a vertical mount gives C.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario card 1 and selects one of the four configurations.
  2. The learner presses Commit. The sim draws the shaft with its two bearings labeled drive end and non-drive end, marks each as fixed or floating according to the correct answer, and shows the feedback.
  3. The learner moves to the next card. Committed cards cannot be changed.
  4. After card 10, the sim shows the score and lists any missed cards with the rule step that decided them. The learner should notice that orientation only matters once a floating bearing is needed.

Feedback: Ten cards, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the Why text and the correct configuration letter. The correct answer is revealed immediately after each commit. A running score "n of 10" is shown, and the final screen states whether the 8 of 10 mastery level was reached.

Starting State: Card 1 is shown with no configuration selected and an unlabeled shaft with two bearings. The question on screen is "Which bearings on this fan should be fixed, and which should float?"

Chapter Anchors: horizontal fans: fixed bearing on the drive side; vertical fans: floating bearing on the drive side; 300°F and below: ball type 2 fixed, roller and split roller 1 fixed and 1 floating; 301°F and above: all types 1 fixed and 1 floating; ball bearings on 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI at 300°F and below may require one fixed and one floating.

docs.title: Lubrication: Grease Fittings and Oil Systems
docs.text:
Nearly all fan bearings are grease lubricated. A grease fitting, often called a zerk, is a small threaded nipple with a spring-loaded check ball, screwed into the bearing housing so that a grease gun can push fresh grease into the bearing while the ball keeps dirt out. FanPedia (p. 101) shows the standard zerk on a pillow block, and the same port is used for a bearing temperature sensor added through a T-fitting (Chapter 16). When a bearing is hard to reach, lube lines carry the fitting to a convenient location; FanPedia's high-temperature pages call for metal lube lines and high-temperature grease. A grease pan on the pedestal collects excess grease purged from the bearings. Do not confuse two different temperatures here. The 300°F and 301°F limits in this chapter are airstream temperatures, but Twin City Fan engineering letter FE-1300 recommends special high-temperature grease when the bearing temperature exceeds 160°F, which a bearing can reach well below a 300°F airstream.

For special applications, FanPedia (p. 95) shows two oil systems instead of grease. Static oil lubrication keeps a constant oil level in a sump in the bearing housing. Each bearing has its own constant-level oiler (FanPedia names the Trico oiler) whose reservoir automatically tops up the sump as oil is used. The supply line enters at the bottom of the bearing, and the bearing needs either a pressure relief line routed back to the oiler or a breather tube or vent on top. The oiler reservoir is placed on the side set by impeller rotation: left for clockwise, right for counterclockwise.

Oil mist lubrication uses one pump unit for both bearings. A metered quantity of oil is broken into fine droplets by a continuous flow of compressed air and carried to the bearings, entering through a line on top of each bearing; liquid oil drains from a line on the bottom and returns to the pump unit. Because the mist keeps the bearing housing at a slight overpressure, dirt is kept away from the bearing, which is a useful side benefit in dusty plants.

Method Supply Hardware per fan Typical use Grease Grease gun through a fitting, on a schedule One fitting per bearing, optional lube lines and grease pan Standard on nearly all fans Static oil Constant-level oiler tops up a sump One oiler per bearing, relief line or vent Special applications Oil mist Pump unit sends oil mist, oil returns One pump unit for both bearings, supply and return lines Special applications; slight overpressure keeps dirt out

docs.title: Bearing Seals and Seal Speed Limits
docs.text:
A bearing seal is part of the bearing itself: it closes the gap between the housing and the shaft so grease stays in and dirt stays out. It is different from the shaft seal on the fan housing, which keeps the airstream in. FanPedia (p. 100) describes three common bearing seals and makes one rule that drives selection: the seal type dictates the speed limit of the bearing.

A labyrinth seal, also called a non-contact seal, uses a winding path of close-clearance grooves between rotating and stationary rings. Nothing rubs, so it adds no friction or heat, and FanPedia lists it for higher-speed applications on spherical roller bearings, both solid and split pillow block. A lip seal, by contrast, is a contact seal that rubs on the shaft and is used for low to moderate shaft surface speeds, typically on ball bearings.

A taconite seal is designed for dirty or abrasive environments, taking its name from the iron-ore pellet plants where it is common. It is used on split pillow block spherical roller bearings and combines a labyrinth with a grease-purged cavity that pushes contaminants back out. The standard type taconite seal has a lower speed limit than a standard labyrinth seal; a Canadian type taconite seal, which is non-contact, is available for higher speeds.

The bearing seal speed limit is the maximum shaft speed (rpm) that the bearing manufacturer allows for a given bearing and seal combination. It is separate from the bearing's own speed rating, and it can be the lower of the two. A fan that must run fast and dirty is therefore a real selection problem: the seal that protects best from dust may not be allowed at the fan's speed. FanPedia refers to Fan Engineering Letter FE-1200 for detail.

A Taconite Seal Makes the Bearing Wider

Adding taconite seals to a quote looks like a simple seal swap, but FanPedia notes they widen the bearing, which can require a longer shaft, moving the bearing on the pedestal, or a larger bearing support such as a bearing bar. Flag the change to engineering before the order is released, not after the shaft is cut.

docs.title: Gas Purge Seals
docs.text:
The bearing seals above protect the bearing. The shaft seals of Chapter 16 protect the surroundings by limiting how much gas leaks through the hole where the shaft passes through the housing. When even a small leak is unacceptable, because the gas is toxic, flammable, odorous or would condense on the bearings, a gas purge seal is used. It is a shaft seal with a connection between its sealing rings through which a clean purge gas is supplied. FanPedia shows two versions (pp. 153 and 155):

  • Double ring mechanical shaft seal (double carbon ring): two split carbon rings with a lantern ring between them, located at the purge hole.
  • Stuffing box type shaft seal with gas purge (also called a graphoil seal or packing gland seal with purge): carbon yarn packing rings and a graphoil split ring, with a Teflon lantern ring at the purge hole.

The lantern ring is a spacer with an open channel around it. Purge gas fed into the purge hole fills that channel and surrounds the shaft. If the purge gas is supplied at a pressure above the gas pressure inside the housing at the shaft, any leakage past the inner ring is clean purge gas flowing into the fan, and any leakage past the outer ring is clean purge gas flowing out. Process gas never reaches the outside. The purge gas is usually clean, dry air or, when the process gas is flammable, an inert gas such as nitrogen; the choice belongs to the customer's process engineer.

The Seal Leaks on Purpose

No shaft seal is perfectly tight, so a purge seal does not try to stop leakage. It decides what leaks, by making sure the gas at the lantern ring is always the cleanest and highest-pressure gas in the neighborhood.

FanPedia notes that the purge hole ships with a 1/8 in. NPT pipe plug, which is replaced in the field with a customer-supplied purge line. That one sentence has a real consequence for the order: the purge gas supply, its piping, its pressure regulation and any flow monitoring are by others.

Worked example (illustrative). A customer needs an Arrangement 1 fan to move solvent-laden air from a coating line to a thermal oxidizer. The fan is downstream of the process blower, so the housing is under positive pressure at the shaft. The specification says "nominally leak-tight construction; no process gas release at the shaft." Working through it:

  1. Find the direction of leakage. Positive pressure at the shaft means process gas will try to leak out. A plain lip seal limits that leakage but does not stop it, so a purged seal is justified.
  2. Check the allowed seal list. FanPedia's nominally leak-tight construction page (Chapter 21) permits lip type, stuffing box (graphoil) and double ring mechanical shaft seals on the fan shaft, with no shaft sleeve or cap. Of these, the stuffing box type and the double ring mechanical type are offered with a purge connection.
  3. Choose the purge gas. The process gas is flammable, so the customer's process engineer specifies nitrogen rather than plant air.
  4. Set the purge pressure. The purge supply must be above the housing pressure at the shaft at every operating point, including start-up and damper changes. The required margin and flow come from the seal vendor's data and the customer's process engineer; the quote should not invent them.
  5. Write the scope split. The quote states that TCF supplies the seal with its purge hole plugged with a 1/8 in. NPT plug, and that the purge line, nitrogen supply and regulation are supplied and installed by others.

Note that the leak-tight requirement also affects the bearings: a sealed, hot housing usually means fixed and floating bearings, so the example connects to the rules earlier in this chapter.

docs.title: Holding the Bearing in Place: Stop Blocks and Dowel Pins
docs.text:
Once a bearing is aligned on its pedestal, something should prevent it from creeping out of position during shipment, start-up or years of vibration. FanPedia calls bearings held this way restrained bearings and offers two methods (pp. 102, 176-177).

Bearing stop blocks are welded brackets, or short pieces of keystock, welded to the pedestal against each side of the bearing base. They confirm and hold the bearing's location along the shaft. Stop blocks are also listed among the pedestal accessories for use next to motors.

Bearing dowel pins are rods fixed to the pedestal that pass through a hole drilled through the bearing base. A doweled bearing can be removed and reinstalled in exactly the same position, which preserves alignment after service.

Restrained bearings matter most in spark resistant construction. FanPedia's Type A spark resistant page lists restrained bearings (bearing dowel pins or bearing stop blocks) as a fan modification, with dowel pins as the first choice, because a bearing that walks along its pedestal can let the impeller rub (see Chapter 20).

docs.title: Fan Pedestals
docs.text:
A fan pedestal is the steel structure that supports the bearings, shaft and often the motor, and through them carries the impeller. FanPedia (pp. 83-87) adds a second job: the pedestal provides the structural stability the assembly needs to be balanced and to meet vibration requirements. A typical pedestal has a top, sides, feet, a front and sometimes a back, built from angled, straight or formed sheet metal. Not every fan has one: an Arrangement 3 fan carries its bearings on the housing, and air kits ship without a pedestal, but every fan needs some support, supplied by TCF or by others in the field.

Several pedestal features follow from choices made earlier in this chapter:

  • Bearing or motor pads, or a machined top, give a flat, stiff surface for bearing alignment.
  • Hand holes give access to bearing and motor fasteners.
  • Reinforcements (angles, flat bar, channels or gussets) stiffen the pedestal; rebar can be welded inside for a concrete fill.
  • Heat shields protect the bearings on high-temperature fans, and buffer strips are used when the customer specifies that a stainless steel housing may not be welded to a mild steel pedestal.
  • Positioners, stop blocks and a grease pan are pedestal accessories.

docs.title: Diagram: Fan Pedestal Features
docs.text:
Run Fan Pedestal Features Fullscreen

Fan Pedestal Features

sim-id: ch17-fan-pedestal-overlay Library: html + FP.Overlay Status: built Bloom Level: Remember Learning Objective: The learner will identify the top, pillow block bearing, hand holes, sides, front, feet and bearing or motor pads of a fan pedestal on FanPedia's drawing, given each feature's job or look.

Content: Seven numbered markers: top, pillow block bearing, hand holes, sides, front, feet, bearing or motor pads.

Provenance: FanPedia page 85, "Pedestals: Features (pedestal on a SWSI fan) with the 'Bearing or Motor Pads' inset", with the printed labels removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 85.

Two pedestal variants deserve their own names. A separated pedestal is used on high-temperature applications. It leaves a gap between the fan housing and the pedestal, which reduces the housing heat conducted into the pedestal and bearings and leaves room for insulation. A bolt-on pedestal bolts to the housing instead of being welded to it. FanPedia lists two kinds: a non-rotatable bolt-on pedestal, used when the pedestal must come off the housing to fit the fan through a smaller opening, to send the pedestal out for special machining, or to join dissimilar metals such as a stainless steel or aluminum housing on a mild steel pedestal; and a rotatable bolt-on pedestal, used on specific models whose housing can be rotated to several discharge positions.

Worked example (illustrative). A quote calls for an Arrangement 1 SWSI fan with a stainless steel housing, handling corrosive exhaust at 550°F. The customer specification says stainless steel may not be welded to carbon steel, and the selection has a 3-7/16 in. shaft. Reading the job against this chapter:

  1. Pedestal material and attachment. The pedestal is mild steel, so it cannot be welded to the stainless housing. Two FanPedia features answer that requirement: buffer strips, or a non-rotatable bolt-on pedestal. The bolt-on pedestal also makes the fan easier to rig into the building if access is tight.
  2. Heat path. At 550°F, a separated pedestal and a heat shield reduce the heat reaching the bearings; the high-temperature construction packages in Chapter 21 set the rest, such as a shaft cooler.
  3. Bearing mount. A 3-7/16 in. shaft is at the four hole mount threshold, so the pillow blocks bolt down with four holes each.
  4. Bearing configuration. Above 301°F, every bearing type uses one fixed and one floating bearing; the fan is horizontal, so the fixed bearing is the drive end bearing, set 3/4 in. in from the end of the pedestal top plate. High-temperature grease is specified.
  5. Retention and lubrication. Stop blocks or dowel pins are added if the customer wants restrained bearings, and a grease pan keeps purged grease off the floor.

Each line on the resulting order traces to a source reason, which is exactly what a reviewer at the factory or the customer's engineer will ask for.

docs.title: Shaft and Coupling Guards
docs.text: The last parts on the drive side protect people rather than bearings. FanPedia's common accessories page (p. 126) shows a shaft/bearing guard, which covers the exposed shaft and bearings, and a coupling guard, which encloses the flexible coupling on direct-drive arrangements where the motor shaft is coupled to the fan shaft. Together these shaft and coupling guards complete the guarding that the belt guard provides on belt-driven fans (see Chapter 7), and a cooler guard covers the shaft cooler on high-temperature fans. Guards are usually bolted to the pedestal or base so they can be removed for bearing service, then must be reinstalled before the fan is restarted. Whether guards are included, and to what standard, should be stated on every quote rather than assumed, because local safety rules require exposed rotating parts to be guarded.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• L-10 bearing life is the hours at which 10% of a bearing population is expected to fail; L-50 (average life) is five times L-10. Convert either to years by dividing by the fan's annual operating hours; 40,000 hours of continuous duty is about 4.6 years.
  • Solid pillow blocks are standard; split pillow blocks split the housing for easy inspection; totally split roller bearings split every part so the shaft can stay in place.
  • Concentric mounts, including the adapter sleeve mount, clamp the whole shaft circumference; keystock carries torque between the shaft and hubs, sheaves and couplings.
  • The TCF standard is a two hole mount for shafts 2-15/16 in. and below and a four hole mount for 3-7/16 in. and above.
  • The drive end bearing (outboard) is nearest the drive; the non-drive end bearing (inboard) is nearest the impeller.
  • The fixed-floating bearing rules: horizontal fans put the fixed bearing on the drive side, vertical fans put the floating bearing there; ball bearings at 300°F and below use two fixed bearings, and every other case uses one fixed and one floating bearing.
  • Bearings are greased through a grease fitting; static oil and oil mist lubrication are for special applications.
  • Labyrinth seals suit higher speeds, taconite seals suit dirty service but widen the bearing, and the bearing seal speed limit can cap fan speed.
  • A gas purge seal feeds clean gas to a lantern ring at higher pressure than the process gas, so only clean gas leaks; the purge line is customer-supplied.
  • Bearing stop blocks and bearing dowel pins restrain bearings; dowel pins are the first choice for Type A spark resistance.
  • The fan pedestal supports and stiffens the rotating assembly; separated pedestals keep heat away from bearings and bolt-on pedestals solve dissimilar-metal, access and rotatable-discharge problems. Shaft and coupling guards finish the drive side.

You Can Specify the Whole Shaft Line

You can now take a bearing life, housing, mount, fixed-floating layout, lubricant, seal and pedestal from a specification and explain each one in shop terms. That shaft line is where most field problems start, and now it is where your quotes are strongest.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals
docs.text: Test your understanding of bearing life ratings, pillow block housings, fixed and floating bearings, lubrication, bearing and gas purge seals, and fan pedestals with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which bearing restraint does FanPedia name as the first choice for Type A spark-resistant construction?
docs.text:
1. Bearing positioners (jacking screws) tightened against the housing
  2. Bearing dowel pins passing through a hole drilled in the bearing base
  3. Bearing stop blocks welded to the pedestal on each side of the bearing
  4. Slotted bolt holes in the pillow block base
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. FanPedia's Type A spark-resistant page lists restrained bearings, by dowel pins or stop blocks, with dowel pins as the first choice. A doweled bearing can also be removed and reinstalled in exactly the same position. Stop blocks (C) are the other accepted method, not the first choice. Positioners (A) adjust a bearing's location but do not restrain it, and slotted holes (D) exist so the bearing can be moved during mounting.

Concept Tested: Bearing Dowel Pins

See: Holding the Bearing in Place

docs.title: 2. What is the Twin City Fan standard for bolting a pillow block bearing to the pedestal on a fan with a 3-7/16 inch shaft?
docs.text:
1. A two hole mount, one bolt on each side of the shaft
  2. A flange mount bolted to a plate perpendicular to the shaft
  3. A four hole mount, two bolts on each side of the shaft
  4. A single center bolt with a dowel pin
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. FanPedia gives the TCF standard by shaft diameter: a two hole mount for shafts of 2-15/16 inch and below, and a four hole mount for 3-7/16 inch and above. More bolts spread the load and resist rocking under larger shaft loads. A two hole mount (A) applies to the smaller shafts. A flange mount (B) is a different housing type, and option D is not a mounting standard in the chapter.

Concept Tested: Two and Four Hole Mount

See: Bolting the Bearing Down

docs.title: 3. When would a totally split roller bearing be specified instead of a standard split pillow block?
docs.text:
1. On a large fan where pulling the shaft to change a bearing would be a major outage
  2. On any fan running above 300°F, because split parts expand freely
  3. On small fans where a lower-cost housing is wanted
  4. On fans whose bearings must carry no axial load
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A totally split roller bearing splits the housing and every internal part, so the bearing can be removed with the shaft left in place. FanPedia lists it as a specialty bearing for special applications only, typically large fans where removing the shaft is a major job. A split pillow block splits only the housing; its insert still slides on the shaft. Temperature (B) is handled by fixed and floating bearings, cost (C) points the other way, and axial load (D) is not the deciding factor.

Concept Tested: Totally Split Roller Bearing

See: Pillow Block Housings

docs.title: 4. A competitor quotes a bearing with a "200,000-hour average life," and the Twin City Fan quote says "L-10 40,000 hours." What is the best interpretation?
docs.text:
1. The competitor's bearing will last five times longer than the TCF bearing
  2. The TCF bearing is better, because L-10 is a stricter test than average life
  3. The two numbers cannot be compared, because one is in hours and one is in years
  4. The two selections may be identical, because L-50 (average life) is five times L-10
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. L-50, also called average life, is the hours at which 50% of a bearing population is expected to fail, and FanPedia gives L-50 as five times L-10. An L-10 of 40,000 hours therefore corresponds to an L-50 of 200,000 hours. Both numbers describe the same bearing at different points on its failure curve, so option A mistakes a different statistic for a longer-lived bearing. Option B overstates the difference, and both figures are in hours (C).

Concept Tested: L-50 Bearing Life

See: Bearing Life: L-10 and L-50

docs.title: 5. A plenum fan in Arrangement 3VA is mounted vertically and uses split roller bearings at 200°F. Which bearing configuration do the fixed-floating rules call for?
docs.text:
1. Two fixed bearings
  2. Fixed bearing at the drive end, floating bearing at the non-drive end
  3. Floating bearing at the drive end, fixed bearing at the non-drive end
  4. Two floating bearings
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Split roller bearings use one fixed and one floating bearing at every temperature, so two fixed bearings (A) are out. Placement then depends on orientation: horizontal fans put the fixed bearing on the drive side, but vertically mounted fans, including plenum Arrangements 3VA and 3VS, put the floating bearing on the drive side. Option B is the horizontal-fan layout. Two floating bearings (D) would leave nothing to locate the shaft axially.

Concept Tested: Fixed-Floating Bearing Rules

See: The Fixed-Floating Bearing Rules

docs.title: 6. A customer asks for the L-50 life, in years, of a bearing rated L-10 20,000 hours on a fan that runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Which answer is closest?
docs.text:
1. 11.4 years
  2. 2.3 years
  3. 22.8 years
  4. 4.6 years
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. First convert the rating: L-50 = 5 × 20,000 = 100,000 hours. Continuous running is 8,760 hours a year, and 100,000 ÷ 8,760 ≈ 11.4 years, which matches FanPedia's table. Option B is the L-10 answer, from forgetting the five-times conversion. Option C is the L-50 of a 40,000-hour bearing, and option D is the L-10 of a 40,000-hour bearing.

Concept Tested: L-50 Bearing Life

See: Bearing Life: L-10 and L-50

docs.title: 7. A horizontally mounted Arrangement 3SI fan uses ball bearings at 250°F. How should the bearing configuration be handled?
docs.text:
1. Order two fixed bearings, as for any ball bearing fan at 300°F and below
  2. Order a fixed bearing at the drive end and a floating bearing at the non-drive end without review
  3. Order a floating bearing at the drive end, because the impeller sits between the bearings
  4. Flag it for engineering review, because ball bearings on 3SI may still need one fixed and one floating
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The general rule allows two fixed ball bearings at 300°F and below, but FanPedia adds a footnote for Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI, where the bearings straddle the impeller and the shaft between them is long: ball bearings there may still require one fixed and one floating bearing. The chapter treats that case as an engineering review item rather than a lookup. Option A ignores the footnote, B skips the review, and C applies the vertical-fan placement rule to a horizontal fan.

Concept Tested: Fixed-Floating Bearing Rules

See: The Fixed-Floating Bearing Rules

docs.title: 8. A fan must run fast in a dusty plant on split pillow block spherical roller bearings, and the fan speed is above the standard taconite seal's limit. Which bearing seal fits best?
docs.text:
1. A lip seal, because contact seals have the highest speed limits
  2. A Canadian type (non-contact) taconite seal
  3. A standard type taconite seal, since the seal does not limit bearing speed
  4. A gas purge shaft seal on the fan housing
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Taconite seals are designed for dirty or abrasive service on split pillow block spherical roller bearings, but the standard type has a lower speed limit than a labyrinth seal. FanPedia notes a non-contact Canadian type taconite seal for higher speeds. The seal type does set the bearing's speed limit, so C is wrong. Lip seals (A) rub on the shaft and suit only low to moderate speeds. A gas purge seal (D) is a shaft seal for the airstream, not a bearing seal.

Concept Tested: Bearing Seal Speed Limit

See: Bearing Seals and Seal Speed Limits

docs.title: 9. In a gas purge shaft seal, why must the purge gas be supplied at a pressure above the gas pressure inside the housing at the shaft?
docs.text:
1. So the purge gas cools the shaft enough to replace a shaft cooler
  2. So the higher pressure lubricates the carbon rings and packing
  3. So any leakage past the inner ring is clean purge gas flowing into the fan, and process gas never reaches the outside
  4. So the lantern ring is pushed tight against the shaft and stops all leakage
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. No shaft seal is perfectly tight, so a purge seal decides what leaks. Purge gas fed to the lantern ring at a pressure above the housing gas means leakage past the inner ring is clean gas entering the fan, and leakage past the outer ring is clean gas leaving it. The lantern ring is an open spacer and does not clamp the shaft or stop all leakage (D). Cooling (A) and lubrication (B) are not the purpose of the purge.

Concept Tested: Gas Purge Seal

See: Gas Purge Seals

docs.title: 10. An Arrangement 1 fan has a stainless steel housing handling 550°F exhaust, and the specification forbids welding stainless steel to carbon steel. Which pedestal approach addresses both the heat and the dissimilar-metal requirement?
docs.text:
1. A separated pedestal with a heat shield, joined to the housing with buffer strips or built as a non-rotatable bolt-on pedestal
  2. A rotatable bolt-on pedestal, because every fan above 500°F must have a rotatable housing
  3. A standard mild steel pedestal welded to the housing, with a grease pan under the bearings
  4. A mild steel pedestal welded to the housing, with taconite seals to keep heat out of the bearings
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A separated pedestal leaves a gap that reduces housing heat conducted into the pedestal and bearings, and a heat shield adds protection. Because the mild steel pedestal cannot be welded to the stainless housing, FanPedia offers buffer strips or a non-rotatable bolt-on pedestal for dissimilar metals. A rotatable bolt-on pedestal (B) is for models whose housing rotates to several discharge positions. Options C and D weld the pedestal, which the specification forbids, and taconite seals keep out dirt, not heat.

Concept Tested: Fan Pedestal

See: Fan Pedestals

docs.title: References: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals
docs.text:
1. Rolling-element bearing - Wikipedia - Covers bearing types, fatigue failure and rated life, including the L10 basic life and the rule of thumb that median life is about five times L10, matching the chapter's L-50 conversion.

  2. Pillow block bearing - Wikipedia - Describes pillow block housings mounted parallel to the shaft, with solid and split styles and their mounting. Background for the chapter's solid, split and totally split housing comparison.

  3. Grease fitting - Wikipedia - Explains the Zerk fitting's check-ball design that admits grease from a gun while keeping dirt out, the standard lubrication port on fan pillow blocks described in this chapter.

  4. Rolling Bearing Analysis (5th ed.) - Tedric A. Harris and Michael N. Kotzalas - CRC Press - Harris is credited with the standard engineering exposition of Lundberg-Palmgren fatigue theory and Weibull life dispersion, the statistics that make L-10 and L-50 two points on one failure curve.

  5. Machinery's Handbook (31st ed.) - Erik Oberg, Franklin D. Jones, Holbrook L. Horton and Henry H. Ryffel - Industrial Press - Its compact reference tables for keys and keyseats, bearing mounting and lubrication are the shop-floor standard for the keystock, adapter mounts and fits discussed here.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Primary source for bearing life tables, pillow block styles and mounts, fixed and floating rules, oil lubrication, bearing seals, gas purge seals, restraints and pedestals.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - Web edition of FanPedia with the Fan Components bearing and pedestal image galleries, handy for recognizing the housings, mounts and pedestal features described in this chapter.

  8. Fan Bearing Selection (FE-1200) - Twin City Fan Engineering Letter - Gives the L-50 equals five times L-10 rule, typical L-10 lives, bearing seal types and speed limits, and Twin City Fan's fixed and expansion bearing practice.

  9. Fan Bearing Maintenance and Troubleshooting (FE-1300) - Twin City Fan Engineering Letter - Practical guidance on grease grades, high temperature greases, relubrication intervals and bearing troubleshooting, extending the chapter's grease fitting and lubrication sections.

  10. Product Catalogs - Twin City Fan - Current product catalogs, the authority the chapter defers to for which L-10 bearing life ratings and bearing options each fan model offers.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers what happens at a fan's inlet and outlet and how airflow is controlled. It introduces inlet funnels, integral and detached inlet boxes, evasés, transition pieces, companion flanges, and inlet and outlet silencers. It then covers flow control: turndown, parallel and opposed blade dampers, outlet and inlet box dampers, gravity, manual, and motorized dampers, variable inlet vanes, and speed control with a VFD or EC motor controller. After completing it, readers can choose a flow-control method and the inlet and outlet accessories an installation needs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans
  • Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views
  • Chapter 8: Centrifugal and Axial Impeller Types
  • Chapter 9: Impeller Construction and Material Handling
  • Chapter 14: Fan Motors and Enclosures
  • Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners

Welcome to Inlets, Outlets and Flow Control

A fan rarely meets its ductwork bare. Somewhere between the drawing and the job site, someone has to decide what bolts onto the inlet, what bolts onto the outlet, and how the customer will turn the airflow down when the process does not need all of it. By the end of this chapter you will make those calls with reasons you can defend on a quote. Let's follow the airflow.

docs.title: The Fan Does Not End at Its Flanges
docs.text:
A fan's catalog rating describes the fan alone, tested with smooth, straight airflow entering the inlet and leaving the outlet.
