Evidence of Mastery: For each of 7 scenarios the learner assigns one of 5 recommendations and then picks one of 3 justifications. A scenario is correct when both match the answer table. Mastery is 6 of 7 on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Every fan needs isolators. (2) Isolators can go under any arrangement. (3) A unitary base can be set on springs. (4) An internally isolated roof ventilator needs external isolators.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level recommendation requires a judgment against criteria, so the learner commits to an option and then to the rule that justifies it; the justification step separates a correct guess from a correct judgment.

Content:

Recommendations (5): Unitary base; Isolation base; Inertia base; Isolators directly under the fan; No added base or isolation.

# Scenario shown to the learner Correct recommendation Correct justification (shown with 2 distractors) 1 Arrangement 7SI fan, slab on grade in a plant, no isolation requested Unitary base 7SI ships on a unitary base as standard; unitary bases are designed for use without isolators. 2 Arrangement 1 belt-driven SWSI fan with motor, on a mezzanine above offices; isolation required Isolation base Isolation bases give fan, motor and drive a common support and sit on spring or RIS isolators. 3 Spec reads "Arrangement 9F with springs under the fan" Isolation base 9F is not suitable for isolators directly under the fan; FanPedia says use Arrangement 1 with a separate isolation base. 4 Long direct-drive Arrangement 8 fan on springs; motor, coupling, shaft and bearings must stay aligned Inertia base Inertia bases are typically used on longer direct-drive fans to mitigate assembly deflection and hold alignment. 5 Commercial roof ventilator on a roof curb No added base or isolation Commercial roof ventilators are internally isolated; no other isolation is required. 6 Arrangement 4 fan with a 30 in impeller; isolation wanted with no separate base Isolators directly under the fan Direct mounting under the fan's foundation holes is usually limited to impellers 36.5 in or less; 30 in qualifies. 7 Fan and detached inlet box mounted together on a base on a plant floor; no isolation Unitary base Fan and inlet box can share one base on the same plane; without isolators that base is a unitary base.

Distractor justifications for every scenario are drawn from the other six rows' justifications, two per scenario, fixed by the seed 22.

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 131–133 (base types, mounting methods, internally isolated fans, 36.5 in limit), p. 143 (inlet box mounting planes), p. 165 (7SI on unitary base), p. 166 (9F). Scenarios are illustrative; the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: Exact match on both recommendation and justification. Scenario order shuffled once with seed 22 and then fixed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a scenario and selects a recommendation.
  2. The learner selects a justification from three choices and presses Submit.
  3. Feedback appears; the learner moves to the next scenario.
  4. After all seven, a summary shows each scenario, the learner's answer and the correct one.

Feedback: Seven scenarios, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ." Incorrect recommendation for scenarios 3 or 6: "Check the arrangement and impeller size against the mounting rules first." Incorrect recommendation otherwise: "Ask whether isolation is needed, then what the arrangement allows." Correct recommendation with wrong justification: "Right choice, wrong reason. Which FanPedia rule decides this case?" After the second wrong attempt the answer and justification are shown and the scenario counts as missed. Score "n of 7 first-attempt correct".

Starting State: Scenario 1 of 7 with no selection made. The prompt reads "What should this fan sit on?"

Chapter Anchors: 7 scenarios; 5 recommendations; 36.5 in impeller limit; Arrangement 9F → Arrangement 1 with isolation base; 7SI on unitary base as standard; commercial roof ventilators internally isolated.

docs.title: Inlet Box Mounting Planes
docs.text:
An inlet box (Chapter 18) can be attached to the fan or detached from it and supported separately. When it is detached, the installer has to know whether the fan and the box share one mounting surface. Inlet box mounting planes describes that relationship. FanPedia shows two cases (p. 143):

  • Same plane: the fan and inlet box both stand on grade (legs to grade), or both stand on one base, unitary or isolation (legs to base). They move together.
  • Different planes: the fan sits on an isolation base or a unitary base while the inlet box stands on grade. Now the fan and box can move relative to each other, and FanPedia requires a flex connector (slip connection) between the fan and the inlet box.

The practical rule follows from the isolation section: if the fan floats on isolators and the inlet box does not, the joint between them must be flexible, exactly as at the duct connections.

docs.title: Installation Accessories: Weather Cover, Zero Speed Switch, Piezometer Ring
docs.text:
Three smaller accessories complete most installations.

A weather cover (FanPedia lists it with the motor cover, p. 126) is a cover that protects the motor from rain, snow and sun when the fan is installed outdoors. It is an option that makes some arrangements suitable for outdoor use: FanPedia describes Arrangement 10 fans, including the lab exhaust version, as suitable for roof or outdoor installations when supplied with the optional weather cover (pp. 167, 175). On spark-resistant construction, the weather cover is one of the mild-steel parts FanPedia lists (p. 109).

A zero speed switch, also called a speed sensor, detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft (FanPedia p. 129). Other designs are provided when the customer requests them. Its usual job is to tell a control or alarm system that a fan has stopped even though its motor starter is still energized, as when a belt breaks.

A piezometer ring is part of an airflow measuring system based on the principle of a flow nozzle, with the fan's own inlet funnel serving as the nozzle (FanPedia pp. 158, 191). Tubing around the throat of the funnel forms the ring, and a tap on the face of the funnel provides the second pressure. The pressure drop between them is measured by a differential pressure transducer: the face tap goes to the high-pressure side and the ring to the low-pressure side. The tubing is nylon for temperatures up to 180°F and copper above. Piezometer rings are available on plenum fans and on SWSI and DWDI housed centrifugal fans (p. 158), and FanPedia also shows inline centrifugal and mixed flow mountings (p. 160). Turning that pressure reading into airflow is covered in Chapter 23.

Accessory What it does Order note Weather cover Protects the motor outdoors Makes some arrangements, such as Arrangement 10, suitable for roof or outdoor use Zero speed switch Detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft Other designs on customer request Piezometer ring Measures inlet funnel pressure drop for airflow Plenum, SWSI and DWDI centrifugal fans; transducer optional

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Fan installation is a set of order decisions (support, base, isolation, connections, environment, monitoring) that must be made before the order, because none of them appear on the fan curve.
  • Vibration is driven mainly by unbalance at the forcing frequency \( f = N/60 \); the lowest forcing frequency sets the isolation requirement.
  • A unitary base is for use without isolators; an isolation base usually sits on spring or RIS isolators (neoprene pads are possible but uncommon) with flex connectors; an inertia base is an isolation base with rebar and customer-poured concrete for longer direct-drive fans.
  • Vibration isolation works only when the frequency ratio exceeds about 1.4; below that an isolator amplifies the force, and at 1 it resonates.
  • Isolator deflection sets the natural frequency, \( f_n \approx 3.13/\sqrt{\delta} \): pads (about 0.0625 in) give minimal isolation, rubber-in-shear (0.2 to 0.5 in) moderate, springs (1 or 2 in) high.
  • The five isolator mounting methods are directly under the fan, isolation rails, mounting angle, isolation base and isolation hangers; some arrangements, such as 9F, cannot take isolators directly under the fan.
  • Internally isolated fans, such as commercial roof ventilators, need no other isolation; seismic restraints keep isolated fans in place during an earthquake.
  • When a fan and a detached inlet box sit on different mounting planes, a flex connector is required between them.
  • Weather covers, zero speed switches and piezometer rings finish the installation: outdoor protection, stop detection and airflow measurement.

You Can Put a Fan in a Building

You can now read a job, pick a unitary, isolation or inertia base, and check a deflection against a fan speed with the frequency ratio. That last calculation is the one that separates an isolator that works from one that makes things worse.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation
docs.text: Test your understanding of fan bases, vibration, isolator deflection and installation accessories with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What distinguishes a unitary (channel) base from the other FanPedia base types?
docs.text:
1. It is filled with concrete by the customer to add mass
  2. It always requires flexible connectors at the inlet and outlet
  3. It is designed for use without isolators and is anchored directly to the floor
  4. It is built only for fans hung from an overhead structure
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A unitary base uses structural channel to support the fan assembly and is designed for use without isolators. It is bolted or anchored directly to the floor or foundation, where vibration is not a concern. Concrete fill describes an inertia base (A). Required flex connectors belong to the isolation and inertia bases, which sit on isolators (B). Hung fans use isolation hangers, not a base (D).

Concept Tested: Unitary Base

See: Unitary Base

docs.title: 2. What does a zero speed switch do?
docs.text:
1. It detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft
  2. It prevents the fan from turning backward when it is idle
  3. It measures airflow through the inlet funnel
  4. It stops the motor whenever vibration exceeds a limit
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. FanPedia describes the zero speed switch, also called a speed sensor, as a device that detects slowing or stopping of the fan shaft. Its usual job is to tell a control or alarm system that a fan has stopped even though its starter is still energized, as when a belt breaks. Preventing reverse rotation is the job of an anti-backspin device (B). Airflow is measured with a piezometer ring (C). Vibration monitoring uses bearing vibration sensors (D).

Concept Tested: Zero Speed Switch

See: Installation Accessories

docs.title: 3. Which statement best describes what vibration isolation does?
docs.text:
1. It balances the impeller so the fan no longer vibrates
  2. It stiffens the floor so it can carry the fan's weight
  3. It increases the fan's speed so it runs above resonance
  4. It limits the force the operating fan transfers to its supporting structure
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FanPedia defines vibration isolation as preventing or limiting the force an operating fan transfers to its supporting structure. It does not reduce the fan's own vibration; it keeps that vibration from travelling into the building. Balancing (A) reduces the unbalance force itself, which is a different remedy. Isolation uses resilient mounts, not a stiffer floor (B). Changing the fan's speed (C) is not what isolators do.

Concept Tested: Vibration Isolation

See: Vibration Isolation

docs.title: 4. A belt-driven fan runs at 900 RPM, driven by a motor at 1,750 RPM. Which forcing frequency sets the isolation requirement?
docs.text:
1. 29.2 Hz, from the motor shaft
  2. 15 Hz, from the fan shaft
  3. 44.2 Hz, the sum of the two shaft frequencies
  4. 14.2 Hz, the difference between the two shaft frequencies
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Forcing frequency is \( f = N/60 \). The fan shaft gives 900/60 = 15 Hz and the motor shaft gives 1,750/60 ≈ 29.2 Hz. The lowest forcing frequency is the hardest to isolate, so 15 Hz sets the requirement. An isolator that handles 15 Hz handles 29.2 Hz even better. The chapter never combines shaft frequencies by adding them (C) or subtracting them (D).

Concept Tested: Vibration

See: Vibration

docs.title: 5. An isolator compresses 0.25 in. under its actual load. Using \( f_n \approx 3.13/\sqrt{\delta} \), what is the natural frequency of the mounted assembly?
docs.text:
1. About 6.3 Hz
  2. About 12.5 Hz
  3. About 3.1 Hz
  4. About 0.8 Hz
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. \( \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5 \), so \( f_n = 3.13/0.5 \approx 6.26 \) Hz. Option B divides by 0.25 instead of its square root, which is the result for a 0.0625 in. pad. Option C is the natural frequency at 1 in. of deflection. Option D multiplies by 0.25 instead of dividing. Deflection sits under a square root, so quadrupling deflection only halves the natural frequency.

Concept Tested: Isolator Deflection

See: Isolator Deflection

docs.title: 6. Why do neoprene pads (about 0.0625 in. deflection) make vibration worse under a 600 RPM fan?
docs.text:
1. Neoprene softens with time, so the pads lose their deflection
  2. The pads add mass, which raises the fan's forcing frequency
  3. The pad's natural frequency (about 12.5 Hz) is above the 10 Hz forcing frequency, so the frequency ratio is below about 1.4 and force is amplified
  4. Pads isolate only horizontal vibration, and a slow fan vibrates vertically
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The pad's natural frequency is \( 3.13/\sqrt{0.0625} = 12.52 \) Hz. At 600 RPM the forcing frequency is 10 Hz, so \( r = 0.80 \). Below \( r \approx 1.41 \), transmissibility exceeds 1, and here the pad passes about 2.8 times the force a rigid mount would. Isolation depends on the frequency ratio, not on material aging (A), forcing-frequency changes (B) or direction (D). Under a 1,170 RPM fan the same pad gives about 30% isolation.

Concept Tested: Vibration Isolation

See: Isolator Deflection

docs.title: 7. An inertia base has a pour cavity 6 ft long, 4 ft wide and 6 in. deep. The fan, motor and steel base weigh 2,500 lb. Using 150 lb/ft³ for concrete, what total weight must the spring isolators be selected for?
docs.text:
1. 2,500 lb
  2. 3,700 lb
  3. 1,800 lb
  4. 4,300 lb
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The volume is \( 6 \times 4 \times 0.5 = 12 \) ft³, so the concrete weighs \( 150 \times 12 = 1{,}800 \) lb. The total is 2,500 + 1,800 = 4,300 lb. Option A sizes springs for the bare fan, and those springs would bottom out once the customer pours the concrete. Option C is the concrete alone. Option B uses 100 lb/ft³ instead of 150 lb/ft³ for the concrete.

Concept Tested: Inertia Base

See: Inertia Base

docs.title: 8. A specification calls for "Arrangement 9F, SWSI, belt driven, spring isolators mounted under the fan." What is FanPedia's stated alternative?
docs.text:
1. Keep Arrangement 9F and place neoprene pads under the fan instead of springs
  2. Use an Arrangement 1 fan with a separate isolation base, with isolators under the base
  3. Use a unitary base under the Arrangement 9F fan and set it on springs
  4. Mount the isolators directly under the 9F motor frame only
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. FanPedia states that Arrangement 9F is not suitable for mounting vibration isolators directly under the fan. When isolators are required, it says to use an Arrangement 1 fan with a separate isolation base, with the isolators under the base's mounting brackets and flex connectors at the inlet and outlet. A unitary base is designed for use without isolators (C). Pads (A) or partial mounting (D) do not change the 9F limit.

Concept Tested: Isolation Base

See: Isolation Base

docs.title: 9. A fan sits on an isolation base while its detached inlet box stands on grade. What does FanPedia require between the fan and the inlet box?
docs.text:
1. A rigid bolted flange so the box steadies the fan
  2. A seismic snubber between the box and the base
  3. A flex connector (slip connection)
  4. Nothing, because the inlet box is not part of the airstream
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. When the fan and the inlet box are on different mounting planes, they can move relative to each other. FanPedia then requires a flex connector, or slip connection, between them. This follows the general isolation rule that rigid duct connections are not allowed on an isolated fan. A rigid flange (A) would short-circuit the isolators. A snubber limits excessive motion but does not seal the joint (B). The inlet box carries the airstream (D).

Concept Tested: Inlet Box Mounting Planes

See: Inlet Box Mounting Planes

docs.title: 10. An engineer changes from 1 in. springs to 2 in. springs under a 1,170 RPM fan. What happens, and why is the gain modest?
docs.text:
1. The natural frequency falls by a factor of √2 (3.13 Hz to about 2.21 Hz); the frequency ratio is already high, so isolation improves only slightly
  2. The natural frequency is halved, so transmitted force is cut in half
  3. The natural frequency doubles, so the springs move closer to resonance
  4. Nothing changes, because deflection does not affect natural frequency
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Natural frequency varies with \( 1/\sqrt{\delta} \), so doubling deflection divides it by √2, not 2 (B). Deflection lowers the natural frequency rather than raising it (C), and it does affect it (D). With 1 in. springs at 1,170 RPM, \( r \) is already 6.23 and isolation is about 97.4%, so 2 in. springs add only a little. As the 600 RPM example shows, the extra deflection matters most on slow fans.

Concept Tested: Isolator Deflection

See: Isolator Deflection

docs.title: References: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation
docs.text:
1. Vibration isolation - Wikipedia - Explains passive isolation with springs, elastomer pads and mounts, including how natural frequency and isolator stiffness decide performance. It is the general background for this chapter's isolator families.

  2. Vibration - Wikipedia - Covers free and forced vibration of a spring-mass system, including the frequency response that underlies transmissibility. It supports the chapter's forcing frequency, natural frequency and frequency ratio calculations.

  3. Mechanical resonance - Wikipedia - Describes what happens when a forcing frequency matches a structure's natural frequency. It explains why an isolator at a frequency ratio of 1 produces large motion instead of isolation.

  4. Mechanical Vibrations (4th edition) - J. P. Den Hartog - McGraw-Hill (reprinted by Dover) - Den Hartog is known for explaining single-degree-of-freedom response and vibration isolation through physical reasoning and minimal mathematics. That approach suits this chapter's practical use of the transmissibility curve.

  5. Harris' Shock and Vibration Handbook - Cyril M. Harris and Charles E. Crede (original editors) - McGraw-Hill - The standard engineering reference on shock and vibration. Crede's isolation work shaped its treatment of isolator selection, deflection and transmissibility for mounted machinery.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - The source for base types and vibration isolation (pp. 131-135), inlet box mounting planes (p. 143), shaft accessories (p. 129), piezometer rings (pp. 158-160) and technical descriptions.

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - The web edition of FanPedia, covering the same accessory and installation topics. Use it with the current catalogs, which take priority when they differ from FanPedia.

  8. Vibration Isolation of Fans (FE-1900) - Twin City Fan Fan Engineering Letter - Charts transmissibility and isolation efficiency against deflection and disturbing frequency. It also discusses springs, pads, structure stiffness and inertia bases, extending the chapter's isolator calculations.

  9. Fan & Fan System Vibration (FE-200) - Twin City Fan Fan Engineering Letter - Discusses fan vibration sources, measurement and how vibration specifications should be written. It is useful context for the chapter's section on why vibration matters.

  10. Centrifugal Fans Installation, Operation and Maintenance Manual (IM-995) - Twin City Fan - Field instructions for centrifugal fans, including a section on foundations and supporting structures. It shows how the base and support decisions in this chapter are carried out on site.

docs.title: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement
Summary
docs.text: This chapter completes installation. It covers spring isolators (open, housed, restrained, and seismic), floor mounted and ceiling hung isolation, direct mounted isolators, isolation rails, mounting angles, snubbers, and thrust restraints that resist the fan's pressure thrust. It also covers shaft and coupling alignment, anti-backspin devices, and measuring airflow in the field with piezometer rings and pressure transmitters. After completing it, readers can specify isolation hardware and explain how installed airflow is verified.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan
  • Chapter 2: Airstreams, Total Pressure and Standard Air
  • Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy
  • Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements
  • Chapter 12: Discharge Positions and Rotation
  • Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners
  • Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals
  • Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation

The Last Few Feet of the Job

A well-selected fan can still disappoint if it rocks on the wrong springs, walks away from its duct at start-up, or spins backward on a windy night. This chapter covers the hardware and checks that make an installation quiet, stable and verifiable. By the end you can read an isolation line on a specification and tell the customer how their airflow will be proven. Let's follow the airflow.

Chapter 22 explained why fans are isolated, what deflection means, and how unitary, isolation and inertia bases support a fan. This chapter turns to the specific hardware on the order: the four kinds of spring isolator, the ways isolators attach to a fan, the snubbers and thrust restraints that limit motion, and three field topics that decide whether the installed fan runs as rated: shaft and coupling alignment, anti-backspin devices, and airflow measurement. The product statements come from the FanPedia vibration isolation pages (pp. 133–135), the piezometer ring pages (pp. 158–160) and the technical descriptions (pp. 162–197).

docs.title: Spring Isolators
docs.text:
A spring isolator is a steel coil spring, with its top and bottom load plates, placed between a fan (or its base) and the supporting structure. Under the fan's weight the spring compresses; that compression is the isolator's static deflection. A soft spring that compresses a lot lets the fan bounce at a low natural frequency, and a fan that runs well above that frequency passes very little of its vibrating force into the floor. Springs reach much larger deflections than rubber-in-shear mounts or neoprene pads, which is why they are the usual choice when isolation really matters.

FanPedia (p. 134) states that most isolators Twin City Fan uses have deflections under 1 inch (25.4 mm), 1 inch, or 2 inches (50.8 mm). Higher deflection is available at additional cost after engineering review. Those three values are the vocabulary of a spring isolator line item: a specification that asks for "2-inch deflection springs" is asking for the high end of the standard range.

Two relationships connect a spring to the fan it carries. The first converts load into deflection.

docs.title: Static Deflection of a Spring
docs.text:
\[ \delta = \frac{W / n}{k} \]

where:

  • \( \delta \) is the static deflection of each isolator, in inches
  • \( W \) is the total weight carried by the isolators (fan, motor, drive and base), in pounds
  • \( n \) is the number of isolators, assuming the load is shared equally
  • \( k \) is the spring rate of one isolator, in pounds per inch of compression

The second, a standard result for an undamped spring and mass, gives the natural frequency of the fan bouncing on its springs.

docs.title: Natural Frequency of a Spring-Mounted Fan
docs.text:
\[ f_n = \frac{3.13}{\sqrt{\delta}} \]

where:

  • \( f_n \) is the natural frequency of the mounted assembly, in hertz (cycles per second)
  • \( \delta \) is the static deflection, in inches
  • 3.13 comes from \( \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g} \) with \( g = 386 \) in/s²

Isolation begins only when the fan's running frequency is more than \( \sqrt{2} \), about 1.41, times the natural frequency. Below that ratio the springs amplify vibration instead of blocking it.

Softer Is Lower, Lower Is Better

Notice that deflection sits under a square root: doubling deflection lowers the natural frequency only by a factor of 1.41. That is why the jump from 1-inch to 2-inch springs matters most on slower fans, whose running frequency sits closest to the springs' bounce.

Worked example (illustrative numbers). A fan, motor and isolation base weigh 2,400 lb and sit on four spring isolators, each with a spring rate of 600 lb/in. The fan runs at 1,180 rpm.

  1. Load per isolator: \( 2{,}400 / 4 = 600 \) lb.
  2. Static deflection: \( \delta = 600 / 600 = 1.00 \) in, a standard 1-inch spring.
  3. Natural frequency: \( f_n = 3.13 / \sqrt{1.00} = 3.13 \) Hz.
  4. Running frequency: \( 1{,}180 / 60 = 19.67 \) Hz.
  5. Frequency ratio: \( r = 19.67 / 3.13 = 6.28 \), far above 1.41, so the springs isolate. The undamped transmissibility \( T = 1/(r^2 - 1) = 0.026 \): about 2.6% of the vibrating force reaches the floor, an isolation efficiency of about 97.4%.

Real bases rarely load four corners equally, because the motor side is heavier. Isolator suppliers then choose a different spring for each corner so that every corner deflects the same amount; the calculation per corner is the same.

docs.title: Diagram: Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator
docs.text:
Run Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator Fullscreen

Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch23-spring-isolator-deflection-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the static deflection of equally loaded spring isolators from total weight, isolator count and spring rate, to within 0.02 in.

Prerequisites: spring isolator, static deflection, spring rate, natural frequency, running frequency, frequency ratio, transmissibility (all defined in the section "Spring Isolators" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge cases, the learner types the deflection in inches before the sim shows it. An answer is correct when it is within ±0.02 in of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Free exploration of the controls afterward is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency (it divides it by 1.41). (2) Any spring isolates, whatever the fan speed (below a ratio of 1.41 the springs amplify). (3) Adding isolators adds deflection (more isolators share the load, so each deflects less).

Instructional Rationale: Calculation at the Apply level needs practice with a check, so the learner commits a number before the answer appears. The exploration mode then shows how deflection, natural frequency and isolation respond to each input, which confronts the three misconceptions with computed values.

Content:

Adjustable quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Total supported weight W 400 8000 100 2400 lb Number of isolators n 4 8 2 4 count Spring rate k (each) 100 3000 50 600 lb/in Fan speed 300 3600 10 1180 rpm

Displayed results: load per isolator (lb), static deflection (in, 2 decimals), natural frequency (Hz, 2 decimals), running frequency (Hz, 2 decimals), frequency ratio (2 decimals), transmissibility (3 decimals), isolation efficiency (%, 1 decimal), and a status line.

Challenge cases, in this order:

# W (lb) n k (lb/in) Model deflection (in) Feedback when wrong 1 2400 4 600 1.00 Divide the weight among the isolators first: 2,400 / 4 = 600 lb, then 600 / 600 = 1.00 in. 2 3600 6 300 2.00 Six isolators share 3,600 lb, so each carries 600 lb; 600 / 300 = 2.00 in. 3 1600 4 1600 0.25 Each isolator carries 400 lb; a stiff 1,600 lb/in spring compresses only 400 / 1,600 = 0.25 in.

All values are labeled "illustrative" on screen.

Provenance: Equations and the 1.41 threshold are standard vibration-isolation results stated in the chapter section "Spring Isolators". The typical deflections (under 1 in, 1 in, 2 in; higher by engineering review) are from FanPedia p. 134. Challenge values are illustrative.

Rules:

  • Load per isolator = W / n. Deflection δ = (W / n) / k.
  • f_n = 3.13 / √δ (Hz). Running frequency f = rpm / 60. Ratio r = f / f_n.
  • If r > 1.41: T = 1 / (r² − 1), efficiency = (1 − T) × 100%, status "Isolating".
  • If r <= 1.41 and r is not within ±0.02 of 1.00: T = 1 / |1 − r²|, efficiency is shown as "none", status "Amplifying: springs too stiff for this speed".
  • If |r − 1.00| <= 0.02: status "Resonance", T shown as "very large".
  • If δ > 2.00 in: add the note "Above the typical 2-inch deflection; higher deflection requires engineering review (FanPedia p. 134)."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 (W, n, k) and types a deflection.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the model deflection, the spring compressed to scale beside an uncompressed spring, and the derived natural frequency.
  3. After all three challenges, exploration unlocks with the default values. Changing any input updates every result at once.
  4. The learner should notice that raising n lowers deflection, that raising fan speed raises the ratio, and that a 0.25-in spring on a 300-rpm fan reaches the Amplifying status.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: δ = in." Hint after a first wrong attempt: "Not quite." plus the slip the typed value points to (the load per isolator typed as the deflection; the weight not shared among the isolators; the division flipped; multiplied instead of divided), or else "Find the load each isolator carries first, then divide it by the spring rate k." The hint states no load or deflection, and the loaded spring and readouts stay hidden. After the final attempt: the model value and the "Feedback when wrong" text with its calculation, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 with an empty answer box, an uncompressed spring drawing, and the question "How far will each spring compress?"

Chapter Anchors: Worked example: 2,400 lb on four isolators at 600 lb/in gives 600 lb each, 1.00 in deflection, 3.13 Hz natural frequency; 1,180 rpm is 19.67 Hz; ratio 6.28; transmissibility 0.026; efficiency about 97.4%. Isolation begins above a ratio of 1.41. Typical deflections under 1 in, 1 in or 2 in.

docs.title: Open, Housed, Restrained and Seismic Springs
docs.text:
FanPedia (pp. 134, 196) names four spring isolator types. They share the same coil spring; what differs is how much of the spring is enclosed and how much motion the enclosure allows.

An open spring isolator is the simplest spring mount: a bare coil between two load plates. It does not offer any restriction of the motion caused by aerodynamic forces, so a fan on open springs is free to shift when its airstream pushes on it. Twin City Fan typically does not use floor mounted open springs. Ceiling hung open springs are mounted in a formed metal surround, and the typical deflection is 1 inch.

A housed spring isolator works the same way as an open spring but sits inside an enclosed housing. The housing can hold one or more springs, depending on the load and application. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches.

A restrained spring isolator is the same design as an open spring with a housing or frame added to restrain the vertical and/or horizontal motion of the spring. The restraint matters when a fan must not drift, rock or lift as its load and aerodynamic forces change. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches.

A seismic spring isolator is similar to a restrained spring, except that the housing nearly surrounds the entire spring so that it can withstand the loads generated during a seismic event such as an earthquake. Typical deflection is 1 or 2 inches. Seismic springs are the isolator-level answer to the seismic restraint requirement introduced in Chapter 22.

The table below lines the four types up against each other.

Spring type Enclosure Limits motion? Typical deflection (FanPedia p. 134) Open None (ceiling hung: formed metal surround) No 1 in Housed Enclosed housing, one or more springs No more than an open spring 1 or 2 in Restrained Housing or frame Yes, vertical and/or horizontal 1 or 2 in Seismic Housing nearly surrounds the spring Yes, built for seismic loads 1 or 2 in

docs.title: Where the Isolators Go
docs.text:
The second half of an isolation specification says how the isolators meet the fan and the structure. FanPedia (p. 133) groups the choices into five mounting styles. Two of them describe which way the load hangs: from the floor up or from the structure down.

Floor mounted isolation places isolators beneath the fan or its base, bearing on the floor, a housekeeping pad or a support frame. It can use springs, rubber-in-shear (RIS) mounts or neoprene pads, and it includes three of the styles below: directly under the fan, isolation rails and mounting angles, plus the isolation base from Chapter 22. FanPedia p. 131 calls for spring or RIS isolators under an isolation base, and p. 133 also lists neoprene pads. Twin City Fan engineering confirms neoprene pads can be used under an isolation base, though it is uncommon; springs or RIS isolators are the usual choice. RIS mounts are themselves a pad-type isolator, and are most often used under isolation rails, with the fan sitting on the rails.

Ceiling hung isolation suspends the fan from an overhead structure, such as a ceiling or roof steel, with the isolators between that structure and the fan. FanPedia calls these isolation hangers, and they can be spring or RIS hangers. The threaded rod that carries them is supplied by others, and ceiling hung springs and RIS mounts sit in a formed metal surround.

Direct mounted isolators sit directly under the foundation holes in the fan's own structure, with no base between. They can be springs, RIS pads or neoprene pads. FanPedia limits this style, usually, to fans with impellers of 36.5 inches in diameter or less. The exception is swingout housed centrifugal fans of any impeller size, with flat pads only. Some arrangements cannot take isolators directly under the fan at all: Arrangement 3F is typically not suitable (p. 163), and Arrangement 9F is not suitable; FanPedia's remedy for 9F is an Arrangement 1 fan on a separate isolation base (p. 166).

Isolation rails put the isolators between two pieces of flat bar. The top bar bolts to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom bar attaches to the floor or other mounting structure. Springs or RIS pads can be used. Rails spread the fan's foundation pattern onto a pair of bars, which gives the isolators a clean place to sit.

An isolator mounting angle is a structural angle mounted between the fan and its isolators. It is usually used when the fan's inlet side has no structural support of its own for an isolator to bear on. Springs or RIS pads can be used.

The list below restates the choices as questions to ask when you read a drawing.

  • Does the fan hang from structure? Use isolation hangers (ceiling hung).
  • Does the fan structure have usable foundation holes and an impeller of 36.5 in or less? Isolators can mount directly under the fan.
  • Do the foundation holes need a continuous member to bolt to? Use isolation rails.
  • Is one side of the fan, usually the inlet side, without structural support? Add a mounting angle.
  • Must fan, motor and drive move together? Use an isolation base (Chapter 22).

Isolation Hardware Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch23-isolation-hardware-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eleven job-site descriptions by the isolation hardware FanPedia calls for, with at least 9 of 11 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: open, housed, restrained and seismic spring isolators; ceiling hung isolation; direct mounted isolators; isolation rails; isolator mounting angle; snubber; thrust restraint (all defined in the chapter above this block, the last two in "Snubbers and Thrust Restraints").

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 11 descriptions to one of 10 bins. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct bin column. Mastery is 9 of 11 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) A snubber and a seismic spring are the same device. (2) Any spring restrains a fan against airflow forces (open springs do not). (3) Every fan can sit on isolators bolted directly under it.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying realistic descriptions makes the learner map features (enclosure, direction of support, where brackets attach) onto hardware names, which is the Understand-level skill used when reading a specification.

Content:

Bins (10): Open spring isolator; Housed spring isolator; Restrained spring isolator; Seismic spring isolator; Snubber; Thrust restraint; Isolation hangers (ceiling hung); Isolators directly under fan; Isolation rails; Isolator mounting angle.

# Description shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The fan hangs from roof steel; the isolators go between the overhead structure and the fan on threaded rod by others. Isolation hangers (ceiling hung) A fan suspended from structure with isolators between structure and fan uses isolation hangers. 2 A horizontal-discharge fan on springs slides back at every start; the spec asks for two devices, 180° apart, tying the fan discharge to the discharge duct with threaded rod. Thrust restraint Thrust restraints are ceiling hung type isolators attached to fan discharge and duct, two per fan, 180° apart. 3 The inlet side of the fan has no structural member for an isolator to bear on. Isolator mounting angle A mounting angle is used when the fan inlet does not have a structural support. 4 Isolators sit between two flat bars; the top bar bolts to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom bar anchors to the floor. Isolation rails That is FanPedia's definition of isolation rails. 5 A fan with a 30-inch impeller (illustrative) gets springs bolted straight under the foundation holes in its own structure, with no base. Isolators directly under fan Direct mounting is usually limited to impellers of 36.5 in or less; 30 in qualifies. 6 A swingout housed centrifugal fan with a large impeller sits on flat pads bolted directly under its own structure. Isolators directly under fan Swingout housed centrifugal fans are the exception: any impeller size, flat pads only. 7 The spec calls for spring mounts whose housings nearly surround the entire spring so they withstand earthquake loads. Seismic spring isolator A housing that nearly surrounds the spring for seismic loads defines a seismic spring. 8 A separate device, one bracket on the base and one on the floor with elastomeric material between them, limits movement in any direction; it is used along with the isolators. Snubber A snubber works with isolators as a shock absorber; the elastomer prevents metal-to-metal contact. 9 Springs with a frame added to limit vertical and horizontal travel; no seismic requirement is stated. Restrained spring isolator A housing or frame that restrains vertical and/or horizontal motion defines a restrained spring. 10 A bare coil spring in a formed metal surround on a ceiling hung fan; it does nothing to resist aerodynamic forces. Open spring isolator Open springs offer no restriction of aerodynamic motion; ceiling hung types sit in a formed metal surround. 11 An enclosed housing holds two springs that act exactly like open springs. Housed spring isolator Housed springs work like open springs inside an enclosed housing that can hold one or more springs.

Provenance: FanPedia pp. 133–135 and 196–197 (all definitions, the 36.5-inch limit, the swingout exception, thrust restraint details). The 30-inch impeller in item 5 is illustrative and is labeled so on screen.

Rules: Each description has exactly one correct bin. Bins can receive more than one description (item 5 and item 6 share a bin). No partial credit.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one description and places it in a bin.
  2. The sim marks the placement correct or incorrect at once and shows the "Why" text.
  3. An incorrect placement returns the card for a second try; the first-attempt result is what counts toward mastery.
  4. After all 11, the sim shows the first-attempt score and lists the descriptions missed with their reasons.

Feedback: 11 items in shuffled order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. ." Hint after a first wrong attempt: "Not quite. Look for .", worded so it never names the correct bin; for items 5, 7, 9 and 11 the feature is "the impeller size limit for mounting with no base", "what the housing must withstand, and how much of the spring it surrounds", "what the added frame does to the spring's travel" and "how the springs behave, and what encloses them". After the final attempt: the card moves to its correct bin and the Why text is shown. Score shown: "First-attempt correct: n of 11; mastery at 9."

Starting State: Ten empty labeled bins and the first card face up, with the prompt "Which hardware does this job call for?"

docs.title: Snubbers and Thrust Restraints
docs.text:
Springs let a fan move. Two devices limit how far.

A snubber is a stop used together with the isolators on a fan or base. It serves as a shock absorber that prevents excessive movement of the fan or base in any direction, and it is often used when the fan must withstand seismic loading (FanPedia p. 135). A snubber is two brackets, one attached to the fan or base and one attached to the floor, with elastomeric (rubberized) material between them that prevents metal-to-metal contact. In normal running the fan floats on its springs; the snubber engages only when an unusual load, such as an earthquake, tries to move the fan too far.

A thrust restraint prevents excessive motion caused by aerodynamic force. Any fan that pushes air feels a reaction force, roughly its pressure rise times its outlet area, in the direction opposite the flow. For an illustrative outlet of 4 ft² at 4 in. wg, with 1 in. wg equal to 5.2 lb/ft², that is about \( 4 \times 5.2 \times 4 = 83 \) lb pushing the fan backward each time it starts. On stiff mounts the force is lost in friction; on soft springs the fan moves, and the flex connector takes the strain.

FanPedia (p. 197) describes the standard thrust restraint: ceiling hung type isolators (springs or spring/RIS pad combinations) attached to both the fan discharge and the discharge duct with threaded rod, adjusted to prevent horizontal motion. Two restraints are used per fan, mounted 180° apart, and FanPedia's drawing shows them for horizontal airflow in either direction.

Provenance: FanPedia page 135, "Vibration Isolation: Isolator Types, snubbers on an isolation base (left, with detail inset) and thrust restraints (right)", with the printed labels removed. Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 135.

Open Springs Do Not Hold a Fan in Place

A common trap is quoting open springs on a high-pressure fan and assuming the flex connector will keep it in place. Open springs offer no restriction of aerodynamic motion, so the fan shifts at every start and the connector tears over time. When pressure is high and discharge is horizontal, add thrust restraints or use restrained springs.

docs.title: Shaft and Coupling Alignment
docs.text:
A coupling connects the fan shaft to the motor shaft, or one fan shaft to another in a twin fan assembly (FanPedia p. 129). Shaft and coupling alignment is the process of positioning the motor and the fan bearings so that the two shaft centerlines run as one straight line through the coupling. Misalignment comes in two forms: offset, where the centerlines are parallel but displaced, and angular, where they meet at an angle. Either form loads the coupling and the bearings on every revolution and shows up as vibration at running speed or twice running speed.

FanPedia hardware exists to make alignment repeatable. Motor positioners, also called motor alignment jacking screws, move the motor in small steps (p. 148). Bearing dowel pins hold a bearing's position once it is aligned (p. 176). A machined pedestal top gives the bearings and motor a flat reference surface (p. 130). Inertia bases are used on longer direct drive fans because their mass and stiffness keep the motor, coupling, shaft and bearings aligned (p. 175).

Align Last, Then Check Again

Do the final alignment after the isolators are adjusted to their working deflection and the duct and flex connectors are attached. Then recheck it after the first run, because a base that settles on its springs can carry the motor out of line.

docs.title: Anti-Backspin Devices
docs.text:
An anti-backspin device, also called an anti-rotation device or anti-rotation clutch (FanPedia p. 125), prevents the rotor from freewheeling in reverse when the fan is not running (p. 162). It is a one-way clutch on the shaft: the fan turns freely in its correct rotation, and the device locks against rotation the other way.

Reverse freewheeling happens when air flows backward through an idle fan. The common causes are a second fan in parallel pushing air back through the stopped one, stack draft in a tall exhaust system, and wind on a roof or wall discharge. A fan spinning backward causes two problems. First, when its motor starts it must stop the rotor and then accelerate it the other way, which lengthens the high-current start and loads belts, couplings and shafts. Second, a rotor that can turn on its own is a hazard for anyone working on a fan that is supposed to be stopped. A zero speed switch, from Chapter 22, can report the motion; an anti-backspin device prevents it.

Where the device mounts depends on how the impeller is supported (p. 162):

  • Overhung impeller designs, where the impeller sits at the end of the shaft (Arrangements 1 and 9, for example): mounted between the bearings.
  • Center hung impeller designs, where the impeller sits between the bearings (Arrangement 3, for example): mounted on a shaft extension on the non-drive end.

Worked example. A plant runs two identical exhaust fans in parallel into one stack. Fan A is an Arrangement 9 SWSI belt drive; Fan B, the standby, is an Arrangement 3 SWSI belt drive. The operator wants to run one fan at a time.

  1. Is reverse flow possible? Yes. When Fan A runs, the shared stack connection is at a higher pressure than Fan B's inlet, so air flows backward through idle Fan B. The same happens to Fan A when Fan B runs.
  2. Which fans need the device? Both, because each will be the idle fan at some point.
  3. Fan A, Arrangement 9: the impeller is overhung, so the device mounts between the two bearings on the pedestal.
  4. Fan B, Arrangement 3: the impeller is center hung, so the shaft must have an extension on the non-drive end to carry the device. That extension is a shaft detail, so it belongs on the order, not as a field add-on.
  5. Line items: anti-backspin device on both fans, plus the non-drive-end shaft extension on Fan B. If the customer also wants a start interlock, add a zero speed switch.

docs.title: Measuring Airflow in the Field
docs.text:
Airflow measurement is the determination of the volume of air a fan actually delivers in its installed system, in cfm. A catalog rating describes the fan on a test stand; a field measurement tells the owner what the system is getting, which is how system effect and duct errors are found. A traditional method is a pitot tube traverse across a duct. The method FanPedia describes uses the fan itself.

The piezometer ring, introduced in Chapter 22, uses the fan's inlet funnel as a flow nozzle (FanPedia p. 158). A tap on the face of the funnel connects to the high-pressure side of a pressure-measuring device; tubing around the throat of the funnel, the ring, connects to the low-pressure side. The air speeds up as it enters the throat, so the throat pressure falls, and that pressure difference rises with the square of the airflow.

docs.title: Flow Through the Inlet Funnel
docs.text:
\[ Q = K \sqrt{\Delta p} \]

where:

  • \( Q \) is the airflow, in cfm
  • \( K \) is the flow coefficient for that fan's inlet funnel, supplied by the fan manufacturer, in cfm per \( \sqrt{\text{in. wg}} \)
  • \( \Delta p \) is the pressure difference between the funnel face tap and the throat ring, in in. wg

With an illustrative \( K = 10{,}000 \), a reading of 1.44 in. wg gives \( 10{,}000 \times 1.2 = 12{,}000 \) cfm. If the reading falls to 1.00 in. wg, the flow is 10,000 cfm: a 31% drop in the reading is only a 17% drop in airflow. Twin City Fan's installation manual IM-105 carries the detailed piezometer information for each fan type (p. 160).

A pressure transmitter is the device that turns that pressure difference into a signal a controls system can use, typically an electrical output for the building automation system, with or without a local display. FanPedia (p. 160) lists two optional versions a customer can buy from Twin City Fan: a pressure transmitter without display, and a pressure transmitter/transducer with display, shown in regular and NEMA 4 enclosures. Either can be mounted on the fan or remotely by others. Transmitters must be sized based on the application and fan performance: the transmitter's range has to cover the pressure difference the fan will produce at its highest expected airflow, without being so wide that normal readings sit at the bottom of the scale.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A spring isolator compresses under load; deflection = load per isolator divided by spring rate, and natural frequency = 3.13 / √deflection (Hz, inches). Isolation needs a running-to-natural frequency ratio above 1.41. Twin City Fan's typical deflections are under 1 in, 1 in and 2 in.
  • Open springs restrain nothing; housed springs enclose one or more springs; restrained springs add a housing or frame to limit vertical and/or horizontal motion; seismic springs have a housing that nearly surrounds the spring for earthquake loads.
  • Floor mounted isolation supports the fan from below; ceiling hung isolation suspends it on isolation hangers. Direct mounted isolators sit under the fan's foundation holes (usually impellers of 36.5 in or less; swingout housed centrifugal fans excepted with flat pads). Isolation rails and isolator mounting angles give isolators a place to bear.
  • Snubbers limit motion in any direction, often for seismic loading; thrust restraints are paired ceiling hung isolators, 180° apart, between fan discharge and duct that resist aerodynamic thrust.
  • Shaft and coupling alignment makes the motor and fan shaft centerlines one line; positioners, dowel pins, machined tops and inertia bases help hold it.
  • An anti-backspin device stops an idle fan from freewheeling in reverse: between the bearings on overhung designs, on a non-drive-end shaft extension on center hung designs.
  • Airflow measurement with a piezometer ring reads the pressure drop across the inlet funnel; airflow varies with its square root. A pressure transmitter, sized to the application, sends that reading to the controls.

Isolation Specified, Airflow Proven

You can now calculate spring deflection, name the right spring and mounting style for a job, explain why thrust restraints and anti-backspin devices go on the order, and describe how a piezometer ring proves installed airflow. That completes the path from a selected fan to a running, verified installation.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement
docs.text: Test your understanding of spring isolators, mounting styles, restraints, anti-backspin devices and field airflow measurement with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. According to FanPedia, what is the defining limitation of an open spring isolator?
docs.text:
1. It can only be used with deflections under 1 in.
  2. It offers no restriction of the motion caused by aerodynamic forces
  3. It must be filled with elastomer to prevent metal-to-metal contact
  4. It can only be installed on seismic projects
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An open spring isolator is a bare coil between two load plates. FanPedia states that it does not offer any restriction of the motion caused by aerodynamic forces, so a fan on open springs can shift when its airstream pushes on it. Twin City Fan typically does not use floor mounted open springs. Ceiling hung open springs have a typical deflection of 1 in. (A). Elastomer between brackets describes a snubber (C). Seismic duty calls for seismic springs (D).

Concept Tested: Open Spring Isolator

See: Open, Housed, Restrained and Seismic Springs

docs.title: 2. What distinguishes a seismic spring isolator from a restrained spring isolator?
docs.text:
1. It uses a rubber element loaded in shear instead of a coil spring
  2. It has no housing, so it can move freely during an earthquake
  3. It is always used with deflections greater than 2 in.
  4. Its housing nearly surrounds the entire spring so it can withstand seismic loads
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FanPedia describes the seismic spring as similar to a restrained spring, except that the housing nearly surrounds the entire spring so it can withstand the loads generated during a seismic event. Both types have typical deflections of 1 or 2 in., so option C is wrong. A rubber element in shear describes a rubber-in-shear isolator (A). An unhoused spring (B) is the open spring, which is the opposite of a seismic design.

Concept Tested: Seismic Spring Isolator

See: Open, Housed, Restrained and Seismic Springs

docs.title: 3. A fan, motor and isolation base weigh 3,200 lb and sit on four equally loaded spring isolators, each with a spring rate of 400 lb/in. What is the static deflection of each spring?
docs.text:
1. 0.5 in.
  2. 8.0 in.
  3. 2.0 in.
  4. 1.0 in.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Using \( \delta = (W/n)/k \), each isolator carries 3,200/4 = 800 lb, and 800/400 = 2.0 in. That is the high end of Twin City Fan's typical deflections. Option B divides the total weight by the spring rate without sharing it among the four isolators. Option A flips the division (400/800). Option D results from assuming each spring carries only 400 lb.

Concept Tested: Spring Isolator

See: Spring Isolators

docs.title: 4. Where does FanPedia mount an anti-backspin device on a center hung impeller design such as Arrangement 3?
docs.text:
1. On a shaft extension on the non-drive end
  2. Between the two bearings on the pedestal
  3. Inside the impeller hub
  4. On the motor shaft, inside the motor housing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. FanPedia ties the mounting location to how the impeller is supported. On overhung designs such as Arrangements 1 and 9, the device mounts between the bearings (B). On center hung designs such as Arrangement 3, the impeller sits between the bearings, so the device goes on a shaft extension on the non-drive end. That extension is a shaft detail that belongs on the order. FanPedia gives no hub or motor-shaft location (C, D).

Concept Tested: Anti-Backspin Device

See: Anti-Backspin Devices

docs.title: 5. A plant runs two identical exhaust fans in parallel into one stack but operates only one at a time. Which fans need an anti-backspin device?
docs.text:
1. Only the fan that runs most often
  2. Only the standby fan, because it is the only one that sits idle
  3. Neither fan, because a zero speed switch prevents reverse rotation
  4. Both fans, because each will be the idle fan at some point while air flows back through it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. When one fan runs, the shared stack connection is at a higher pressure than the idle fan's inlet, so air flows backward through the idle fan and can spin it in reverse. Each fan takes the idle role at some time, so both need the device. A zero speed switch can report the motion but does not prevent it (C). Options A and B overlook that the roles switch.

Concept Tested: Anti-Backspin Device

See: Anti-Backspin Devices

docs.title: 6. Which description matches FanPedia's standard thrust restraint?
docs.text:
1. A single snubber bolted between the fan base and the floor
  2. Two ceiling hung type isolators, 180° apart, connecting the fan discharge to the discharge duct with threaded rod
  3. A rigid steel strap that replaces the flex connector at the fan outlet
  4. A seismic spring placed under the fan's inlet side
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A thrust restraint prevents excessive motion caused by aerodynamic force. FanPedia's standard version uses ceiling hung type isolators, springs or spring/RIS combinations, attached to both the fan discharge and the discharge duct with threaded rod, adjusted to prevent horizontal motion. Two are used per fan, mounted 180° apart. A snubber (A) limits motion in any direction, and a rigid strap (C) would defeat isolation.

Concept Tested: Thrust Restraint

See: Snubbers and Thrust Restraints

docs.title: 7. A fan's inlet funnel has a flow coefficient \( K = 8{,}000 \) cfm per \( \sqrt{\text{in. wg}} \). The piezometer reading is 2.25 in. wg. Using \( Q = K\sqrt{\Delta p} \), what is the airflow?
docs.text:
1. 12,000 cfm
  2. 18,000 cfm
  3. 3,556 cfm
  4. 5,333 cfm
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. \( \sqrt{2.25} = 1.5 \), so \( Q = 8{,}000 \times 1.5 = 12{,}000 \) cfm. Option B multiplies K by the pressure difference directly instead of by its square root. Options C and D divide instead of multiply. The square-root relationship is why the chapter notes that a large drop in the reading corresponds to a much smaller drop in airflow.

Concept Tested: Airflow Measurement

See: Measuring Airflow in the Field

docs.title: 8. A piezometer ring reading falls to one-quarter of its commissioning value. Assuming the same flow coefficient, what has happened to the airflow?
docs.text:
1. It has fallen to one-quarter of the original value
  2. It has fallen to one-sixteenth of the original value
  3. It has fallen to one-half of the original value
  4. It is unchanged, because the ring measures pressure, not flow
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Airflow varies with the square root of the pressure difference, \( Q = K\sqrt{\Delta p} \). A reading at one-quarter gives \( \sqrt{1/4} = 1/2 \), so airflow is half the original. Option A assumes a linear relationship. Option B squares the ratio instead of taking its root. Option D ignores that the ring's pressure difference is used precisely because it changes with the square of airflow.

Concept Tested: Airflow Measurement

See: Measuring Airflow in the Field

docs.title: 9. What is a snubber, as FanPedia describes it?
docs.text:
1. Two brackets, one on the fan or base and one on the floor, with elastomeric material between them, used with the isolators to prevent excessive movement in any direction
  2. A spring isolator whose housing nearly surrounds the coil
  3. A one-way clutch that stops the shaft from turning backward
  4. A flat bar that bolts to the fan's foundation holes to carry isolators
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A snubber works alongside the isolators as a shock absorber that prevents excessive movement of the fan or base in any direction. It is often used when the fan must withstand seismic loading. Its elastomeric material prevents metal-to-metal contact, and in normal running the fan floats free of it. Option B is a seismic spring, option C is an anti-backspin device, and option D describes isolation rails.

Concept Tested: Snubber

See: Snubbers and Thrust Restraints

docs.title: 10. A housed (non-swingout) centrifugal fan has a 44 in. impeller, and the specification asks for springs bolted directly under the fan's foundation holes. What is the best assessment?
docs.text:
1. Acceptable, because direct mounting has no size limit when springs are used
  2. Acceptable, provided flat neoprene pads are used instead of springs
  3. Not usually acceptable, because direct mounting is generally limited to impellers of 36.5 in. or less; use another method such as an isolation base
  4. Not acceptable, because centrifugal fans can never be isolated
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. FanPedia usually limits isolators directly under the fan to impellers of 36.5 in. diameter or less. The exception is swingout housed centrifugal fans, which may be any size but only on flat pads. This fan is not a swingout, so option B misapplies the exception, and option A ignores the limit. Larger fans are isolated by other methods, such as rails, a mounting angle or an isolation base, so option D is wrong.

Concept Tested: Direct Mounted Isolators

See: Where the Isolators Go

docs.title: 11. When sizing a pressure transmitter for a piezometer ring, what does FanPedia's guidance require?
docs.text:
1. Always choose the widest available range to avoid over-ranging
  2. Always choose a NEMA 4 enclosure with a display
  3. Mount it remotely, never on the fan
  4. Size it based on the application and fan performance, so its range covers the highest expected pressure difference without leaving normal readings at the bottom of the scale
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FanPedia states that transmitters must be sized based on the application and fan performance. The range must cover the pressure difference at the highest expected airflow, yet not be so wide that normal readings sit at the bottom of the scale, which option A would cause. FanPedia offers versions with and without a display in regular and NEMA 4 enclosures (B). They can be mounted on the fan or remotely (C).

Concept Tested: Pressure Transmitter

See: Measuring Airflow in the Field

docs.title: References: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement
docs.text:
1. Shaft alignment - Wikipedia - Explains offset and angular misalignment between coupled shafts and the methods used to correct them. It supports the chapter's section on shaft and coupling alignment.

  2. Freewheel - Wikipedia - Describes one-way clutch mechanisms that turn freely in one direction and lock in the other. It explains the principle behind the anti-backspin devices that stop idle fans from turning in reverse.

  3. Flow measurement - Wikipedia - Surveys flow measurement methods, including differential-pressure devices such as nozzles and venturis. It is background for the chapter's piezometer ring and the square-root relationship \( Q = K\sqrt{\Delta p} \).

  4. Mechanical Vibrations - Singiresu S. Rao - Pearson - Rao's worked examples on static deflection, natural frequency and transmissibility of spring-mounted machines are widely used in engineering courses. They match the step-by-step spring calculation in this chapter.

  5. Flow Measurement Engineering Handbook (3rd edition) - Richard W. Miller - McGraw-Hill - Miller's handbook is known for its detailed treatment of differential-pressure flowmeters and their coefficients. It is the theory behind using a fan's inlet funnel as a flow nozzle.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - The source for spring isolator types and mounting styles (pp. 133-135), piezometer rings and transmitters (pp. 158-160), and anti-backspin devices and thrust restraints (pp. 162-197).

  7. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan - The web edition of FanPedia, covering the same isolation and accessory topics. Use it with the current catalogs, which take priority when they differ from FanPedia.

  8. Vibration Isolation of Fans (FE-1900) - Twin City Fan Fan Engineering Letter - Gives the deflection, natural frequency and transmissibility relationships for fan isolators in chart form. It also discusses spring constants, structure stiffness and inertia bases.

  9. Piezometer Airflow Measurement System (IM-105) - Twin City Fan - The installation, operation and maintenance manual FanPedia cites for piezometer details. It covers installing and using the airflow measuring system described in this chapter.

  10. Field Testing of Fans (FE-900) - Twin City Fan Fan Engineering Letter - Describes field fan tests, including system evaluations, acceptance tests and pitot tube traverses. It is the traditional alternative to the piezometer method for verifying installed airflow.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter returns to fan arrangements with the variants that build on motors, bases, and installation: Arrangements 8, 9, and 10; plug arrangements 1P, 4P, 8P, and 9P; plenum arrangements 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VA, 3VS, and 4V; Arrangements 3F, 9F, 9H, and 9ST/9SS; vertical and horizontal inline variants; and swingout and clamshell fans and their door assemblies. It closes with motor positions L and R, the standard and swingout motor position rules, inline motor positions A to H, and ventilating sets. After completing it, readers can identify any arrangement code in a FanPedia or catalog drawing.
