Base operating point: 10,000 CFM, 4.0 in. wg, 9.0 BHP, 70% static efficiency, on the system curve P = 4.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)².

Adjustable ratios:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Speed ratio N2/N1 0.50 1.50 0.01 1.00 ratio Diameter ratio D2/D1 0.80 1.25 0.01 1.00 ratio Density ratio ρ2/ρ1 0.40 1.30 0.01 1.00 ratio

Readouts: new speed (RPM, whole number), new airflow (CFM, nearest 10), new static pressure (in. wg, two decimals), new BHP (two decimals), static efficiency (%, one decimal). The base curve and the new curve are both drawn, with the operating point on each.

Challenges, in this order:

# Question shown Model answer Feedback when wrong 1 The same system needs 11,500 CFM. What speed (RPM)? 1,587 Airflow goes with speed: 1,380 × 11,500 ÷ 10,000 = 1,587 RPM. 2 At 1,587 RPM, what BHP? 13.69 Power goes with speed cubed: 9.0 × 1.15³ = 13.69 BHP, not 9.0 × 1.15. 3 The fan is slowed to 1,104 RPM. What static pressure (in. wg)? 2.56 Pressure goes with speed squared: 4.0 × 0.8² = 2.56 in. wg. 4 The next size up has a diameter ratio of 1.12 and runs at 1,380 RPM. What BHP at the corresponding point? 15.86 Power goes with diameter to the fifth power: 9.0 × 1.12⁵ = 9.0 × 1.762 = 15.86 BHP.

Provenance: Curve A is the illustrative curve from Chapter 10, "The Fan Curve" section, and the sim labels it "illustrative." Model answers are computed from the Rules. The fan laws are standard fan engineering relations.

Rules: Q2 = Q1 × (N2/N1) × (D2/D1)³. P2 = P1 × (N2/N1)² × (D2/D1)² × (ρ2/ρ1). BHP2 = BHP1 × (N2/N1)³ × (D2/D1)⁵ × (ρ2/ρ1). Each point of Curve A is mapped by these rules to draw the new curve; static efficiency at mapped points is unchanged. New speed = 1,380 × speed ratio. Model answers are rounded to whole RPM and two decimals for pressure and BHP. A density ratio changes pressure and BHP but never CFM, and the sim says so the first time the density ratio is changed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types a number. The ratio controls are locked during challenges.
  2. On Check, the sim sets the matching ratio, redraws the new curve and operating point, and shows the model value beside the learner's answer.
  3. Challenges 2 to 4 repeat steps 1 and 2.
  4. After challenge 4, exploration unlocks. The learner changes any ratio and the new curve and readouts update at once. With only the speed ratio changed, the learner should notice that the operating point moves along the system curve and the efficiency readout stays at 70.0%.

Feedback: Four challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: ." Hint after a first wrong attempt: "Not quite." plus the slip the typed value points to (the scaling factor typed instead of the scaled value; the ratio raised to the wrong power, followed by the law: speed with airflow, power with speed cubed, pressure with speed squared, power with diameter to the fifth; the ratio upside down), or else the step for that challenge (which law, which ratio, which starting value) with no worked numbers. The new curve and the model value stay hidden. After the final attempt: the model answer and the "Feedback when wrong" text, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 4" is shown.

Starting State: Curve A at 1,380 RPM with the operating point at 10,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg; challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box. The question on screen is "The same system needs 11,500 CFM. What speed?"

Chapter Anchors: Curve A: 10,000 CFM, 4.0 in. wg, 9.0 BHP at 1,380 RPM, 70% static efficiency. Speed-up to 11,500 CFM: 1,587 RPM, 5.29 in. wg, 13.69 BHP. Diameter ratio 1.12: airflow × 1.405, pressure × 1.254, power × 1.762. Power at 80% speed is 0.512 of the original.

docs.title: Cold Start Horsepower
docs.text:
The density term in the fan laws matters most for hot fans. Cold start horsepower is the brake horsepower a fan selected for hot air absorbs when it starts and runs on cold, denser air before the airstream reaches its operating temperature. At the same speed the fan moves the same CFM, but BHP rises in proportion to density. Chapter 10's oven exhaust fan absorbs 3.7 BHP on 200°F air; on 70°F air at start-up it absorbs the full standard-air value of 4.6 BHP, about 24% more, and on 0°F air it would absorb \( 4.6 \times 1.152 = 5.3 \) BHP. For high-temperature fans the gap is larger: a fan running on 600°F air has a temperature factor of 0.500, so its cold start horsepower is twice its running horsepower. The motor must be sized for the cold start condition, or the start-up must be managed with a damper, inlet vanes or speed control, a choice developed in Chapter 27.

Sanity-Check Any Fan-Law Answer With the Exponents

Here's a quick self-check: for a speed change, the pressure ratio must equal the airflow ratio squared and the power ratio must equal the airflow ratio cubed. If 15% more air came out with less than 50% more power, an exponent is wrong somewhere.

docs.title: Specific Speed
docs.text: Specific speed is a single number that characterizes a fan design by combining its speed, airflow and pressure at the point of rating, usually the peak efficiency point.

docs.title: Specific Speed
docs.text:
\[ N_s = \frac{N \sqrt{Q}}{P^{3/4}} \]

where:

  • \( N_s \) is specific speed (in the units used; not dimensionless as written)
  • \( N \) is speed in RPM, \( Q \) is airflow in CFM and \( P \) is pressure in in. wg

Because the fan laws leave it unchanged when speed or size changes, specific speed belongs to the design, not to one fan. Curve A at its rated point gives \( 1{,}380 \times \sqrt{10{,}000} / 4.0^{0.75} \approx 48{,}800 \). Low specific speeds suit high-pressure, low-flow duties, the territory of radial and narrow centrifugal impellers; high specific speeds suit high-flow, low-pressure duties, the territory of axial fans. Values compare only when computed in the same units and pressure basis.

docs.title: Where to Select: Duty Point and Fan Energy Index
Duty Point
docs.text: The duty point is the airflow and pressure, at a stated air density, that a specification requires the fan to deliver: for example, "10,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg fan static pressure, standard air." It is the customer's target. The operating point from Chapter 10 is what actually happens where the fan and system curves cross, and the selection point is the catalog speed and BHP at which the fan meets the duty. On a good job all three coincide. When they do not, the gap usually traces to a missing density correction, a system resistance estimated wrong, or system effect, which this chapter covers next. The duty point is also where efficiency requirements are judged.

docs.title: Worked Example: Restoring the Duty Point After System Effect
docs.text:
Chapter 10 left Curve A short of air: an elbow on its inlet added an illustrative 0.5 in. wg of system effect at 10,000 CFM, so the effective system curve passes through 4.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM, and the fan at 1,380 RPM settles at about 9,560 CFM and 4.11 in. wg, absorbing about 8.80 BHP. The duty point is still 10,000 CFM. The fan laws find the fix.

  1. Speed ratio. Airflow goes with speed: \( 10{,}000 / 9{,}560 = 1.046 \).
  2. New speed. \( 1{,}380 \times 1.046 = 1{,}444 \) RPM.
  3. Pressure check. \( 4.11 \times 1.046^2 = 4.50 \) in. wg, matching the effective system curve at 10,000 CFM.
  4. Power. \( 8.80 \times 1.046^3 = 10.08 \) BHP.
  5. Motor. 10.08 BHP is above a 10 hp nameplate. Service factor is margin, not capacity (Chapter 14), so the motor goes to 15 hp, or the elbow is replaced with an inlet box or straight duct and the original 1,380 RPM and 10 hp stand.

The 9,560 CFM point sits at about 70% efficiency on Curve A, so the speeded-up fan still operates at peak efficiency. The cost of the elbow is about 1.1 BHP, around 12% more power, every hour the fan runs.

docs.title: Fan Energy Index
docs.text: Efficiency at the duty point is now regulated. The Fan Energy Index (FEI) is the ratio of the electrical input power of a reference fan to the electrical input power of the actual fan, both delivering the same airflow and pressure. It is defined in AMCA Standard 208. The reference fan's power comes from a formula based only on the duty's airflow and pressure, so it is the same for every manufacturer.

docs.title: Fan Energy Index
docs.text:
\[ FEI = \frac{FEP_{ref}}{FEP_{act}} \]

where:

  • \( FEP_{ref} \) is the fan electrical input power of the reference fan at the duty point, in kW
  • \( FEP_{act} \) is the fan electrical input power of the actual fan at the same duty point, in kW, including motor, drive and any speed-control losses

An FEI of 1.00 means the fan uses exactly the reference power; above 1.00 it uses less, below 1.00 it uses more. Because FEI is calculated at a duty point, one fan model has a different FEI at every point on its curve. Energy codes and standards, including ASHRAE Standard 90.1 and several state regulations, set minimum FEI values at the design point, so FEI is now part of many specifications. The older Fan Efficiency Grade, which rated a fan by its peak efficiency alone, is covered in Chapter 27.

docs.title: Worked Example: Same Fan, Two Duty Points
docs.text:
Curve A is driven by a belt with 97% efficiency and a motor with 93% efficiency (illustrative). The reference powers below are illustrative values of the kind selection software reports from the AMCA 208 formula.

Step Duty 1: 10,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg Duty 2: 14,000 CFM at 2.0 in. wg BHP from Curve A 9.0 9.4 Shaft power, kW (× 0.746) 6.71 7.01 Actual electrical input, kW (÷ 0.97 ÷ 0.93) 7.44 7.77 Reference electrical input, kW (illustrative) 9.0 6.8 FEI 9.0 ÷ 7.44 = 1.21 6.8 ÷ 7.77 = 0.88

At Duty 1, near peak efficiency, the fan passes a 1.00 minimum with room to spare. At Duty 2, the same fan at the same speed sits far right on its curve at 47% static efficiency and fails. Nothing about the fan changed; its position on the curve did. A selection that fails FEI is usually fixed by choosing a different size so the duty lands closer to peak efficiency.

docs.title: System Effect in Detail
docs.text: Chapter 10 introduced system effect as the loss of fan performance caused by the way a fan is connected to its system, and its values come from AMCA Publication 201, Fans and Systems. This section separates the inlet and outlet cases and adds the vocabulary AMCA uses to rate and correct for them.

docs.title: AMCA Installation Type
docs.text:
A fan's catalog rating depends on whether ducts were connected to its inlet and outlet during the test, because a duct changes how air approaches and leaves the impeller. The AMCA 210 test standard therefore defines four AMCA installation types, by whether each side of the fan is free (open to the surroundings) or ducted:

  • Type A: free inlet, free outlet
  • Type B: free inlet, ducted outlet
  • Type C: ducted inlet, free outlet
  • Type D: ducted inlet, ducted outlet

A certified catalog rating states which installation type it applies to. Applying a rating made for one type to a job installed as another is a common source of field shortfall: a fan rated with a ducted outlet but installed discharging straight into a plenum loses the benefit of the outlet duct, and that loss is an outlet system effect. The installation type is part of the duty statement, just as density is.

docs.title: Worked Example: Classify the Job, Then Check the Rating
docs.text:
An outside sales engineer is quoting four fans on one project and must confirm each rating basis:

  1. A plug (plenum) fan in an air handler cabinet. It draws from the open cabinet and discharges into the cabinet: free inlet, free outlet, Type A.
  2. A centrifugal fan with an open inlet funnel in an equipment room, discharging into a supply duct. Free inlet, ducted outlet, Type B.
  3. A roof upblast exhaust fan connected to a kitchen exhaust duct from below, discharging to atmosphere. Ducted inlet, free outlet, Type C.
  4. An inline fan in the middle of a duct run. Ducted on both sides, Type D.

For each, the engineer compares the job's type with the type printed on the catalog rating. Where they match, the rating applies as published. Where they differ, the engineer either asks for a selection at the job's installation type or adds the appropriate system effect from AMCA 201 to the design pressure before selecting. A fan in the field never knows which page of the catalog it was selected from; it only knows how it was installed.

Use the sorter below to practice the classification on eight installations.

docs.title: Diagram: AMCA Installation Type Sorter
docs.text:
Run AMCA Installation Type Sorter Fullscreen

AMCA Installation Type Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: ch25-amca-installation-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify fan installations into AMCA installation types A, B, C and D from a description of what is connected to the fan's inlet and outlet, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: AMCA installation type, free inlet, ducted inlet, free outlet, ducted outlet, system effect (defined in "AMCA Installation Type" above and in Chapter 10).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 8 descriptions to one of four bins (Type A, Type B, Type C, Type D) and commits each assignment. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct type column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the type definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The installation type depends on the fan type rather than on the connections. (2) A short connection to a plenum or cabinet counts as a ducted side. (3) Exhaust fans are always Type C.

Instructional Rationale: Classification is an Understand-level task; asking the learner to state, for each description, which side is ducted before seeing the answer makes them apply the two-question rule rather than match fan names to letters.

Content:

Bin definitions, shown at all times: Type A, free inlet and free outlet. Type B, free inlet and ducted outlet. Type C, ducted inlet and free outlet. Type D, ducted inlet and ducted outlet.

# Description shown to the learner Correct type Why (shown as feedback) 1 A plug fan inside an air handler cabinet, drawing from the cabinet and discharging into it A Neither side has a duct; the cabinet is open space around the fan. 2 A propeller wall fan drawing from a warehouse and discharging outdoors, with no ductwork A Both the inlet and the outlet are open to their surroundings. 3 A utility set with an open inlet in an equipment room and a supply duct bolted to its outlet B The inlet is free and the outlet is ducted. 4 A pressure blower with an open inlet funnel in a work area, discharging into a process duct B An open funnel is a free inlet; the process duct makes the outlet ducted. 5 A roof upblast exhaust fan fed by a kitchen exhaust duct from below, discharging to atmosphere C The inlet is ducted and the discharge is open to the air. 6 A centrifugal fan drawing through a duct from a process hood and discharging directly outdoors with no outlet duct C Ducted inlet, free outlet, whatever the fan type. 7 An inline fan installed in the middle of a duct run D Both sides are connected to ductwork. 8 A centrifugal fan with an inlet duct from a dust collector and an outlet duct to a stack D Both sides are ducted.

Provenance: Type definitions follow the four installation types of the AMCA 210 test standard (standard engineering knowledge). The descriptions are illustrative installations written for this chapter, built from fan types described in Chapters 5, 6 and 18; the sim labels them "illustrative."

Rules: Two questions decide the type: is the inlet ducted, and is the outlet ducted? No/No is A, No/Yes is B, Yes/No is C, Yes/Yes is D. A cabinet, plenum or room is open space, not a duct.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads description 1 and predicts, by choosing Yes or No, whether the inlet is ducted and whether the outlet is ducted.
  2. The learner places the description in one of the four bins and commits it.
  3. The sim marks the answer correct or incorrect and shows the Why text; the next description appears.
  4. After all 8, the sim shows the four bins with their correct contents and the learner's score.

Feedback: 8 descriptions, shuffled order, one committed answer each counted for the score; after an incorrect answer the learner may move the item once more, but only the first answer counts. Correct: "Correct: Type . ." Incorrect: "Not quite. " followed by the correct letter. A running count "Correct on first try: n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Four empty bins with their definitions and the first description shown, with the question "Is each side of this fan free or ducted?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example classifies a plug fan in an air handler as Type A, a centrifugal fan with an open inlet funnel and a supply duct as Type B, a roof upblast exhaust fan on a kitchen duct as Type C, and an inline fan as Type D. The sorter has 8 items; mastery is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Inlet System Effect
docs.text: Inlet system effect is the loss of fan performance caused by conditions at the fan inlet that keep air from entering the impeller smoothly and evenly. The impeller is designed for air arriving straight and uniform; anything else makes some blades work harder than others. The common causes are an elbow bolted directly to the inlet, which crowds air to one side; a plenum wall or obstruction too close to an open inlet; and swirl, or prerotation, in the incoming air. Swirl in the direction of impeller rotation reduces airflow and pressure much as an inlet vane does; swirl against rotation raises power. Inlet losses are usually larger than outlet losses for the same fault. FanPedia's answer to the elbow case is the inlet box, which "is designed to minimize the system effect of a 90 degree turn into the fan" (FanPedia p. 187).

docs.title: Effective Duct Length
docs.text: Air leaves a centrifugal fan outlet with a lopsided velocity profile, fastest along the outer wall of the scroll. It needs a length of straight duct to even out. Effective duct length is the length of straight outlet duct needed for that profile to become uniform, which AMCA 201 defines from the outlet velocity and the duct's equivalent diameter.

docs.title: Effective Duct Length
docs.text:
\[ L_e = D_e \left( 2.5 + \frac{V - 2{,}500}{1{,}000} \right) \text{ for } V > 2{,}500 \text{ fpm}, \qquad L_e = 2.5\,D_e \text{ for } V \le 2{,}500 \text{ fpm} \]

where:

  • \( L_e \) is the effective duct length (100% recovery), in the units of \( D_e \)
  • \( D_e \) is the equivalent duct diameter, \( \sqrt{4ab/\pi} \) for a rectangular outlet of sides \( a \) and \( b \)
  • \( V \) is the outlet velocity in fpm

For a 24 × 30 in. outlet at 3,500 fpm, \( D_e = \sqrt{4 \times 24 \times 30 / \pi} = 30.3 \) in., and \( L_e = 3.5 \times 30.3 = 106 \) in., about 8.8 ft of straight duct before the first elbow.

docs.title: Outlet System Effect
docs.text: Outlet system effect is the loss of fan performance caused by the outlet connection: no outlet duct, an outlet duct shorter than the effective duct length, an elbow or damper too close to the outlet, or an abrupt expansion. Its size depends on how much of the effective duct length is present and on the outlet velocity, so a high-velocity fan with an elbow right at the outlet pays the most. An elbow placed after a full effective duct length adds only its ordinary duct loss; the same elbow bolted to the outlet adds a system effect on top. Where the outlet orientation forces a turn, choosing the discharge position so the elbow turns in the same direction as the scroll (Chapter 12) reduces the loss.

docs.title: System Effect Curve
docs.text:
A system effect curve is a chart in AMCA 201 that gives system effect, in in. wg, against the velocity at the fan inlet or outlet. AMCA 201 presents a family of these curves, identified by letter, and tables that assign a curve to each connection: a given elbow at a given distance from the inlet, an outlet duct of a given fraction of the effective duct length, and so on. Because system effect is a velocity pressure loss, each curve rises with velocity squared. The procedure is to identify each faulty connection, look up its curve, read the system effect at the job's velocity, and add the result to the design pressure, as in the worked example above. Adding system effect to the designer's system curve produces the effective system curve the fan actually works against.

System Effect Takes a Second Pass

If the inlet cases, outlet cases, effective duct length and lettered curves feel like a lot, that's normal; most people need to work one real job before the tables make sense. Start with the two questions you already know, "What is on the inlet?" and "What is on the outlet?", and look up only what is actually there.

docs.title: Controlling Flow Efficiently
docs.text:
Flow control efficiency describes how much of the possible power saving a flow-control method delivers when airflow is reduced. Chapter 18 compared the three methods at 70% airflow with illustrative values: an outlet damper needs about 86% of design power, variable inlet vanes about 67% and speed control about 34%. The damper is least efficient because it throws away pressure the fan has already made; FanPedia notes that outlet damper horsepower savings are "usually much less than other methods" (FanPedia p. 182).

The 34% figure is the ideal cube law, and it holds only when the system curve passes through zero. Many systems have a fixed pressure component: a VAV system holding duct static pressure for its terminal units, or a process that must overcome a fixed back-pressure. Suppose 1.5 in. wg of a 4.0 in. wg design must be held at every flow. At 70% airflow the system needs \( 1.5 + 2.5 \times 0.7^2 = 2.73 \) in. wg, not \( 4.0 \times 0.7^2 = 1.96 \) in. wg, so air power falls to \( 0.7 \times 2.73 / 4.0 = 48\% \) of design rather than 34%. Speed control still wins, but by less, and the fan's efficiency shifts as the slowed curve crosses the system curve at a new relative position. Drive and motor losses at low load reduce the saving further.

docs.title: Fans in Parallel and in Series
docs.text:
Two fans can be combined to serve one system, and the combination is predicted by adding their curves, not their ratings.

Fans in parallel draw from and discharge into a common system side by side. At any pressure, their airflows add: the combined curve is found by doubling the airflow of each point of a single fan's curve. Parallel fans give redundancy and staging, and they add the most air when the system is flat (low resistance). On a steep system the second fan adds little, because more airflow costs a great deal more pressure. Parallel fans must each operate right of the peak pressure point, or one fan can take most of the flow while the other stalls, a form of the surge problem described above, and each needs a backdraft damper if it may run alone.

Fans in series move the same air one after the other, outlet of one to inlet of the next. At any airflow, their pressures add: the combined curve is found by doubling the pressure of each point of a single fan's curve. Series fans suit steep, high-resistance systems. A multi-stage blower is a series arrangement inside one housing.

The table below shows Curve A combined two ways on two illustrative systems: the steep design system from Chapter 10 (4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM) and a flat system needing only 1.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM.

System One fan Two in parallel Two in series Steep (4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM) 10,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg about 11,000 CFM at 4.8 in. wg about 12,300 CFM at 6.0 in. wg Flat (1.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM) about 14,000 CFM at 2.0 in. wg 20,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg about 15,100 CFM at 2.3 in. wg

On the steep system a second fan in parallel adds only about 10% more air. On the flat system it adds over 40%. The explorer below lets you predict each case before the curves are drawn.

Two Fans Never Simply Double the Air

Think of the system curve as a referee. Parallel fans double the airflow at each pressure, series fans double the pressure at each airflow, but the operating point still has to land on the system curve. Which combination wins depends on how steep that curve is, not on the fans.

docs.title: Diagram: Fans in Parallel and Series Explorer
docs.text:
Run Fans in Parallel and Series Explorer Fullscreen

Fans in Parallel and Series Explorer

Type: chart sim-id: ch25-parallel-series-explorer Library: Plotly Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare one fan, two fans in parallel and two fans in series on a steep and a flat system curve, correctly predicting which combination delivers more airflow on each system.

Prerequisites: fan curve, system curve, operating point, fans in parallel, fans in series, peak pressure point, stall region (defined in "Fans in Parallel and in Series" above and in Chapter 10).

Evidence of Mastery: Three predictions committed before the curves are drawn: (1) on the steep system, parallel or series gives more airflow; (2) on the flat system, parallel or series gives more airflow; (3) on the steep system, the airflow gain from adding a second fan in parallel is about 10%, about 50% or about 100%. Each is correct when it matches the Content. Mastery is 3 of 3. Switching configurations and hovering curves after the predictions is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Two fans in parallel deliver twice the airflow. (2) Series fans are only useful for pressure and never increase airflow. (3) The better combination is a property of the fans rather than of the system.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level comparison needs the learner to relate the combined curves to the system curve's shape. Committing predictions before the reveal exposes misconception 1, and toggling between the two systems makes the dependence on system steepness visible.

Content:

Single-fan curve (Curve A, illustrative, 1,380 RPM, standard air):

Airflow (CFM) 0 2,000 4,000 6,000 8,000 10,000 12,000 14,000 16,000 Static pressure (in. wg) 4.6 4.8 4.9 4.8 4.5 4.0 3.2 2.0 0.4

Systems: Steep, P = 4.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)². Flat, P = 1.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)².

Operating points (shown after the predictions):

System One fan Two in parallel Two in series Steep 10,000 CFM at 4.00 in. wg 10,980 CFM at 4.83 in. wg 12,300 CFM at 6.05 in. wg Flat 14,040 CFM at 1.97 in. wg 20,000 CFM at 4.00 in. wg 15,080 CFM at 2.27 in. wg

Prediction answers: (1) Steep: series, 12,300 vs. 10,980 CFM. (2) Flat: parallel, 20,000 vs. 15,080 CFM. (3) About 10% (10,980 vs. 10,000 CFM).

Provenance: Curve A is the illustrative curve from Chapter 10, "The Fan Curve" section. Operating points are computed from the Rules and rounded to the nearest 10 CFM and 0.01 in. wg. The sim labels all curves "illustrative."

Rules: Single-fan pressure between table points is linearly interpolated; beyond 16,000 CFM it is extended along the 14,000 to 16,000 CFM segment to zero. Parallel curve: pressure at total airflow Q equals single-fan pressure at Q ÷ 2. Series curve: pressure at Q equals 2 × single-fan pressure at Q. The operating point is the airflow, searched in 1 CFM steps, where |combined pressure − system pressure| is smallest, using only the part of each curve where each fan's own airflow is >= 4,000 CFM (right of the peak pressure point). The portion of each combined curve where each fan's airflow is < 4,000 CFM is drawn and marked "stall region."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the steep system curve and the single-fan curve and commits prediction 1.
  2. The learner switches to the flat system and commits prediction 2.
  3. The learner commits prediction 3 for the steep system.
  4. All combined curves and operating points are revealed with the readout table. The learner can now switch system (steep, flat) and configuration (one fan, parallel, series) in any combination; the operating point and readout update at once. The learner should notice that the configuration that wins on one system loses on the other.

Feedback: Three predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct." followed by the operating points that prove it. Incorrect for (1): "On a steep system, more airflow costs much more pressure, so the pressure-adding series pair wins: 12,300 vs. 10,980 CFM." Incorrect for (2): "On a flat system, little extra pressure is needed, so the airflow-adding parallel pair wins: 20,000 vs. 15,080 CFM." Incorrect for (3): "Parallel fans double airflow only at the same pressure; on a steep system the operating point climbs the system curve, so the gain is about 10%." Score "Predictions correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The steep system curve and the single-fan curve with its operating point at 10,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg. The question is "Add a second fan: in parallel or in series for more air?"

Chapter Anchors: Steep system: one fan 10,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg; parallel about 11,000 CFM at 4.8 in. wg; series about 12,300 CFM at 6.0 in. wg. Flat system: one fan about 14,000 CFM at 2.0 in. wg; parallel 20,000 CFM at 4.0 in. wg; series about 15,100 CFM at 2.3 in. wg. A second parallel fan adds about 10% on the steep system and over 40% on the flat one.

docs.title: Sound Pressure and Octave Bands
docs.text: Chapter 10 described fan sound by its sound power level, the total acoustic power a fan radiates, independent of where it is installed. A listener, a microphone or a property-line noise ordinance does not hear sound power. They respond to sound pressure.

docs.title: Sound Pressure Level
docs.text: Sound pressure level (Lp) is the magnitude of the pressure fluctuations of sound at one location, expressed in decibels relative to a reference pressure of 20 micropascals, roughly the threshold of human hearing.

docs.title: Sound Pressure Level
docs.text:
\[ L_p = 20 \log_{10} \left( \frac{p}{20 \times 10^{-6}} \right) \]

where:

  • \( L_p \) is the sound pressure level in dB
  • \( p \) is the root-mean-square sound pressure in pascals

Unlike sound power, sound pressure depends on the surroundings: the distance from the fan, the size and hardness of the room, and reflections from nearby surfaces. Outdoors, away from reflecting surfaces, sound pressure level falls about 6 dB each time the distance from the source doubles. A sound pressure figure is therefore meaningless without its distance and setting. Manufacturers publish sound power because it belongs to the fan; acoustical consultants convert it to sound pressure at the listener's location for the actual room or site.

Ask Three Questions About Any Noise Limit

Want to save yourself an hour of rework? When a specification says "85 dB," ask: sound power or sound pressure, at what distance and in what setting, and overall or by octave band. The answers decide whether the catalog data can show compliance at all.

docs.title: Octave Band
docs.text:
Fan sound is not one tone but a spread of frequencies, and its effect depends on where the energy falls: low-frequency rumble passes through walls and silencers more easily, while the ear is most sensitive in the middle range. An octave band is a range of frequencies whose upper limit is twice its lower limit, identified by its center frequency. Fan sound data is published in eight octave bands:

Band Center frequency (Hz) Approximate range (Hz) 1 63 44 to 88 2 125 88 to 177 3 250 177 to 354 4 500 354 to 707 5 1,000 707 to 1,414 6 2,000 1,414 to 2,828 7 4,000 2,828 to 5,657 8 8,000 5,657 to 11,314

Chapter 10's 10-blade impeller at 1,770 RPM has a blade pass frequency of 295 Hz, which falls in the 250 Hz band, so that band will usually stand out in the fan's data. Octave band data lets an acoustical engineer choose a silencer that attacks the right frequencies; a single overall number, such as an A-weighted level that discounts low frequencies to match the ear, cannot. Reading octave band sound data in a submittal is part of Chapter 27.

You Can Predict a Fan's Next Move

You can now take one fan curve and predict what happens when the speed, size or air density changes, find the speed that restores a duty point lost to system effect, and judge a selection by its efficiency and FEI. That is the core of every "what if?" call an application engineer takes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Landmarks: shutoff pressure is the pressure at zero airflow, free delivery the airflow at zero static pressure, and the peak pressure point the top of the pressure curve. Select right of the peak; left of it the fan can stall and surge.
  • Fan power equation: \( BHP = Q \times P / (6356 \times \eta) \). Static efficiency uses fan static pressure; compare candidate fans only on the same pressure basis.
  • The efficiency curve is zero at shutoff and free delivery and peaks in between. Selections near peak efficiency use less power and make less noise.
  • Fan laws: airflow varies with speed, pressure with speed squared, power with speed cubed. Airflow varies with diameter cubed, pressure with diameter squared and power with diameter to the fifth. Pressure and power vary directly with density; CFM does not.
  • Speed change: a 15% airflow increase on the same system needs 15% more speed, 32% more pressure and 52% more power. Always recheck the motor and the maximum safe speed.
  • Cold start horsepower is the BHP on cold, dense air; a 600°F fan absorbs twice its running power at a 70°F start.
  • Duty point and FEI: the duty point is what the specification requires; FEI compares the fan's electrical input power with a reference fan at that point, and the same fan can pass at one duty point and fail at another.
  • System effect: classify the job by AMCA installation type (A, B, C, D), allow an effective duct length of straight outlet duct, keep elbows off the inlet, and add any system effect from AMCA 201 curves to the design pressure.
  • Flow control: speed control saves the most power, but less than the ideal cube law when the system has a fixed pressure component.
  • Combining fans: parallel fans add airflow at the same pressure and help most on flat systems; series fans add pressure at the same airflow and help most on steep systems.
  • Sound: sound power belongs to the fan; sound pressure depends on distance and surroundings. Fan sound data comes in eight octave bands from 63 to 8,000 Hz.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Fan Laws, System Effect and Sound
docs.text: Test your understanding of fan curve landmarks, efficiency, the fan laws, system effect, combined fans and fan sound with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a fan's shutoff pressure?
docs.text:
1. The static pressure at which the fan reaches its peak static efficiency
  2. The static pressure the fan develops at zero airflow, with the inlet or outlet blocked
  3. The highest static pressure anywhere on the fan curve, at the boundary of the stall region
  4. The static pressure at which the motor must be shut off to avoid overload
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Shutoff pressure is the static pressure a fan develops at zero airflow, when the inlet or outlet is completely blocked; Curve A's is 4.6 in. wg. It is not a zero-power condition, since the fan still absorbs power churning the trapped air. The highest pressure on the curve is the peak pressure point (C), which on Curve A is 4.9 in. wg at 4,000 CFM, not the shutoff value. Peak efficiency (A) occurs far from shutoff.

Concept Tested: Shutoff Pressure

See: Landmarks on the Fan Curve

docs.title: 2. Why is a fan's static efficiency zero at free delivery, even though the fan is moving the most air it can?
docs.text:
1. Because the motor draws no power when the fan discharges into open air
  2. Because the impeller stalls at free delivery and stops doing useful work
  3. Because free delivery is always to the left of the peak pressure point
  4. Because static pressure is zero there, so air power based on static pressure is zero
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Static efficiency is airflow times fan static pressure divided by 6356 times BHP. At free delivery the fan discharges against zero static pressure, so the numerator is zero even though airflow is at its maximum. The fan still absorbs power (Curve A takes 8.8 BHP near 16,000 CFM), so option A is wrong. Free delivery sits at the far right of the curve, not left of the peak (C), and the fan is not stalled there (B).

Concept Tested: Free Delivery

See: The Efficiency Curve

docs.title: 3. A fan runs at 1,000 RPM and delivers 8,000 CFM at 2.0 in. wg, absorbing 5.0 BHP, on a system whose curve passes through zero. The owner wants 9,200 CFM through the same system. About what brake horsepower will the fan need?
docs.text:
1. 5.75 BHP
  2. 6.61 BHP
  3. 7.60 BHP
  4. 8.75 BHP
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Airflow goes with speed, so the speed ratio is 9,200 ÷ 8,000 = 1.15. Power goes with speed cubed: 5.0 × 1.15³ = 5.0 × 1.521 = 7.60 BHP. Option A scales power linearly with speed, option B uses the square (the pressure law), and option D raises the ratio to the fourth power. A 15% airflow increase costing about 52% more power is the same result as the chapter's Curve A speed-up example.

Concept Tested: Power Varies With Speed Cubed

See: Speed Change Calculation

docs.title: 4. A fan selected for 600°F air absorbs 20 BHP at its operating temperature. At the same speed, about how much will it absorb when it starts on 70°F air?
docs.text:
1. 40 BHP
  2. 20 BHP
  3. 30 BHP
  4. 10 BHP
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. At the same speed the fan moves the same CFM, but BHP rises in proportion to air density. The chapter gives a temperature factor of 0.500 for 600°F air, so 70°F air is twice as dense and the cold start horsepower is 20 ÷ 0.500 = 40 BHP. Option B assumes density does not affect power, and option D applies the density factor in the wrong direction. The motor must be sized for this cold start, or the start-up load must be managed.

Concept Tested: Cold Start Horsepower

See: Cold Start Horsepower

docs.title: 5. A centrifugal fan draws air through a duct from a process hood and discharges directly outdoors with no outlet duct. Which AMCA installation type describes this job?
docs.text:
1. Type A
  2. Type B
  3. Type C
  4. Type D
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Two questions decide the type: is the inlet ducted, and is the outlet ducted? Here the inlet is ducted and the outlet is free, which is Type C. Type A is free on both sides, Type B is a free inlet with a ducted outlet, and Type D is ducted on both sides. The installation type depends on the connections, not on the fan type, and a rating made for one type does not describe a job installed as another.

Concept Tested: AMCA Installation Type

See: AMCA Installation Type

docs.title: 6. On the chapter's steep system (4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM), adding a second Curve A fan in parallel raises airflow only from 10,000 CFM to about 11,000 CFM. What is the underlying reason?
docs.text:
1. Parallel fans add pressure at the same airflow, and the steep system needs airflow instead
  2. The combined curve doubles airflow only at equal pressure, and on a steep system more airflow costs much more pressure
  3. The second fan always stalls when two identical fans share one system
  4. Each fan loses half its efficiency when it shares an inlet plenum with another fan
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Parallel fans add airflow at the same pressure, but the operating point must still land on the system curve. On a steep system, extra airflow requires much more pressure, so the operating point climbs to about 4.8 in. wg, where each fan delivers far less than at 4.0 in. wg. Option A describes series fans. Stall (C) is a risk only if each fan runs left of its peak pressure point. On a flat system the same parallel pair adds over 40% more air.

Concept Tested: Fans in Parallel

See: Fans in Parallel and in Series

docs.title: 7. A VAV system must hold 1.5 in. wg of its 4.0 in. wg design pressure at every flow. At 70% airflow, air power falls to about 48% of design with speed control, not the ideal 34%. What causes the difference?
docs.text:
1. The fixed pressure component keeps system pressure from falling with airflow squared, so the fan must still develop more pressure than the cube law assumes
  2. Variable frequency drives lose about 14% of their input power at any reduced speed
  3. The fan laws apply only to speed changes of less than 20%, so the cube law fails at 70% airflow
  4. Static efficiency always rises at reduced speed, which increases the power the fan draws
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The ideal cube law holds only when the system curve passes through zero. With 1.5 in. wg held constant, the system needs 1.5 + 2.5 × 0.7² = 2.73 in. wg at 70% airflow instead of 1.96 in. wg, so air power is 0.7 × 2.73 ÷ 4.0 = 48% of design. Speed control still saves the most, but by less. Drive and motor losses (B) reduce savings further, yet they are not the cause of the 48% figure.

Concept Tested: Flow Control Efficiency

See: Controlling Flow Efficiently

docs.title: 8. A fan has an FEI of 1.21 at one duty point but 0.88 at the project's actual design point, which lies far to the right on its curve. The energy code requires a minimum FEI of 1.00 at the design point. Which response is best?
docs.text:
1. Accept the fan, because FEI is judged at the fan's best operating point
  2. Fit a larger motor, because more motor capacity raises the fan's FEI
  3. Keep the fan and add an outlet damper to move the duty to the left
  4. Choose a different fan size so the design point lands closer to peak efficiency
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FEI compares the electrical input power of a reference fan with that of the actual fan at the same duty point, so one fan model has a different FEI at every point on its curve. The code judges the design point, not the best point (A). A larger motor (B) does not reduce the power the fan needs, and a damper (C) adds pressure loss rather than meeting the duty more efficiently. The chapter's remedy for a failing selection is a different size.

Concept Tested: Fan Energy Index

See: Fan Energy Index

docs.title: 9. An elbow bolted to Curve A's inlet adds about 0.5 in. wg of system effect, so the fan delivers about 9,560 CFM instead of the 10,000 CFM duty. Speeding up to 1,444 RPM would need about 10.08 BHP, more than the 10 hp motor. Which redesign restores the duty point without changing the motor?
docs.text:
1. Speed the fan up to 1,444 RPM and rely on the motor's service factor to carry the extra load
  2. Add a second identical fan in series immediately downstream of the elbow
  3. Replace the inlet elbow with an inlet box or straight inlet duct and keep 1,380 RPM and the 10 hp motor
  4. Throttle an outlet damper so the operating point moves back to the design airflow
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The shortfall comes from inlet system effect, so removing its cause restores the original effective system curve, and the fan returns to 10,000 CFM at 1,380 RPM on its 10 hp motor. Service factor is margin, not capacity, so option A is not a sound design. A series fan (B) adds cost and does not remove the loss, and a damper (D) adds resistance and reduces airflow further. FanPedia describes the inlet box as designed to minimize the system effect of a 90 degree turn into the fan.

Concept Tested: Inlet System Effect

See: Restoring the Duty Point After System Effect

docs.title: 10. A fan has a 10-blade impeller running at 1,770 RPM, giving a blade pass frequency of 295 Hz. In which octave band will this tone appear in the fan's sound data?
docs.text:
1. The 250 Hz band
  2. The 125 Hz band
  3. The 500 Hz band
  4. The 1,000 Hz band
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Blade pass frequency is the number of blades times revolutions per second: 10 × 1,770 ÷ 60 = 295 Hz. The 250 Hz octave band covers roughly 177 to 354 Hz, so 295 Hz falls inside it and that band will usually stand out. The 125 Hz band ends at about 177 Hz, and the 500 Hz band starts at about 354 Hz. Octave band data lets an acoustical engineer choose a silencer that attacks the right frequencies.

Concept Tested: Octave Band

See: Octave Band

docs.title: References: Fan Laws, System Effect and Sound
docs.text:
1. Affinity laws - Wikipedia - States the fan and pump affinity laws for changes in speed and impeller diameter. A compact cross-check for the chapter's fan laws, speed change and size change calculations.

  2. Sound pressure - Wikipedia - Defines sound pressure and sound pressure level in decibels referenced to 20 micropascals, and how level falls with distance. Supports the chapter's distinction between sound pressure and sound power.

  3. Octave band - Wikipedia - Explains octave and fractional-octave bands, their center frequencies and band limits. Background for the eight-band fan sound data table and the blade pass frequency example in this chapter.

  4. Fan Engineering: An Engineer's Handbook on Fans and Their Applications (9th ed.) - Robert Jorgensen (editor) - Howden Buffalo - Jorgensen's handbook treats speed, size and density changes as one family of similarity relations applied at the same point of rating, the framing this chapter uses for the fan laws and specific speed.

  5. Noise and Vibration Control Engineering: Principles and Applications (2nd ed.) - Leo L. Beranek and István L. Vér - Wiley - Beranek's clear separation of a source's sound power from the sound pressure a listener receives in a room or outdoors underlies how this chapter tells students to read a noise limit.

  6. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan - Source for the inlet box and outlet damper statements this chapter quotes (pp. 182 and 187); also available as FanPedia online.

  7. AMCA Publication 201, Fans and Systems - AMCA International - Publication page for the fan application manual that defines system effect, effective duct length and the lettered system effect curves used in this chapter.

  8. ANSI/AMCA Standard 210, Laboratory Methods of Testing Fans for Certified Aerodynamic Performance Rating - AMCA International - Standard page for the laboratory test method that defines installation types A, B, C and D behind catalog ratings.

  9. About Fan Energy Index - AMCA International - Explains FEI and fan electrical power as duty-point metrics, with links to ANSI/AMCA Standard 208, the calculation standard the chapter cites.

  10. ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1 - ASHRAE - Bookstore page for the energy standard that sets minimum fan efficiency requirements at the design point, one of the codes this chapter names as requiring FEI.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter teaches how to read a current Twin City Fan catalog. It covers catalog structure, fan size and model codes, performance tables and their headers, class shading, interpolation, rating conditions and AMCA certified ratings, transmission losses and appurtenance effects, actual operating conditions, catalog operating limits, first critical speed, balance grade, material specification tables, and the fan selector software. It explains why current catalogs take precedence over FanPedia where they disagree, and introduces fan family and motor selection. After completing it, readers can find a fan's speed and brake horsepower for a duty point in a catalog.

docs.title: Why the Catalog Is the Last Word
docs.text:
Every earlier chapter described fans in general terms: what an arrangement is, why a class limits speed, how density changes pressure. A customer does not order a general fan. They order a specific model, in a specific size and class, at a speed and horsepower that someone read out of a Twin City Fan catalog or the Fan Selector software. This chapter teaches you to do that reading accurately, and to know which numbers the catalog gives you, which it leaves to you, and which it deliberately leaves out.

From Duty Point to Order Line

A customer gives you an airflow and a pressure; by the end of this chapter you will turn that into a fan size, a class, a speed and a brake horsepower you can defend line by line. That is the moment a conversation becomes an order. Let's follow the airflow, from the catalog cover to the last footnote under the performance table.

The examples in this chapter use three current Twin City Fan publications posted on tcf.com: Catalog 300 for the BC backward inclined fan (dated April 2024), Catalog 902 for the RBA, RBO, RBR, RBW and RBP radial bladed industrial fans (dated November 2017), and the Engineering Resource Guide ERG-100 (dated May 2024). Numbers quoted from them are real catalog values and are labeled with their source. Numbers that are not from a catalog are labeled illustrative. Before you quote any of them to a customer, check the catalog on tcf.com for a newer edition; that habit is the first lesson of the chapter.

docs.title: The Product Catalog
docs.text:
A product catalog is the manufacturer's published document for one product line: the models in the line, the sizes and classes built, the arrangements and options offered, the construction details, the engineering limits and, for many lines, the rated performance. Twin City Fan publishes one numbered catalog per line and lists them on the tcf.com Product Catalogs page. Catalog 300 covers the BC-SW and BC-DW backward inclined fans, Catalog 600 covers the BCV, BAV and FCV utility sets, Catalog 902 covers the radial bladed industrial fans, and so on through the axial, plenum, mixed flow and roof lines. Each catalog's cover carries its number and its edition date.

A catalog answers three kinds of question, and it helps to know which kind you are asking before you start turning pages:

  • Can it be built? Which sizes, classes, arrangements, materials and temperatures are offered. These answers are yes or no, and a "no" ends the discussion.
  • How will it perform? Speed and brake horsepower for a stated airflow and pressure, either in printed performance tables or, for newer lines, in the Fan Selector software the catalog points to.
  • What will it look like on the job? Dimensions, weights, shaft and bearing sizes, and the paragraphs an engineer copies into a specification.

The catalog is also a legal document of sorts. Its performance is certified under stated conditions, its dimension pages carry the warning "Dimensions not to be used for construction. Certified drawings available upon request," and its statements about what is standard and what is optional decide what a customer receives for the quoted price. Reading a catalog carelessly is how quotes go wrong.

docs.title: Worked Example: Answering a Customer Question from the Catalog
docs.text:
A plant engineer asks whether a BC-SW fan in Arrangement 9 can exhaust air at 600°F. Here is how the question is answered from Catalog 300 alone.

  1. Find the product. The cover and the overview (pages 2–3) confirm that the BC-SW is the single width, single inlet backward inclined fan and that Arrangement 9 is offered for it.
  2. Find the limit. The high temperature section (page 5) contains Table 1, High Temperature Construction Requirements. It has three temperature bands: –20°F to +300°F, 300°F to 500°F, and 500°F to 800°F.
  3. Read the row. In the 500°F to 800°F row, the bearings are ball or roller with one expansion bearing, lubricated with high temperature grease, and the fan needs high temperature aluminum paint, a shaft cooler and a shaft seal, with a motor heat shield included for Arrangement 9 and 10 fans. The available arrangements are 1, 8, 9, 9F and 10, with the note that Arrangements 9 and 10 are limited to 600°F.
  4. Read the footnote that follows. The same page says that high temperature reduces impeller strength, so maximum safe speed must be derated, and directs you to the Fan Selector (FS10) software for the derated speeds.

The answer is "yes, at exactly the 600°F limit for Arrangement 9, with high temperature construction, and only if the selection speed is below the derated maximum speed from Fan Selector." A good answer names the construction it requires and the check that is still open.

Read the Edition Date First

Before you quote anything from a catalog PDF saved on your laptop, compare its cover date with the copy on tcf.com. Thirty seconds spent checking the date saves you from quoting an arrangement, option or limit that the current edition has changed.

docs.title: Catalog Structure
docs.text:
Catalog structure is the standard order of sections inside a Twin City Fan product catalog. The order is close to the same from line to line, so once you know it in one catalog you can find your way in any other. Catalog 300 runs in this sequence:

  1. Overview (pages 2–3): models, impeller diameters, airflow and pressure range, arrangements, standard and optional construction, certifications and typical applications.
  2. Construction features (page 4): how the impeller, housing, shaft and bearings are built, including balance grade, shaft critical speed and bearing life.
  3. High temperature modifications and energy regulations (page 5): Table 1 and the derating note, plus a statement on DOE and state efficiency rules.
  4. Arrangements (pages 6–9): a picture and paragraph for every arrangement offered.
  5. Options and accessories (pages 10–12): numbered callouts for guards, bases, dampers, inlet vanes, flanges, seals, doors and drives.
  6. Motor positions and standard configurations (page 13), inlet boxes (page 14) and vibration isolation (page 15).
  7. Engineering data (page 16): maximum RPM, impeller weight and WR² (the moment of inertia of the rotating impeller, in lb-ft², used to check that a motor can start it) for every size and class.
  8. Material specifications (page 17 onward): housing gauges, shaft diameters, bearing types and bare fan weights.
  9. Dimensions: one drawing and table per arrangement and size range.
  10. Typical specifications (pages 50–51): ready-to-copy specification paragraphs.

Catalog 902 follows the same pattern but adds a section that Catalog 300 does not have: performance data, printed tables of RPM and brake horsepower for each model and size, starting on page 20. Catalog 300 instead says on its overview page that "certified performance data may be found in Twin City Fan & Blower's Fan Selector software." Whether performance is printed or lives in software is the single biggest structural difference between catalogs, and you should check which kind you are holding before you look for a table.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Questions, Three Sections
docs.text:
A representative is preparing a quote for a BC-SW and has three questions. Each one maps to a section by the kind of answer it needs:

Question Kind of answer Section What the catalog says What is the highest speed a size 365 Class II can run? Engineering limit Engineering data, page 16 1,283 RPM What shaft diameter and bearing does a size 365 Class I use in Arrangement 1? Construction detail Material specifications, page 17 1-15/16 in. shaft, ball bearings Can the outlet damper modulate airflow over the whole range? Option choice Options and accessories, page 12 Opposed blade dampers are recommended for modulation over the entire range

None of the three questions needed a performance table. Most of the questions a sales or application engineer fields in a day are "can it be built" and "what does it look like" questions, and they are answered in the front and back of the catalog, not in the middle.

The MicroSim below gives you practice at the same skill: matching a question to the catalog section that answers it, before you start searching.

docs.title: Diagram: Catalog Section Finder
docs.text:

Catalog Section Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch26-catalog-section-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify ten customer questions by the Twin City Fan catalog section that answers them, getting at least 8 of 10 right on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: product catalog, catalog structure, engineering data, material specifications, performance data, typical specifications (all defined in the sections "The Product Catalog" and "Catalog Structure" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each question card to one of ten section bins. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct section column. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Opening a section's description before assigning is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every catalog has printed performance tables (Catalog 300 does not; it points to Fan Selector). (2) Maximum speed is found in the performance tables rather than in engineering data. (3) Dimension pages can be used for construction (they cannot; certified drawings are required).

Instructional Rationale: Classifying questions by the kind of answer they need builds the mental map of catalog structure that makes later lookups fast. Committing each card before feedback makes the learner predict, which an Understand objective needs.

Content:

Ten section bins, each with a one-line description shown on request:

Bin Description Overview Models, diameters, airflow and pressure range, arrangements, certifications Construction Features How the impeller, housing, shaft and bearings are built High Temperature Modifications Temperature bands, bearing and lubrication requirements, derating Arrangements Picture and paragraph for each arrangement offered Options/Accessories Guards, bases, dampers, inlet vanes, flanges, seals, doors, drives Engineering Data Maximum RPM, impeller weight and WR² by size and class Material Specifications Housing gauges, shaft diameters, bearing types, bare fan weights Performance Data Printed RPM and BHP tables by model and size Dimensions Drawings and dimension tables by arrangement and size Typical Specifications Specification paragraphs ready to copy

Ten question cards, shown in shuffled order:

# Question Correct section Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the maximum RPM of a BC-SW size 365 Class II? Engineering Data Maximum RPM by size and class is engineering data (Catalog 300, page 16: 1,283 RPM). 2 What shaft diameter and bearing type does a BC SWSI Class I size 365 use in Arrangement 1? Material Specifications Shaft and bearing sizes by size and class are in the material specifications table. 3 What RPM and BHP does an RBA 913 need for 4,092 CFM at 12 in. wg? Performance Data Speed and power at a duty point are read from the performance tables (Catalog 902, page 24). 4 What bearing and grease does a BC-SW need at 450°F? High Temperature Modifications Table 1 lists bearing type and lubrication for each temperature band. 5 Where does the motor mount on an Arrangement 9H? Arrangements Each arrangement's paragraph describes the motor location. 6 Is an opposed blade or parallel blade outlet damper better for modulating over the full range? Options/Accessories Damper types and where to use each are described with the accessories. 7 Are lifting lugs standard on BC housings? Construction Features Housing construction, including lifting lugs, is described in construction features. 8 What is the highest airflow the BC-DW line covers? Overview The overview states the airflow and pressure range for each model (344,300 CFM for BC-DW). 9 How tall is a BC-SW size 300 in Arrangement 9? Dimensions Overall dimensions are in the dimension tables, which are not for construction. 10 What paragraph can an engineer paste into a project specification for a BC-DW? Typical Specifications Specification paragraphs are collected at the back of the catalog.

Provenance: Section names and contents from Twin City Fan Catalog 300 (April 2024) and Catalog 902 (November 2017), https://tcf.com/resources/product-catalogs/. Values 1,283 RPM and 344,300 CFM from Catalog 300 pages 16 and 3.

Rules: Each card has exactly one correct bin. A card's first assignment is scored. Each bin can hold any number of cards.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a question card and may open any bin's description.
  2. The learner assigns the card to a bin. The card is marked correct or incorrect and the feedback is shown.
  3. An incorrect card returns to the deck once; the learner may reassign it, but only the first attempt is scored.
  4. After all ten cards, the learner sees the score and the list of missed cards with their reasons.

Feedback: Ten cards, shuffled, two attempts each, first attempt scored. Correct: "Correct: " plus the Why text. Hint after a first wrong attempt: "Not quite. " plus a hint about what kind of information the question asks for, which never names a section (1: a mechanical limit by size and class, not a duty point; 2: the size and type of particular parts, not how the fan is built in general; 3: a duty point turned into speed and power; 4: the 450°F airstream is what makes it special; 5: motor location depends on the configuration; 6: a damper is added to the fan, not part of its standard build; 7: add-on or part of how the standard housing is built; 8: the range a whole product line covers; 9: a physical size, drawings with tables; 10: ready-written wording, not data). After the final attempt: "Not quite. " plus the Why text and the correct bin. A running score "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown.

Starting State: The ten bins are shown with card 1 of the shuffled deck. The prompt reads "Which catalog section answers this question?"

Chapter Anchors: BC-SW size 365 Class II maximum RPM is 1,283 RPM. BC-DW airflow range is to 344,300 CFM. Catalog 300 has no printed performance tables. Mastery is 8 of 10.

docs.title: Technical Descriptions and the Typical Specification
docs.text:
A catalog explains in words as well as in tables. A technical description is a short written paragraph that defines one component, arrangement or option and states its restrictions. FanPedia collects these in its Technical Descriptions section (pages 161–197), alphabetically from Anti-Backspin Devices onward, and the product catalogs carry similar paragraphs beside each arrangement and accessory. Technical descriptions often hold rules that never appear in a table. FanPedia's description of Arrangement 1 SWSI (page 162), for example, says the motor can go in any of the four AMCA motor positions W, X, Y or Z, and then lists the exceptions: on a bottom horizontal discharge (BHD), motor position Z is not allowed on a CW fan and position W is not allowed on a CCW fan, because the motor would block the outlet. A table of arrangements would simply show "W, X, Y, Z"; the description is where the exception lives.

The typical specification at the back of each catalog is the same idea written for an engineer's project manual. Catalog 300's BC-SW paragraph requires, among other things, AMCA certified ratings for sound, air and fan energy index (FEI, the AMCA 208 efficiency metric), shafts sized for a first critical speed of at least 1.43 times maximum speed, and balance to AMCA 204 grade BV-3. When a specification on a bid looks familiar, it has often been copied from one of these paragraphs.

docs.title: FanPedia Versus the Current Catalog
docs.text:
FanPedia (©2021) is Twin City Fan's encyclopedia of terms, arrangements, components and construction across all its product lines. It explains what things are. A product catalog states what one line offers today: its sizes, limits, options and ratings. FanPedia vs current catalog is the rule for when they disagree: the current catalog wins, because it is the document that describes what the factory builds and certifies now. FanPedia carries almost no size-specific numbers at all; it does not list maximum speeds, performance or dimensions, and it points to the product catalogs for details such as bearing life by model.

"Current" means the latest edition on tcf.com, not "newer than FanPedia." Catalog 300 (April 2024) is newer than FanPedia, but Catalog 902 (November 2017) is older, and it is still the current catalog for the radial bladed line. Use FanPedia to understand a feature, then confirm the specific offering, limit or option in the current catalog for the model you are quoting, and use Fan Selector or the factory when the catalog is silent.

docs.title: Fan Size
docs.text:
Fan size is the number Twin City Fan uses to identify one impeller diameter within a model. The industrial fans in Catalog 902 state that their sizes and impeller diameters conform to AMCA Standard 2402 (Sizes for Industrial Centrifugal Fans), and every performance page heads its table with the size number and the impeller diameter it stands for. Fan size is not the outlet dimension, the inlet diameter or the housing width; it is a label for the impeller, and every other dimension follows from it.

Two numbering styles appear in the catalogs used in this chapter:

  • In Catalog 300, the BC size number tracks the impeller diameter in inches with the decimal point dropped. The BC-SW line runs from 12.25-inch to 98.25-inch impeller diameters, and its sizes run from 122 to 982.
  • In Catalog 902, the radial bladed sizes are a 900-series code. Size 905 is an 8.75-inch impeller, size 913 is 22.625 inches, and size 960 is 104.25 inches. The digits after the 9 are not the diameter; you read the diameter from the performance page.

The table below gives a few real size-to-diameter pairs from Catalog 902's performance pages, so you can see that the size code climbs with diameter but is not equal to it:

Size (Catalog 902) Impeller diameter (in.) Tip speed factor (FPM per RPM) 905 8.75 2.29 913 22.625 5.92 921 36.5 not used in this chapter 960 104.25 not used in this chapter

Size also decides which classes and arrangements exist. In Catalog 902's RB Series Availability table (page 13), size 905 is offered only in Class 22, while sizes 913 through 919 are offered in Classes 22, 32 and 45. Class 22, 32 and 45 are Twin City Fan's own industrial categories (about 22, 32 and 45 in. wg of static pressure), not the Class I to IV of Chapter 10; Catalog 300 uses the Roman numerals. In Catalog 300, Arrangement 10 units of Class I and II in sizes 122 through 365 are the fans commonly called ventilating sets. So the first question about any size is not "how big is it?" but "what does this size let me build?"

The header of each performance page turns the size into the numbers you need for calculations. For size 913 it reads: impeller diameter 22.625 in., tip speed (FPM) 5.92 × RPM, inlet area 0.87 ft², inlet diameter 13 in. O.D., outlet area 0.93 ft², outlet dimension 10-7/8 in. × 12-3/16 in.

docs.title: Tip Speed Factor
docs.text:
\[ TS = k \times N, \qquad k = \frac{\pi \times D}{12} \]

where:

  • \( TS \) is the impeller tip speed in FPM
  • \( k \) is the catalog's tip speed factor in FPM per RPM
  • \( N \) is the fan speed in RPM
  • \( D \) is the impeller diameter in inches

docs.title: Worked Example: What Size 913 Tells You
docs.text:
Check the header against itself, then use it.

  1. Tip speed factor. \( k = \pi \times 22.625 / 12 = 5.92 \) FPM per RPM, which matches the printed "5.92 × RPM."
  2. Tip speed at a selection. The RBA 913 table gives 2,167 RPM for 4,092 CFM at 12 in. wg (Catalog 902, page 24). The tip speed is \( 5.92 \times 2{,}167 = 12{,}829 \) FPM.
  3. Outlet velocity. Outlet velocity is airflow divided by outlet area: \( 4{,}092 / 0.93 = 4{,}400 \) FPM. That is the number printed in the OV column on the same row, which confirms that the OV column is computed from the outlet area in the header.

Three numbers from the header (diameter, tip speed factor, outlet area) let you check the table, compute tip speed for comparison with other sizes (Chapter 10), and size the duct transition at the outlet. A size number with no header beside it tells you very little.

Size Is Not Interchangeable Across Models

A common trap is assuming that "size 365" or "size 913" means the same impeller in every model. Size numbering belongs to a model's catalog, and the same digits can mean different diameters in different lines. Always read the diameter from that model's own performance page or engineering data before comparing two fans.

docs.title: Model Code
docs.text:
A model code is the short letter designation that identifies a Twin City Fan product line and impeller type, such as BC-SW, RBA or TCTA. On its own it names a family; combined with a size, a class and an arrangement, it names one buildable fan. Twin City Fan's catalogs are titled by model code, so the code is also how you find the right catalog:

Model code Catalog title (tcf.com) Catalog BC-SW, BC-DW Backward Inclined Fans (single width, double width) 300 BAE Airfoil Fans 370 RBA, RBO, RBR, RBW, RBP Industrial Fans (radial bladed) 902 BCV, BAV, FCV Utility Sets 600 EPF, EPFN, EPQ, EPQN E-Series Plenum Fans 470 TCTA Tubeaxial Fans AX200 TCVA Vaneaxial Fans AX100 QSL, QSLSH, QSLR, QFE Mixed Flow Fans 1060

Inside a line, the letters often separate impeller types that share a housing. Catalog 902 uses one housing family with five impellers: RBA (air handling, backward inclined blades welded to a back plate and front ring), RBO (open radial paddle), RBR (paddle with blade end rings for larger sizes and higher RPM), RBW (back plate wool impeller for stringy material) and RBP (paper handling, a modified RBW with trapezoidal gussets). The performance of each impeller differs, so each has its own table on the same size page: RBO 913 and RBA 913 share a header but not their numbers.

A model code can also end in a suffix. Twin City Fan engineering says PL at the end of a model name means the customer wants that style of wheel in a plug fan arrangement, so BCPL is a BC style wheel built as a plug fan (see Chapter 6). A complete order line adds the rest of the designation. A typical written form is model, size, class and arrangement, for example "RBA 913, Class 32, Arrangement 9." Rotation and discharge (Chapter 13), motor position and construction options are then added for a full fan description, which Chapter 27 builds in full.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is This Designation Buildable?
docs.text:
Catalog 902's RB Series Availability table (page 13) lists the arrangements offered for each impeller type, size and class. For RBA sizes 913 through 919 it reads:

Class Arrangements offered Class 22 1, 4, 8, 10, 4VI, 9A, 9B, 9F Class 32 1, 4, 8, 9, 4VI, 9F Class 45 1, 8, 9, 9F

Now check three designations a customer might send:

  1. RBA 913, Class 22, Arrangement 10. Arrangement 10 appears in the Class 22 list. Buildable.
  2. RBA 913, Class 32, Arrangement 10. Arrangement 10 is not in the Class 32 list. Not buildable; offer Arrangement 9 or 9F, which are the belt-drive arrangements listed for Class 32.
  3. RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 4. Arrangement 4 (impeller on the motor shaft) is not in the Class 45 list. Not buildable; a Class 45 RBA 913 must have its own shaft and bearings, as in Arrangements 1, 8, 9 or 9F.

The second and third designations look reasonable and would pass a casual read. They fail only when you check the model, size and class together against the availability table, which is why a model code is never checked one field at a time.

The MicroSim below gives you eight designations to check in the same way, using real Catalog 300 and Catalog 902 data.

docs.title: Diagram: Model Code Decoder
docs.text:
Run Model Code Decoder Fullscreen

Model Code Decoder

Type: microsim sim-id: ch26-model-code-decoder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret a Twin City Fan designation (model code, size, class, arrangement) by judging whether it is offered and reading its class maximum RPM from catalog extracts, for at least 7 of 8 designations.

Prerequisites: model code, fan size, fan class, arrangement, maximum RPM (defined in the sections "Fan Size" and "Model Code" above and in Chapters 10 and 11).

Evidence of Mastery: For each designation the learner commits two answers: Offered or Not offered, and the class maximum RPM chosen from the extract. A designation is correct when both answers match the answer table. Mastery is 7 of 8 designations correct on the first attempt. Browsing the extracts is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) If a size is offered in a class and an arrangement is offered in the line, every combination is offered. (2) A direct-drive arrangement is available in every class. (3) A size number means the same diameter in every model.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting a designation requires reading three catalog tables together; judging real designations with feedback makes the learner cross-reference rather than recall.

Eight designations, in this order:

# Designation Offered? Class maximum RPM Why (shown as feedback) 1 RBA 913, Class 22, Arrangement 10 Offered 2,812 Arrangement 10 is in the Class 22 list for RBA 913. 2 RBA 913, Class 32, Arrangement 10 Not offered 3,337 Arrangement 10 is offered only in Class 22 for this size; Class 32 lists 1, 4, 8, 9, 4VI, 9F. 3 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 4 Not offered 4,000 Class 45 lists only 1, 8, 9 and 9F; the direct-drive Arrangement 4 is not offered at Class 45. 4 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 9 Offered 4,000 Arrangement 9 is in the Class 45 list. 5 RBO 905, Class 22, Arrangement 9A Offered 5,296 Size 905 offers 9A in Class 22; selections above 4,000 RPM are not recommended without consulting the factory. 6 RBO 905, Class 32, Arrangement 1 Not offered none Size 905 is built only in Class 22. 7 BC-SW 365, Class II, Arrangement 9 Offered 1,283 Arrangement 9 is offered for BC-SW, and Class II size 365 runs to 1,283 RPM. 8 BC-DW 365, Class I, Arrangement 9 Not offered 1,015 Arrangement 9 is a single width arrangement; BC-DW is offered in 3, 3F, 3DI, 7 and 7DI.

Provenance: Catalog 902 (November 2017), page 13 (RB Series Availability) and performance pages 20 and 24 (maximum RPM, diameters). The class maximum RPM answer is the value in the extract for that class, or "none" when the class is not built. Both answers must match for the designation to count as correct.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads designation 1 and opens whichever extract they need.
  2. The learner chooses Offered or Not offered, and chooses the class maximum RPM from the values in that model's row plus "none".
  3. The learner submits; both answers are marked and the Why text appears.
  4. The learner moves to the next designation. After designation 8, the score and missed items are shown.

Starting State: Designation 1 is shown with both extracts collapsed. The prompt reads "Can the factory build this fan, and how fast can it run?"
