docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the density ratio for a stated air temperature and site altitude, and use it to correct a static pressure between catalog and job conditions, to within ±0.005 on the ratio and ±0.03 in. wg on the pressure (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Air density and standard air (70°F, sea level, 0.075 lb/ft³)
  • Density ratio, air temperature, altitude and absolute pressure
  • Static pressure
  • The two correction rules: multiply to predict, divide to select

All are covered in the Chapter 1 sections "Air Density", "Air Temperature" and "Altitude".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (8 min): Place the marker first, then calculate and check each entry. Two attempts each.
  2. Explore (4 min): Hover the curves at 250°F and 600°F. Then find an altitude where 70°F air is as thin as 120°F air at sea level.
  3. Discussion (3 min): A fan selected for a 5,000 ft site straight from the catalog at 2.0 in. wg: is it short of pressure or oversized, and by how much?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Hot air or high altitude reduces the CFM a fan moves at a given speed: the Explore readout states that CFM and RPM stay the same while pressure and BHP scale with DR.
  • The temperature correction can be done in °F directly (70 ÷ 250): challenge 1 recognizes 0.28 and points to absolute temperature; challenge 4 recognizes a missing 460.
  • To select a fan for thin air you multiply the required pressure by DR: challenge 2 recognizes the multiplied answer and explains that it would undersize the fan.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score shown as "Entries correct: n of 6"; mastery is 6 of 6 entries correct within two attempts each. The summary shows "Mastery reached (6 of 6 needed)." or what is still needed, and lists any missed entry with its calculation.
  • Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Follow up: a motor sized only for the hot running condition of challenge 1 starts up cold. What happens to its load?

docs.title: Airstream Classifier
docs.text:
Run the Airstream Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen

To run this sketch in the p5.js editor, first add the kit files it uses (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html, then paste ch01-airstream-classifier.js as the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A fan's impeller and housing sit in the airstream, so what the air carries decides the impeller, the arrangement, the accessories and the construction. This sorter gives you ten airstreams and five bins, each with its definition on screen:

  • A. Clean air: no significant solids, moisture, corrosives, flammables or hazardous fumes, at any temperature.
  • B. Solids: contaminated with solids that wear or build up on the impeller.
  • C. Corrosive or moisture: contaminated with corrosive gases or heavy moisture that attack materials.
  • D. Flammable: contaminated with flammable vapors, gases or dusts that make a spark dangerous.
  • E. Hazardous fumes: contaminated with fumes hazardous to people, which must be diluted and discharged away from the building.

The ten cards range from office supply air and outdoor make-up air to paper trim, a foundry shakeout, a plating tank, a dishwasher room, a paint booth, lab fume hoods, a battery charging room and a 400°F drying oven. They appear one at a time in a shuffled order that is fixed for the session.

Your first placement of each card is scored. A correct placement shows "✓ Correct: ." with the reason. A wrong one shows "✗ Not quite." with the reason, and the card stays on screen until you place it in the correct bin; those retries are marked "Practice (not scored)". After a second wrong placement the sim reveals the correct bin (→ on its button and an orange outline on the bin). Placed cards collect in the bin you first chose, as ✓ (solid border) or ✗ (dashed border) chips. The running score reads "First-attempt correct: n of 10". Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

After the tenth card a summary lists every card with your first choice and the correct bin. Sort again starts a new round in a new order.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the five bin definitions.
  2. Read the airstream card and decide what in the air matters to the fan or to people. Press the bin's button below the drawing (or a key, A to E or 1 to 5).
  3. Read the reason. If the card was wrong, place it again until it lands in the correct bin.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After the tenth card, read the summary and press Sort again to practice in a new order.

Keyboard: A to E or 1 to 5 place the card; Enter goes to the next card. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Bins from the chapter section "Contaminated Airstreams"; FanPedia pp. 4, 6, 32, 110-116", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will distinguish clean airstreams from contaminated ones and assign each contaminated airstream to its main threat category, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Analyze, verb: distinguish).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airstream, and "in the airstream" versus "out of the airstream"
  • Air temperature
  • Contaminated airstream

All are covered in the Chapter 1 sections "The Airstream", "Air Temperature" and "Contaminated Airstreams".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (6 min): Place all ten cards, committing to a bin before you read the reason.
  2. Summary (2 min): For each miss, name the word in the card that should have decided it.
  3. Discussion (2 min): The 400°F oven air is clean, yet the fan still needs special construction. What question does that answer, and what question does the bin answer?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Hot air is contaminated air: the 400°F drying oven card belongs in Clean air, and its reason points to high-temperature construction instead.
  • Any airstream from a factory is contaminated: the outdoor make-up air card for a warehouse is clean.
  • If the fan survives the airstream, it is not a concern: the lab fume hood card belongs in Hazardous fumes, because the threat is to people, not the fan.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. The summary shows "Mastery reached (8 of 10 needed)." or what is still needed.
  • Retries after a miss are practice and are not evidence of mastery. Follow up: a request form lists only CFM and static pressure. Which three questions about the airstream do you ask before quoting?

docs.title: Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Duct Airflow and Velocity Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

To run this sketch in the p5.js editor, first add the kit files it uses (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html, then paste ch01-duct-airflow-velocity-calculator.js as the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator gives practice with the airflow equation \( Q = V \times A \) on the kinds of ducts that appear on drawings. Duct sizes come in inches, but the equation needs the flow area in square feet. A rectangular duct's area is \( (W \times H) \div 144 \) ft², and a round duct's area is \( \pi D^2 \div 576 \) ft².

The sim opens with four fixed challenges. Each one asks for a single number:

# Given Asked Model answer 1 2,400 CFM in a 16 in × 12 in rectangular duct Velocity 1,800 ft/min 2 5,000 CFM in a 24 in round duct Velocity 1,592 ft/min 3 A 20 in × 10 in rectangular duct at 1,500 ft/min Airflow 2,083 CFM 4 10,000 CFM with velocity no higher than 2,000 ft/min Minimum flow area 5.00 ft²

Challenge 1 uses the machine-shop worked example from Chapter 1. Challenges 2 to 4 are illustrative values, and the sim labels them that way.

An answer within ±2% of the model value is correct. Each challenge allows two attempts. A non-numeric or empty entry gets "Enter a number" and does not use an attempt. A correct answer shows "✓ Correct: model value is …"; a wrong one shows ✗ with the challenge's worked feedback, and a second wrong answer reveals the model value and counts as missed. After every check the sim shows your number beside the model value, lays out the worked calculation, and highlights the step where your number departs from it. It recognizes common slips: forgetting to divide by 144, treating a round duct as a square of side D, using π D² ÷ 144, multiplying where you should divide, and giving the area in square inches. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 4" stays on screen. Mastery is 4 of 4 correct, with at most two attempts each.

Explore mode (the free mode) unlocks after challenge 4 and is never scored. You can change the duct shape, width, height or diameter, and the airflow. The flow area (3 decimals), the velocity (to the nearest 10 ft/min) and the substituted equation update immediately. The first time you enlarge the duct while the airflow stays fixed, the sim points out that the CFM did not change and only the velocity fell. Explore mode also shows your challenge results and the mastery line, and Start over runs the four challenges again.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1 and calculate the velocity on paper or a calculator.
  2. Type the number in the Your answer box and press Check (or Enter).
  3. Read the feedback and the highlighted step. If you have an attempt left, correct your work and try again.
  4. Press Next challenge to continue. After challenge 4, press Start explore mode and read the mastery line.
  5. In Explore mode, set 2,400 CFM in a 16 in × 12 in duct, then change it to 24 in × 16 in. Velocity falls from 1,800 to 900 ft/min while the airflow stays at 2,400 CFM. Explore mode is never scored.
  6. Press Start over to work the four challenges again.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer; after a challenge is answered, Enter goes to the next one. Tab reaches every control, and the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Values from the chapter's machine-shop worked example" (challenge 1) or "Illustrative values" (challenges 2 to 4), shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate air velocity, airflow volume or required flow area from the other two quantities for rectangular and round ducts, to within 2 percent of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airflow volume in cubic feet per minute (CFM)
  • Air velocity in feet per minute
  • Flow area in square feet and the equation \( Q = V \times A \)
  • Converting duct dimensions in inches to square feet

All are covered in the Chapter 1 sections "Airflow Volume and Cubic Feet Per Minute" and "Air Velocity".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (8 min): Work the four challenges in order. Commit to a number before checking. Two attempts each.
  2. Explore mode (5 min): Hold the airflow at 2,400 CFM and enlarge the duct. Then switch to a round duct and find the diameter whose area is closest to a 16 in square. It is not 16 in.
  3. Discussion (2 min): Why does a bigger duct not move more air when the fan delivers the same CFM?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Dividing CFM by the duct dimensions in inches without converting to square feet (challenge 1).
  • Believing a bigger duct moves more air at the same fan airflow. In fact the CFM is the same and only the velocity drops (Explore mode note).
  • Believing a round duct of diameter D has the same area as a square duct of side D (challenge 2).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score shown as "Challenges correct: n of 4"; mastery is 4 of 4 challenges correct within ±2%, with at most two attempts each. The sim shows "Mastery reached (4 of 4 needed)." or what is still needed.
  • Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Follow up: why does a bigger duct not move more air at the same fan CFM?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan - The "Air Velocity" section and its worked example "Velocity in a Rectangular Duct".
  2. FanPedia online, Twin City Fan - The fan and blower encyclopedia this textbook is built from.
  3. Volumetric flow rate, Wikipedia - Defines Q = V × A for flow through a cross-section.
  4. Duct (flow), Wikipedia - Background on rectangular and round ductwork.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Fan Duty Statement
docs.text: Run the Anatomy of a Fan Duty Statement MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A duty statement is the line on a schedule or specification that tells you what a fan must do. This infographic shows the one built from Chapter 1's worked examples:

12,000 CFM at 3.0 in. wg static pressure, 1,173 RPM, 7.9 BHP, at 0.075 lb/ft³ (70°F, sea level), clean air.

Its six parts are marked as clickable segments, each with its quantity name underneath:

# Segment Quantity name What it tells you 1 12,000 CFM Airflow volume Cubic feet of air per minute, measured at the fan inlet conditions. 2 3.0 in. wg static pressure Static pressure The system's resistance at this airflow, which the fan must overcome. 3 1,173 RPM Fan speed Impeller revolutions per minute; here set by a 6 in motor sheave and a 9 in fan sheave on a 1,760 RPM motor. 4 7.9 BHP Brake horsepower Power required at the fan shaft; a 10 hp motor would run at 79 percent load. It is not the motor size. 5 0.075 lb/ft³ (70°F, sea level) Air density The density the rating assumes; here standard air. Hot air or a high site changes pressure and power. 6 clean air Airstream condition What the air carries; contaminated airstreams change the impeller, arrangement and construction.

In Explore mode, clicking a segment opens its callout. A ✓ badge marks each part you have opened ("Visited n of 6").

In Quiz mode the names are hidden. The sim highlights one segment at a time, in an order shuffled once per session, and you choose its name from the six quantity names. Each segment has one scored attempt. A correct choice shows "✓ Correct: ." with the callout text. A wrong one shows "✗ Not quite. That segment is the ." with the callout text, and the answer is marked on the line. The running score reads "Correct on first attempt: n of 6". Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. After the sixth segment a summary lists any missed parts, with Start over and Back to explore.

The duty statement is illustrative, not a catalog selection, and the infographic says so.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. In Explore mode, click each part of the rating line (or Tab to it and press Enter) and read its callout.
  2. When you know all six, press Quiz.
  3. For each highlighted part, choose its name (or press 1 to 6). Read the feedback, then press Next prompt.
  4. Read the summary. Press Back to explore to review the parts, or Start over for a new quiz.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the parts and the buttons; Enter or Space opens a part; in the quiz, keys 1 to 6 pick a name, and Enter on Next prompt goes on.

Data label: "Illustrative duty statement, not a catalog selection · Values from the Chapter 1 worked examples", shown under the rating line.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify each of the six parts of a fan duty statement by its quantity and unit, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airflow volume and cubic feet per minute
  • Static pressure and inches of water gauge
  • Fan speed and RPM
  • Brake horsepower
  • Air density and standard air
  • Airstream

All are defined earlier in Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all six callouts. For each, say which unit tells you what the quantity is.
  2. Quiz (3 min): Name the six highlighted parts without the labels.
  3. Discussion (2 min): A customer's schedule gives only "12,000 CFM at 3.0 in. wg". What two parts are missing, and why can the line not be checked against a catalog without them?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• BHP is the motor nameplate size: the brake horsepower callout says it is the power at the fan shaft, with a 10 hp motor running at 79 percent load.
  • Static pressure is a property of the fan alone: its callout calls it the system's resistance at this airflow.
  • The density can be left off because every catalog uses standard air: its callout says hot air or a high site changes pressure and power.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Correct on first attempt: n of 6"; mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt. The summary shows "Mastery reached (5 of 6 needed)." or what is still needed.
  • Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Follow up: rewrite the line for 250°F air. Which parts change, and which stay the same?

docs.title: References
docs.text:

docs.title: Reading Static Pressure with a Manometer
docs.text:
Run the Reading Static Pressure with a Manometer MicroSim Fullscreen

To run this sketch in the p5.js editor, first add the kit files it uses (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html, then paste ch01-manometer-static-pressure.js as the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A U-tube manometer has one leg connected to the duct and one leg open to the room. The difference between the two water levels, in inches, is the static pressure in inches of water gauge (in. wg). When the duct is above room pressure, the water is pushed down on the duct leg. When the duct is below room pressure (suction), the room pushes the water up the duct leg.

The sim draws the supply system from the chapter's worked example "Adding Up a System's Resistance": intake louver, filter, coil, fan, ductwork, diffuser and room, with each part's pressure drop. You step through six measurement points in order. At each one the manometer's water levels are hidden behind a shutter. You choose a sign and type the size of the reading, then press Check. The shutter opens to show both water levels on a ruler, and the reading is labeled on the system drawing, so the pressure profile builds up across the system.

# Point Correct reading (in. wg) Water on the duct leg 1 After the intake louver −0.15 Up 2 After the filter −0.65 Up 3 Fan inlet, after the coil −1.40 Up 4 Fan outlet +1.10 Down 5 Before the diffuser +0.15 Down 6 In the room 0.00 Level

Question 7 asks how much static pressure the fan must add. The answer is 2.50 in. wg: outlet minus inlet, \( 1.10 - (-1.40) \). This treats the air velocity at the fan inlet and outlet as equal, as the chapter states.

A reading is correct when the sign matches and the size is within ±0.05 in. wg. A reading of 0 for point 6 is correct with or without a sign. Each item has one scored attempt. A correct answer shows "✓ Correct: in. wg." A wrong answer shows ✗ with the reason for that point and the correct reading. The sim also names common slips: the right size with the wrong sign, and, for question 7, the outlet reading alone or the two sizes subtracted. After a miss you may retry once; that retry is marked "Practice (not scored)" and does not change the score. An empty entry, or a nonzero reading with no sign, does not use the attempt. The running score reads "First-attempt correct: n of 7". Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

After question 7 the sim switches to Review mode, which is never scored. Pick any point to see its manometer, its reading and the reason again. The summary shows the first-attempt score, the mastery line and a ✓ or ✗ for each item. Start over runs all seven again.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and the pressure drops under the drawing. Decide whether the duct at the marked point is above or below room pressure.
  2. Choose + above room or − below room, type the size of the reading in the Reading box, and press Check (or Enter). You can also type the sign in the box, for example -0.15.
  3. Compare the water levels with your answer. If you missed, you may enter the reading again and press Retry (not scored).
  4. Press Next point to move on. After point 6, answer question 7 with the fan's static pressure rise.
  5. In Review mode, choose a point from the Review menu (or press 1 to 7, or click a numbered point) to see its manometer again. Press Start over to repeat the seven items.

Keyboard: Tab reaches every control; the arrow keys change the sign; Enter checks the answer, and after an answer Enter goes to the next point. In Review mode, keys 1 to 7 choose a point.

Data label: "Illustrative values from the chapter worked example", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will interpret U-tube manometer readings taken at six points in a supply system as signed static pressures in inches of water gauge, and infer the fan's static pressure rise, with at least 6 of 7 answers correct (Bloom: Understand, verb: interpret).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Air pressure, atmospheric pressure, gauge pressure and suction
  • Inches of water gauge and the manometer
  • Static pressure and pressure drop

All are covered in the Chapter 1 sections "Air Pressure", "Inches of Water Gauge" and "Static Pressure".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Readings (6 min): Work points 1 to 6 in order. Commit to a sign and a size before each check, and watch which leg the water moves on.
  2. Fan rise (2 min): Use the inlet and outlet readings on the drawing to answer question 7.
  3. Review (3 min): Open point 3 and point 4 side by side in your mind: the same fan, the water pulled up on one side of it and pushed down on the other.
  4. Discussion (2 min): Why is a reading at the fan inlet negative even though the fan is "making pressure"?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Static pressure is always positive: points 1 to 3 are negative, and the sim names a right-size, wrong-sign answer.
  • The water rises on the duct leg when the duct is pressurized: the revealed manometer shows the water pushed down on the duct leg at points 4 and 5, and the caption says which way it moved.
  • The fan's pressure rise is the outlet reading alone: question 7 recognizes 1.10 and explains that the inlet suction counts too.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt correct: n of 7"; mastery is 6 of 7 on the first attempt. The summary shows "Mastery reached (6 of 7 needed)." or what is still needed.
  • The unscored retry and Review mode are not evidence of mastery. Follow up: a filter loads up and its drop doubles. Which readings change, and does the fan's required rise change?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: Air, Pressure and the Fan - The "Static Pressure" section and its worked example "Adding Up a System's Resistance".
  2. FanPedia online, Twin City Fan - The fan and blower encyclopedia this textbook is built from.
  3. Pressure measurement: manometers, Wikipedia - How a liquid column measures a pressure difference.
  4. Inch of water, Wikipedia - The unit used for fan and duct pressures.

docs.title: Airstream Condition Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Airstream Condition Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html before pasting ch02-airstream-condition-sorter.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Real airstreams often have more than one condition at once, and an inquiry has to name each one. The sorter shows ten short application descriptions, one at a time, in shuffled order. For each, select every condition tag that applies and press Submit:

Tag Definition (shown by the tag's ⓘ button) Hot Temperature high enough to change performance or call for construction beyond the standard catalog build. Wet Enough water vapor, mist or steam that liquid can condense and collect in the fan. Corrosive Gases, vapors or mists that chemically attack the fan's materials. Particulate-laden Carries solid material such as dust, grit, chips, fibers or lint. Explosive atmosphere Contains flammable gases, vapors or combustible dusts that a spark could ignite. Clean None of the above; ordinary air near standard conditions.

Selecting Clean clears every other tag, and selecting any other tag clears Clean. An empty selection cannot be submitted. An item is correct only when your set matches the key exactly; a partly matching set is incorrect. There is one attempt per item. The feedback reads "✓ Correct: tags. Why." or "✗ Not quite. Missing: tags. Extra: tags. Why.", and the correct tags are shown at once. After ten items the sim shows your score as "n of 10", the mastery line, and every missed item with its correct tags. Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first run. Start over deals a new shuffle; later runs are practice and are labeled as such, because only the first run counts as evidence.

The descriptions are illustrative applications written for this sim. The temperature judgments for the kiln dryer (450°F) and the heat-treating oven (700°F) rest on the high-temperature package ranges from FanPedia pp. 110–116 summarized in the chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the description. Press a tag's ⓘ button to read its definition below the item.
  2. Select every tag that applies (click it, or press keys 1 to 6). Selected tags show a ✓ and a heavier outline.
  3. Press Submit (or Enter). Read the verdict, the reason and the correct tags, then press Next item (or Enter).
  4. After item 10, read the score and the list of missed items. Start over deals a new shuffle for practice.

Keyboard: 1 Hot, 2 Wet, 3 Corrosive, 4 Particulate-laden, 5 Explosive atmosphere, 6 Clean; Enter submits, then goes to the next item. Tab reaches every tag, every ⓘ button and the action buttons.

Data label: "Illustrative applications", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

        height="567px"
        width="100%"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify ten application descriptions by every airstream condition they present (hot, wet, corrosive, particulate-laden, explosive atmosphere, or clean), matching the answer key on at least 8 of 10 (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read "The Airstreams Fans Handle" in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airstream
  • Hot, wet, corrosive and particulate-laden airstreams
  • Explosive atmosphere

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5-6 min): Tag all ten items on the first run, judging each condition separately against its definition.
  2. Review (2 min): For each missed item, say which definition you misapplied.
  3. Discuss (2 min): Name a combined airstream from your own territory and the questions you would ask about each of its conditions.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Each airstream has only one condition: the swimming pool hall, feed-mill elevator and laundry dryer items each need two tags, and a single tag is marked with the missing one.
  • Warm, humid air is "hot": the dishwashing, pool hall and laundry items are warm, and their feedback says warm is not hot.
  • Combustible dust is only a particulate problem: the grain dust item needs the explosive atmosphere tag too.
  • Any chemical exhaust is an explosive atmosphere: the chlorine storage room is corrosive only, while the solvent-recovery room with flammable vapors is explosive.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The end screen shows "Score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first run. Later runs are practice. Reading the tag definitions is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a paint booth exhaust carries solvent vapor and overspray. Which tags apply, and which product decisions does each one drive?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Corrosion - Wikipedia article on the chemical attack of metals, the basis of corrosive-airstream material choices.
  2. Dust explosion - Wikipedia article on why fine grain, wood and metal dusts are explosion hazards.
  3. Electrical equipment in hazardous areas - Wikipedia article on hazardous-location classes, divisions and groups for motors.
  4. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on high-temperature, wet-service, corrosion-resistant and spark-resistant construction.

docs.title: Density Ratio by Temperature and Altitude
docs.text: Run the Density Ratio by Temperature and Altitude MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The chart plots the density ratio, actual air density divided by the standard-air density of 0.075 lb/ft³, against airstream temperature from 0°F to 1,000°F. There is one curve per site elevation, using the barometric pressures from the chapter's table (standard atmosphere):

Elevation Barometric pressure Ratio at 70°F 0 ft 29.92 in. Hg 1.000 2,500 ft 27.31 in. Hg 0.913 5,000 ft 24.89 in. Hg 0.832 7,500 ft 22.65 in. Hg 0.757

Every point follows the chapter's density ratio equation:

density ratio = (Pb ÷ 29.92) × (530 ÷ (T + 460)), and density = 0.075 × ratio

with T in °F and Pb in in. Hg. A dotted line at 1.000 marks standard air. The orange diamond is the temperature marker (0 to 1,000°F in 10°F steps) on the elevation you choose; the line under the chart gives its density ratio to three decimals, its density in lb/ft³ to four decimals, and the two factors that make it up. Hovering any curve shows the same values.

Five challenges follow, in this order:

# Question Answer 1 Density ratio at 300°F, sea level? 0.697 2 Density ratio at 70°F, 5,000 ft? 0.832 3 Density ratio at 300°F, 5,000 ft? 0.580 4 Density ratio at 600°F, sea level? 0.500 5 A system needs 3.00 in. wg at 300°F, sea level. What standard-air pressure do you select from the catalog? 4.30 in. wg

A density ratio is correct within ±0.01 and a pressure within ±0.05 in. wg. You get two attempts. A wrong first answer shows the worked calculation; a second wrong answer shows the answer and counts the challenge as missed. While a challenge is open, the marker, the elevation list and the hover readouts are locked, so you calculate the value instead of reading it off the chart. When the challenge resolves, the chart marks its point on the right curve: a circle with ✓ for correct, a square with ✗ for missed. At the end the sim shows "n of 5 correct on first attempt" and the mastery line; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt. Exploring the chart is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Move the Temperature marker and switch the Elevation. Check that the ratio at 600°F is exactly half the ratio at 70°F, and that each elevation curve is the sea-level curve multiplied by a constant (its barometric factor).
  2. Press Start challenges. Type each value in the answer box and press Check (or Enter). A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: value." in a solid green box; a wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the worked calculation in a dashed red box.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter). After challenge 5, press See score to read the first-attempt score, the mastery line and any missed challenges.
  4. The marker and hover readouts unlock again: confirm each marked point. Start over clears the marks and the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Tab reaches the marker (arrow keys move it), the elevation list and every button. In the answer box, Enter checks; Enter again goes to the next challenge.

Data label: "Density ratio = (Pb ÷ 29.92) × (530 ÷ (T + 460)) · barometric pressures: Chapter 2 elevation table, standard atmosphere", under the chart.

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

<iframe src="https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/ch02-density-ratio-temperature-altitude/main.html"
        height="882px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the air density ratio for a given airstream temperature and site elevation, to within ±0.01, and use it to convert a required pressure into a standard-air catalog pressure (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the "Barometric Pressure", "Standard Air" and "Hot Airstreams" sections of Chapter 2.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Standard air (0.075 lb/ft³, 70°F, 29.92 in. Hg)
  • Barometric pressure and its fall with elevation
  • Air density and the density ratio equation
  • Hot airstreams, and the rule that pressure and power scale with the density ratio

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Read the ratio at 70°F, 300°F and 600°F on the sea-level curve; then switch to 5,000 ft and compare.
  2. Challenges (6-8 min): Work each challenge on paper first, writing the temperature in degrees Rankine (°F + 460).
  3. Review (2-3 min): Compare each marked point with your working. For challenge 5, say in words why the catalog pressure is higher than the job pressure.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Temperature in °F can be used without adding 460: challenges 1 and 4 and their feedback require 530 ÷ (T + 460); using 530 ÷ 300 gives a ratio above 1 that the chart shows cannot be right for hot air.
  • Hot air raises the pressure a fan develops: every curve falls as temperature rises.
  • To find the catalog pressure, multiply by the density ratio: challenge 5's feedback names 2.09 as the result of multiplying and explains that it would under-select the fan.
  • Altitude and temperature corrections cannot be combined: challenge 3 multiplies the 0.832 barometric factor by the 0.697 temperature factor, and the 5,000 ft curve shows the product at every temperature.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• At the end the sim shows "n of 5 correct on first attempt"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt. Moving the marker and hovering are exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a fan for a 400°F airstream at 2,500 ft draws 12.0 bhp on the catalog page. What does it draw in service at 400°F, and what does it draw on a cold start at 70°F? (0.913 × 530 ÷ 860 = 0.563, so 6.75 bhp hot; 0.913 × 12.0 = about 11.0 bhp cold at 2,500 ft.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Density of air - Wikipedia article on how air density depends on temperature and pressure, and on standard conditions.
  2. Barometric formula - Wikipedia article on how atmospheric pressure falls with altitude in the standard atmosphere.
  3. Standard conditions for temperature and pressure - Wikipedia article comparing reference conditions, including 70°F and 29.92 in. Hg.
  4. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan performance at non-standard air densities and high-temperature construction.

docs.title: Duct System Pressure Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Duct System Pressure Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js, fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html before pasting ch02-duct-system-pressure-explorer.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The sim draws one exhaust system in flow order: a hood, a 24 in. × 24 in. inlet duct (4.00 ft²), Station 1 at the fan inlet, the fan, Station 2 at the fan outlet, a 20 in. × 20 in. outlet duct (2.78 ft²) and a discharge stack. Three readout panels show velocity V, velocity pressure VP, static pressure SP and total pressure TP at each station, and fan total pressure FTP, fan static pressure FSP and air power AHP for the fan. Click any label in the schematic, or pick it under Definition of…, to read what that part is.

The system is illustrative, chosen so that 10,000 CFM reproduces the chapter's worked example. Air is standard air (0.075 lb/ft³). The model:

  • V1 = Q ÷ 4.00 and V2 = Q ÷ 2.78 (fpm); VP = (V ÷ 4005)² (in. wg)
  • TP1 = −0.81 × (Q ÷ 10,000)² and TP2 = +2.81 × (Q ÷ 10,000)² (the system resistance relation)
  • SP = TP − VP at each station; FTP = TP2 − TP1; FSP = FTP − VP2; AHP = Q × FTP ÷ 6356

Velocities are shown to the nearest 10 fpm, pressures to 0.01 in. wg and air power to 0.01 hp, all computed from unrounded intermediates.

Five challenges come first, in this order. The readout each one asks for (and any readout that would give it away) shows "?" until you check an answer:

# Question Answer Tolerance 1 At 10,000 CFM, what is the velocity in the inlet duct (fpm)? 2,500 fpm ±25 2 At 10,000 CFM the outlet velocity is 3,600 fpm. What is the outlet velocity pressure? 0.81 in. wg ±0.02 3 Inlet SP −1.20, inlet VP 0.39, outlet SP +2.00, outlet VP 0.81. What is the fan total pressure? 3.62 in. wg ±0.03 4 What is the air power at 10,000 CFM and 3.62 in. wg fan total pressure? 5.70 hp ±0.05 5 The airflow is raised to 12,000 CFM in the same system. What fan total pressure is now required? 5.21 in. wg ±0.05

You get two attempts at each. A wrong first answer shows the worked calculation and leaves one attempt; a second wrong answer shows the answer with the calculation, and the challenge counts as missed. Before challenge 5 the airflow moves to 12,000 CFM. After challenge 5, Explore mode unlocks the airflow slider (4,000 to 14,000 CFM in 500 CFM steps) and every value updates at once. Mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type a number in Your answer and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: value unit." in a solid green box, followed by the worked calculation. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the worked calculation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) for the next one. "Challenges correct: n of 5" counts first-attempt answers only.
  4. After challenge 5, press Start exploring. Move the airflow and check that SP1 is always negative, that TP1 is always smaller in magnitude than SP1, and that going from 5,000 to 10,000 CFM multiplies FTP by 4 and air power by 8. The panel shows the airflow, FTP and air-power ratios against 10,000 CFM. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, the buttons, the Definition of… list and the airflow slider; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative system · standard air, 0.075 lb/ft³", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate duct velocity, velocity pressure, total pressure, fan total pressure and air power for a simple exhaust duct system, to within the tolerance stated for each challenge (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the first half of Chapter 2.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airflow continuity equation and feet per minute
  • Velocity pressure and the velocity pressure equation
  • Static pressure, total pressure, fan total pressure and fan static pressure
  • Air power, duct system and the system resistance relation

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (6-8 min): Work each challenge on paper before typing an answer. Write every pressure with its sign.
  2. Review (2 min): For any missed challenge, compare your working with the worked calculation the sim shows.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Set the airflow to 5,000 and then 10,000 CFM and record FTP and air power at each. Confirm the ratios are 4 and 8. Then sweep the airflow and watch SP1 and TP1.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Inlet static pressure is added as a positive number: challenge 3 and its feedback keep the sign, and the Station 1 panel always shows a negative SP.
  • Velocity pressure is proportional to velocity: challenge 2 squares the velocity ratio, and the outlet VP is about double the inlet VP although the area is only 30% smaller.
  • A 20% airflow increase needs 20% more pressure: challenge 5's feedback names 3.62 × 1.20 as the wrong step, and Explore mode shows FTP × 1.44 at 12,000 CFM.
  • Static pressure always falls in the direction of flow: the readouts show SP rising from −1.20 to +2.00 across the fan while total pressure carries the energy budget.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Challenges correct: n of 5"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt. Moving the airflow slider is exploration, not evidence.
  • Ask the learner: a customer wants 30% more air from this system. By how much do the pressure and the air power rise? (1.69 and 2.20 times.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Dynamic pressure - Wikipedia article on the pressure of a moving fluid brought to rest, the basis of velocity pressure.
  2. Stagnation pressure - Wikipedia article on stagnation (total) pressure as the sum of static and dynamic pressure.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan performance, pressure and system terms.
  4. AMCA International - publisher of the fan application manuals and test standards that define fan total and fan static pressure.

docs.title: Bearing Life in Years by Operating Schedule
docs.text: Run the Bearing Life in Years by Operating Schedule MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A bearing's L-10 rating is given in hours: the operating hours at which 10 percent of a large group of identical bearings are expected to have failed. The L-50 life, or average life, is five times the L-10 life. A customer needs the rating in years of their own running schedule:

  • Hours per year = hours per day × days per week × 52
  • L-10 years = L-10 hours ÷ hours per year
  • L-50 years = 5 × L-10 hours ÷ hours per year

The bar chart shows five schedules, from around-the-clock service (24 h/day, 7 days/week, 8,736 h per year) down to 2 h/day, 5 days/week (520 h per year). Each schedule has an L-10 bar (solid) and an L-50 bar (light, with a heavy outline), and every bar carries its value. The vertical axis is a log scale, so a 4-year bar and a 900-year bar both stay readable; each gridline is 10 times the one below. Hover over or tap a bar to see the rating, the schedule, the hours per year and both lives.

The sim starts with three challenges, in this order:

# L-10 rating Schedule L-10 life 1 40,000 h 16 h/day, 5 days/week 9.6 years 2 40,000 h 24 h/day, 7 days/week 4.6 years 3 20,000 h 8 h/day, 5 days/week 9.6 years

The bars are hidden until you check your answer. An answer is correct when it is within ±0.1 year of the model value. You get two attempts: a wrong answer shows the calculation, and a second wrong answer shows the model value and the challenge counts as missed. When a challenge is resolved, the chart shows that rating, outlines the matching schedule, and prints the chart value next to your answer. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.

After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks the L-10 rating menu: 20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000 or 100,000 hours. All ten bars update at once. Every bar scales in proportion to the rating, and the 2 h/day bar is always about 17 times (16.8 times) the 24/7 bar. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type the L-10 life in years (one decimal is enough) and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: 9.6 years." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the calculation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) for challenges 2 and 3. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score, and the numbered chips show each challenge as ✓, ✗ or current.
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. The summary box shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Change the L-10 rating and compare the bars. Start over clears the score.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, the buttons and, after challenge 3, the rating menu; the arrow keys change the rating.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia, page 90 (L-10 and L-50 ratings) · 52-week year · Log scale", below the chart.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the L-10 and L-50 bearing life in years from a rated L-10 life in hours and an operating schedule, to within 0.1 year (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read "Bearing Life" in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Bearing, L-10 life and L-50 life (Chapter 3)
  • Operating schedule in hours per day and days per week

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5 min): Work each challenge with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the hours per year first, then the years.
  2. Exploration (3 min): At 40,000 h, read the L-50 years for 16 h/day, 5 days/week (48.1 years) and check that it is five times the L-10 bar. Switch to 80,000 h and confirm every bar doubled.
  3. Discussion (2 min): A customer says "40,000-hour bearings last 40,000 hours." Use the chart to explain what L-10 means and why their schedule matters.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• L-10 life is the life of every bearing: the chart labels it L-10, and the chapter's wording "by about 9.6 years, roughly 1 in 10 of these bearings will have failed" is the reading to use.
  • L-50 life is twice L-10: the L-50 bar sits five times higher on every schedule.
  • A rating in hours lasts the same number of years for every customer: the same rating spans from a few years to centuries across the five schedules.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 within ±0.1 year on the first attempt.
  • Reading the chart in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner to convert a 60,000-hour rating for a 24 h/day, 5 days/week schedule (9.6 years) without the chart.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rolling-element bearing - Wikipedia article covering bearing life ratings, including L10 life.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; page 90 defines L-10 and L-50 life and gives the example values used here.
  3. Bearing (mechanical) - Wikipedia overview of bearing types, including the ball and roller bearings used in fan pillow blocks.

docs.title: Belt Drive Speed Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Belt Drive Speed Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch03-belt-drive-speed-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A belt drive sets the fan speed with two grooved wheels: the motor sheave and the fan sheave. The fan speed follows from the motor speed and the ratio of the two pitch diameters:

  • Fan speed = motor speed × motor sheave pitch diameter ÷ fan sheave pitch diameter

The drawing shows both sheaves to scale, joined by a V-belt. The readout gives the ratio (motor sheave ÷ fan sheave) to three decimals, the fan speed in RPM and a label: "fan slower than motor", "fan same as motor" or "fan faster than motor". Belt slip is not modeled, so the sim gives the ideal speed.

The sim starts with three challenges, in this order:

# Motor speed Motor sheave Fan sheave Fan speed 1 1,760 RPM 5.0 in 8.0 in 1,100 RPM 2 1,760 RPM 6.0 in 12.0 in 880 RPM 3 1,160 RPM 9.0 in 6.0 in 1,740 RPM

Type the fan speed before the drive turns. An answer is correct when it is within ±10 RPM. You get two attempts: a wrong answer shows the calculation, and a second wrong answer shows the fan speed and the challenge counts as missed. When a challenge is resolved, the drive turns and the fan speed appears next to your answer. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.

After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks. Choose a motor speed (1,160, 1,760 or 3,500 RPM, illustrative nominal speeds) and move either sheave: the motor sheave from 3.0 to 12.0 inches and the fan sheave from 4.0 to 24.0 inches, in 0.2-inch steps. The drawing, ratio, label and fan speed update at once, from 145 RPM up to 10,500 RPM. The first time you enlarge the fan sheave, the sim notes "Bigger fan sheave: fan speed went down." Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1 and type the fan speed in RPM in Your answer. Press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: 1,100 RPM." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the calculation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score.
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Enlarge the fan sheave and watch the fan speed fall; then make the motor sheave larger than the fan sheave and read the label. Start over clears the score.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, every button, the motor speed menu and both sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative nominal motor speeds · Belt slip not modeled", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the fan shaft speed of a belt drive from the motor speed and the two sheave pitch diameters, to within ±10 RPM (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read "The Drive Train" in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Drive train, direct drive and belt drive (Chapter 3)
  • Sheave, V-belt and pitch diameter (Chapter 3)
  • Motor speed in RPM

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5 min): Solve the three drives with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the ratio for each one.
  2. Exploration (3 min): At 1,760 RPM, set the motor sheave to 5.0 inches and move the fan sheave from 8.0 to 16.0 inches. Record the fan speed at 8.0 and 16.0 and explain why it halves.
  3. Misconception check (2 min): Find two sheave pairs with the same difference (for example 5.0 and 8.0, and 9.0 and 12.0) and show that they give different fan speeds, because the ratio, not the difference, sets the speed.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A larger fan sheave makes the fan turn faster: Explore mode shows the fan speed fall as the fan sheave grows, and says so the first time.
  • A belt drive always slows the fan down: challenge 3 has a larger motor sheave, and the fan turns faster than the motor.
  • Fan speed depends on the difference between the sheave sizes: the readout shows the ratio, and the activity compares pairs with the same difference.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 within ±10 RPM on the first attempt.
  • Changing sheaves in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner which sheave to change, and in which direction, to speed up a fan by about 8 percent (the chapter's 5.0 to 5.4 inch motor sheave example: 1,100 to 1,188 RPM).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Belt (mechanical) - Wikipedia overview of belt drives, sheaves and speed ratios.
  2. Pulley - Wikipedia article on pulleys (sheaves) and belt and pulley systems.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; page 173 notes that belt-driven fans reach the exact point of rating through a sheave change.

docs.title: Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan Parts
docs.text: Run the Direct Drive Centrifugal Fan Parts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts twelve numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded view of a direct drive centrifugal fan (page 9). The fan is an Arrangement 8: the bearing pedestal is extended to carry the motor, and a coupling joins the motor shaft to the fan shaft, so the impeller turns at motor speed. An inset at the lower left shows the inlet side of the assembled fan with a flanged inlet.

The twelve parts are the inlet collar, inlet funnel, impeller, housing, outlet flange, access hole for mounting bolts, pedestal, bearings, shaft, coupling, motor and inlet flange. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. Where a part is small (the bearings, shaft and coupling), its marker sits just above it with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select the part that joins the motor shaft to the fan shaft.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 12 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 12".
  4. After the twelfth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (10 of 12), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 9", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the twelve labeled parts of an Arrangement 8 direct drive centrifugal fan on an exploded view, given each part's function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 3, sections "The Fan Housing", "The Impeller", "The Fan Inlet", "The Fan Outlet", "The Fan Shaft", "Bearings", "The Fan Motor" and "The Drive Train" (direct drive through a coupling, Arrangement 8).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all twelve parts. Sort them aloud into the air path (inlet collar, inlet funnel, impeller, housing, outlet flange), the connections (inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange) and the drive train and its support (shaft, bearings, coupling, motor, pedestal).
  2. Compare (2 min): Open the belt-driven exploded view in Exploded Centrifugal Fan. Which parts of that drive train are missing here, and which part replaces them?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all twelve parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The inlet collar and the inlet flange are the same connection: the collar is a plain sleeve that a duct slips over and clamps to, the flange is a drilled ring that bolts face to face (the inset shows it on the assembled fan).
  • A direct drive fan has no shaft or bearings of its own: in Arrangement 8 the fan keeps its own shaft and two bearings on the pedestal, and only the coupling links it to the motor.
  • The pedestal is just a stand for the motor: it carries the bearings and shaft, and Arrangement 8 extends it to carry the motor too.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a site asks for the fan to run slower than motor speed. Which part on this drawing would have to change, and what would replace it?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 9 is the direct drive exploded view used here, p. 174 describes Arrangement 8, p. 188 the inlet funnel, pp. 79-80 the shaft and p. 97 the bearings.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy - the section "The Drive Train", where this MicroSim is embedded, and the sections that define each part.
  4. Exploded Centrifugal Fan - the belt driven Arrangement 9 counterpart (FanPedia p. 10).

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 9. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan
docs.text: Run the Exploded View of a Belt-Driven Centrifugal Fan MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows a belt-driven single-width, single-inlet (SWSI) centrifugal fan in Arrangement 9, pulled apart along its shaft line the way an exploded view in FanPedia or a submittal drawing shows it. It names 14 parts, from the inlet collar and flanged inlet through the drive train to the pedestal.

The drawing is a simplified schematic drawn in code, modeled on the FanPedia page 10 exploded view. It is not to scale and does not show a specific Twin City Fan model.

The flanged inlet sits in its own "Inlet option" box because it is the alternative to the inlet collar. A fan ships with one or the other, not both.

The quiz has 10 prompts in a fixed order, with two attempts each. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Select any part to open its infobox. Only one infobox is open at a time. Each part you have opened gets a ✓ mark and a shaded label, and the counter shows how many of the 14 you have visited.
  2. Assemble / Explode. Press Assemble to slide the parts into place. The inlet funnel and impeller disappear inside the housing, and the shaft, bearings, sheave, belts and motor drop onto the pedestal. Press Explode to pull them apart again. Labels are shown only in the exploded view.
  3. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels are hidden and the drawing stays exploded. Ten prompts appear in a fixed order. Select the part that matches each one. You get two attempts per prompt:
    • Correct: you see "✓ Correct:" with the reason, and that part's label appears.
    • First miss: you see "✗ That is the …" naming the part you picked, with the reason for the correct answer, and you try again.
    • Second miss: the correct part is highlighted and marked "Answer", and the prompt counts as missed.
  4. Press Next prompt after each answer. After the tenth prompt, a summary shows your score ("Correct on first attempt: n of 10"), whether you reached mastery (9 of 10), and lists the prompts you missed or got on the second attempt, with their reasons. Press Start over to retake the quiz or Back to explore to review parts.
  5. Start over in the toolbar clears your visited parts and the quiz and returns to the exploded view in explore mode.

Keyboard: Tab moves between parts and buttons; Enter or Space selects a part. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Simplified schematic, not to scale · Source: FanPedia, page 10 (exploded view, Arrangement 9)", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify each of the 14 labeled parts in an exploded view of a belt-driven Arrangement 9 centrifugal fan when given the part's name or function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and facilities staff who will read exploded views and submittal drawings of centrifugal fans.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3, Basic Fan Anatomy, through the drive-train sections.
  • The terms exploded view, fan housing, impeller, inlet funnel, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange, shaft, bearing, sheave, V-belt, motor, slide base and pedestal.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 min): Open all 14 infoboxes. For each part, say out loud whether it touches the air.
  2. Assemble and explode (2 min): Press Assemble and watch where the funnel, impeller and drive parts go. Note that the bearings, sheave and motor end up outside the housing.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and answer the ten prompts without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the reasons for any missed prompts, return to explore mode for those parts, then retake the quiz.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The inlet funnel and the inlet collar are the same part. The funnel shapes the air into the impeller; the collar is a duct connection.
  • The pedestal is part of the housing. It is a separate support for the bearings and shaft.
  • The fan sheave and the motor sheave are the same size. Their ratio sets fan speed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Correct on first attempt: n of 10"; mastery is 9 of 10 on the first attempt in quiz mode.
  • Opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration and does not count as evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; page 10 is the exploded view of belt-driven centrifugal fans, Arrangement 9, that this drawing is modeled on.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy - the sections on the housing, impeller, inlet, outlet and drive train, which cite FanPedia pages 59, 79, 90 and 188 for the infobox definitions.

docs.title: Follow the Airflow Through a Centrifugal Fan
docs.text:
Run the Follow the Airflow Through a Centrifugal Fan MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch03-follow-the-airflow.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The drawing is a side view of a ducted, belt-driven SWSI centrifugal fan in Arrangement 9, the fan in the FanPedia exploded view on page 10. Air enters from the duct on the left and leaves through the duct at the top. Eight numbered slot buttons sit along the air path, and a bin at the top right is labeled "Not in the air path".

Eleven part cards start in a shuffled pile. Eight of them are stages the air passes through, in this order:

Slot Part Why 1 Inlet ductwork Air arrives from the upstream duct. 2 Inlet flange (with companion flange) The bolted joint where the duct meets the fan inlet. 3 Inlet funnel Funnels the air smoothly into the eye of the impeller. 4 Impeller The only part that adds energy to the air; air enters at the center and is thrown outward between the blades. 5 Housing scroll Collects the air leaving the impeller and guides it toward the outlet. 6 Cutoff The point of the scroll closest to the impeller, just before the outlet. 7 Outlet flange The bolted joint where the fan outlet meets the downstream duct. 8 Outlet ductwork Air leaves the fan system through the downstream duct.

The other three, the shaft, the bearings and the motor, belong in "Not in the air path": in an Arrangement 9 fan the bearings sit on the pedestal and the motor beside it, outside the airstream, and the shaft only passes through the housing side.

Each slot holds one card; the bin holds any number. A submission counts only when all 11 cards are placed. You get two submissions. Correct cards lock with a ✓. On the first submission, wrong cards go back to the pile marked ✗, with their Why text and the misconception the placement suggests (for example, that air enters the impeller at the blade tips, or that the cutoff is at the inlet). After the second submission every card is shown in its correct place, missed cards are marked ✗, and the air animates once from slot 1 to slot 8, naming each part as it arrives. Mastery is all 11 cards correct within two submissions.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Select a card in the pile, then select a numbered slot or Not in the air path. The card shows where it went ("3 · Inlet funnel", or "Out · Motor" for the bin). Placing a card in an occupied slot sends the card that was there back to the pile.
  2. To move a placed card, select it (or its slot) and choose a new place, or press Back to pile.
  3. When all 11 cards are placed, press Submit. The status line shows "Cards correct: n of 11". Select any card marked ✗ to read why, place it again and press Submit (2 of 2).
  4. After the final submission, watch the air path, select any card to read its feedback, press Replay airflow to see it again, or Start over for a new shuffle.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the cards, the slots and the buttons; Enter or Space selects. With a card selected, keys 1-8 place it in that slot, 0 (or N) puts it in "Not in the air path", P returns it to the pile and Escape deselects.

Data label: "Belt-driven SWSI fan, Arrangement 9 (FanPedia p. 10)", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will list, in airflow order, the eight parts that air passes through in a ducted, belt-driven SWSI centrifugal fan, and set aside the three parts that stay out of the air path (Bloom: Remember, verb: list).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read "The Fan Housing" through "The Fan Outlet" in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan housing, housing scroll and cutoff (Chapter 3)
  • Impeller, inlet funnel, inlet flange and outlet flange (Chapter 3)
  • Shaft, bearing and motor, as named in the chapter introduction

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Placement (5 min): Place all 11 cards from memory and submit. Do not look back at the chapter before the first submission.
  2. Correction (3 min): Read the feedback on every ✗ card, place them again and submit.
  3. Recall (2 min): Watch the airflow animation and say each part's name out loud as the air reaches it, as the chapter's mascot tip suggests.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Air enters the impeller at the blade tips: placing the impeller before the inlet funnel brings the reminder that air enters at the center, through the funnel.
  • The cutoff is at the inlet: placing the cutoff in slots 1 to 3 brings the reminder that it is just upstream of the outlet.
  • Every part of a fan touches the air: placing the shaft, bearings or motor in the air path brings the reminder that they sit outside the airstream in an Arrangement 9 fan.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Cards correct: n of 11" after each submission; mastery is all 11 cards correct within two submissions.
  • Moving cards around before a submission is exploration, not evidence. Follow up by asking the learner to name the slot just before and just after the impeller without the drawing.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia article on centrifugal fans, their impellers, housings and the path the air takes.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; page 10 shows the exploded view of a belt-driven Arrangement 9 centrifugal fan used here.
  3. Duct (flow) - Wikipedia overview of the ductwork that carries air to and from a fan.

docs.title: Which Housing Feature Does the Job?
docs.text:
Run the Which Housing Feature Does the Job? MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch03-housing-feature-classifier.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A customer calls with a request, and you choose the housing feature or opening accessory that does the job. There are twelve requests, always in the same order, each with four options. The wrong options are features that share a location or a word with the right one, such as a bird screen and a safety screen, or an inlet collar and an inlet flange.

# Request (short) Feature that does the job 1 Look at the impeller between cleanings without opening a door Inspection port 2 Pull the impeller without disconnecting the ducts Pie split housing 3 Fit through a doorway smaller than the housing 3-way split housing 4 Open the door on an insulated fan Raised access door 5 Flexible sleeve slips over the inlet with clamps Inlet collar 6 Part for the duct so the bolt holes match the fan inlet Companion flange 7 Downstream duct bolts rigidly to the discharge Outlet flange 8 Birds nest in the roof exhauster's discharge Bird screen 9 Panel fan inlet within reach of people on a ladder Safety screen 10 Cold air blows in through the idle wall fan at night Backdraft damper 11 Fume exhaust must go straight up, away from the roof Stack cap 12 No bolted seams in the scroll Welded housing

You get two attempts per request. A correct choice shows "✓ Correct:" and the reason. A wrong first choice does not explain the option you picked; instead a hint names the job of the right feature without naming it (for request 1: "Think of the smallest opening that still lets you see inside."). A second wrong choice reveals the answer with its reason, and the request counts as missed. After request 12, a summary lists every request with your choice, the correct option and the reason. Retry missed runs a practice round over the missed requests; it is not scored, and the first-attempt score is kept. Mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the request in the speech bubble and press one of the four options (or keys 1-4).
  2. A correct choice turns green with a ✓. A wrong first choice is marked ✗ and a hint appears; choose again. After a second miss the right option is marked ✓.
  3. Press Next request (or Enter). "Requests correct: n of 12" keeps the running score, and the numbered chips show each request as ✓, ✗ or current.
  4. After request 12, press See summary. Read the first-attempt score, the mastery line and the list of every request (scroll the list). Press Retry missed to practice the misses, or Start over to begin again.

Keyboard: keys 1-4 choose an option, Enter goes to the next request; Tab reaches every option and button, and the summary list scrolls with the arrow keys once focused.

Data label: "Illustrative job-site requests", at the bottom left of the drawing.
