docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify 12 job-site requests by the housing feature or opening accessory that meets each one, choosing from four options per request (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read Chapter 3 through "Putting It All Together".

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Welded, bolted and split housings; access door and inspection port (Chapter 3)
  • Inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange and companion flange (Chapter 3)
  • Bird and safety screens, backdraft and gravity dampers, stack cap and hood (Chapter 3)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classification (6-8 min): Answer all twelve requests. Before choosing, say which job the request needs done (view, reach in, connect, protect, close, discharge or seal).
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary and the reason for every miss.
  3. Practice (2-4 min): Press Retry missed and answer the missed requests again.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Bird screens and safety screens are interchangeable: requests 8 and 9 offer both, and the hints separate "meant for animals" from "meant for people".
  • An inspection port allows cleaning and impeller removal: request 1 pairs it with the access door.
  • A collar and a flange are the same connection: requests 5 to 7 separate slip-fit from bolted.
  • A backdraft damper controls airflow while the fan runs: request 10's hint, "acts only when the fan stops", corrects it.
  • A split housing is only for maintenance: request 3 uses a 3-way split for a tight opening.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Requests correct: n of 12" counts requests solved on either attempt. The summary shows "First-attempt score: n of 12" and the mastery line; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.
  • The Retry missed round is practice and does not change the score. Follow up by asking the learner to write one new request for each feature they missed.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Damper (flow) - Wikipedia article on dampers, including backdraft (gravity) dampers.
  2. Flange - Wikipedia article on flanged connections and companion flanges.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on housing construction, access doors, split housings and fan accessories.

docs.title: Induction Motor Parts
docs.text: Run the Induction Motor Parts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts ten numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded view of a typical electric induction motor (page 69). The motor is pulled apart along its shaft: at the left the cooling parts of a totally enclosed fan cooled (TEFC) motor, in the middle the frame with the stator windings inside it, and at the right the rotor assembly with its bearings and the front endplate.

The ten parts are the fan cover, endplates, nameplate, stator, rotor assembly, external fan, conduit box, frame, motor bearings and motor shaft. The stator, rotor assembly (with its motor shaft), motor bearings, endplates, conduit box and nameplate are the parts Chapter 3 names; the fan cover, external fan and the ribbed frame belong to the TEFC enclosure described in Chapter 14. On a wide screen the labels sit in two strips, above and below the drawing, with leader lines; on a narrow screen they move below it as a numbered list. The motor bearings and the motor shaft are small, so their markers sit in the white space below them with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select where the power wiring connects.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 10".
  4. After the tenth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 69", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the ten labeled parts of an electric induction motor on an exploded view, given each part's function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3, section "The Fan Motor" (the induction motor and its parts).
  • Optional: Chapter 14, sections "Induction Motor", "The Motor Nameplate", "TEFC Motor" and "Conduit Box".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten parts. Sort them aloud into the parts that turn with the shaft (rotor assembly, motor shaft, external fan), the parts that hold and support them (stator, frame, endplates, motor bearings), and the parts you deal with on the outside (nameplate, conduit box, fan cover).
  2. Trace the power (2 min): Starting at the conduit box, name the parts the electrical energy passes through until it leaves the motor as rotation at the shaft end.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all ten parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The rotor is wired to the supply like the stator: in an induction motor the rotor current is induced by the stator's magnetic field, so there is no electrical connection to the rotor.
  • The external fan cools the windings directly: on a TEFC motor it blows air over the outside surface of the motor only; the ribs on the frame give that air more surface.
  • The motor bearings sit in the frame: they support the rotor at each end, inside the endplates.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a motor arrives and the paperwork does not match the order. Which part on this drawing tells you what was actually shipped?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 69 is the induction motor exploded view used here and names its parts, p. 68 defines the induction motor, and p. 73 describes the TEFC enclosure with its external fan and fan cover.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy - the section "The Fan Motor", where this MicroSim is embedded.
  4. Chapter 14: Fan Motors and Enclosures - the sections "Induction Motor", "The Motor Nameplate", "TEFC Motor" and "Conduit Box".

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 69. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Airflow Path Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Airflow Path Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch04-airflow-path-explorer.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows seven fan configurations, one at a time, as side-view drawings with the shaft horizontal and the air coming in from the left. No airflow is drawn at first. For each fan you predict two directions, relative to the shaft:

  • Impeller exit: parallel to the shaft, at a right angle to the shaft, or diagonal (between parallel and right angle).
  • Fan exit: parallel to the shaft, at a right angle to the shaft through one outlet, or outward in all directions around the impeller.

When you commit both predictions, an animation shows the air entering along the shaft, passing through the impeller and leaving the fan, and each prediction is marked. On the tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans the particles also rotate around the shaft to show swirl; on the vaneaxial fan the swirl stops at the guide vanes.

# Configuration Impeller exit Fan exit 1 SWSI housed centrifugal fan in a scroll housing At a right angle At a right angle, through one outlet 2 DWDI housed centrifugal fan in a scroll housing At a right angle At a right angle, through one outlet 3 Plenum fan (unhoused centrifugal) in an air handler cabinet At a right angle Outward in all directions 4 Tubular inline centrifugal fan with straightening vanes At a right angle Parallel 5 Tubeaxial fan (no guide vanes) Parallel Parallel 6 Vaneaxial fan (guide vanes downstream) Parallel Parallel 7 Mixed flow fan in a tubular housing with straightening vanes Diagonal Parallel

The fans come in this fixed order. Each prediction gets one attempt, so the 14 predictions are all first attempts, and mastery is 12 of 14. Replaying the animation is exploration and is never scored. The paths follow FanPedia pp. 4–7 (fan types), p. 186 (axial versus centrifugal impellers) and the exploded views on pp. 15–17; the drawings are schematic, and the animation speed and particle counts are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the fan's name and study the drawing: where are the inlet, the impeller, the housing or tube, any vanes and the outlet?
  2. Choose a direction in Impeller exit and in Fan exit, then press Commit predictions (or Enter). You cannot change a prediction once it is committed.
  3. Watch the animation. Each prediction is marked "✓ Correct." or "✗ Not quite. The answer is …", and the reason appears below. After the animation, arrows tagged "impeller exit" and "fan exit" stay on the drawing. Press Replay animation (or R) as often as you like.
  4. Press Next fan (or Enter). After fan 7, the summary shows your first-attempt score out of 14, whether you reached mastery, and every prediction you missed with your choice and the answer. Press Start over to reset the score and begin again at fan 1.

Keyboard: Tab reaches the two lists and the buttons; arrow keys change a list; Enter commits the predictions, then goes to the next fan; R replays the animation. Feedback is also announced to screen readers.

Data label: "Paths: FanPedia pp. 4–7, 15–17, 186 · Animation illustrative", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify seven fan configurations by the direction air leaves the impeller and the direction air leaves the fan, relative to the fan shaft (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: impeller, fan shaft, fan housing.
  • Chapter 4: fan family, centrifugal fan, axial fan, mixed flow fan, scroll housing, unhoused centrifugal fan, plenum fan, tubular housing, guide vanes, straightening vanes, inline centrifugal fan.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): Work through the seven fans in order, committing both predictions before each animation.
  2. Compare (3 min): In the summary, read the notice about fans 4, 6 and 7. Which part of each fan decides its family, and which part decides where the air leaves?
  3. Discuss (3 min): Why does the plenum fan's air go out in all directions, while the SWSI fan's air leaves through one outlet, when both impellers are centrifugal?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A fan in a round, straight-through tube must be an axial fan: fans 4 and 7 have tubes and leave the fan parallel to the shaft, but their impellers send air out radially or diagonally.
  • Air leaves a centrifugal fan in the same direction it leaves the impeller in every case: fan 4's impeller exit is at a right angle, but its fan exit is parallel to the shaft.
  • Guide vanes add pressure by speeding the air up: on the vaneaxial fan the animation shows the vanes stopping the swirl without changing the main direction.
  • A mixed flow fan discharges at a diagonal out of the fan: only the impeller exit is diagonal; the tube and vanes return the air to the duct direction.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running count "Predictions correct: n of 14"; one attempt per prediction, so every prediction is a first attempt. Mastery is 12 of 14.
  • Watching and replaying the animation is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer calls a fan "axial" because it is a round tube in a duct. What would you look at to check, and what would you expect to see for a tubular inline centrifugal fan?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; pp. 4–7 describe the fan types, p. 186 compares axial and centrifugal impellers, and the exploded views on pp. 15–17 show where the guide vanes and straightening vanes sit.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans - the fan families, housings, guide vanes and straightening vanes behind every configuration.
  4. Twin City Fan & Blower - current catalogs for the tubeaxial, vaneaxial, inline centrifugal and mixed flow lines.

docs.title: Fan Family Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Fan Family Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch04-fan-family-sorter.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The sorter deals fifteen current Twin City Fan product lines, one card at a time, in a shuffled order. Each card shows a model designation and a short description of the fan: the wheel or impeller, the housing, the mounting and sometimes the application. The cards never name the family. You decide whether each line is Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow from the clues about how air passes through the impeller.

Several cards are look-alikes on purpose. A tubular inline centrifugal fan sits next to a tubeaxial in the same kind of round tube; a centrifugal roof exhauster and an axial roof ventilator both sit on a roof; two lab exhaust fans belong to two different families. The relevant clue is always the airflow path through the impeller: in along the shaft and out at a right angle (centrifugal), in and out along the shaft (axial), or out on a diagonal (mixed flow). Housing shape, roof location and application name are distractors.

Each placement is final. The card locks into the bin you chose, is marked correct or incorrect, and the reason appears beneath it. Only first placements count toward the score.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the face-up card and press Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow (or the keys 1, 2 or 3).
  2. Read the feedback under the card. A correct placement reads "✓ Correct: family." and an incorrect one reads "✗ This one is family.", each followed by the reason. Correct cards get a solid green border and incorrect ones a dashed red border, so the verdict never depends on color alone; screen readers hear the verdict too.
  3. Press Next card (or Enter) to turn up the next card. The placed card stays in its bin as a chip marked with a check or a cross.
  4. After the fifteenth card, press Show summary. The summary shows the score as "Correct: n of 15", the mastery line, a per-family tally and every misplaced card with its correct family and reason. Use More misses to page through a long list.
  5. Press Sort again to reshuffle all fifteen cards and reset the score.

Keyboard: keys 1, 2 and 3 place the card in Centrifugal, Axial or Mixed flow; Enter (or N) turns up the next card. Tab reaches every button, and Enter or Space presses the focused one.

Data label: "Source: Twin City Fan product catalog, tcf.com, retrieved 2026-10-08", at the bottom left of the drawing, with the keyboard hint when it fits.

docs.text:

        height="612px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate fifteen Twin City Fan product lines into the centrifugal, axial and mixed flow families from a short description of each, correctly placing at least 13 of 15 on the first placement (Bloom: Analyze, verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and plant staff who need to identify fans by family. This is an adult professional-development activity.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes for one sort, plus 5 minutes of discussion.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: From Chapter 4: fan family, centrifugal fan, axial fan, mixed flow fan, scroll housing, tubular housing, guide vanes, unhoused centrifugal fans (plenum and plug types), inline centrifugal fan, panel fan, power roof ventilator, centrifugal roof exhauster, roof ventilator, wall mounted fan and laboratory fume exhaust fan.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. First sort (5 to 8 min): Each learner sorts all fifteen cards alone, without notes. Mastery is 13 of 15 on the first placement.
  2. Diagnose the misses (3 to 5 min): For each misplaced card in the summary, the learner names the clue that misled them: housing shape, roof location or application name.
  3. Discussion (5 min): Compare the look-alike pairs. Why are TSL and TD both in a round tube but in different families? Why are DCRD and TUD both roof fans but in different families? Why do BCIFE and TVIFE, both induced flow lab exhaust fans, land in different families?
  4. Second sort (optional): Learners who scored below 13 review the chapter sections on tubular housings and power roof ventilators, then press Sort again.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any fan in a tubular housing is axial (TSL, QSL and QCLB are not).
  • Any roof fan, or any power roof ventilator, is centrifugal (TUD is axial).
  • Lab exhaust fans are their own family (BCIFE is centrifugal; TVIFE is mixed flow).
  • A fan without a housing cannot be centrifugal (plenum and plug fans are).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Score of 13 or more of 15 on the first sort shows mastery; the summary reads "Mastery reached."
  • For each miss, the learner can state the airflow-path clue on the card that identifies the correct family.
  • Follow-up question: given a new model description that names only a "round tube" and "vanes," what extra information would you need to name the family?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan, current product catalog pages on tcf.com (products: centrifugal fans, plenum fans, plug fans, inline centrifugal fans, axial fans, wall mounted fans, roof ventilators, centrifugal roof and wall exhausters, mixed flow fans, laboratory and fume exhaust fans), retrieved 2026-10-08 - source of the model designations and their family groupings.
  2. Twin City Fan, FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (2021), pp. 4-8, 17 and 32 - source of the housing and impeller descriptions.
  3. Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans - the chapter this sorter closes.

docs.title: Parts of a Centrifugal Scroll Housing

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a drawing of a single width, single inlet (SWSI) housed centrifugal fan seen from the inlet side. Part of the inlet-side sheet is cut away so you can see the impeller inside the scroll, and an inset shows a section through the inlet, where the inlet flange, inlet collar and inlet funnel sit one behind the other. Ten parts are outlined with dashed lines: the housing scroll, housing side, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet funnel, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet (discharge) flange, framing and pedestal.

The drawing is a simplified illustration based on FanPedia p. 60 (the SWSI housing construction drawing) and p. 59 (housing features). It is not to scale and is not a specific Twin City Fan model.

The quiz names each of the 10 parts once, in a shuffled order, and you click where that part is. You get two attempts per part. Only first-attempt answers count toward the score, and mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Hover over an outlined part to see its name; click it to open its infobox. Parts you have opened get a ✓ mark and keep their label, and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels disappear and a prompt such as "Click the cutoff." appears above the drawing. Click that part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" and the part name. The part keeps a solid outline and its label for the rest of the quiz.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ That is the" part you clicked, then "Try again."
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the correct part is highlighted and marked "Answer", its infobox text is shown, and the item counts as missed.
    • Clicking an empty area of the drawing does nothing and uses no attempt.
  3. Press Next part after each answer. The toolbar shows "First-attempt correct: n of 10".
  4. After the tenth part, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (9 of 10), and every missed part with its infobox text. Press Retake quiz to reshuffle and start again with the score reset, or Back to explore to review.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the parts (outlet flange, cutoff, scroll, side, wiper bar, framing, pedestal, then the inset parts) and the buttons; Enter or Space selects a part. After an answer, focus moves to Next part, so Enter goes on.

Narrow screens: when the drawing is narrower than about 640 px, the callouts become numbers, and the names of the parts you have opened appear in a key list below the drawing.

Data label: "Simplified illustration, not to scale · Based on FanPedia pp. 59–60 (SWSI housing)", shown below the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will identify the ten named parts of a single width, single inlet centrifugal scroll housing on a drawing of the fan (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 4, section "Scroll Housings": scroll housing, housing scroll, housing side, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet funnel, inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet (discharge) flange, framing and pedestal.
  • Chapter 2: velocity pressure and static pressure, for the idea that the growing scroll slows the air and recovers static pressure.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Hover over and open all ten parts. For each one, say whether it shapes the airflow (scroll, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet funnel), connects to ductwork (inlet collar, inlet flange, outlet flange) or holds the fan up (housing side, framing, pedestal).
  2. Trace (2 min): Put a finger on the cutoff and follow the scroll the way the gap grows. Which way does the impeller turn, seen from this side?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and locate all ten parts without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Retake quiz for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The scroll housing is only a protective cover: the scroll's infobox explains that its growing passage slows the air and recovers static pressure.
  • The cutoff and the outlet flange are the same thing: they are separate parts at opposite ends of the outlet, the cutoff inside the housing next to the impeller tips and the flange on the outside rim where the duct bolts on.
  • The inlet collar and the inlet funnel are the same part: the inset shows the collar as the outside duct connection and the funnel as the curved piece that guides air into the impeller eye.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt correct: n of 10"; mastery is 9 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Hovering and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a technician reports a "dented bolting rim where the duct leaves the fan." Which part is it, and why is it not the cutoff?

  3. Chapter 4: Centrifugal, Axial and Mixed Flow Fans - the section "Scroll Housings", which defines every part in this drawing.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts eleven numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded views of vaneaxial fans (page 16). The two drawings on the left are direct drive fans: the motor sits inside the tube, in the airstream, with the impeller on its shaft. The two on the right are belt driven fans: the motor sits on a motor base on top of the tube, and a belt runs down through a belt tube to the fan shaft in the middle of the tube. The upper pair is pulled apart so the guide vanes and the inside of the tube show.

The eleven parts are the tubular housing, guide vanes, shaft, impeller, motor, motor support, motor base, impeller access door, sheave, belt tube and bearing housing. On a wide screen the labels sit in two columns, left and right of the drawing, with leader lines; on a narrower screen (including the chapter page) they move below it as a numbered list. The shaft and the sheave are small, so their markers sit just beside them with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job or its look ("Select the passage that shelters the belt in the airstream.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 9 of 11 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 11 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 11".
  4. After the eleventh prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (9 of 11), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 16", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the eleven labeled parts of direct drive and belt driven vaneaxial fans on FanPedia's exploded views, given each part's function or appearance (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 4, sections "Axial Fans" (tubeaxial and vaneaxial fans), "Tubular Housings" and "Guide Vanes".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all eleven parts. Sort them aloud into the parts every fan on the page has (tubular housing, guide vanes, impeller, shaft, motor, impeller access door), the part only the direct drive fans need (motor support) and the parts only the belt driven fans need (motor base, sheave, belt tube, bearing housing).
  2. Compare (2 min): Look at the two left drawings and the two right drawings. Where does the motor sit in each, and what keeps the belt out of the airstream on the belt driven fan?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all eleven parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A vaneaxial fan is just a tubeaxial fan with a different impeller: the difference is the vane section, the fixed guide vanes downstream of the impeller that straighten the swirling air.
  • The guide vanes turn with the impeller: they are fixed in the housing; only the impeller rotates.
  • A belt driven axial fan has its motor in the airstream like a direct drive one: the motor sits outside the tube on a motor base, and only the belt passes through the airstream, sheltered by the belt tube.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 11"; mastery is 9 of 11 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer needs the motor out of a hot or dirty airstream. Which of the two drive types on this drawing would you start from, and which parts make that possible?

docs.title: Lab Exhaust Entrained Flow Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Lab Exhaust Entrained Flow Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A laboratory exhaust fan dilutes fume hood air twice. Bypass air enters through the bypass air plenum and mixes with the contaminated air before the fan, so it passes through the impeller. Entrained air is pulled into the plume by the jet leaving the nozzle, so it never passes through the impeller. The flow diagram shows all four flows; the MicroSim uses the chapter's three equations:

  • Fan flow = contaminated air + bypass flow
  • Total flow = fan flow + entrained flow
  • Plume concentration = hood concentration × contaminated air ÷ total flow

Three illustrative cases come in a fixed order, all at a hood concentration of 100 ppm:

Case Contaminated (CFM) Bypass (CFM) Entrained (CFM) Fan flow (CFM) Total flow (CFM) Plume (ppm) 1 8,000 2,000 7,000 10,000 17,000 47.1 2 6,000 0 9,000 6,000 15,000 40.0 3 12,000 4,000 0 16,000 16,000 75.0

For each case you type all three values and press Check. Flows must equal the model value exactly; the plume concentration (rounded to 0.1 ppm) is correct within ±0.5 ppm. Each value has two attempts. A correct value reads "✓ Correct: ."; a first wrong attempt reads "✗ Not yet. Check which air passes through the impeller."; a second wrong attempt shows the case's explanation, reveals the value and counts it as missed. As each value is settled, the diagram fills it in. The running count reads "Values correct: n of 9"; mastery is all nine values correct with at most two attempts each.

After case 3, Explore mode unlocks four sliders (contaminated air, bypass flow, entrained flow and hood concentration). Fan flow, total flow and plume concentration update at once. The first time you double the entrained flow, the sim shows the plume concentration before and after, and that it does not halve.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the givens on the diagram: hood air and its concentration, bypass air and entrained air.
  2. Type fan flow, total flow and plume concentration in the three boxes, then press Check (or Enter).
  3. Fix any value marked ✗ and check again; a value missed twice is revealed with the explanation.
  4. Press Next case. After case 3, press Start exploring.
  5. In Explore mode, move the sliders. Try doubling the entrained flow, then setting bypass or entrained flow to zero. Case 1 values resets the sliders; Start over clears the score.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the boxes, buttons and sliders. Enter in an answer box checks all three values; Enter again goes to the next case. Arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · Flow definitions: FanPedia pp. 4, 6", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the fan flow, total flow and plume concentration of a laboratory exhaust fan from its contaminated, bypass and entrained flows, with flows exact and concentration within 0.5 ppm (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Contaminated air, bypass flow, fan flow, entrained flow and total flow
  • Concentration in ppm
  • The three equations in "Entrained Flow in Laboratory Exhaust" in Chapter 5

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (8 min): Work the three cases. Before typing, point to the air that passes through the impeller.
  2. Compare (2 min): Note that case 2 has fan flow equal to the hood air (no bypass) and case 3 has total flow equal to fan flow (no entrainment).
  3. Explore (5 min): Double the entrained flow and read the before and after concentrations. Then trade entrained air for bypass air at the same total and compare the fan flow.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the fan selected for the fan flow and not for the total flow?
  2. Bypass air and entrained air both dilute the plume. What does each cost the owner?
  3. Why does doubling the entrained flow not halve the plume concentration?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The fan must be sized for the total flow, including entrained air: every case asks for fan flow and total flow separately.
  • Entrained air passes through the impeller: the diagram joins entrained air above the nozzle, and case 2 shows fan flow equal to the hood air.
  • Only one of bypass and entrained air reduces the plume concentration: case 3 shows bypass air alone diluting the plume, and the plume equation uses the total flow.
  • Doubling the entrained flow halves the plume concentration: Explore mode shows the before and after values the first time you double it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running count shown as "Values correct: n of 9"; mastery is all nine values correct with at most two attempts each.
  • Explore mode is not scored.
  • Follow-up: a lab adds a second fume hood; ask learners which of the three results changes first and why.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, pp. 4 and 6 (bypass air plenum, entrained flow through the nozzle or windband, lab exhaust fans). PDF
  2. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia online - the same encyclopedia in web form.
  3. Twin City Fan. Laboratory exhaust fans (TVIFE, QIFE, BAIFE, BCIFE induced flow fans; QFE and TFE venturi nozzle fans) - current catalog lines and their discharge velocity and plume height ratings.
  4. Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans, "Entrained Flow in Laboratory Exhaust" - the worked example that case 1 repeats.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts nine numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded views of two centrifugal roof exhausters (page 19). The left column is an upblast unit and the right column a downblast unit, each stacked from the top of the fan down to the roof curb it sits on. Both columns show a direct drive and a belt driven motor plate side by side.

The nine parts are the ones FanPedia names for both roof exhauster types: motor cover, motor housing, motor, bird screen, impeller, shroud, skirt, curb cap and roof curb. Each marker sits on one example of the part, in whichever column shows it best. On a wide screen the labels sit in two columns with leader lines, left and right of the drawing; on a narrower screen, including the chapter page, they move below it as a numbered list. The motor is small, so its marker sits just above it with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select the drum that encloses the motor.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 9 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 9".
  4. After the ninth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 9), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the nine labeled parts of a centrifugal roof exhauster on FanPedia's upblast and downblast exploded views, given each part's function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 5, sections "On the Roof and Through the Wall", "Upblast Discharge" and "Downblast Discharge".
  • Chapter 3, sections "The Impeller" and "The Fan Motor".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all nine parts. Sort them aloud into the parts that move or guide the air (impeller, shroud, skirt, motor cover), the parts that carry or shelter the drive (motor, motor housing), and the parts that protect the opening or mount the fan on the roof (bird screen, curb cap, roof curb).
  2. Compare (3 min): Find each marked part in the other column too. Which parts look nearly the same on the upblast and the downblast unit, and which part changes the direction the air leaves?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all nine parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The motor cover is only a rain lid: on a downblast unit the mushroom-shaped cover turns the rising air back down so it spills out around the base.
  • The curb cap and the roof curb are the same part: the curb cap is the fan's flat base plate, and it rests on and covers the roof curb, the raised frame built into the roof around the opening.
  • Upblast and downblast exhausters are built from different parts: FanPedia's exploded view names the same nine parts for both types; what differs is where the air is sent after it leaves the impeller.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 9"; mastery is 8 of 9 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer asks for a downblast unit on a kitchen hood. Which part on this drawing sends the exhaust back toward the roof, and which discharge type should the quote use instead?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 19 is the roof exhauster exploded view used here, p. 5 describes the roof ventilator configurations by discharge direction and p. 181 the butterfly gravity damper on upblast units.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 5: Roof, Wall and Specialty Exhaust Fans - the section "Downblast Discharge", where this MicroSim is embedded, and "Upblast Discharge".
  4. Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer - predict the air path through roof and wall units on schematic cutaways.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 19. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Roof and Wall Exhaust Path Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Roof and wall ventilation units differ mainly in the parts above the impeller: an open top, a motor cover, a hood, a louvered penthouse, a short stack or a wall mounting. Those parts decide where the exhaust air goes. This MicroSim shows seven units one at a time, in an order shuffled once per session, as schematic cutaways with the discharge hidden. You predict the path, then the sim draws the true path with arrows for the air entering and leaving the unit.

Unit Path Upblast centrifugal roof exhauster Straight up Downblast centrifugal roof exhauster Up, then down and out Hooded roof exhauster Up, then down and out Louvered roof exhauster Up, then down and out Low profile roof ventilator, upblast version Straight up Centrifugal wall exhauster Straight out from the wall Gravity relief ventilator Up, then down and out

Each unit gets one attempt. A correct prediction reads "✓ Correct: ." followed by the reason; an incorrect one reads "✗ Not quite: this unit's air goes ." followed by the reason. The running score reads "Paths correct: n of 7". After the seventh unit a yes/no question asks whether a gravity relief ventilator needs a fan to move air. Mastery is 6 of 7 paths plus the gravity question, all on the first attempt.

Clicking a part of a cutaway (or choosing it in Read a part) shows its name and definition. That is exploration and is never scored. After the gravity question a summary table lists every unit, your prediction and the correct path, and the Review list reopens any unit's cutaway and path without changing the score.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Study the cutaway. Click any part, or use Read a part, to read what it is.
  2. Choose a path: Straight up, Up, then down and out or Straight out from the wall, then press Commit.
  3. Read the feedback and watch the arrows: which part above the impeller set the path? Press Next unit.
  4. After unit 7, answer the gravity question, then press Show summary.
  5. Use Review to reopen any unit. Press Start over to clear the score and repeat the seven units in the same order.

Keyboard: keys 1–3 choose a path (1 = Yes and 2 = No for the gravity question) and move focus to Commit; Enter commits, then Enter goes to the next unit. Tab reaches every button and list; Enter or Space presses a focused button.

Data label: "Schematic cutaways, not to scale · Source: FanPedia pp. 5, 19, 181", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify seven roof and wall ventilation configurations by the path the exhaust air takes as it leaves the unit, given a cutaway of each unit with its discharge hidden (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Upblast and downblast discharge
  • Hooded and louvered roof exhausters, low profile roof ventilators
  • Centrifugal wall exhausters and gravity relief ventilators
  • Roof curb and gravity damper

All are covered in "On the Roof and Through the Wall" in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): For each unit, name the part above the impeller before you commit, and say which way it sends the air.
  2. Check (2 min): Compare the drawn arrows with your prediction. Answer the gravity question by looking for the impeller.
  3. Review (5 min): In the summary, reopen the hooded, louvered and downblast units side by side and note that three different covers give the same path.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why would you never quote a downblast exhauster for kitchen exhaust, even though the air still leaves the building?
  2. The low profile ventilator uses an axial propeller, the upblast exhauster a centrifugal wheel. Why do both send air straight up?
  3. A supply fan runs and a gravity relief ventilator lets the air out. What moves the air through the relief unit?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every roof exhauster blows air straight up: three of the roof units send it up, then down and out.
  • A hood or louvers change the fan type inside the unit: the hooded and louvered units keep the same centrifugal wheel; only the path cover changes.
  • Downblast units suit any exhaust because the air still leaves the building: the downblast feedback and the chapter warning show the air laid back onto the roof.
  • A gravity relief ventilator contains a small fan: its cutaway has no impeller, and the gravity question asks about it directly.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Paths correct: n of 7"; mastery is 6 of 7 paths plus the gravity question, on first attempts.
  • Reading part definitions and reviewing units in the summary are exploration and are not scored.
  • Follow-up: ask learners to sketch the path for a roof unit they have seen and name the part that sets it.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A customer describes a job; you recommend the product line built for it. This MicroSim gives you twelve illustrative job cards, shuffled once per session. For each card you choose one of twelve product lines and the one deciding factor, then commit both:

  • Air contents: what the air carries (grease, smoke and heat, corrosive vapor).
  • Discharge path: where the air must go when it leaves the unit.
  • Mounting location: where the fan can sit.
  • Occupant exposure: whether people stand in the airflow.

The twelve product lines are kitchen exhaust fan, smoke and heat exhaust fan, fiberglass fan, mancooler, downblast centrifugal roof exhauster, laboratory exhaust fan with entrained flow, plenum fan, cabinet ventilator, gravity relief ventilator, square inline centrifugal fan, centrifugal wall exhauster and tubeaxial fan. Each fits exactly one card.

Each card gets one attempt. The product line is marked "✓ Correct: ." or "✗ A better fit is .", followed by the reason. The deciding factor is marked separately: "✓ Right reason." or "✗ The deciding factor here is ." Two running scores are shown: "Product lines correct: n of 12" and "Reasons correct: n of 12". Mastery is 10 of 12 product lines on the first attempt; the reasons score makes your reasoning visible but is not part of mastery. After the twelfth card a summary lists each job, your choice and the correct choice, grouped by deciding factor.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job card. Ask what is in the air, where it must go, where the fan can sit and whether people are in the airflow.
  2. Choose a product line in Product line, or click it in the list of twelve.
  3. Choose the deciding factor (keys 1–4 or the four buttons), then press Commit.
  4. Read both verdicts and the reason, then press Next card. After card 12, press Show summary.
  5. Press Start over to clear both scores and repeat the twelve cards in the same order.

Keyboard: Tab reaches the product line list, the factor buttons and the other buttons. Keys 1–4 choose the factor (when focus is not in the list) and move focus to Commit once a product line is chosen; Enter commits, then Enter goes to the next card.

Data label: "Job cards are illustrative · Sources: tcf.com product pages; FanPedia pp. 4–6, 170", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will recommend the product line that fits each of twelve building ventilation jobs, judged by the air contents, discharge path, mounting location and occupant exposure described in the job (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Housed centrifugal, plenum, square inline centrifugal and tubeaxial fans; upblast and downblast discharge; centrifugal wall exhausters, gravity relief and cabinet ventilators; kitchen, smoke and heat, and fiberglass fans; mancoolers; and entrained flow, all in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recommend (10 min): Work the twelve cards. Say the deciding factor aloud before choosing the product line.
  2. Review (3 min): In the summary, notice that air contents decide the grease, smoke and corrosive jobs, while the cleanroom, ceiling, duct-turn and wall jobs turn on where the fan can sit.
  3. Discuss (2 min): Pick one missed card and explain which word in the job description should have pointed to the right line.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. A customer asks for a cheaper downblast unit for a grill hood. What do you tell them, and why?
  2. Why is stainless steel not the only answer for corrosive exhaust?
  3. When does a relief opening need no fan at all?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any roof exhauster can handle any exhaust air: the kitchen and restroom cards put grease and clean air side by side.
  • A smoke exhaust job only needs a large ordinary fan: the smoke card's reason gives the temperature rating an ordinary fan lacks.
  • Stainless steel is the only answer for corrosive air: the wastewater card's reason compares FRP with stainless steel.
  • A mancooler is an exhaust fan: the foundry card turns on occupant exposure, not on exhaust.
  • Every relief opening needs a powered fan: the warehouse card has no second motor.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Product lines correct: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 product lines on the first attempt.
  • "Reasons correct: n of 12" is shown beside it and is not part of mastery.
  • Follow-up: write a thirteenth job card for a product line that is not in this set and trade it with a colleague.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
On a real inquiry you rarely get a product name; you get a job. This MicroSim gives you 13 illustrative jobs, shuffled for each round, and the same list of 13 product lines from Chapter 6 for every job:

Plug fan · Vaneaxial fan · Roof mounted panel fan · Radial bladed fan · Radial tip fan · Pressure blower · Utility set · Duct fan · Filtered supply fan · Air kit · Paint booth exhaust fan · Dust collection fan · Inline lab exhaust fan

Each job has two steps, each with one scored attempt:

  1. Product line. Choose a line from the list and press Check line. A correct choice reads "✓ Correct: line. reason"; a wrong one reads "✗ The better fit is line. reason".
  2. Deciding feature. Three features then appear in shuffled order: the one that decides the job and two distractors taken from other product lines. Choose one and press Check feature. The sim answers "✓ Right: feature decides this job." or "✗ The deciding feature is feature."

The running scores "Lines correct: n of 13" and "Features correct: n of 13" are shown at the top. Mastery is 10 of 13 product lines correct on the first attempt; the feature score is reported separately and does not count toward mastery. After job 13 the summary shows both scores, the mastery line and every missed job with its reason (on a narrow screen with many misses the list shortens to the answers).

The jobs reflect the chapter's deciding facts: backward inclined fans on the clean side of a filter versus radial bladed fans for cyclones, radial tip fans that are more efficient than radial blade fans at high airflow, pressure blowers for high pressure at relatively low volume, and air kits whose enclosure and insulation are provided by others.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job, choose a product line from the Product line list (Tab to it, then the arrow keys or the first letter) and press Check line (or Enter).
  2. Read the verdict and reason, then choose the deciding feature with the option buttons or keys 1–3, and press Check feature (or Enter).
  3. Press Next job (or Enter). After job 13 read the summary; Start over begins a new scored round in a new order.

Keyboard: Enter checks the line, then the feature, then goes to the next job; keys 1–3 choose a feature option. Tab reaches the list and every button.

Data label: "Illustrative jobs · Source: Chapter 6, FanPedia and tcf.com product pages", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Duration

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • Utility sets, duct fans, filtered supply fans and air kits (Chapter 6)

docs.text:

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any dirty-air job takes a radial bladed fan: the clean-side dust collector job takes a backward inclined dust collection fan.
  • An air kit is a complete fan: its job and reason say the enclosure and insulation are provided by others.
  • Pressure blowers are chosen for large airflow: their job is high pressure at relatively low volume.
  • Plug fans and plenum fans are the same thing: the plug fan job turns on the mounting panel that keeps the drive out of the process air.

docs.title: Lab Exhaust Flow Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Lab Exhaust Flow Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A laboratory exhaust fan dilutes contaminated fume hood air with outside air and throws the mixture high above the roof. Two streams of outside air do the diluting, and they join at different places (FanPedia pp. 4 and 6):

  • Bypass flow enters through the bypass air plenum, controlled by a bypass damper, before the impeller, so it passes through the fan.
  • Entrained flow is pulled into the jet at the nozzle or windband after the fan; it never passes through the impeller.

The sim uses the chapter's flow bookkeeping:

  • Fan flow = contaminated + bypass (CFM)
  • Total flow = fan flow + entrained (CFM)
  • Contaminated share = contaminated ÷ total × 100, to the nearest whole percent ("not defined" when the total is 0, and no plume is drawn)

Three challenges, in a fixed order, give the contaminated, bypass and entrained flows. For each you type the fan flow, the total flow and the contaminated share before the diagram fills in.

# Contaminated Bypass Entrained Fan flow Total flow Share 1 6,000 0 9,000 6,000 15,000 40% 2 5,000 5,000 10,000 10,000 20,000 25% 3 12,000 3,000 15,000 15,000 30,000 40%

Flows must match the model exactly; the share is correct within ±1 percentage point. Each value is marked ✓ or ✗ after a check. You get two attempts; a wrong answer shows the challenge's worked explanation, and a second wrong answer shows the model values and the challenge counts as missed. When a challenge resolves, the stack diagram shows the value on every stream, and the arrow weights grow with flow. Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges with all three values right on the first attempt.

After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks three sliders (contaminated air 0–20,000, bypass flow 0–10,000, entrained flow 0–30,000 CFM, in 500 CFM steps). The diagram and the worked sums update at once. The first time you lower contaminated air and raise bypass by the same amount, the sim points out that the fan flow stayed constant, which is what the bypass damper does as fume hood sashes close. In a real fan, entrained flow depends on the fan flow and the nozzle design and comes from the manufacturer's rating; the sim treats it as an independent input for practice and says so on screen. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the given flows, then type the fan flow, the total flow (CFM) and the contaminated share (%) and press Check (or Enter in any box). Commas and a trailing % are accepted.
  2. Read the ✓/✗ marks for each value and the feedback. "✓ Correct: fan flow …, total flow …, contaminated share …%." appears in a solid green box; a wrong answer shows the worked explanation in a dashed red box. Fix the boxes and check again if an attempt is left.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter). After challenge 3 press Start exploring to read the first-attempt score and mastery line and unlock the sliders.
  4. In Explore mode, try the night setback: lower contaminated air and raise bypass by the same amount, and watch the fan flow. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the three answer boxes and the buttons; Enter checks the answer, then goes to the next challenge. In Explore mode the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · Stream names: FanPedia pp. 4, 6, 138", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the fan flow, the lab exhaust total flow and the contaminated share of the plume from given contaminated, bypass and entrained flows, matching the model values exactly on at least 3 of 3 challenges (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Contaminated air, bypass flow, bypass air plenum, entrained flow, fan flow, lab exhaust total flow and plume dilution (Chapter 6, "Laboratory Exhaust: Dilute, Then Throw It High")
  • Entrained flow (Chapter 5)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-7 min): Work each challenge on paper before typing. Say where each stream joins: before or after the impeller.
  2. Explore (4-6 min): Reproduce the chapter's worked example (8,000 contaminated, 2,000 bypass, 10,000 entrained: 20,000 CFM total, 40%), then the night case (5,000 and 5,000: 25%).
  3. Discussion (2 min): Why is the fan selected on contaminated plus bypass flow, and not on the total flow?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Entrained air passes through the fan, so the fan must be sized for total flow: the diagram shows entrained air joining at the windband, after the fan.
  • Bypass air is wasted air that does not help dilution: the share falls when bypass rises.
  • When fume hood exhaust drops, the fan flow must drop too: the constant-fan-flow note in Explore mode shows the bypass damper making up the difference.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt; the summary shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line. Mastery is 3 of 3 with all three values right on the first attempt.
  • Explore mode is not evidence. Follow-up: a lab drops from 9,000 to 6,000 CFM of hood exhaust at night; what bypass keeps a 10,000 CFM fan flow, and what happens to the contaminated share?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - lab exhaust diagrams naming contaminated air, bypass flow, fan flow, entrained flow and total flow (pp. 4, 6) and bypass dampers (p. 138).
  2. Twin City Fan - current laboratory and fume exhaust fan catalog pages (TVIFE, QIFE, QFE, TFE, BAIFE, BCIFE).
  3. Fume hood - Wikipedia overview of fume hoods, sash operation and variable-air-volume exhaust.

docs.title: Plug Fan Arrangement Picker
docs.text:
Run the Plug Fan Arrangement Picker MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A plug fan is an unhoused centrifugal fan mounted through the wall of a plenum: the impeller sits inside with the process air, and the mounting panel keeps the motor and drive outside. FanPedia defines seven plug fan arrangements (pp. 170–172) and this sim offers all of them. Not every model is built in every one: the current catalogs list 1P, 9, 9P, 4 and 8P for all four plug lines, plus 4P on the BEPL and BFPL, and none lists a plain Arrangement 8. They differ on two questions: is the fan direct drive or belt driven, and does the customer's wall carry the fan, or does it stand on grade? The "P" suffix marks the same arrangement mounted to grade.

The sim gives you nine illustrative jobs in a fixed order. For each one you choose one arrangement and press Check; there is one scored attempt per job. The decision rules are:

  1. Drive: direct drive or belt drive, from the job description.
  2. Temperature: with direct drive and a hot airstream, Arrangement 4/4P is excluded (the impeller would sit on the motor shaft), so 8/8P is used.
  3. Support: if the wall is not sufficient, or the job states a low-vibration requirement, use the P version; otherwise the wall-mounted version. For belt drive on grade, a motor on its own base separate from the fan is 1P; a motor on the fan's pedestal is 9P.
# Job (short form) Answer 1 Warm enclosure, no belts or fan bearings, stiff wall 4 2 Same as #1, wall cannot carry the fan 4P 3 General belt-driven recirculation, adequate wall 9 4 Large belt-driven fan, wall cannot carry it 9P 5 Direct drive, hot airstream, adequate wall, room for length 8 6 Coupled direct drive, large motor, weak wall 8P 7 Belt drive, strict low-vibration requirement 9P 8 Most compact and lowest maintenance, room temperature, adequate wall 4 9 Large belt-driven fan on grade, motor on its own separate base 1P

After each check the sim shows the reason, marks the deciding rule with "◆ deciding rule" in the rule list, and sketches the correct arrangement in side view: plenum wall, impeller and inlet funnel inside, motor, bearings, coupling or belts outside, and either a wall bracket or a pedestal on grade (the mounting panel is drawn dashed on P versions, where it is optional). The sketch is schematic, not to scale.

The seven reference cards (drive, what carries the fan, and FanPedia's notes for each arrangement) can be opened at any time. Opening them is exploration and is not scored. A checked scenario can be revisited with Back; it shows your answer and the reason but cannot be re-answered. Mastery is 7 of 9 on the first (only) attempt.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario and choose an arrangement with the buttons below the drawing (or keys 1–7), then press Check (or Enter).
  2. Read the verdict: "✓ Correct: Arrangement n." with the reason in a solid green box, or "✗ Not quite. The answer is Arrangement n." with the reason in a dashed red box. The rule list marks the deciding rule and the sketch shows the correct arrangement.
  3. Press Next scenario (or Enter). After scenario 9 press See summary to read the first-attempt score, the mastery line and every missed scenario with its reason.
  4. Use Back and Forward to review checked scenarios, Reference cards to compare the seven arrangements, and Start over for a new scored round.

Keyboard: keys 1–7 choose Arrangement 1P, 4, 4P, 8, 8P, 9 or 9P; Enter checks, then goes to the next scenario (and closes the reference cards when they are open). Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative scenarios · Source: FanPedia pp. 170–172", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the drive, support and temperature rules for plug fan arrangements to choose the correct arrangement (1P, 4, 4P, 8, 8P, 9 or 9P) for a described job, getting at least 7 of 9 scenarios right on the first attempt (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Plug fan, plenum fan and mounting panel (Chapter 6, "Plug Fans: The Impeller Goes In, the Drive Stays Out")
  • Arrangement, direct drive, belt drive and grade (Chapter 6; arrangements in full in Chapter 11)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Open the reference cards and say, for each pair (4/4P, 8/8P, 9/9P), then find 1P and say how it differs from 9P, what the P changes and what it does not.
  2. Scenarios (6-8 min): Work the nine scenarios. Before pressing Check, say which rule decides the job.
  3. Review (3 min): Use Back to revisit any miss and read the deciding rule; compare with the chapter's worked example (hot oven, belt drive, weak wall: Arrangement 9P).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Arrangement 4 is always best because it has the fewest parts: scenario 5 shows a hot airstream ruling it out.
  • The P versions are different fans: the sketch shows the same drive on a pedestal, with the mounting panel optional.
  • Arrangement 8 is common: the reference card says it is the least common plug arrangement, and it is the answer only when direct drive is required and Arrangement 4 is ruled out.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Scenarios correct: n of 9" counts correct first (only) attempts; the summary shows "First-attempt score: n of 9" and the mastery line. Mastery is 7 of 9.
  • Opening the reference cards is exploration, not evidence. Follow-up: a customer wants belt drive on a wall that can carry the fan but has a low-vibration specification; which arrangement, and which rule decides it?

  2. Twin City Fan - current plug fan catalog pages (BEPL, BFPL, AFPL, BCPL) with mounting panel, temperature and pedestal options.
  3. BEPL High Efficiency Plug Fans Catalog 355 (PDF) and BCPL AFPL Plug Fans Catalog 350 (PDF) - Twin City Fan, April 2024 - arrangements available per plug fan line.
  4. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's reference on fan types and arrangements.

docs.title: Belt Driven Plug Fan Parts
docs.text: Run the Belt Driven Plug Fan Parts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts ten numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded view of a belt driven plug fan (page 14). The fan is an Arrangement 9P, a grade-mounted plug fan: it stands on a pedestal, the impeller hangs inside the customer's plenum, the mounting panel fastens the fan to the plenum wall, and the insulation plug fills the wall opening around it. The drive parts (shaft, bearings, sheave, belts and motor) are laid out to the left of the fan.

The ten parts are the impeller, insulation plug, mounting panel, pedestal, motor slide base, motor, belt, sheave, bearings and shaft. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. Where a part is small (the sheave, the bearings and the shaft), its marker sits just above it with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select the plate that fastens the fan to the customer's wall.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 10".
  4. After the tenth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 14", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 3, sections "The Fan Shaft", "Bearings" and "The Drive Train" (sheaves, V-belts and the slide base).
  • Chapter 6, section "Plug Fans: The Impeller Goes In, the Drive Stays Out".
  • Chapter 7, sections "Reading an Exploded View" and "Plug Fan Hardware: Mounting Panel and Insulation Plug".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten parts. Sort them aloud by which side of the plenum wall they end up on: inside (impeller), in the wall (mounting panel, insulation plug) and outside the process airstream (shaft, bearings, sheave, belt, motor, motor slide base, pedestal).
  2. Compare (2 min): Open Plug Fan Arrangement Picker. On the Arrangement 9 plug fan the wall carries the whole fan; which part on this drawing carries it instead on the grade-mounted 9P?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all ten parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The mounting panel and the insulation plug are the same part: the panel is the flat plate that fastens the fan to the wall, and the plug is the insulated section mounted with it that fills the wall opening around the fan.
  • A plug fan's motor and belts sit inside the plenum with the impeller: only the impeller is inside; the shaft, bearings, belts and motor stay outside the process airstream.
  • The mounting panel always holds up the fan: on the grade-mounted versions, such as this 9P, the fan stands on the foundation on its pedestal, and FanPedia lists the mounting panel as optional.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: the plug fan serves a hot oven. Which part on this drawing keeps the plenum wall insulated where the fan passes through it?

docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 14 is the belt driven plug fan exploded view used here, pp. 13-14 both plug fan exploded views, pp. 5 and 172 the mounting panel, pp. 66 and 113 the insulation plug.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the section "Plug Fan Hardware: Mounting Panel and Insulation Plug", where this MicroSim is embedded.

docs.text:
Run the Which Exploded View Shows This Part MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
FanPedia names every housing part on an exploded view (pp. 9–19) or a housing detail page (pp. 59–66). This MicroSim gives you twelve part cards, shuffled, and four bins, one per fan family:

  • Housed Centrifugal (scroll housing)
  • Tubular (axial, inline centrifugal, mixed flow)
  • Plug Fan
  • Centrifugal Roof Exhauster

Put each card in the bin of the family whose FanPedia drawing labels the part. Decide from what the part does: does it shape a scroll, take swirl out of air in a tube, seal a plenum wall, or sit on a roof curb? For the Curb Cap, the roof exhauster exploded view on p. 19 decides, and the feedback notes that roof mounted axial fans use one too (p. 7).

Cards move freely until you press Check, which needs all twelve cards placed. The first check is scored: "First check: n of 12", with mastery at 10 of 12. Retry sends the incorrect cards back to the pool so you can place them again; retries are practice, not scored, and you can retry as often as you like.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Drag each card from the pool into a bin. You can drag cards between bins, or back to the pool, as often as you like before you check. You can also click a card to select it and then click an empty part of a bin.
  2. Press Check (or C). Every card is marked ✓ (solid green border) or ✗ (dashed red border), and the first-check score and mastery line appear.
  3. Click any card to read why:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" the part "belongs to" the family, with the reason and the FanPedia page.
    • Incorrect: "✗ Not" the family you chose, with the reason. Straightening Vanes in Housed Centrifugal also explains why a scroll needs no vanes.
  4. Press Retry (or R) to send the incorrect cards back to the pool, place them again and press Check (practice). Practice checks never change the first-check score.
  5. Press Start over to reshuffle all twelve cards for a new scored first check.

Keyboard: choose a card in the Card list, then press 1–4 to put it in a bin or 0 to return it to the pool (the bin buttons do the same). The next card in the pool is selected for you. C checks and R retries when a button has focus.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia exploded views pp. 9–19 and housing details pp. 59–66", shown at the bottom left of the drawing area.
