docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will attribute twelve housing parts to the fan family whose FanPedia exploded view or housing detail shows them, using what each part does to decide (Bloom: Analyze, verb: attribute).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 7, every section from "Reading an Exploded View" to "Rooftop Hardware".
  • The terms housing side plate, scroll wrapper, cutoff, straightening vanes, guide vanes, discharge cone, belt tube, mounting panel, insulation plug, roof exhauster shroud, curb cap and motor cover.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5 min): Place all twelve cards before checking. For each one, say out loud what the part does to the air or to the structure.
  2. Check and read (4 min): Press Check, then click every card, not just the incorrect ones, and read its reason and page.
  3. Retry (3 min): Retry the misses until every card is correct.
  4. Discuss (3 min): Which two cards could plausibly belong to more than one family, and what decided the answer key?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Straightening vanes belong to scroll housings: the card goes to Tubular, and placing it in Housed Centrifugal adds that a scroll turns the air with its spiral shape, so vanes are needed only when air leaves the impeller swirling inside a tube.
  • A plug fan has a scroll: the plug fan's own parts are the mounting panel and insulation plug at the plenum wall; the scroll parts belong to the housed centrifugal fan.
  • A belt tube is the same as a belt guard and appears on every belt driven fan: the belt tube card belongs only to tubular housings, where the belts must cross the airstream.
  • Curb caps are only for centrifugal roof exhausters: the Curb Cap feedback notes that roof mounted axial fans use one too (p. 7).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-check score shown as "First check: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first check. Retries are practice and do not count toward mastery.
  • Follow-up question: a belt driven inline fan has both a belt tube and a belt guard. What does each one protect?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; exploded views pp. 9–19 and housing details pp. 59–66, cited on each card.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the sections on tubular housings, plug fan hardware and rooftop hardware that define every card.

docs.title: Inline Centrifugal and Mixed Flow Fan Parts
docs.text: Run the Inline Centrifugal and Mixed Flow Fan Parts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts twelve numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded views of inline centrifugal and mixed flow fans (page 17). Both fans are built in a tubular housing. The left column shows a direct drive inline centrifugal fan, exploded at the top and assembled at the bottom with its motor inside the tube. The right column shows a belt driven mixed flow fan: exploded at the top, and assembled at the bottom with its belt guard, belt tube and discharge cone.

The twelve parts are the tubular housing, straightening vanes, shaft, impeller (inline centrifugal), inlet funnel, motor, impeller (mixed flow), bearing housing, belt guard, belt tube, sheave and discharge cone. Some parts appear on both fans; each has one marker. On a wide screen the labels sit in two columns with leader lines, the left half of the markers on the left; on a narrower screen (including the chapter page) the labels move below the drawing as a numbered list. Where a part is small or crowded (the shaft, the belt tube and the sheave), its marker sits in nearby white space with a short pointer to the part.

The quiz describes each part by its job or its look ("Select the passage that shields the belts from the airstream.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 12 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 12".
  4. After the twelfth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (10 of 12), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 17", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the twelve labeled parts of a direct drive inline centrifugal fan and a belt driven mixed flow fan on FanPedia's exploded views, given each part's function or appearance (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 4, sections "Tubular Housings", "Guide Vanes", "Inline Centrifugal Fans" and "Mixed Flow Fans".
  • Chapter 3, section "The Drive Train" (sheaves, V-belts and the belt guard).
  • Chapter 7, sections "Reading an Exploded View" and "Tubular Housings: Straightening Vanes, Discharge Cone and Belt Tube".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all twelve parts. Sort them aloud into the air path (inlet funnel, the two impellers, straightening vanes, tubular housing, discharge cone) and the drive (motor, shaft, bearing housing, sheave, belt tube, belt guard).
  2. Compare (2 min): The left fan is direct drive and the right one is belt driven. Which parts on the right fan exist only because the motor sits outside the tube?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all twelve parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order. Then try Which Exploded View Shows This Part.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The belt tube and the belt guard do the same job: the belt tube shields the belts where they cross the airstream inside the tube, and the belt guard encloses the belts and sheaves outside the housing where people could reach them. A belt driven inline fan has both.
  • A fan in a round tube must be an axial fan: these tubes carry a centrifugal impeller (left) and a mixed flow impeller (right), told apart by the impeller, not the housing.
  • Straightening vanes move the air: they are fixed, and they only turn the swirling air leaving the impeller back into straight-through flow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: on the direct drive fan, where is the motor, and why does that fan need no belt tube?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 17 is the inline centrifugal and mixed flow exploded view used here (straightening vanes, discharge cone, belt tube and belt guard), pp. 15-16 the axial exploded views, p. 64 the straightening vanes on the housing detail.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the section "Tubular Housings: Straightening Vanes, Discharge Cone and Belt Tube", where this MicroSim is embedded, and "Guards and Covers".
  4. Which Exploded View Shows This Part - sorts the same parts into the fan family whose exploded view shows them.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 17. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Split Housing Selector
docs.text:
Run the Split Housing Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A split housing is built in sections that bolt together. FanPedia names three kinds for centrifugal fans, each by where the cut runs: the horizontal split (the standard split, along the horizontal centerline), the three-way split (three sections, up to 180 degrees) and the pie split (a wedge at 90 degrees or greater, in Mohawk or standard style). This MicroSim gives you eight illustrative job situations in a fixed order and asks which split, if any, each one calls for.

For each situation you make two decisions:

  1. Recommend. Choose one of five recommendations: Horizontal split; Three-way split; Pie split, Mohawk style; Pie split, standard style; No split recommended. The choice locks.
  2. Justify. Four FanPedia rules appear in shuffled order. Pick the one that justifies the right choice for this fan. The options are the situation's own rule plus the rules of the next three situations whose recommendation is different, so no wrong option is a valid reason for the same split.

A situation counts as correct only when both the recommendation and the justification are right. Situations 3, 4, 5 and 7 all involve a pie split; the style follows only from the facts stated in each situation (inlet side left whole, double width, attached inlet box, matching an older split).

There is one attempt per situation. Mastery is 6 of 8 situations correct on the first attempt.

# Correct recommendation FanPedia rule 1 Horizontal split Standard split on the horizontal centerline; the shop may split size 807 and above for shipping 2 Three-way split Needed to ship a fan or to enter a specific sized opening 3 Pie split, Mohawk style Splits between the scroll and the inlet side; the inlet side has no split 4 Pie split, standard style The Mohawk style is not used on double width fans 5 Pie split, standard style Arr. 3SI includes a pie split; no Mohawk with attached inlet boxes 6 No split recommended Split housings are not recommended for nominally leak-tight construction 7 Pie split, standard style The older standard style runs down to the funnel or inlet plate 8 Three-way split Fits the opening; needs extra drafting and engineering time in the quote

Work through the sim before you read the table.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the situation and the question "Which split, if any, should this fan have?"
  2. Choose a recommendation with the buttons in the Split row or keys 1 to 5. It locks and shows a ✓ mark.
  3. Read the four rules, A to D, and choose one with the Reason buttons or keys A to D.
  4. Read the feedback:
    • Both right: "✓ Correct:" with the recommendation and its rule.
    • Wrong recommendation: "✗ Not quite. The better choice is" the right split, followed by its rule.
    • Right recommendation, wrong rule: "✗ Right split, wrong reason." followed by the rule. The right rule is marked ✓ in the list and your pick, if different, ✗. The running count "Situations correct: n of 8" is at the top.
  5. Press Next situation (or Enter). After situation 8, See summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery, and a table of your answers beside the correct splits. Press Start over to try again.

Keyboard: 1–5 choose the split, A–D choose the reason, Enter goes to the next situation. After a split locks, focus moves to the reason buttons; after a reason, to Next situation.

Data label: "Illustrative situations · Source: FanPedia pp. 120, 156–157, 164–168, 194", shown at the bottom left of the drawing area.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will recommend a horizontal, three-way, Mohawk pie, standard pie or no split housing for eight described centrifugal fan situations, justifying each choice with a FanPedia rule (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 7, section "Split Housings", and the warning on splits in leak-tight housings.
  • Chapter 3: split housing, attached inlet box, double width fan.
  • The term nominally leak-tight construction (Chapter 21 gives the details).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Situations (8 min): Work through all eight situations. Before you press a reason, say out loud which fact in the situation text decided the split.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary table. For every "wrong reason" row, find the rule in the chapter's split table.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Situations 3, 4, 5 and 7 all need a pie split. List the facts that rule the Mohawk style out, and the one fact that rules it in.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any split will let the impeller out without touching the ductwork: only the pie split is described as removing the impeller "without disturbing inlet or outlet"; situations 1, 2 and 8 use other splits for shipping and openings.
  • The Mohawk pie split works on any fan: situations 4 and 5 rule it out for double width fans and fans with attached inlet boxes.
  • Adding a split is always harmless: situation 6 asks for no split in nominally leak-tight service, and situation 8 costs drafting and engineering time.
  • A horizontal split is only for maintenance, never shipping: situation 1 is a shipping split for size 807.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt score: n of 8"; mastery is 6 of 8 situations with both the recommendation and the justification correct. The running line shows "Situations correct: n of 8".
  • Follow-up question: a quote calls for a three-way split on an RTO fan. What two concerns should you raise before it goes out?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; pp. 156–157 and 194 describe the split housing types and styles, pp. 164–168 the arrangements with pie splits, and p. 120 the leak-tight limitation.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the section "Split Housings" and its summary table.
  4. Chapter 21: High-Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - gasketing, bolt spacing and centering plates when a split is used on a tight housing.

docs.title: SWSI Housing Callout Explorer
docs.text: Run the SWSI Housing Callout Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a line drawing of a single width, single inlet (SWSI) housed centrifugal fan with ten callouts: the housing side, housing scroll and cutoff of the shell; the inlet collar, inlet funnel (with the wiper bar on its inner end, as FanPedia p. 60 draws it) and inlet flange, pulled off the inlet along the shaft line the way an exploded view shows them; the outlet (discharge) flange; the framing; and the pedestal that carries the bearings. No other parts are labeled.

The drawing is based on FanPedia p. 60 (Centrifugal Fans SWSI). It is a simplified schematic, not to scale, and not a specific Twin City Fan model. Rubbing bars, which p. 60 shows on spark-resistant fans only, are left out; Chapter 20 covers them.

The quiz shows the ten part descriptions once each in shuffled order. You get one attempt per description, and mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Click any part to read what it does. You can click as often as you like. Each part you have opened gets a ✓ mark and a shaded label, and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels are hidden and a description appears above the drawing. Click the part it describes. You get one attempt:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" and the part name and the part's label appears.
    • Incorrect: "✗ That is the" part you clicked, followed by "The" correct part "is" and its description The correct part is highlighted and marked "Answer". If you mix up the cutoff and the wiper bar, the feedback adds where each one sits.
    • Clicking an empty area of the drawing does nothing and uses no attempt.
  3. Press Next description after each answer. The running count "Correct: n of 10" sits in the toolbar.
  4. After the tenth description, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and the parts you missed with their descriptions. Press Start over to retake the quiz with a new shuffle, or Back to explore to review.
  5. Start over in the toolbar clears your visited parts and the quiz at any time and returns to explore mode.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the parts (in the callout order, Housing Side to Pedestal) and the buttons; Enter or Space selects a part. After an answer, focus moves to Next description, so Enter goes on.

Narrow screens: when the drawing is narrower than about 650 px, the callouts become numbers with a key list below the drawing, so the text stays readable.

Data label: "Simplified line drawing, not to scale · Based on FanPedia p. 60. Rubbing bars, shown there on spark-resistant fans only, are covered in Chapter 20.", shown below the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify ten labeled parts of a single width, single inlet centrifugal fan housing from a one-sentence description of each part's job (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 7, sections "Reading an Exploded View" and "The Scroll Housing: Side Plates, Wrapper and Cutoff".
  • Chapter 3, Basic Fan Anatomy: inlet collar, inlet funnel, inlet and outlet flanges, pedestal.
  • The terms exploded view, housing side plate, scroll wrapper, cutoff, wiper bar and housing framing.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten callouts. For each one, say whether it is part of the shell, the inlet hardware, or the support structure.
  2. Compare (2 min): Open the cutoff and the wiper bar one after the other and note where each sits: the cutoff at the outlet end of the scroll, the wiper bar near the inlet funnel. Do the same for the inlet collar, inlet funnel and inlet flange.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and answer the ten descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, return to explore mode for those parts, then press Start over for a new shuffle.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The cutoff and the wiper bar are the same piece in the same place: the drawing puts the cutoff at the outlet end of the scroll and the wiper bar on the inner end of the inlet funnel, and the quiz feedback for that pair says so.
  • The side plate and the scroll are one continuous part: they are separate callouts, the flat side and the curved wrapper between the two sides.
  • The inlet collar and the inlet funnel are interchangeable names: they are pulled off the inlet as separate pieces, a plain short cylinder and a shaped bell.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt in quiz mode. The running line shows "Correct: n of 10".
  • Clicking callouts in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer reports a "bent piece of sheet metal near the outlet." Which part is it most likely, and which FanPedia page would you open to confirm it?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 60 is the SWSI housing view this drawing is based on, p. 59 gives the cutoff and wiper bar function, and pp. 59 and 185 the housing and framing roles.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the section "The Scroll Housing: Side Plates, Wrapper and Cutoff", which defines every callout.
  4. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy - the inlet and outlet hardware and the pedestal.

docs.title: Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator
docs.text:
Run the Axial Airflow and Hub Position Configurator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch08-axial-airflow-hub-configurator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An axial fan order has to say which way the air goes, and that one choice fixes two more words on the order. FanPedia gives each airflow code an alternative name based on where the hub faces, and its left hand and right hand pages pair each code with a hub bore (FanPedia PDF pp. 36–43):

Airflow code Air path Hub position Hub bore PM Through the impeller, then over the motor Hub on intake side Reverse bore hub MP Over the motor, then through the impeller Hub on discharge side Standard bore hub

Impeller hand (left or right) and pitch type (fixed or adjustable) do not change the rule. A reversible impeller runs standard flow as MP and reverse flow as PM (FanPedia PDF p. 41).

The sim shows a side view of a direct-drive axial fan with the motor at the left of the tube and the impeller at the right. For each of eight orders, in a fixed order, you choose the hub position and the hub bore and press Check. Until you do, the fan is drawn without its hub and the ends of the tube are not labeled. After Check, the hub appears with its boss highlighted, the ends are labeled Intake and Discharge, and the air moves from intake to discharge: right to left for PM, left to right for MP. The heavier blade edge is the leading edge, which always faces the intake.

# Order Hub position Hub bore 1 Airflow = PM, adjustable pitch Intake side Reverse bore 2 Airflow = MP, fixed pitch cast Discharge side Standard bore 3 Air passes over the motor first, then through the impeller Discharge side Standard bore 4 Air passes through the impeller first, then over the motor Intake side Reverse bore 5 Reversible impeller, standard flow Discharge side Standard bore 6 Reversible impeller, reverse flow Intake side Reverse bore 7 Right hand adjustable pitch impeller, airflow = MP Discharge side Standard bore 8 Left hand fixed cast impeller, airflow = PM Intake side Reverse bore

Each order has one scored attempt and counts as correct only when both answers are right. Mastery is 7 of 8 orders correct on the first attempt. There is no retry of a single order; Start over restarts the whole set.

After order 8 the free model (Explore mode) unlocks. It has two settings: the airflow code (PM or MP) and the rotation (correct for the impeller, or reversed). With the correct rotation, air enters at the leading edges and leaves at the discharge. With the rotation reversed, the intended airflow arrow is crossed out and the sim reads "Wrong rotation: no airflow in the proper direction (FanPedia note 2)." Rotation is always labeled as viewed from the discharge side. The rotation arrow is a symbol for "as the impeller needs" or "reversed"; the actual direction depends on the impeller hand, which this sim does not set.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the order. Choose Intake side or Discharge side for the hub, and Standard bore or Reverse bore for the hub bore. Your choice is marked with a ✓ and a heavier outline.
  2. Press Check (or Enter). A correct order reads "✓ Correct." with the reason, in a box with a solid green border. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the right hub position and bore and the reason, in a box with a dashed red border. "Orders correct: n of 8" keeps the running count.
  3. Press Next order (or Enter) and repeat. After order 8, press Open free model. The panel shows the first-attempt score, the mastery line and any missed orders.
  4. In the free model, switch the airflow between PM and MP and watch the Intake and Discharge labels and the hub label change; then set the rotation to Reversed and see the airflow stop in the intended direction. The free model is never scored. Start over returns to order 1 and clears the score.

Keyboard: I and D choose the hub side, S and R choose the bore, Enter checks the order and then goes to the next one. Tab reaches every button and, in the free model, both menus.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia PDF pp. 36–43", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply FanPedia's axial airflow rules to state the hub position and hub bore for an axial fan order, given its airflow code or air path, with at least 7 of 8 orders correct (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Axial impeller and blade leading edge (Chapter 8)
  • Airflow = PM and airflow = MP; hub on intake side and hub on discharge side (Chapter 8)
  • Standard bore hub and reverse bore hub; reversible impeller (Chapter 8)
  • Rotation viewed from the discharge side (Chapter 8)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Orders (5-7 min): Work through the eight orders. Before each Check, say the air path out loud ("impeller, then motor") and name the build.
  2. Review (2-3 min): For any missed order, reread its reason and the section "Hub on Intake Side and Hub on Discharge Side". Note that orders 7 and 8 add an impeller hand that does not change the answer.
  3. Free model (3-5 min): Switch PM and MP and note which end becomes the intake. Then reverse the rotation and explain why the result is no useful airflow rather than less airflow.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• "Hub on intake" means the motor is on the intake side: in PM the air meets the impeller first, so the motor is on the discharge side of the impeller.
  • PM and MP are rotation codes: they are airflow codes, read left to right as the air's path; rotation is a separate setting in the free model.
  • A reversible impeller has a fixed hub position: orders 5 and 6 give the same impeller two answers, one for each flow mode.
  • Running an axial impeller backward gives less airflow in the same direction: the free model shows no airflow in the proper direction, as FanPedia's note says.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Orders correct: n of 8" counts orders with both answers right. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 8" and the mastery line; mastery is 7 of 8 orders on the first (and only) attempt.
  • Running the free model is exploration, not evidence. Follow-up question: a customer orders a reversible fan for supply in summer and exhaust in winter; which hub position does each mode have?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - pp. 36–43 give the axial airflow codes, the "aka" hub names, the reversible impeller modes and the standard and reverse bore hubs.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's reference on fan types, arrangements and axial fan configuration.
  3. Axial fan design (Wikipedia) - background on axial impellers, blades and hubs.

docs.title: Impeller Balance Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Impeller Balance Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch08-impeller-balance-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An impeller is balanced until its residual unbalance is within a limit set by a balance quality grade G. The sim uses the formulas from the chapter section "Impeller Balancing":

  • Permissible residual unbalance: U = 6.015 × G × W / N, with G in mm/s, W the impeller weight in lb, N the maximum service speed in rpm and U in oz·in.
  • Correction mass at radius r: m = U / r, with r in inches and m in ounces.
  • Rotating force from that unbalance: F ≈ 1.77 × U × (N/1000)², in lbf.

The sim starts with three challenges, in this order. All values are illustrative.

# W (lb) N (rpm) G r (in) U (oz·in) m (oz) 1 200 1,200 G6.3 15 6.32 0.42 2 200 1,200 G2.5 15 2.51 0.17 3 600 1,800 G6.3 20 12.63 0.63

For each challenge you type both U and m. The challenge is correct when both values are within ±2% of the unrounded model values. You get two attempts. A wrong answer shows the worked calculation for that challenge (and says which of your two values was within 2%); a second wrong answer shows the model values and the challenge counts as missed. Once a challenge is resolved, your answers, the model values and the worked calculation appear together, and the end view and force bars are revealed.

The drawing shows an end view of the impeller with an orange correction mass at radius r (40 in is drawn at the rim) and an arrow for the outward force. The bars compare the force from the same residual unbalance U at half, the selected and double speed, when those speeds lie within 300–3,600 rpm. Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges with both values correct on the first attempt. After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks the weight, speed and radius sliders and the grade menu (G16, G6.3, G2.5, G1.0); U, m and F update at once. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1. Type U in the U (oz·in) box and m in the m (oz) box, then press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: U = 6.32 oz·in, m = 0.42 oz." in a solid green box. A wrong one shows the worked calculation in a dashed red box; use your second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat for challenges 2 and 3. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running count.
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Set N to 1,200 rpm, then 2,400 rpm: U halves, because the grade allows less unbalance at a higher speed, while the bars show that the same impeller, with the same U, would push four times as hard at double the speed. Start over returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches both answer boxes, every button, the grade menu and the three sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the permissible residual unbalance and the matching correction mass for an impeller from its weight, speed, balance grade and correction radius, to within 2% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Impeller balancing and residual unbalance (Chapter 8)
  • Balance quality grade G (Chapter 8)
  • Ounce-inch and correction radius (Chapter 8)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-7 min): Solve the three challenges with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down U first, then divide by r.
  2. Review (2 min): Compare challenges 1 and 2, which differ only in grade, and say which grade is tighter.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Double the weight and watch U double. Then double the speed and compare the change in U with the change in the force bars.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A heavier impeller is allowed less unbalance: U rises in proportion to W, so a heavier wheel is allowed more.
  • Force from unbalance grows in proportion to speed: the bars show four times the force at double the speed for the same U.
  • A larger grade number means tighter balance: G2.5 gives a smaller U than G6.3, so the smaller number is the tighter grade.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 challenges with both values within ±2% on the first attempt.
  • Moving the sliders is not evidence. Follow-up question: a customer wants to run an impeller balanced at 1,200 rpm at 1,800 rpm. What happens to the force from the same unbalance, and what has to be checked first?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Balancing of rotating masses (Wikipedia) - background on static and dynamic unbalance and how it is corrected.
  2. ISO 21940-11:2016, Mechanical vibration - Rotor balancing - Part 11 - the standard that defines balance quality grades G and permissible residual unbalance.
  3. AMCA International - publisher of AMCA 204, which assigns balance grades to fan application categories.
  4. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's reference on impellers and fan construction.

docs.title: Impeller Type Classifier
docs.text:
Run the Impeller Type Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch08-impeller-type-classifier.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Naming an impeller from a description follows a fixed order: first the air path (outward, straight through, or partway), then for a centrifugal impeller the blade shape against rotation, and for an axial impeller the pitch type, material and flow modes. This sorter gives you ten descriptions like the ones on field photos and catalog pages, one at a time in shuffled order, and six bins:

  1. Backward inclined (centrifugal)
  2. Forward curved (centrifugal)
  3. Mixed flow
  4. Axial, fixed pitch
  5. Axial, adjustable pitch
  6. Axial, reversible
# Card (short name) Bin 1 Flat, single-thickness blades whose tips trail rotation; air leaves at a right angle to the shaft Backward inclined (centrifugal) 2 Many short, shallow blades curved with rotation, held by an end ring and tie rods Forward curved (centrifugal) 3 Airfoil blades tapering from the front plate to the hub end; air leaves partly along the shaft Mixed flow 4 Cast impeller with blades formed at one angle Axial, fixed pitch 5 Separate blades whose shanks clamp into the hub Axial, adjustable pitch 6 One impeller in two modes: standard flow MP and reverse flow PM Axial, reversible 7 Fiberglass blades on an aluminum hub, the "F4/F6" impeller Axial, adjustable pitch 8 Fiberglass "TF" impeller with molded blades Axial, fixed pitch 9 SWSI wheel with backward-tilted flat blades in an inline (tubular) centrifugal fan Backward inclined (centrifugal) 10 "TCTA" impeller from FanPedia's axial impeller types Axial, fixed pitch

Each card gets one scored placement. The placement locks, the card turns green with a solid border and "✓ Correct: ." or red with a dashed border and "✗ This one is .", followed by the reason, and a chip with ✓ or ✗ lands in the bin you chose. Misplaced cards go to a review pile. After card 10 the summary shows the first-attempt score (n of 10), the mastery line and the review pile with each card's correct bin. Redo review pile runs those cards again, unscored; the review pile never changes the score. Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card and ask the starting question: where does the air go, and what do the blades look like?
  2. Press the bin button (or key 1 to 6). Read the verdict and the reason.
  3. Press Next card (or Enter). After card 10, press Show summary.
  4. On the summary, press Redo review pile to place the misplaced cards again (not scored), or Start over to reshuffle all ten cards and clear the score.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 6 place the card in that bin; Enter goes to the next card. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia PDF pp. 6, 31–35, 41", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify written descriptions of impellers into the impeller types named in Chapter 8, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Centrifugal, axial and mixed flow impellers (Chapter 8)
  • Backward inclined and forward curved impellers; single width single inlet (Chapter 8)
  • Fixed pitch, adjustable pitch, fiberglass axial and reversible impellers (Chapter 8)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5 min): Place all ten cards. Before each placement, say the air path first, then the blade feature that decides the bin.
  2. Review pile (2-3 min): Redo the misplaced cards and read each reason.
  3. Discussion (2 min): Why is card 9 centrifugal even though the fan is tubular? Why is card 7 adjustable even though it is fiberglass?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Many narrow blades always means forward curved: card 2 is decided by blade tips pointing with rotation, not by blade count.
  • Any impeller in a tubular housing is axial: card 9 is a backward inclined wheel in an inline centrifugal fan.
  • Adjustable pitch means the blades can be changed while the fan runs: card 5 describes blade shanks clamped into the hub, so the angle is reset by re-clamping the blades, a hardware adjustment rather than a running control.
  • Fiberglass impellers are always fixed pitch: card 7 (F4/F6) is adjustable, card 8 (TF) is fixed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Cards correct: n of 10" counts first placements. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 10" and the mastery line; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. The review pile is practice and does not change the score.
  • Follow-up question: a photo shows a tubular fan with a wheel whose blades taper toward the hub. Which two bins are possible, and what would you look for to decide?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - p. 31 (centrifugal impeller captions), pp. 6 and 32 (mixed flow), pp. 33–35 (axial impeller types, fixed and adjustable), p. 41 (reversible impeller).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's reference on impeller types.
  3. Centrifugal fan (Wikipedia) - background on backward inclined and forward curved blades.
  4. Axial fan design (Wikipedia) - background on axial impellers and blade pitch.

docs.title: DWDI Housing Parts Explorer
docs.text: Run the DWDI Housing Parts Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is an exploded view of a double width, double inlet (DWDI) centrifugal fan housing. The housing sits in the middle. The wiper bar, inlet funnel and bearing structural support are pulled away from each inlet along the shaft line, and the setback outlet flange is lifted off the outlet. Eight parts are labeled: housing side, housing scroll, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet funnel, bearing structural support, setback outlet flange and framing. The wiper bar, inlet funnel and bearing structural support appear twice, once at each inlet, and either copy counts as that part.

The drawing is a simplified illustration based on FanPedia p. 61 (Housing Construction, Centrifugal Fans (DWDI)). The wiper bar and inlet funnel wording comes from pp. 59 and 188, and the bearing location in the airstream comes from p. 167 (Arrangement 3 DWDI). It is not to scale and is not a specific Twin City Fan model.

The check phase shows eight function descriptions in a fixed order. You click the part that matches each one and get two attempts per description. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. The explore phase is never scored.

# Description Part 1 Carries a bearing in front of an inlet, in the airstream. Bearing structural support 2 Where the discharge duct is bolted to the fan. Setback outlet flange 3 Separates air leaving the fan from air that would recirculate. Cutoff 4 Directs air into the impeller from each side. Inlet funnel 5 Collects air leaving the impeller and guides it toward the outlet. Housing scroll 6 Reduces turbulence in the inlet funnel area. Wiper bar 7 Flat sheet that carries an inlet. Housing side 8 Stiffens the housing and carries it to its mounting. Framing

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore (the starting phase). All eight labels are visible. Click any part to open its infobox. The parts list under the drawing ticks off each part you have opened, and the toolbar counts them.
  2. Check. Press Check after you have opened all eight, or sooner to skip ahead. The labels are hidden and a description appears above the drawing. Click the part it describes:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" and the part name.
    • Wrong: the feedback for that description, for example "The cutoff is the scroll tongue at the outlet; the wiper bar sits at the inlet funnel." You get one more attempt.
    • Wrong twice: the correct part is highlighted and marked "Answer", and the description counts as missed.
  3. Press Next description after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts identified: n of 8", and "✓ Mastered" appears once 7 descriptions are correct on the first attempt.
  4. After the eighth description, the summary shows your first-attempt score and lists any missed parts with their infobox text. Press Restart check to run the check again with the labels hidden, or Back to explore to review.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the parts and the buttons; Enter or Space selects a part. After an answer, focus moves to Next description, so Enter goes on.

Narrow screens: when the drawing is narrower than about 640 px, the callouts become numbers that match the numbered parts list.

Data label: "Simplified exploded view, not to scale · Based on FanPedia p. 61 (DWDI housing construction)", shown below the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the eight labeled parts of a double width double inlet housing from a description of each part's job, with at least 7 of 8 correct (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 9, section "Double Width Double Inlet Fans": double width double inlet, bearing structural support, setback outlet flange.
  • Chapter 7: housing side, housing scroll, cutoff, wiper bar, inlet funnel, framing.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all eight parts. Name the three parts that appear twice and explain why a DWDI housing needs two of each.
  2. Check (5 min): Answer the eight descriptions without going back to the explore phase.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, reopen those parts, then press Restart check.
  4. Apply (2 min): The bearing structural supports sit in the airstream. What does that mean for a standard Arrangement 3 DWDI fan handling 160°F air?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The bearing structural support is part of the motor base: it is drawn at each inlet carrying a bearing, and the feedback for that description says it is not a motor base.
  • The cutoff and the wiper bar are the same part: the cutoff is at the outlet and the wiper bars are at the inlet funnels, and the feedback for both descriptions says where each one works.
  • A DWDI fan has one inlet funnel, like an SWSI fan: the exploded view shows a funnel at each inlet, and either one is accepted.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running count "Parts identified: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt, shown as "✓ Mastered".
  • Opening infoboxes in the explore phase is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: standard Arrangement 3 DWDI fans are limited to clean air at 130°F. Which part in this drawing is the reason?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 61 is the DWDI housing construction drawing this view is based on, pp. 59 and 188 describe the wiper bar and inlet funnel, and p. 167 places the bearings in the airstream on Arrangement 3 DWDI fans.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 9: Impeller Construction and Material Handling - the section "Double Width Double Inlet Fans", which defines the bearing structural support and setback outlet flange.
  4. Chapter 7: Housing Construction and Exploded Views - the SWSI housing parts this DWDI housing repeats.

docs.title: Impeller Recommender for Real Airstreams
docs.text:
Run the Impeller Recommender for Real Airstreams MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch09-impeller-recommender.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Ten job cards describe real airstreams, such as a boiler forced draft fan, cyclone exhaust, buffing threads and corrugated box trim. They appear in a shuffled order. For each card you recommend one of seven impeller types, each tied to a current Twin City Fan model:

Bin What it is built for Airfoil (HAF) Hollow airfoil blades; highest efficiency; clean air, high pressure. Backward curved (HIB) Single thickness curved blades; clean air or light dust loading. Radial tip (RTF) Curved at entry, radial at tip; large volumes of clean or dirty gas. Air handling radial (RBA) Heavy blades welded to back plate and front plate; relatively clean air, fumes, light contaminant. Open radial paddle (RBO) Open paddles, no plates; coarse, sticky, heavy or abrasive material. Back plate wool, material handling (RBW) Radial blades on a full back plate; long, stringy or fibrous material. Paper handling (RBP) Full back plate with gussets and a deflector cone; paper trim, fibrous material, metal trim, high impact.

Some bins take more than one card, and you are not told how many. You get two attempts per card, and mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first try. The bin descriptions and every job card come from the application statements on Twin City Fan's current product pages (retrieved 2026-10-08) and FanPedia pp. 31–32. Job settings such as "process tank" and "stamping line" are illustrative wrappers around those statements.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job card. Each bin tile shows its description; press Bin descriptions (or D) to see all seven in full.
  2. Press the impeller you recommend (or keys 1–7). A correct choice shows "✓ Correct:" with the impeller and the catalog reason.
  3. A wrong first try shows "Not the best fit. Ask what the material does in this airstream: does it stick, wrap, strike, or pass through?" and the card comes back for a second try. A wrong second try shows the best fit and why, and the card counts as missed.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). The status line shows "Recommendations correct on first try: n of 10", and "✓ Mastered" appears at 8 or more.
  5. After card 10, the summary lists every card with your first choice and the best fit. Press Start over to reshuffle the cards and reset the score.

Keyboard: keys 1–7 choose a bin, Enter goes to the next card, D shows or hides the bin descriptions. Tab also reaches every button.

Data label: "Source: tcf.com product pages, retrieved 2026-10-08; FanPedia pp. 31–32", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will recommend one of seven impeller types for each of ten airstream descriptions, judged against Twin City Fan's catalog application statements, with at least 8 of 10 correct (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 9: airfoil impeller, backward curved impeller, high efficiency centrifugal fan, radial tip impeller, radial bladed impeller, air handling impeller, open radial paddle impeller, material handling impeller, paper handling impeller.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recommend (8 min): Work through the ten cards. Before each choice, say aloud whether the material sticks, wraps, strikes or passes through.
  2. Review (3 min): In the summary, find each first choice that missed and name the misconception behind it.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Why does the cyclone exhaust card go to the radial tip fan and not a radial bladed fan, even though both handle dirty gas?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The most efficient impeller is always the best choice: the airfoil wins only for clean air; dirty, sticky or stringy jobs go to more rugged wheels.
  • Any radial bladed impeller handles any dirty airstream: the RBA, RBO, RBW and RBP each match a different material behavior.
  • Paper shreddings and corrugated trim need the same impeller: threads that wrap go to the back plate wool wheel; trim that strikes goes to the paper handling wheel.
  • Radial tip fans are only for clean air: the catalog lists them for large volumes of dirty gas, such as incinerator induced draft and cyclone exhaust.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-try score shown as "Recommendations correct on first try: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first try, shown as "✓ Mastered".
  • Reading the bin descriptions before committing is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer needs to exhaust lint-laden air from a textile dryer. Which impeller would you start with, and what would you ask first?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower product pages - Radial Bladed Fans (RBA, RBO, RBW, RBP) and Radial Tip & High Efficiency Fans (RTF, HAF, HIB): the application statements every card and bin is based on.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; pp. 31–32 describe the centrifugal and radial impeller types.
  3. Chapter 9: Impeller Construction and Material Handling - the sections "Clean-Air Impellers Built for Efficiency" and "Impellers for Dirty Airstreams".

docs.title: Density Correction Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Density Correction Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch10-density-correction-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Catalog ratings assume standard air (0.075 lb/ft³ at 70°F and sea level). This calculator practices the density corrections from the section "Density Corrections" in Chapter 10:

  • Temperature factor: Kt = 530 ÷ (T + 460), with T in °F
  • Altitude factor: Ka = (1 − 6.875 × 10⁻⁶ × h)^5.2559, with h in feet
  • Combined factor: Kd = Kt × Ka
  • Standard-air pressure for catalog selection = actual pressure ÷ Kd
  • Actual BHP = catalog BHP × Kd

The sim starts with three challenge jobs, in this fixed order (illustrative values; job 3 is the chapter's worked example "A Hot Fan at Altitude"):

# Job Asked Model answer 1 200°F air at sea level (0 ft) Combined factor 0.803 2 70°F air at 5,000 ft Combined factor 0.832 3 200°F air at 5,000 ft, 3.0 in. wg actual static pressure, 10,000 CFM Combined factor, then standard-air pressure 0.668, then 4.49 in. wg

A factor is correct within ±0.01 of the model value and a pressure within ±0.05 in. wg. Every answer gets two attempts; after the second wrong attempt the model value is shown and the answer counts as missed. Job 3 has two parts: the pressure question appears only after the factor is checked, and the job counts as correct only when both parts are. Two common slips get an extra line: a job-1 factor near 70 ÷ 200 = 0.35 ("Add 460 to each temperature first.") and a job-3 pressure near 3.0 × 0.668 = 2.00 ("That multiplies by the factor; to enter a standard-air catalog, divide by it."). After each answer the sim shows the model value and the one-line calculation, and the factor chain Kt × Ka = Kd on the right fills in.

Mastery is 3 of 3 jobs fully correct on the first attempt. After job 3, Explore mode unlocks four sliders: air temperature (0 to 800°F), site elevation (0 to 10,000 ft), actual static pressure (0.5 to 15.0 in. wg) and catalog BHP at the standard-air point (1.0 to 200.0 BHP). The three factors, the standard-air pressure and the actual BHP update at once. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read job 1, type the combined factor in Your answer and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: model value." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the calculation hint in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) for job 2, then job 3: type the factor, press Next: part 2, and type the standard-air pressure. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score.
  4. After job 3, press Start exploring. Set 800°F at sea level and see the combined factor fall to 0.421, so the catalog pressure is more than twice the job pressure. Set 200°F, 5,000 ft, 3.0 in. wg and 11.0 BHP to see the chapter's dryer example: 4.49 in. wg in, 7.35 BHP out. Start over clears the score and returns to job 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next part or job. Tab reaches the answer box, every button and the four sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · standard air 0.075 lb/ft³ at 70°F, sea level", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the combined density correction factor for a stated air temperature and site elevation, and use it to convert an actual static pressure to the standard-air pressure used for catalog selection, to within ±0.01 on the factor and ±0.05 in. wg on the pressure (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the section "Density Corrections" in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Standard air and the density correction factor
  • Temperature correction and degrees Rankine (°F + 460)
  • Altitude correction

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): Work each job with a calculator before pressing Check. Write Kt and Ka separately, then multiply.
  2. Review (2 min): For job 3, say aloud which way each value goes: pressure into the catalog is divided by Kd; horsepower out of the catalog is multiplied by Kd.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Find the temperature at which the catalog pressure is half again the job pressure at sea level (Kd about 0.667, near 335°F), then add elevation and watch it grow.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The fan moves less CFM in hot or thin air at the same speed: the sim repeats that airflow volume is the same at any density for a fan at fixed speed.
  • The actual pressure is multiplied by the factor to get the catalog pressure: a job-3 answer near 2.00 in. wg gets the "divide by it" correction.
  • Temperature in °F can be used directly in the ratio: a job-1 answer near 0.35 gets the "add 460" correction.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts jobs solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 jobs fully correct on the first attempt.
  • Moving the sliders in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner why a hot fan needs a cold-start motor check.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Density of air - Wikipedia article on how air density varies with temperature and pressure.
  2. Barometric formula - Wikipedia article on the standard-atmosphere pressure change with altitude behind the altitude factor.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan ratings at standard air and corrections for temperature and altitude.

docs.title: Fan Curve Explorer
docs.text: Run the Fan Curve Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Two illustrative centrifugal fans, labeled Curve A and Curve B, are drawn at one fixed speed each and at standard air. The top plot shows fan static pressure (in. wg) against airflow (CFM); the bottom plot shows brake horsepower (BHP) against the same airflow axis. Hovering any data point shows its airflow, fan static pressure and BHP.

Six questions, asked in a fixed order, ask the learner to decide whether four duty points sit in the stall region, which fan has a non-overloading power curve, and how large a motor Curve A needs so that it cannot be overloaded at this speed. Each question has one scored attempt. Each answer marks the point or curve it is about on the chart: a round marker with a solid green ring and ✓ for a correct answer, a square marker with a red ring and ✗ for an incorrect one. The feedback shows the reason, and after a miss it also shows the correct answer. After the last question the stall region of each fan is shaded so the two can be compared, and the score is shown as "n of 6 correct". Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.

Both curves are illustrative. They are shaped after typical backward inclined (Curve A) and forward curved (Curve B) fan behavior described in standard fan engineering texts and are not Twin City Fan published ratings. Curve A is the same illustrative fan curve tabulated in Chapter 10.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover along both pressure curves and both BHP curves to read values. Find the airflow at which each pressure curve reaches its peak (for Curve B, the right-hand peak after the dip).
  2. Answer each question by pressing Yes / No or Curve A / Curve B. Question 6 needs a typed number of BHP; press Submit or Enter. Each question has one attempt.
  3. Read the feedback, look at the point the sim just marked, then press Next question.
  4. After question 6, press See score. The score reads "n of 6 correct", followed by "Mastery reached" at 5 or more, or by what to review. Start over clears the marks and starts again at question 1; it is available at any time.

Keyboard: keys 1 and 2 choose the first or second answer; Enter submits a typed value, goes to the next question, and starts over from the score screen. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Illustrative data, standard air, one fixed speed per fan", shown at the bottom left of the chart.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate stable from stall-region operating points, and overloading from non-overloading power curves, by reading the pressure and BHP curves of two illustrative fans (Bloom: Analyze, verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and specifying engineers who read fan curves to judge a selection.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Fan curve, fan static pressure, brake horsepower, stall region, overloading power curve and non-overloading power curve, as defined in the section "The Fan Curve" of Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (4 min): Hover along Curve A and find the airflow of peak pressure (4,000 CFM, 4.9 in. wg). Then find Curve B's right-hand peak. Ask: which fan has more of its airflow range to the left of its peak?
  2. Committed answers (6 min): Work through the six questions without looking back at the chapter tables. Before pressing an answer, say out loud which side of the peak the point is on.
  3. Debrief (5 min): With the stall regions shaded, compare their extent. Discuss why the highest-pressure point is the edge of the stall region rather than the best place to select a fan, and why a 10 hp motor protects Curve A at this speed while Curve B's motor must be sized for the highest airflow the fan could realistically see.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any point the pressure curve passes through is a safe operating point, including points left of the peak (questions 1-4).
  • A fan's BHP always rises with airflow (question 5).
  • The highest-pressure point is the best place to select a fan (debrief and final summary).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running score reads "Questions correct: n of 6"; the final score reads "n of 6 correct". Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt (one scored attempt per question).
  • Hovering to read values is exploration and does not count as evidence. Question 6 accepts any value within 0.1 of 9.5 BHP.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 10: Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings - the fan curve, stall region and power curve sections this MicroSim exercises.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan's reference on fan types, performance and selection.
  3. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online fan and blower encyclopedia.
  4. Plotly JavaScript Open Source Graphing Library - the charting library used to draw the curves.

docs.title: Fan Power and Efficiency Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Fan Power and Efficiency Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch10-fan-power-efficiency-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator practices the power equations from the section "Brake Horsepower and Fan Efficiency" in Chapter 10:

  • Static air power (hp) = Q × FSP ÷ 6356
  • BHP = air power ÷ (static efficiency ÷ 100)
  • Static efficiency (%) = 100 × air power ÷ BHP

where Q is the airflow volume in CFM and FSP is the fan static pressure in in. wg. The sim starts with three challenge duties, in this fixed order. All three are illustrative values; challenge 1 is the chapter's worked example.

# Given Asked Model answer 1 10,000 CFM, 4.0 in. wg FSP, static efficiency 70% BHP 8.99 BHP 2 20,000 CFM, 6.0 in. wg FSP, static efficiency 75% BHP 25.17 BHP 3 5,000 CFM, 2.0 in. wg FSP, 2.5 BHP Static efficiency (%) 62.9%

An answer is correct when it is within 2% of the model value. You get two attempts per challenge. A wrong answer shows the worked calculation; an answer about 100 times too small also gets a reminder about decimals and percent. After the second wrong attempt the model value is shown and the challenge counts as missed. Once a challenge is resolved, the sim shows your answer next to the model value, the three-line calculation (air power, division, result) and two bars: air power, and BHP split into air power and losses.

Mastery is 3 of 3 challenges correct on the first attempt. After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks three sliders: airflow volume (1,000 to 50,000 CFM), fan static pressure (0.5 to 15.0 in. wg) and static efficiency (40% to 90%). The air power and BHP readouts and the bars update at once. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type a number in Your answer (BHP for challenges 1 and 2, percent for challenge 3) and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: model value." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the worked calculation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat for challenges 2 and 3. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score.
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Set 10,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg, then lower the efficiency from 70% to 50%: BHP rises from 8.99 to 12.59 hp. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, every button and the three sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · standard US fan units, constant 6,356", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate a fan's brake horsepower or static efficiency from its airflow volume, fan static pressure and one of the other two quantities, to within 2% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the section "Brake Horsepower and Fan Efficiency" in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Airflow volume (CFM) and fan static pressure (in. wg)
  • Air power and the constant 6,356
  • Brake horsepower and static efficiency

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): Solve each challenge with a calculator before pressing Check. Write the air power first, then divide by the efficiency as a decimal.
  2. Review (2 min): Compare your answer with the three-line calculation. If you were 100 times off, find where the percent should have become a decimal.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): At 10,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg, record BHP at 80%, 70%, 60% and 50% and compare with the chapter's table (7.87, 8.99, 10.49 and 12.59 BHP). Pick the motor size for each.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• BHP equals air power: the bars show BHP as air power plus losses, always larger.
  • Efficiency entered as a whole number (70 instead of 0.70): the sim spots an answer about 100 times too small and says so.
  • A less efficient fan needs less power because it "does less work": in Explore mode, lowering the efficiency at a fixed duty makes the BHP bar longer, not shorter.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.
  • Moving the sliders in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner why a fan selected far from its peak efficiency costs money twice (a larger motor and a larger electric bill).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fan (machine) - Wikipedia overview of fan types, performance and power.
  2. Brake horsepower - Wikipedia section on shaft power measured at the output shaft.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan performance, horsepower and efficiency.

docs.title: Operating Point Finder
docs.text:
Run the Operating Point Finder MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-curves.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch10-operating-point-finder.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The chart shows Curve A, the illustrative backward inclined fan from Chapter 10 at one fixed speed and standard air (solid indigo line, straight segments between the table points), and a duct system curve (dashed orange parabola):

  • System curve: P = R × (Q ÷ 10,000)², where R is the system resistance in in. wg at 10,000 CFM.
  • Operating point: the airflow, searched in 1 CFM steps from 0 to 16,000 CFM, where the fan pressure and the system pressure are closest.
  • The hatched band left of 4,000 CFM is Curve A's stall region (left of its pressure peak).

For each of three challenge systems, you predict the operating point before it is drawn. The systems come from the chapter section "The Operating Point":

# System Model operating point BHP 1 As designed: 4.0 in. wg at 10,000 CFM (R = 4.0) 10,000 CFM, 4.00 in. wg 9.0 2 Filters loaded: 4.0 in. wg at 8,000 CFM (R = 6.25) 8,390 CFM, 4.40 in. wg 8.3 3 Resistance overestimated: 2.5 in. wg at 10,000 CFM (R = 2.5) 11,600 CFM, 3.36 in. wg 9.4

A prediction is correct when its airflow is within ±300 CFM and its pressure within ±0.15 in. wg of the model intersection. You get two attempts per challenge; after the second wrong attempt the intersection is revealed and the challenge counts as missed. Each reveal marks the operating point (orange diamond) and shows the operating airflow (nearest 10 CFM), pressure (two decimals), BHP (one decimal, interpolated from the table) and whether the point is in the stall region.

Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt. After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks a slider for the system resistance at 10,000 CFM (1.0 to 35.0 in. wg). The system curve, the operating point and the readouts update at once; above about R = 30.6 in. wg the point falls below 4,000 CFM and the sim flags "In the stall region: select a different fan." Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the system for challenge 1. Type your predicted airflow (CFM) and pressure (in. wg) in the two boxes, or click the chart where you think the curves cross; the click fills both boxes.
  2. Press Check (or Enter). A correct prediction reads "✓ Correct: the curves cross at …" in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with an explanation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) for systems 2 and 3. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score.
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring and move the resistance slider. Watch the point move left as the system gets steeper and right as it gets flatter, and find where it enters the stall region. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Tab reaches the two prediction boxes, every button and the slider. Enter checks the prediction, and Enter again goes to the next challenge; the arrow keys move the focused slider. Clicking the chart is optional; typing gives the same result.

Data label: "Illustrative fan curve · Curve A, standard air, one fixed speed", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will solve for the operating point of an illustrative fan in a stated duct system by predicting where the fan curve and system curve intersect, to within ±300 CFM and ±0.15 in. wg (Bloom: Apply, verb: solve).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the sections on the fan curve, the system curve and the operating point in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan curve and stall region
  • System resistance and the system curve (square law)
  • Operating point
  • Brake horsepower

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): For each system, compute the system pressure at two or three airflows (for example 8,000, 9,000 and 10,000 CFM), compare with the fan curve, and commit a prediction.
  2. Review (2 min): For any miss, find the airflow where the system's need passes the fan's offer, as the feedback describes.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Find the resistance at which the operating point first enters the stall region, and the BHP at R = 1.0 in. wg. Explain why a non-overloading fan still protects its motor there.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A fan always delivers its rated airflow, whatever the system: three systems give three different airflows from the same fan at the same speed.
  • A dirtier, more resistant system makes the fan move more air "because it works harder": the loaded-filter system crosses further left, at less air.
  • The system curve is a straight line: the dashed curve is a parabola, so 20% more air needs 44% more pressure.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.
  • Moving the slider in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner what would change the operating point if the system curve stayed the same (a change in fan speed).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fan (machine) - Wikipedia overview of fan types and fan performance.
  2. Affinity laws - Wikipedia overview of how fan curves move with speed, the other way to move an operating point.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan curves, system resistance and flow control.

docs.title: Arrangement Identifier
docs.text:
Run the Arrangement Identifier MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch uses the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files from ../shared-libs/ (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js and fan-drawings.js, or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An arrangement number is a short answer to three questions: how is the fan driven, where is the impeller relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor? This MicroSim shows ten schematic side views of centrifugal fans, one for each of Arrangements 1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10, in shuffled order. For each drawing you first answer the three feature questions and commit them, and only then name the arrangement. Splitting the drawing into features before naming it is the skill the activity practices.

The parts in each drawing are left unlabeled until you check your arrangement answer, so you have to read the picture: look for belts and sheaves or a coupling, look for anything on the inlet side of the impeller, and look at what holds the bearings and the motor.

Each question allows one attempt per drawing. Mastery is 8 of 10 arrangements correct on the first attempt; the feature answers are scaffolding and are scored separately (out of 30). There is no Explore mode: after the round, Start over deals a new shuffled set.

The schematics are simplified teaching drawings, not manufacturer outline drawings. Twin City Fan's arrangement drawings are on FanPedia pp. 20–23. Arrangement 2 comes from the AMCA arrangement standard and is not shown in FanPedia.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the drawing. Answer Drive (Belt, Direct with coupling, or Direct on motor shaft), Impeller (Overhung or Center hung) and Bearings carried by (Pedestal, Fan housing, Independent pedestals outside inlet boxes, or Motor only).
  2. Press Check features. Each feature is marked ✓ correct or ✗ incorrect, with the correct answer shown (green solid or red dashed outline on the control). If all three features are right, the arrangements consistent with them are highlighted in bold with an outline (for example, Belt, Overhung and Pedestal highlight 1, 9 and 10). If any feature is wrong, nothing is highlighted.
  3. Choose an arrangement and press Check arrangement. The parts of the drawing are labeled and the reason for the answer appears, with an extra hint when your choice is a common confusion (for example, picking 4 for a coupled fan, or 1 for an Arrangement 9 or 10).
  4. Press Next drawing. After ten drawings, See results lists each drawing and shows separate scores for arrangements (out of 10) and features (out of 30), the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Start over starts a new shuffled round at any time.

Keyboard: Tab moves between controls; the arrow keys choose within a list or the arrangement options; Enter checks the features, checks the arrangement or goes to the next drawing. Feedback is announced to screen readers.

Data label: "Schematics are simplified. Twin City Fan arrangement drawings: FanPedia pp. 20–23. Arrangement 2 is from the AMCA standard and is not shown in FanPedia.", shown under the drawing with the keyboard hint.
