docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will distinguish ten centrifugal fan arrangements (1, 2, 3, 3SI, 3DI, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10) from schematic side-view drawings by identifying the drive type, the impeller position relative to the bearings, and what carries the bearings and the motor (Bloom: Analyze, verb: distinguish).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and others who read fan drawings and quotes.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes for one round of ten drawings.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Direct drive, belt drive, shaft coupling and sheave
  • Overhung and center hung impellers
  • Bearing pedestal, inlet box, SWSI and DWDI
  • The arrangement definitions in Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm-up (2 min): Recall the three questions that make an arrangement number: drive, impeller position, and what carries the bearings and motor.
  2. Round one (8 min): Complete a full round of ten drawings. Before pressing Check arrangement, say aloud which feature rules out the other highlighted arrangements.
  3. Debrief (5 min): Compare the misses on the results screen. Discuss the common confusions the hints target.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every direct drive fan is Arrangement 4: choosing 4 for a coupled fan (3SI, 3DI, 7 or 8) adds "There is a coupling and a separate fan shaft, so this is not Arrangement 4."
  • Any fan with a coupling is Arrangement 7, whatever the impeller position: choosing 7 for Arrangement 8 points out that the impeller is overhung.
  • Arrangements 1 and 9 differ in impeller position: they share the same three features, and the hint says they differ only in motor location (as does 10).
  • Arrangements 2 and 1 are the same: choosing 1 for Arrangement 2 points out that the bearings are on a bracket carried by the housing, not on a pedestal.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Arrangements correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt in one round.
  • "Features correct: n of 30" shows whether a miss came from misreading the drawing or from mapping correct features to the wrong number.
  • Discussion check: explain why drawings 1, 9 and 10 share the same three features but have different arrangement numbers.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan; pp. 20–23 (centrifugal arrangement drawings and captions), p. 30 (impeller orientation), pp. 162–168 (arrangement technical descriptions).
  2. AMCA Standards - Air Movement and Control Association International, ANSI/AMCA Standard 99, Standards Handbook: drive arrangements for centrifugal fans (source of the Arrangement 2 definition used here).
  3. Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements - the arrangement definitions and worked examples in this textbook.

docs.title: Belt Drive Speed Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Belt Drive Speed Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch11-belt-drive-speed-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator puts the three belt drive formulas from Chapter 11 side by side:

  • Fan speed: fan rpm = motor rpm × motor sheave pitch diameter ÷ fan sheave pitch diameter
  • Belt speed: V (ft/min) = π × motor sheave pitch diameter (in) × motor rpm ÷ 12
  • Belt count: design hp = motor hp × drive service factor; belts = design hp ÷ rating per belt, rounded up to a whole belt (a whole-number quotient is not rounded up)

The motor sheave and the fan sheave are drawn to scale relative to each other and joined by a V-belt. Once a drive is checked, each sheave turns at its own computed speed, so the larger sheave visibly turns slower. The outputs panel lists the fan speed, the speed ratio (motor rpm ÷ fan rpm), the belt speed, the design horsepower and the belts required.

The sim starts with four challenge drives, in this order:

# Motor rpm Motor sheave (in) Fan sheave (in) Motor hp Drive SF hp per belt Fan rpm Belt speed (ft/min) Belts 1 1,760 5.0 8.0 15 1.3 6.0 1,100 2,304 4 2 1,760 6.0 8.4 10 1.2 5.0 1,257 2,765 3 3 1,170 9.0 6.0 20 1.4 8.5 1,755 2,757 4 4 3,500 4.0 10.0 7.5 1.2 4.5 1,400 3,665 2

For each drive you type a fan speed and a belt count. The two answers are judged separately: the fan speed is right within ±5 rpm of the model value, and the belt count is right only when it is exactly the model value. You get two attempts per drive. A field you got right on the first attempt stays fixed, and you correct only the other one. A wrong answer shows the worked calculation; if your fan speed is the ratio turned upside down, or your belt count was rounded down, the feedback says so. After a second wrong attempt the model values are shown and the drive counts as missed. Mastery is all four drives with both answers right on the first attempt.

After drive 4, Explore mode unlocks six sliders (motor speed 860 to 3,540 rpm, motor sheave 3.0 to 12.0 in, fan sheave 3.0 to 24.0 in, motor power 1 to 100 hp, drive service factor 1.0 to 1.8, rating per belt 1.0 to 20.0 hp) and every output updates at once. A belt speed above 6,500 ft/min shows a note to check the drive manufacturer's limits. Explore mode is never scored.

All numbers are illustrative; challenge 1 matches the chapter's worked examples. Real per-belt ratings and drive service factors come from the drive manufacturer's current tables.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1: the motor speed and power, both sheave sizes, the drive service factor and the rating per belt. Type the fan speed in Fan speed (rpm) and the number of belts in Belts, then press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct drive reads "✓ Correct: 1,100 rpm and 4 belts." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the worked calculation in a dashed red box; fix the field that was wrong and check again.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat for drives 2 to 4. In drive 3, watch the fan sheave turn faster than the motor sheave. "Challenges fully correct: n of 4" keeps the running score.
  4. After drive 4, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Make the fan sheave bigger and watch the fan slow down; raise the motor sheave and motor speed until the belt speed note appears. Reset to defaults returns to drive 1's values; Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answers, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches both answer boxes, every button and the six sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Motor speeds, per-belt ratings and service factors are illustrative. Use the current drive manufacturer's tables for real selections.", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the fan speed, belt speed and required belt count of a V-belt fan drive from the motor speed, the two sheave pitch diameters, the motor horsepower and the drive service factor, with fan speed within ±5 rpm and belt count exact (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the "Belt Drive" section of Chapter 11.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Belt drive, sheave, pitch diameter, motor sheave and fan sheave
  • V-belt and belt speed
  • Drive service factor and design horsepower

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): Work each drive with a calculator before pressing Check. Before calculating, say which sheave is bigger and whether the fan should turn slower or faster than the motor.
  2. Review (2 min): Read the worked calculation for any missed drive and redo it on paper.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Starting from the defaults, raise the fan sheave from 8.0 to 10.0 in and record the fan speed. Then find a motor speed and motor sheave that push the belt speed past 6,500 ft/min. Finally, set a drive whose belt quotient is exactly a whole number and confirm it is not rounded up.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A larger fan sheave makes the fan run faster: the turning sheaves and the fan rpm readout show it slowing, and Explore mode says "Bigger fan sheave, slower fan."
  • The speed ratio equals the fan/motor diameter ratio the same way up: an inverted answer gets "Your ratio is inverted: the larger sheave turns slower."
  • A belt count of 3.25 rounds down to 3: a rounded-down answer gets "Round belt counts up; a partial belt cannot carry its share."
  • The motor's nameplate service factor is the drive service factor: every drive lists the drive service factor separately from the motor horsepower, and the chapter contrasts it with the motor service factor example from FanPedia p. 69.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges fully correct: n of 4" counts drives with both answers right on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 4" and the mastery line; mastery is 4 of 4 drives with both answers right on the first attempt.
  • Moving the sliders in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner to explain why the fan in challenge 3 turns faster than its motor.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Belt (mechanical) - Wikipedia overview of belt drives, V-belts, speed ratio and belt power transmission.
  2. Pulley - how pulley (sheave) diameters set the speed ratio of a belt drive.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan drives, arrangements and the motor service factor (p. 69).

docs.title: Overhung or Center Hung Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Overhung or Center Hung Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch11-overhung-center-hung-sorter.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every centrifugal arrangement number is built on one of two impeller positions (FanPedia p. 79): an overhung impeller sits on the end of the shaft, beyond both bearings, and a center hung impeller sits between the two bearings. Where the impeller sits decides where the bearings must stand, and that decides whether a bearing is in the airstream.

Each card gives a one-line description of an arrangement. You make two choices:

  • Impeller: Overhung or Center hung
  • Bearings: All out of airstream, At least one in airstream, or No fan bearings

A card is correct only when both choices match; there is no partial credit, but the feedback says which choice was wrong and why. After Check, a side-view schematic of that arrangement appears with the impeller and the bearings highlighted and the airstream shaded between dashed edges, so you can see which bearings the air reaches.

Card Impeller Bearings Arrangement 1 SWSI Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 3 SWSI Center hung At least one in airstream Arrangement 3 DWDI Center hung At least one in airstream Arrangement 3SI Center hung All out of airstream Arrangement 3DI Center hung All out of airstream Arrangement 4 SWSI Overhung No fan bearings Arrangement 7 DWDI Center hung At least one in airstream Arrangement 7SI Center hung All out of airstream Arrangement 7DI Center hung All out of airstream Arrangement 8 SWSI Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 9 SWSI Overhung All out of airstream Arrangement 10 SWSI Overhung All out of airstream

The twelve cards come in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. The schematics are simplified side views; the Twin City Fan arrangement drawings are in FanPedia pp. 20–23, and the impeller groups come from FanPedia p. 30.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the card. Choose Overhung or Center hung, then one of the three bearing options. Check turns on once both are chosen.
  2. Press Check (or Enter). A correct card reads "✓ Correct: Overhung, All out of airstream." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." in a dashed red box, names the wrong choice and gives the reason. The schematic appears either way.
  3. Press Next card (or Enter). "Correct: n of 12" keeps the running score.
  4. After card 12 the summary shows the first-attempt score, the mastery line and every missed card with its answer. Retry missed runs the missed cards again as practice (not scored); Start over deals a new shuffled round.

Keyboard: 1 Overhung, 2 Center hung, 3 All out of airstream, 4 At least one in airstream, 5 No fan bearings; Enter checks the card, and Enter again goes to the next one. Tab reaches every button; Space on a focused option picks it.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 30, 79, 162–168 · Schematics simplified", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify twelve fan arrangements as overhung or center hung and state whether each arrangement's bearings sit in or out of the airstream, from a one-line description of each arrangement (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read "Where the Impeller Sits on the Shaft" in Chapter 11.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Overhung impeller and center hung impeller
  • Bearing pedestal and airstream
  • SWSI and DWDI fans, inlet box
  • Direct drive, belt drive and shaft coupling

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (6-8 min): Work through the twelve cards. Before choosing, say where the impeller sits relative to the two bearings.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the missed cards on the summary, then press Retry missed and sort them again (not scored).
  3. Discuss (2-4 min): Compare the Arrangement 3 SWSI and Arrangement 3SI schematics. What does the inlet box change, and what does it leave the same?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Direct drive means center hung: Arrangements 4 and 8 are direct drive and overhung; marking the Arrangement 4 or Arrangement 8 card center hung adds "Direct drive does not decide impeller position."
  • Arrangement 4 has fan bearings in the airstream: its only bearings are inside the motor, so its bearing answer is "No fan bearings."
  • Every Arrangement 3 has its bearings out of the airstream: Arrangement 3 SWSI and 3 DWDI both put a bearing in the inlet.
  • Center hung fans always have a bearing in the airstream: 3SI, 3DI, 7SI and 7DI use inlet boxes to move the bearings out, and their schematics show the bearings outside the shaded airstream.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Correct: n of 12" is the running score. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 12" and the mastery line; mastery is 10 of 12 cards with both choices right on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: why does FanPedia limit standard DWDI fans to clean air at 130°F, and which arrangement removes that limit?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia overview of centrifugal fan construction, impellers, housings and drives.
  2. Plain bearing and rolling-element bearings - the shaft bearings whose location the sorter asks about.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; p. 30 lists the overhung and center hung arrangements and pp. 162–168 describe each arrangement.

docs.title: Discharge Position Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Discharge Position Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch12-discharge-position-explorer.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A centrifugal fan's rotation and discharge are always named as seen from the drive side (Chapter 12). The discharge angle N counts from upblast (360) in the direction of rotation, in 45° steps, so the direction the air leaves, measured clockwise from straight up as seen from the drive side, is θ = N for a CW fan and θ = 360 − N for a CCW fan. A view from the inlet side is the mirror image: the drawing flips left to right and the rotation arrow appears reversed, but the name does not change.

The sim opens in Explore mode. Set the rotation (CW or CCW), step the discharge angle from 45 to 360, and switch the viewpoint between the drive side and the inlet side. The housing redraws with its rotation arrow and outlet, and the panel shows the abbreviation and full name, the designation ("CW 90"), the FanPedia "also known as" form ("Clockwise 90°") and the direction the air leaves as seen from the drive side. The small dial shows the angle counted from upblast.

The eight positions are UBD Upblast 360, TAU Top Angular Up 45, THD Top Horizontal 90, TAD Top Angular Down 135, DBD Downblast 180, BAD Bottom Angular Down 225, BHD Bottom Horizontal 270 and BAU Bottom Angular Up 315 (FanPedia pp. 46–47).

Press Start challenge for ten drawings in a fixed order. Each shows a housing from the drive side or, for drawings 8 and 9, from the inlet side. Choose a rotation and a discharge abbreviation as seen from the drive side and press Check. Both must match; there is no partial credit. You get two attempts. A wrong first attempt gets a hint: a wrong rotation on an inlet-side drawing says to mirror the view, a wrong rotation on a drive-side drawing says to read the arrow as drawn, and a wrong abbreviation says to count 45° steps from upblast in the direction of rotation. A second wrong attempt shows the answer and the reason, and the drawing counts as missed. Only first-attempt answers count; mastery is 8 of 10. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. In Explore mode, keep CW and press + 45° repeatedly from 360. Predict where the outlet goes before each step.
  2. Switch to CCW at the same angle: the housing mirrors and the air direction changes side, while the name and angle stay the same.
  3. Choose Inlet side: only the picture changes; the name and designation do not.
  4. Press Start challenge. For each drawing choose CW or CCW and one of the eight abbreviations, then press Check (or Enter). A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: CW THD (CW 90)." in a solid green box; a wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with a hint in a dashed red box.
  5. Press Next drawing (or Enter). After drawing 10 the summary lists the score, the mastery line and any missed drawings with their reasons. Explore mode goes back to free exploration; Start over runs the ten drawings again.

Keyboard: Tab reaches every button and the angle slider (arrow keys move it). Space picks a rotation or an abbreviation; Enter checks the drawing, and Enter again goes to the next one.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 46–47 · Directions as seen from the drive side", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text:

        height="642px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the drive-side viewing rule and the discharge-angle convention to name the rotation and discharge position of ten SWSI centrifugal housing drawings, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the "Viewed From the Drive Side", "Rotation", "Discharge Position" and "Discharge Angle" sections of Chapter 12.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Drive side and viewed from the drive side
  • Rotation (CW and CCW)
  • Discharge position, discharge angle and the eight position names and abbreviations
  • Mirror image of an opposite-side view

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Step the angle all the way around for CW, then for CCW. Find the two positions whose air direction is the same for both rotations, and say how their housings differ.
  2. Challenge (6-8 min): Name the ten drawings. For drawings 8 and 9, mirror the view before naming the rotation.
  3. Review (2 min): Read the missed drawings on the summary and recreate each one in Explore mode.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The rotation seen from the inlet side is the fan's rotation: drawings 8 and 9 are inlet-side views, and a wrong rotation there gets "Check the viewpoint".
  • The discharge angle is a fixed compass bearing: switching CW to CCW at the same angle in Explore mode moves the air to the other side while the name stays.
  • Upblast and downblast housings are the same for both rotations: the explorer shows the CW upblast outlet on the left of the top and the CCW one on the right.
  • "Top Horizontal" alone tells which way the air goes: the "Air leaves toward" line changes with the rotation.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is the running score; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: a submittal says CCW 135. Without the sim, say which way the air leaves and where the outlet sits.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia overview of centrifugal fan housings, rotation and discharge.
  2. Mirror image - why a view from the opposite side reverses left and right and the apparent rotation.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; pp. 46–49 define the discharge positions viewed from the drive side.

docs.title: Inlet Box Position Dial
docs.text:
Run the Inlet Box Position Dial MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch12-inlet-box-position-dial.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An inlet box's position states where its opening faces. FanPedia measures it around the fan as seen from the drive side, in 45° steps from 45 to 360, with 360 at the top and the angle increasing clockwise (FanPedia p. 144). Unlike the discharge angle, it does not change direction with rotation.

Position Description Box location (drive side) 45 Angular Down Intake Upper right 90 Horizontal Right Intake Right 135 Angular Up Intake Lower right 180 Bottom Up Intake Bottom 225 Angular Up Intake Lower left 270 Horizontal Left Intake Left 315 Angular Down Intake Upper left 360 Top Down Intake Top

The sim opens in Explore mode with a CW fan and the box at 360. Move the box around the housing and read each number and description; switch the drawn rotation between CW and CCW and watch the box and its number stay where they are. Once you have visited both members of a pair, the panel points out that 45 and 315 (and 135 and 225) share a description.

Press Start challenge for eight duct descriptions in a fixed order. Move the box to meet the duct and press Check. The position numbers stay hidden until you check, so you place the box by where the duct arrives; the check then shows the number. An answer is correct when the position equals the answer; there is no partial credit. You get two attempts. A wrong first attempt gets a hint: the mirror position with the same description says "Same description, other side"; on duct 8, which is drawn on a CCW fan, the counterclockwise count says the angle does not follow rotation; anything else says to find where the duct arrives. A second wrong attempt marks the correct position with a dashed ✓ ring, shows the answer and the reason, and counts the duct as missed. Only first-attempt answers count; mastery is 7 of 8. Explore mode is never scored.

The housing is drawn with a top horizontal discharge so the drawing has an outlet; the inlet box is on the inlet face, so it may pass behind the outlet in this end view.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. In Explore mode, press Clockwise ⟳ (or the Right arrow key) to walk the box around the housing, reading each number and description. Clicking near a position also moves the box.
  2. Switch the rotation to CCW: the box and its number do not move.
  3. Press Start challenge. Read the duct description, move the box to meet the duct and press Check (or Enter). A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: position 90, Horizontal Right Intake." in a solid green box; a wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with a hint in a dashed red box.
  4. Press Next duct (or Enter). After duct 8 the summary lists the score, the mastery line and any missed ducts with their reasons. Explore mode returns to free exploration; Start over runs the eight ducts again.

Keyboard: Left and Right arrow keys move the box; Enter checks the duct, and Enter again goes to the next one. Tab reaches every button; Space presses a focused button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia p. 144 · Positions as seen from the drive side", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text:

        height="602px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will use the drive-side inlet box angle convention to set the correct inlet box position for eight duct-approach descriptions, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Apply, verb: use).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the "Inlet Box Position" section of Chapter 12.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Inlet box and inlet box position
  • Viewed from the drive side
  • The eight inlet box position numbers and their descriptions
  • The difference between the inlet box angle and the discharge angle

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Walk the box all the way around. Name the two pairs of positions that share a description, then switch to CCW and confirm nothing moves.
  2. Challenge (5 min): Set the eight ducts. Say the number aloud before pressing Check.
  3. Review (2 min): For each missed duct, find the mirror position and explain why the number, not the description, pins down the side.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The inlet box angle counts in the direction of rotation: duct 8 is drawn on a CCW fan, and the counterclockwise count gets "The inlet box angle does not follow rotation".
  • The description alone identifies one position: ducts 5 to 8 use the shared descriptions in pairs.
  • The inlet box angle is read from the inlet side: the drawing and every duct are described from the drive side, and a mirrored answer gets "Same description, other side".

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Correct on first attempt: n of 8" is the running score; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: an order reads CCW 90 discharge with the inlet box at 90. Which side is the box on, and why does the rotation not change it?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Duct (flow) - Wikipedia overview of air ducts and how they connect to fans.
  2. Centrifugal fan - centrifugal fan construction, including inlets and housings.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; p. 144 defines the inlet box positions determined from the drive side.

docs.title: Motor Position Restriction Checker
docs.text: Run the Motor Position Restriction Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A centrifugal fan's motor can sit in one of the AMCA floor positions W, X, Y or Z, but not every position works with every discharge. On SWSI Arrangements 1, 3 and 3F, FanPedia forbids the position where the motor would block the outlet opening (BHD and TAD discharges) and calls for a height check where the motor may not fit below a Top Horizontal outlet (THD). Arrangement 9SS swingout fans have only two buildable pairings: CW with (L) and CCW with (R).

This MicroSim shows ten order lines in a fixed order. For each line you choose one verdict, Allowed, Not allowed or Height check needed, and submit it. Each line has one scored attempt. After you submit, the sim:

  • marks your verdict ("✓ Correct: Not allowed." or "✗ Not quite: Not allowed.") and shows the reason for the line;
  • opens the reference rule card and highlights the row (and the rotation) that decides the line;
  • marks the drive-side sketch: a dashed box with ✗ for a position that is not allowed, a dashed box with ↕ for a height check.

The running score reads "Verdicts correct: n of 10". After line 10, Show summary lists each line with your verdict and the correct verdict side by side, and states the first-attempt score and whether mastery (9 of 10 on the first attempt) was reached. Opening the rule card is exploration and never changes the score.

The rule the sim applies (FanPedia PDF pp. 53, 162–163, 166):

Discharge CW CCW Reason BHD Z not allowed W not allowed Motor interferes with the outlet opening TAD W not allowed Z not allowed Motor interferes with the outlet opening THD W, height check Z, height check Motor may not fit below the discharge; on Arrangement 1 the pedestal can be lengthened Arrangement 9SS (L) only (R) only Fixed swingout pairings

Every other combination is allowed. The verdicts come from the kit's FP.codes.checkMotorPosition, the same table the chapter prints. The order lines are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the order line: arrangement, rotation, discharge and motor position.
  2. Pick a verdict (click it or press 1, 2 or 3), then press Submit verdict.
  3. Read the feedback, compare the highlighted rule-card row and the sketch, and press Next line.
  4. After line 10, press Show summary to see your verdicts beside the correct ones. Press Start over at any time to clear the score and return to line 1.

Keyboard: 1 Allowed, 2 Not allowed, 3 Height check needed. Enter submits the chosen verdict, then goes to the next line (Enter on a focused verdict button picks it and submits). R opens or closes the rule card. Tab moves between the buttons.

Data label: "Order lines are illustrative · Source: FanPedia PDF pp. 53, 162–163, 166", shown at the bottom of the drawing column.

        height="718px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will judge whether each proposed combination of arrangement, rotation, discharge and motor position can be ordered as written, using the FanPedia restriction rules (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: judge).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and order-entry staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan arrangements (1, 3, 3F, 9SS)
  • CW and CCW rotation, seen from the drive side
  • Discharge letter codes (BHD, TAD, THD, UBD)
  • Motor positions W, X, Y and Z, and (L) and (R)
  • Motor position restrictions, from Chapter 13

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judge (7 min): Work through the ten order lines. Before each verdict, say the rotation and the discharge together and name the restricted position for that pair.
  2. Review (3 min): Compare the summary table with your verdicts. For each miss, find the rule-card row that decided it.
  3. Discuss (5 min): Look at lines 1 and 3. Why does BHD forbid Z for CW but W for CCW? Write the corrected line for each line that was not allowed (the chapter's worked example moves line 1 to position W).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A restriction on a position holds for both rotations: lines 1–3 and 4–6 pair the same discharge with both rotations, and the sketch shows the outlet mirror left to right.
  • The THD restriction forbids the position outright: lines 7 and 8 need "Height check needed", not "Not allowed".
  • Arrangement 9SS lets the buyer choose either side for the motor: line 10 shows the two fixed pairings.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Verdicts correct: n of 10"; mastery is 9 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: a CCW BHD fan arrives with the motor in W. What would you change, and why?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia, pp. 52–53 (motor positions, swingout arrangements) and pp. 162–166 (Arrangements 1, 3, 3F and 9SS technical descriptions and motor position restrictions). PDF
  2. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia online - the online edition of the same reference.
  3. AMCA International. ANSI/AMCA Standard 99, Standards Handbook - drive arrangements and motor positions for centrifugal fans. AMCA

docs.title: Rotation and Discharge Code Builder
docs.text:
Run the Rotation and Discharge Code Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A centrifugal fan's rotation and discharge code tells the factory which way the wheel turns and where the outlet points, both as seen by an observer on the drive side. The code can be written in letter form (CW THD) or angle form (CW 90). This MicroSim gives you eight job cards, in a fixed order, each describing a fan and its outlet in words. For each card you choose a rotation and one of the eight discharge letter codes, or "Not offered", and submit.

After every submission the sim draws the drive-side outline of the housing with the outlet in the answer's direction, a rotation arrow, a small dial showing the angle measured from straight up in the direction of rotation, and both code forms. The first submission on each card is scored; one unscored retry follows. A correct submission reads "✓ Correct: ."; an incorrect one shows the card's reason followed by the correct answer. The running score reads "Codes correct: n of 8", and mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt.

After card 8, free practice (the sim's Explore mode, never scored) unlocks and the summary shows your first-attempt score, the mastery line and any missed cards. Choose SWSI or DWDI, a rotation, and a discharge angle from 45° to 360° in 45° steps, and the outline and code update at once. On a DWDI fan, 225° (Bottom Angular Down) shows "Not offered on DWDI".

The job cards are illustrative scenarios. Discharge names, letter codes, angle forms and the DWDI discharge list come from FanPedia (PDF pp. 46–49) and Chapter 13.

docs.title: The rule the sim uses
docs.text:
Start with the outlet pointing straight up (360°) and turn it through the discharge angle in the direction of rotation: clockwise for CW, counterclockwise for CCW.

Code Angle CW outlet points CCW outlet points UBD Upblast 360 up up TAU Top Angular Up 45 up and right up and left THD Top Horizontal 90 right left TAD Top Angular Down 135 down and right down and left DBD Downblast 180 down down BAD Bottom Angular Down 225 down and left (SWSI only) down and right (SWSI only) BHD Bottom Horizontal 270 left right BAU Bottom Angular Up 315 up and left up and right

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job card: fan type, rotation and outlet direction, all from the drive side.
  2. Choose a rotation and a discharge (or "Not offered") under Your code, then press Submit code.
  3. Read the feedback and study the drawn housing. Use Retry (unscored) if you want another try; it never changes the score.
  4. Press Next card. After card 8, press Start free practice (or change any Free practice control), read the summary, and explore fan type, rotation and angle.
  5. Press Start over at any time to clear the score and return to card 1.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the controls and the arrow keys change a selection. Enter submits your code, or goes to the next card once the feedback is shown. Enter or Space also presses a focused button.

Data label: "Job cards are illustrative · Source: FanPedia PDF pp. 46–49", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the drive-side rotation and discharge-angle conventions to write the correct rotation and discharge code, in letter form and angle form, for a described centrifugal fan (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Fan sales, application and order-entry staff, and engineering students who specify or order centrifugal fans.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Drive side, clockwise (CW) and counterclockwise (CCW) rotation, discharge position, discharge angle, SWSI and DWDI fans, Bottom Angular Down discharge, and DWDI discharge limits, all covered in Chapter 13.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (8 min): Work through the eight job cards. Before each submission, say the outlet direction aloud and count quarter turns from straight up in the direction of rotation.
  2. Check (2 min): After each card, compare the drawn outlet and the angle dial with your prediction; use the unscored retry on any card you missed.
  3. Explore (5 min): In free practice, fix the angle at 90° and switch between CW and CCW. Note that the outlet mirrors left to right. Repeat at 45° and 315°, then try 225° on a DWDI fan.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does CW 90 blow right but CCW 90 blow left, while 360 and 180 are the same for both rotations?
  2. Why must rotation be judged from the drive side and not the inlet side?
  3. A layout calls for a DWDI fan blowing bottom angular down. What could you offer instead?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The same angle number points the same way for CW and CCW fans.
  • Rotation can be judged from the inlet side.
  • Every discharge is available on every centrifugal fan, including DWDI.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Codes correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt.
  • Free practice is exploration and is not scored.
  • Ask learners to explain card 6: why is "Not offered" the right code?

docs.title: Motor Enclosure Selector
docs.text:
Run the Motor Enclosure Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A motor enclosure decides how the motor gets rid of its heat and how well its windings are protected from the air around it. FanPedia (page 73) lists five enclosures used by Twin City Fan: open drip proof (ODP), totally enclosed fan cooled (TEFC), totally enclosed air over (TEAO), totally enclosed non-ventilated (TENV) and explosion proof (EXPL).

This MicroSim shows ten illustrative fan jobs in a fixed order. For each job you recommend one enclosure. Your first choice on each job is the scored one:

  • a choice in the job's accepted set reads "✓ Correct:" followed by the reason;
  • any other choice reads "✗ Not this one. Reread the job and the card for the enclosure you chose, then try again." and that enclosure is crossed out;
  • you keep choosing until you reach an accepted enclosure; later tries never change the score. The reason and the accepted answer appear only once you reach a correct choice.

Job 1 accepts two answers: ODP is acceptable in a clean, dry room, and TEFC also works. Picking TEFC there adds "ODP would also have been acceptable here."

Five reference cards, one per enclosure, can be opened at any time. Each shows a side-view sketch of the motor with its cooling path (room air through the windings, an external fan blowing over the frame, the fan's own airstream, or heat leaving through the frame) and the IP ratings and duties FanPedia maps to it. Reading a card is exploration and is never scored.

The running count reads "First-try correct: n of 10". After job 10 a summary lists each job, your first choice and the accepted answer, and states whether mastery (8 of 10 on the first try) was reached.

# Job (short) Accepted 1 Clean, dry indoor supply fan ODP, TEFC 2 Rooftop exhaust, rain and dust TEFC 3 Vaneaxial, motor in the housing airstream TEAO 4 Belt drive, motor in the air stream TEAO 5 Textile plant, lint, larger frame accepted TENV 6 Solvent paint spray room, classified for gases EXPL 7 Grain handling, classified for combustible dust EXPL 8 Paper mill, IEEE 841 specified TEFC 9 IP55, general purpose, non-hazardous TEFC 10 IP22, clean indoor ODP

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job. Open any reference card with the Card list (or press C to step through them).
  2. Press an enclosure button under Recommend (or keys 1–5). Read the feedback.
  3. If the choice was wrong, choose again; crossed-out enclosures are already ruled out.
  4. Once you reach an accepted enclosure, press Next job (or Enter). After job 10, read the summary and press Start over to try again.

Keyboard: 1 ODP, 2 TEFC, 3 TEAO, 4 TENV, 5 EXPL; C steps through the reference cards; Enter goes to the next job once the job is solved. Tab reaches every button and the card list; Enter or Space presses a focused button.

Data label: "Illustrative jobs · Source: FanPedia p. 73", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will recommend a motor enclosure (ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV or EXPL) for each of ten described fan jobs, with at least 8 of 10 first-attempt choices falling in the accepted set (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Motor enclosure; ODP, TEFC, TEAO, TENV and explosion proof motors
  • Intended duty (GD, SD, IEEE 841, IEEE 45, DFG) and IP ratings
  • Hazardous locations, from Chapter 14

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recommend (8 min): For each job, ask the chapter's two questions first: is the area classified as hazardous, and what is in the air around the motor? Then commit a choice.
  2. Compare (3 min): Open the cards for TEFC and EXPL side by side in turn. Both have an external fan; what makes EXPL different, and why is it not the answer for job 9?
  3. Review (4 min): Use the summary to find the jobs you missed and say which fact on the card would have decided each.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• ODP is fine anywhere indoors, even in dirty or wet air: jobs 1, 2 and 10 separate clean, dry air from wet and dirty air.
  • An explosion-proof motor is needed whenever the air is dirty: job 2 is dirty but not classified, so it is TEFC.
  • A TEAO motor cools itself the way a TEFC motor does: the TEAO card shows no fan of its own, only the fan's airstream (jobs 3 and 4).
  • IP55 always means explosion proof: job 9 maps IP55 to TEFC in a non-hazardous area.
  • TENV is simply a better TEFC with no downside: job 5 states the cost, a hotter motor in a larger frame.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-try score shown as "First-try correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: a European specification asks for ATEX motors. What does the chapter say about substituting a standard EXPL motor?

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  2. Twin City Fan & Blower. FanPedia online - the online edition of the same reference.
  3. NEMA. ANSI/NEMA MG 1, Motors and Generators - enclosure and duty definitions for industrial motors. NEMA
  4. NFPA. NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, Article 500 - classes, divisions and groups for hazardous locations. NFPA

docs.title: Motor Line Decoder
docs.text: Run the Motor Line Decoder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A Twin City Fan order describes the motor in one coded line (FanPedia p. 71):

50 HP, 1800 RPM, IN, P, 3 Phase, 60 Frequency, 460 Volt, SD, TEFC, 326T

This MicroSim shows the whole line with one field highlighted at a time. For each of the ten fields you pick one of four meanings before anything is revealed; the four choices appear in a fixed shuffled order. Each field has one scored pick. After the pick:

  • the correct meaning is marked ✓ (solid green) and a wrong pick ✗ (dashed red);
  • the feedback reads "✓ Correct:" or "✗ Not quite:" followed by the field's explanation, and for five common slips a one-line note (for example, "Phase appears later as 3 Phase; P here is efficiency.");
  • a short decoded meaning stays visible under that field of the line.

The running count reads "First-try correct: n of 10". After field 10 the whole line is shown decoded with the first-try score and whether mastery (8 of 10 on the first try) was reached. Any answered field in the line can be selected to reread its explanation; that is exploration and never changes the score.

Field Meaning Why 50 HP Rated power 50 horsepower About 37 kW using kW = HP × 0.7457 1800 RPM Synchronous speed of a 4-pole 60 Hz motor 120 × 60 / 4 = 1800; the motor runs slightly slower because of slip IN Induction technology The alternative is EC (electronically commutated) P Premium Efficiency Comparable to NEMA Premium and IEC IE3 3 Phase Three-phase AC supply Electric power field: phase 60 Frequency 60 Hz supply frequency Electric power field: frequency 460 Volt 460 V supply voltage Electric power field: voltage SD Severe Duty GD is general duty; DFG is explosion proof TEFC Totally enclosed fan cooled Sealed windings; an external fan blows air over the frame 326T NEMA 326 frame, T-frame foot mount Shaft height 32/4 = 8 inches from the bottom of the feet

The distractor meanings are illustrative and are not real codes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the highlighted field (▸) in the motor line and the question below it.
  2. Pick a meaning (click it or press 1–4). Read the explanation and see the correct meaning marked.
  3. Press Next field (or Enter). After field 10, press Show decoded line to see the whole line decoded with your score.
  4. Select any answered field in the line to reread its explanation. Press Start over to clear the score and begin again at field 1.

Keyboard: 1–4 pick a meaning; Enter goes to the next field. Tab reaches the meanings, the answered fields of the line and the buttons; Enter or Space presses a focused button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 71–74 (motor line and field meanings) · distractor meanings are illustrative, not real codes", shown under the motor line.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will interpret each of the ten fields of a Twin City Fan motor specification line, choosing the correct meaning for at least 8 of 10 fields on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: interpret).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Horsepower, synchronous speed and poles
  • Induction and EC motor technology
  • Efficiency class; phase, frequency and voltage
  • Intended duty and motor enclosure
  • NEMA frame size and frame letters, from Chapter 14

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (6 min): For each field, say the meaning aloud before picking, then compare with the explanation.
  2. Review (2 min): Select the fields you missed in the decoded line and reread their explanations.
  3. Transfer (2 min): Rewrite the line for a 25 HP, 1200 RPM, EC, Standard Efficiency, single-phase 230 V general-duty ODP motor, and check each field against the chapter's table.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• "1800 RPM" is the exact running speed: field 2 explains synchronous speed and slip.
  • "P" means phase: field 4 notes that phase appears later as 3 Phase.
  • "SD" means standard duty: field 8 notes that general duty is GD.
  • "T" in 326T means TEFC: field 10 notes that T marks the T-frame foot mount.
  • "60 Frequency" is a speed: field 6 notes that it is the supply's 60 cycles per second.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-try score shown as "First-try correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up: what is the shaft height of a 184T motor, and how do you know?

docs.title: Motor Base Selector
docs.text:
Run the Motor Base Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Choosing a motor base for a belt-driven fan is a procedure: check the motor frame against each base's frame range, then the fan type and arrangement against its typical mountings, then the industry. This MicroSim gives eight illustrative cases, one at a time and always in the same order. For each one you choose one of five base styles and commit it with Check.

The reference table, which you can open at any time, holds the rules:

Base style Frame range Typical mounting NEMA type slide base 48 to 445 Arr. 1, 3, 9, 9F, 9H, 9ST; plenum 1, 3, 3HS, 3VS, 3SM; pedestal plug 1P, 9P Heavy-duty slide rails 440, 500 and 5000 series On base; on pedestal for Arr. 9H only Automotive pivot base Not stated Arr. 9H pedestal, Arr. 9SS swingout, Arr. 3 specially mounted; mostly automotive Standard post mount 48 to 215 Tubular centrifugal and axial Arr. 9; plenum 3HA, 3VA; plug Arr. 9 Pivot/bolted adjustable base 254 to 445 Tubular centrifugal and axial Arr. 9; plenum 3HA, 3VA; plug Arr. 9

Frame comparisons use the number in the frame designation (326T is 326). A 440-series frame above 445 (such as 449T) is beyond the NEMA slide base and has only heavy-duty slide rails.

Each case has one attempt. A correct choice reads "✓ Correct: . "; an incorrect one reads "✗ Not quite. The correct base is . ". The correct base is shown at once, and a checked case cannot be changed. Each checked case stays marked on the base you chose, as a chip with its case number and ✓ (solid border) or ✗ (dashed border). The running line reads "Correct: n of 8".

After case 8 the summary gives the first-attempt score, says whether the mastery level (7 of 8 on the first attempt) was reached, and lists every case with your choice, the correct base and the reason. On narrow screens the summary and the reference table are split over pages.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the case and the prompt "Which motor base fits this fan and motor?"
  2. Press Reference table (or R) whenever you want to look up the frame ranges and mountings. On a narrow screen, press More rows for the rest of the table.
  3. Choose a base with its button or keys 1 to 5 (the choice is outlined; you can change it until you check).
  4. Press Check (or Enter). The table closes so the verdict and the rule are visible.
  5. Press Next case (or Enter). After case 8, press Finish and read the summary.
  6. Start over clears the score and starts again at case 1.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 5 choose a base; R opens, pages or closes the reference table; Enter checks, then goes to the next case; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative cases · Rules: FanPedia pp. 76-78", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply FanPedia's motor base frame ranges and typical mountings to choose the motor base style for a belt-driven fan, given the motor frame, the fan type and arrangement, and the industry, with at least 7 of 8 cases correct (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Motor base, slide base and heavy-duty slide rails (Chapter 15, "Slide Base")
  • Pivot motor base and automotive pivot base (Chapter 15, "Pivot Motor Base")
  • Post mount motor base and pivot/bolted adjustable base (Chapter 15, "Post Mount Motor Base")
  • NEMA frame size (Chapter 14) and fan arrangements (Chapter 11)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Select (7 min): Work the eight cases. For each, say the frame number, then which bases its range allows, then which of those the arrangement allows, before you press Check.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary. For each miss, name the step of the procedure (frame, arrangement or industry) that decided it.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Cases 3 and 4 are both plenum or tubular Arrangement 9-family fans. What single fact moves a motor from the post mount to the pivot/bolted base?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any motor up to 449T fits a NEMA slide base. Case 7 (449T) is above the 445 limit; the feedback names the limit.
  • Post mount and pivot/bolted bases are interchangeable. Cases 3, 4 and 5 split them by frame: 48 to 215 versus 254 to 445.
  • Automotive pivot bases can use any motor position. Case 6's feedback states that clockwise rotation puts the motor in position L on Arrangement 9SS.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Correct: n of 8".
  • Follow-up question: the motor on case 3 is upsized from 184T to 256T. Does the base change, and why?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 76 (slide bases and rails), p. 77 (automotive pivot bases), p. 78 (adjustable bases) and p. 74 (the 5008S special frame).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners - the section "Mounting the Motor on a Belt-Driven Fan" and its frame-range table.
  4. Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements - the fan arrangements named in the cases.

docs.title: Motor Intended Duty Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Motor Intended Duty Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The intended duty on a motor line (the "SD" in FanPedia's example line) says how well the whole motor stands up to its surroundings. Choosing it is a judgment against FanPedia's stated rules, not a recall of a list. This MicroSim shows eight illustrative inquiries, one at a time and always in the same order. For each one you choose one of five duty bins and commit it with Check.

Bin Definition (shown when the bin is open) GD (General Duty) General purpose motor for normal, clean and cool air around the motor. SD (Severe Duty) Used where a severe duty motor is needed but IEEE 841 is not specified; also called Mil/Chem duty or chemical duty. IEEE 841 Industry standard for severe duty motors begun in 1986, used in process industries when specified. DFG Explosion proof enclosure motor for a hazardous location classified under the NEC. Washdown Special-basis motor for food applications that are washed down.

Each case has one attempt. A correct choice reads "✓ Correct: . "; an incorrect one reads "✗ Not quite. The correct duty is . ". The correct duty is shown at once, and a checked case cannot be changed. Each checked case stays marked in the bin you chose, as a chip with its case number and ✓ (solid border) or ✗ (dashed border). The running line reads "Correct: n of 8".

After case 8 the summary gives the first-attempt score, says whether the mastery level (7 of 8 on the first attempt) was reached, and lists all eight cases with your bin, the correct bin and the reason. On narrow screens the list is split over two pages.

The rules come from FanPedia p. 73 as presented in Chapter 15: a case that names IEEE 841 is IEEE 841; a severe case that does not name it is SD; only the owner's NEC area classification makes a location hazardous (DFG). The cases are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the case and the prompt "Which intended duty does this motor need?"
  2. Choose a bin with its button or keys 1 to 5. Choosing a bin opens its definition; you can change your choice until you press Check. Press Open all definitions (or D) to open all five at once.
  3. Press Check (or Enter). Read the verdict and the reason.
  4. Press Next case (or Enter). After case 8, press Finish and read the summary.
  5. Start over clears the score and starts again at case 1.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 5 choose a bin; D opens or closes all definitions; Enter checks, then goes to the next case; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative cases · Rules: FanPedia p. 73", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will judge which motor intended duty (GD, SD, IEEE 841, DFG or Washdown) an application requires, given a short description of the motor's environment and the customer's specification, with at least 7 of 8 cases correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: judge).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Motor intended duty and general duty (Chapter 15, "Motor Intended Duty")
  • Severe duty motor and IEEE 841 (Chapter 15, "Severe Duty Motor")
  • Hazardous location motor, NEC class, division and group, DFG (Chapter 15, "Hazardous Location Motor")
  • Washdown duty motors ordered on a special basis (Chapter 15)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (6 min): Work through the eight cases. Before pressing Check, say which words in the case decide the duty.
  2. Review (4 min): Read the summary. For each miss, name the FanPedia rule that decides it.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Cases 3 and 7 and cases 2 and 8 describe similar environments but get different duties. What in the specification makes the difference?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any severe environment calls for IEEE 841. Cases 3 and 7 are severe but do not name IEEE 841, so the answer is SD; the feedback states the rule.
  • A dusty or dirty environment is automatically a hazardous location. Only the cases with an owner's NEC classification (4 and 6) are DFG.
  • General duty is acceptable anywhere the motor has a TEFC enclosure. The mining case names a TEFC motor and still needs IEEE 841; GD fits only clean, cool air.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Correct: n of 8".
  • Follow-up question: a refinery inquiry describes oil mist around the motor and the plant's motor standard calls for IEEE 841. A second inquiry from the same refinery is for a fan in an area the owner classifies Class I, Division 2, Group D. Which duty goes on each motor line?

docs.title: VFD Frequency and Fan Law Calculator
docs.text:
Run the VFD Frequency and Fan Law Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js and fan-models.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A variable frequency drive (VFD) changes the supply frequency, and with it the motor's synchronous speed and the fan speed. On a fixed system the fan laws then set the new airflow, pressure and power, with the frequency ratio as the speed ratio. This MicroSim uses the base duty of the chapter's worked example (illustrative values): 10,000 CFM at 2.00 in. wg static pressure, 8.0 bhp, on 60 Hz power with a 4-pole motor.

The model, with r = f / 60:

  • Synchronous speed = 120 × f / 4 RPM
  • Airflow = 10,000 × r CFM
  • Static pressure = 2.00 × r² in. wg
  • Brake horsepower = 8.0 × r³ bhp

It ignores motor slip, drive losses and any fixed system pressure. Frequencies above 60 Hz are not offered: running a fan above 60 Hz starts with checking its maximum safe speed in the current catalog.

# Frequency Airflow Static pressure Brake horsepower 1 45 Hz 7,500 CFM 1.13 in. wg 3.38 bhp 2 30 Hz 5,000 CFM 0.50 in. wg 1.00 bhp 3 50 Hz 8,333 CFM 1.39 in. wg 4.63 bhp

For each challenge you type all three values and press Check. All three are checked together, and each must be within ±2% of the unrounded model value. Each box gets ✓ (solid green border) or ✗ (dashed red border). You have two attempts. A wrong first attempt shows the challenge's hint (the ratio and its square and cube); after a second wrong attempt the model values and the worked calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed. The running line reads "Challenges correct: n of 3"; mastery is all three challenges (all nine values) correct within two attempts.

After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks the frequency slider (20 to 60 Hz). Every value in the readout updates at once, each with its percent of the 60 Hz value, and a plot shows percent airflow (r), pressure (r²) and power (r³) against frequency. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge ("The drive is turned down to 45 Hz. What will the fan deliver, and what will it draw?") and the base duty in the readout.
  2. Type the airflow (CFM), static pressure (in. wg) and brake horsepower (bhp) in the three boxes and press Check (or Enter).
  3. Read the verdict and the marks beside each box. With an attempt left, fix the values marked ✗ and check again.
  4. Press Next challenge (or Enter). After challenge 3, press Start exploring.
  5. In Explore mode, move the frequency slider. At 30 Hz, notice that airflow is still 50% while power is 12.5%.
  6. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the boxes and buttons; Enter checks, then goes to the next challenge; in Explore mode the arrow keys move the focused slider one hertz at a time.

Data label: "Illustrative values · Base duty 10,000 CFM, 2.00 in. wg, 8.0 bhp at 60 Hz · 4-pole motor", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the airflow, static pressure and brake horsepower of a belt-driven fan at a reduced VFD frequency, using the fan laws with the frequency ratio as the speed ratio, to within 2% of the model values (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Synchronous motor speed, poles and frequency (Chapter 15, "Synchronous Motor Speed")
  • Variable frequency drive (Chapter 15, "Variable Frequency Drive")
  • Airflow (CFM), static pressure (in. wg) and brake horsepower
  • The fan laws (Chapter 25)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (7 min): Work the three frequencies on paper first, then type and check. Write down r, r² and r³ for each.
  2. Review (2 min): For any miss, compare your numbers with the worked calculation and name the step that went wrong.
  3. Explore (4 min): Move the slider from 60 Hz down to 20 Hz. Find the frequency where power falls to about half (about 48 Hz) and compare the airflow there.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Power falls in the same proportion as frequency. At 45 Hz power is 42% of full, not 75%; the hint after a wrong attempt gives the cube, and the plot shows the r³ curve far below the r line.
  • Pressure is unchanged by a speed change. The pressure box is checked against 2.00 × r², and the plot shows the r² curve.
  • The VFD changes the motor's poles or the sheave ratio. The formula card states that only f changes; the synchronous speed in the readout follows 120 × f / 4 with the same 4 poles.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line reads "Challenges correct: n of 3"; mastery is all three challenges correct within two attempts, and the summary in Explore mode says whether it was reached.
  • Follow-up question: an owner wants to cut a fan's airflow by 20% overnight. What frequency should the drive run at, and what fraction of full power will the fan draw?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 71 (synchronous speeds by poles and frequency) and p. 170 (the VFD as a way to change fan performance in the field).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 15: Motor Ratings, Speed Control and Positioners - the sections "Synchronous Motor Speed" and "Variable Frequency Drive", with the 45 Hz worked example.
  4. Chapter 25: Fan Laws, System Effect and Sound - the fan laws in full.
  5. Variable-frequency drive (Wikipedia) - background on how a VFD sets motor speed.

docs.title: Rotating Assembly Callout Map
docs.text: Run the Rotating Assembly Callout Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a schematic side cross-section of an overhung (Arrangement 1 style) centrifugal fan: the impeller inside the housing at the left, the shaft passing through the housing's drive-side wall, two pillow block bearings on a pedestal, and a drive sheave on the right-hand shaft end. Ten parts of the rotating assembly carry callouts:

# Callout What it does 1 Shaft keyway A groove cut into the shaft that accepts keystock so torque passes to the hub or sheave. 2 Shaft turndown A length of shaft machined to a smaller diameter to fit a bearing, seal, hub or coupling. 3 Shaft sleeve A tube over the shaft inside the housing that shields the shaft from the airstream when materials differ. 4 Shaft locking collar A ring clamped to the shaft that keeps the shaft from sliding axially into another part. 5 Shaft seal A seal mounted on the housing wall where the shaft passes through, limiting air leakage in or out. 6 Non-drive end bearing (inboard) The bearing nearer the impeller, farther from the sheave. 7 Drive end bearing (outboard) The bearing nearer the sheave or coupling. 8 Bearing seal A seal built into the bearing that keeps dirt out of the bearing. 9 Bearing positioner A threaded bolt on a bracket beside the bearing, used for fine adjustment of bearing location. 10 Vibration sensor tap A drilled and tapped hole in the bearing housing where a vibration sensor is mounted.

The quiz shows the ten descriptions once each in shuffled order. You get two attempts per description. A first wrong click names the part you clicked and its job; a second wrong click highlights the correct part with an "Answer" badge and the description counts as missed. The running line reads "Correct on first try: n of 10", and mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

The drawing is schematic and not to scale. It is based on FanPedia pp. 79-81 (shaft, keyways and turndowns), p. 91 (drive end and inboard bearings), pp. 100-102 (bearing seals, vibration sensor tap, bearing positioner) and p. 129 (shaft collar and shaft sleeve).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Click any part to read what it does. Each part you have opened gets a ✓ mark and a shaded label, and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels are hidden and a description appears above the drawing. Click the part it describes.
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" and the part name; its label appears.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite. That callout is the" part you clicked, with what that part does. Try again.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the correct part is highlighted and marked "Answer", and the description counts as missed.
    • Clicking an empty area of the drawing does nothing and uses no attempt.
  3. Press Next description after each answer. After the tenth, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and the parts you missed. All labels return. Press Start over to retake the quiz with a new shuffle, or Back to explore to review.
  4. Start over in the toolbar clears your visited parts and the quiz at any time and returns to explore mode.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the parts (from the shaft sleeve at the housing to the keyway at the shaft end) and the buttons; Enter or Space selects a part. After an answer, focus moves to Next description, so Enter goes on.

Narrow screens: when the drawing is narrower than about 650 px, the callouts become numbers with a key list below the drawing.

Data label: "Schematic, not to scale · Overhung (Arrangement 1 style) fan · Based on FanPedia pp. 79-81, 91, 100-102 and 129", shown below the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify ten parts of an overhung fan's rotating assembly, given a one-sentence description of each part's job (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Rotating assembly and overhung impeller (Chapter 16, "The Rotating Assembly"; Chapter 3)
  • Shaft keyway, turndown, sleeve and locking collar (Chapter 16, "Shaft Features")
  • Pillow block bearings, bearing seals, bearing positioners and vibration sensors (Chapter 16, "Bearings" and "Monitoring the Bearings")
  • Shaft seal (Chapter 16, "Shaft Seals")

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten callouts. Sort them aloud into three groups: on the shaft, on the bearings, on the housing.
  2. Compare (2 min): Open the shaft seal and the bearing seal one after the other. Say what each one keeps in or out. Do the same for the shaft locking collar and the shaft sleeve.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and answer the ten descriptions.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, return to explore mode for those parts, then press Start over for a new shuffle.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The shaft sleeve is a bearing part. The sleeve sits inside the housing, over the shaft in the airstream, far from both bearings.
  • The shaft locking collar and a bearing's locking collar are the same part. The shaft collar is drawn on its own on the shaft between the shaft seal and the inboard bearing.
  • The shaft seal keeps grease in the bearing. The shaft seal sits on the housing wall and limits air leakage; the bearing seal is built into the bearing. A wrong click on either one names the clicked part's job.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Correct on first try: n of 10".
  • Follow-up question: a nominally leak-tight fan is ordered for a stainless airstream with a steel shaft. Which callout on this drawing is left off, and why? (The shaft sleeve and cap: FanPedia's leak-tight construction does not use them.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; shaft p. 79, keyways and turndowns pp. 80-81, drive end and inboard bearings p. 91, bearing seals p. 100, vibration sensor tap p. 101, bearing positioner p. 102, shaft collar and sleeve p. 129.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - the sections "Shaft Features", "Bearings", "Monitoring the Bearings" and "Shaft Seals".
  4. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy - overhung and center hung bearing layouts.

docs.title: Shaft Seal Identifier
docs.text:
Run the Shaft Seal Identifier MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every shaft seal is identified by what touches the shaft. This MicroSim shows FanPedia's seven shaft seal types as bins, grouped in their three families:

Family Bin Identifying parts (reference infobox) Contact seals Friction shaft seal Soft seal material (tacky cloth, Teflon, Viton, Nomex mineral wool, silicone sheet or Fiber Frax ceramic felt) held by a cover plate, typically aluminum. The standard type. V-ring shaft seal Teflon plate design with Chekseal and PTFE joint sealant; also called axial or Teflon shaft seal. Lip shaft seal Elastomer lip (Buna-N standard, Viton special) in a seal housing with a grease fitting. Carbon ring seals Single carbon ring seal One split carbon ring in a seal housing behind a cover plate; vendor supplied; also called labyrinth shaft seal. Double carbon ring seal Two split carbon rings with a lantern ring at a purge hole; vendor supplied. Stuffing box seals Stuffing box seal Graphoil split inner rings and carbon yarn packing outer rings between an inside plate and an outside plate with a retaining ring. Stuffing box seal with gas purge A stuffing box with a Teflon lantern ring at a purge hole, shipped with a 1/8-inch NPT pipe plug.

In explore mode (the start) each bin opens its reference infobox and a schematic cross-section of the seal: housing wall at the left, shaft along the bottom, seal parts outside the wall. Exploring is never scored.

The quiz deals twelve cards in shuffled order. Each describes a seal by its parts, its materials or its order-line name. You commit a card by pressing a bin, with two attempts per card:

  • Correct: "✓ Correct: . "
  • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not this one. Look again at the parts named on the card." The wrong bin gets a dashed red outline.
  • Wrong on the second attempt: "✗ This is a . " and the card counts as missed.

    After every answer the correct bin's infobox opens, and the committed card appears as a chip in the bin you chose (✓ solid, ✗ dashed). The running line reads "First-try correct: n of 12". After card 12 the summary gives the first-attempt score, the mastery line (10 of 12 on the first attempt; when it is reached: "You can identify FanPedia's seven shaft seal types from their parts.") and every card that was not correct on the first try, with its correct bin. Start over reshuffles the cards.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press each bin (keys 1 to 7) and compare the cross-sections: which part touches the shaft, and is there a purge?
  2. Press Start the quiz (or Enter).
  3. Read the card and press the bin it belongs in. With a wrong first attempt, read the card again and press another bin.
  4. Read the verdict and the infobox, then press Next card (or Enter).
  5. After card 12, read the summary. Press any bin to review its infobox, and Summary to return. Start over deals a new shuffle.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 7 press a bin; Enter starts the quiz and goes to the next card; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Schematic cross-sections, not to scale · Source: FanPedia pp. 149-155", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.
