docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify a fan shaft seal into one of seven FanPedia seal types from a description of its parts, materials or order-line name, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Shaft seal and the three seal families (Chapter 16, "Shaft Seals")
  • Friction, V-ring and lip shaft seals (Chapter 16, "Lip and Friction Shaft Seals")
  • Single and double carbon ring seals, lantern ring, purge (Chapter 16, "Carbon Ring Seals")
  • Stuffing box seal, stuffing box with gas purge, Graphoil, carbon yarn packing (Chapter 16, "Stuffing Box Seals")

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all seven bins. For each, name the part that touches the shaft and say whether the seal can be purged.
  2. Quiz (6 min): Classify the twelve cards. Before pressing a bin, point to the word on the card that decides it.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the summary. For each card not correct on the first try, open its bin and find the identifying part in the cross-section.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any seal with a purge is a carbon ring seal. Cards 7 and 12 are purged stuffing boxes; the stuffing box with gas purge bin sits in its own family.
  • A lip shaft seal and a bearing lip seal are the same part. The lip seal cross-section shows it on the fan housing wall with its own greased housing.
  • "Labyrinth" always means a bearing seal. The single carbon ring infobox lists "labyrinth shaft seal" as another name.
  • Single and double carbon ring seals differ only in size. The double ring cross-section adds the lantern ring and the purge.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt. The running line reads "First-try correct: n of 12".
  • Follow-up question: a nominally leak-tight fan handles a gas that must not escape. Which two of the seven seal types would you offer, and what must the customer supply?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; Shaft Seals pp. 149 (friction), 150 (V-ring), 151 (lip), 152 (single ring mechanical), 153 (double ring mechanical), 154 (stuffing box) and 155 (stuffing box with gas purge).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - the "Shaft Seals" section and its subsections.
  4. Gland (engineering) (Wikipedia) - background on packing glands and stuffing boxes.

docs.title: Contact and Carbon Ring Shaft Seals
docs.text: Run the Contact and Carbon Ring Shaft Seals MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks five numbered zones on FanPedia's exploded shaft seal drawings (pages 149 to 153), set in two rows on one image. The top row shows the three contact seals: the friction shaft seal, with soft seal material clamped by a cover plate; the V-ring shaft seal, a Teflon plate design; and the lip shaft seal, with an elastomer lip in a seal housing that carries a grease fitting. The bottom row shows the two carbon ring seals: the single carbon ring seal, with one split carbon ring behind a cover plate, and the double carbon ring seal, with a lantern ring between two split carbon rings at a purge hole. The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one drawing at a time ("Which drawing has a lantern ring between two rings, for a purge?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 5 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one drawing:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 5".
  4. After the fifth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (4 of 5), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, pp. 149-153", shown under the drawing.

docs.text:

        height="825px"
        width="100%"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the friction, V-ring and lip contact seals and the single and double carbon ring seals on FanPedia's exploded drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 16, sections "Shaft Seals", "Lip and Friction Shaft Seals" and "Carbon Ring Seals".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all five drawings. For the top row, say what rubs on the shaft in each contact seal. For the bottom row, say which drawing can take a purge supply and which part makes that possible.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all five descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A carbon ring seal is one more rubbing contact seal: the split carbon rings float with the shaft and run against it with low friction at very small clearance, so leakage is lower than through a soft contact seal.
  • The double carbon ring seal is a single ring seal with a spare ring: the lantern ring between the two rings sits at a purge hole, and purge gas fed there slightly above fan pressure means any leakage is purge gas flowing into the fan.
  • The grease fitting on a lip seal lubricates the bearing: a shaft seal does not touch the bearings; the grease lubricates the lip and fills the gap, which is why the lip seal is also called a grease seal.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 5"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a nominally leak-tight fan handles a gas the customer must not release, and the customer will pipe a purge line. Which bottom-row drawing fits, and which part receives the purge gas?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; pp. 149-153 hold the friction (p. 149), V-ring (p. 150), lip (p. 151), single ring mechanical (p. 152) and double ring mechanical (p. 153) shaft seal drawings used here.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - the sections "Lip and Friction Shaft Seals" and "Carbon Ring Seals"; this MicroSim is embedded at the end of "Carbon Ring Seals".
  4. Shaft Seal Identifier - sorts text cards into seven seal types with schematic cross-sections, including these five.
  5. Stuffing Box Seal With Gas Purge - the stuffing box seal, the third seal family, on FanPedia's exploded view.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, pp. 149-153. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Stuffing Box Seal With Gas Purge
docs.text: Run the Stuffing Box Seal With Gas Purge MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts ten numbered markers on FanPedia's exploded view of a stuffing box type shaft seal with gas purge (page 155). The seal is drawn pulled apart along the shaft, in the order it goes together on the fan housing wall: the joint sealant, the inside plate with its seal housing, the ring stack, and the outside plate that presses the stack. Dash-dot lines show how the nuts run onto the mounting rods. An inset at the upper right shows the same seal assembled.

The ten parts are the shaft, fan housing wall, threaded mounting rods, 1/8-inch NPT pipe plug, PTFE joint sealant, inside plate with seal housing, carbon yarn packing, Graphoil split ring, Teflon lantern ring and outside plate with retaining ring. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. The three rings of the stack are small, so their markers sit just below the stack with a short pointer to each ring.

The quiz describes each part by its job or material ("Select the ring that lets purge gas reach the shaft.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 10".
  4. After the tenth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 155", shown under the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will identify the ten labeled parts of a stuffing box shaft seal with gas purge on an exploded view, given each part's job or material (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 16, sections "Shaft Seals" (what a shaft seal does and how every seal assembly mounts to the housing), "Carbon Ring Seals" (the lantern ring and purge on the double carbon ring) and "Stuffing Box Seals".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten parts. Sort them aloud into what is already on the fan (shaft, fan housing wall, threaded mounting rods), what holds and presses the packing (PTFE joint sealant, inside plate with seal housing, outside plate with retaining ring), the ring stack (carbon yarn packing, Graphoil split ring, Teflon lantern ring) and the purge connection (1/8-inch NPT pipe plug).
  2. Trace the purge (2 min): Start at the yellow plug on the seal housing and say where purge gas goes once the customer's line replaces it. Which ring must sit under the purge hole, and why?
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all ten parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order. Then try the Shaft Seal Identifier to tell this seal apart from the other types.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The stuffing box ships ready to connect to a purge line: it ships with a 1/8-inch NPT pipe plug in the purge hole, and the customer-supplied purge line replaces the plug in the field.
  • All the rings in the stack are the same packing: in Twin City Fan's design the outer rings are carbon yarn packing, the inner rings are Graphoil split rings, and the Teflon lantern ring is a spacer at the purge hole, not packing.
  • The seal is tightened once at the factory: because the packing is compressed against the shaft by the outside plate on the threaded mounting rods, it can be retightened to take up wear.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: an order line reads "Graphoil Stuffing Box" without "With Purge". Which parts on this drawing would not ship?

docs.title: Bearing Life to Calendar Years
docs.text:
Run the Bearing Life to Calendar Years MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch17-bearing-life-calendar-years.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A bearing's L-10 life is the number of operating hours at which 10% of a population of identical bearings is expected to fail; its L-50 (average) life is five times as long. Both are hours of running, not calendar time. This MicroSim converts a rating to years for a stated duty schedule, the way Chapter 17 does:

  • Annual hours = hours per day × days per week × 365/7
  • Years = rated hours ÷ annual hours, rounded to 0.1 year
  • L-50 hours = 5 × L-10 hours

The sim starts with five challenges, in this order. Each asks for one number, in years:

# Rating Schedule Model answer 1 L-10 40,000 h 24 h/day, 7 days/week 4.6 years 2 L-10 40,000 h 8 h/day, 5 days/week 19.2 years 3 L-50 of a bearing rated L-10 20,000 h 24 h/day, 7 days/week 11.4 years 4 L-10 60,000 h 16 h/day, 5 days/week 14.4 years 5 L-10 100,000 h 12 h/day, 6 days/week (illustrative schedule) 26.6 years

An answer is correct when it is within 2% of the model answer. You get two attempts. A wrong first answer gets a hint that names the slip or the step (no numbers); a second wrong answer shows the model answer and the worked conversion, and the challenge counts as missed. Once a challenge is resolved, the sim shows the annual operating hours, the model answer and your answer side by side, writes out the calculation, and fills in bars comparing the L-10 and L-50 years of the same bearing. A week grid (7 days by 24 hours) shades the hours the fan runs.

Mastery is 4 of 5 challenges correct on the first attempt. After challenge 5, Explore mode unlocks the four inputs (L-10 rating 20,000 to 100,000 hours in 20,000-hour steps, 1 to 24 hours per day, 1 to 7 days per week, and the rating shown, L-10 or L-50), and a table compares FanPedia's published years (p. 90) with the model. The model lands within 2% of every published cell; the small differences come from rounding and from FanPedia counting some cells with a 52-week year. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type the number of years in Your answer and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: n years." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with a hint in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat for challenges 2 to 5. Challenge 3 asks for an L-50 life from an L-10 rating, so multiply by five first. "Challenges correct: n of 5" keeps the running score.
  4. After challenge 5, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Move the sliders and switch Rating shown between L-10 and L-50: the hours and years update at once. Notice that switching to L-50 multiplies the years by exactly five while the bearing is unchanged, and that cutting the hours per day changes the calendar life as much as a different rating does. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, every button, the rating selector and the three sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia p. 90 · 365/7 weeks per year" (challenge 5 reads "Illustrative schedule · Source: FanPedia p. 90"), at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the expected calendar life in years of an L-10 or L-50 bearing rating for a stated daily and weekly duty schedule, to within 2% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Bearing life as a statistical estimate (Chapter 17)
  • L-10 and L-50 bearing life, and the L-50 = 5 × L-10 conversion (Chapter 17)
  • The years formula (Chapter 17, "Bearing Life: L-10 and L-50")

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-7 min): Work each challenge with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the annual hours for each schedule.
  2. Review (2 min): Compare your annual hours with the sim's, and redo any missed challenge by hand from the worked calculation.
  3. Explore (3-5 min): Keep the rating at L-10 40,000 hours and move hours per day from 24 to 8. Then switch Rating shown to L-50. Find the FanPedia table row that matches the inputs (it is highlighted) and compare its published years with the model.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• L-50 is a better or longer-lived bearing than L-10: the sim shows both bars for the same bearing, and switching the rating changes the years by exactly five times while the L-10 rating is unchanged.
  • L-10 hours equal calendar hours whatever the schedule: challenges 1 and 2 use the same bearing and get 4.6 and 19.2 years.
  • L-10 is the time at which every bearing fails: every prompt and the L-10 definition speak of 10% of a population.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 5" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 5" and the mastery line; mastery is 4 of 5 challenges within 2% of the model value on the first attempt.
  • Changing the inputs in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner to explain to a customer why "200,000-hour average life" and "L-10 40,000 hours" may describe the same bearing.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; p. 90 (Bearing Life Overview) gives the L-10 and L-50 definitions, the five-times rule and the published year tables.
  2. Rolling-element bearing: life - Wikipedia overview of bearing fatigue life and the L10 rating.
  3. Twin City Fan & Blower - current product catalogs, which state the L-10 life offered on each fan model.

docs.title: Fan Pedestal Features
docs.text: Run the Fan Pedestal Features MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts seven numbered markers on FanPedia's drawing of pedestal features (page 85). The main drawing shows a sheet-metal pedestal beside the housing of a single width centrifugal fan, carrying the shaft on two pillow block bearings. An inset below it shows a bare pedestal with a stepped top and purple bearing or motor pads.

The seven features are the top, the pillow block bearing, the hand holes, the sides, the front, the feet and the bearing or motor pads. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. The pillow block bearing is small, so its marker sits just above it with a short pointer to the bearing.

The quiz describes each feature by its job or its look ("Select the openings that give access to fasteners.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the feature and counts as missed. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the feature's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened features get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 7 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that feature too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one feature:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the feature name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the feature you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 7".
  4. After the seventh prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (6 of 7), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 85", shown under the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will identify the top, pillow block bearing, hand holes, sides, front, feet and bearing or motor pads of a fan pedestal on FanPedia's drawing, given each feature's job or look (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 17, sections "Pillow Block Housings: Solid, Split and Totally Split", "Bolting the Bearing Down: Two and Four Hole Mounts" and "Fan Pedestals".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all seven features. Sort them aloud into the pedestal's structure (top, sides, front, feet), the features that serve the bearings (pads, hand holes) and the part it carries (the pillow block bearing).
  2. Compare (2 min): Look at the inset. Which feature does it add that the main drawing's flat top does not show, and which other feature does the same job?
  3. Quiz (3 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all seven features from their descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (2 min): Read the missed list, open those features in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The pedestal is just a stand: it supports the bearings, shaft and often the motor, and it gives the rotating assembly the stiffness it needs to be balanced and meet vibration requirements.
  • The hand holes are only for looking in: they give access to the bearing and motor fasteners.
  • Bearing or motor pads are needed on every pedestal: a machined top gives the same flat, stiff surface for bearing alignment.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 7"; mastery is 6 of 7 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a pillow block bearing has to be unbolted for service. Which pedestal feature does the mechanic reach through, and which feature sets how true the new bearing will sit?

docs.title: Fixed or Floating Bearing Assignment
docs.text:
Run the Fixed or Floating Bearing Assignment MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch17-fixed-floating-bearing-assignment.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A shaft grows as it warms. If both bearings clamp it axially, the growth becomes an axial load that shortens bearing life, so FanPedia (pp. 97-99) lets only one bearing locate the shaft: the fixed bearing. The floating bearing carries the shaft radially but lets its outer ring slide axially in the housing. This MicroSim applies the rules from Chapter 17 in their decision order:

  1. At 301°F and above, every bearing type uses one fixed and one floating bearing. Go to step 3.
  2. At 300°F and below, ball bearings use two fixed bearings (A), except on Arrangements 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI, where FanPedia's footnote says one fixed and one floating may be required (D, engineering review). Roller and split roller bearings use one fixed and one floating.
  3. With a floating bearing, a horizontal mount puts the fixed bearing at the drive end (B) and a vertical mount puts the floating bearing at the drive end (C).

Each of ten illustrative scenario cards gives the fan type, arrangement, mounting orientation, bearing type and operating temperature. You choose one of four configurations: A, two fixed bearings; B, fixed at the drive end and floating at the non-drive end; C, floating at the drive end and fixed at the non-drive end; D, flag for engineering review. The cards come in a fixed order, with one attempt each. After you commit, the sim draws the shaft (horizontal or vertical, as the card says) with its sheave or coupling, impeller and two pillow blocks, labels the drive-end and non-drive-end bearings, marks each one fixed (clamped between locating rings) or floating (double arrow along the shaft), and names the rule step that decided the card.

Mastery is 8 of 10 cards correct on the first (and only) attempt. After card 10 the sim shows the score, whether mastery was reached, and each missed card with the rule step that decided it.

The shaft drawing is a schematic: a vertical fan is drawn with its drive end at the top, and the impeller sits between the bearings on Arrangement 3 family fans and outboard of them on Arrangements 1, 8 and 9.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read scenario card 1 and choose a configuration with the A, B, C or D button (or keys 1-4 or A-D). The full text of each option is listed on the card.
  2. Press Commit (or Enter). The answer locks. "✓ Correct." or "✗ Not quite." appears with the reason, the correct configuration letter, and the rule step that decided it; the shaft drawing now shows which bearing is fixed and which floats.
  3. Press Next card (or Enter) and repeat. "Cards correct: n of 10" keeps the running score.
  4. After card 10, press See results. Read the missed cards, then press Start over to try all ten again. Notice that orientation only matters once a floating bearing is needed.

Keyboard: keys 1-4 or A-D choose a configuration; Enter commits, then goes to the next card. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative scenarios · Source: FanPedia pp. 91, 97–99", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the fixed-floating bearing rules to assign the correct bearing configuration to ten fan scenarios defined by mounting orientation, bearing type, operating temperature and arrangement, with at least 8 of 10 correct (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Drive end and non-drive end bearings (Chapter 17)
  • Fixed and floating bearings (Chapters 16 and 17)
  • Ball, roller and split roller bearing types (Chapters 16 and 17)
  • Horizontal and vertical mounting, and the fixed-floating bearing rules (Chapter 17)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Scenario cards (6-8 min): Ask the four questions in order for each card (horizontal or vertical, ball or roller, above or below 300°F, straddle arrangement or not) before committing.
  2. Review (2-3 min): On the results screen, read the rule step for every missed card and say which question you skipped.
  3. Discussion (2-3 min): Cards 6 and 10 differ by one degree. Explain why that degree changes the answer.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every fan needs a floating bearing: cards 1, 5 and 6 use two fixed ball bearings.
  • The fixed bearing is always on the drive end: cards 4 and 9 are vertical and float at the drive end.
  • Temperature does not matter for ball bearings: cards 6 (300°F, two fixed) and 10 (301°F, fixed and floating).
  • The 300°F cutoff works the same way on straddle arrangements: card 8 (Arrangement 3SI, ball, 250°F) is an engineering review item.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Cards correct: n of 10" counts first-attempt answers (there is only one attempt). At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 10" and the mastery line; mastery is 8 of 10.
  • Looking at the shaft drawing before committing is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner why the floating bearing moves to the drive end on a vertical fan.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; pp. 97-99 (Fixed & Floating Bearings) give the placement and quantity rules and the 3SI, 7SI, 3DI and 7DI footnote, and p. 91 defines drive end and non-drive end bearings.
  2. Rolling-element bearing - Wikipedia overview of ball and roller bearings and how they carry radial and axial loads.
  3. Thermal expansion - why a warm shaft grows longer and needs one bearing free to slide.

docs.title: Pillow Block Bearings and Shaft Mounts
docs.text: Run the Pillow Block Bearings and Shaft Mounts MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks six numbered zones on FanPedia's bearing drawings (page 92). The top row shows three pillow block housings: a solid pillow block with ball rolling elements, a solid pillow block with spherical rollers, and a split pillow block whose cap lifts off. The bottom row shows three ways the bearing's inner ring is locked to the shaft: the set screw mount, the D-Lok / Skwezloc style concentric mount and the adapter mount. The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one drawing at a time ("Which drawing shows a housing whose cap lifts off?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 6 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one drawing:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 6".
  4. After the sixth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (5 of 6), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 92", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the solid (ball and spherical roller) and split pillow block housings and the set screw, D-Lok / Skwezloc and adapter shaft mounts on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 17, sections "Pillow Block Housings: Solid, Split and Totally Split" and "Locking the Bearing to the Shaft".
  • Chapter 16, "Mounting the Bearing to the Shaft", for the set screw mount.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all six drawings. For the top row, say which housing lets a mechanic inspect the bearing by lifting off a cap. For the bottom row, say which mounts clamp evenly around the shaft.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all six descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A split pillow block is a different kind of bearing: it is a different housing; FanPedia offers it with ball or spherical roller elements, like the solid housing.
  • Every mount pushes the bearing to one side of the shaft: only the set screw mount does; the D-Lok / Skwezloc and adapter mounts are concentric and clamp the segmented inner ring evenly around the shaft.
  • One set screw is enough: FanPedia says two set screws are always required, spaced 65 to 120 degrees apart depending on the manufacturer.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 6"; mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a heavy fan with spherical roller bearings needs a mount that will not fret the shaft. Which bottom-row drawing fits, and which tool tightens it?

docs.text:

  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 17: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals - the section "Locking the Bearing to the Shaft", where this MicroSim is embedded.
  4. Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - the set screw mount.

docs.title: Flow Control Method Selector
docs.text:
Run the Flow Control Method Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch18-flow-control-method-selector.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every device in Chapter 18's flow-control section answers one of three needs: stopping reverse flow when the fan is off, setting airflow once, or changing airflow while the fan runs. This MicroSim gives ten illustrative job cards and the same ten devices for each:

A. Butterfly gravity damper · B. Wall or ceiling gravity damper · C. Manual damper · D. Motorized damper · E. Parallel blade outlet damper · F. Opposed blade outlet damper · G. Parallel blade inlet box damper · H. External variable inlet vanes · I. Speed control with a VFD · J. EC motor speed controller

For each card you recommend a device, and then the three possible deciding conditions appear (the correct one and two others, in a shuffled order); you pick the one that decided your choice. A card is correct only when both the device and the condition are right. The cards come in a shuffled order, so the first card differs from learner to learner. You get two attempts. A wrong device gets a hint chosen by your answer: picking a gravity or manual damper for a job that needs control while the fan runs, picking speed control for an infrequent reduction, or mixing up the parallel and opposed blade ranges each has its own hint; any other wrong device gets a hint that points at the card's deciding job condition without naming the device. A right device with the wrong condition says so. After a second wrong attempt the device, the condition and the reason are shown and the card counts as missed.

"Recommendations correct: n of 10" counts cards with both selections right on the first attempt. Mastery is 8 of 10. After card 10 the summary lists every card with your first device, your second device if you used one, and the correct device, marked ✓ (right first time), ½ (device right, condition wrong) or ✗ (device wrong). Review card shows the reason for any card.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job card and choose a device in the Device list. The ten devices are also listed beside the card.
  2. Choose the deciding condition in the Condition list (it appears after the device), then press Check (or Enter). The device and the condition are marked ✓ or ✗ separately.
  3. If a hint appears, change your device or condition and check again.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter) and continue. After card 10, press See summary, read the reason for each card with Review card, and press Start over for a new shuffled round.

Keyboard: Tab reaches both lists, every button and the review list; the arrow keys change a focused list; Enter checks, then goes to the next card.

docs.text: The learner will recommend the flow-control or backdraft device that best fits each of ten job descriptions and justify the choice by naming the deciding job condition, scoring at least 8 of 10 (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Gravity, butterfly, manual and motorized dampers (Chapter 18)
  • Parallel and opposed blade outlet dampers and the inlet box damper (Chapter 18)
  • External and variable inlet vanes, speed control, VFDs and EC motor speed controllers (Chapter 18)
  • Turndown and blade flutter (Chapter 18)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Job cards (8-10 min): Before choosing a device, sort the job into one of the three needs: stop backflow, set once, or change while running.
  2. Summary review (3 min): Read every card marked ½ or ✗ with Review card and say which word in the job decided it.
  3. Discussion (2 min): Cards 5 and 9 both reduce airflow. Why is a parallel blade outlet damper right for one and a VFD for the other?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any damper can control airflow in operation: choosing a gravity or manual damper for a running reduction gets a dedicated hint.
  • Speed control is always right: the hot, dirty process fan with a monthly trim is an outlet damper job, and choosing a VFD there gets a hint.
  • Parallel and opposed blade dampers are interchangeable: the modulation-range hint separates them.
  • An outlet damper saves about as much power as inlet vanes, and a gravity damper works at any airflow: the inlet vane, inlet box damper and motorized damper cards turn on exactly those points.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Recommendations correct: n of 10" counts first-attempt cards with both selections right; mastery is 8 of 10. The summary shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line.
  • The ½ marks show where a learner picks the right device for the wrong reason; ask them to restate the deciding condition for each.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; pp. 181-183 cover gravity, manual, motorized, outlet and inlet box dampers, pp. 139 and 188 inlet vanes, pp. 68 and 70 EC motors and the GridPoint controller.
  2. Damper (flow) - Wikipedia overview of dampers in air-handling systems.
  3. Variable-frequency drive - Wikipedia overview of VFD speed control and its energy savings on fans.

docs.title: Flow Control Power Comparator
docs.text: Run the Flow Control Power Comparator MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Three common ways to turn a fan down are an outlet damper, variable inlet vanes and speed control. All three reduce airflow, but they need very different shaft power to do it. This MicroSim plots shaft power (% of design) against airflow (% of design) from 50% to 100% for the three methods and asks you to predict their order before you see the curves.

All three curves are labeled illustrative. The speed-control curve is the ideal fan-law relation, power = 100 × (airflow / 100)³, for a system curve that passes through zero. The outlet-damper and inlet-vane values are illustrative values written for this chapter to show the typical ordering; they are not Twin City Fan test data. FanPedia supports the ordering: outlet damper horsepower savings are "usually much less than other methods" (FanPedia p. 182), and inlet box dampers and inlet vanes save horsepower at reduced loads by pre-spinning the air (FanPedia pp. 145, 183, 188). Values between table rows are found by straight-line interpolation. Real speed control has small drive losses, and a system with fixed static pressure saves less than the ideal cube value.

Airflow (% of design) Outlet damper (% power) Variable inlet vanes (% power) Speed control (% power) 100 100 100 100.0 90 96 88 72.9 80 91 77 51.2 70 86 67 34.3 60 80 59 21.6 50 74 52 12.5

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge (80%, then 70%, then 50% airflow). The chart shows only its axes.
  2. Choose the three methods in order from lowest to highest shaft power, type the saving of the best method compared with the outlet damper in percentage points, and press Check.
  3. A challenge is correct when the ranking is right and the saving is within ±3 percentage points. You get two attempts (the attempt line shows "Attempt 1 of 2"). When the challenge ends (correct, or missed after the second wrong attempt), the three curves are drawn and the powers at that airflow are marked with their values. Press Next challenge; the curves are hidden again.
  4. After challenge 3 a summary shows your first-attempt score and whether you reached mastery (3 of 3 on the first attempt), the curves stay visible and Explore mode unlocks the airflow selector (50% to 100% in 5% steps, starting at 70%). Move it from 100% down to 50% and watch the readout of the three powers and the two savings. Hover any point for its airflow, method and power. Explore mode is never scored. Press Start over at any time to begin again from challenge 1.

Keyboard: Tab moves between controls; Enter in a ranking list or the saving box checks your answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge; the arrow keys move the airflow selector.

Data label: "Illustrative values", shown below the chart with the footnote on real speed control. The legend also marks each series "(illustrative)".

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate outlet dampers, variable inlet vanes and speed control by the shaft power each needs at reduced airflow, correctly ranking the three methods and estimating the savings gap at a stated airflow between 50% and 100% of design (Bloom level: Analyze; verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives and specifying engineers who discuss flow-control options with customers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Flow control
  • Operating point
  • Fan curve
  • System curve
  • Outlet damper
  • Variable inlet vanes
  • Speed control
  • Brake horsepower

These are defined in Chapter 18's "What Flow Control Means" section and in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (6 min): Complete the three challenges in order. Commit a ranking and a saving before each reveal.
  2. Explore (4 min): With the selector unlocked, move from 100% to 50% airflow. Note that the damper curve is nearly flat while the speed-control curve drops steeply, so the gap between them grows as flow falls.
  3. Connect (3 min): Compare the 70% readout with the chapter's worked example "The Same 70% Flow Three Ways" (damper 86%, vanes 67%, speed control 34%) and the 80% value with the Speed Control worked example (51.2%).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Closing a damper to half flow cuts power roughly in half (at 50% flow the damper still needs about 74%).
  • All flow-control methods save about the same energy.
  • Inlet vanes save as much as speed control.
  • Power falls in proportion to airflow under speed control, rather than with roughly the cube of airflow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score shown as "Challenges correct: n of 3"; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt, and the summary after challenge 3 shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" with "Mastery reached (3 of 3 needed)." or "Mastery needs 3 of 3 on the first attempt."
  • Hovering points and moving the airflow selector are exploration, not evidence.
# Airflow Correct ranking, lowest to highest Saving of best method vs. damper 1 80% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 39.8 points (91 − 51.2) 2 70% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 51.7 points (86 − 34.3) 3 50% Speed control, inlet vanes, outlet damper 61.5 points (74 − 12.5)

  2. Wikipedia. Affinity laws: the fan-law relation between speed, flow, pressure and power.
  3. Wikipedia. Variable-frequency drive: how motor speed control is applied to fans.
  4. Chart.js. Line chart documentation.

docs.title: Industrial Grade Dampers
docs.text: Run the Industrial Grade Dampers MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks five numbered zones on FanPedia's industrial grade damper drawings (page 137). On the left, the parallel blade outlet damper (top) and the opposed blade outlet damper (bottom) each sit on a fan outlet, with two close-ups of their blades: Type 1 flat blades and Type 2 airfoil blades. On the right are the parallel blade inlet box damper, with red arrows showing the air turning through the blades and into the fan, the manual outlet damper and the outlet damper with actuator. The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one damper at a time ("Which damper suits modulation over the entire range?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 5 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one damper:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 5".
  4. After the fifth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (4 of 5), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 137", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the parallel blade and opposed blade outlet dampers, the parallel blade inlet box damper, the manual outlet damper and the outlet damper with actuator on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 18, sections "Damper", "Outlet Damper", "Parallel Blade Damper", "Opposed Blade Damper", "Inlet Box Damper", "Manual Damper" and "Motorized Damper".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all five drawings. Sort them aloud by where the damper sits (on the fan outlet or in an inlet box) and by how its blades are moved (by hand, by an actuator, or not shown).
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all five descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order. For field situations that call for a gravity damper or a slide gate instead, try Flow Control Device Sorter.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Parallel and opposed blade dampers do the same job: FanPedia recommends parallel blades for modulation from full open to about 75% open and opposed blades for modulation over the entire range, at about 10% more cost.
  • An inlet box damper is an outlet damper moved to the inlet: partly closed, its parallel blades pre-spin the air in the direction of impeller rotation, which saves horsepower at reduced loads, and it needs an inlet box.
  • A manual damper is for day-to-day flow control: FanPedia says manual dampers are typically used to balance a system, set once and left in place; a control loop needs an actuator.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 5"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a temperature controller must vary airflow continuously over nearly the whole range on a constant-speed fan. Which two drawings together describe the damper to quote, and why?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 137 holds the industrial grade damper drawings used here, p. 136 the commercial grade dampers and pp. 182-183 the damper descriptions.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 18: Inlets, Outlets and Flow Control - the damper sections from "Damper" to "Motorized Damper"; this MicroSim is embedded after "Motorized Damper".
  4. Flow Control Device Sorter - sorts field situations into damper and vane types.

docs.title: Inlet Box Features
docs.text: Run the Inlet Box Features MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts seven numbered markers on FanPedia's colour-coded drawing of a centrifugal fan with an inlet box (page 145). The box sits on the inlet side of the fan and takes its air from above, through a damper mounted on top of it, and turns the air into the fan inlet. FanPedia colours each feature: the damper green, the flange at the box inlet orange, the access door blue, the connection to the fan yellow and the drain connection red.

The seven features are the inlet box, inlet box damper, flange at inlet, access door, flange or collar, drain connection and fan housing. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. The drain connection is a small fitting, so its marker sits just to the left of it with a short pointer to the part. FanPedia's insets for the FGR connection, the insulated box and the damper airflow are not shown, so the FGR connection has no marker.

The quiz describes each feature by its job ("Select the fitting that lets condensation out of the box.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the feature and counts as missed. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the feature's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened features get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 7 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that feature too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one feature:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the feature name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the feature you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 7".
  4. After the seventh prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (6 of 7), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 145", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the inlet box, its damper, its two connections, its access door and drain connection, and the fan housing it feeds on a drawing, given each feature's function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 18, sections "Inlet Box" (purpose, styles and the list of features and accessories), "Inlet Box Damper" and "Companion Flange".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all seven features. Sort them aloud into the two connections (flange at inlet, flange or collar), the standard accessories (access door, drain connection) and the flow-control device (inlet box damper).
  2. Position (2 min): The box on this drawing takes its air from above. Using the position table in the "Inlet Box" section, which position is it? Then check your reading of positions in Inlet Box Position Trainer.
  3. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all seven features from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (1 min): Read the missed list, open those features in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• An inlet box has one flange: it has two connections, the flange at inlet to the customer's ductwork and the flange or collar to the fan.
  • The access door and drain connection are special options: FanPedia lists both as standard on most inlet boxes.
  • The inlet box damper is just added resistance like an outlet damper: partly closed, its parallel blades pre-spin the air in the direction of impeller rotation, which saves horsepower at reduced loads.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 7"; mastery is 6 of 7 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a quote line reads "inlet box, position 360, with access door and drain." Which three features on this drawing does that line name, and which way does the box opening face?

docs.text:

  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 18: Inlets, Outlets and Flow Control - the section "Inlet Box", where this MicroSim is embedded, and the section "Inlet Box Damper".
  4. Inlet Box Position Trainer - assigns the inlet box position, the other half of an inlet box order.

docs.title: Inlet Box Position Trainer
docs.text:
Run the Inlet Box Position Trainer MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch18-inlet-box-position-trainer.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An inlet box position names where the box opening sits on a dial drawn on the fan as seen from the drive side: 360 at the top, numbers increasing clockwise in 45° steps (FanPedia p. 144). The position does not change with rotation or discharge.

Position FanPedia description Opening (drive side) 45 Angular down intake Upper right 90 Horizontal right intake Right 135 Angular up intake Lower right 180 Bottom up intake Bottom 225 Angular up intake Lower left 270 Horizontal left intake Left 315 Angular down intake Upper left 360 Top down intake Top

A picture drawn from the inlet side mirrors left and right, so the drive-side position is 360 − p, where p is the angle read on the inlet-side picture (0 is written 360; 180 stays 180).

The sim shows eight illustrative installations in a fixed order: four drive-side views, three inlet-side views and one text-only description. Each picture is an end view of a fan housing with its inlet box, a viewpoint label and an arrow showing the air entering the box. You choose one of the eight positions and press Check. You get two attempts: a wrong first answer gets a hint that names the slip (for example an inlet-side picture read without mirroring) but not the position, and a second wrong answer reveals the position with its explanation and counts as missed. When an item is resolved, the drive-side dial is drawn over the picture with the answer highlighted; an inlet-side picture first flips to the drive side, and a dashed outline marks where the box appeared before the flip.

"Positions correct: n of 8" counts first-attempt answers only. Mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. After item 8, free practice unlocks: drag the box around the housing (or use Turn and the arrow keys) and switch the viewpoint. Free practice is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read installation 1, note the viewpoint label, and choose a position with the 45 to 360 buttons (or keys 1-8).
  2. Press Check (or Enter). A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: position n, description." A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with a hint; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next installation (or Enter) and continue through item 8, then press See score.
  4. In free practice, move the box and press View to switch between the drive side and the inlet side. Notice that switching the view changes 90 to 270 and 45 to 315 on the picture, while 360 and 180 never change. Start over clears the score and returns to item 1.

Keyboard: keys 1-8 choose 45 to 360; Enter checks, then goes to the next item. In free practice the left and right arrow keys turn the box and V switches the view. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative installations · Source: FanPedia p. 144", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the drive-side viewing convention to assign the correct inlet box position (45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315 or 360) to eight described or pictured installations, including views drawn from the inlet side (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Inlet box and inlet box position (Chapter 18)
  • Drive side and inlet side (Chapter 12)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Installations (5-6 min): For each item, say aloud which side the picture is drawn from before choosing a position.
  2. Free practice (3 min): Put the box at 90, switch to the inlet side and read the picture; then repeat for 45, 180 and 360.
  3. Transfer (1-2 min): Rework the chapter example "Elbow or Inlet Box?" (duct from the ceiling) and confirm position 360.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The position can be read from either side: items 5, 6 and 8 are inlet-side pictures, and each one flips to the drive side when it is resolved.
  • 45 and 315 (or 135 and 225) are interchangeable: item 3 is upper left (315), and the feedback points out that 45 is upper right.
  • 180 means the box faces up because the air moves up: items 4 and 7 have the opening at the bottom, and the number names where the opening is.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Positions correct: n of 8" counts first-attempt answers; mastery is 7 of 8. The summary shows the first-attempt score, the mastery line and the missed items.
  • Moving the box in free practice is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner to explain why 180 and 360 are the only positions that read the same from both sides.

docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference; p. 144 gives the inlet box position descriptions and states that positions are determined from the drive side.
  2. Twin City Fan & Blower - current catalogs and drawings showing inlet box options on centrifugal fans.
  3. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia overview of centrifugal fan construction, housings and inlets.

docs.title: Damper Throttling Operating Point Explorer
docs.text: Run the Damper Throttling Operating Point Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The chart shows one illustrative fan curve and the system curve it works against. Damper throttling multiplies the system's resistance coefficient by a factor m, so the system curve becomes steeper each time the damper closes:

  • Fan curve: P = 6.0 − (Q / 10,000)² in. wg
  • System curve: P = 5.0 × m × (Q / 10,000)² in. wg
  • Operating point: Q = 10,000 × √(6.0 / (1 + 5.0m)) and P = 6.0 − 6.0 / (1 + 5.0m)

The damper closes in five fixed steps. Before each new system curve is drawn, the learner predicts whether airflow will be higher, lower or the same, and whether static pressure will be higher, lower or the same. Pressing Check locks the pair, draws the new system curve and its operating point, and keeps the previous system curve (dotted grey) and the previous operating point (open circle) on the chart for comparison. A table beside the chart lists every operating point revealed so far.

Damper setting Multiplier m Airflow (CFM) Static pressure (in. wg) Wide open 1.0 10,000 5.00 Step 1 1.5 8,402 5.29 Step 2 2.0 7,385 5.45 Step 3 3.0 6,124 5.63 Step 4 4.0 5,345 5.71 Step 5 6.0 4,399 5.81

Each step has one scored attempt. A prediction is correct only when both directions are right (airflow lower, static pressure higher). A wrong pressure direction and a wrong airflow direction each get their own explanation. After Step 5 the summary reads "Predictions correct: n of 5", gives the mastery line (mastery is 5 of 5) and notes that m rose 6 times while airflow fell by only 56%. Reset then returns to wide open for unscored stepping.

All values are illustrative, chosen to make the pattern easy to see. They are not Twin City Fan published ratings; real fan curves are read from the catalog.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the wide-open operating point: 10,000 CFM at 5.00 in. wg.
  2. Press Close damper one step. Choose Higher, Lower or Same for airflow and for static pressure, then press Check.
  3. Read the feedback and compare the new operating point (diamond) with the previous one (open circle) on the chart and in the table.
  4. Repeat through Step 5. Then read the summary, press Reset and step through the settings freely; nothing is scored in this explore mode. Start over clears the score and restarts the challenge at any time.

Keyboard: keys 1, 2 and 3 choose airflow higher, lower or same; keys 4, 5 and 6 choose static pressure higher, lower or same; Enter closes the damper one step or checks the prediction. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Values are illustrative. Real fan curves are read from the catalog.", shown at the bottom left of the chart.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will interpret how closing an outlet damper moves a fan's operating point along its fan curve, predicting the direction of change in airflow and static pressure before each new damper setting is revealed (Bloom: Understand, verb: interpret).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan curve, system curve and operating point (Chapter 10)
  • Damper throttling and the resistance multiplier m (section "Damper Throttling" of Chapter 19)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predictions (6 min): Work through the five closing steps. Before pressing Check, say out loud why the new intersection must sit where you predict.
  2. Review (4 min): Read the table from Wide open to Step 5. Compare the change in m with the change in airflow, and notice that pressure rises by less than 1 in. wg in total.
  3. Explore (3 min): Press Reset and step through again, watching only the fan curve. Ask: did the fan curve ever move?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Closing a damper lowers the pressure the fan produces: every step reveals a higher static pressure, and the wrong-pressure feedback explains why.
  • Closing a damper changes the fan curve: the fan curve is drawn once and never moves; only the system curve steepens.
  • Airflow falls in proportion to how far the damper is closed: the summary contrasts the 6-fold rise in m with the 56% drop in airflow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score "Predictions correct: n of 5"; mastery is 5 of 5 steps with both directions correct, one attempt per step.
  • Viewing the chart after a reveal is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: why does damper throttling save less horsepower than other flow-control methods? (The fan still develops more pressure at the throttled point.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 19: Damper Details and Duct Connections - the "Damper Throttling" section this MicroSim exercises.
  2. Chapter 10: Fan Performance, Curves and Ratings - fan curves, system curves and the operating point.
  3. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - pp. 182-183 describe outlet damper control shifting the operating point to the left of the rating point, with smaller horsepower savings than other methods.
  4. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online fan and blower encyclopedia.
  5. Plotly JavaScript Open Source Graphing Library - the charting library used to draw the curves.

docs.title: Fan-to-Duct Connection Chooser
docs.text:
Run the Fan-to-Duct Connection Chooser MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch19-fan-duct-connection-chooser.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Eight illustrative job descriptions appear in a fixed order. For each one the learner selects one of seven options and presses Submit:

  1. Bolted flange connection
  2. Slip connection
  3. Flexible connector
  4. Tube adapter and rubber sleeve
  5. Bolt-on inlet box
  6. Free-standing inlet box
  7. Inlet box horn

Each option has a definition the learner can open with Definition at any time; opening a definition is exploration and is never scored. Each job is scored on its first submission and then locks. Job 2 accepts either a slip connection or a flexible connector, because FanPedia calls for a flex connector in the form of a slip connection there. Jobs 3 and 4 come back to back and differ only in temperature: the tube adapter's rubber sleeve is judged by its rating (up to 5 psi and 180°F), so it fits job 3 (3 psi, 150°F) but not job 4 (220°F), where the blower bolts to the matching 125# ASA pipe flange instead.

Feedback starts with "Correct." or "Not this one." and gives the deciding fact; an incorrect answer also shows the accepted answer. Choosing the tube adapter for job 4 adds "Check the temperature against the sleeve's 180°F rating." The running count reads "Correct: n of 8". After job 8, the summary lists every job with the learner's answer and the accepted answers, followed by "Mastery: 7 or more of 8" or "Review the sections on the items you missed." Start over clears all answers.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job description and find the deciding fact: isolation, separate support, different planes, a pressure or temperature limit, or intersecting airflows.
  2. Select an option. Press Definition to read what the selected option is, if you need to.
  3. Press Submit. Read the feedback, then press Next.
  4. After job 8, press See summary. Press Start over to try all eight again.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 7 select an option; D opens or hides the selected option's definition; Enter submits the selection, then goes to the next job. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Illustrative jobs · Source: FanPedia pp. 67–194", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will use the support, alignment, temperature and pressure facts in a job description to choose the inlet box style or fan-to-duct connection that fits it, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Apply, verb: use).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Bolted flange connection, slip connection, flexible connector, tube adapter and sleeve, 125# ASA pipe flange bolt pattern, bolt-on inlet box, free-standing inlet box and inlet box horn, all defined in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Choose (6 min): Work through the eight jobs. Before submitting, underline (mentally or on paper) the one fact that decides the answer.
  2. Compare (3 min): Put jobs 3 and 4 side by side. What changed, and which rating does it cross? Then compare jobs 6 and 8: both use a free-standing box, so what decides job 8?
  3. Review (3 min): Read the summary and reopen the definitions of the options you missed.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A rubber sleeve connector can be used at any temperature: job 4 exceeds the sleeve's 180°F rating, and choosing the tube adapter there triggers a temperature reminder.
  • A bolted joint is fine on a spring-isolated fan: job 1 requires a flexible connector.
  • Any detached inlet box is supported by the fan: job 6 is a free-standing box supported at the floor.
  • A horn is a sound-control device: job 7 uses the horn to keep the inlet duct clear of the discharge airflow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running count "Correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
  • Opening definitions is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a pressure blower runs at 4 psi and 170°F into a pipe line. Which connection, and what changes if the temperature rises to 200°F?

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Eight situation cards describe real order questions: an exhaust opening in a ceiling or a wall, a pressure blower outlet that must shut off, a cast aluminum blower that needs a set-once inlet adjustment, a clean hot airstream that needs flow control with horsepower savings, and two lab exhaust problems. The learner places each card in one of seven device bins:

  1. Ceiling type gravity damper
  2. Wall type gravity damper
  3. Blast gate
  4. Slide gate damper
  5. Nested inlet vanes
  6. Lab exhaust isolation damper
  7. Lab exhaust bypass damper

The cards come in a shuffled order. Each card is scored on the first bin it is placed in and then locks. The sim marks the placement correct (✓, solid green border) or incorrect (✗, dashed red border) and shows why. A missed card moves to its correct bin as a chip marked "missed". Blast gate is the correct bin for two cards (situations 3 and 4); every other bin is correct for exactly one card.

The running count reads "Correct: n of 8". After the last card the summary reads "Mastery: 7 or more of 8" or "Review the sections on the devices you missed, then try again." and names the devices missed. Try again reshuffles all eight cards for a practice round; practice rounds are not scored and never change the first-round result.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the situation on the face-up card and find the detail that decides it: mounting plane, full shutoff, automatic control, manual set-once trim, clean air and the vane location, or the job a lab damper does.
  2. Press the bin button for the device that fits. Read the feedback and, after a miss, look where the card landed.
  3. Press Next card and continue until all eight are placed, then read the summary.
  4. Press Try again for an unscored practice round over all eight cards.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 7 place the card in that bin; Enter goes to the next card, shows the summary after the last card, and starts a practice round from the summary. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Illustrative scenarios · Source: FanPedia pp. 125–192", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will classify eight field situations by the damper or vane device that fits each one, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Ceiling type and wall type gravity dampers, blast gate, slide gate damper, nested inlet vanes, pre-spin, and lab exhaust isolation and bypass dampers, all defined in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5 min): Place all eight cards. Before each placement, name the one detail in the situation that rules out the other devices.
  2. Review (3 min): Reread the chapter section for each device you missed. Compare cards 3 and 4 (both blast gates) with card 5 (slide gate): what makes a slide gate the wrong shutoff device?
  3. Practice (2 min): Press Try again and sort the reshuffled deck without looking back.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Ceiling and wall gravity dampers are interchangeable: cards 1 and 2 differ only in the mounting plane.
  • A slide gate is the shutoff device for any pressure blower: cards 3 and 4 need full shutoff and automatic control, which only the blast gate offers.
  • Nested and external inlet vanes suit the same airstreams: card 6 asks for clean air with the vanes inside the inlet funnel.
  • Isolation and bypass dampers on a lab fan do the same job: cards 7 and 8 contrast direction control with flow make-up.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running count "Correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
  • Practice rounds are not evidence of mastery.
  • Follow-up question: a plant wants to throttle a cast aluminum pressure blower automatically. Which device, and why not a slide gate?
