docs.title: Inlet Box Styles
docs.text: Run the Inlet Box Styles MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks four numbered zones on FanPedia's inlet box drawings (pages 141 and 142), with the inlet box drawn in green on each fan. The top row shows the two integral (attached) styles from page 141: an integral inlet box without a horn, and one with a horn that carries the inlet connection out over the fan. The bottom row shows the two detached styles from page 142: a bolt-on box fastened to the fan's inlet flange, and a free-standing box supported at the floor and joined to the fan by a slip connection. The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one style at a time ("Which drawing shows a detached box fully supported at the floor?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 4 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 4 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one drawing:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 4".
  4. After the fourth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (4 of 4), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, pp. 141-142", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the integral inlet box without horn, the integral inlet box with horn, the bolt-on inlet box and the free-standing inlet box on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 18, sections "Inlet Box", "Integral Inlet Box" and "Detached Inlet Box".
  • Chapter 19, section "Inlet Box Styles and the Horn".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all four drawings. For each one, say what carries the box: the fan, a base angle, or a base plate at the floor.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all four descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every inlet box bolts to the fan's inlet flange: an integral box shares a common plate with the fan inlet housing sideplate; only the detached styles connect at the inlet flange or collar.
  • A horn is a separate detached box: it is an extension on an integral box, used when the inlet and discharge airflows would intersect.
  • A free-standing box is just a bolt-on box with a longer leg: it is mounted separately from the fan and fully supported at the floor, and it connects either by a bolted round outlet flange or by a slip collar with a rubber sleeve and clamps.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 4"; mastery is 4 of 4 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: the inlet duct of an integral box would run into the discharge duct. Which drawing shows the fix, and what does the added part do?

docs.title: External and Nested Inlet Vanes
docs.text: Run the External and Nested Inlet Vanes MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts six numbered markers on FanPedia's industrial grade inlet vane drawings (page 139). The top drawing is a centrifugal fan with external inlet vanes, a vane ring in its own housing bolted to the inlet, and beside it a close-up photo of that vane section. The bottom drawing is a fan with nested inlet vanes, built into the inlet funnel, and beside it a close-up photo of the funnel with its vanes. Both drawings show the housing cut away and red arrows for the air turning as it enters.

The six parts are the manual handle, external inlet vanes, impeller, pre-spin, nested inlet vanes and inlet funnel. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. The handle's marker sits just to its right with a short pointer, so the lever stays visible.

The quiz describes each part by its job or look ("Select the part the nested vanes are built into.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 6 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 6".
  4. After the sixth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (5 of 6), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 139", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the external inlet vanes, nested inlet vanes, inlet funnel, manual handle, impeller and the pre-spin arrows on FanPedia's inlet vane drawings, given each part's job or look (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 18, sections "Variable Inlet Vanes" and "External Inlet Vanes".
  • Chapter 19, section "Nested Inlet Vanes and Pre-Spin".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all six parts. Compare the two close-up photos and say where each vane ring sits: in its own bolted housing, or inside the curved entry of the funnel.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all six parts from their descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Nested and external inlet vanes suit the same airstreams: nested vanes are for clean air up to 600°F; external vanes are the choice for contaminated air, or high temperature air up to 600°F.
  • Replacing either vane set is the same job: external vanes come out as their own section; replacing nested vanes means replacing the entire inlet funnel assembly.
  • Inlet vanes save power by blocking the air like a damper: they pre-spin the entering air in the direction the impeller rotates, so the impeller does less work on each pound of air.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 6"; mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.

  • Follow-up question: a fan handles dusty exhaust and the owner wants to clean the vanes without pulling the inlet funnel. Which close-up photo shows the right vane style, and why?

docs.title: Construction Class Advisor
docs.text:
Run the Construction Class Advisor MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, first add the kit files fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/ (or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html, then paste ch20-construction-class-advisor.js as the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The advisor presents six illustrative inquiries, in a fixed order, of the kind that reach an application engineer. Each inquiry gives a short description of the fan and the job, and tags for the airstream conditions present: hot, wet, corrosive, explosive, personnel exposure or recirculated gas. Four construction recommendations follow, labeled A to D. One of them is consistent with the FanPedia rules in Chapter 20; the other three each break a specific rule.

The six inquiries cover the decisions a construction line most often gets wrong:

  • high moisture construction for steam in an Arrangement 9 axial fan, with a drain;
  • the rule that high moisture construction cannot be combined with high temperature construction (at 220°F the axial fan needs a high temperature package, so the job goes to engineering review);
  • Type B, not Type C, when a radial bladed fan already has a non-ferrous impeller as standard;
  • the 601°F-800°F centrifugal package plus insulation when workers can touch a 700°F housing;
  • an FGR connection and an insulated inlet box when hot flue gas is returned to the fan inlet;
  • buffer strips or a bolt-on pedestal when stainless steel must not be welded to mild steel.

You commit a recommendation before the reason is shown. The first answer to each inquiry is the one scored; one extra practice attempt is allowed. The summary lists every first answer, the correct answer and the reason, and builds the construction line for inquiry 4 as an example. The score line at the top reads "Inquiries correct: n of 6" and counts first answers only. Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.

The inquiries are illustrative, not customer orders; the rules come from FanPedia.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the inquiry and its airstream tags. The prompt asks: "What should the construction line say?"
  2. Press A, B, C or D (or the A to D keys) to select a recommendation, then press Recommend (or Enter) to commit it.
  3. Read the feedback. A sound choice reads "Recommended construction is sound." and a wrong one reads "That breaks a rule." followed by a hint that names the rule the choice breaks. After a correct first answer the reason follows and the correct option is marked at once.
  4. After a wrong first answer you may choose again once for practice. The practice attempt is not scored; afterwards the reason is shown and the correct option is marked.
  5. Press Next inquiry to continue. After inquiry 6, press See summary for the first-attempt score "First-attempt score: n of 6" and the review list. A score of 5 or more reads "Mastery reached (5 of 6 needed). You can turn an airstream into a construction line." On narrow screens the review list has two pages; press Inquiries 4-6 and Inquiries 1-3 to switch.
  6. Press Start over to reset all six inquiries and the score.

Keyboard: keys A to D select an option; Enter recommends the selected option, or moves to the next inquiry once the first answer is committed. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative inquiries · Rules: FanPedia pp. 85-145", shown at the bottom left of the drawing. The inquiries are illustrative; every rule and reason comes from FanPedia.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will recommend the construction choice for six stated airstream inquiries, consistent with the FanPedia rules in Chapter 20, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: New application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and plant staff who write or check the construction line on a fan order. This is an adult professional-development activity.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes for one pass, plus 5 to 10 minutes of discussion.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: From Chapter 20 and Chapter 18: construction class, construction material, stainless steel construction, buffer strips, spark resistant Types A, B and C, non-ferrous material, high temperature construction and packages, high moisture construction, housing drain, insulated fan, insulated jacket, double wall construction, flue gas recirculation and inlet box.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. First pass (8 to 10 min): Each learner works all six inquiries alone, without notes, committing each recommendation before reading the reason. Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.
  2. Name the broken rule (3 to 5 min): For every wrong first answer in the summary, the learner states which chapter rule that option breaks (for example, "high moisture and high temperature construction cannot be stacked").
  3. Discussion (5 to 10 min): Why does a specification that says Type C end with a Type B recommendation in inquiry 3? Why is insulation the deciding item in inquiry 4 when the temperature band is the same in options B and C? What makes an FGR job more than a normal inlet box?
  4. Write a line (optional): Learners write the full construction line for inquiry 5 in the same form as the summary's example for inquiry 4, then compare.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• High moisture and high temperature construction can be stacked (they cannot).
  • Type C is always the lowest-cost answer, even when the impeller is already non-ferrous (use Type B).
  • Insulation is only for heat (it also addresses condensation, sound and personnel protection).
  • A stainless housing can always be welded to a mild steel pedestal (use buffer strips or a bolt-on pedestal when the specification forbids it).
  • An FGR job is just a normal inlet box (it needs an FGR connection on the front of the inlet box, and the hot gas makes an insulated inlet box appropriate).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Inquiries correct: n of 6"; mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt, and the summary then reads "Mastery reached (5 of 6 needed). You can turn an airstream into a construction line."
  • For each wrong first answer, the learner can name the FanPedia rule the chosen option breaks.
  • Follow-up question: an Arrangement 9 axial fan handles condensing exhaust at 150°F. Which construction applies, and what would change if the temperature rose to 240°F?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan. Source of every rule and reason in the sim: buffer strips and bolt-on pedestals p. 85; spark resistant radial bladed fans p. 107 (note 2); centrifugal high temperature packages p. 110; axial high temperature packages p. 116; insulated jackets p. 119; high moisture construction p. 122; inlet box FGR connection and insulated inlet box p. 145.
  2. Chapter 20: Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance - the chapter this sim closes, in this book.
  3. FanPedia (PDF edition) - Twin City Fan, the printable edition with the same page numbers.

docs.title: Fan Temperature Limits Ruler
docs.text: Run the Fan Temperature Limits Ruler MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every part of a hot fan carries its own temperature limit, and the lowest one wins. This ruler puts the limits from Chapter 20 on one horizontal temperature axis, 0°F to 1,200°F, so you can see where they overlap. Each row is one limit drawn as a range:

# Limit Range (°F) Source 1 Aluminum rotating parts, Arr. 4 centrifugal and Arr. 4 plug fans 0 to 250 FanPedia pp. 111, 114 2 Standard aluminum axial impeller 0 to 275 FanPedia p. 116 3 High temperature grease required, axial fans over 275 and above FanPedia p. 116 4 Shaft cooler recommended over 300 and above FanPedia p. 192 5 Arr. 4 centrifugal package 181 to 300 FanPedia p. 111 6-9 Centrifugal packages (Arr. 1, 8, 9, 9F, 10) 301-500, 501-600, 601-800, 801-1,000 FanPedia p. 110 10 Centrifugal package, engineering review 1,001 and above FanPedia p. 110 11 Type C centrifugal: steel funnel with rubbing band and rubbing bars 501 and above FanPedia p. 106 12 Nominally leak-tight construction recommended 0 to 600 FanPedia p. 120

Rows 1 and 5 are FanPedia's Arrangement 4 figures. Twin City Fan engineering (2026-10-09) advises that current practice does not use Arrangement 4 for high-temperature applications (standard ranges are typically up to about 180°F), so read those two rows as FanPedia's description, not a current ordering path.

A row is active at the marker temperature T when T lies in its range. "To" ranges include both ends (301 ≤ T ≤ 500), "over 275" means T > 275 and "over 300" means T > 300; open-ended rows have no upper bound and are labeled "and above". Active rows are drawn in full colour, with a ✓ and bold text in their axis label; inactive rows are dimmed but stay readable. The readout under the chart lists every active row in words.

Five questions follow, in a fixed order, one attempt each. When you submit, the marker jumps to the question's temperature, the row that decides it is outlined and marked ▶, and the feedback gives the reason. The question temperatures are illustrative design points chosen for practice. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Moving the marker is exploration and is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Move the temperature marker (it starts at 70°F, where rows 1, 2 and 12 are active) and watch which limits switch on and off. Hover or tap a bar for its full label, range and source.
  2. Read question 1, choose an option (click it or press 1-4) and press Submit (or Enter).
  3. Read the feedback: "Correct." or "Not quite." followed by the reason. The correct option is marked ✓ at once, and a wrong choice is marked ✗. The running score reads "Questions correct: n of 5".
  4. Press Next question and continue through question 5, then See summary for the first-attempt score, the mastery line and every question's reason. At 4 or more the summary adds "You can place a design temperature against the catalog limits."
  5. Press Start over to reset the questions, the score and the marker.

Keyboard: the arrow keys move the marker in 10°F steps; keys 1-4 choose an option; Enter submits, then goes to the next question; Tab reaches every control.

Data label: "Illustrative design temperatures · Limits: FanPedia pp. 106, 110, 111, 114, 116, 120, 192", shown under the chart.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will use FanPedia's temperature limits to decide, for five stated fans and design temperatures, which package, material or construction rule applies, answering at least 4 of 5 correctly (Bloom: Apply, verb: use).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• High temperature construction and temperature packages
  • Maximum operating temperature
  • Aluminum construction
  • Shaft cooler and high temperature grease
  • Spark resistant Type C
  • Nominally leak-tight construction

All are introduced in Chapter 20 above the sim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Sweep the marker from 70°F to 1,200°F. Name the temperatures where a row switches on or off (250, 275, 300, 500, 600, 800, 1,000).
  2. Questions (6 min): Answer the five questions in order, committing each answer before the reason appears.
  3. Review (3 min): In the summary, find the row behind each reason on the chart.
  4. Discuss (3 min): Why do rows 1 and 2 end at different temperatures? At 600°F, is nominally leak-tight construction still recommended, and why does 650°F change the answer?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• One aluminum limit applies to every fan type: rows 1 and 2 end at 250°F and 275°F, side by side.
  • A temperature exactly at a boundary always belongs to the lower band: bands are inclusive as written, so 600°F is inside "0 to 600" and not "over 600°F".
  • If the package fits, nothing else needs checking: at 320°F the package row and the shaft cooler row are both active, and at 550°F the Type C funnel row switches on too.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score "Questions correct: n of 5"; the summary shows "First-attempt score: n of 5" with "Mastery reached (4 of 5 needed)." or "Mastery needs 4 of 5 on the first attempt."
  • Follow-up: an Arrangement 4 centrifugal fan runs at 260°F. Which package applies, and may its impeller be aluminum?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan. High temperature packages pp. 110-111 and 114, axial high temperature construction p. 116, Type C centrifugal p. 106, nominally leak-tight construction p. 120, shaft cooler p. 192.
  2. FanPedia (PDF edition) - Twin City Fan, the printable edition with the same page numbers.
  3. Chapter 20: Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance - the chapter section this sim belongs to.
  4. Chart.js bar chart documentation - the floating-bar form used for the ranges.

docs.title: Spark Resistance Parts Matrix
docs.text: Run the Spark Resistance Parts Matrix MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Spark resistant Types A, B and C differ in which airstream parts they make non-ferrous. This matrix asks you to commit a prediction for every part before you see FanPedia's answer. The rows are six components of a centrifugal fan; the columns are the three types. Each of the 18 cells takes one of three states: Non-ferrous, Steel or Not listed (the type's page does not list the part).

The answer table comes from the "Non-Ferrous Construction" and "Steel Construction" lists on FanPedia's centrifugal fan pages for Type A (p. 104), Type B (p. 105) and Type C (p. 106):

Component Type A Type B Type C Housing / frame Non-ferrous Steel Steel Impeller Non-ferrous Non-ferrous Steel Inlet funnel Non-ferrous Steel Non-ferrous Rub plate Not listed Non-ferrous Non-ferrous Shaft Steel Steel Steel Pedestal Steel Steel Steel

The pattern is the point: Type A makes almost every airstream part non-ferrous, Type B makes the impeller (and its rub plate) non-ferrous, and Type C protects only the likely contact points, the inlet funnel and the rub plate. The shaft and the pedestal are steel in all three. After the answers are revealed, a note adds two rules: bearings are not allowed in the airstream in any of the three types, and Type C at 501°F and above uses a steel funnel with a rubbing band and rubbing bars instead of the aluminum funnel.

The first Check is the recorded score. Mastery is 15 of 18 cells correct on the first Check.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Open any component name (Housing / frame, Impeller, …) to read what the part is. The description appears in the line under the question. Opening a description is exploration, not evidence.
  2. Set every cell to Non-ferrous, Steel or Not listed. Check stays unavailable until all 18 cells are set; the line beside it says how many cells remain empty.
  3. Press Check. Each cell is marked ✓ Correct (solid green border) or ✗ Not quite (dashed red border), and every row with a wrong cell shows a hint underneath (the question to ask for that component, not the answer). The feedback reads "You matched n of 18 cells." followed by "You can tell the three types apart part by part." (15 or more) or "Look at the Impeller and Inlet funnel rows first; they carry the main difference between B and C." (below 15).
  4. Press Try Again to clear only the wrong cells (the correct ones stay locked), set them again and press Check a second time. The first-Check score stays the recorded score.
  5. The second Check, or Show Answers at any time after the first Check, reveals the answer in every cell, every row's reason and the note on bearings and the 501°F funnel.
  6. Press Start over to clear the matrix and the score.

Keyboard: Tab moves from cell to cell and to the buttons. In a cell, the arrow keys change the state (or type S for Steel, N for Non-ferrous or Not listed). Enter or Space on a component name opens its description; Enter on a button presses it.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia, Spark Resistant Construction, Centrifugal Fans, pp. 104-106", shown under the matrix.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate spark-resistant Types A, B and C on a centrifugal fan by predicting, for six fan components, whether each type makes the component non-ferrous, leaves it steel, or does not list it, with at least 15 of 18 cells correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Analyze, verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Spark resistant construction and Types A, B and C
  • Non-ferrous material
  • Rub plate and inlet funnel
  • Pedestal (Chapter 3)

All are defined in the section "Spark Resistant Construction" of Chapter 20.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Fill all 18 cells without notes and press Check. This first Check is the recorded score.
  2. Repair (3 min): Read the hints under the wrong rows, press Try Again, fix the cleared cells and Check again.
  3. Find the pattern (3 min): With the answers revealed, describe each type in one phrase (A: almost everything in the airstream; B: the impeller; C: the contact points).
  4. Discuss (3 min): Why does Type A's list have no rub plate? Why is a stainless steel set screw not "non-ferrous"? What does the 501°F note change on a Type C order?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Type C makes the impeller non-ferrous: the Impeller row shows Steel for Type C.
  • Type B makes the whole airstream non-ferrous: only the impeller and the rub plate are non-ferrous; the housing and the inlet cone stay steel.
  • Spark-resistant construction makes the shaft non-ferrous: the Shaft row is Steel in all three types.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-Check score shown as "First Check: n of 18 cells (recorded)"; mastery is 15 of 18 on the first Check, and the feedback adds "Mastery reached (15 of 18 needed)." or "Mastery needs 15 of 18 on the first attempt."
  • Follow-up: a Type B fan has an outside protruding hub. Which cell of the matrix could change, and why? (FanPedia p. 105: the rub plate is then not required.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: Spark Resistant Construction, Centrifugal Fans - Twin City Fan. Type A (p. 104), Type B (p. 105) and Type C (p. 106) component lists, the source of every cell in the answer table.
  2. FanPedia (PDF edition) - Twin City Fan, the printable edition with the same page numbers.
  3. Chapter 20: Construction Classes, Materials and Spark Resistance - the chapter section this sim belongs to.
  4. Non-ferrous metal - Wikipedia, background on why iron-free metals are used where sparks matter.

docs.title: High Temperature Fan Construction
docs.text: Run the High Temperature Fan Construction MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts seven numbered markers on FanPedia's general construction drawing for high temperature centrifugal fans (page 110). The large drawing is a belt driven centrifugal fan on its base, with its housing prepared for insulation. Down the left side are three close-ups of the drive end, where the shaft leaves the hot housing: the top one shows the shaft seal, shaft cooler and bearing of the high temperature style pedestal, and the bottom one shows the same corner on a housing studded with insulation pins, with a guarded open frame around the shaft cooler. The middle close-up (a shaft cooler with a stuffing box or mechanical seal) carries no marker.

The seven parts are the shaft seal, bearing, shaft cooler, insulation pins, raised access door, safety screen and cooler box. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select the part that sheds heat from the shaft before it reaches the bearings.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 7 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 7".
  4. After the seventh prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (6 of 7), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 110", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the seven labeled high temperature construction features of a centrifugal fan (shaft seal, bearing, shaft cooler, insulation pins, raised access door, safety screen and cooler box) on FanPedia's drawing, given each feature's job (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 21, sections "How Heat Moves Through a Fan" and "Shedding and Blocking Heat at the Shaft" (shaft cooler, cooler box, insulation pins).
  • Chapter 3, sections "Access Door" (raised access door) and "Bird and Safety Screens".
  • Chapter 16, section "Shaft Seals".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all seven parts. Trace the shaft in the top close-up from the housing wall outward: which part meets the shaft first, which comes next, and which part is all of that there to protect?
  2. Compare (2 min): Compare the top and bottom close-ups. What was added around the shaft cooler once the housing was insulated, and why is that area left open?
  3. Quiz (3 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all seven parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Classify (2 min): Go on to High Temperature Fan Heat Path, which sorts the shaft cooler, cooler box and insulation pins (and seven other parts) by whether they block heat, shed heat or allow growth.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A cooler box is an insulated enclosure: it is an uninsulated open area left around the shaft cooler so the cooler has air to shed heat into.
  • Insulation pins are themselves insulation: they only hold the field- or vendor-applied insulation on the housing.
  • The shaft cooler cools the airstream: it sheds the heat that has travelled along the shaft from the airstream, to protect the bearings.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 7"; mastery is 6 of 7 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a customer orders this fan with aluminum clad insulation. Which part on the drawing would otherwise be buried, and which feature keeps it working?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 110 is the high temperature general construction drawing used here (cooler box, insulation pins, safety screen, raised access door), p. 90 the high temperature style pedestal, p. 117 the raised access door and p. 192 the shaft cooler.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 21: High Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - the section "Shedding and Blocking Heat at the Shaft", where this MicroSim is embedded.
  4. Chapter 3: Basic Fan Anatomy and Chapter 16: Bearings, Shafts and Shaft Seals - the safety screen, the raised access door and the shaft seal.
  5. High Temperature Fan Heat Path - the companion sim that classifies these parts by job.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 110. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: High Temperature Fan Heat Path
docs.text: Run the High Temperature Fan Heat Path MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every high temperature feature on a fan drawing does one of three jobs: it blocks heat from reaching the bearings, it sheds heat that has already reached the shaft, or it allows parts to grow without binding. This MicroSim shows two illustrative side views with ten labeled parts. View A is a composite: FanPedia p. 112 draws the separated pedestal and the motor heat shield on different pedestal forms, and this drawing puts both on one fan so the parts can be compared. The two views are:

  • A. A belt-driven centrifugal fan on a high temperature style pedestal: shaft cooler, cooler box, insulation pins, floating bearing, separated pedestal, high temp angle, motor heat shield and fixed bearing.
  • B. An Arrangement 9 plug fan through an insulated wall: recess cone and insulated plug.

For each part you choose a job before its description is shown, so every answer is a prediction. The parts may be answered in any order; each takes one answer and cannot be re-answered. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct:" followed by the part's description; an incorrect one reads "✗ Not quite." followed by the description and the part's job. The running line shows "n of 10 correct". Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first (and only) attempt.

# Part Job 1 Shaft cooler Shed 2 Recess cone Shed 3 Cooler box Shed 4 Insulation pins Block 5 Floating bearing Allow 6 Separated pedestal Block 7 High temp angle Block 8 Motor heat shield Block 9 Insulated plug Block 10 Fixed bearing Allow

The fixed bearing is scored Allow: by locating one end of the shaft, it sends all of the growth toward the floating bearing.

After all ten parts are answered, Explore mode unlocks (select any part to reread its description) and the Show buttons filter the drawing to only the Block, Shed or Allow parts. Exploring is never scored.

The drawings are generic illustrations, not to scale and not a specific Twin City Fan model. Part names and jobs come from FanPedia pp. 85, 90, 110-113 and 192 and from Chapter 17 (fixed and floating bearings).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The quiz starts with the shaft cooler highlighted and marked "?". Choose its job from the three buttons, or select any other labeled part first to answer that one instead.
  2. Read the verdict and the part's description. The part gets a ✓ or ✗ badge, and its label gets a solid (correct) or dashed (missed) border.
  3. Press Next part to go to the next unanswered part, or select any unanswered part on the drawing. After the tenth answer, press See summary to see your first-attempt score, the mastery line and the parts you missed with their jobs.
  4. After the quiz, use Show: Block / Shed / Allow to filter the drawing. Count the parts in each group: five block, three shed, and only the two bearings allow. Back to explore lets you reread any description. Start over (or Quiz) clears every answer.

Keyboard: Tab moves between parts and buttons (parts in label order 1-10); Enter or Space selects a part; keys 1, 2 and 3 choose Block, Shed or Allow; after an answer, focus moves to Next part, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Illustrative drawing, not to scale · Part names and jobs: FanPedia pp. 85, 90, 110-113, 192", shown at the bottom of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify ten high temperature fan parts by whether each one blocks heat, sheds heat, or allows thermal growth, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Thermal expansion, and fixed and floating bearings (Chapters 17 and 21)
  • Shaft cooler, cooler box and insulation pins
  • Recess cone and insulated plug
  • High temperature pedestal, separated pedestal and heat shield

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (6 min): Answer all ten parts. For each, say why the part is on the drawing before you choose its job.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary. For each missed part, reread its description and name the heat path (shaft or pedestal) it deals with.
  3. Explore (3 min): Filter by Block, Shed and Allow. Notice that five parts block, three shed, and only the two bearings allow growth.
  4. Discuss (3 min): Which parts would a drawing of a fan below 300°F leave out, and why?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A cooler box is an insulated enclosure. It is deliberately left uninsulated so the shaft cooler can shed heat; the sim scores it Shed and its description says so.
  • Insulation pins are themselves insulation. They hold the housing insulation in place; the insulation they hold is what blocks heat.
  • Every high temperature part keeps heat out. The floating and fixed bearings do not block or shed anything; together they let the shaft grow.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt score: n of 10" in the summary (running line "n of 10 correct"); mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt.
  • Opening descriptions after answering, in the summary or Explore mode, is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: on a 700°F oven fan, which of the ten parts deal with the shaft heat path, and which with the pedestal heat path?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; pp. 85 and 90 (pedestal features, high temperature style pedestal), pp. 110-113 (high temperature packages, cooler box, insulation pins, separated pedestal, plug fan recess cone and insulated plug) and p. 192 (shaft cooler).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 21: High Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - the sections on thermal expansion, shedding and blocking heat at the shaft, and high temperature pedestals.
  4. Chapter 17: Bearing Details, Lubrication and Pedestals - fixed and floating bearings.

docs.title: High Temperature Package Finder
docs.text:
Run the High Temperature Package Finder MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
FanPedia groups high temperature construction into packages by airstream temperature band, and the bands depend on the fan family. This MicroSim gives you eight illustrative job tickets in a fixed order. Each ticket names a fan, an application and an airstream temperature. You choose a band from the band list for that ticket's family and mark whether engineering review is required, then press Check. A ticket is correct only when both the band and the review answer match.

# Ticket Band Review 1 Arr. 1 centrifugal, kiln exhaust, 450°F 301-500°F No 2 Arr. 4 centrifugal, dryer, 250°F 181-300°F No 3 Arr. 4 centrifugal, oven, 400°F 301°F and over Yes 4 Arr. 9 plug fan, oven, 650°F 601-800°F No 5 Air kit Arr. 3, furnace, 1,100°F 1,001°F and over Yes 6 Axial Arr. 4, warm exhaust, 180°F 151-195°F Yes 7 Axial Arr. 9, drying air supply, 240°F 201-250°F No 8 Arr. 10 centrifugal, process fume exhaust, 520°F 501-600°F No

The Arrangement 4 bands (tickets 2, 3 and 6) are FanPedia's. Twin City Fan engineering (2026-10-09) advises that current practice does not use Arrangement 4 for high-temperature applications, so these tickets practice reading FanPedia's tables, not a current ordering path.

A temperature belongs to a band when lower bound ≤ temperature ≤ upper bound; "and over" bands have no upper bound. On ticket 7, 240°F lies in both Arr. 9 axial bands; the answer is the general 201-250°F band, because 201-300°F is for select models only.

You get two attempts per ticket. A first miss reads "Check the band list for again." with a hint (for example "450°F is below the bottom of the band you chose") and does not mark the halves; a second miss says whether each half (band and review) is correct, shows the answer and the reason, and the ticket counts as missed. A correct check reads "✓ Correct: , review . ." The running line shows "Tickets correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

After each final check, the right panel opens a band chart for the family: every band on a °F scale, dashed bars for bands that need engineering review, the job's temperature as a dashed line and the answer band outlined. After ticket 8, Explore mode (never scored) lets you pick any family and any temperature from 100°F to 1,200°F in 10°F steps and see its band and review flag.

Bands and review requirements come from FanPedia pp. 110, 111, 113, 114, 115 and 116 (2021 edition), as summarized in Chapter 21. The job tickets are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the ticket: fan, application and airstream temperature.
  2. Open the Band menu (the band list for this ticket's family) and choose one band.
  3. Mark Engineering review required: Yes or No.
  4. Press Check and read the verdict. On a first miss, try again; after the final check, read the band chart and press Next ticket.
  5. After ticket 8, press Explore. Pick a family and move the temperature slider. Notice that the listed axial bands stop at 300°F, and that Arrangement 4 centrifugal fans switch to engineering review above 300°F.
  6. Start over clears the score and returns to ticket 1.

Keyboard: Tab moves between the band menu, the Yes/No buttons and the buttons; arrow keys choose inside the menu and the Yes/No group; Y or N marks review (when the band menu does not have focus); Enter checks, then goes to the next ticket.

Data label: "Illustrative jobs · Bands: FanPedia pp. 110-116", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will determine the FanPedia high temperature package band, and whether engineering review is required, for a stated fan family and airstream temperature, with at least 7 of 8 jobs correct (Bloom: Apply, verb: determine).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• High temperature package and axial high temperature package (Chapter 21)
  • Fan arrangements (Chapter 11)
  • Plug fans and air kits (Chapters 4 and 11)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Tickets (8 min): Work the eight tickets. Before choosing a band, say the family out loud, then the temperature.
  2. Review (3 min): For any missed ticket, read the band chart and the reason. Which misconception caught you?
  3. Explore (4 min): Compare Centrifugal Arr. 1 and Arr. 4 at 290°F, 310°F and 650°F, then try both axial families at 280°F and 350°F.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• All fans share one set of temperature bands. Each ticket opens its own family's band list, and the band chart shows how different the families are.
  • An Arrangement 4 centrifugal at 400°F has a standard package. Ticket 3 scores review Yes; Arrangement 4 above 300°F always goes to engineering review.
  • Axial packages reach the same temperatures as centrifugal packages. Tickets 6 and 7 and Explore mode show the listed axial bands stopping at 300°F.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in Explore mode as "First-attempt score: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. The running line "Tickets correct: n of 8" also counts second-attempt successes.
  • Follow-up question: a customer asks for an Arrangement 4 plug fan at 290°F. Which band applies, and what should you confirm with the factory?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; high temperature package pages for centrifugal fans (pp. 110-111), plug fans (pp. 113-114), air kits (p. 115) and axial fans (p. 116).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 21: High Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - the "High Temperature Packages" section and its package band table.
  4. Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements - fan arrangements, plug fans and air kits.

docs.title: Leak-Tight Versus RTO Requirement Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Leak-Tight Versus RTO Requirement Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
FanPedia's nominally leak-tight page (p. 120) and its RTO page (p. 121) share most of their lines, which is why the two options blur together. This MicroSim deals twelve requirement cards, one at a time, in a shuffled order that is the same for every learner (seed 21). For each card you choose a bin, Leak-Tight Only, Both or RTO Only, and lock the placement. A locked card cannot be moved.

# Requirement Bin 1 Solid drive side on housing (no drive plates) Both 2 Not recommended for applications over 600°F Both 3 Bolted connections on 3 in. to 4 in. centers Both 4 Centering plates if the housing is split Both 5 Soap bubble test at the shop, recorded on the inspection form Both 6 Arrangements 1, 8 and 9 only Leak-Tight Only 7 Shaft seal: lip, Graphoil stuffing box, or double carbon ring Leak-Tight Only 8 Drain: pipe coupling type with plug Leak-Tight Only 9 Silicone sponge gasket and silicone caulk, with an alternative on automotive jobs RTO Only 10 Dampers, if required, must have stuffing boxes RTO Only 11 Sales must specify VFD, cycling and bake-out conditions RTO Only 12 Shaft seal: friction, single carbon ring, or commercial carbon ring RTO Only

A correct placement reads "✓ Correct: "; an incorrect one reads "✗ This one belongs in . ". Each locked card appears as a chip in the bin you chose, with ✓ and a solid border or ✗ and a dashed border. The running line shows "Cards correct: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first (and only) attempt.

After the twelfth card, a summary lists your score, the mastery line and any missed cards with their right bins. Compare the two lists then shows the leak-tight and RTO lists side by side, with the five shared requirements linked across the middle.

Requirements and wording come from FanPedia p. 120 (nominally leak-tight) and p. 121 (RTO), 2021 edition, as summarized in Chapter 21.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the requirement card and decide which construction calls for it.
  2. Choose a bin: press 1 Leak-Tight Only, 2 Both or 3 RTO Only (the selected bin is outlined). You can change your choice until you lock.
  3. Press Lock placement. Read the verdict and the reason, then press Next card.
  4. After the twelfth card, press Finish, read the summary, and press Compare the two lists. Count the linked rows: 5 of the 12 requirements are shared. Show the bins returns to your placements.
  5. Start over deals all twelve cards again (in a new order, the same for every learner) and clears the score.

Keyboard: keys 1, 2 and 3 choose a bin; Enter locks the placement, then goes to the next card; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia p. 120 (leak-tight) and p. 121 (RTO)", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate FanPedia's nominally leak-tight and RTO construction requirements by sorting 12 requirements into Leak-Tight Only, RTO Only, or Both, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Analyze, verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan leakage, nominally leak-tight fan, gasketing (Chapter 21)
  • Continuous seal weld, centering plate, soap bubble test (Chapter 21)
  • Regenerative thermal oxidizer and RTO service conditions (Chapter 21)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (6 min): Place all twelve cards. Before locking, say which page the requirement is on.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary. For each missed card, name the question a salesperson should have asked.
  3. Compare (4 min): Open the side-by-side lists. Write down the shared core once, then the three leak-tight-only and four RTO-only lines.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• RTO construction is just leak-tight construction under another name. The comparison view shows seven requirements that belong to only one list.
  • Leak-tight fans may be any arrangement. The Arrangements 1, 8 and 9 card belongs in Leak-Tight Only.
  • Silicone gasketing is acceptable on every RTO job. The silicone card includes the automotive alternative and belongs in RTO Only.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.
  • Follow-up question: an RTO builder serving an automotive paint shop asks for "leak-tight construction". Which lines from each list go on the order?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 120 (nominally leak-tight fans) and p. 121 (regenerative thermal oxidizer construction).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 21: High Temperature, Leak-Tight and RTO Construction - the "Nominally Leak-Tight Fans" and "Regenerative Thermal Oxidizer (RTO) Service" sections.
  4. Regenerative thermal oxidizer (Wikipedia) - background on how an RTO destroys pollutants and reverses flow through its ceramic media.

docs.title: Fan Base and Isolation Selector
docs.text:
Run the Fan Base and Isolation Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, first add the kit files fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/ (or their published URLs under https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/shared-libs/) to the editor's index.html, then paste ch22-fan-base-isolation-selector.js as the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Bases, isolators and mounting methods come down to one decision taken in order: does this fan need isolation, and what does the arrangement allow underneath it? The selector gives seven illustrative installations. For each one you choose one of five recommendations and then one of three justifications. A scenario is correct only when both match, so a lucky guess with the wrong reason does not count.

The five recommendations are Unitary base, Isolation base, Inertia base, Isolators directly under the fan and No added base or isolation.

Scenario Correct recommendation Rule (FanPedia) Arrangement 7SI fan, slab on grade in a plant, no isolation requested Unitary base 7SI ships on a unitary base as standard; unitary bases are designed for use without isolators (pp. 131, 165) Arrangement 1 belt-driven SWSI fan with motor, on a mezzanine above offices; isolation required Isolation base Common support for fan, motor and drive, usually on spring or RIS isolators (p. 131); neoprene pads are possible but uncommon (Twin City Fan engineering) Spec reads "Arrangement 9F with springs under the fan" Isolation base 9F is not suitable for isolators directly under the fan; use Arrangement 1 with a separate isolation base (p. 166) Long direct-drive Arrangement 8 fan on springs; alignment must hold Inertia base Used on longer direct-drive fans to mitigate assembly deflection (p. 132) Commercial roof ventilator on a roof curb No added base or isolation Internally isolated; no other isolation is required (p. 133) Arrangement 4 fan with a 30 in impeller; isolation wanted with no separate base Isolators directly under the fan Usually limited to impellers 36.5 in or less (p. 133) Fan and detached inlet box on one base on a plant floor; no isolation Unitary base Fan and inlet box can share one base on the same plane (p. 143); without isolators it is a unitary base

Each scenario's two distractor justifications are drawn from the other six rows. The scenario order and the distractors are fixed by seed 22, so every learner sees the same sequence, and Start over repeats it. Each scenario allows two attempts. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario. The prompt asks: "What should this fan sit on?"
  2. Choose a recommendation with the buttons 1 to 5 (or keys 1-5), then a justification with Reason A, B or C (or keys A-C). The justifications are written out in the drawing as cards A, B and C.
  3. Press Submit (or Enter). Feedback:
  4. both right: "Correct: ."
  5. wrong recommendation on the 9F or 30 in impeller scenarios: "Check the arrangement and impeller size against the mounting rules first."
  6. wrong recommendation otherwise: "Ask whether isolation is needed, then what the arrangement allows."
  7. right recommendation, wrong justification: "Right choice, wrong reason. Which FanPedia rule decides this case?" After a wrong first attempt you choose again. After a second wrong attempt the answer and its justification are shown and the scenario counts as missed.
  8. Press Next scenario. After scenario 7, See summary lists every scenario with your first answer and the correct one, the first-attempt score and the mastery line. On narrow screens the summary has two pages; press Scenarios 5-7 and Scenarios 1-4 to switch.
  9. Press Start over to reset all seven scenarios and the score.

    10. Keyboard: keys 1-5 choose the recommendation and A-C the justification; once both are chosen, Submit takes focus and Enter submits; Enter again goes to the next scenario. Tab reaches every button.

    Data label: "Illustrative scenarios · Rules: FanPedia pp. 131-133, 143, 165, 166", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will recommend a base or mounting for a described fan installation and justify it with the FanPedia rule that governs the case, with at least 6 of 7 scenarios correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: recommend).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Unitary, isolation and inertia bases
  • Isolator mounting methods and internally isolated fans
  • Flexible connectors (Chapter 19)
  • Arrangements 1, 7SI, 8 and 9F (Chapter 11)

Defined in Chapter 22.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recommend (8 min): Work all seven scenarios without notes, committing the recommendation and the reason together.
  2. Review (3 min): In the summary, read the rule for every scenario that was not correct on the first attempt.
  3. Discuss (3 min): Why is the 9F specification answered with an isolation base and not with springs? Why does the roof ventilator need nothing added?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every fan needs isolators: the 7SI slab, roof ventilator and inlet box scenarios need none.
  • Isolators can go under any arrangement: the 9F scenario cannot take them under the fan.
  • A unitary base can be set on springs: unitary bases are designed for use without isolators.
  • An internally isolated roof ventilator needs external isolators: it needs no other isolation.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Score line "n of 7 first-attempt correct"; the summary shows "First-attempt score: n of 7" with "Mastery reached (6 of 7 needed)." or "Mastery needs 6 of 7 on the first attempt."
  • Follow-up: an Arrangement 3F SWSI fan must be isolated. What do you recommend, and why?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan. Base types and mounting methods pp. 131-133, inlet box mounting planes p. 143, Arrangement 7SI p. 165, Arrangement 9F p. 166.
  2. FanPedia (PDF edition) - Twin City Fan, the printable edition with the same page numbers.
  3. Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation - the chapter section this sim belongs to.

docs.title: Fan Base Types
docs.text: Run the Fan Base Types MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts six numbered markers on FanPedia's drawings of the three base types for centrifugal fans (pages 131 and 132). The top row shows two fans; under them, the middle row shows the unitary base and the isolation base on their own, each carrying only a motor. The bottom row shows the bare inertia base above its optional bottom pan, and a fan on an inertia base. The fans themselves carry no marker.

The six parts are the unitary base, the isolation base, the spring isolators under it, the inertia base, its reinforcing rods (rebar) and the bottom pan. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list.

The quiz describes each part by its job ("Select the base the customer fills with concrete.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the part's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 6 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the part name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 6".
  4. After the sixth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (5 of 6), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, pp. 131-132", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the unitary, isolation and inertia bases, the spring isolators, the reinforcing rods (rebar) and the bottom pan on FanPedia's base drawings, given each part's function (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 22, sections "Fan Bases", "Unitary Base", "Isolation Base" and "Inertia Base".
  • Chapter 22, "Vibration Isolation", for what an isolator does.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all six parts. Say which of the three bases is designed for use without isolators, and what the inertia base adds to an isolation base.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all six parts from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order. Then try Fan Base and Isolation Selector to pick a base for a job.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any fan base can go on isolators: the unitary (channel) base is designed for use without isolators; the isolation and inertia bases are the ones built to sit on them.
  • An inertia base ships full of concrete: it ships as steel and rebar, and the customer fills it with concrete; the optional bottom pan makes that pour easier in the field.
  • An inertia base is a different kind of frame from an isolation base: FanPedia defines it as an isolation base with reinforcing rods, filled with concrete.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 6"; mastery is 5 of 6 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at markers and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a long direct-drive fan on springs must keep its motor, coupling and bearings aligned. Which base on this drawing fits, and what does the customer have to supply for it?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; pp. 131-132 hold the base type drawings used here, and pp. 175-176 give the technical descriptions of the three bases.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation - the section "Inertia Base", where this MicroSim is embedded, and the sections "Unitary Base" and "Isolation Base".
  4. Fan Base and Isolation Selector - recommends a base and isolation for text scenarios.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, pp. 131-132. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Isolator Mounting Methods
docs.text: Run the Isolator Mounting Methods MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks five numbered zones on FanPedia's vibration isolation mounting drawings (page 133), one for each of the five isolator mounting methods. The top row shows isolators directly under the fan, isolation rails (in two versions, one on rubber-in-shear pads and one on springs, sharing one zone) and a mounting angle. The bottom row shows an isolation base carrying the fan and motor, and a fan hung from isolation hangers. The isolators and the hanger rods are drawn in green; the rails, the angle and the base in purple. The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one mounting at a time ("Which drawing suspends the fan from structure overhead?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 5 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one mounting:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 5".
  4. After the fifth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (4 of 5), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 133", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the five isolator mounting methods (directly under the fan, isolation rails, mounting angle, isolation base and isolation hangers) on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 22, sections "Vibration Isolation", "Neoprene Isolation Pads", "Rubber-in-Shear Isolators" and "Isolator Mounting Methods".
  • Chapter 22, "Isolation Base", for the base itself.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all five drawings. For each, say what sits between the fan's foundation holes and the isolators: nothing, a pair of flat bars, an angle or a structural base; and for the hung fan, where the isolators are.
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all five descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Isolators can always go directly under any fan: FanPedia says this is usually limited to impellers 36.5 in in diameter or less, with swingout housed centrifugal fans of any size as the exception, on flat pads only.
  • Isolation rails and an isolation base are the same thing: rails are two flat bars, the top one bolted to the fan's foundation holes and the bottom one to the floor; a base is a structural frame that can carry the motor and other components too.
  • A mounting angle is only for looks: it is usually used when the fan inlet has no structural support of its own.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 5"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: a housed centrifugal fan (not a swingout) with an impeller larger than 36.5 in must be isolated on a floor. Which method is usually ruled out, and which drawings show the floor-mounted alternatives?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 133 holds the vibration isolation mounting drawings used here and the description of each method.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation - the section "Isolator Mounting Methods", where this MicroSim is embedded.
  4. Chapter 23: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement - the section "Where the Isolators Go", which works through each method's hardware.
  5. Isolation Hardware Sorter - sorts job descriptions into isolation hardware, including four of these mounting styles.

Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 133. Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved. See Copyright and License.

docs.title: Isolator Transmissibility Explorer
docs.text: Run the Isolator Transmissibility Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
How much of a fan's unbalance force gets through its isolators depends on how far apart the fan's speed and the isolators' bounce are. This MicroSim uses the undamped single-degree-of-freedom model from Chapter 22:

  • forcing frequency f = N / 60 (Hz), from the fan speed N in RPM;
  • natural frequency fn = 3.13 / √δ (Hz), from the static deflection δ in inches (the rounded form of (1/2π)√(386.1/δ));
  • frequency ratio r = f / fn;
  • transmissibility T = 1 / |r² − 1|, and percent isolation (1 − T) × 100.

The chart plots T on a log scale against r from 0 to 10. The band below r = 1.414 (√2) is shaded and labeled Amplification, the rest Isolation, and the dotted line at r = 1 marks Resonance. The readouts give f, fn, r, T and the percent isolation; when T is greater than 1 they show "amplified ×T" instead of a negative percentage, and within 0.05 of r = 1 they show "at or near resonance" (the plotted T is capped at 10). Values are shown to 3 significant figures; answers are judged against the unrounded model.

Three challenges come first, in a fixed order. You type T before the curve is shown; an answer within ±5% of the model counts as correct. Each challenge allows two attempts.

# Fan speed Deflection Model T What it shows 1 1170 RPM 1.0 in (spring) 0.0264 about 97.4% isolation 2 1170 RPM 0.0625 in (neoprene pad) 0.701 only about 30% isolation 3 600 RPM 0.0625 in (neoprene pad) 2.76 r = 0.80, the pad amplifies the force

Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt. After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks the fan speed (300 to 3,600 RPM in 30 RPM steps) and the six deflections from FanPedia p. 134: 0.0625 in (neoprene pad), 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 in (rubber-in-shear), 1.0 and 2.0 in (spring). The fan speeds are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1. The fan speed and deflection are set for you; the readouts show "?".
  2. Type T as a decimal in Transmissibility T and press Check (or Enter). A correct answer reads, for example, "Correct: T = 0.0264, 97.4% isolation." A wrong first answer shows the challenge's worked numbers and "Try again (1 attempt left)."; after a second wrong answer the answer and worked calculation are shown and the challenge counts as missed.
  3. Once a challenge ends, the curve appears with the model's operating point (square) and your answer (open diamond) side by side, and the readouts fill in. Press Next challenge.
  4. After challenge 3, press Finish for the summary ("First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line). Explore mode then unlocks: move the Fan speed slider and change the Deflection; the point, readouts and region label update at once. Try 420 RPM with 0.2 in (resonance), and any pad setting below about 1,060 RPM (amplification). Explore mode is never scored.
  5. Press Start over at any time to begin again from challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks your answer, then goes to the next challenge. In Explore mode the arrow keys move the speed slider in 30 RPM steps and change the deflection; Tab reaches every control.

Data label: "Illustrative fan speeds · Deflections: FanPedia p. 134 · Undamped model: f = N/60, fn = 3.13/√δ, T = 1/|r² − 1|", shown under the chart.

docs.text: The learner will calculate the transmissibility of an undamped isolator from the fan speed and the isolator's static deflection, to within 5% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Prerequisites

All are defined in the "Vibration", "Vibration Isolation" and "Isolator Deflection" sections of Chapter 22.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min): Work the three challenges with a calculator, committing T before the curve appears.
  2. Explore (5 min): Repeat the chapter's 600 RPM table (pad, rubber-in-shear 0.3 in, springs 1 in and 2 in). Find the speed where the pad leaves the amplification region (about 1,060 RPM) and the resonance at 420 RPM with 0.2 in.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any isolator reduces transmitted force: challenge 3 gives T = 2.76, more force than a rigid mount, because r < 1.414.
  • An isolator that works on one fan works on any fan: challenges 2 and 3 use the same pad at two speeds, with opposite results.
  • Doubling the deflection halves the natural frequency: in Explore mode, 1 in gives 3.13 Hz and 2 in gives 2.21 Hz, a factor of √2.

Run the Isolation Hardware Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js and fanpedia-p5.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An isolation line on a specification names hardware by its features: what encloses the spring, which way the load hangs, and where the brackets attach. This MicroSim deals eleven job-site descriptions, one at a time and in a shuffled order, and asks you to place each one in the bin for the hardware FanPedia calls for. There are ten bins:

  • Spring types: open, housed, restrained and seismic spring isolators.
  • Motion limiters: snubber and thrust restraint.
  • Mounting styles: isolation hangers (ceiling hung), isolators directly under the fan, isolation rails and isolator mounting angle.

Each description has exactly one correct bin, and one bin (isolators directly under the fan) receives two descriptions: a 30-inch impeller (an illustrative size within FanPedia's 36.5-inch limit) and the swingout housed centrifugal exception on flat pads.

Each card allows two attempts. A correct placement reads "✓ Correct. ". A wrong first placement reads "✗ Not quite. Look for ." and the card comes back for a second try; the bin you chose is marked "not this one". A second wrong placement shows the right bin and the reason, and the card moves to its correct bin as a ✗ chip with a dashed border. Placed cards appear in their bins with their deal number. The running line reads "First-attempt correct: n of 11; mastery at 9." Mastery is 9 of 11 on the first attempt; a card right on the second try is placed but does not count.

After the eleventh card, a summary shows the first-attempt score, the mastery line and every description you missed on the first attempt with its correct bin and reason. When the list is long, More missed turns its pages.

The definitions, the 36.5-inch limit, the swingout exception and the thrust restraint details come from FanPedia pp. 133–135 and 196–197, as summarized in Chapter 23.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the job description on the card and decide which hardware it calls for.
  2. Press the bin's button (or its key: 1 to 9, and 0 for the tenth bin). The verdict appears at once.
  3. If the verdict says "Not quite", look for the named feature and place the card again.
  4. Press Next card (or Enter). After the eleventh card, press Finish and read the summary.
  5. Start over deals all eleven cards again in a new order and clears the score.

Keyboard: keys 1-9 and 0 place the card in a bin; Enter goes to the next card; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 133-135, 196-197 · Item 5 impeller size is illustrative", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A snubber and a seismic spring are the same device. The snubber card (two brackets with elastomer, used along with the isolators) and the seismic spring card (a housing that nearly surrounds the spring) go to different bins.
  • Any spring restrains a fan against airflow forces. The open spring card says the spring does nothing to resist aerodynamic forces, and the thrust restraint card shows what a fan that slides back at start-up needs.
  • Every fan can sit on isolators bolted directly under it. The direct mounting card names the 36.5-inch limit, and the swingout card shows the one exception, on flat pads only.
