docs.title: Piezometer Ring Components
docs.text: Run the Piezometer Ring Components MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts ten numbered markers on FanPedia's drawing of the piezometer ring components on a fan inlet funnel (page 158). A piezometer ring is part of an airflow measuring system based on the principle of a flow nozzle, and the fan's own inlet funnel is the nozzle. The main drawing shows the funnel with the ring tubing around its throat, the tubing that runs from the ring to the low pressure tap, and the loose tubing and tap fittings beside the funnel. Three close-ups below it show the union tee, the two tap fittings and a coupling with its rivnut.

The ten components are the inlet funnel, tubing around the throat, couplings with "T" fittings, union tee, tubing to low pressure tap, tubing to high pressure tap, low pressure tap fitting, high pressure tap fitting, hanger clip and rivnut. On a wide screen a label column with leader lines sits to the right of the drawing; on a narrow screen the labels move below it as a numbered list. Where a component is small (the hanger clip, the two tap fittings, the coupling and the rivnut), its marker sits beside it with a short pointer to the component.

The quiz describes each component by its job ("Select the part the system uses as its flow nozzle.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the component and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered marker, or Tab to it, to see the component's name and description in the panel below the drawing. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened components get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 10 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that component too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one component:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the component name and its description; the marker turns green with a ✓ badge and its label comes back.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the component you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 10".
  4. After the tenth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 10), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the markers in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a marker. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 158", shown under the drawing.

docs.text: The learner will identify the ten labeled components of a piezometer ring airflow measuring system on a fan inlet funnel, given each component's function or location (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 22, section "Installation Accessories: Weather Cover, Zero Speed Switch, Piezometer Ring" (what a piezometer ring is and which fans offer it).
  • Chapter 23, section "Measuring Airflow in the Field" (the inlet funnel as a flow nozzle and the high- and low-pressure sides).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all ten components. Trace the two pressure paths aloud: the throat pressure from the tubing around the throat, through the union tee and the tubing to the low pressure tap, to the low pressure tap fitting; and the face pressure, which leaves through the high pressure tap fitting and the tubing to the high pressure tap.
  2. Sort (2 min): Group the components into tubing (three runs), fittings (couplings, union tee, the two tap fittings) and mounting hardware (hanger clip, rivnut).
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all ten components from their jobs without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those components in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A piezometer ring is a separate flow meter added to the duct: the fan's own inlet funnel is the flow nozzle, and the ring is tubing around its throat.
  • Both pressures are taken in the throat: the high pressure tap is on the face of the funnel on the inlet side; only the ring senses the throat.
  • The ring connects to the high-pressure side because it is the measuring ring: the air speeds up in the throat, so the ring's pressure is the lower one and it goes to the low-pressure side.

docs.text:

  • Follow-up question: a fan's inlet runs above 180°F. Which component on this drawing changes material, and to what?

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts nine numbered markers on two FanPedia drawings from page 135. On the left, a steel isolation base sits on isolators and carries snubbers, with a close-up inset of one snubber at the lower left. On the right, a fan discharge is joined to its discharge duct by a flex connector, and two thrust restraints, one above and one below the joint, tie the two sides together.

The nine parts are the two snubber brackets (one attached to the fan or base, one attached to the floor), the elastomeric (rubberized) material between them, the isolators, the discharge duct, the flex connector, the fan discharge, the ceiling hung type isolator and the threaded rod. On a wide screen the labels sit in strips above and below the drawing with leader lines; on a narrow screen they move below it as a numbered list. The elastomeric strip is small, so its marker sits just right of the inset with a short pointer to the part; the fan discharge marker sits in the white space above the grey fan section.

The quiz describes each part by its job or its place ("Select the material that prevents metal-to-metal contact.") instead of naming it, in a shuffled order. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the part and counts as missed. Mastery is 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened parts get a ✓ in the label list and the counter shows how many of the 9 you have visited. Clicking a name in the label list opens that part too.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The labels and leader lines disappear and a prompt describes one part:

    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the part you picked, and a hint. The hint never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Parts correct: n of 9".
  4. After the ninth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (8 of 9), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises only the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the labels.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the nine labeled parts of a snubber on an isolation base and of a thrust restraint across a fan-to-duct joint, given each part's function or location (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 23, sections "Spring Isolators", "Open, Housed, Restrained and Seismic Springs", "Where the Isolators Go" and "Snubbers and Thrust Restraints".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all nine parts. Sort them aloud into the snubber (the two brackets and the elastomeric material), what the snubber works with (the isolators) and the thrust restraint across the joint (ceiling hung type isolator, threaded rod, and the fan discharge and discharge duct it is attached to). Where does the flex connector fit, and why does it need the restraint?
  2. Compare (2 min): Name the force each device answers: the snubber limits movement in any direction, such as seismic loading; the thrust restraint limits horizontal motion caused by aerodynamic force.
  3. Quiz (5 min): Switch to quiz mode and find all nine parts from their jobs or places without going back to explore mode.
  4. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those parts in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order. Then sort the job cards in Isolation Hardware Sorter.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A snubber holds the fan rigidly in place: in normal running the fan floats on its isolators, and the snubber engages only when an unusual load, such as an earthquake, tries to move the fan too far.
  • The snubber's two brackets touch when it engages: elastomeric (rubberized) material between them prevents metal-to-metal contact.
  • The flex connector keeps a spring-mounted fan in place: open springs offer no restriction of aerodynamic motion, so the fan moves at every start and the connector takes the strain; the thrust restraint's threaded rod is adjusted to prevent that horizontal motion.

docs.text:

docs.title: Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Spring Isolator Deflection Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A spring isolator compresses under the share of the fan's weight it carries. This MicroSim asks you to calculate that static deflection before it shows the answer, then lets you change every input and watch the whole isolation calculation respond.

The model follows the chapter's rules:

  • Load per isolator = W / n, and static deflection δ = (W / n) / k.
  • Natural frequency fₙ = 3.13 / √δ (Hz), running frequency f = rpm / 60, and frequency ratio r = f / fₙ.
  • Above r = 1.41 the springs isolate: transmissibility T = 1 / (r² − 1) and isolation efficiency = (1 − T) × 100%.
  • At or below 1.41 the status reads "Amplifying: springs too stiff for this speed", T = 1 / |1 − r²| and efficiency is "none". Within ±0.02 of r = 1.00 the status reads "Resonance" and T is "very large".
  • Above 2.00 in of deflection a note says that higher deflection requires engineering review (FanPedia p. 134).

The three challenges come in this order:

# W (lb) n k (lb/in) Model deflection (in) 1 2,400 4 600 1.00 2 3,600 6 300 2.00 3 1,600 4 1,600 0.25

An answer within ±0.02 in of the model is correct. Each challenge allows two attempts: a wrong first answer shows the calculation hint, and a second wrong answer shows the model value and counts as missed. While you answer, every result that depends on the deflection shows "?" and the loaded spring is hidden. After you check, the loaded spring appears to scale beside a free spring (an illustrative 4-inch free height), together with its natural frequency and the isolation results at the default 1,180 rpm. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.

After challenge 3, Explore mode unlocks the four sliders with the default values (2,400 lb, 4 isolators, 600 lb/in, 1,180 rpm). Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the challenge: the total weight W, the number of isolators n and the spring rate k of each isolator.
  2. Type the deflection in inches and press Check (or Enter). If you get a hint, use your second attempt.
  3. Read the loaded spring and the results panel, then press Next challenge (or Enter).
  4. After challenge 3, press Start exploring. Move the sliders and notice that raising n lowers the deflection, that raising the fan speed raises the frequency ratio, and that a 0.25-in spring (W = 1,600 lb, n = 4, k = 1,600 lb/in) on a 300-rpm fan reaches the Amplifying status.
  5. Start over returns to challenge 1 and clears the score.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer or goes to the next challenge; Tab reaches every control; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · Typical deflections: FanPedia p. 134", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the static deflection of equally loaded spring isolators from total weight, isolator count and spring rate, to within 0.02 in (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Spring isolator, static deflection and spring rate (Chapter 23)
  • Natural frequency, running frequency and frequency ratio (Chapters 22 and 23)
  • Transmissibility and isolation efficiency (Chapter 22)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5 min): Work the three deflection challenges. Write the load per isolator before typing each answer.
  2. Review (3 min): Compare the loaded springs of challenges 2 and 3. Which spring isolates better at 1,180 rpm, and why?
  3. Explore (5 min): Set the challenge 3 spring and slow the fan to 300 rpm. Then find the slowest fan speed at which that spring isolates.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency. Change k to double δ and read fₙ: it falls by a factor of 1.41, not 2.
  • Any spring isolates, whatever the fan speed. A 0.25-in spring on a 300-rpm fan shows the Amplifying status and a transmissibility above 1.
  • Adding isolators adds deflection. Raising n spreads the same weight over more springs, so each one deflects less.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "First-attempt score: n of 3"; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Challenges correct: n of 3".
  • Follow-up question: a 600-rpm fan sits on 1-inch springs. Is it isolated, and what would 2-inch springs change?

docs.title: References

1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; p. 134 lists the typical spring deflections (under 1 in, 1 in or 2 in; higher by engineering review).
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 23: Spring Isolators, Restraints and Field Measurement - the "Spring Isolators" section, with the equations and the worked example.
  4. Chapter 22: Fan Bases and Vibration Isolation - deflection, natural frequency and transmissibility.
  5. Vibration isolation (Wikipedia) - background on passive isolation and transmissibility.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Arrangement variants differ by one feature: where the motor sits, what holds the fan up, or what opens when the door swings. This MicroSim shows twelve written fan descriptions, one at a time, in an order that is shuffled once per session. For each one you choose a code from the same answer list of 22 and press Check:

8, 9F, 9H, 10, 3F, 4, 4VI, 7DI, 3HS, 3HA, 3SM, 3VS, 4V, 1P, 4P, 8P, 9P, 9ST, 9SS, 4SO, 9SO, 9CS.

# Description (shortened) Code 1 Overhung impeller on a long pedestal, motor coupled at the end 8 2 Belt drive, motor too large for the pedestal, on an extended frame 9F 3 Belt drive, motor inside the bearing pedestal, ventilating set 10 4 Direct drive, hung from its inlet flange, vertical shaft 4VI 5 Coupled DWDI fan with integral inlet boxes 7DI 6 Horizontal plenum fan, motor on top, adjustable base, below size 182 3HA 7 Horizontal plenum fan, motor on the side of the frame on a slide base 3SM 8 Vertical direct drive plenum fan, inlet under the motor 4V 9 Belt driven plug fan at grade, motor on its own base 1P 10 Direct drive plug fan, floor mounted 4P 11 Swingout housed SWSI, motor on the side of the pedestal on a pivot base 9SS 12 Inline fan whose casing opens while the rotor stays in place 9CS

Each item has one scored attempt. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: Arrangement ." An incorrect one reads "✗ This is Arrangement . ", with an added sentence for the common traps: 4 or 4P for item 1, 9F for item 3, 9P for item 9 and 9SO for item 12. After Check the answer list marks your choice (✓ or ✗) and the right code (→). The running line reads "Correct: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt.

Show hint lists the description's features by category (drive, impeller, support, motor). Hints are never scored. After item 12 the summary lists every missed item with its correct code and the code you chose. Retry missed presents only those items again as a practice round: every message starts "Practice (not scored)" and the score does not change.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the description. If you want, press Show hint (or H).
  2. Choose a code from the answer list, then press Check (or Enter).
  3. Read the verdict and the reason, then press Next item (or Enter).
  4. After item 12, read the summary. Press Retry missed to practise the missed items, or Start over to run all twelve again in the same order.

Keyboard: Tab into the answer list, use the arrow keys to move between codes (the focused code is selected), and press Enter to check; Enter then goes to the next item; H shows or hides the hint; Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 20-28, 163-173", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will differentiate twelve arrangement variants by naming the arrangement code that matches a written description of a fan's drive, motor location, support and access features, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Analyze, verb: differentiate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Overhung and center hung impellers, direct drive and belt drive, bearing pedestal (Chapter 11)
  • Slide base and adjustable motor base, plenum fan, plug fan and pedestal plug (Chapters 11 and 24)
  • Swingout and clamshell construction (Chapter 24)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Decode (6 min): Work the twelve items. Before choosing, say which one feature separates the right code from its nearest neighbour.
  2. Review (3 min): Read the summary. For each miss, name the feature you overlooked.
  3. Retry (3 min): Use Retry missed until every item is right, then explain one pair aloud: 9P against 1P, or 9SS against 9CS.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Any direct drive fan is Arrangement 4. Items 1 (8), 5 (7DI) and 8 (4V) are direct drive with different codes; choosing 4P for item 1 explains the coupling and separate fan shaft.
  • The P suffix changes the drive. Item 10 (4P) keeps the Arrangement 4 drive on a floor-mounted fan, and item 9 separates 1P from 9P by motor location only.
  • Swingout and clamshell are the same construction. Items 11 (9SS) and 12 (9CS) differ in what moves when the door opens.
  • 9F is the right fix whenever a large motor needs isolators. Item 3 shows that a motor inside the pedestal is Arrangement 10, not 9F.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 12"; mastery is 10 of 12 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Correct: n of 12".
  • Follow-up question: a customer wants a belt driven plenum fan with the motor on top, size 165. Which code do you quote, and why not 3HS?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan & Blower; arrangement drawings on pp. 20–28 and technical descriptions on pp. 163–173.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 24: Advanced Arrangements and Configuration Variants - the sections on each arrangement variant.
  4. Chapter 11: Drives and Standard Fan Arrangements - the base arrangements 1 to 10 that the variants modify.

docs.title: Motor Position Rule Checker
docs.text:
Run the Motor Position Rule Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

This p5.js sketch is built on the shared FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the kit files (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-codes.js and fan-drawings.js from ../shared-libs/, or their published URLs) to the editor's index.html before pasting the sketch.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An order desk checks every motor position before a fan is released. This MicroSim shows ten order lines, in a fixed order (pedestal arrangements, then swingout, then plenum and inline). For each line you give a verdict:

  • Standard: the pairing FanPedia lists as standard.
  • Allowed with condition: a FanPedia option tied to a stated condition.
  • Not allowed: a pairing FanPedia excludes ("only", "must", "no options", or a position not shown for that mount). For these you also choose the fix: change motor to (L) or (R), change to the F2 conduit box, change to Top Center (TC), remove the motor position, or choose a position from G, H, A, B or C.
# Order line Verdict Fix 1 Arr. 9, CW, motor (L), F1 Standard 2 Arr. 9F, CCW, motor (R) Standard 3 Arr. 9, CW, motor (L), F2, wall close to conduit side Allowed with condition 4 Arr. 9SS right swing, CW, motor (R) Not allowed change motor to (L) 5 Arr. 9SS left swing, CCW, motor (R), F1 Not allowed change to F2 conduit box 6 Arr. 9ST left swing, motor (L) Standard 7 Arr. 10, CW, motor (L) Not allowed remove motor position 8 Plenum 3SM, motor (R) Standard 9 Arr. 9 inline, horizontal, floor mount, motor position E Not allowed choose from G, H, A, B or C 10 Plenum 3HA, motor (L) Not allowed change to Top Center (TC)

The verdicts and fixes come from the kit's rule table (FP.codes.checkMotorLine), which restates FanPedia pp. 52, 53, 55 and 56. Each line has one scored attempt, and an item counts only when the verdict and (for Not allowed) the fix are both right. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct. ". A wrong verdict reads "✗ Check the rule for Arr. : "; a right verdict with the wrong fix reads "✗ Right verdict; the fix is ." Either way the answer is then shown. After Check, a schematic sketch shows the fan in its reference view (drive side, or the discharge view for the inline fan) with the motor in the correct position. The running line reads "Correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. After line 10 the summary lists the missed lines with their rules.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the order line and decide whether it would ship as written.
  2. Choose a verdict: 1 Standard, 2 Allowed with condition or 3 Not allowed.
  3. For Not allowed, choose the fix from the Fix list.
  4. Press Check (or Enter). Read the verdict, the rule and the sketch, then press Next line (or Enter).
  5. After line 10, read the summary. Start over clears the score and returns to line 1.

Keyboard: keys 1-3 choose a verdict; choosing Not allowed moves focus to the Fix list, where the arrow keys pick the fix; Enter checks, then goes to the next line; Tab reaches every control.

Data label: "Source: FanPedia pp. 52, 53, 55, 56 · Item 3 clearance is illustrative", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply FanPedia's motor position rules to ten order lines, judging each as standard, allowed with a condition, or not allowed, and stating the correct position or conduit box when the line is wrong, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Apply, verb: apply).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Drive side, CW and CCW rotation (Chapter 12)
  • Motor positions L and R, the standard motor position rule, swing side and the swingout motor position rule (Chapter 24)
  • Conduit boxes F1 and F2, plenum positions S, O and TC, and inline motor positions A to H (Chapters 13 and 24)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Check the lines (6 min): Work all ten. Before each verdict, say which FanPedia rule applies.
  2. Review (3 min): For each missed line, write the rule in one sentence.
  3. Discuss (4 min): On a 9SS, why does a late change of swing side change the discharge?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• L and R are free choices on every pedestal-mounted motor. Lines 1 to 3 show the CW (L) / CCW (R) standard and the F2 condition.
  • A 9SS can take either motor position on either swing. Lines 4 and 5 are not allowed: right swing is CW (L) only, and left swing needs the F2 conduit box.
  • Arrangement 10 has a motor position to choose. Line 7's fix is to remove the motor position.
  • A floor mounted inline fan can take any of A to H. Line 9's sketch shows D, E and F blocked by the floor supports.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. The running line reads "Correct: n of 10".
  • Follow-up question: an order reads "Arr. 9SS, left swing, CW, motor (L)". What has to change, and what is the cheapest fix?

docs.text:

  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan & Blower's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 24: Advanced Arrangements and Configuration Variants - the section "Motor Positions for Arrangement Variants".

docs.title: Swingout and Clamshell Fans
docs.text: Run the Swingout and Clamshell Fans MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim marks five numbered zones on FanPedia's special construction drawings (page 123). The top row shows three swingout fans, where the rotating assembly rides out of the fan on a door: a housed centrifugal fan (Arrangements 4S, 9ST and 9SS), an axial fan and an inline centrifugal fan (both Arrangements 4SO and 9SO). The bottom row shows clamshell fans, where the casing opens and the rotor stays in place: a pair of double door clamshell fans and a pair of single door clamshell fans (Arrangements 4CS and 9CS). The names sit in a numbered list under the drawing.

The quiz describes one drawing at a time ("Which drawings show a casing that opens on two doors?") in a shuffled order, and you select the matching zone. You get two attempts per prompt. The first wrong answer shows a hint about where to look; the second reveals the drawing and counts as missed. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Explore mode (the starting mode). Point at a numbered zone, or Tab to it, to see its name, a one-line summary and the key facts in the panel below. Click it (or press Enter) to open it; opened drawings get a ✓ in the name list and the counter shows how many of the 5 you have visited.
  2. Quiz mode. Press Quiz. The names disappear and a prompt describes one drawing:
    • Correct: "✓ Correct:" with the name and summary; the zone gets a green solid border and a ✓ badge.
    • Wrong on the first attempt: "✗ Not quite.", the name of the drawing you picked, and a hint that never names the answer.
    • Wrong on the second attempt: the answer is marked "Answer" and named, and the prompt counts as missed.
  3. Press Next prompt after each answer. The toolbar shows "Drawings correct: n of 5".
  4. After the fifth prompt, the summary shows your first-attempt score, whether you reached mastery (4 of 5), and each missed prompt with its answer. Retry missed practises the misses (not scored), Start over reshuffles and resets the score, and Back to explore returns to the names.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the zones in number order and then the buttons; Enter or Space selects a zone. After an answer, focus moves to Next prompt, so Enter goes on.

Data label: "Drawing: FanPedia, Twin City Fan, p. 123", shown under the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the housed centrifugal, axial and inline centrifugal swingout fans and the double door and single door clamshell fans on FanPedia's drawings, given a description of each (Bloom: Remember, verb: identify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 24, section "Swingout and Clamshell Construction", with its subsections "Swingout Fan", "Arrangement 4S Swingout", "Arrangement 9ST and 9SS", "Arrangement 4SO and 9SO", "Clamshell Fan", "Double Door Clamshell" and "Arrangement 4CS and 9CS".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Open all five drawings. For each one, say what moves when the door opens: the rotor (swingout) or the casing (clamshell).
  2. Quiz (4 min): Switch to quiz mode and match all five descriptions without going back to explore mode.
  3. Review (3 min): Read the missed list, open those drawings in explore mode, then press Start over for a new order.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Swingout and clamshell are two names for the same thing: in a swingout fan the rotor swings out with the door; in a clamshell fan the casing opens and the rotor stays put.
  • Swingout construction is only for housed centrifugal fans: FanPedia offers it for centrifugal, inline centrifugal and axial fans (4S, 9ST and 9SS for housed centrifugal; 4SO and 9SO for axial and inline).
  • The second door of a double door clamshell is only for cleaning: FanPedia says one of the two doors is wide enough for impeller removal.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown in the summary as "First-attempt score: n of 5"; mastery is 4 of 5 on the first attempt.
  • Pointing at zones and opening infoboxes in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.
  • Follow-up question: an impeller must come out of a vertical inline fan for a blade change without removing the duct. Which bottom-row drawings fit, and why?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (PDF) - Twin City Fan; p. 123 holds the swingout and clamshell drawings used here, pp. 164 and 166 describe Arrangements 4S, 9ST and 9SS, pp. 172-173 Arrangements 4SO, 9SO, 4CS and 9CS, and p. 195 the swingout door.
  2. FanPedia online - Twin City Fan's online version of the encyclopedia.
  3. Chapter 24: Advanced Arrangements and Configuration Variants - the section "Swingout and Clamshell Construction", where this MicroSim is embedded under "Arrangement 4CS and 9CS".
  4. Arrangement Variant Decoder - decodes the arrangement codes (S, ST, SS, SO, CS) that this drawing shows opened.

docs.title: AMCA Installation Type Sorter
docs.text:
Run the AMCA Installation Type Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-drawings.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch25-amca-installation-type-sorter.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A catalog rating applies to one AMCA installation type, set by what was connected to the fan during the AMCA 210 test. This sorter practices the classification from Chapter 25. Two questions decide the type: is the inlet ducted, and is the outlet ducted?

Inlet ducted? Outlet ducted? Type No No A (free inlet, free outlet) No Yes B (free inlet, ducted outlet) Yes No C (ducted inlet, free outlet) Yes Yes D (ducted inlet, ducted outlet)

A cabinet, plenum or room is open space, not a duct. The fan type does not matter: an exhaust fan, a plug fan or a centrifugal fan can be any of the four types.

The sim shows eight illustrative installations in shuffled order:

Description Correct type A plug fan inside an air handler cabinet, drawing from the cabinet and discharging into it A A propeller wall fan drawing from a warehouse and discharging outdoors, with no ductwork A A utility set with an open inlet in an equipment room and a supply duct bolted to its outlet B A pressure blower with an open inlet funnel in a work area, discharging into a process duct B A roof upblast exhaust fan fed by a kitchen exhaust duct from below, discharging to atmosphere C A centrifugal fan drawing through a duct from a process hood and discharging directly outdoors with no outlet duct C An inline fan installed in the middle of a duct run D A centrifugal fan with an inlet duct from a dust collector and an outlet duct to a stack D

For each description you answer the two questions, place the description in one of the four bins and commit it. Only the first committed answer counts toward the score. After an incorrect answer you may move the item once more, as unscored practice. After each commit a schematic draws the correct answer: a grey duct on a ducted side and open dashed arrows on a free side. When all eight are placed, the bins show their correct contents, marked against your first answers. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the description and answer Inlet ducted? and Outlet ducted? (No, free or Yes, ducted).
  2. Choose a bin, Type A to Type D, and press Commit. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: Type letter. Why" in a solid green box. An incorrect one reads "✗ Not quite. Why Correct type: letter." in a dashed red box. The line below compares your two answers with the bin you chose.
  3. After a miss you may pick another bin and press Commit again (not scored) once. Press Next description to go on. "Correct on first try: n of 8" keeps the running score; each committed item appears in its bin as a numbered chip with ✓ or ✗.
  4. After description 8, press See the bins. The summary shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Start over reshuffles the eight descriptions and clears the score.

Keyboard: Tab reaches the two Yes/No groups (arrow keys change the choice), the bins and the buttons. Keys A, B, C and D choose a bin; Enter commits, then goes to the next description.

Data label: "Illustrative installations", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify fan installations into AMCA installation types A, B, C and D from a description of what is connected to the fan's inlet and outlet, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• AMCA installation type, free inlet, ducted inlet, free outlet and ducted outlet (Chapter 25)
  • System effect (Chapter 10)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5 min): Classify the eight descriptions. Say out loud which side is ducted before choosing a bin.
  2. Review (2 min): Read the end view of the bins. For each ✗, find the word in the description that decides the side (cabinet, funnel, duct, atmosphere).
  3. Apply (3 min): Name a fan on a current job, state its installation type, and compare it with the type printed on the catalog rating used to select it.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The installation type depends on the fan type: the two exhaust fans and the three centrifugal fans land in different bins, so the fan name cannot decide the type.
  • A short connection to a plenum or cabinet counts as a ducted side: the plug fan in its cabinet is Type A, and the feedback says the cabinet is open space.
  • Exhaust fans are always Type C: the propeller wall fan is an exhaust fan with no duct, Type A.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Correct on first try: n of 8" counts first committed answers only. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 8" and the mastery line; mastery is 7 of 8.
  • Follow-up question: a fan rated as Type D is installed discharging straight into a plenum. What is the job's installation type, and what has to be added to the design pressure?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. AMCA International - publisher of AMCA 210 (laboratory test methods that define installation types A to D) and AMCA 201, Fans and Systems.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan types, inlets, outlets and system effect.
  3. Chapter 25: Fan Laws, System Effect and Sound - the installation type definitions and the worked example this sorter practices.

docs.title: Fan Law Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Fan Law Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js, fan-curves.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch25-fan-law-calculator.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This calculator applies the three fan laws to Curve A, the illustrative fan curve from Chapter 10. The base fan runs at 1,380 RPM on standard air and operates at 10,000 CFM, 4.0 in. wg and 9.0 BHP, at 70% static efficiency, on the system curve P = 4.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)².

Every point of Curve A is mapped through the fan laws for geometrically similar fans:

  • Airflow: Q2 = Q1 × (N2/N1) × (D2/D1)³
  • Pressure: P2 = P1 × (N2/N1)² × (D2/D1)² × (ρ2/ρ1)
  • Power: BHP2 = BHP1 × (N2/N1)³ × (D2/D1)⁵ × (ρ2/ρ1)

Static efficiency at mapped (corresponding) points is unchanged. The readout panel shows the base and new speed, airflow, static pressure, BHP and static efficiency, with the ratio between them, so you can see at a glance that power moves with the cube of speed and the fifth power of diameter.

The sim starts with four challenges, in this order. Each one asks for a single number:

# Question Model answer 1 The same system needs 11,500 CFM. What speed? 1,587 RPM 2 At 1,587 RPM, what BHP? 13.69 BHP 3 The fan is slowed to 1,104 RPM. What static pressure (in. wg)? 2.56 in. wg 4 The next size up has a diameter ratio of 1.12 and runs at 1,380 RPM. What BHP at the corresponding point? 15.86 BHP

An answer is correct when it is within 2% of the model answer. You get two attempts; a wrong answer shows the worked fan-law calculation, and a second wrong answer shows the model answer and the challenge counts as missed. When a challenge is resolved, the sim sets the matching ratio, shows your answer beside the model answer, and draws the new curve (solid indigo) and the new operating point (orange diamond) beside Curve A (solid grey) and its base operating point (dark dot). The ratio sliders are locked until all four challenges are done; then Explore mode unlocks. Mastery is 4 of 4 on the first attempt. Explore mode is never scored.

Notes on the model:

  • Curve A is illustrative, not a catalog curve. Its 9.0 BHP is rounded, so Q × P ÷ (6,356 × BHP) gives 69.9%; the sim uses the stated 70% as the base efficiency and carries it unchanged to every corresponding point.
  • A change in air density scales the system's resistance as well as the fan's pressure, so the sim draws a second, density-scaled system curve (orange, dashed). The corresponding point stays on it at the same CFM.
  • With a diameter change, the orange point is the fan-law corresponding point. It no longer lies on the original system curve, and the sim says so.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1, type a number in Your answer and press Check (or Enter).
  2. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: model answer." in a solid green box. A wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the worked calculation in a dashed red box; use the second attempt.
  3. Press Next challenge (or Enter) and repeat for challenges 2 to 4. "Challenges correct: n of 4" keeps the running score.
  4. After challenge 4, press Start exploring. The panel shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line. Move the speed ratio alone and watch the orange operating point slide along the system curve while efficiency stays at 70.0%. Then try the diameter and density ratios. Reset ratios to 1.00 returns to Curve A; Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer, and Enter again goes to the next challenge. Tab reaches the answer box, every button and the three sliders; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative values · Curve A, Chapter 10", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.text:

<iframe src="https://moroshek.github.io/FanTASTIC-textbook/sims/ch25-fan-law-calculator/main.html"
        height="642px"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will solve fan-law problems for a new speed, pressure or brake horsepower after a change in speed, impeller diameter or air density, to within 2% of the model value (Bloom: Apply, verb: solve).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff who have read the fan-law section of Chapter 25 and the fan-curve material in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan laws, speed change calculation and size change calculation (Chapter 25)
  • Fan curve, system curve and static efficiency (Chapter 10)
  • Density correction factor (Chapter 10)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (5-8 min): Solve the four challenges with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the ratio and exponent used for each.
  2. Exploration (3-5 min): Change only the speed ratio and record airflow, pressure, BHP and efficiency at 0.80, 1.00 and 1.15. Confirm that BHP at 0.80 is 0.512 of the original.
  3. Misconception check (2 min): Set the density ratio to 0.80 and explain why the CFM does not change. Set the diameter ratio to 1.25 and explain why airflow nearly doubles rather than rising by 25%.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Power rises in proportion to speed (it rises with speed cubed).
  • Doubling the diameter doubles the airflow (airflow goes with diameter cubed).
  • Changing speed changes efficiency on a pure-resistance system (it does not; the point slides along the system curve).
  • Hotter, lighter air changes the CFM a fan moves (it changes pressure and power, not CFM).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 4" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 4" and the mastery line; mastery is 4 of 4 challenges answered within 2% of the model value on the first attempt.
  • Moving the ratio sliders in Explore mode is not evidence of mastery. Ask the learner to explain, from the exponents, why 15% more airflow needs about 52% more power.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Affinity laws - Wikipedia overview of the fan and pump affinity laws for speed and diameter changes.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan performance, fan laws and system effect.
  3. AMCA International - publisher of the fan application manuals and test standards that use the fan laws to adjust rated performance.

docs.title: Fans in Parallel and Series Explorer
docs.text: Run the Fans in Parallel and Series Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Two fans can serve one system side by side (in parallel) or one after the other (in series). This explorer combines Curve A, the illustrative fan curve from Chapter 10 (1,380 RPM, standard air), both ways and sets the result against two system curves from Chapter 25:

  • Steep system: P = 4.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)², the Chapter 10 design system.
  • Flat system: P = 1.0 × (Q ÷ 10,000)².

The combined curves follow two rules:

  • Parallel: airflows add at each pressure. Pressure at total airflow Q equals one fan's pressure at Q ÷ 2.
  • Series: pressures add at each airflow. Pressure at Q equals 2 × one fan's pressure at Q.

Curve A is interpolated linearly between its table points and extended along its 14,000 to 16,000 CFM segment to zero pressure (16,500 CFM). Each operating point is the airflow, searched in 1 CFM steps, where the combined curve and the system curve are closest, using only the part of the curve where each fan's own airflow is at least 4,000 CFM (right of the peak pressure point). The part where each fan is below 4,000 CFM is drawn faded and marked "stall region". Results are rounded to 10 CFM and 0.01 in. wg:

System One fan Two in parallel Two in series Steep 10,000 CFM at 4.00 in. wg 10,980 CFM at 4.83 in. wg 12,300 CFM at 6.05 in. wg Flat 14,040 CFM at 1.97 in. wg 20,000 CFM at 4.00 in. wg 15,080 CFM at 2.27 in. wg

The sim starts with three predictions, in this order, one attempt each, before the combined curves are drawn:

# Prediction Answer 1 Steep system: parallel or series for more airflow? Series (12,300 vs. 10,980 CFM) 2 Flat system: parallel or series for more airflow? Parallel (20,000 vs. 15,080 CFM) 3 Steep system: a second fan in parallel adds about 10%, 50% or 100%? About 10% (10,980 vs. 10,000 CFM)

Mastery is 3 of 3. After the third prediction every combined curve, the operating points and a readout table appear, and Explore mode lets you switch the system and the configuration in any combination. Explore mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question under the plot, which shows one fan on the steep system with its operating point at 10,000 CFM and 4.0 in. wg. Press Parallel or Series.
  2. A correct prediction reads "✓ Correct." with the operating points that prove it, in a solid green box. An incorrect one explains why in a dashed red box. "Predictions correct: n of 3" keeps the score. Press Next prediction; the plot switches to the flat system for prediction 2 and back to the steep system for prediction 3.
  3. After prediction 3, press Reveal the curves. The summary shows the first-attempt score and the mastery line.
  4. Explore: choose Steep or Flat and One fan, Parallel or Series. The chosen combined curve is drawn thicker, its operating point is the filled diamond, and the readout gives its airflow and pressure with the gain over one fan. Notice that the configuration that wins on one system loses on the other. Hover any curve or point for values. Start over clears the predictions.

Keyboard: keys 1, 2 and 3 choose a prediction; Enter goes to the next one. In Explore mode, S and F choose the system and O, P and R choose one fan, parallel or series. Tab reaches every button.

Data label: "Illustrative data · Curve A, Chapter 10 · standard air, 1,380 RPM per fan", below the plot.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare one fan, two fans in parallel and two fans in series on a steep and a flat system curve, correctly predicting which combination delivers more airflow on each system (Bloom: Analyze, verb: compare).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan curve, system curve, operating point, peak pressure point and stall region (Chapter 10)
  • Fans in parallel and fans in series (Chapter 25)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (3 min): Commit the three predictions. Write a one-line reason for each before pressing a button.
  2. Explore (5 min): On the steep system, step through one fan, parallel and series and record each airflow. Repeat on the flat system. Mark which configuration wins on each.
  3. Explain (3 min): Use the plot to explain why a second parallel fan on the steep system raises pressure from 4.0 to 4.8 in. wg instead of doubling the airflow.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Two fans in parallel deliver twice the airflow: prediction 3 and the steep-system readout show about 10% more.
  • Series fans are only useful for pressure and never increase airflow: on the steep system the series pair moves the most air, 12,300 CFM.
  • The better combination is a property of the fans: the same two fans win in series on the steep system and in parallel on the flat one.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• "Predictions correct: n of 3" counts first-attempt predictions; mastery is 3 of 3. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line.
  • Switching configurations and hovering curves after the predictions is exploration, not evidence. Follow-up question: a VAV system holds a fixed duct static pressure. Is its system curve closer to the steep or the flat case here, and which pairing would you test first?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 25: Fans in Parallel and in Series - the combining rules and the operating points this explorer draws.
  2. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan curves, system curves and fan application.
  3. AMCA International - publisher of AMCA 201, Fans and Systems, which covers fan and system curve interaction, including multiple-fan systems.

Run the Catalog Section Finder MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch26-catalog-section-finder.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Ten question cards are the kind a sales or application engineer fields in a day: a maximum speed, a shaft and bearing size, the RPM and BHP at a duty point, bearings and grease for a hot airstream, where a motor mounts, which damper modulates, whether lifting lugs are standard, a line's airflow range, an overall height, and a paragraph for a project specification. The learner assigns each card to one of ten catalog sections, in the order a Twin City Fan catalog uses them:

Key Section What it contains 1 Overview Models, diameters, airflow and pressure range, arrangements, certifications 2 Construction Features How the impeller, housing, shaft and bearings are built 3 High Temperature Modifications Temperature bands, bearing and lubrication requirements, derating 4 Arrangements Picture and paragraph for each arrangement offered 5 Options/Accessories Guards, bases, dampers, inlet vanes, flanges, seals, doors, drives 6 Engineering Data Maximum RPM, impeller weight and WR² by size and class 7 Material Specifications Housing gauges, shaft diameters, bearing types, bare fan weights 8 Performance Data Printed RPM and BHP tables by model and size 9 Dimensions Drawings and dimension tables by arrangement and size 0 Typical Specifications Specification paragraphs ready to copy

Each card has exactly one correct section. The cards come in a shuffled order and each has two attempts. Only the first attempt is scored: a correct first try reads "✓ Correct:" with the reason; a wrong one reads "✗ Not quite." with the reason, marks the section you tried, and lets you try once more without score. After a second miss the correct section is named. The placed card then appears in its correct section as a chip: solid with ✓ for a first-try success, dashed with ✗ for a first-try miss.

The running score reads "First-try correct: n of 10". Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. After the tenth card the summary gives the score, the mastery line and every card missed on the first try with its reason. Start over reshuffles all ten cards and clears the score.

Remember the structural difference the chapter stresses: Catalog 902 prints performance tables, Catalog 300 does not (it points to the Fan Selector software). The Performance Data section exists only in catalogs that print tables.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the question and decide what kind of answer it needs: a yes/no on what can be built, an engineering limit, a construction detail, a duty-point reading, or a drawing.
  2. Point at a section, or Tab to it, to read its description in the strip above the sections. Reading descriptions is exploration and is never scored.
  3. Press the section button (or its number key). Read the feedback; after a first-try miss, try once more.
  4. Press Next card and continue. After the tenth card read the summary, then press Start over for a fresh, reshuffled deck.

Keyboard: keys 1 to 9 and 0 assign the card to that section; Enter goes to the next card, shows the summary after the last card, and starts over from the summary. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Source: TCF Catalog 300 (Apr 2024), Catalog 902 (Nov 2017)", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify ten customer questions by the Twin City Fan catalog section that answers them, getting at least 8 of 10 right on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Product catalog, catalog structure, engineering data, material specifications, performance data and typical specifications, all defined in the sections "The Product Catalog" and "Catalog Structure" of Chapter 26.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort (5 min): Assign all ten cards. Before each one, say aloud which kind of answer it needs: can it be built, how will it perform, or what will it look like on the job.
  2. Review (3 min): Reread the reason for every card you missed. Compare question 1 (maximum RPM) with question 3 (RPM at a duty point): why do they live in different sections?
  3. Practice (2 min): Press Start over and sort the reshuffled deck without the descriptions.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Every catalog has printed performance tables: Catalog 300 has none and points to Fan Selector; the Performance Data card uses Catalog 902.
  • Maximum speed is found in the performance tables: question 1 lives in Engineering Data, by size and class.
  • Dimension pages can be used for construction: the Dimensions feedback says the tables are not for construction; certified drawings are required.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Running score "First-try correct: n of 10"; mastery is 8 of 10 on the first attempt. Second tries and descriptions are not evidence of mastery.
  • Follow-up question: a customer asks for the WR² of a BC-SW size 445 Class III impeller to check motor starting. Which section, and why not the material specifications?

  2. Twin City Fan Product Catalogs - current editions of Catalog 300 (BC backward inclined fans, April 2024) and Catalog 902 (RB radial bladed industrial fans, November 2017).

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A designation names one buildable fan: model, size, class and arrangement, such as "RBA 913, Class 22, Arrangement 10". For each of eight designations the learner commits two answers:

  • Offered or Not offered. Offered when the arrangement appears in the list for that model, size and class; Not offered otherwise, including when the class is not built for that size.
  • Class maximum RPM. The value in the extract for that class, chosen from the values in that model's row, or "none" when the class is not built.

A designation is correct only when both answers match. Two catalog extracts can be opened and closed at any time (they start collapsed):

  • Extract A, Catalog 902 (November 2017): RB Series availability (page 13) and maximum RPM (pages 20 and 24) for RBO 905 (8.75 in. impeller, Class 22 only) and RBA 913 (22.625 in. impeller, Classes 22, 32 and 45: 2,812, 3,337 and 4,000 RPM).
  • Extract B, Catalog 300 (April 2024): arrangements by model (pages 2-3 and 9) and maximum RPM by class (page 16) for BC-SW 365 and BC-DW 365.
# Designation Offered? Class maximum RPM 1 RBA 913, Class 22, Arrangement 10 Offered 2,812 2 RBA 913, Class 32, Arrangement 10 Not offered 3,337 3 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 4 Not offered 4,000 4 RBA 913, Class 45, Arrangement 9 Offered 4,000 5 RBO 905, Class 22, Arrangement 9A Offered 5,296 6 RBO 905, Class 32, Arrangement 1 Not offered none 7 BC-SW 365, Class II, Arrangement 9 Offered 1,283 8 BC-DW 365, Class I, Arrangement 9 Not offered 1,015

The designations come in this fixed order, the first three matching the chapter's worked example. Each has one scored attempt. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct:" with the reason. A wrong one names which of the two answers was wrong, gives the reason, marks each answer ✓ right or ✗ wrong, and allows one Practice try that is never scored; the practice feedback gives the full answer. The score reads "Designations correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. After the eighth designation the summary lists every missed designation with its answer. Start over clears the score.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the designation, then open the extract that covers its model.
  2. Find the row for the model and size, then the list for the class. Is the arrangement in it?
  3. Choose Offered or Not offered, choose the class maximum RPM (or none if the class is not built for this size), and press Check.
  4. Read the feedback. After a miss, change your answers and press Practice try if you want an unscored second look. Press Next designation to continue; after the eighth, read the summary.

Keyboard: O chooses Offered and N Not offered; keys 1 to 5 choose a maximum RPM button from the left; Enter checks, then goes to the next designation (and starts over from the summary); A and B open or collapse the extracts. After a shortcut key chooses both answers, focus moves to Check. Tab and Space or Enter work on every button.

Data label: "Source: TCF Catalog 902 (Nov 2017) pp. 13, 20, 24; Catalog 300 (Apr 2024) pp. 2-3, 9, 16", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will interpret a Twin City Fan designation (model code, size, class, arrangement) by judging whether it is offered and reading its class maximum RPM from catalog extracts, for at least 7 of 8 designations (Bloom: Understand, verb: interpret).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Model code, fan size, fan class, arrangement and maximum RPM, defined in the sections "Fan Size" and "Model Code" of Chapter 26 and in Chapter 10 and Chapter 11.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Decode (6 min): Judge all eight designations. Say which table row and which class list you used before pressing Check.
  2. Review (3 min): Compare designations 1 and 2: same model, size and arrangement, different class. Compare 7 and 8: same size number in two models of the same catalog.
  3. Discuss (3 min): A customer insists on a Class 45 RBA 913 in Arrangement 4. What do you offer instead, and why?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• If a size is offered in a class and an arrangement is offered in the line, every combination is offered: designations 2 and 3 use arrangements the line offers, in classes that do not list them.
  • A direct-drive arrangement is available in every class: designation 3 (Arrangement 4 at Class 45) is not offered.
  • A size number means the same diameter in every model: Extract A shows size 905 at 8.75 in. and 913 at 22.625 in.; BC-SW 365 and BC-DW 365 have different arrangement lists and maximum speeds.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Score "Designations correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. Practice tries are not evidence of mastery.
  • Follow-up question: why does designation 2 still have a class maximum RPM answer (3,337) when the designation is not offered?

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  2. Twin City Fan Catalog 902, RB Industrial Fans (PDF) - RB Series Availability (page 13) and performance pages 20 and 24.
  3. Twin City Fan Product Catalogs - Catalog 300 (BC backward inclined fans, April 2024), pages 2-3 and 9 arrangements by model (page 3's BC-DW list omits Arrangement 7, which page 2 lists and page 9 describes) and page 16 maximum RPM.
  4. p5.js - the JavaScript library used to draw the decoder.

docs.title: Performance Table Reader
docs.text:
Run the Performance Table Reader MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch26-performance-table-reader.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The grid is the RBA 913 excerpt from Twin City Fan Catalog 902 (November 2017), page 24, exactly as printed in the chapter: five airflow rows (3,348 to 4,836 CFM, with outlet velocity 3,600 to 5,200 FPM) and eight static pressure columns (4 to 32 in. wg), each cell an RPM and a BHP at standard air. The header and footer are shown as on the page: impeller diameter 22.625 in., tip speed 5.92 × RPM, outlet area 0.93 ft², FEG80; maximum RPM Class 22 = 2,812, Class 32 = 3,337, Class 45 = 4,000; installation type B and D; BHP without transmission losses; no appurtenance effects. The two underlined cells (4,836 CFM at 28 and 32 in.) mark maximum static efficiency.

For each of six duty points the learner types an RPM and a BHP and picks Class 22, 32 or 45, then presses Check:

# Duty Method RPM BHP Class 1 4,092 CFM at 12 in. Direct 2,167 11.72 22 2 3,720 CFM at 24 in. Direct 2,879 21.02 32 3 4,836 CFM at 32 in. Direct 3,340 35.65 45 4 4,000 CFM at 12 in. Interpolate CFM 2,157 11.42 22 5 4,000 CFM at 14 in. Interpolate CFM then SP 2,291 13.18 22 6 4,464 CFM at 30 in. Interpolate SP 3,224 31.08 32

Rules: linear interpolation \( y = y_1 + \frac{x - x_1}{x_2 - x_1}(y_2 - y_1) \); for a point between two pressure columns, interpolate airflow in each bracketing column first, then pressure between the two results. Direct readings must match exactly (±1 RPM, ±0.01 BHP); interpolated answers must be within ±1% of the RPM and BHP above. Class is 22 when RPM ≤ 2,812, 32 when 2,812 < RPM ≤ 3,337, and 45 when 3,337 < RPM ≤ 4,000. A duty point is correct only when all three answers are.

Each point has two attempts; the first is scored. Check marks each of RPM, BHP and class with ✓ or ✗. Once the point is resolved (correct, or the second attempt) the class overlay turns on (shaded bold = Class 32, shaded italic = Class 45), so both answers must come from the footer speeds. A correct answer gives the row, column and class reasoning; a first wrong attempt names which answers are wrong and gives a hint (the slip or the method step, never a value or the class); after the second attempt the answer and its calculation are shown. The overlay turns off when the next point loads. The score reads "Duty points correct: n of 6" (first attempts); mastery is 5 of 6. After point 6 the summary lists the points not right on the first attempt with their answers.

The scratch panel is a notepad: click cells to pin up to four bracketing values (or move with the arrow keys and press S) and type the fraction f you worked out. It echoes what you entered and never computes the answer. Hovering a cell highlights its row and column heads. All values must be confirmed in Fan Selector before quoting.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the duty point. Is it on a printed row and column, between two rows, between two columns, or both?
  2. Find the bracketing cells; pin them in the scratch panel if that helps.
  3. Type the RPM and BHP, choose the class by comparing your RPM with the footer, and press Check. If you have an attempt left, correct the marked answers and check again.
  4. Press Next duty point. After point 6 read the summary, explore the grid with the overlay, and press Start over to repeat.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the RPM box, the BHP box, the class buttons and the other buttons; Enter checks (from either box), then goes to the next point and starts over from the summary. Outside a text box, the arrow keys move a cell cursor over the grid (each cell is read aloud) and S pins or unpins that cell.

Data label: "Source: TCF Catalog 902 (Nov 2017) p. 24 · Confirm in Fan Selector before quoting", shown at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will use an excerpt of the RBA 913 performance table to find the RPM and BHP for a duty point, by direct reading or linear interpolation within ±1%, and to name the fan class the point requires (Bloom: Apply, verb: use).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Performance table, performance table header, outlet velocity, class shading and interpolation, all defined in the section "Performance Tables" of Chapter 26.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read (4 min): Points 1 to 3 are direct readings. Before checking point 3, compare its RPM with the Class 32 limit digit by digit.
  2. Interpolate (8 min): Points 4 to 6. Write f and each intermediate RPM and BHP in the scratch panel before typing the answer. For point 5, interpolate airflow in both the 12 in. and 16 in. columns before interpolating pressure.
  3. Explore (3 min): After the summary, turn the overlay on and trace where Class 32 begins in each row. Why does the boundary not follow a straight column?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The class is decided by the static pressure column alone: points 2, 3 and 6 put Class 32 and Class 45 in columns that also hold other classes; the 32 in. column holds both.
  • Interpolation can use the nearest cell instead of the two bracketing cells: the ±1% tolerance on points 4 to 6 rejects a nearest-cell reading.
  • A duty point between two pressure columns can be interpolated in one step: point 5's feedback spells out the two steps.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Score "Duty points correct: n of 6" counts first attempts; mastery is 5 of 6. Second attempts, hovering and the overlay are not evidence of mastery.
  • Follow-up question: a duty of 4,836 CFM at 30 in. comes out near 3,246 RPM. Which class do you order, and what would you check before quoting it?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 26: Reading Catalogs and Performance Tables - performance table header, reading a table, class shading and interpolation worked examples.
  2. Twin City Fan Catalog 902, RB Industrial Fans (PDF) - page 24, RBA 913 performance table, maximum RPM by class and rating notes.
  3. Twin City Fan Product Catalogs - current editions and the Fan Selector software that computes points directly.
  4. p5.js - the JavaScript library used to draw the table.

docs.title: Capstone Specification Builder
docs.text:
Run the Capstone Specification Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch27-capstone-specification-builder.js. The .csb-desc style for the description box is in this sim's main.html.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The builder walks you through the chapter's dryer exhaust fan decision by decision: 20,000 ACFM at 12.0 in. wg, 500°F gas at sea level, moderately sticky, abrasive, combustible wood dust, reduced flow during warm-up, spring isolators on a mezzanine, an outlet duct that leaves the top of the fan horizontally to the right (viewed from the drive side), a 70°F cold start, a selected speed of 1,450 RPM, 96.0 BHP cold and 53.0 BHP hot (illustrative values from the chapter's worked example).

You choose an option for each of ten attributes and write a one-sentence justification beside it:

# Attribute Options 1 Impeller / model RTF radial tip; RBO open radial paddle; HIB backward curved; HAF airfoil 2 Arrangement 1; 4; 8; 9; 9F 3 Drive Belt drive; direct coupled at 1,780 RPM without VFD; direct coupled with VFD set to 1,450 RPM 4 Rotation and discharge CW THD; CCW THD; CW UBD; CCW BHD 5 Motor 60 HP; 75 HP; 100 HP; 125 HP 6 Temperature package None; to 300°F; to 500°F (grease, bearings, shaft seal, shaft cooler); to 600°F 7 Spark resistance None; AMCA Type A; AMCA Type B; AMCA Type C 8 Abrasion protection None; welded 7-gauge scroll liner; bolt-on scroll liner 9 Flow control None; parallel blade outlet damper with actuator; nested inlet vanes 10 Base and isolation Unitary base, no isolators; isolation base with spring isolators and flex connectors; spring isolators without flex connectors

Check specification evaluates all fifteen violation rules and four advisories together and lists every triggered message beside its attribute. A violation (✗, red dashed border) blocks completion; an advisory (ℹ) does not. Rules that join two attributes are listed beside one of them: the 9F rule (no valid 9F design exists on isolators) beside the arrangement, the arrangement-and-drive rules beside the drive, and the turndown rule beside flow control. Nothing is revealed before you choose.

The specification is complete when all ten attributes are chosen, all ten justifications contain text and the check reports zero violations. The sim then says "Specification complete: ten attributes, zero conflicts, n checks." and composes the complete fan description in the format of the chapter's worked example, followed by your justifications, in a box you can select or copy with Copy description. Checks are unlimited; the number of checks needed and your justifications are recorded, not scored.

Some fixes cascade: changing the arrangement to 8 forces a direct drive, and a direct drive needs the VFD to meet the 1,450 RPM speed. Arrangement 9 with a belt drive is the chapter's worked selection; Arrangement 1 with a belt drive and Arrangement 8 with the VFD also pass, with an advisory to check the length against the 10 ft by 8 ft pad.

Sources: FanPedia pp. 110, 162, 165, 166, 171 and 187 (arrangement and isolation rules); Twin City Fan's Model RTF guide specification, Section 23 34 16 (temperature tier, spark-resistance limits, liners, inlet vanes); Chapter 12's discharge table (CW THD); Chapter 9 (impeller and dust).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the application card.
  2. For each attribute, choose an option and type one sentence saying why, citing the fact on the card or the source that decides it.
  3. Press Check specification. Read every message beside its attribute; the sim turns to the page with the first flagged attribute.
  4. Revise and check again until no violations remain. The composed description then appears. Back to attributes returns to the form; Show fan description reopens the description.

Keyboard: Tab moves through each drop-down, justification box and button in order; the arrow keys change a focused drop-down; Enter or Space presses a focused button. On narrow screens the attributes are split into pages; More attributes is in the Tab order after the last visible row.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compose a complete, internally consistent fan specification for the dryer exhaust application by choosing all ten attributes and writing a one-sentence justification for each, finishing with zero rule violations (Bloom: Create, verb: compose).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Impeller, arrangement, drive and construction selection (Chapter 27)
  • Cold start motor sizing and accessory selection (Chapter 27)
  • Complete fan description and specification review (Chapter 27)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Build (8-10 min): Choose and justify all ten attributes before the first check. Cite the card fact or source in each justification.
  2. Revise (3-5 min): Check, read each conflict, and revise. Note which fixes cascaded into other attributes.
  3. Write up (3-5 min): Copy the composed description into your capstone document and compare it with the chapter's worked example line by line.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The most efficient impeller is always the right one: HIB and HAF trigger the dust rule.
  • Any arrangement works if the motor is large enough: Arrangements 4 and 9F fail whatever the motor.
  • Spark resistance of any type works at any temperature: Types A and B fail at 500°F.
  • A damper or VFD is optional when the process needs turndown: no flow control without the VFD fails.
  • Isolators can be added without flex connectors: the springs-only option fails.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Evidence: a submitted specification with ten choices, ten justifications and zero violations; the sim records the number of checks needed and the justifications as written. Justifications are reviewed by the instructor, not scored by the sim.
  • Follow-up: rewrite one justification so it names its source (FanPedia page or guide specification paragraph), then explain which advisory you accepted and why.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. MasterFormat - Wikipedia article on the CSI numbering system used for construction specifications.
  2. Centrifugal fan - Wikipedia overview of centrifugal fan impeller types, from airfoil to radial blades.
  3. Twin City Fan product specifications - CSI-format guide specifications, including the Model RTF section 23 34 16 behind the construction rules.
  4. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference for arrangements, high temperature construction, isolation and flex connectors.

docs.title: Fan Selection Workflow
docs.text: Run the Fan Selection Workflow MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Fan selection runs through twelve steps in a fixed order, from collecting the application requirements to writing the specification. Each step consumes particular information about the job, and knowing which step uses which fact is what tells an engineer where to loop back when a requirement changes. The flowchart shows the twelve steps, the information that passes from each step to the next, and the dashed loop from the sound and dimension check back to the arrangement when a candidate fails a space or noise limit. The key above the flowchart groups the steps into five phases by step number as well as by color.

Every step in the flowchart is clickable. Clicking a step opens a short explanation of what that step decides; this is exploration and is never scored. The panel on the right holds eight information cards from one worked job, always in the same order. For each card you choose the step that uses it. Each card allows one attempt and locks once submitted. The sim checks the answer immediately, outlines the correct step with a solid green border and a ✓ (and your choice with a dashed red border and a ✗ if it was wrong) and explains why. The running score reads "Cards correct: n of 8". Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt; below that, the summary links to the chapter sections behind the cards you missed.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any step in the flowchart to read what it does.
  2. Read the card in the right panel, choose a step from the list and press Submit.
  3. Read the feedback. Each card allows one attempt and locks once submitted.
  4. Press Next card to continue. After card 8 the panel shows your score out of 8 and whether you reached mastery. Below 7, it lists the chapter sections to reread, with links.
  5. Press Start over at any time to sort the same eight cards again in the same order.

Keyboard: Tab to a flowchart step and press Enter or Space to read it. In the step list, Enter submits the chosen step; Enter again goes to the next card.

Data label: "Illustrative values · job values on the cards are the chapter's worked example", shown at the bottom left of the flowchart. The 1,450 RPM table speed, the 1,180 and 1,780 RPM motor speeds, the 500°F design and 70°F cold start temperatures, the 95 dB A-weighted outlet limit and the 10 ft by 8 ft pad are not data for a specific catalog fan.

docs.text: The learner will classify eight pieces of application information by the selection step that uses them, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt (Bloom: Understand, verb: classify).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, inside and outside sales staff, manufacturer's representatives, distributors and specifying engineers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Fan selection and duty point
  • Standard air
  • Arrangement, drive and construction
  • Cold start motor sizing
  • Accessories
  • Sound data and dimensional data

These are covered in this chapter and in Chapters 2, 10 and 11.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (4 min): Click all twelve steps and read each explanation. Trace the information labels on the arrows and find the one loop in the workflow. Ask what would send a selection back along it.
  2. Sorting (6 min): Sort the eight cards. Before submitting each one, say which step uses the fact and why.
  3. Discussion (5 min): Look at the cards you missed and reread the linked sections. Then discuss the misconceptions below.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• Selection is finished once a size is read from the performance table: eight of the twelve steps come after the catalog size, and two cards belong to the sound and dimension check.
  • The motor is sized from the operating brake horsepower at the hot design temperature: the 70°F winter startup card belongs to motor and cold start sizing.
  • Dimensions are checked only after the order is placed: the 10 ft by 8 ft pad card belongs to the sound and dimension check, before candidates are compared.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• First-attempt score shown as "Cards correct: n of 8"; mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. Clicking steps to read their explanations is exploration and does not count toward the score.
  • Follow-up: give the learner a requirement change, such as a lower noise limit, and ask which step the selection loops back to.
