docs.title: Octave Band A-Weighting Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Octave Band A-Weighting Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js, fan-models.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch27-octave-band-a-weighting.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A fan's sound power is published in eight octave bands, centered at 63, 125, 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 Hz. To compare band data with an A-weighted limit, add the standard A-weighting correction to each band and add the weighted bands logarithmically:

  • Weighted band = band level + A-weighting correction
  • LwA = 10 log10(Σ 10^(weighted/10)), rounded to 0.1 dB
  • Unweighted overall = 10 log10(Σ 10^(L/10))

The corrections are the standard IEC 61672 octave-band values: −26.2, −16.1, −8.6, −3.2, 0, +1.2, +1.0 and −1.1 dB. The bar chart draws each band's unweighted level as an outline; after Check, the A-weighted level fills each bar, the largest contributor is outlined in orange and labeled, and the two totals appear beside a dashed line at the limit. The limit line spans only the totals, because a limit on the overall level says nothing about any single band.

Three challenges, in this fixed order (all spectra illustrative):

# Bands 63 to 8,000 Hz (dB) Limit (dB, A-weighted) Model LwA (dB) Verdict 1 98, 96, 94, 90, 87, 83, 78, 72 95 92.5 Meets 2 90, 92, 95, 97, 96, 93, 88, 82 95 100.2 Exceeds 3 105, 100, 92, 86, 82, 78, 74, 68 95 90.0 Meets

Challenge 1 is the chapter's worked example: 92.5 dB A-weighted against 101.6 dB unweighted, with the 500 and 1,000 Hz bands dominating. A challenge is correct when the level you type is within ±0.5 dB of the model value (rounded to 0.1 dB) and the meets/exceeds choice is right. You get two attempts. If the level you type matches the unweighted total or the arithmetic average of the bands, the feedback says so. After a second wrong attempt the model value and the weighted band table are shown and the challenge counts as missed. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.

After challenge 3, free mode unlocks: each band slider runs from 50 to 110 dB in 1 dB steps (starting at challenge 1's spectrum) and the limit from 70 to 110 dB (starting at 95 dB). The weighted values, both totals, the verdict, the largest contributor and the change from the starting spectrum update as you move a slider. Free mode is never scored.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read challenge 1's eight band levels and the limit. Work out the weighted bands and the logarithmic sum with a calculator.
  2. Type the overall A-weighted level in LwA (dB), choose Meets or Exceeds, and press Check.
  3. Read the feedback. A correct answer reads "✓ Correct: LwA = 92.5 dB, which meets the 95 dB limit." in a solid green box; a wrong one starts with "✗ Not quite." in a dashed red box. Use the second attempt if one is left.
  4. Press Next challenge and repeat. "Challenges correct: n of 3" keeps the running score.
  5. After challenge 3, press Start free mode. Raise the 63 Hz band by 10 dB and note the change in LwA; press Reset bands, raise the 1,000 Hz band by 10 dB and compare. Start over clears the score and returns to challenge 1.

Keyboard: Enter checks the answer and then goes to the next challenge. M picks Meets and E picks Exceeds when the cursor is not in the answer box (Tab to the radio buttons and use the arrow keys or Space works too). Tab reaches every slider; the arrow keys move a focused slider.

Data label: "Illustrative spectra · A-weighting: IEC 61672 octave-band values", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the overall A-weighted sound power level from eight octave band levels and judge it against a limit, to within ±0.5 dB (Bloom: Apply, verb: calculate).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Octave band and sound power level (Chapter 25 and the Octave Band Sound Data section of Chapter 27)
  • A-weighting and logarithmic addition of decibels
  • Noise limits and their forms (Chapter 27, Noise Limits)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Challenges (6-8 min): Solve the three spectra with a calculator before pressing Check. Write down the weighted value of each band and which band is largest after weighting.
  2. Review (2 min): Compare the A-weighted and unweighted totals for challenge 3. Explain why the 105 dB band at 63 Hz does not control the A-weighted total.
  3. Free mode (3-5 min): Raise the 63 Hz band by 10 dB, then reset and raise the 1,000 Hz band by 10 dB. Record the change in LwA each time and decide which band a silencer should attack.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• The overall level is the arithmetic average or sum of the band levels: the feedback names the average when you type it, and the totals bar shows the logarithmic sum.
  • The loudest unweighted band controls the A-weighted total: challenge 3 and the free-mode 63 Hz test show that a loud low band barely moves LwA.
  • An unweighted overall level can be compared with an A-weighted limit: challenge 1's unweighted 101.6 dB would wrongly fail the 95 dB limit; the feedback names the unweighted total when you type it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The running line "Challenges correct: n of 3" counts challenges solved on either attempt. At the end the sim shows "First-attempt score: n of 3" and the mastery line; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt, with the level within ±0.5 dB and the verdict right.
  • Follow-up: a limit of 90 dB applies to challenge 1's fan. Which two bands would you attenuate, and roughly how much?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. A-weighting - Wikipedia article on the A-weighting curve and its octave-band corrections.
  2. Octave band - Wikipedia article on octave bands and their center frequencies.
  3. Sound power - Wikipedia article on sound power level, the source quantity a fan catalog publishes.
  4. Twin City Fan product specifications - CSI-format guide specifications, including the Model RTF section 23 34 16 that asks for sound power in eight octave bands with an A-weighted overall value.
  5. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference on fan sound and selection.

Run the Specification Error Detector MicroSim Fullscreen

This sketch is built on the FanPedia MicroSim kit. To run it in the p5.js editor, add the ../shared-libs/ files it loads (fanpedia-sim.css, fanpedia-core.js, fanpedia-p5.js), or their published URLs, to the editor's index.html before pasting ch27-specification-error-detector.js.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A reviewer reads every clause of a specification with the selection checklist beside it and asks two questions: is the requirement stated so it can be proven, and does any clause contradict another clause or a source? This sim gives you a ten-clause draft written for the chapter's dryer exhaust fan (20,000 ACFM at 12.0 in. wg, 500°F gas at sea level, moderately sticky, abrasive, combustible wood dust, spring isolators on a mezzanine, cold start at 70°F).

For each clause, the drop-down offers Acceptable or Defective with one of seven reasons:

Letter Reason (a) duty has no air condition (b) arrangement unsuited to the temperature (c) spark-resistance type not allowed at this temperature (d) motor not sized for cold start (e) sound data in the wrong form (f) isolated fan without flex connectors (g) arrangement cannot sit directly on isolators

Seven clauses are defective and three are acceptable; each defective clause has exactly one right reason. A clause is judged correctly when the acceptable/defective mark matches and, for a defective clause, the reason letter matches too. Marks can be changed freely until you press Submit review; the sim asks for every clause to be marked first. The first submission is the recorded evidence: the score reads "n of 10 clauses judged correctly", and mastery is 9 of 10.

After submission every clause turns green with a solid border and "✓ Correct" or red with a dashed border and "✗ Incorrect: you marked … ; it is …", followed by the reason the answer is right. Show corrected specification rewrites the seven defective clauses (for example, clause 3 becomes "Provide AMCA Type C spark-resistant construction."). Try again clears the marks and keeps the clause order; later submissions are labeled "Practice (not scored)" and the first-submission score stays recorded.

When the clauses do not all fit (a narrow screen, or after submission), they are split into pages; More clauses and Previous clauses move between them.

Sources: clauses 2, 9 and 10 from FanPedia pp. 110, 171, 187 and 166; clauses 3, 6, 7 and 8 from Twin City Fan's Model RTF guide specification (Section 23 34 16); clauses 1 and 5 and the application card from the chapter's illustrative worked example.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the application card.
  2. For each clause, open the drop-down and choose Acceptable or the Defective reason that names what is wrong. Check pairs of clauses against the card: temperature against the arrangement and the spark-resistance type, the cold start against the motor, isolators against the duct connection.
  3. Press Submit review. Read each clause's result and the reason.
  4. Press Show corrected specification to see the rewritten clauses, and Show my review to go back. Press Try again to practice with the marks cleared.

Keyboard: Tab moves through the ten drop-downs and then the buttons; the arrow keys change a focused drop-down (Alt+Down opens it); Enter or Space presses a focused button.

Data label: "Illustrative worked example · Sources: FanPedia pp. 110, 166, 171, 187; TCF Model RTF guide spec 23 34 16", at the bottom left of the drawing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will critique a ten-clause draft fan specification by flagging each clause as acceptable or defective and choosing the reason for each defect, with at least 9 of 10 clauses judged correctly (Bloom: Evaluate, verb: critique).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Specification review and the fan selection checklist (Chapter 27)
  • Airstream conditions and the density correction (Chapters 2 and 27)
  • Arrangement selection, including Arrangements 4, 9 and 9F (Chapters 11 and 27)
  • Spark-resistant construction types (Chapter 20)
  • Cold start motor sizing, octave band sound data and flex connectors (Chapter 27)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Review (6-8 min): Mark all ten clauses before submitting. For each defective clause, write in the margin which other clause or which fact on the card it conflicts with.
  2. Debrief (3 min): Read every result, then open the corrected specification and compare each rewrite with the guide-specification wording in the chapter.
  3. Practice (2-4 min): Press Try again and redo any clause you missed.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions Addressed
docs.text:
• A clause that sounds technical is complete: clause 1 states a duty with no air condition.
  • Spark-resistant Types A and B work at any temperature: clause 3 (Type B at 500°F).
  • The motor is sized for the hot operating point: clause 5 (60 HP against a 96 BHP cold start).
  • An overall dBA value is the sound data a specification asks for: clause 6.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• The first submission is the evidence: "n of 10 clauses judged correctly", with mastery at 9 of
  • Later submissions are practice and do not change the recorded score.
  • Follow-up: write the corrected clause 9 so that it also says who furnishes the flex connectors.

docs.text:
1. MasterFormat - Wikipedia article on the CSI numbering system that organizes construction specifications, including Division 23.
  2. Specification (technical standard)
  3. Wikipedia article on what a technical specification must state so compliance can be checked.
  4. Twin City Fan product specifications - CSI-format guide specifications, including the Model RTF section 23 34 16 used for clauses 3, 6, 7 and 8.
  5. FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia - Twin City Fan's reference for arrangements, high temperature construction, isolation and flex connectors.
